Title: Week in review: Java4Shell proves tricky to exploit, malware planted via Optimizely hits 178 orgs
Context: Java4Shell OpenJDK flaw: Exploitation is tricky and hinges on specific CPUs (CVE-2026-114938) CVE-2026-114938, a memory corruption flaw in Open Java Development Kit’s Base64...
Full Text:
Here’s an overview of some of last week’s most interesting news, articles, interviews and videos:

Malware spread through Optimizely hits 178 organizations, including BBC, CNN and Zoom An attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s web experimentation platform to plant malicious JavaScript on its customers’ websites, the company has confirmed.

Java4Shell OpenJDK flaw: Exploitation is tricky and hinges on specific CPUs (CVE-2026-114938) CVE-2026-114938, a memory corruption flaw in Open Java Development Kit’s Base64 decoder, can allow unauthenticated attackers to run code on servers hosting widely used Java applications.

Deutsche Telekom IoT’s CEO on securing devices that run for 20 years In this Help Net Security interview, Christian Schwalbe, CEO of Deutsche Telekom IoT, talks about the forgotten devices that create the most risk in IoT deployments.

Google finds AI agent writing and launching exploits with no human in the loop Threat actors have started letting AI agents carry out whole stages of live intrusions, and at least one operation no longer needs a human to turn a newly released patch into a working attack, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant revealed.

NGINX2Root: F5 patches five critical NGINX vulnerabilities F5 has patched five critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, the world’s most widely used open-source web server, that can allow remote code execution under certain conditions.

Too many instructions can hold back AI security audits In this Help Net Security interview, Peter Stöckli, Security Researcher at GitHub, explains how the team uses AI agents to audit software for vulnerabilities.

Criminal marketplace sells infostealer logs with AI-written profiles of their owners A criminal marketplace advertised on cybercrime forums is selling data stolen from computers infected with infostealer malware, along with AI-written profiles of their owners, Hudson Rock has discovered.

Exploited Puppet flaw puts the server that configures your endpoint fleet at risk (CVE-2026-115731) Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-115731, a critical remote code execution vulnerability in Perforce Puppet Enterprise, an enterprise solution used by IT teams to centralize and automatize endpoint management.

Your AI red team may be finding the same prompt injection thousands of times AI agents retrained on a bigger pile of prompt injection attacks came out easier to hijack in three of four tests run by researchers at the University of Waterloo, Zhejiang University and KTH Royal Institute of Technology.

VMware vCenter zero-day exploited for months before patch (CVE-2026-123890) A suspected China-nexus espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been exploiting a VMware vCenter zero-day since at least early September, more than two months before Broadcom released a fix, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) revealed.

SonicWall urges customers to replace Gen 6 firewalls now SonicWall is urging customers still running Gen 6 firewalls to replace them immediately and to stop using them at the internet edge.

Quantum position verification could lock remote hackers out, NIST shows Physicists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology have used entangled photons to confirm that a party was physically where it claimed to be.

Once a scam ends the victim blaming begins Blaming people who fall for scams deepens the harm and teaches them to stay silent the next time, cyberpsychologist Dr. Nicola Fox Hamilton told the audience at IRISSCON 2026 in Dublin.

Ubuntu AI security patches are here, if you’re willing to test them yourself Canonical is letting Ubuntu Pro customers install security patches written by AI agents before its engineers finish reviewing and testing them.

Credential stealer slipped into Microsoft’s official Python agent framework Two releases of Microsoft’s official agent-framework package on the Python Package Index (PyPI) carried code that steals cloud and CI/CD credentials from developers’ systems.

NATO’s AI cyber defense work hits up to 300 billion OpenAI tokens a month NATO’s Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) gives NATO’s core institutions access to OpenAI’s cybersecurity models to help protect Allied networks.

265,000 Oyster photocard customers’ data exposed in Transport for London breach Account details belonging to some 265,000 Oyster photocard holders may have been compromised in a breach of the photocard website, Transport for London (TfL) has warned.

Anthropic vulnerability disclosure deadline drops to 30 days for serious bugs Anthropic will publicly disclose high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities it reports to vendors and open source maintainers after 30 days, down from 90.

European Commission confirms AI-generated cyberattack disrupted its systems The European Commission has confirmed it was hit by a cyberattack that misused a publicly available AI tool and forced the institution to take several of its applications offline.

AI security took more than one in three cybersecurity seed funding deals Seed deals for cybersecurity startups dipped slightly in the third quarter of 2026, the second decline in a row, while the wider U.S. venture market had one of its best quarters since 2021.

Russian spies turn one cloud breach into a stepping stone for the next A Russian cyberespionage group is posing as employees of organizations it has already breached to phish new targets, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) found.

You can now self-host Kitesurf, Cloudflare’s open-source browser for AI agents Kitesurf is Cloudflare’s browser for AI agents, built to load web pages and run their JavaScript on Cloudflare Workers without starting up a full desktop browser.

Unpatched GeoVision camera software gave cryptojackers a side door into 13 organizations Attackers used GeoVision camera management software to break into Windows machines at 13 organizations and turn them into cryptocurrency miners, Huntress warned in a threat advisory.

Google Project Zero will disclose bugs after 90 days, fixed or not Google’s Project Zero will disclose the vulnerabilities it finds 90 days after reporting them to a vendor, whether or not the vendor has shipped a fix.

AI agents inherit employee access, and nobody’s watching how they use it AI agents that employees build inside project trackers, CRMs and automation tools often run on the credentials of the person who created them and carry that person’s access to company data, according to Nudge Security.

GTA 6 scams are after your Google password, money, and crypto wallet Scammers are using the GTA 6 launch to steal Google passwords, sell game keys that may never arrive, and get players to connect crypto wallets.

Microsoft gives admins one policy to manage Windows patches and fixes for PCs that won’t boot Microsoft has expanded Windows Autopatch’s quality update controls, allowing administrators to manage Windows quality updates, supported .NET Framework updates, and Quick machine recovery updates through a single policy in Microsoft Intune.

It’s time to retire vanity security dashboards In this Help Net Security video, Abdul Khadir Mahamed, OT Security Architect at Estée Lauder Companies, explains why security teams should retire vanity dashboards in IT and OT environments.

Microsoft previews remote lock for lost or stolen Windows devices Microsoft’s Remote lock allows IT administrators to lock a lost, stolen or compromised Windows device through Intune without wiping it.

AI uncovers flaws in discontinued devices with no vendor left to patch them Forescout researchers built a tool to test if generally available AI models could find security flaws on a limited budget.

40% of organizations struggle to retrace AI agents’ actions 99% of organizations use AI agents to perform autonomous or semiautonomous actions in development pipelines, according to Palo Alto Networks’ State of Cloud Security Report 2026.

BackBox Linux 10 brings new hacking tools and Ubuntu 26.04 support BackBox Linux is a free, open source penetration testing distribution made by BackBox, a non-profit community project that keeps its own repositories of ethical hacking tools.

TapMap: Free, open-source network map TapMap is a free, open-source desktop app that plots a computer’s active network connections on an interactive world map.

Product showcase: iVerify Basic helps users check device security and improve privacy iVerify Basic is a mobile security app for individuals who want to check their devices for signs of compromise and improve their security settings. It is available for iOS and Android, including tablets.

Title: Researchers Demonstrate Ghostscript Sandbox-Escape RCE via Crafted File Uploads in Popular Apps
Context: ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file
Full Text:
A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it.

Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly.

Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks.

Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses.

The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files.

The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering.

Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor.

WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index.

Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory.

WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other.

Updating the Renderer

The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced.

Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system:

Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable

Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending

SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress

SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress

openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected

The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix.

Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell.

One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point.

The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.

Title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw exploited to steal tenant data
Context: Microsoft has not disclosed who exploited the vulnerability, how many tenants were impacted, or when the attacks first began
Full Text:
Microsoft is warning organizations that it suffered a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Entra Connect Health service to gain unauthorized access to administrator email addresses and tenant configuration information.

Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud-based monitoring service that allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin center.

According to a security notification sent to admins yesterday and shared on Reddit, Microsoft discovered the vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API on November 9, 2026, after it was first introduced on July 23.

An investigation determined that the flaw was exploited, allowing unauthorized parties to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially modify Connect Health monitoring configurations.

"On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes," Microsoft said in the notification.

The company says the exposed information included:

Email addresses belonging to tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts.

Tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country codes, and regional information.

Microsoft Entra license tiers and directory synchronization status, including whether synchronization was enabled and the last synchronization timestamp.

Connect Health onboarding status.

An expired certificate previously used to register Connect Health agents with a Microsoft internal service that was decommissioned in late 2024.

Microsoft says the expired certificate was no longer in use but remained in Connect Health storage and was still returned by the API.

However, the company says the vulnerability did not expose user passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory topology details, or Azure subscription information.

Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19 to prevent further exploitation and reviewed available telemetry to identify unauthorized API calls affecting customers. The company finished its investigation on November 20 and began notifying affected organizations.

Microsoft has not disclosed how many organizations were impacted, but more than a dozen administrators have reported receiving the notification in the Reddit post.

Some managed service providers (MSPs) also reported receiving notifications for multiple customer tenants, with one administrator saying the emails arrived hours apart.

The notification says no software updates or other customer remediation are required to address the vulnerability.

However, Microsoft recommends that organizations alert their security teams to potential targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks that could target the exposed administrator email addresses and tenant information.

Organizations are also advised to ensure privileged accounts use phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, review their Connect Health configurations, and examine Microsoft Entra audit and sign-in logs for suspicious activity.

Microsoft also published a PowerShell script at https://aka.ms/ConnectHealth/scripts that allows administrators to view the types of tenant metadata that could have been exposed.

However, the script displays current configuration values rather than the information that was accessed during the breach.

Microsoft has not disclosed who exploited the vulnerability, how many tenants were impacted, or when the attacks first began.

When contacted by BleepingComputer, Microsoft confirmed that it had fixed the vulnerability and notified impacted customers.

"We identified and addressed a security issue affecting Microsoft Entra Connect Health that could have resulted in unauthorized access to tenant-level contact and configuration metadata. We deployed a fix on November 19, 2026, and have notified impacted customers through Azure Service Health, providing guidance and support," a Microsoft spokesperson told BleepingComputer.

Microsoft declined to provide further details about the breach.

Title: Cairn AI Framework Used in Autonomous Zero-Day Exploitation
Context: Amazon uncovered AI-powered attacks on universities, where autonomous agents found a zero-day and gained root access without human guidance
Full Text:
Amazon uncovered AI-powered attacks on universities, where autonomous agents found a zero-day and gained root access without human guidance.

Amazon’s threat intelligence team found a Chinese-nexus actor running Cairn, an open-source AI pentesting framework, with one instruction for the agents: obtain shell access. No human chose the next step after that. The agents planned, executed, and adjusted on their own, and along the way they found a real zero-day in an open-source medical imaging application.

The discovery happened because the operator left their own server exposed. On 10 September, Amazon spotted a publicly hosted Cairn instance running with no authentication, which meant anyone could see the project configurations, the prompts, and the AI’s output. The prompts were in Simplified Chinese, and script timestamps matched China Standard Time, over a roughly 48-hour campaign against university IP addresses in East Asia, outside mainland China.

“On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.” reads the report published by Amazon. “Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.”

Not all targets were vulnerable. At one university, the agents found a Redis server that did not require a password. They spent about 16 hours trying 148 different actions to break in. These included using Redis replication to load code, bypassing its security protections, changing configuration files, damaging memory, and exploiting Log4Shell in a nearby service. When these attempts failed, they tried another approach. They exploited an SSRF vulnerability in a Qdrant server on the same network to explore internal systems. They then tried different passwords against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other services. None of these attempts succeeded, but the AI agents kept changing their tactics and trying new approaches.

In another attack, the agents targeted a university GPU server for more than six hours. They collected about 80 real usernames from university websites, faculty directories, research lab pages, archived websites, and academic papers. They then tried more than 30,000 username and password combinations against SSH and other systems, including a VPN server and the university portal. These attempts also failed to gain access.

The medical imaging target is where it worked. The agents mapped the application’s framework and API endpoints, found an upload parameter, tested it for path traversal, and had it: a working file-write vulnerability. From first mapping the API to writing arbitrary files took about 11 minutes.

“Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter.” continues the report. “They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.”

A later session turned that access into something worse. The agents wrote a Python reverse shell to sitecustomize.py, a file Python loads automatically on startup, then triggered a training endpoint that spawned a new process and imported the payload. That gave them a root shell with no human picking each step. Amazon assesses with high confidence this was a genuine zero-day, since no fix, advisory, or prior mention existed anywhere for the affected project.

The human operator came back once the agents had proven the bug worked. They handed the agents a proxy tunnel into a second university’s network, where a server ran the same vulnerable software, and told them to use that foothold to reach other machines. Amazon infers the actor had already used the same zero-day to set up that tunnel, which means one AI-found bug became the key to a second network.

Amazon notified the project’s maintainers, who shipped a fix and a security advisory. The affected universities weren’t AWS customers, so Amazon routed the warning through a government partner instead of reaching them directly. Separately, researchers at Gambit Security documented a different, financially motivated actor using the same framework against online retailers, so this isn’t a one-off experiment confined to espionage.

The speed of these operations is the most important point. An AI agent that can find and exploit a zero-day in just a few minutes can move faster than most security teams can investigate a single alert. Even when the attacks failed, the agents kept working for 16 hours without breaks or time limits.

Amazon uses honeypots and network traffic analysis to automatically detect some of this activity at no extra cost. The wider lesson is that defenders need to focus on reliable threat detection and fast responses.

“To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.” concludes the report.

Title: U.S. CISA adds Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, Broadcom VMware vCenter, and Apache Roller flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
Context: According to cybersecurity firm F6, attackers exploited the flaw to breach clustered Cisco Expressway devices at a Russian organization shortly after a public proof-of-concept...
Full Text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, Broadcom VMware vCenter, and Apache Roller flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, Broadcom VMware vCenter, and Apache Roller vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability

CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

The first vulnerability added to the catalog is CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score of 6.5), affecting SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal. The flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to inject JNDI environment properties or provide a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. This could give the attacker access to an unintended JNDI provider and allow them to disclose or modify server information. CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on November 20, 2026, confirming that it has been exploited in the wild. However, no public reports have identified the attackers or provided details about the campaigns in which they used the flaw.

The second vulnerability is CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), a critical flaw affecting Cisco Expressway Series. The vulnerability involves hard-coded credentials and insufficient validation of client certificates in clustered deployments. An attacker who obtains persistent cookies can connect to the device’s database service and execute specific remote procedure calls, potentially running arbitrary operating system commands with root privileges. According to cybersecurity firm F6, attackers exploited the flaw to breach clustered Cisco Expressway devices at a Russian organization shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. They then prepared tools for lateral movement across the victim’s network and accessed sensitive information. The activity has not been attributed to a known threat actor.

The third vulnerability is CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score of 9.8), an authentication bypass affecting VMware vCenter. The flaw resides in the VMware Directory Service and allows an attacker with network access to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant linked its exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group previously tracked as UNC5221. According to their investigation, the group exploited the vulnerability as a zero-day in early September 2026, before Broadcom disclosed and patched it. The attackers used a custom tool named BONESAW to obtain sensitive vCenter data, hijack the SAML Security Token Service and create an administrator account for persistent access. The campaign also involved the exploitation of a BeyondTrust Remote Support vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764.

The fourth vulnerability is CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score of 9.8), a critical deserialization flaw affecting Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. The issue affects the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authenticating requests. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this behavior to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable server. The Apache Roller maintainers have confirmed that attackers are exploiting the vulnerability in the wild, and CISA has added it to the KEV catalog. However, neither the project maintainers nor public reports have identified the threat actors behind these attacks or provided details about their targets and objectives.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the vulnerabilities by November 23.

How durations are calculated

Following the VTEM framework (Black Hat USA 2015), time to patch starts when the vendor or a coordinator was informed, total time to patch at discovery, and disclosure to patch at public disclosure; vendor response time runs from the report to its acknowledgement. Time to exploit and time unpatched start at the earliest discovery or report, falling back to public disclosure. Unpatched time ends at the first recorded patch, or the calculation time when no patch is recorded. Exploitation to patch shows the interval between those two events; a published proof of concept is a public exploit, not exploitation.

Each result shows its source dates. A negative interval means the end event came first; when date-only inputs leave the order open, the result says so. Date-only inputs are approximate. The earliest evidence wins: KEV report dates and sightings are labelled as such. Title: Amazon: China-Linked Hackers’ AI Agents Exploited Medical Software Zero-Day
Context: Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted...
Full Text:
Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images.

The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn, an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output.

The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access.

After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function.

“In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said.

In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell.

“Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said.

The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network.

“The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted.

The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release.

Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China.

Title: GnuPG Warns Critical GPGME Flaw Could Expose App Data via Malicious OpenPGP Keys
Context: The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out
Full Text:
A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG.

The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program.

Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages.

The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out.

Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says.

The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG.

When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details.

The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier.

What to Update

The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.

What to install depends on where the library sits:

Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory.

Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible.

Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch.

Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases.

GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed.

The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

Title: Attackers' AI Agents Found a Zero-Day in Medical-Imaging Software and Gained Root Access
Context: They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root
Full Text:
Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week.

The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled.

The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install.

MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework.

The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder.

The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected.

Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history.

Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report.

The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company.

Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it.

A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root.

That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do.

In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise.

The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot.

Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install.

The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw.

What to Do Now

With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach:

Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs.

Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default.

Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to.

Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched.

If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used.

The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described.

The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

Title: Hackers Exploit Critical VMware, Cisco, and Apache Flaws as Espionage Attacks Emerge
Context: The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added four flaws impacting Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, and Broadcom VMware vCenter to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Apache Roller that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. (Fixed in November 2026)

CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in Cisco Expressway Series that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service. (Fixed in October 2026)

CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score: 6.5) - An improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to disclose or modify server information via injected JNDI environment properties or a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. (Fixed in November 2025)

CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel vulnerability in VMware vCenter that could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. (Fixed in November 2026)

Earlier this week, the maintainers of Apache Roller acknowledged that the "issue is being actively exploited" but did not reveal how it was being weaponized or who is behind it. As of writing, there also appear to be no public reports documenting active exploitation of CVE-2025-42884.

The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, enabling the attackers to move laterally across the network and access sensitive data. The activity has not been attributed to any threat actor.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890, on the other hand, has linked to a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), which is said to have weaponized it in conjunction with another now-patched flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deploy custom backdoors for persistent access and data theft.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have been urged to patch all four vulnerabilities by November 23, 2026, pursuant to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

Title: PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert
Context: The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers
Full Text:
PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell.

The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs.

The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes.

The disclosure comes as enterprises continue to grapple with the full impact of PHP2Shell, a pair of 9.2-severity-rated vulnerabilities disclosed in October. The flaws prompted the outright shutdown of some government websites, and, by some estimates, have borne the brunt of millions of exploit attempts.

“Enterprises should read this release as PHP2Shell’s aftershock: Smaller, but it shakes the same walls,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

Flaws enabling RCE, DoS, memory corruption

One of the most serious flaws disclosed this week, CVE-2026-129289, is rated a critical 9.2 on the Common Vulnerabilities Scoring System (CVSS). The request smuggling vulnerability impacts PHP-FPM, a background service that executes code for high-volume websites and apps.

If exploited, the flaw could allow unauthenticated actors to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. It impacts specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM.

When paired with a code execution bug, it can “carry an attacker from the web worker toward the whole server,” Dickson explained.

Several of the other patches also address vulnerabilities that could allow remote code execution (RCE). Still others address issues including information disclosure, memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS) interruptions, potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs, and cross-site scripting.

While there may be heavy focus on the 9.2-rated CVE-2026-129289, the lesser flaws still matter, Dickson said. For instance, in one case, one capital letter turned off encryption; a URL written as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// with an uppercase S could send passwords, tokens, form data, and files in plaintext, even through a redirect, to anyone watching the network.

Not quite PHP2Shell level, but still high priority

An attacker who exploits a PHP code-execution flaw gains access to whatever the PHP worker can touch, “which is just about everything,” Dickson said. Successful exploitation executes code with the privileges of the PHP worker, which holds the database password, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data.

For example, he described what he called an “ugly” attack path:

The threat actor gets in through the web application.

Reads the configuration file;

Dumps the customer database;

Plants a web shell to come back later.

He pointed out that PHP warned that PHP2Shell puts every installation serving web requests at risk, with no login required. “This release returns to the same neighborhood: session upload progress, fatal error backtraces, and how PHP behaves when it runs out of memory,” he said.

Fritz Jean-Louis, principal cybersecurity advisor at Infotech, agreed that this is a high-priority patching event, if not a PHP2Shell-level emergency. Although several of the critical vulnerabilities require specific configurations or uncommon deployment scenarios, “they still affect one of the most widely deployed web runtimes in the world,” he noted.

RCE is the most concerning outcome, as it can give an attacker control over the application server. From there, they may be able to access sensitive business data, steal credentials or session tokens, deploy persistent backdoors, modify application behavior, or use the compromised system as a foothold for deeper intrusion.

“Even vulnerabilities that appear less severe, such as information disclosure or memory corruption, can become highly impactful when chained together by a determined attacker,” Jean-Louis said.

What enterprises should do now

Dickson emphasized the a PHP version number alone will not tell security teams whether they are exposed. Checking the version number is the easy part, but Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version string, so the package changelog tells more than the version number does.

The hard part is finding every copy: Web servers, containers, hosting control panels, and appliances can all quietly bundle PHP, Dickson said. Then check the settings that matter:

Is session upload progress on?

Do PHP 8.5 workers include arguments in error backtraces?

Does php-cgi face the internet?

Is the PHP-FPM status page reachable from outside?

He advised security teams to start with internet-facing PHP 8.5 servers, anything with session upload progress enabled, and any setup where several applications share one session store. PHP 8.5 should be first because it is the only branch exposed to the new backtrace flaw, and fatal error backtraces are on by default there, he explained.

“Then patch everything else on a normal fast cycle,” Dickson said.

He pointed out that PHP 8.2 has just six weeks to live; it will receive no security fixes after December 31, 2026. That means this release may be one of the last it receives. Running 8.2 into January is a risk decision; PHP 8.1 and older, meanwhile, receive no fixes from the PHP project.

Interestingly, PHP’s advisory for the new PHP 8.5 backtrace flaw says a change in 8.5.12, the PHP2Shell release, is what made the new attack path reachable. “Emergency fixes are built fast, and fast work sometimes creates a new vulnerability,” Dickson noted.

In light of this, his advice is to preserve the PHP inventory built for PHP2Shell, “and keep it current,” because no one ever said during an incident, “We knew about too many of our PHP servers.”

Understanding everywhere PHP runs

Jean-Louis agreed that security teams should immediately inventory all PHP deployments, including those embedded in vendor products and appliances. They should also prioritize internet-facing systems, verify PHP-FPM and session management configurations, and deploy the latest supported PHP versions “as quickly as operationally feasible.”

Organizations should view this as a continuation of the lesson learned from PHP2Shell, he said: Runtime vulnerabilities deserve the same attention as application vulnerabilities. While PHP2Shell was more “immediately exploitable” and quickly attracted real-world attacks, this release reinforces the need for strong asset inventory, rapid patch deployment, and visibility into underlying software components.

“The biggest question for CISOs is not whether they run PHP; it’s whether they know everywhere it runs,” Jean-Louis said.

Title: CVE-2026-23871: WhatsApp Bug Helped Scammers Make Messages Look Legitimate
Context: The company’s security team found that a scammer was exploiting the issue to make fraudulent messages appear more credible
Full Text:
WhatsApp patched three security flaws, including one exploited in a real scam campaign to make fraudulent messages appear more credible.

WhatsApp’s November security advisory fixes three flaws, including CVE-2026-23871, a vulnerability in Click to WhatsApp ads affecting WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android versions earlier than 2.26.17.4.

“Incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4 could have caused a target’s device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread.” reads the advisory. “This issue may have been abused in conjunction with specific spam messages.”

The issue was caused by incomplete checks on external ad-reply URLs. An attacker could use a server under their control to send media through a crafted ad-reply message. When the message appeared in a chat, it could cause the victim’s device to reveal its IP address to the attacker.

SecurityWeek reported that WhatsApp discovered the flaw while investigating a real scam campaign. The company’s security team found that a scammer was exploiting the issue to make fraudulent messages appear more credible.

“Our team found this issue while disrupting a scam campaign, and we believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.” a WhatsApp spokesperson told SecurityWeek.

The second fix is more serious on paper, though WhatsApp has seen no sign it was ever used. CVE-2026-102769 is a SQL injection on WhatsApp for Android before 2.26.35.74, triggered when someone taps a specially crafted “order details” message sent from an unofficial client.

“A SQL injection vulnerability when the recipient tapped on a specially crafted “order details” message from an unofficial client in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 could have allowed deletion of locally-stored WhatsApp files and, only if the user is online at time of receipt, leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user’s chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing sidechannel.” continues the report.

The company is not aware of attacks in the wild exploiting this flaw.

The third, CVE-2026-44908, lives deeper in WhatsApp’s infrastructure than in the app itself. It affects the remote-attestation verifier that confirms trust with Meta AI’s confidential computing backend, across WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business on iOS, Android and Mac. Someone positioned inside Meta’s own infrastructure could, in theory, have presented a certificate signed by the wrong key to bypass the hardware root of trust, but such a certificate would first need to appear on a public transparency ledger, and WhatsApp says that ledger shows every published certificate checks out clean.

These issues come after two fixes released in May. One addressed a bug in Instagram Reels message handling that could make another person’s device load media from an attacker-controlled URL. The other fixed a Windows attachment-spoofing trick. By adding a NUL byte to a filename, an attacker could make an executable file look like a normal document. Meta received reports of both flaws through its bug bounty program, and there is no evidence that attackers exploited them.

Of the three new flaws, only one was used in a real-world scam. It also had the lowest technical impact. This shows that scammers don’t always need to exploit serious vulnerabilities or gain access to a device. A convincing message can be enough to deceive a victim. Make sure you update WhatsApp on all your devices. The fixed versions vary across iOS, Android, Mac, Windows and WhatsApp Business.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Title: How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
Context: Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score Memory corruption is usually only the first step
Full Text:
On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10.

The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure.

Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases.

The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise.

What we know about ruby2shell

Ruby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length.

The German sharp s (ß) breaks that assumption. Its uppercase form is two characters, SS. In 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, Ruby writes those two bytes but checks for room for only one. According to Veria Labs, a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. The methods that reach the bug are upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

A one-byte overflow can look harmless. In a memory-corruption exploit, though, a single byte written past the end of a heap buffer can be enough to corrupt an adjacent object or allocator metadata. Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after.

Why default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposed

HTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a _method parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of _method to uppercase. Rails includes this middleware by default, and classic-style Sinatra applications enable it. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose _method part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs.

Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from.

Who is affected

Condition

Details

Ruby version

Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.

Framework

Rails and classic-style Sinatra in their default configuration. Any other code that changes the case of attacker-controlled strings in a legacy single-byte encoding.

Bundled software

As of November 19, 2026, Veria Labs lists GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 as bundling an affected Ruby in their latest release. Discourse moved its Docker base image to Ruby 4.0.10 on November 19, so rebuilding a Docker install picks up the fix.

Distribution packages can backport fixes without changing the Ruby version number, so check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.

Six more Ruby flaws in the same release

Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 also fix six other memory safety flaws, and Ruby says several of them can lead to code execution. One, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, is an integer overflow in the same string case conversion code, and our second WAF rule covers it. The other five are in Ruby's regular expression engine. Most of them require the application to compile or match a regular expression pattern supplied by the attacker. That is uncommon in web applications, but it does happen in search features, filtering rules and admin tools.

How Cloudflare WAF protects you

Upgrading every Ruby runtime takes time, especially when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products and container images. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.

New managed rules, on for every customer

Both rules are part of the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee), with Block as the default action.

On the Free plan, the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset runs automatically, so there is nothing to turn on. On paid plans, the rules are active wherever the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed. Because paid plans give you more control over how rulesets are deployed, the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset may not be active on every zone. We recommend checking its status to confirm that it is running. You can use the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules in your dashboard.

What the WAF cannot see

A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious input arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable code:

Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. Requests sent directly to your origin IP address, and traffic between internal services, never reach the WAF. Configure your origin to accept traffic only from Cloudflare, for example with Cloudflare Tunnel or Authenticated Origin Pulls.

Other entry points into the same code. Ruby code that changes the case of strings from email, file imports, message queues or background jobs can reach ruby2shell without an HTTP request.

Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score

Memory corruption is usually only the first step. To run commands, an attacker still has to deliver a second-stage payload, such as shell commands or a reverse shell, and then interact with the compromised server. WAF attack score uses machine learning to score each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch exploit variations and post-exploitation traffic that signature-based rules can miss. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.

Impact on Cloudflare infrastructure

Cloudflare has patched its systems that use Ruby against ruby2shell. We have found no indication of compromise and continue to monitor.

Patch now

ruby2shell turns a one-byte miscalculation in string case conversion into a pre-authentication path to code execution in default Rails and Sinatra apps. With a public proof of concept expected within days, the window to patch is short. Here is what to do:

Check your WAF coverage. On the Free plan, the ruby2shell rules are already blocking. On paid plans, confirm the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and the rules have not been overridden.

Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 and restart every Ruby process, including background workers. Rebuild container images. Move applications on Ruby 3.2 or earlier to a supported series.

Update self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject and Chatwoot, as each vendor releases a fix. Rebuild Discourse Docker installs now.

Inventory your runtimes. The Zero Wire briefing includes a prompt you can give an AI agent to find every affected Ruby runtime in your infrastructure.

Our WAF analysts will keep updating protections as new techniques appear. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates.

Title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws
Context: That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell
Full Text:
On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a vulnerability in PHP's default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project fixed it the same day in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases fix 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of them also rated critical.

Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF) blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns, including for customers on the Free plan. The protection comes from a PHP remote code execution rule we first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities. That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell. The rule is part of both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, is enabled by default, and its default action is Block.

In the same WAF release, we added three new rules to the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset for paid plans: one for a request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), and two for flaws in PHP's SOAP extension (CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506) that PHP fixed in the same releases. These rules are enabled by default with the Log action, because the request patterns they look for can also appear in legitimate traffic, and blocking by default could disrupt it. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the action to Block once they confirm the rules do not affect legitimate traffic.

The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart every worker. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and follow how the vulnerabilities develop in the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

There appears to be no indication so far that these vulnerabilities have been exploited. As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no source we reviewed reports exploitation in the wild.

What we know about phpAfterShell

PHP stores session data in files by default. When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array. When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.

phpAfterShell is triggered when that write is interrupted. The session file can then hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the end of the old one. On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker controlled the old data, PHP can end up deserializing objects of the attacker's choice.

An attacker trying to exploit the flaw is likely to first search for a way to place controlled data in the session. PHP's advisory names two:

Session upload progress, a PHP feature that writes information about a running file upload into the session. A remote client can use it to shape the stored data.

Applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session.

According to PHP, code execution also requires an interruption at a useful point in the write and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application. depthfirst reports that it reached code execution without an application gadget by chaining a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. The sources we reviewed do not establish whether that second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.

depthfirst says it discovered and reported phpAfterShell. The CVE record credits Leo Lin and Asahi as reporters.

The other critical flaws

The same releases fix six more critical vulnerabilities. Each one needs a specific configuration to be exploitable:

CVE

Component

Impact

Conditions

CVE-2026-129289

PHP-FPM

An unauthenticated attacker can smuggle a second FastCGI request into PHP-FPM and run PHP code as the worker.

A front end that reuses backend FastCGI connections (nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, or HAProxy), an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end, and the path of an existing PHP script.

CVE-2026-115560

Session serializer

Object injection through a mismatch between session serializers. First covered in our php2shell briefing, now fixed.

Session upload progress enabled. PHP widened the scope: applications, pools or command-line jobs that use different serializers and share a session store are affected.

CVE-2026-129496

Timezone cache

Use-after-free that can crash a fresh worker and possibly run code. PHP demonstrated code execution locally with known memory addresses.

Non-thread-safe builds where a startup diagnostic has been written to a PHP error log file.

CVE-2026-129481

Session shutdown

Use-after-free, described by PHP as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619. No code execution demonstrated.

PHP 8.3 and later.

CVE-2026-129474

Fatal error backtraces

Use-after-free in magic method backtraces.

PHP 8.5 and later, where fatal error backtraces are enabled by default. Setting zend.exception_ignore_args=1, the php.ini-production default, blocks the demonstrated attack.

CVE-2026-129182

Fatal error backtraces

Use-after-free. No code execution demonstrated.

PHP 8.5, specific path-level settings, and an Apache per-directory configuration or front end that produces an early diagnostic.

Who is affected

The vulnerable versions are PHP 8.2 before 8.2.36, 8.3 before 8.3.37, 8.4 before 8.4.28, 8.5 before 8.5.13, and the 8.6.0 release candidates. Whether a deployment is exposed depends on the conditions of each flaw.

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life. depthfirst says the official 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 end-of-life mitigation branches are not affected by phpAfterShell, but PHP says CVE-2026-129289 was introduced in PHP 5.6.0 and that releases older than 8.2 may also be affected by CVE-2026-115560.

Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the PHP version number. Check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.

How Cloudflare WAF protects you

PHP runs a large share of the web, often inside content management systems, plugins, and container images that teams do not update directly. Patching every PHP runtime takes time. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.

phpAfterShell: protection on every plan

We released the original PHP remote code execution rules in an emergency release on October 21, 2026, after the php2shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) were disclosed. We extended them to CVE-2026-115560 on October 23 and refined them several times in the following weeks, based in part on reports from security researchers who took part in a PHP Capture the Flag (CTF) challenge.

phpAfterShell shares an attack technique with php2shell: an attacker plants serialized PHP data in session storage and waits for PHP to deserialize it. Because of that overlap, the existing rule already matched part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before disclosure. On November 19, we updated the rule's detection logic to cover phpAfterShell and added CVE-2026-126714 to its description.
