What the WAF cannot see

A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious data arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to these vulnerabilities, including:

The deserialization step. phpAfterShell's final step happens inside PHP, when it reads a corrupted session file. The WAF can block the requests that plant the payload, not the read itself.

Session data from other sources. If an application copies user-controlled data into the session from a database, a queue or an upstream API, that data may never cross the WAF in a recognizable form.

Flaws triggered by server state. CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 depend on error logs, diagnostics and worker lifecycle. They do not have dedicated WAF rules, and the patch and the configuration changes below are the way to address them.

Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services and PHP-FPM listeners exposed directly to a network.

Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score

WAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for attack payloads. It is available on Business plans (cf.waf.score.class) and, with a dedicated remote code execution sub-score (cf.waf.score.rce) along with an overall score (cf.waf.score), on Enterprise plans.

Attack score complements the managed rules. It will not recognize every serialized object or smuggled FastCGI record on its own, but a working exploit chain usually needs more than one request, and the later stages carry payloads the model is trained to score:

Second-stage payloads. Once an attacker can run code, they still need to send commands: shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, system(), passthru()), PHP code evaluation (eval(), assert()) or reverse-shell strings in headers, query parameters or request bodies.

Webshell traffic. Attackers often drop a small PHP webshell after the initial compromise. Requests that pass operating system commands to that webshell remain visible to attack score.

Deploy protections and patch

You can find more information on how to deploy managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide. In short:

Check that phpAfterShell protection is active. On the Free plan, no action is needed. On paid plans, make sure the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and that the PHP Remote Code Execution Attack #6 rule is set to Block.

Review the new rules and switch them to Block. The CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506 rules are in Log mode by default. Review their matches in Security Events, then change their action to Block.

Layer attack score. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with a low remote code execution score, for example cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.

Upgrade PHP. Move to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0. Rebuild container images and restart the PHP-FPM master or Apache so every worker loads the new binary, then verify the version that serves web requests. After upgrading, check that no php.ini, FPM pool or virtual host still sets session.upload_progress.enabled=1, because an explicit setting overrides the new default.

Apply interim mitigations if you cannot upgrade right away. Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and limit the untrusted data you store in sessions. Turn off FastCGI connection reuse. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Fix configuration errors that produce PHP startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a file. Keep PHP-FPM listeners off untrusted networks. These steps reduce exposure; they do not fix the flaws.

For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your PHP deployments and check each one against all seven critical CVEs, see the phpAfterShell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire.

Update every PHP runtime now

phpAfterShell turns an interrupted file write in PHP's default session handler into a path to code execution, and it arrived in the same release as six other critical flaws. With technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow. Cloudflare WAF blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns for every customer, including the Free plan, and paid plans have new rules for the PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws. The fix is still to upgrade PHP and restart the services that use it.

Title: PHP Discloses Three New Critical Vulnerabilities
Context: 5, an attacker may be able to exploit this to run code as the PHP process
Full Text:
TL;DR

PHP disclosed three additional critical vulnerabilities, separate from the PHP2Shell issues covered in our October analysis.

Upgrade to PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, or 8.2.36, as appropriate for your branch; check with your vendor for package availability or backported fixes.

Inventory PHP deployments and confirm each has an owner and a patch path. For background on the earlier PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, read our October analysis.

PHP2Shell reminded us that PHP powers a vast range of websites, applications, and products, often running behind the scenes in places organizations may not immediately think to look. With three new advisories now drawing attention to PHP’s internals, security teams face a familiar challenge: understanding where the runtime is deployed, how it is configured, and who can move quickly when a fix is available.

New Flaws Impact Memory Safety and Session Handling Issues in PHP

PHP’s three critical advisories point to different failure points in the runtime, from memory cleanup to session parsing. Their impact depends on the PHP version and, in some cases, how the application is configured.

Vulnerability

Description

Fixed Version / Remediation

Backtrace use-after-free (CVE-2026-129474)

When PHP records an error’s history, it can mistakenly refer to memory that has already been cleared while handling certain method calls. Under specific conditions in PHP 8.5, an attacker may be able to exploit this to run code as the PHP process.

Upgrade to PHP 8.5.13

Timezone-cache use-after-free (CVE-2026-129496)

A startup warning can leave PHP pointing to timezone data that is no longer in use. If another warning occurs during an early request, PHP may crash or mishandle memory; in some conditions, that could let an attacker run code as the PHP process.

Upgrade to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13

Session serializer mismatch (CVE-2026-115560)

PHP can save session data in one format and later read it as another. If upload-progress tracking is enabled and the application has the right code available, an attacker may be able to turn that mismatch into code execution.

Disable upload progress (workaround) or upgrade to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, or 8.5.13.

Memory-safety flaws are especially consequential in a language runtime because they can let an attacker influence how a process handles data or control flow. Here, the affected paths include backtrace generation and timezone-cache handling, which are operations that may sit outside the application code teams typically review. Under the right conditions, the outcome can range from a worker crash to code execution with the PHP worker’s privileges.

Session handling carries a different risk: the same stored data can be interpreted differently by different readers. If one component writes session data using one format and another reads it using a different format, attacker-controlled content may be treated as serialized objects. Teams should check for upload-progress settings, shared session stores, and applications or processes that use different serializers.

Finding PHP is Only Half the Job

The fixes are available, but applying them across an organization can take more than updating a public-facing server. PHP may also run in internal services, containers, test environments, appliances, and products maintained by another vendor

Start with an inventory, then track each deployment through to a verified fix:

Find every PHP runtime. Include internet-facing and internal services, containers, test environments, appliances, and products that bundle PHP.

Identify the owner and patch path. Note who maintains each deployment and whether it comes from PHP, an operating system distributor, hosting provider, or product vendor.

Confirm the fix for its branch. Apply the appropriate patched release or a vendor backport, and verify that the update reached each deployment.

Review session settings. Where session upload progress is enabled, use the advisory’s workaround while arranging the upgrade.

A patch plan is only complete when teams can confirm that affected deployments have been updated or mitigated, including less visible systems and bundled runtimes. For more on the inventory and ownership challenge, see our October analysis of PHP2Shell.

Title: WhatsApp Patches 3 Security Flaws, Including Android Bug Suspected of Use in Scams
Context: When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign
Full Text:
Meta-owned WhatsApp has addressed security vulnerabilities, including one impacting its Android app that it suspects may have been exploited in connection with scam messages.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-23871, has been described as a case of incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4.

The issue could have "caused a target's device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread," WhatsApp said.

The messaging platform said it may have been "abused in conjunction with specific spam messages." Internal researchers on the WhatsApp Security Team have been credited with discovering and reporting the issue.

When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign. "We believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible," the spokesperson added.

WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity, and if those efforts were successful.

Also addressed by the company are two other flaws -

CVE-2026-102769 - An SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 that occurred when a recipient tapped on a specially crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client, causing locally-stored WhatsApp files to be deleted.

CVE-2026-44908 - A trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure that affects WhatsApp for iOS before 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before v2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before v2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before v2.26.23.70.

Interestingly, CVE-2026-102769 is also capable of leaking one bit of information through a timing-based side channel if the user is online at the time of receipt of the malicious message.

It "leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user's chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel," WhatsApp added. There is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.

Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-44908, on the other hand, could have allowed a bad actor positioned within Meta infrastructure to bypass the hardware root of trust using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key.

"Any such VCEK Cert would first have to be published to the third-party binary transparency ledger used by WhatsApp Private Processing," WhatsApp noted. "The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation."

WhatsApp is advising users to keep their apps and devices up to date to ensure optimal protection. The company also said that it continuously works to strengthen its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions towards keeping the platform secure.

Title: Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own
Context: Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability...
Full Text:
Amazon Threat Intelligence is sharing findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor using autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The actor gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server. These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable.

Discovery

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.

Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.

Cairn and an overview of this campaign

Cairn was built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple. Given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. That same ease of use makes it attractive to threat actors. In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to “obtain shell access.” Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step.

The campaign included several operations that varied widely in complexity and outcome. The following operations show both the persistence and the capability of autonomous AI agents.

Persistence against a hardened target

The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. Redis is a database that keeps frequently used data in memory so applications can retrieve it quickly, which can make it a valuable foothold inside a network. Over roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, the agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. These included abusing Redis’s replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted Log4Shell injection against another service running on the same system.

When those attempts failed, the agents mapped the internal Docker network topology through a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance and launched credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and several other services. None of these attempts succeeded.

A separate operation ran for more than 6 hours and targeted a university GPU server, which is a group of high-performance computers built for computing-intensive research. The agents first built a list of about 80 real usernames by researching the university’s public presence, including faculty directories, lab websites, archived web pages, and academic papers. Then, they tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against the server’s remote login (SSH), and, on other systems across the university network, an admin dashboard, a network storage device, a VPN server, and the university’s campus portal. They never found a working login.

Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction.

Zero-day discovery

Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.

In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup. The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root.

At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.

Subsequent use

In another session, the threat actor stepped in. After the agents discovered the zero-day, the actor then provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network. The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel. The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.

Attribution

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that this is a Chinese-nexus threat actor based on the Simplified Chinese prompts, the China Standard Time script timestamps, and the targeting of universities likely of strategic interest to China.

Actions taken by AWS

Amazon Threat Intelligence notified the project’s maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a GitHub Security Advisory.

The affected organizations were non-AWS customers that AWS had no direct path to notify. Instead, AWS worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.

Adoption is growing

Gambit Security was one of the first organizations in the industry to document the use of Cairn by a threat group. Its research describes a separate, financially motivated actor using Cairn to target online retailers. Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations. Additional details are available in Gambit Security’s report.

What this means for defenders

The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response. An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints. To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.

Behind the scenes, AWS active defense systems use global honeypots (decoy systems that attract threat actors) and network traffic analysis to identify actors that are scanning for vulnerable systems, and then help restrict that activity at the network level. These protections are built into the AWS network at no extra cost to customers.

Indicators of compromise

The following addresses appear in records dated September 8 to 10, 2026. 142[.]4.98.145 142[.]4.107.34

His mission is to enable Amazon businesses by making the benefits of security the path of least resistance. CJ joined Amazon in December 2007, holding various roles including Consumer CISO, and most recently AWS CISO, before becoming CISO of Amazon Integrated Security September of 2023.

Prior to joining Amazon, CJ led the technical analysis of computer and network intrusion efforts at the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Cyber Division. CJ also served as a Special Agent with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI). CJ led several computer intrusion investigations seen as foundational to the security industry today.

Title: Hackers use autonomous AI tool Cairn to find zero-day, take over server
Context: Hackers used an autonomous AI agent platform called "Cairn" to discover a zero-day vulnerability in a medical imaging application and exploit it to take complete control of a...
Full Text:
Hackers used an autonomous AI agent platform called "Cairn" to discover a zero-day vulnerability in a medical imaging application and exploit it to take complete control of a server.

According to Amazon Threat Intelligence, the suspected Chinese-linked attackers simply instructed the AI agents to "obtain shell access," leaving them to independently discover and exploit the flaw.

Amazon Threat Intelligence uncovered the campaign after discovering that the attackers had left their Cairn instance publicly accessible without authentication, exposing their hacking operations.

According to the researchers, the attacks were launched by a Chinese-nexus threat actor between September 8 and 10, 2026, targeting mainly East Asian educational institutions outside China.

Cairn is a legitimate pentesting tool that can be used to coordinate multiple AI agents in cyber-operations, created for research and defense strengthening.

Gambit Security documented cases of Cairn abuse as part of a large-scale credit card stealing operation in September. More recently, Google reported it was deployed in an attack against an aerospace organization in the U.S.

During the campaign investigated by Amazon, the AI agents were not always successful. For example, a 16-hour and 148-action effort to take control of a Redis server failed.

In a separate case targeting a university GPU server, the agents tried over 30,000 credential combinations over six hours but failed to brute-force their way in.

Finding and using a zero-day

According to Amazon, Cairn's AI agents found a path traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging application that uses AI to help researchers label medical images.

The flaw enabled the agents to write files to arbitrary locations on the server, and within 11 minutes, they went from mapping the application's API to exploiting the vulnerability.

In a subsequent session, the AI agents used the flaw to write a Python reverse shell to the sitecustomize.py file that automatically loads when Python starts, then triggered an API endpoint to establish root access to the server.

After discovering the zero-day, the operator provided the agents with a proxy into a second university network running the same vulnerable software and directed them to target other machines.

Amazon reported the flaw to MONAI Label maintainers, and they released a security update to address it on November 18.

The researchers attributed the campaign to a Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language of the retrieved prompts, the activity timestamps, and the choice of targets.

Amazon also shared two IP addresses associated with the campaign, observed between September 8 and 10, 2026:

142[.]4.98.145

142[.]4.107.34

Amazon warned that AI agents can find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than security teams can react, urging organizations to rely more on automated defenses rather than manual investigations.

The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time. Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools. Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents. "Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote. Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server. "The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server." Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root. In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code. Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies. This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies. "Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

Title: In Other News: Norwegian Energy Firm Cyberattacks, Supercomputer Hack, New Nightmare Eclipse Exploit
Context: This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help...
Full Text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights:

Gemini agents targeted Epoch AI

AI evaluation firm Trajectory Labs says Gemini 4 Argon agents it stress-tested in October, with Gemini’s API safeguards turned on, tried to hack Epoch AI’s live website while hunting for answers to non-existent FrontierMath problems, attempting SQL injection and impersonating Epoch staff. Trajectory has paused all misalignment testing. Epoch says no private information was accessed.

Google brings Gemini 4 Neon to defenders

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Google has released Gemini 4 Neon, a faster, lower-cost model for coding and enterprise work, and says a cyber-focused version will reach eligible members of its Fairwind Program for trusted defenders in the coming days. Google claims the model performs at frontier level across finding, validating and patching vulnerabilities. It also says Neon keeps Carbon-level safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse while turning down far fewer legitimate requests in those areas.

Compromised migration vendor opens door to Infoblox data theft

Networking and security company Infoblox has confirmed that hackers accessed certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor, which TechCrunch’s sources say handled SharePoint migration. The Register has since reported that the stolen files included NIOS configuration snapshots for some customers and personal details of employees and their dependents. Infoblox says it has no indication that its products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved.

EU adds NoName057(16) to cyber sanctions list

The Council of the EU has sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities over Russian information manipulation and cyber activity, including the Moscow-based Social Design Agency, 24 of its employees, and several pro-Kremlin propagandists. Under its cyber sanctions regime, the Council also listed NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has claimed attacks on government bodies, critical infrastructure and companies in Ukraine, the US and EU member states.

Japanese supercomputer offline after intrusion

Japan’s Riken research institute has suspended operations of the Fugaku supercomputer and cut off external access after detecting suspicious traffic on its user authentication system. In a November 17 notice, Riken said an outside party used a public dashboard showing Fugaku’s operational status to break into the system’s internal operations network and tamper with multiple servers. Names, email addresses and user IDs of up to 4,597 Fugaku and RIKYU users may have been exposed.

Ukraine arrests ransomware suspects, 8-Digits member extradited to US

Ukrainian police, working with the FBI, have arrested four alleged key members of a ransomware gang that posed as IT support in calls powered by an AI voice platform to obtain credentials or get remote access software installed. Separately, Kazakh national Roman Khlynovskiy has appeared in US court after being extradited from Italy over his alleged role in the 8-Digits Team, an INC and Lynx ransomware affiliate accused of stealing data from US hospitals, healthcare entities and schools and making over $500 million in ransom demands. In Florida, five people were arrested in a nationwide crackdown on account-takeover fraud schemes linked to more than $54 million in losses at over 65 US financial institutions.

Test environment intrusion exposes Rakuten Securities customer data

Japanese online brokerage Rakuten Securities says login IDs and branch codes for up to 11.25 million accounts, and personal and financial information for up to 4.47 million accounts, may have been exposed after attackers accessed a test environment system on November 11. The exposed details include names, dates of birth, addresses, employers, withdrawal bank account numbers, and declared annual income and financial assets.

Equinor stops cyberattack as Skagerak Energi reports attempted intrusion

Norwegian energy giant Equinor says it has stopped a cyberattack against some of its IT systems that it detected on November 17, adding that production was not affected and there is no sign that data was stolen or altered. The company said the attack was not a virus attack and did not appear to be specifically targeting it. A day after Equinor’s disclosure, Norwegian power company Skagerak Energi reported activity that may have been an attempted cyberattack on some of its IT systems, saying operations and production were not affected and there is no sign that information was leaked.

Nightmare Eclipse drops unpatched Windows lock screen escape

Researcher Nightmare Eclipse has published FastUnlock, an unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and run code as the lock screen account. The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account.

Malware targets CACs left in personal computers

The NSA says threat actors are using malware against the personal computers that Department of War (DoW) employees use with Common Access Card (CAC) readers. Once the malware has recorded the card’s PIN, it can use the CAC’s credentials to sign into federal and DoW websites for as long as the card stays in the reader. That often gives attackers access to anything the cardholder can normally reach.

Title: How exposure management can help public sector prepare for PHP2Shell-like vulnerabilities
Context: What set PHP2Shell apart from a typical critical vulnerability wasn’t simply its severity, but also how quickly exploitation followed disclosure
Full Text:
PHP2Shell showed how fast a runtime-level flaw can go from disclosure to confirmed exploitation. Here’s how federal, state, local, and education teams can prepare for PHP2Shell-like flaws.

Key takeaways

PHP2Shell went from disclosure to confirmed exploitation within days. With AI shortening the disclosure-to-exploitation window, new critical flaws will likely move just as fast.

Most security teams’ primary challenge with PHP2Shell was knowing where the vulnerabilities were in their environment. Teams that already knew where PHP ran across their IT infrastructure, web applications, and cloud assets were in a position to act quickly.

Initial access flaws will continue to impact your network edge, so work backward from the foothold. Map what an attacker could reach after breaching an edge device, such as root access, management servers, and directory services. Then close those escalation paths by patching kernels and restricting unprivileged user namespaces.

To prioritize, factor in exploitation evidence, not severity alone. Weigh KEV status, exploit prediction scores, and your own internet exposure, as well as pre-approve a plan for systems you can’t patch immediately.

When two critical PHP vulnerabilities, nicknamed PHP2Shell, leaked ahead of their coordinated disclosure date on Oct. 20, and their alarming scope and severity became clear, cybersecurity teams sprung into “all hands on deck” mode, much in the same way they did in late 2021 in response to the Log4Shell bug.

Many organizations, including government agencies, rushed to take down their websites as an early, stopgap preventive measure against attackers’ already active attempts to exploit these two memory management vulnerabilities, which were cataloged as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and given a CVSS score of 9.2.

Thrust into a furious race against time, security teams scrambled to detect and patch their instances of PHP, the popular server-side scripting language that around 70% of websites use. If exploited, the vulnerabilities, which impact PHP’s runtime, can allow attackers to execute unauthenticated code remotely on compromised web servers.

As the dust begins to clear, here are Tenable’s recommendations for how public-sector cybersecurity teams can ensure they’re well prepared to respond to vulnerabilities that trigger urgent, global responses like PHP2Shell.

What happened with PHP2Shell

PHP’s maintainers shipped emergency patches a day early on Oct. 21. Within days, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed attackers were actively exploiting PHP2Shell, added the flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, and issued a three-day remediation deadline for federal civilian agencies under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04.

What set PHP2Shell apart from a typical critical vulnerability wasn’t simply its severity, but also how quickly exploitation followed disclosure.

For public-sector security teams, identifying what needed to be patched presented a major challenge. Because the vulnerability sits in the PHP runtime itself, an organization’s own application code could be free from significant flaws and still be exposed.

Fact

Detail

CVEs

CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619

Severity

CVSS v4.0 9.2 (Critical)

Disclosure

Oct. 20–21, 2026 (PHP’s maintainers rushed out patches a day ahead of schedule after details leaked)

Fixed versions

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35 (PHP2Shell). The Nov. 19 releases (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36) also fix a separate critical flaw, CVE-2026-115560, so upgrade to those.

Exposure

About 30.3M PHP services on affected versions as of Oct. 29 (Source: Internet-wide scanning)

Public agencies urging action

CISA, NSA, FBI (U.S.); NCSC (U.K.); CERT-EU; ACSC (Australia); CISA KEV listing Oct. 26 with a federal civilian deadline of Oct. 29

Technical guidance

Tenable® Research PHP2Shell FAQ

CISA, the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA), and the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), as well as the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and the EU’s CERT-EU told organizations to either patch immediately or to take affected systems offline.

On Oct. 28, CISA added the Linux kernel flaw Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300) to KEV and warned that it can be chained with PHP2Shell to implant PHP webshells. Indeed, Palo Alto Networks has confirmed exploitation of internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces. Dream Research reported that attackers chained PHP2Shell with Fragnesia to gain root access to 25 servers, including firewalls at a U.S. government-affiliated organization, and Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 team says it independently verified the tooling and results. Tenable Research’s testing found that exploits generally had to be tuned to each target, but systems that share one build, such as network appliances, are a glaring exception.

Even the criminal underground reacted: forums including BreachForums and DarkForums took themselves offline within hours of disclosure, likely to protect their PHP infrastructure.

The researchers credited with finding the flaws say AI assisted the discovery. The pattern, faster discovery followed by faster exploitation, is worth taking seriously.

On Nov. 19, PHP shipped fixes for a separate critical flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the same runtime. It is harder to exploit, because it depends on how session handling is configured and which libraries an application uses. No exploitation had been reported at release.

As we’ve seen in recent weeks, security teams have had to pivot increasingly frequently and quickly to address critical vulnerabilities with a broad impact scope, including Brotli2Shell, NGINX2Root, Java4Shell, and Able2Shell.

This means PHP2Shell isn’t a one-off. Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), disclosed Nov. 17, is a good example of why this scenario is becoming a new normal for security teams. Like PHP2Shell, it is a memory corruption flaw in a language runtime that researchers say can give attackers code execution in applications built on it. Within a day of Java4Shell's disclosure, researchers reported exploitation attempts and a working exploit, though it isn’t yet in CISA’s KEV catalog and exposure is narrower. Thus, now is the time to find where PHP and Java run in your environment, and which of those assets face the internet.

What federal agencies should know about PHP2Shell

The task for U.S. federal civilian agencies is to now verify remediation and check for compromise.

BOD 26-04 replaces flat deadlines with a four-variable model: whether the asset is publicly exposed, whether the CVE is in KEV, whether an adversary can automate exploitation, and what the technical impact is. Agencies must determine the first variable themselves. An agency that can’t say which assets run PHP, and which of those face the internet, can’t place a single finding in the right tier. State, local, and education teams aren’t bound by BOD 26-04, but CISA "strongly encourages all partners to adopt similar actions in their vulnerability management policy", and many organizations outside of the federal government use KEV for prioritization. It is a defensible benchmark for your own program.

Why runtime flaws like PHP2Shell are a challenge for public sector agencies

Three structural realities make a runtime-level flaw hard for government teams to address quickly:

Legacy footprint: According to Tenable Research, about 59% of internet-facing PHP hosts run end-of-life branches. Due to long procurement cycles, public sector organizations often find themselves running software that vendors no longer maintain.

Indirect exposure: PHP runs underneath websites, content management systems, and other commercial software that IT and security teams may not associate with PHP. That’s why a runtime-level flaw is so dangerous: an agency can discover it is exposed through a vendor or a plugin, only after the fact.

Resourcing constraints: State and local security teams are being asked to respond to critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities with limited staff and budget.

None of this is a criticism of any single agency’s diligence. It is a description of why “patch quickly” is necessary but not sufficient as a strategy.

How exposure management can help public sector agencies

The teams best positioned to respond to PHP2Shell were those that could answer two critical questions before the PHP2Shell CVEs were even assigned:

What is running everywhere, including in internet-facing commercial products and cloud workloads?

How fast can we act on what we find?

An exposure management platform allows organizations to answer those two questions by replacing the outdated model of periodic scans with continuous, comprehensive asset and vulnerability visibility, paired with workflows that operate at the speed of modern, AI-boosted cyber threats.

“PHP2Shell is a preview of what’s becoming the new normal, not an outlier. The agencies that were best positioned to respond weren’t necessarily those with the biggest patching teams. They were the ones that already knew what they ran, what faced the internet, and what an attacker could reach from there. Exposure management gives you this comprehensive, continuously updated visibility, so the next time a critical flaw emerges, your first question is ‘what do we fix first?’ instead of ‘do we even have this?’”

— Christopher Day, Public Sector CTO, Tenable

The traditional patch-management model assumes a predictable sequence: disclosure, a grace period to assess and plan, and scheduled remediation. PHP2Shell compressed that chain with early and unplanned disclosure, and exploitation within days of disclosure. Plus, the vulnerability sat below the application layer, where many security teams lack day-to-day visibility. For many organizations, the first question wasn’t: “How do we patch this?” It was: “Do we even have these vulnerabilities?”

AI is shortening the distance between a vulnerability’s discovery and its exploitation. The researchers who found the PHP2Shell flaws say AI assisted their discovery. Tenable Research expects AI-assisted tooling to accelerate exploit creation.

Your security program can’t depend on periodic scans and scheduled patch windows. Teams asking “Do we even run PHP anywhere?” on Oct. 21 have a visibility gap. A point-in-time scan, run on last quarter’s schedule, cannot answer this question. You need a continuously updated view of on-prem systems, web applications, cloud assets, and their vulnerabilities.

How to protect your network edge

PHP2Shell will not be the last critical flaw to reach the edge. Tenable Research’s analysis of edge infrastructure exploitation found the same edge product lines exploited repeatedly, with some appliance lines seeing a newly exploited CVE every eight and a half to thirteen months. Network appliances often share builds, so one tuned exploit can reach every exposed, unpatched device running the same build.

You can’t know which flaw will give an attacker their first foothold, but you can decide what that foothold lets them do. The PAN-OS compromises reported by Dream Research show the difference. PHP2Shell gave the attackers code execution as a low-privilege user. Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300), a Linux kernel flaw with a public proof-of-concept available since May, turned that into root access. From there, the attackers opened a tunnel, reached a management server, and went after Active Directory credentials. Every step after the first existed before PHP2Shell was disclosed.

That is the lesson for addressing initial-access flaws. The entry point changes with every disclosure, but what an attacker can do next depends largely on your own environment: unpatched kernels, unprivileged user namespaces, and edge devices with broad reach into management networks and directory services.

Map those attack paths now, before the next disclosure, and close them. Patch kernels on internet-facing hosts and appliances, restrict unprivileged user namespaces, and limit what each edge device can reach internally. Done ahead of time, this removes attack paths for vulnerabilities that haven’t been discovered yet.

How Tenable helps you find and address PHP2Shell exposure

For many organizations, the hardest part of PHP2Shell wasn’t applying the fix. It was finding every place PHP runs. The Tenable One Exposure Management Platform helps public sector teams detect their PHP instances across their attack surface, then act on it:

To see this in action, watch the on-demand product deep-dive webinar, explore the step-by-step demos, or read how to discover and remediate PHP2Shell exposure with Tenable.

How public sector leaders can prepare for the next PHP2Shell-like flaw

Headline-grabbing flaws like PHP2Shell will test these three things:

How quickly you can find affected assets

How well you can prioritize their remediation

How far an attacker can get once they’re inside

These six steps can help you prepare:

Prioritize by exploitation evidence, not severity alone. A CVSS score describes the worst case. It doesn’t tell you whether anyone is exploiting the flaw, whether it’s reachable from the internet, or what it takes to exploit. Weigh KEV status, exploit prediction scores such as the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS), Tenable’s Vulnerability Priority Rating (VPR), and your own internet exposure. Start with internet-facing management interfaces, network appliances, and end-of-life PHP instances, and include the kernel underneath them.

Create a comprehensive asset inventory. Catalog your exposure to PHP instances across on-premises systems, cloud workloads, and vendor-hosted or SaaS products, not just your own internal code. Record how each instance is configured, not just its version. Exposure to flaws like CVE-2026-115560 depends on settings such as session handling. Systems that haven’t been inventoried become likely places for critical vulnerabilities to remain unpatched.

Limit what an edge breach unlocks. Treat a local privilege escalation flaw on an internet-facing host or appliance as urgently as the remote flaws that breach it. Fragnesia’s severity has a lower score than PHP2Shell, yet it turned a contained breach into root access. Then map what each edge device can access, including management servers, directory services, and stored credentials.

Treat remediation speed as a risk metric. Track and report time-to-remediate for critical, actively discussed vulnerabilities the way you would track any other operational risk, with executive visibility when timelines slip.

Plan for the “can’t patch immediately” case. Proactively establish compensating controls, web application firewall rules, and the ability to take a system offline.

Extend your asset visibility to your trusted third parties, such as SaaS providers. A vendor’s unpatched CMS or plugin puts you at risk. Contractually require timely disclosure and patching commitments from your vendors and other third parties. Ask network appliance vendors for their kernel status, not just their application status, because their operating system matters as much as their PHP version.

Where to go from here

Many organizations that struggled to respond to PHP2Shell had difficulty confirming where the vulnerability lived across their infrastructure, cloud workloads, and their internet-accessible vendor platforms.

After comprehensively detecting PHP, you need to identify what an attacker can reach. Initial access flaws will continue to impact your network edge. The ones that find an open path to root access, to a management server, or to the directory will become breaches.

Title: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Flaw CVE-2026-76466 to Breach Russian Organization
Context: Attackers have exploited a critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9
Full Text:
Cisco Expressway flaw CVE-2026-76466 is being exploited to gain root access and move from exposed devices into internal networks.

Attackers have exploited a critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8) in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization, and they moved fast once a working exploit went public.

“A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.” reads the advisory.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger the flaw to run commands as root on an affected device. Cisco shipped a fix on 21 October, so this wasn’t a zero-day by the time it got used.

The vulnerability is caused by persistent cookies and weak client certificate checks when TLS Verify Mode is enabled for clustering. An attacker with access to these cookies could connect to the database service and send specific RPC commands, potentially executing arbitrary commands with root privileges on the affected device.

Russian security firm F6 says this is the first known case of the flaw being exploited in the wild, and it happened on Expressway X15.5.3 devices after a proof-of-concept exploit appeared on GitHub. The attackers started with two internet-facing Expressway boxes.

“The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices.” reads the advisory by F6. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.”

The attackers used custom Python scripts to scan networks, find accessible SMB resources, connect to SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories. Their goal was to steal credentials and other sensitive information.

F6’s analysts think AI tools helped write those scripts, judging by the comments and fix descriptions left inside them, which is a strange kind of courtesy from an intruder.

F6 published indicators tied to the activity: two IP addresses, a telltale “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log on affected devices, and Python scripts staged under a specific disk path.

“One of the key indicators of successful exploitation is the appearance of a nodeup ‘wombat@127.0.0.1’ entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices.” states F6. “Such an entry indicates that a connection was established with an Erlang node whose identifier corresponds to the known exploitation mechanism — CVE-2026-76466. When such events are detected, organizations should review other logs and artifacts to confirm whether compromise has occurred.”

Nobody has linked the attack to a known group yet, so treat this as an active technique without a named author. If you run Expressway, update now, hunt for those indicators, and don’t assume a clean edge device means a clean network behind it.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Cisco)

Title: Industry Reactions to Major Outages and AI Patching Debate: Feedback Friday
Context: When a critical Java vulnerability lands, teams must push OpenJDK updates into production within hours, often with less testing than they would normally do and with far more...
Full Text:
A series of major technology outages have hit the United States, disrupting email, air travel, banking and government operations.

The incidents included a nearly day-long Microsoft 365 outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that slowed transactions at other banks, and an outage affecting the NSA’s classified internal network. United Airlines and Apple also experienced disruptions.

Officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or a link between the incidents. Microsoft traced its outage to a months-old software defect, the FAA blamed a newly installed router, and the NSA cited routine maintenance.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, however, linked the NSA disruption to patching for a PHP vulnerability found with the help of AI. Sen. Mark Warner said AI-driven vulnerability discovery is pushing organizations to patch many systems at once, putting strain on infrastructure that wasn’t built for that pace of change.

Industry professionals have commented on whether AI-accelerated patching played a role, the need for tested rollback plans, and the fragility of interconnected systems.

And the feedback begins…

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Gil Tene, Chief Technology Officer & Co-founder, Azul:

“We have strong reason to believe that AI-accelerated patch velocity is already causing major operational incidents. Based on direct experience with customers, we know that urgently deploying large, non-security-only OpenJDK updates does cause stability incidents. These rollouts sometimes fail and have to be reverted, leaving organizations exposed and delaying the remediation of the very vulnerabilities they are meant to address until teams find a workaround they can roll out without compromising stability.

As AI accelerates the discovery of critical flaws, patch cycles are compressing rapidly. In the past four weeks alone, the Java community has had to absorb four update events, including three separate critical vulnerability events and a multitude of high-severity CVEs that couldn’t wait. When a critical Java vulnerability lands, teams must push OpenJDK updates into production within hours, often with less testing than they would normally do and with far more urgency to get the change rolled out before attackers can exploit it. When the fix for a vulnerability is available only as part of a much wider full update that brings along hundreds of unrelated changes, the rollout carries much more risk, because change is risk.

The outage risk doesn’t come from the vulnerabilities themselves. It comes from the volume of change forced by compressed timelines. Hurried, urgent change is risky to begin with. The more change a hurried rollout carries, the greater the risk of instability and widespread incidents. Security-only updates minimize that risk by limiting the change to what is necessary to resolve the vulnerabilities, and nothing more.”

Samuel Hassine, CEO and Co-founder, Filigran:

“I think [faster patching pace driven by AI] plays a part, but I would be careful not to make it the whole story. From what has been made public so far, these outages look less like an AI problem than a change problem: updates and upgrades pushed onto systems that can’t take much change. AI is making that visible, because the list of flaws to fix now grows faster than most companies can safely roll out the fixes.

For years our industry has told companies to patch faster and has measured them on that alone. But a fix that takes the service down is a security failure too, because being available is the first thing a customer expects from you. So the question I would put to every CEO is who owns the choice between leaving a flaw open a few more days and risking the service by closing it tonight. In most companies those are two teams with two different targets, and at this pace it has to be one person who answers for both.”

Ken Barth, CEO, Catalogic Software:

“AI is finding vulnerabilities faster than many remediation processes were built to handle. Microsoft fixed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities in its October security release, a monthly record, and 1,094 in November. The company has said AI-assisted discovery will put more fixes into each release. Each fix is a change to a live system. With the same staff and maintenance windows, a higher volume leaves less time to test each update, and less testing leaves more room for something to break. Nothing published so far links this pressure to the recent Microsoft 365 outage, but Microsoft’s own explanation shows how easily planned work can take a service down.

Waiting longer is not a safe answer either. Google has reported attackers using AI to reverse-engineer patches and quickly build exploits for the flaws the patches address, so every published fix also tells attackers where to look. That makes being able to undo a change a security control in its own right. Before it reaches production, each update needs a verified restore point for the systems it touches, a tested rollback plan, and a clear owner for the decision to use it.

The same discipline applies after something breaks. Microsoft restored services in stages to keep them stable, which is what careful recovery looks like. Organizations should know before the next incident which services must come back first, what each one depends on, and how long the full sequence takes. A recovery time that has never been tested is only an estimate, and boards should treat it as one.”

Brian Contos, Field CISO, Mitiga:

“Faster patching isn’t the problem by itself. AI is shrinking the time between a vulnerability being disclosed and being exploited, so defenders are under real pressure to ship fixes faster, and every change is a chance to break something. Look at the past week. Officials tied the FAA disruption to a network equipment upgrade, sources told CBS News the NSA outage followed routine patching, and JPMorgan Chase attributed its problems to a software issue. None of those appear to be attacks. What turns a routine change into a national outage is pushing it without being able to see its effects or quickly undo it. Speed is fine if every change is staged, watched for how the system behaves afterward and backed by a rollback someone has tested.

The other lesson is how far a single failure travels. One router change at the FAA destabilized 17 of its 22 en route centers, and Chase said its issue may have slowed transactions at other banks. Redundancy alone doesn’t protect against a healthy component that’s misbehaving, because everything around it trusts it. Segmentation, independent failure domains and a rehearsed process for isolating a bad component quickly are what keep one problem from becoming everyone’s problem.

The preparation for failures and cyberattacks is largely the same. An adversary can deliberately create these same disruptions, coordinate them across multiple locations and interfere with recovery. If a system can’t survive an accident, it won’t survive an adversary.”

Benny Czarny, CEO and Founder, OPSWAT:

“Faster patching can actually contribute to outages when testing and recovery cannot keep up. AI is increasing the pressure to fix vulnerabilities quickly, but you can’t attribute anything to AI without evidence from the investigation.

Failures this week have resulted from cloning systems and their weaknesses along with them. When a primary system and its backup run the same software, receive the same update, and depend on the same network, then they really aren’t that independent.

From a cybersecurity standpoint, critical infrastructure needs the same design mindset as an airplane cockpit, where primary and secondary systems use different hardware and software to reduce the chance that one defect disables every way of performing a critical function.”

Bryson Byrd, Cybersecurity Advisor, Huntress:

“Right now, there is no definitive link between these outages, and we should be careful about rushing to conclusions that AI or cyberattacks are responsible without having all the facts. What we do know is that there is a significant AI race going on between defenders and threat actors. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, defenders are under increasing pressure to engineer, test and push patches quickly to stay one step ahead. When companies are focused on speed of development, mistakes can happen. In the age of rapid patching, testing and verifying updates is arguably more important than ever.

My concern is that these outages will cause organizations to start dialing back patches out of fear of being the next Microsoft or FAA. We cannot afford to go back to a time when system administrators could wait several days before deploying critical security updates. The window between vulnerability discovery and potential exploitation is shrinking, and slowing down patches could leave organizations exposed to threats they already know about. So we cannot stop updates or sacrifice testing for speed. We need to double down on resilience and make sure organizations are prepared when an update doesn’t go as planned.

When it comes to critical patches and updates, there should always be a fallback plan in place, whether that’s a known, good backup or the last working code push that teams can quickly return to. We often see security teams with these plans documented, but the mechanisms haven’t actually been tested and verified to work. As infrastructure continues to evolve, these plans need to be tested regularly. Otherwise, when a bad update happens, organizations may not be prepared to respond, and a relatively contained issue can quickly grow into a much larger disruption.”

Grayson North, Principal Threat Intelligence Consultant, GuidePoint Security:

“This situation is a combination of increased media attention and a flurry of technical changes caused by AI’s rapid acceleration of vulnerability discovery. Outages are fairly common, but a few hours of downtime on a highly-visible system draws heightened attention. It can be compared to the DCA airline crash last year in a sense. After that incident, every near miss got national attention rather than being the usual footnote.

We are also clearly in a period of flux in regards to vulnerability discovery/patch management. AI has made discovery of vulnerabilities trivial for those willing to spend tokens. As such the pure number of vulnerabilities being reported is through the roof (thus the “Vulnpocalypse” that some have dubbed the moment). Some of these discoveries lead to big, scary cyberattacks, yes, but all of them lead to patches to fix the problem. Every time you make a change to a production system, you risk causing an unforeseen issue. This risk scales exponentially with the number of patches and number of underlying systems. There are questions of whether or not holiday code freezes are forcing organizations to hurry up and implement more changes than usual this time of year. Every organization handles its change windows differently but this could certainly be exacerbating the issue.

Optimistically I believe that the number of vulnerabilities that exist and are waiting to be discovered is finite, so (hopefully) we just have to wait for all the major organizations to shake out a few years of technical debt and we will return to relative normalcy. The “Patchpocalypse” to address the “Vulnpocalypse,” if you will.”

Patrick Harr, Chief Executive Officer, DataVisor:

“What stands out to me with these outages is the breadth. Banks, major technology companies, and government systems all experienced disruptions. Separate organizations can face the same pressure at the same time. When AI uncovers vulnerabilities faster than teams can test the fixes, systems that run reliably on an ordinary day can struggle with the pace of change. That’s a form of fragility we need to take seriously.

AI can find a flaw in minutes. It can take much longer to understand what happens to every service that depends on the software you’re about to change. Imagine a bank patches its sign-in system. The fix can close the security hole and pass its own tests, yet customers could still lose access if the mobile app can no longer authenticate them. That’s why I’d prioritize testing the whole customer journey and rolling the fix out in stages. Whether a particular organization missed a test is a question for its incident review.

Security teams need to change their monitoring, incident response and recovery plans. First, monitor what customers can actually do. Again, taking banks as an example, can customers sign in, see a balance, and complete a payment? Give the incident lead the authority to pause a rollout when those checks fail and rehearse how to restore service while keeping the vulnerable component isolated. Second, look across accounts for signs of coordination. One new account, one login, or one small transfer can look perfectly ordinary. When dozens of apparently unrelated accounts start moving money in the same sequence toward the same destinations, the pattern tells a different story.”

Chris Hughes, Vice President of Security Strategy, Noma Security:

“Artificial Intelligence (AI) has industrialized vulnerability discovery, organizations are racing to fix what’s being found, and the patching itself can disrupt operations. That’s the availability piece of the CIA triad. We’ve seen industrialized vulnerability discovery all year, in programs like Patch the Planet and Project Glasswing and in a steady stream of findings from frontier labs and researchers. Vulnerability trackers reported the 2026 CVE count passing 100,000 earlier this month, more than double last year and a record. That volume is outpacing the ability to patch and test safely, and when teams compress testing windows to keep up, they raise the risk of exactly these kinds of outages. The work that matters is risk-based prioritization around exploitability, known exploited vulnerabilities, and reachability, along with better testing, rollback plans, and resilience.

So, what technical indicators would support an AI-driven, coordinated attack as an explanation for these incidents? You’d want indicators that actually tie the incidents together: shared tooling or TTPs, artifacts consistent with autonomous offensive frameworks, and timing or targeting that can’t be explained by a common vendor, a maintenance window, or a shared patch cycle. Based on what’s public, we can’t say that’s what happened, and many of these disruptions have been described as planned maintenance or the result of accelerated patching. The coincidences are hard to ignore, which is why the speculation has taken off, but the better-supported story right now is accumulated technical debt and rushed remediation under the pressure of industrialized discovery. Organizations should still prepare for agentic offensive frameworks, even if this cluster isn’t ultimately attributed to them.”

Alex Orleans, Head of Threat Intelligence, Sublime Security:

“What I feel AI is more likely contributing to these outages is not patching speed or the discovery of vulnerabilities but code of dubious quality. As more and more development and engineering is devolved to vibe-coding, the internals of the resultant code are less and less understood by both the organizations deploying it and the engineers who maintain it. This makes crashes and outages more likely.

I would also say that across the outages we’ve seen, there hasn’t been a firmly identified shared type of cause (AI related or otherwise). Each outage should be taken on its own technical merits, not viewed as if there is some sort of unidentified overlap based on coincidental timing.”

Gerasimos Marketos, Chief Product Officer, Hack The Box:

“These incidents make security teams realize that attackers may use the same AI (used to discover the vulnerability x) to turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours. The answer is to give defenders and red teamers the same advantage.

A red team working with AI can show within hours which of a thousand flaws are actually exploitable in your environment, so only those few get the emergency treatment. A SOC working with AI can put detection and containment around a new flaw the same day, which buys the time to roll the patch out safely.”

Patrick Quirk, President, Opengear:

“We don’t have specifics on these incidents, and outages have many causes, so I’ll speak to the pattern. AI is accelerating how quickly vulnerabilities are found, which means patches are arriving faster, and that speed is an advantage only when every rollout is tested in a staging environment first. Skip that step or miss a key dependency and the fix becomes the failure.

Speed doesn’t change the question that matters on the day something breaks: can your team get back into the affected systems and start recovery? That’s where many organizations fall short. They manage and troubleshoot their infrastructure over the same production network that just went down, so when it fails, IT and security lose access to the very systems they need to restore. In a cyberattack that dependency is dangerous, because visibility and control are what contain the threat.

Design your infrastructure assuming it will fail and build an independent management path that stays reachable when the primary network does not. That gives your team a way to diagnose the problem, isolate affected systems, and begin recovery without relying on the infrastructure that failed.”

Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist, Sysdig:

“We swung the pendulum too far one way. For years, the security mantra was “patch faster.” Don’t get me wrong, that’s still the right approach. But many orgs have taken it to an extreme where the answer to every finding is “ship the fix, now, everywhere.” Pair that with a software delivery culture that already moves at breakneck speed, plus an AI-driven firehose of findings, and you get change volume that surpasses their ability (or desire?) to test and stage before deploying.

System fragility is the ultimate issue here. Systems are toppling over when you try to fix them because they were already broken. It’s like pulling the final brick in Jenga. These are architecture and infrastructure debts coming back to haunt us. AI-speed vulnerability discovery just delivered the bill to our doorstep.

Patching is prevention, and prevention is necessary, but it has a limit. What we’re seeing is what happens when you blow past that limit. So to bridge that gap while you fix your architecture, you need to turn to detection, which doesn’t have those limits.”
