Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Check Your Java Services Now
Context: Check Point IPS protection for the public PoC is available now, but patching is still the only complete fix
Full Text:
Bottom line: A single malformed Base64 string can give an attacker code execution on unpatched Java runtimes, often without logging in. Fixes were released on November 17, 2026. Inventory your Java runtimes, patch identity providers first, and use a startup flag where you cannot patch today. Check Point IPS protection for the public PoC is available now, but patching is still the only complete fix. Our full advisory has every detail.

What we see

The flaw: On recent Intel and AMD x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI, Java’s hand-tuned Base64 decoder miscalculates the output length for the padded tail of a short malformed input. The result is a write of 62 or 63 bytes past the end of its buffer, depending on the padding. Java rejects the input, but only after the write.

The impact: The bytes written are fixed, so on its own the overflow usually crashes Java. Calif, the firm that found the flaw, reports shaping server memory so the overflow enlarges a neighboring array, which gives read and write access and then code execution. It demonstrated this without authentication against default installations of Keycloak, self-managed Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login against Apache Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. The same corruption can also expose heap memory, including private keys, session tokens, and credentials, without any code execution.

Why login is often not needed: Applications decode Base64 before authentication, in HTTP Basic authentication headers, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and file uploads.

Side effects: Failed attempts often crash the Java process, and an attacker can often retry. Calif also reports that a Java client can be compromised by connecting over TLS to a malicious server.

Exploitation status (as of November 18, 2026):We are not aware of confirmed exploitation. However, the root cause is public, and a triggering input has been visible since September 9, 2026. Several independent teams have reproduced crashes and the memory leak in lab conditions, though not code execution as of November 18.

Important Note : There is no universal exploit, because each product needs its own memory layout and timing. That slows mass exploitation but does not protect a specific, high-value target such as an identity provider.

Are you affected?

A system is vulnerable only when all three conditions are true: an unpatched runtime, a specific processor, and attacker-controlled Base64 that reaches Java’s standard decoder.

Condition

Affected

Not affected

Java runtime

Unpatched OpenJDK-based builds from 17.0.6 onward on Java 17, and all Java 21, 25, and 27 builds before the fix, from any vendor. Oracle also lists its Java 8 performance build.

Java 17 releases before 17.0.6, standard Java 8 and Java 11, and fixed builds (Oracle: 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1)

Processor

x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI, including Intel Xeon Ice Lake through Granite Rapids and AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 and newer. The CPU must expose avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2

ARM64, and x86-64 processors without AVX-512 VBMI

Reachability

Attacker-controlled Base64 reaches Java’s standard decoder (login headers, tokens, uploads)

No path for external input to reach the standard Base64 decoder

How to check

Runtime: Build an inventory of the runtime each application actually uses. Bundled runtimes do not get OS updates, so check the one each application ships with.

Processor: Run the Linux command in the advisory. A host is affected only if avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2 all appear in its CPU flags (/proc/cpuinfo). Use the result to prioritize, not to dismiss a finding, because a cloud resize can silently move a workload onto an affected processor.

Reachability: This is the hardest to settle from the inside, because it depends on how each application is deployed and what sits in front of it.

What else is in scope

Self-managed Jira and Confluence: The risk applies to self-managed Data Center deployments. Atlassian manages the Java runtime for Atlassian Cloud. Atlassian installers typically ship their own bundled runtime, so operating system patches alone do not fix a self-managed instance.

Spring Boot: Treat every Spring Boot service on an affected runtime as in scope. Researchers reached code execution in sample Spring Boot applications, where login handling, tokens, and file uploads often decode Base64 before a user is authenticated.

Apache Tomcat: It was not tested and no advisory links it to this CVE. It runs a large share of Java web applications and is embedded in Spring Boot by default, so include every Tomcat server in your inventory.

Anything else: If you cannot rule out that attacker input reaches Java’s built-in Base64 decoder, assume it does. Vendor advisories cover only Java 17, 21, 25, and 27, so move any other release to a fixed build rather than assuming it is safe.

What to do: patch first

Updating the Java runtime is the only complete fix.

Fix availability (as of November 18, 2026)

Fixed builds shipped: Oracle, Amazon (Corretto), Azul (Zulu). For Oracle, only builds ending in .1 are patched.

Not yet released: Red Hat and Eclipse Temurin

Status unconfirmed: Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, BellSoft Liberica. Check each vendor’s page.

Bundled runtimes: Products that ship their own Java runtime need an update from the product vendor.

Patch in this order

Identity providers: Keycloak and PingFederate

Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and Artifactory (for Jira and Confluence, apply Atlassian’s update or the startup flag)

Other internet-facing Java services that handle logins, tokens, or uploads

Internal systems and Java clients

If you cannot patch today

Add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to the Java startup options and restart the service. This turns off only the accelerated Base64 decoder. Applications that decode large volumes of Base64 may slow down, so test first.

Alternatively, use -XX:UseAVX=2. It turns off AVX-512 entirely, at a broader performance cost. Java on ARM64 rejects this option and will not start.

Remove either option after you have patched.

Avoid: -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock on its own. It can stop Java from starting.

Verify: A patch or a flag takes effect only after Java restarts. Confirm on the running process:

jcmd <pid> VM.version

jcmd <pid> VM.flags

VM.version should show a fixed build. For Oracle that is a version ending in .1, such as 17.0.21.1, and other vendors use their own version strings. If you set the startup flag, VM.flags should list -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics.

Elasticsearch

Elasticsearch ships with a bundled Java runtime, and Calif demonstrated code execution against it after login. Some attacks depend on a request arriving in pieces, so a reverse proxy that waits for complete requests (nginx does by default) blocks those. This attack works in a single complete request, so request buffering does not stop it. Treat clusters with anonymous access or weak credentials as exposed without a login. Apply Elastic’s update, or add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics in a new .options file under config/jvm.options.d/ (/etc/elasticsearch/jvm.options.d/ for DEB and RPM installs) and restart each node. Do not edit the root jvm.options file.

Block known exploit attempts at the gateway

Check Point has released an IPS protection, [protection name / ID], that detects and blocks the public proof-of-concept for CVE-2026-114938. Make sure it is set to Prevent on your Quantum gateways, especially for traffic going to internet-facing Java services. This reduces exposure while you patch. It does not replace the runtime update, because it targets the known triggering input and not every possible variant

How to spot attempts

Failed attempts often crash Java, so watch for unexpected service restarts and new hs_err_pid<pid>.log files, which the JVM writes on a fatal crash. Crashes during garbage collection are also a known sign of this corruption. Then list every place where attacker-controlled Base64 reaches Java before login: HTTP Basic headers, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and file uploads.

Find the Java services you expose to the internet

Check Point Exposure Management can identify internet-facing assets that appear to run Java, including the version, so you know where to start. This is a passive check of technologies and versions. It does not exploit anything or send attack traffic to your services.

A technology check shows where Java is present. It cannot confirm the processor or whether attacker-controlled input reaches Java’s Base64 decoder, so use the results to prioritize and still run the runtime and processor checks above.

Beyond this flaw, Exposure Management helps you find, prioritize, validate, and fix the exposures that matter most across your environment:

Threat Intelligence: Know which threats and vulnerabilities attackers are targeting.

CAASM: Get a continuously updated view of your assets and where they are exposed.

Vulnerability Prioritization: Focus on the exposures with real risk, not the longest list.

Agentic Exposure Validation (AEV): Test whether an exposure is exploitable.

Safe Remediation: Fix confirmed exposures without disrupting the business.

Title: Hackers Exploiting Critical Puppet RCE Flaw Affecting Enterprise Management Servers
Context: "If the certificate authority automatically signs requests without strong verification, an unauthenticated network attacker can obtain a valid certificate and exploit the...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical security flaw impacting Perforce Puppet, an enterprise infrastructure-as-code (IaC) and configuration management platform, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing reports of active exploitation.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS score: 9.4), is a case of deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution.

"Perforce Puppet Enterprise contains a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Puppet's report-processing code that allows a client with any CA-signed agent certificate to execute arbitrary code on the Puppet Server as the service user by submitting a report containing a crafted rich-data type through a PUT request," CISA said.

"If the certificate authority automatically signs requests without strong verification, an unauthenticated network attacker can obtain a valid certificate and exploit the vulnerability."

The shortcoming impacts the following versions -

Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.0 before 2026.0.1

Puppet Enterprise 2025.0.0 before 2025.12.1

Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.0 before 2023.8.13

Puppet Core 9.0.0 before 9.1.3

Puppet Core 8.x before 8.22.2

It was addressed by Perforce Software on November 3, 2026, in the following versions -

Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1 (Puppet Core 9.1.3)

Puppet Enterprise 2025.12.1 (Puppet Core 8.22.2)

Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.13 (Puppet Core 8.22.2)

Puppet Core 9.1.3

Puppet Core 8.22.2

It's worth noting that the issue also affects OpenVox, an open-source implementation of Puppet, and has been resolved in the following versions -

OpenVox Agent 9.3.0 and 8.32.0

OpenVox Server 9.2.0 and 8.18.0

Alain Rödel, a security researcher at Neodyme AG, has been credited with discovering and reporting CVE-2026-115731 along with CVE-2026-115732 (CVSS score: 9.0), a critical certificate-name authorization bypass affecting both Puppet and OpenVox. The issues were discovered with artificial intelligence (AI) assistance and precise steering, the German cybersecurity company added.

"The impact highly depends on the Puppet server configuration and the orchestration protocols used, if any are enabled at all," Neodyme said in a report published this month. "Independent of the configuration, an attacker with RCE on a Puppet server can grab the CA signing keys and impersonate other hosts."

"Puppet is a powerful software, often with full access to a fleet of systems in a corporate network. Remote Code Execution on such a central and important system can lead to worst-case scenarios: Deployment of ransomware, mass data exfiltration, and potentially lateral movement to other parts of the network."

As of writing, there are no details on how the vulnerability is being weaponized in the wild. However, a Reddit user named transdimensia noted in a November 4 post that it was being exploited shortly after public disclosure.

"After finding a severely misconfigured CA in my fleet, I traced the actions backwards on a [CVE-2026-]115731 intrusion," the user said.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are advised to apply the fixes by December 1, 2026, to secure their networks under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

Title: CISA Urges Immediate Patching of Java4Shell Flaw That Could Allow Remote Code Execution
Context: "This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as 'Java4Shell,' affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged organizations to immediately patch a newly disclosed critical security flaw impacting Oracle Java.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS score: 8.1), refers to a case of out-of-bounds write that can lead to denial-of-service (DoS) or remote code execution under certain conditions.

"This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as 'Java4Shell,' affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK)," CISA said. "Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution."

Patches for the flaw have been released by Oracle and OpenJDK. As of writing, there is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.

As reported previously by The Hacker News, Java4Shell can enable attackers without an account to execute arbitrary code on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, under default settings.

Advisories for the flaw have been released by numerous security and software vendors, including Aikido, Amazon Linux, Blackpoint Cyber, Chainguard, Cisco Talos, Cycode, Datadog, Dynatrace, Endor Labs, Field Effect, Hadrian, Horizon3.ai, Miggo, Orca Security, Qualys, Rapid7, Red Hat, SentinelOne, Sophos, Tanium, Tenable, Upwind, VulnCheck, watchTowr, and Wiz.

In an update shared on November 18, 2026, the Keycloak team said an instance can be considered at risk if the following conditions apply -

It runs an unpatched OpenJDK build from 17.0.6 onward, including unpatched OpenJDK 21 and 25 builds

Its x86-64 host or virtual machine exposes the avx512vbmi CPU feature to Java

The running JVM has Base64 intrinsics enabled and has not been limited to AVX2 with -XX:UseAVX=2

"The x86-64 Keycloak container images tagged 26.8.2-1 and 26.8.2-2 bundle an affected OpenJDK 21.0.13 build," the team said. "These image tags alone do not establish whether your deployment is exploitable: check the CPU feature and effective JVM flags."

"A Keycloak ZIP or TAR.GZ distribution started directly on a host can also be affected; the conditions depend on its Java runtime and CPU, not on whether it runs in a container."

Keycloak is also recommending that users run the below command to check the CPU feature on a host or virtual machine -

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | grep -qw avx512vbmi && echo 'AVX-512 VBMI available'

If the output of the command returns nothing, it indicates that the CPU does not expose AVX-512 VBMI and is not known to be affected by the flaw. Keycloak has released temporary mitigations that users can apply until it releases updated Keycloak and Keycloak Operator container images once patched OpenJDK builds are available for them.

"The vulnerability could be reached through a local Spring Boot application using Spring Security," Blackpoint Cyber researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal said.

"In this environment, approximately 28,000 unauthenticated HTTP requests carrying a malformed Base64 authentication value caused the JVM to terminate after roughly 20 seconds of sustained requests. Additional testing confirmed corruption of nearby Java objects and changes to live application data without necessarily causing an immediate crash."

CISA is recommending that organizations take the following steps -

Identify affected Java installations.

Review software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances.

Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available.

"If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access," CISA said.

Title: Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps
Context: ” Talos’s analysis of Java4Shell includes the interesting observation that it “has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet
Full Text: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November, which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products. Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938, which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning. The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes. By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE. Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw, says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.” “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:” Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10. Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.” “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.” Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised. Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled. Akamai’s Chief Information Security Architect Jan Schaumann, writing on the Openwall project’s mailing list, expressed a little discomfort with Calif’s work. “Calif.io set their priorities on publicity-maxxing, it seems,” he wrote, pointing out that the flaw-finding firm’s announcement of Java4Shell opens by stating “After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.” Talos’s analysis of Java4Shell includes the interesting observation that it “has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.” That second sentence perhaps supports Calif’s assertion that news of the flaw leaked before disclosure. The rest of Big Red’s flaws Java4Shell deserves a place high up on patch priority lists. So do the six 10.10 flaws Oracle reported, three in its Access Manager product, one in the Oracle Platform Security for Java, another in the WebLogic Server, and one in Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition. Big Red also repaired five 9.9-rated bugs, in Oracle Text, Hyperion, RDBMS, and Autovue. The November patch dump also includes 28 flaws rated 9.8/10. By Tenable Security’s count, 249 of the patches are for high severity bugs. Oracle’s Hyperion enterprise performance management accounts for 267 of the bugs. Such is life in the age of AI-powered flaw finders – which Calif says burned through just $200 worth of tokens to find Java4Shell. ®

Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Frequently asked questions about OpenJDK remote code execution vulnerability
Context: Later that day, Oracle released its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU), and the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group published its own advisory
Full Text:
Java4Shell is a flaw in how Java decodes Base64 data. Calif, which found it, says it can let attackers run code on widely used Java applications without logging in. Oracle released fixed Java builds on November 17, and Calif is withholding its exploits for individual applications for now.

Key takeaways

CVE-2026-114938, dubbed Java4Shell, is an OpenJDK memory corruption vulnerability that Oracle scores 8.1 on CVSS 3.1, and Calif says its testing showed attackers could run code without logging in on applications such as Atlassian Jira and Jenkins.

As of November 17, Tenable is not aware of any reports that attackers have exploited this flaw, though Calif has published a PoC that triggers the bug without taking control of the system and a second researcher reports building a working exploit.

Oracle released fixed builds on November 17, and according to Calif, only systems running an affected Java version on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI can be affected.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Java4Shell, a vulnerability in OpenJDK that was patched on November 17, 2026.

FAQ

When was Java4Shell first disclosed?

On November 17, security firm Calif said on X that it had found and reported the flaw, and that details of Java4Shell, as Calif named it, had leaked ahead of a fix. Later that day, Oracle released its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU), and the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group published its own advisory. Calif then published its technical write-up. Oracle credits Quang Luong of Calif.io and Albert Yang for reporting the vulnerability.

Since the vulnerability has leaked: Calif discovered and reported Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938).We're publishing technical details by 1 PM Pacific today, after Oracle releases a patch.Stay tuned! https://t.co/No5hJXK1Zx

— Calif (@calif_io) November 17, 2026

What is CVE-2026-114938?

CVE

Description

CVSSv3.1

CVE-2026-114938

OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Memory Corruption Vulnerability (Java4Shell)

8.1

CVE-2026-114938 is a memory corruption vulnerability in the part of Java that decodes Base64, a common format that applications use to send data such as login details and file uploads. Oracle assigned it a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 and rates its attack complexity as high. Calif says it scores 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. An attacker does not need to log in to exploit it remotely. According to Oracle, the flaw can only be exploited when an application passes untrusted data to the affected Java APIs, such as through a web service.

Is CVE-2026-114938 among the Java fixes in Oracle's November 2026 CSPU?

Yes. CVE-2026-114938 is addressed by one of the 11 Java SE security patches in Oracle's November 2026 CSPU, released November 17. For a breakdown of all the patches in this release, see our blog post on Oracle's November 2026 CSPU.

What is known about CVE-2026-114938?

The flaw is in a performance shortcut that Java uses to decode Base64 data faster on certain Intel and AMD processors. When the shortcut receives a specially crafted Base64 string, it writes data beyond the memory it set aside. That can corrupt other information the application is holding in memory.

According to Calif, an attacker can use this flaw in two ways. The first, which Calif calls "JavaBleed," lets an attacker read the application's memory. That memory may hold secrets such as keys and tokens. The second lets an attacker run their own code on the server. Calif also says that each application needs its own exploit, and that a failed attempt can crash the application, though an attacker can often try again.

Exposure depends on the processor as well as the Java version. According to Calif, Java uses the affected code only on x86-64 processors that support a feature called AVX-512 VBMI. These include Intel Xeon processors from the Granite Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Sapphire Rapids and Ice Lake families, as well as AMD processors based on Zen 4 or newer. Calif says systems with ARM64 processors are not affected. On Linux, a system meets this requirement when its processor reports all four of the avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2 flags.

Which versions of Java are affected?

The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group lists the Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 release lines as affected by CVE-2026-114938. Calif says OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer are affected. Oracle lists the following Oracle builds as affected:

Oracle lists only builds it supports and says earlier versions are likely also affected. The Java 8 build on Oracle's list is its Enterprise Performance Pack. The OpenJDK advisory does not list standard Java 8 or Java 11 as affected by this vulnerability.

I don't use Oracle's Java builds. Am I affected?

Possibly. The flaw is in OpenJDK code, and according to Calif, the following Java distributions built from OpenJDK are also vulnerable:

Each vendor releases fixed builds on its own schedule, so check with your distribution's vendor for its fixed versions.

Which applications are known to be affected?

Calif says its initial testing showed that an attacker could run their own code on the following applications in their default configurations, when they run on an affected version of Java on a processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI. The list is not exhaustive, according to Calif.

Calif also said it ran its own code on sample applications built on frameworks including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Calif adds that everyday functions, including authentication and file uploads, can lead to the vulnerable code, so more applications than the ones Calif tested may be exposed. Calif says researcher samczsun gave it a client-side exploit, and that a Java program can be compromised when it connects over TLS to a server an attacker controls, even if the program offers no service of its own. Calif says it will publish its exploits for individual products at a later date.

Has Java4Shell been exploited in the wild?

As of November 17, we are not aware of any reports of exploitation of CVE-2026-114938, and it is not listed in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Yes. Calif published a PoC alongside its write-up that triggers the flaw without taking control of the system. It shows whether a given Java version and processor reproduce the bug. It does not show whether a particular application is exposed.

On November 17, Kevin Breen of Immersive said on X that they had developed a working exploit for CVE-2026-114938. According to Breen, the exploit has to be adapted to each application. It works only on a vulnerable version of Java running on a processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, and only against applications that decode Base64 data. Breen also said that Apache Tomcat's Basic authentication and the java-jwt library provide ways to exploit the flaw before a user logs in. The post does not say that the exploit has been released.

Are there any mitigations?

Calif identified two Java startup options that keep the vulnerable code from running. The first, -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, turns off the Base64 shortcut. The second, -XX:UseAVX=2, turns off AVX-512 instructions. According to Calif, the second option applies only to x86-64 systems, and Java on ARM processors fails to start with it. Neither Oracle nor the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group mentions these options in its advisory.

Yes. CISA's KEV catalog includes 13 vulnerabilities in Oracle Java SE and the Java Runtime Environment (JRE), six of which are known to have been used in ransomware campaigns. Those six are:

Yes. CVE-2026-114938 has been classified as a "Vulnerability of Interest" as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Are Tenable products affected by this vulnerability?

Tenable is aware of this vulnerability and is investigating whether it affects any Tenable products.

Title: CVE-2026-114938: Critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java
Context: This vulnerability does require a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI; these include commonly deployed processors from both Intel and AMD, resulting in a...
Full Text:
Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java (CVE-2026-114938), dubbed “Java4Shell,” with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 that may lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). This vulnerability can be triggered by sending a malformed Base64 input to affected JVMs, which can result in RCE.

Details

This vulnerability affects OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed.

This vulnerability does require a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI; these include commonly deployed processors from both Intel and AMD, resulting in a large potential attack surface of vulnerable systems, including both on-premise and cloud environments.

Cisco Talos would like to thank Calif.io for sharing the details of the vulnerability in advance of public disclosure.

Observed exploitation

Talos has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure. Talos will continue to monitor for exploitation attempts and will provide updates accordingly.

Recommendations and guidance

Talos recommends applying the software update for this vulnerability. If immediate patching is not possible, other mitigations can be implemented in the interim. The primary mitigation is starting the JVM with AVX-512 support disabled. This can be done by starting the application with “=XX:UseAVX=2”. Note that this is only applicable for x86-64 systems, as ARM-based processors will not recognize the command, likely resulting in failure to start.

Cisco is following its well-established process to evaluate its products and will provide updates shortly. Customers should reach out to their sales teams with specific questions

Coverage

Snort3: 1:301754, 1:67502 - 1:67513

These rules detect malformed base64 data in specific HTTP request fields associated with the vulnerability. This vulnerability is implementation specific. Title: Patches released for critical ‘NGINX2Root’ vulnerabilities
Context: Sophos countermeasures SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this vulnerability and will deliver detections and protections as available
Full Text:
On November 18, 2026, F5 published security advisories for five critical (CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2) vulnerabilities that Xint has collectively dubbed ‘NGINX2Root’: (K000163925, K000163926, K000163927, K000163928, and K000163931). The issues affect NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus configurations. Exploitation could lead to crashes, denial of service, memory corruption, or code execution. According to F5, code execution requires ASLR to be disabled or bypassed.

Two of the vulnerabilities relate to NGINX HTTP/2 handling, and Wiz Research reports that they can be used to bypass Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR):

CVE-2026-123007 is an integer underflow issue in HTTP/2 flow control

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free issue affecting HTTP/2 connections that are proxied to a backend

The other three issues are use-after-free flaws that require specific configurations:

CVE-2026-123634 affects the NGINX resolver in some NGINX Open Source versions when NGINX proxies to a server name that contains variables and an SSI or mirror directive sends a subrequest that resolves the same name

CVE-2026-121810 affects HTTP/3 configurations in some NGINX Open Source versions

CVE-2026-113425 affects some NGINX Open Source versions when configured as a mail proxy server

Xint reports that each vulnerability can be chained with a separate Linux kernel SCTP vulnerability to obtain root privileges on the host, including when NGINX runs in a Docker container.

Recommended actions

Organizations should review the F5 advisories and upgrade vulnerable versions as appropriate. Updated source code and Linux packages for NGINX Open Source are also available from the NGINX website. Packages may not be immediately available for older, unsupported distributions. Xint notes that nginx -s reload does not load the new binary, so NGINX must be restarted or its binary upgraded after updating. If immediate upgrades are not possible, F5 advises avoiding SSI or mirror directives and proxied server names with variables (CVE-2026-123634), and restricting mail proxy listeners to trusted networks (CVE-2026-113425). For the HTTP/2 flaws, Wiz and Xint recommend disabling HTTP/2 on affected listeners but note that there may be implications for that action.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this vulnerability and will deliver detections and protections as available.

An internal investigation is also underway to determine if Sophos products or services are affected.

Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Pre-auth RCE in OpenJDK, and the challenge of image and feature bloat
Context: Calif, the firm that discovered the vulnerability, says that with 64 A characters and one =, a remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, leak it Heartbleed-...
Full Text:
DISCLAIMER: This blog reflects public findings as of 1:36 UTC, Nov. 18, 2026, and it will be updated as new information is released.

Java promised that users would never have to think about memory again. Java's Base64 decoder, however, had other plans.

On November 17, 2026, Oracle and OpenJDK shipped fixes for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a heap memory corruption bug in the AVX-512 accelerated Base64 decoder. Calif, the firm that discovered the vulnerability, says that with 64 A characters and one =, a remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, leak it Heartbleed-style, and in the products they tested, get remote code execution (RCE).

Calif made a suggestion that Java4Shell’s Base64 optimization and the Squidbleed flaw that they also discovered are calls for vibe-uncoding, or the use of AI to find and remove system bloat to reduce an attack surface. This is the same point that’s been made in multiple Sysdig Cloud Native Security and Usage Reports since 2023 with regard to image bloat.

Let’s explore what's confirmed, what's still theoretical, and why after combating and cleaning up image bloat for years, the next fight appears to be feature bloat.

Important facts to know now about Java4Shell

What: Heap out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. Pre-authentication on common login paths.

Who: OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later (17, 21, 25, 27) on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI. ARM is out. Java 11 and standard Java 8 are out. Oracle also lists the Java 8 performance build (8u511b33-perf) as vulnerable.

Severity: 9.2 critical on CVSS 4.0 per Calif, and 8.1 on CVSS 3.1 per OpenJDK's advisory.

Exploitation: Calif confirms working RCE in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate without authorization, plus five more post-auth. The researcher says OpenAI Codex helped find the bug in an hour and build an exploit in two hours for less than $200. Calif stated the exploit will not be publicly shared until organizations have patched the vulnerability.

Fix: Oracle builds ending in .1, or -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as the bridge.

What happened

Time

Event

Nov 12

Oracle's pre-release notice: 11 Java SE fixes, all remotely exploitable without authentication, max CVSS 3.1 of 8.1. No CVE IDs.

Nov 17

Calif says the bug leaked ahead of the patch and moves its disclosure to 1 p.m. PT (21:00). Confirmed discussions about the report appear on X as early as 10:22.

Nov 17, 17:44 UTC

OpenJDK's advisory lists CVE-2026-114938 as hotspot/compiler, affecting 17, 21, 25, and 27.

Nov 17, 17:53 UTC

CISA KEV catalog is released. CVE not included.

Nov 17, 20:00 UTC

A lab reproduction of the overflow is published and says RCE isn't proven.

Nov 17, 21:00 UTC

Calif publishes its write-up, with RCE demos across named products.

Who's affected by Java4Shell

Calif's list of vulnerable builds is broad because everything downstream of OpenJDK inherits the code: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE, and Oracle GraalVM for JDK.

For non-Oracle distributions, researchers said the Temurin, Corretto, and Zulu fixes were still pending at 20:00 UTC. To determine if your organization is affected, check with your vendor.

The hardware filter may be a silver lining for some organizations. The vulnerable code only runs on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. Use Calif's check to see if your Linux hosts are vulnerable:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

All four flags must show up. Then run java -version inside the container, not on the host. Your host's JDK is not your container's JDK, and your container's JDK is the one that matters.

How Java4Shell works

Per Calif's write-up, HotSpot's C2 compiler uses AVX-512 intrinsics to decode Base64 fast. The hand-rolled assembly that handles the padded tail miscalculates the output length for certain inputs, ending up with -1, which turns the write mask fully open. The result is that 64 bytes get written where two were expected, and 62 of them land past the end of the output array. Java then notices the input is bad and throws an exception, but the write already happened.

The trigger is 64 A characters followed by = (128 A plus = on Java 17). The decoder has to be JIT-compiled first, which means warm-up traffic. The overflowing bytes are fixed, so an attacker picks where the write lands, not what it writes.

That sounded like a dead end to some researchers, whose lab tests found that a typical token wasn’t able to corrupt anything, leading them to the early assumption that RCE was yet to be proven, but not impossible. However, Calif found the way around it: a classic heap grooming move borrowed from JavaScript engine exploitation. Use the fixed write to overwrite a neighboring array's length, and now you have a buffer that accepts chosen bytes. Do it again to get a reader; writer plus reader gives you a heap leak and a path to code execution.

What's reachable before login

Researchers found that standard Basic auth handling in Spring Security, Tomcat, and Jetty 12 passes the raw token to Base64.getDecoder() before validating it. Auth0's java-jwt decodes JWT headers and payloads the same way before checking the signature.

Calif adds that ordinary features like file uploads can expose the decoder too, and that samczsun contributed a client-side exploit: A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised even if it exposes no service. Ultimately, that means that your login page is likely the attack surface.

What's been demonstrated vs. what’s been claimed

Demonstrated by researchers:

Calif reports RCE in default configurations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate (pre-auth), and Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker (post-auth). It also reports RCE in sample Struts and Spring Boot applications and publishes a demo video.

Theori and other firms have independently reproduced the overflow itself.

Calif says discovery took one hour, the first working exploit took two more, and the total token cost was under $200.

Constraints:

There is no universal exploit. Each target needs its own profile: a decoder route, a live writer, a feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action.

Wrong heap placement can crash the JVM. Calif says in many cases it can just retry.

The attack is sensitive to network latency. Calif's fix for that was renting a VM in the same region as the target.

Some chains need partial request bodies to reach the application. Request buffering (which nginx does by default) breaks those chains but isn't a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from a single complete request, and WebSocket tunnels bypass buffering.

What's public so far:

Calif published a self-contained Java program that warms the decoder and reproduces the 62-byte overwrite inside a bounded array.

Calif says it is holding back the weaponized, product-specific chains "until everyone has had a chance to upgrade," and will publish them later.

As of 21:10 UTC, GitHub repositories for the CVE ID were a placeholder README, Theori's mitigation tool, and a BigFix scanner. No exploit code. A search for java4shell exploit returned nothing. So far, researchers have shared a public trigger, a documented technique, named targets, and a promise of more to come. Leaked bugs often attract fake exploits, as researchers have already warned. So if a repo promises a shell, read it before you run it, and run it in a sandbox.

Reigning in image bloat

Calif closes its write-up with what it calls vibe-uncoding: If you don't need something, stop running it. They explicitly point to Base64 optimization as an example. It helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data and ships to everyone else too, and so "an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk."

As a cybersecurity strategist, this is a soapbox I’ve been on for about three years. Our annual cloud-native security and usage reports have continually made the same case: The unused packages that ride along with open source images do nothing for your use case and everything for an attacker's. The 2025 report specifically called for shrinking image bloat through consolidation, smart application building, and discovering shadow AI and other shadow IT.

And then organizations actually did it, and I’d like to think they used AI to do so, just as Calif suggests. In the 2026 Cloud-Native Security and Usage Report, we analyzed nearly 13 billion packages for image bloat. Less than one percent of packages in images were unused, a 50% reduction year over year. Teams matured their CI/CD pipelines and moved to leaner images, which in turn shrinks the attack surface. And, as a bonus, it makes images build, scan, and pull faster and cost less to store. Fewer packages means fewer surprises, faster patching, and clearer ownership.

That’s a win. Image bloat will probably never hit 0%, but it’s a material reduction that came from boring, disciplined work.

Here's the catch, and the real lesson of Java4Shell: The cleanup got the unused packages, but it didn't touch the unused code inside the packages you do use. Nobody's image scan flags a hand-rolled AVX-512 Base64 stub sitting inside java.base, because Java is in use, Base64 is in use, and the optimization is part of the thing. Package-level bloat is mostly handled. Feature-level bloat is the next frontier, and it lives upstream, in runtimes and libraries that ship everything to everybody.

Calif's answer is to point AI at that problem too: Find the dead code and needless optimizations, then remove them. I think this question of "What can we delete?" is the right one, aimed one layer deeper than most of us have been looking.

But slimming your images will not stop this specific bug. The vulnerable code is in the JDK itself, in the thing you actually use. Two things do apply, however:

The flag is vibe-uncoding at runtime. -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics turns off a feature you probably didn't need. That mitigation works because most workloads never notice.

Blast radius is a real control. If an attacker lands code execution in a minimal image with no shell, no package manager, no curl, and no compiler, they have a much worse afternoon than in an image with everything. Leftover tooling doesn't cause the bug, but it's the toolkit the attacker finds afterward.

And there’s another important lesson CISOs can learn from this: Calif's researcher found this by prompting Codex over an audit of the JIT compiler, intrinsics, and crypto and in the researcher's own words, "ignoring slops for around 20 minutes." Discovery to working exploit in three hours. That’s the new math for defenders. If your patch cycle is measured in weeks and the other side's exploit cycle is measured in an afternoon, you’ve lost the race.

That is the same theme running through our 2026 report and other Sysdig threat research identified throughout the year: shifting from manual effort to machine-speed defense, with runtime detection as the signal teams trust most.

How to detect Java4Shell

This exploit leaves almost nothing at the application layer. The server answers 401 and moves on. Defenders should look for the shape, noise, and aftermath of an attack.

Request shape: Flag Base64-alphabet tokens of 32 or more characters that end in = and whose length isn't a multiple of 4. Valid padded Base64 is always a multiple of 4. Start with Authorization headers.

Application logs: Researchers saw IllegalArgumentException: Input byte array has wrong 4-byte ending unit on every attempt in their tests.

Retry and warm-up behavior: Calif's chain warms the decoder with valid decodes, then triggers, and retries on bad placement. That implies bursts of requests from one source, repeated malformed tokens, and potentially many half-sent request bodies held open and released together. However, this has not been observed in the wild as of this publication.

JVM crashes: Wrong placement means crashes: SIGSEGV, hs_err_pid*.log files, and bursts of worker restarts.

Post-exploitation: If the chain lands, the aftermath looks like any other Java compromise: the JVM spawning a shell, dropping and executing a binary, or opening connections it never opened before.

What defenders can do to get ahead of Java4shell today

Patch Oracle JDK immediately. 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1, and 8u513 for the performance build.

Linux users don’t have to self-patch: Java installed from your Linux distribution's package manager gets fixed through the distribution's normal update channel, but only after the distro ships a fix and only on hosts that apply updates. Containers and vendor JDK builds don’t update themselves. Rebuild and redeploy.

Inventory everything else. Check Temurin, Corretto, Zulu, Microsoft, and distribution builds against your vendor's advisory. Several were pending as of this publication.

Prioritize by exposure and hardware. Internet-facing services on AVX-512 VBMI instances, especially anything using Basic auth, java-jwt, or the products on Calif's list, go first.

Mitigate with a JVM flag if you can’t patch yet. -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics stopped the overflow on every affected version Upwind tested. -XX:UseAVX=2 also works but turns off all AVX-512 paths and fails to start on ARM hosts, so apply it to x86-64 only. Both need a restart.

Make sure you use the right flag, or you may break something. -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock fails without -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions. Pushed fleet-wide through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, that's an outage you caused yourself.

Think hard before running someone's runtime patch. Some proposed tools attach an agent to live JVMs without a restart, distributed via curl | sh with pinned certificates and hash checks, which attaches code to production. Read it, test it, schedule it, and expect a temporary throughput dip.

Hunt backward. Search Authorization headers and application logs for the shapes above, and check for hs_err_pid files and unexplained restarts since before today.

Keep deleting, and go a layer deeper. Unused packages are down to under one percent of what's in images, so keep that discipline. Then ask what feature, shell, or optimization you could turn off inside the things you do use.

Conclusion

Java4Shell is the third entry in a pattern defenders should have memorized by now: a widely deployed platform, a bug in the low-level code underneath the safe layer, and a researcher with an AI assistant who went from audit to exploit in a few hours. The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) has been tracking the same theme across vulnerabilities like PHP2Shell, Node2Shell, and the Apache HTTP Server mod_http2 bug. The names may change (slightly), but the story remains familiar.

The next iteration may look like a library or runtime a team forgot was in its stack, hit through a field they didn’t know was parsed before auth. The defenses that hold up are the basic ones we know all too well: Know what you run, patch what's exposed first, run less of what you don’t need, and watch what it does at runtime so you aren't relying on the exploit having the courtesy to announce itself early.

Memory safety comes with an asterisk that is often written in assembly. Teams have cleaned up the packages, and now it’s time to pare down the features.

Title: Google and Anthropic push for faster patches as AI collapses bug discovery timelines
Context: In a report published this week, Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) documented the first fully automated AI-powered vulnerability discovery-and-exploitation pipeline it...
Full Text:
AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has made it untenable for software vendors to sit on privately reported flaws for months, and Google Project Zero is responding by shrinking its vulnerability disclosure deadline from 90 to 60 days, with plans to drop it to 30 days a year from now. Anthropic is following suit with an even more aggressive timeline.

Project Zero is Google’s elite vulnerability research team that regularly reports vulnerabilities in widely used open-source and proprietary software, much of which is critical to internet infrastructure. Its 90-day deadline for vendors to produce patches before the team releases vulnerability details publicly was a major stake in the ground for the security research community when it was announced in 2014, and it has become the de facto standard for coordinated disclosure.

The team’s announcement Friday that it will reduce this deadline to 60 days starting in February and 30 days starting in January 2028 is important because when Project Zero speaks, the security industry listens. And it did. On Monday, Anthropic announced it will adjust its disclosure policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, starting in January. Other security companies and researchers will likely follow.

The rationale is explicitly due to the offensive cyber capabilities of large language models: not only in discovering new vulnerabilities, but in reverse engineering patches and using them as blueprints for finding additional flaws in the same code.

“LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug,” Project Zero researcher Natalie Silvanovich said in a blog post. “A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.”

Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team said essentially the same: “A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can, and these changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.”

‘Soak time’ has become meaningless

Since 2021, Project Zero’s policy has actually been “90+30” with 90 days to develop a patch, plus 30 days of grace while the patch rolled out to users. The team referred to these extra 30 days as “soak time.”

But in a world where AI agents can analyze patches to determine flaw details in minutes and then write exploits for them, waiting for a patch to propagate before releasing vulnerability details only creates a false sense of secrecy. As a result, the Project Zero’s previous 30-day grace is gone effective immediately.

In a report published this week, Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) documented the first fully automated AI-powered vulnerability discovery-and-exploitation pipeline it has observed in the wild. Called exploit_agent, the framework is designed to analyze application code changes following security patches, identify vulnerabilities, and generate exploits without requiring an operator to direct each step.

While Anthropic has different deadlines based on vulnerability severity, Project Zero decided to abandon severity as a disclosure metric because attackers are just as likely to discover low-risk flaws as they are to find the high-risk ones.

“When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances,” Project Zero’s Silvanovich said. “But this doesn’t change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality.”

Google’s team will also no longer check whether a vendor’s patch fixes the issue when deciding whether to release details or not, because this back-and-forth can quickly become unmanageable, especially because the team now finds vulnerabilities using AI assistance at a much faster pace and because vendors might choose alternative mitigation strategies such as temporarily disabling a vulnerable feature or code path until a full patch can be developed.

“We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly,” Silvanovich said.

The road ahead will be bumpy for users

The shorter patch deadlines come at a time when open-source projects and software vendors are already drowning in vulnerability reports and must resort to either AI-assisted patching or hiring more developers, if they can afford it. As of last week, the number of CVEs issued this year exceeded 100,000, more than double last year’s count.

Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team noted that “models can now help develop fixes” as one justification for the more aggressive disclosure deadlines, and said it will include “actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible,” to help maintainers confirm flaws and fix them.

However, multiple studies and developers have reported in recent months that AI-generated patches are often incomplete, failing to address the root causes of a flaw, to eliminate all instances of the bug from the codebase, or to block all exploit variations.

Security firm XOR built a benchmark that pitted frontier coding systems against vulnerabilities the company had discovered in a private software stack. No public fix existed for any of the flaws when the evaluation ran, so the systems had to work from the vulnerable code alone. The best models produced complete fixes for only about a third of the flaws: 35.3% for GPT-6 Astra and 28.6% for Claude Fable 5.1. Across all systems, just 11.9% of patch attempts earned full credit.

According to an analysis by VulnCheck, seven months after launching its Mythos-powered Glasswing vulnerability-hunting program, Anthropic’s public ledger counts 37,966 findings, but only 217 of the 7,349 flaws made public so far have been fixed.

Project Zero acknowledges the friction between the need to patch faster and devs being overloaded. The team solicited feedback from the vendors it reports to most and chose the phased schedule because an immediate change could push vendors to stop trying to meet the disclosure deadlines.

“To respond to these new timelines, organizations should be better prepared to assess whether compensating controls can reduce the risk of a vulnerability when it’s disclosed,” Ramy Rahman, senior principal solutions engineer at ArmorCode, tells CSO. “With disclosures arriving sooner, and sometimes before a fix is available, teams need a process for evaluating exposure, applying available mitigations, and tracking remediation.”

“Consider hardening systems at deployment time and removing software you don’t use,” he said. “Leaner, more deliberate deployments can reduce exposure and make vulnerability findings easier to manage.”

Title: Java4Shell Vulnerability: How Should Security Teams Identify and Reduce Exposure?
Context: Even after CVE-2026-114938 becomes available in Aquasec vulnerability feeds, detection coverage may vary depending on the Java distribution and package format
Full Text:
TL;DR: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a high severity vulnerability affecting the OpenJDK HotSpot compiler, with a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1. The published advisory identifies Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 release lines as affected, although exact vulnerable versions vary by distributor. Security teams should identify affected Java installations, prioritize production workloads and apply available security updates.

Aquasec expects CVE-2026-114938 to be available in its vulnerability feeds around 04:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Online CyberCenter) and 07:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Offline CyberCenter), after which customers can use native vulnerability scanning and Image Assurance Policies to identify images with matching findings.

What is the Java4Shell vulnerability?

Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a vulnerability in the OpenJDK HotSpot compiler, a component of the Java runtime responsible for compiling Java bytecode into native machine code during application execution.

The vulnerability carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1 (High) and affects multiple supported OpenJDK release lines.

According to the published OpenJDK advisory, the following Java release lines are affected:

Java release line

Status

Java 17

Affected

Java 21

Affected

Java 25

Affected

Java 27

Affected

The exact affected and fixed builds depend on the Java distributor. Organizations should consult their distributor’s security advisory to determine whether their installed Java version is vulnerable and which update resolves the issue.

Why does Java4Shell matter to cloud native environments?

Java is widely used in enterprise applications, including services deployed in containers and Kubernetes environments. A vulnerability affecting the Java runtime can therefore create exposure across multiple applications even when their underlying application code has not changed.

In containerized environments, Java installations are frequently packaged directly into application images. Updating Java on the underlying host does not necessarily update the version embedded within those images. Organizations may need to rebuild and redeploy applications to remove vulnerable versions from production.

This creates an immediate challenge for security teams. They need to identify which container images contain affected Java versions, determine where those images are deployed and prioritize remediation based on the applications and services potentially exposed.

Why is vulnerability scanning alone insufficient to address Java4Shell?

Vulnerability scanning is essential for identifying affected Java installations, but its effectiveness depends on the availability and accuracy of vulnerability intelligence.

When a vulnerability is newly disclosed, there may be a delay before it becomes available in vulnerability feeds. During that period, a scan may not report the newly disclosed CVE even when an image contains an affected software version.

This is particularly relevant to Java4Shell because Aquasec expects CVE-2026-114938 to become available in its vulnerability feeds around 04:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Online CyberCenter) and 07:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Offline CyberCenter).

Security teams should therefore avoid treating the absence of a CVE finding as confirmation that an image is unaffected. Reviewing installed Java versions against distributor advisories remains important, particularly while vulnerability content is being updated.

Once the updated vulnerability information becomes available, organizations should rescan relevant images to identify matching findings and support remediation.

What does an effective Java4Shell response look like?

An effective response begins with identifying affected Java installations across container images and deployed applications.

Security teams should review the Java distributions and versions used throughout their environments, paying particular attention to images supporting internet facing or business critical applications.

Once affected images have been identified, organizations should update Java to the fixed version recommended by their distributor, rebuild the affected images and redeploy the corrected applications.

Teams should then rescan the updated images to confirm that the vulnerability finding has been resolved. This verification step is particularly important in containerized environments where older images may remain available in registries or continue to be deployed across multiple services.

How is Aquasec addressing Java4Shell?

Aquasec is updating its vulnerability feeds to include CVE-2026-114938, with availability expected around 04:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Online CyberCenter) and 07:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Offline CyberCenter).

Once the updated vulnerability content is available, customers can use native vulnerability scanning and Image Assurance Policies to identify container images with a matching CVE finding.

Customers can configure an Image Assurance Policy to evaluate images against CVE-2026-114938 using the built in CVEs Blocked control. A custom Rego check is not required for this workflow.

After the vulnerability content becomes available, customers should rescan relevant images, particularly those scanned before the update. They can then use Image Inventory to review images that failed the relevant policy and examine the associated vulnerability details, Java package and version, registry information and deployed workloads.

For customers using Image Assurance Policies for investigation, policy enforcement and CI/CD actions should be reviewed to avoid unintentionally blocking deployments or failing pipelines.

For detailed instructions, see the Aquasec Knowledge Base article on identifying affected Java4Shell images.

What should security teams know about Java4Shell detection results?

Even after CVE-2026-114938 becomes available in Aquasec vulnerability feeds, detection coverage may vary depending on the Java distribution and package format. A missing finding does not necessarily mean an image is unaffected. Organizations should verify their Java vendor and installed version against the appropriate security advisory, particularly when investigating images they believe may contain vulnerable software.

Similarly, an Image Assurance Policy failure does not automatically mean Java4Shell was detected. If the policy includes multiple controls, teams should review the specific failed check to confirm that CVE-2026-114938 triggered the result.

If a known affected image is not detected after the vulnerability content becomes available, customers should contact Aquasec Support for further investigation.

What should organizations do now to address Java4Shell?

Organizations should prioritize the following actions:

Identify affected Java installations. Review container images and deployed applications for Java 17, 21, 25 and 27, confirming the exact affected versions against the relevant distributor advisory.

Prioritize production exposure. Focus first on affected images supporting internet facing or business critical applications.

Apply available security updates. Update Java to the fixed version recommended by the distributor, then rebuild and redeploy affected container images.

Rescan when updated vulnerability content is available. Aquasec expects CVE-2026-114938 to be available in its vulnerability feeds around 04:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Online CyberCenter) and 07:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Offline CyberCenter).

Verify remediation. Confirm that corrected images are deployed and that the vulnerability finding has been resolved.

Once CVE-2026-114938 is available in Aqua’s vulnerability feeds, Aquasec customers can use native vulnerability scanning and Image Assurance Policies to identify affected images and verify remediation. Customers who believe a known affected image is not being detected should contact the Aquasec Support Portal for assistance.

Java4Shell reinforces the importance of maintaining accurate software inventories and responding quickly when new vulnerabilities are disclosed. While updated vulnerability intelligence supports more efficient identification, organizations should not delay reviewing affected Java versions or applying available security updates.

What is CVE-2026-114938?

CVE-2026-114938, also known as Java4Shell, is a high severity vulnerability affecting the OpenJDK HotSpot compiler. It carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1 and affects multiple Java release lines.

Which Java versions are affected by Java4Shell?

The published OpenJDK advisory identifies Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 release lines as affected. Exact vulnerable and fixed builds vary by distributor, so organizations should consult their Java vendor’s security advisory.

Can Aquasec detect Java4Shell?

Aquasec customers should update Java to the fixed version recommended by their distributor, rebuild and redeploy affected images, then rescan them using updated vulnerability content. They should also confirm that corrected images are deployed in production.

Does a missing Java4Shell finding mean an image is unaffected?

No. A missing finding does not confirm that an image is unaffected. Vulnerability content may not yet be available, and detection coverage can vary by Java distribution or package format. Organizations should verify installed Java versions against their distributor’s advisory.

Title: How to Find, Mitigate, and Patch the Critical Java4Shell Flaw (CVE-2026-114938) Now
Context: Executive Summary Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. The researchers who found it rate it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can corrupt Java heap memory, read secrets from it, and reach remote code execution. Researchers demonstrated pre-authentication RCE on default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Unpatched OpenJDK builds from 17.0.6 onward, from any vendor, are affected when they run on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI, which includes Intel Xeon from Ice Lake through Granite Rapids and AMD EPYC from Zen 4 onward. Oracle released fixes on November 17, 2026, and a single JVM flag closes the exposure where patching has to wait. CISA has issued an alert urging organizations to patch immediately. Start with internet-facing identity, CI/CD, and collaboration systems, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched.

What’s at Risk

A Critical Java Flaw Could Hand Attackers Your Identity and Build Servers.

Java4Shell is in the Java runtime itself, so no application or library has to be at fault for a service to be exposed. The flaw sits in handwritten assembly that speeds up Base64 decoding with AVX-512 instructions. A short malformed input makes that code write 62 bytes past the end of a buffer before Java rejects the input.

Base64 carries login headers, tokens, and file uploads, so the vulnerable code often runs before a user has authenticated. Calif, the firm that discovered the flaw, demonstrated remote code execution against the following products in their default configurations:

Access required

Products

None (pre-authentication)

Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, PingFederate

Authenticated user

Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, Netflix Spinnaker

The researchers say these lists are not exhaustive. They also reached RCE in sample applications built on Apache Struts and Spring Boot.

The pre-authentication list is where the business risk concentrates. Identity providers issue the tokens every other system trusts, and build and artifact servers sign and ship your software. A compromise of either can expose downstream systems that trust its identities, tokens, or software artifacts.

Code execution is not the only outcome. A successful exploit chain can read Java heap memory before it runs any attacker code. That memory can hold private keys, tokens, and personal data. CISA also warns that crafted input can crash the JVM, so availability is at risk too. Java clients are exposed as well. The researchers report a client-side exploit in which a Java program is compromised simply by connecting over TLS to a malicious server.

Are You Affected?

A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, attacker-controlled data must also reach the vulnerable Base64 decoding path in the application.

Condition

Affected

Not affected

Releases before 17.0.6, including standard OpenJDK 8 and 11. Also any vendor build that contains the fix

Processor

x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids), AMD EPYC and Ryzen (Zen 4 and newer)

ARM64, and x86-64 without AVX-512 VBMI

The runtime condition covers every OpenJDK-based distribution: Oracle Java SE, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, and Red Hat OpenJDK. There is one exception on Java 8. Oracle lists the 8u511b33-perf build of Java SE 8 as vulnerable.

On Linux, run this command to check the processor. The host meets the hardware condition only if all four flags appear.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’

Two cautions when scoping:

Check the runtime each application actually runs. Many products and container images bundle their own JDK, which operating system updates do not touch. CISA notes that bundled runtimes, including those in appliances, may not appear as separate entries in a software inventory.

Use the processor condition to order the work, not to close findings. A workload on an unaffected CPU today can land on an affected one after an instance resize or a move to newer hardware.

Exploitation Status

As of November 17, 2026, we have not seen public confirmation of exploitation in the wild. Do not plan around that. The trigger is a short malformed Base64 string; the root cause and exploitation technique are public, and the researchers have said details of the bug leaked before the patch.

The researchers are holding back their product-specific exploits until organizations have had time to upgrade, and plan to publish them later. They report finding the bug with AI assistance in about an hour and having a first working exploit two hours after that, for under $200 in AI token costs. Expect others to repeat that work.

There is one limit worth knowing. No universal exploit exists: each product needs its own chain, and the technique is sensitive to network conditions. That slows mass exploitation. It does not protect a specific target such as your identity provider.

What to Do Now

Updating the Java runtime is the only complete fix. Oracle released fixed builds on November 17, 2026.

Oracle Java SE

Fixed build

Other OpenJDK vendors publish on their own schedules. As of November 17, 2026, Amazon had released Corretto 17.0.21.1.2 with the fix. Use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed build and confirm it addresses CVE-2026-114938.

If you cannot patch today, there is a temporary workaround. It is a startup setting for Java, applied by the team that runs the application, and it takes effect after a restart. You need only one of the two options below.

Preferred: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. This turns off the fast Base64 decoder where the bug lives. Java falls back to its standard decoder, and everything else runs as before. Applications that decode large amounts of Base64 may run slower, so test first.

Alternative: -XX:UseAVX=2. This turns off a wider set of processor optimizations, including the vulnerable one, so the performance cost is broader. Use it only on Intel and AMD servers. Java on ARM does not accept this setting and will not start.

Neither option replaces the patch.

Either way, restart every Java process. A patch or a flag takes effect only when the JVM restarts, so verify the running process and not only the installed package. Do not rely on a reverse proxy as a control. Request buffering breaks some exploit chains but is not a general mitigation.

Reduce exposure while you wait for a patch. Take identity, build, and collaboration consoles off the open internet, or put them behind a VPN, until they are patched. CISA also suggests validating Base64 input and enforcing input-size limits at the application boundary. Size limits alone will not stop this bug, because the malformed input is very short. The JVM flag above is the more direct stopgap because it removes the vulnerable code.

Work in this order:

Internet-facing identity providers such as Keycloak and PingFederate.

Internet-facing Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and Artifactory.

Other internet-facing Java services that handle logins, tokens, or file uploads.

Internal Java systems, starting with Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.

Assign an owner and a remediation deadline to every system that is waiting on a vendor build.

What to Watch For

CISA advises monitoring for rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. Qualys TRU suggests starting with these checks:

Java processes that start a shell or open outbound connections they have not made before.

Java runtimes on a host that your inventory does not account for.
