Title: Critical OpenJDK RCE CVE-2026-114938: What to Know
Context: A critical OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can allow an attacker to inject and remotely execute arbitrary code without authentication or user interaction
Full Text:
TL;DR

Calif disclosed Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, as an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in OpenJDK.

The flaw is in the Java runtime's Base64 decoding path, not a third-party library. Reachability depends on the runtime build, processor, and whether an application decodes untrusted Base64 data.

Oracle released updated Java builds as part of its November 2026 security update, but its pre-release notice does not map those Java fixes to this CVE by name.

Finding exposure requires checking runtimes on hosts and in container images. Project dependency scans alone will not identify every affected system.

For the current advisory and response guidance, see our Security Event page for the Critical OpenJDK Vulnerability.

A critical OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can allow an attacker to inject and remotely execute arbitrary code without authentication or user interaction. Calif calls the vulnerability Java4Shell.

The disclosure coincided with Oracle's Java security update on November 17, 2026. That timing has raised questions about which Oracle builds address Java4Shell and what organizations should check.

Teams need to identify vulnerable runtimes across their environments, prioritize network-accessible systems, and apply the patched OpenJDK build through the appropriate vendor.

Java4Shell Is a Runtime Vulnerability, Not a Library Flaw

Java4Shell is a memory corruption vulnerability in the Java runtime itself, not in a third-party library or framework. Because the flaw sits in the runtime, project dependency scans will not identify every affected installation.

Base64 decoding is common in applications that receive data over a network. Our research indicates that a Java 17 application could, in principle, be reachable when it decodes Base64 data from an untrusted source on an affected runtime build and processor.

That does not mean every Java application is exposed in the same way. The runtime build and processor matter, as does whether untrusted input can reach the decoder. The vulnerability is described as pre-authentication, because an attacker may be able to supply that input before logging in or interacting with the application.

Third-party analysis has also reported affected Java versions beyond Java 17. Upwind says it reproduced the memory corruption in tests on Java 17, 21, and 25, and identified Java 27 through code analysis. These are research findings, not a vendor's final affected-version list. Organizations should use vendor guidance to confirm the status of each runtime they operate.

Oracle's November Update Does Not Define the CVE’s Full Scope

Oracle released updated Java builds as part of its November 17 security update. Its November security notice lists 11 Java SE security fixes, all described as remotely exploitable without authentication, with a maximum CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1. Oracle also lists builds for Java SE 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, and 27, along with versions of GraalVM and JavaFX.

The notice is a pre-release announcement and does not identify the 11 issues by CVE. It therefore does not establish which update addresses Java4Shell. The Java versions Oracle lists as affected should not be treated as the confirmed affected-version range for this CVE.

Early coverage reports a 9.2 score for Java4Shell under CVSS 4.0. Oracle reports a maximum score of 8.1 under CVSS 3.1 for its Java SE fixes. Those scores use different CVSS versions and refer to different sets of vulnerabilities. They are not competing scores for the same confirmed issue.

Patch Confirmed Systems and Reduce Exposure

Treat systems confirmed to run a vulnerable OpenJDK build as exposed until the patched runtime is installed. Apply the update supplied by the vendor or distribution responsible for that runtime. Build numbers can vary across distributions, so confirm the fixed version with the supplier rather than assuming a particular version string applies everywhere.

Replacing runtime files on a host does not update a JVM process that is already running. Restart affected services after updating. Rebuild container images using a patched base image, and update products that bundle their own Java runtime. Then verify that the deployed service is running the patched build.

If a product bundles the vulnerable runtime and has no direct upgrade path, contact its maintainers for an update. If no update is available, investigate an alternative component or a mitigating control while tracking the issue to resolution.

Calif’s recommendations describe two possible temporary mitigations: disabling the Base64 intrinsic or limiting AVX use to version 2. The AVX setting applies only to x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and may fail to start. These controls are not replacements for a patched runtime. Test them for compatibility and performance impact, and follow the relevant vendor's guidance.

What Teams Should Do Now

Organizations should:

Inventory runtimes: Check the Java runtime used by each running service, including runtimes on hosts, in container images, and bundled with products. Record the build, vendor, processor, deployment location, and owner. Package inventories can help, but they do not replace checking the runtime a service actually uses.

Assess reachability: Check for the relevant AVX-512 processor support and whether the Java Base64 intrinsic is enabled. Identify which Java services listen for network connections.

Prioritize exposure: Start with internet-facing and other network-accessible systems, then review the rest of the environment.

Confirm and apply the fix: Check Oracle or the relevant OpenJDK supplier for the patched build that applies to each runtime. Restart affected services and rebuild images as needed.

Reduce interim risk: Restrict or monitor network access to confirmed vulnerable systems while updates are being applied. Test any temporary mitigation and follow vendor guidance.

Connect Vulnerability Intelligence to Runtime Inventory

Java4Shell is a reminder that vulnerability response depends on knowing what runs across the environment, including the runtimes beneath applications.

CVE-2026-114938 requires organizations to look beneath project dependencies and account for the runtime installed across their environments. Finding each vulnerable OpenJDK build, assigning an owner, and verifying the patch are essential steps in reducing exposure.

Check Sonatype Guide and the associated Security Event page, which contain current details and response guidance as organizations identify affected OpenJDK deployments and verify remediation.

Title: CVE-2026-114938 OpenJDK RCE (Java4Shell): Everything You Need to Know
Context: The "Java4Shell" vulnerability and exploit were discovered and disclosed by security firm Calif
Full Text:
On November 17, 2026, details emerged exposing a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in OpenJDK, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (dubbed "Java4Shell") with a CVSSv4.0 score of 9.2. The bug exists in the optimized assembly code handling AVX-512 Base64 decoding, allowing remote unauthenticated attackers to cause heap memory corruption. Triggering this flaw on affected systems can lead to remote code execution.

The "Java4Shell" vulnerability and exploit were discovered and disclosed by security firm Calif.

What is CVE-2026-114938?

CVE-2026-114938 is a memory-corruption vulnerability residing in the optimized Base64 decoding intrinsic engine of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). To maximize performance, OpenJDK uses an optimized implementation on supported x86-64 processors, based on AVX-512 VBMI instructions. However, the optimized assembly code miscalculates the output array bounds when handling inputs that contain an unexpected number of trailing padding characters (=).

When an input containing a specific sequence -such as 64 A characters followed by a single = - is parsed, the decoder's length calculation underflows to a negative value. This calculation mismatch causes an out-of-bounds write past the allocated heap memory buffer. Attackers can leverage this to overwrite adjacent object metadata, which can lead to code execution. We have proved that remote exploitation is feasible against standard Java applications such Jenkins, Confluence, and Apache Tomcat.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

Like other memory safety issues, exploitation is possible with AI, but is not trivial. Our AI based vulnerability research harness, Wiz Atlas, managed to find and build a proof-of-concept exploit for this vulnerability within 2 hours, even before the full details were disclosed. Having said that, generalizing the exploit for an arbitrary target is difficult. We should expect adversaries to target commonplace Java applications, where specific builds and memory layouts repeat across targets. Motivated adversaries may tailor exploits with AI for specific targets, including home-grown applications.

Web Application Firewalls can help mitigate some of the exploits as they emerge in the wild. Since this vulnerability is rooted in OpenJDK itself, many possible code paths using user inputs may lead into the vulnerable code path, so it’s unlikely that WAF rules will be able to cover all possible paths, and will never be able to cover home grown applications completely. The best solution is upgrading to the latest OpenJDK version.

Prioritize externally facing, packaged Java applications, and make sure they are either patched or restricted from public access. Upgrade home-grown Java applications and update to the latest OpenJDK version containing the fix.

Which products are affected?

The vulnerability affects OpenJDK versions 17.0.6 and later, as well as downstream distributions, provided they run on x86-64 hardware supporting AVX-512 VBMI instruction sets (ARM64 processors are unaffected). Affected software distributions and hardware include:

OpenJDK Distributions: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, and Oracle Java SE (specifically versions 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3).

Vulnerable CPU Architectures: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids) and AMD EPYC/Ryzen (Zen 4 or newer).

Proven Vulnerable Applications (Pre-Auth RCE): Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and custom frameworks built on Spring Boot, Apache Struts, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, Netflix Spinnaker and Apache Tomcat.

Which actions should security teams take?

Security teams should immediately prioritize the following mitigation steps:

Audit and Patch: Identify all systems running OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later on AVX-512-capable x86-64 hardware. Apply the official security patches released on November 17, 2026, or update to downstream vendor-supplied builds immediately.

Verify Hardware Vulnerability: Run the following command on Linux systems to check if your infrastructure is physically affected:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

If all four CPU flags are present in the output, the host runs the vulnerable hardware execution path.

Implement JVM Runtime Workarounds: If immediate patching is not possible, apply one of the following flags to JVM startup parameters to completely neutralize the vulnerability. They may have performance impact on the application.

Disable Base64 Intrinsics (Recommended): -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

Disable AVX-512 execution (x86-64 only): -XX:UseAVX=2

Isolate Internet-Facing Services: Temporarily restrict external network access to vulnerable management portals (e.g., Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak) until mitigations or updates are deployed.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

Title: Defending Against Java4Shell: Vulnerability in OpenJDK Enables RCE on AVX-512 CPUs
Context: 2 Critical), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder that allows malformed Base64 input to trigger remote code execution (RCE)
Full Text:
On November 17, 2026, security researchers at Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS 4.0: 9.2 Critical), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder that allows malformed Base64 input to trigger remote code execution (RCE).

Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in default configurations of Apache Kafka Broker, Atlassian Confluence and Jira, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, Keycloak, Gerrit, PingFederate, and Spring Boot applications, and post-authentication execution against Elasticsearch.

Oracle released patches addressing this flaw in its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update. Organizations running OpenJDK 17.0.6 or newer on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI support are affected. Additionally, affected Oracle Java SE versions include 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, and 27.0.1.0.3.

What Is Java4Shell

The flaw sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application. Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.

Recommended Next Steps

Inventory every Java runtime. Record the vendor, full build version, OS, CPU architecture, and owner across your environment—including containers, bundled installations, and vendor appliances. Prioritize internet-facing applications, authentication services, and business-critical systems.

Mitigate immediately by disabling AVX-512 (if unable to patch right away). Start x86-64 JVMs with the flag -XX:UseAVX=2. Note: Apply this flag on x86-64 hosts only; ARM JVMs do not recognize it and will fail to start.

Apply Oracle’s security updates once available. Monitor Oracle and your specific OpenJDK distribution vendor for patched builds addressing CVE-2026-114938, and upgrade affected runtimes as soon as fixes are released. For products that bundle their own Java runtime, follow the vendor’s supported update path.

Hunt and audit logs. Where your WAF, reverse proxy, or application logs capture Base64 values (HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens), inspect them after normal application parsing, and flag any that meet all of the following conditions:

Total length L (including padding) is 65 or more

$L \pmod{64}$ is 1, 2, or 3

Ends with one or two = characters (not exceeding $L \pmod{64}$)

All other bytes belong to the standard Base64 alphabet

SentinelOne’s Defense Against Java4Shell

The exploit arrives as a malformed Base64 string that corrupts memory inside the running JVM, so there is no file to scan at that stage. Instead of relying on CVE-specific signatures, SentinelOne protects against what an attacker does next.

Real-Time Behavioral & Static Protection

Across both Windows and Linux, the SentinelOne Agent’s behavioral engines continuously monitor JVM-hosted services and web servers in real time to detect malicious post-exploitation activity – regardless of the initial exploit vector. If an attacker achieves RCE and acts on the host, the Agent monitors for common post-exploitation behaviors, including a JVM process spawning a shell to run a remote or obfuscated one-liner (such as downloading a payload and piping it to a shell), suspicious child processes, credential access, persistence, and payload execution. Files written to disk during an attack, including JSP web shells and second-stage binaries, are evaluated by the Agent’s static engines across both operating systems.

Linux: In addition to general JVM behavioral monitoring, the Linux Agent applies deeper behavioral checks across web and application servers. These monitor for web shell drops, server-initiated file-transfer utilities, user enumeration, access to sensitive credential stores (such as shadow files and SSH keys), password changes, and use of AWS IMDS tokens– a common indicator of cloud credential theft following exploitation.

Windows: Alongside JVM and post-exploitation behavioral monitoring (such as suspicious child processes, credential access, and persistence), the Windows Agent specifically monitors web server processes for spawning suspicious child-processes as well as unauthorized file drops and execution.

Customers across all OS platforms with Live Security Updates enabled benefit from our most up to date detection capabilities.

Platform Detection Rules

For an added layer of visibility on top of Agent telemetry, SentinelOne provides Platform Detection Rules that can alert on post-exploitation activity from Java application servers and general Java-based exploitation. SentinelOne customers have access to these rules and can enable them today.

Threat Hunting

Our Wayfinder Threat Hunting teams provide an additional 24/7 layer of protection using AI-powered hunting systems that continuously look for post-exploit activity, persistence, and lateral movement across web servers and other potentially vulnerable applications. They add human review and agentic technology to find attacker activity that may originate from this or other application vulnerabilities.

Title: “Java4Shell”: Critical OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Flaw Could Allow Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution

Full Text:
A critical vulnerability dubbed “Java4Shell” (CVE-2026-114938) has been reported in OpenJDK. According to early reports, it lets unauthenticated attackers achieve remote code execution by sending a crafted Base64 string to a Java application running on x86 servers with AVX-512 support. Early reports rate it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. Java runs a large share of enterprise and cloud backends, so organizations should start inventorying their Java runtimes now and prepare to patch as soon as vendor builds are confirmed.

Security firm Calif, which says it discovered and reported the flaw, disclosed it publicly on November 17 because the details had already leaked, and says it will publish full technical details later that day, after Oracle releases its patch. Neither Oracle nor the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group has published an advisory that names this CVE, and as of this writing CVE records are only reserved but unpublished . [VERIFY @23:00]

x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI for the reported path

Patch

Oracle Nov 17 builds released; CVE not yet confirmed among fixes

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation or public PoC

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?

The issue is a memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated (intrinsic) Base64 decoder, the native code the JVM uses in place of the Java implementation of java.util.Base64 decoding on supported CPUs. A crafted 65-byte input reportedly causes an integer underflow in padding handling. The result is a 62-byte heap buffer overflow that can corrupt adjacent Java objects and lead to code execution. Base64 decoding of untrusted input is very common in Java applications (such as authentication headers, tokens and encoded API payloads), so the reachable attack surface can be large. Exploitation still requires attacker-controlled data to reach the decoder.

Which Java versions could be affected by Java4Shell?

Public reports so far say “OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later”. Orca Research reviewed the OpenJDK source history to see which Java versions contain the reported vulnerable code. Containing the code does not by itself confirm that a version is exploitable; confirmation is expected once full technical details and vendor advisories are published:

The 17.0.6 boundary matches the code. The AVX-512 Base64 decoding intrinsic (JDK-8268276) was backported to the JDK 17 update line in November 2022 and first shipped in OpenJDK 17.0.6 (January 2023). It is not present in 17.0.5.

Newer Java lines likely carry the same code. The same decoder was added to mainline OpenJDK in 2021 and first released in JDK 18. JDK 21, 25 and 27 therefore contain it. Early reports mention only Java 17, and it has not been confirmed whether these newer lines are affected; until Oracle or OpenJDK clarifies the scope, organizations may want to treat them as potentially exposed. [VERIFY @23:00]

Java 8 and 11 do not contain this decoder intrinsic in OpenJDK, so they are unlikely to be affected by Java4Shell. Oracle released updates for these lines on November 17 (8u513 and 11.0.33.1) as part of the same patch update.

Hardware matters. On Java 17, the Base64 intrinsic is enabled only on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512; on Java 21 and later it is also enabled on CPUs with AVX2. However, the AVX-512 decoding path that early reports point to runs only on CPUs with the AVX-512 VBMI extension (e.g., Intel Ice Lake and later, AMD Zen 4 and later). ARM-based hosts (e.g., AWS Graviton) use different decoder code and are not known to be affected.

All distributions are in scope. The code is in upstream OpenJDK, so Oracle JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Red Hat and distro OpenJDK packages built from affected versions should all be considered potentially affected, including JDKs bundled inside applications and container images.

Is there a patch for CVE-2026-114938?

On November 17, Oracle released new builds for Java 8, 11, 17, 21, 25 and 27 (8u513, 11.0.33.1, 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1) as part of its November Critical Security Patch Update. According to Oracle’s pre-release announcement, the update contains 11 Java SE fixes, all remotely exploitable without authentication (highest CVSS 3.1 score 8.1). The 9.2 figure in early reports is a CVSS 4.0 score, while Oracle uses CVSS 3.1, so Oracle’s 8.1 maximum neither confirms nor rules out that CVE-2026-114938 is among the fixes. Oracle’s release notes for these builds do not name CVE-2026-114938. Oracle has not confirmed that CVE-2026-114938 is among the fixes, and other OpenJDK vendors (Temurin, Corretto, Zulu and others) release on their own schedules. [VERIFY @23:00 – confirm fixed versions per vendor]

How to mitigate Java4Shell before a patch is confirmed

No vendor-validated workaround has been published. It can be suggested to limit AVX usage or disable Base64 intrinsics as temporary measures. In HotSpot, the JVM option -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics disables the Base64 intrinsic entirely, while -XX:UseAVX=2 prevents the JVM from using the AVX-512 decoding path (on Java 21 and later the intrinsic remains active through its AVX2 path). These options exist in affected JDKs, but they have not been validated by Oracle or OpenJDK as a fix for this CVE, they may affect performance, and they do not replace patching. Recommended steps:

Inventory every Java runtime: OS packages, tarball/zip installs, JDKs bundled in applications and container base images, on both Linux and Windows.

Prioritize internet-facing Java services that decode untrusted Base64 input.

Apply vendor updates as soon as fixed builds for CVE-2026-114938 are confirmed, and rebuild container images on patched base images.

Is Java4Shell being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, there are no reports of in-the-wild exploitation and no public proof-of-concept. Technical details are expected to become public within hours, which typically shortens the time to working exploits significantly. Organizations should treat this as urgent.

How can Orca help?

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running potentially vulnerable Java versions across installation methods – OS packages, standalone JDK installations and JDKs bundled in container images – on both Linux and Windows. Customers can understand each asset’s exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk.

Title: Researchers Claim Two RCE Exploits That Bypass Telegram’s New Android Defenses
Context: The malware allows attackers to control the infected system and steal data from crypto wallets and Telegram accounts
Full Text:
A malicious widget can bypass the security filter that Telegram added to its Android app last week and run code outside it, according to NebuSec, a security company.

Widgets are small interactive blocks that bots send inside chat messages, and their JavaScript runs on the user's phone. The researchers ran their demonstration on a Telegram test server, because only approved bots can send widgets on the live service now.

Bots could start sending widgets last week. Two days later, an account called V12 posted a video on X claiming that any Telegram message could now be used to execute remote code.

Telegram then put QuickJS, the small engine that runs widget JavaScript, into its own process on Android. It also added a seccomp filter, which can block or record the system calls that the process makes. Both changes appear in the source code it published for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303).

NebuSec said in a technical analysis published earlier this week that its researchers got code running outside that filter in two separate ways. One uses a widget bug the filter does not cover, and the other chains a widget bug the filter does cover with a kernel bug.

In their video, a bot's Telegram widget on Android 13.2.2 (7303) bypasses the filter and opens the phone's calculator app, the researchers say.

Their write-up and their demonstration post on X do not say what the code could reach beyond that, such as the app's messages or the rest of the phone. They also do not say whether the user had to start the bot or tap the widget first.

The researchers are holding back the details for now. Their write-up names no CVE identifier and does not say whether the bugs were reported to the app's developers.

The widget documentation says widgets run in a sandbox, with rules such as no network access. Those rules live in the engine's own code, the researchers say. A single use-after-free or out-of-bounds write bug in QuickJS lets a script read and write the process's memory, and then the rules no longer protect anything.

The new filter names a few dozen system calls, such as ptrace, bpf, and mount, and lets every other call through. The filter's source code leaves ioctl unfiltered. The filter sits on top of Android's own limits on the engine process.

One process also runs every widget, so a hijacked widget from one bot shares memory with the widgets of every other bot, the researchers say.

In the published source code for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303), that filter is set to an audit mode, The Hacker News found. In audit mode, it still blocks attempts to start new programs or processes, but it only records the other listed calls and lets them run.

A comment above the setting says how long that will last: "Audit until the logs from the devices say the engine never makes them." The published code does not show whether the version people install uses the same setting.

"Yes, currently, general bots aren't allowed to use widgets even in private chats," a contributor to the telegram-bot-api project wrote late last week in a bug report thread on GitHub. As of this week, no later message in the thread says which bots are still allowed or that the limit has been lifted.

The researchers' write-up lists no fixed version, and the published Android source code is no newer than 13.2.2 (7303) as of this week.

"No one could be hacked just by receiving a message," Pavel Durov, Telegram's chief executive, wrote late last week in a channel post. His post addressed reports of code execution through widgets in the Android and Windows apps, and came before the researchers' demonstration. He added that a user first had to start a third-party service, and that even that was fully patched on the server side.

The company had earlier said that the problem in V12's first demonstration was fixed and that the fix had reached all users.

Separately, the security vendor Kaspersky said late last week that it had detected suspected exploitation of a flaw in Telegram widgets when people visited some Telegram channels.

In that activity, a PowerShell script ran without the user noticing and downloaded and launched WebRAT, also known as Salat Stealer. The malware allows attackers to control the infected system and steal data from crypto wallets and Telegram accounts.

The vendor's malware warning does not identify the flaw or the Telegram version, does not report the number of victims, and does not link the activity to either demonstration. It advises not running widgets until a fix is released.

Title: Anthropic Cuts Disclosure Deadline to 30 Days For Serious Bugs
Context: On the same day, Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported finding an exposed server hosting an attacker framework, dubbed exploit_agent, built to research vulnerabilities and...
Full Text:
Anthropic has cut the time vendors get to fix serious flaws found by its Claude models before it makes them public from 90 days to 30. The change applies to vulnerabilities Anthropic reports to vendors and maintainers, not generally to bugs reported to Anthropic by external researchers.

The company's Frontier Red Team announced the change in a November 16 post, with the new timelines applying to vulnerabilities reported on or after January 1, 2027. Reports already in progress then will keep their existing deadlines.

Anthropic said disclosure norms, including its own, had assumed fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery was unlikely, but that "neither assumption holds today." It said bugs one model could find were increasingly likely to be found by another.

What Changes in Anthropic's Disclosure Policy

Under the updated policy, high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities will have a 30-day disclosure deadline, while all other issues will have 45 days. Anthropic will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days without a maintainer response, rather than 30.

The company will also wait 30 days after a patch becomes available before publishing full technical details, down from 45 days. The seven-day disclosure window for vulnerabilities under active exploitation remains unchanged.

Anthropic said it would work with vendors on a remediation timeline for flaws in hard-to-deploy software such as critical infrastructure, or flaws that need specification or RFC changes. The policy will not cover AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those from its OSS Scanner.

Acknowledging that shorter timelines could put more pressure on maintainers, Anthropic said it would keep sending actionable guidance with each report, plus a patch or mitigation where possible.

Read more on vulnerability disclosure: AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours

How Anthropic's Deadlines Compare With Project Zero's

The change puts Anthropic's serious-bug deadline ahead of Project Zero's schedule. Google's team, which now publishes details 90 days after reporting a bug whether or not it is fixed, will cut that to 60 days on February 2, 2027 and 30 days on January 3, 2028.

The approaches also differ on severity. Anthropic will set different disclosure windows based on severity, while Project Zero argued that a vulnerability's severity does not affect how likely attackers are to find it.

On the same day, Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported finding an exposed server hosting an attacker framework, dubbed exploit_agent, built to research vulnerabilities and weaponize them.

Anthropic said it was now giving maintainers 30 more days on high- and critical-severity bugs that had passed its current 90-day deadline, before publishing them on its disclosure dashboard.

Title: Oracle to Patch 11 Java Flaws Today as Critical OpenJDK RCE (CVE-2026-114938) Report Emerges
Context: Oracle is preparing to release security patches for 11 vulnerabilities in Java SE on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, all of which may be exploited remotely without authentication,...
Full Text:
Oracle is preparing to release security patches for 11 vulnerabilities in Java SE on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, all of which may be exploited remotely without authentication, as separate reports warn of a potentially critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw affecting OpenJDK.

The 11 vulnerabilities carry a maximum CVSS 3.1 severity score of 8.1, according to Oracle's advance security notice. The company has not disclosed their CVE identifiers, affected components, or the individual consequences of exploitation.

The separate OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, has reportedly been assigned a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later. However, those details remain unconfirmed, and there is no evidence yet that the reported flaw is among the 11 vulnerabilities Oracle plans to patch.

Security firm Calif said in a post on X that it discovered and reported the flaw, which it calls Java4Shell, and that the vulnerability had leaked. Calif said it would publish technical details by 1 p.m. Pacific time on November 17, after Oracle releases a patch.

Security company watchTowr acknowledged the reports in a post on X, but cautioned that the technical details were still unconfirmed.

Separate analyses of the OpenJDK source code by security companies Upwind and Equixly point to a flaw in Java's Base64 decoder whose likely result is a crash of the Java virtual machine (JVM) rather than code execution.

The vulnerability's CVE record remains reserved without a public description. No official advisory has specified the vulnerable component, precise exploitation requirements, affected version range, or the availability of a fix.

Oracle's ops.java site now lists the replacement builds below as its current releases. Oracle's advance notice, release notes and download page still showed the earlier builds as of 16:59 UTC.

Oracle Prepares Java Security Updates

Oracle advises customers to stop using its current builds of Java 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, and 27 after the November 17 security update and move to the corresponding replacement releases.

The November security notice identifies the following affected Oracle products and versions:

Oracle Java SE: 8u511, 8u511-perf, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1.

Oracle GraalVM for JDK: 17.0.21 and 21.0.13.

Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3.

Oracle JavaFX: 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1.

Oracle says all 11 Java SE vulnerabilities may be exploited over a network without requiring credentials. That does not necessarily mean they all allow remote code execution or that every application running an affected Java version can be attacked directly.

The advance notice does not identify the vulnerable Java components or specify what an attacker could accomplish by exploiting each flaw.

Oracle also warns that the information may change before the complete security advisory is published.

Critical OpenJDK RCE Report Remains Unverified

The reported CVE-2026-114938 vulnerability introduces a separate concern for organizations operating Java applications, particularly those exposed to the internet.

However, the public information does not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed.

However, Oracle's notice and the OpenJDK advisories do not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed.

Upwind said in a technical analysis that its reading of the OpenJDK source points to a flaw in Java's AVX-512 Base64 decoder, and Equixly reached the same finding in a separate analysis. The flawed code runs only on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support, when untrusted data reaches the basic or URL decoder of java.util.Base64. ARM servers do not run it.

The code is in Java 17.0.6 and later and in Java 21, 25 and 27, but not in standard Java 8 or 11. A crash is the likely result because the bytes written past the buffer are fixed and not chosen by the attacker. Neither firm reported reproducing the overflow on AVX-512 hardware.

Oracle's 8u371-perf release notes show that its Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack added a "Base64 Decoding optimization for x86 using AVX-512". Neither firm said whether the Performance Pack is affected.

Both firms named two JVM options as stopgaps to keep the flawed code from running: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which turns off the Base64 intrinsics, and -XX:UseAVX=2, which turns off all AVX-512 code paths and can slow other work. Neither option has been confirmed by a vendor for this flaw, the firms said.

Oracle's November notice covers Oracle products and does not establish the patch status of third-party OpenJDK distributions.

The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group, which coordinates security disclosures affecting OpenJDK source code, had not published an advisory newer than October 24 at the time of the earlier review.

Until official details are available, organizations cannot determine from the reported CVE alone whether their Java deployments are vulnerable or which specific update addresses the issue.

Oracle began a monthly security patch cycle on May 28, introducing targeted security releases between its quarterly Critical Patch Updates.

Its Java security update plan, last updated September 10, identified November 17 as the next scheduled monthly release.

Organizations should inventory deployed Java runtimes, identify internet-facing applications, and prepare to test and install the relevant vendor updates once they become available.

This is a developing story. We will update this article as Oracle publishes its full vulnerability advisory and additional verified details about CVE-2026-114938, affected versions, and available patches emerge.

Title: Your Vulnerability Scanner Found 10,000 Issues. Which Ones Actually Matter?
Context: By combining vulnerability data with exploitability, asset criticality, exposure, attacker activity and existing controls, security teams can turn a growing volume of findings...
Full Text:
Finding vulnerabilities is rarely the hardest part of Vulnerability Management.

Modern vulnerability scanning services can continuously examine internal and external networks, web applications, APIs, databases and cloud environments, producing thousands, or even tens of thousands, of findings. The challenge begins after the scan finishes.

Which vulnerability should your team fix first?

A list of 10,000 findings may look comprehensive, but treating every vulnerability as equally urgent can overwhelm remediation teams, consume resources and distract attention from the weaknesses attackers are most likely to exploit.

Effective threat and vulnerability management requires a shift in perspective: from counting vulnerabilities to understanding risk.

Why vulnerability volume can be misleading

In 2025 alone, 48,185 new CVEs were published which was >20% more than were released in 2024. This ever-increasing rate of issues released makes it increasingly difficult for organizations to effectively keep up with the threat. Security teams have traditionally relied on vulnerability severity scores to organize remediation. A critical vulnerability goes to the top of the queue. A medium-severity vulnerability can wait.

That's useful as a starting point, but severity alone doesn't tell the entire story.

Consider two vulnerabilities:

A critical vulnerability exists on an isolated internal system protected by multiple security controls, with no evidence of active exploitation.

A high-severity vulnerability affects an internet-facing system containing sensitive information, and attackers are actively exploiting the weakness.

If remediation is based strictly on severity, the critical vulnerability may receive attention first. From a risk perspective, however, the second issue may represent the more immediate threat.

This distinction becomes increasingly important as both vulnerability inventories and assets within an organization’s attack surface rapidly grow. Simply generating more findings isn't necessarily improving security, especially when raw scanner output includes false positives that consume remediation time without reducing risk. The real measure of an effective vulnerability program is whether the organization can identify and reduce its most meaningful risks.

Identify and address risks with LevelBlue Vulnerability Management.

Learn More

Five factors that reveal which vulnerabilities matter

Risk-based vulnerability prioritization adds context to scanner findings. Rather than asking only, "How severe is this vulnerability?" security teams can consider several factors together.

1. Exploitability

A vulnerability that can realistically be exploited deserves different treatment from one that requires highly specific conditions, substantial attacker access or a complex exploit chain.

Teams should consider whether exploit code is publicly available, what level of access exploitation requires and how difficult the vulnerability is to exploit in the organization's specific environment.

Where the answer is unclear, penetration testing or proof-of-concept validation can confirm whether a finding is truly exploitable.

The distinction matters because a vulnerability's theoretical severity isn't synonymous with its practical likelihood of exploitation.

2. Asset criticality

Not every asset has the same value to the business.

A vulnerability on an employee test machine and the same vulnerability on a production server supporting a critical business process create different levels of organizational risk. That’s not to say you shouldn’t fix the vulnerability on the employee test machine, as it could still be leveraged as a pivot by an attacker to other areas of the network; however, it might take a backseat to the production instance.

Effective vulnerability management tools should help teams combine technical findings with asset context. Relevant questions include:

What business process does this asset support?

Does it store or process sensitive data?

Would compromise disrupt essential operations?

What systems could an attacker reach from it

Asset context helps transform a scanner finding into a business risk decision.

3. Exposure

Where the vulnerable asset sits also matters.

An internet-accessible system presents a fundamentally different attack surface from a tightly segmented internal asset. Network accessibility, security architecture, identity requirements and potential attack paths should all influence remediation priority.

Teams need to look beyond whether a vulnerability exists and ask: Can an attacker actually reach it?

That question can dramatically change a remediation queue.

4. Real-world attacker activity

Threat intelligence provides another critical piece of context.

Attackers do not exploit every known vulnerability equally. Some vulnerabilities rapidly become part of ransomware campaigns or automated exploitation, while others may see little meaningful attacker activity.

Understanding whether threat actors are actively targeting a vulnerability allows teams to adjust priorities as the threat environment changes.

A vulnerability that was a lower priority yesterday may require immediate action if new exploitation activity emerges today. That is why effective threat and vulnerability management is an ongoing process rather than a periodic scanning exercise.

5. Compensating controls

A vulnerability doesn't exist in isolation from the rest of the security environment.

Endpoint protection, network segmentation, application controls, identity protections, increased logging / monitoring, and other safeguards may reduce the likelihood or potential impact of exploitation. They don't necessarily eliminate the need to mitigate an identified weakness, but they can influence how urgently remediation is required.

Conversely, the absence or weakness of those controls can increase priority.

Understanding compensating controls helps security teams make remediation decisions based on the environment they actually operate, rather than on vulnerability data alone.

From vulnerability findings to meaningful risk reduction

This broader context is where managed vulnerability scanning evolves into a comprehensive vulnerability management strategy.Scanning establishes visibility into weaknesses across the environment. Mature vulnerability management enriches those findings with asset, exposure and threat context, enabling teams to determine appropriate remediation priorities.

A repeatable process can help operationalize this approach:

Discover → Validate → Prioritize → Remediate → Retest

Discovery identifies vulnerabilities across an organization’s entire, ever expanding attack surface, including IT assets, cloud environments, SaaS applications, APIs, IoT and OT systems, and other externally exposed technologies. Expert validation confirms which findings are real and exploitable, removing false positives before they consume remediation time. Prioritization then applies asset, exposure, and threat context to direct attention toward the findings that present the greatest risk. Remediation addresses that risk through activities such as patching, configuration changes, or compensating controls whether performed by internal teams, supported through patch management capabilities, or delivered through managed remediation services for assets requiring hands-on intervention. Retesting confirms that the vulnerability or exposure has been effectively mitigated.

This process also makes vulnerability data more actionable for the teams responsible for remediation. Infrastructure, application, cloud and operations teams often balance security work against availability requirements, development priorities, and other business demands. Providing those teams with contextualized priorities creates a clearer path to addressing the exposures that can have the greatest impact.

That need is growing as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery. Assessments such as SentinelOne's Wayfinder Frontier AI Services can surface validated, exploitable weaknesses across source code, software dependencies and exposed secrets in days, widening the remediation gap between finding a weakness and eliminating it. Closing that gap takes the same discipline: prioritize by real-world risk, give developers actionable guidance and retest to confirm each fix holds.

A risk-based program prioritizes remediation by exploitability and business impact. It expands scope to the full attack surface and focuses that effort around several key principles:

Evaluate exploitability: Determine how practical exploitation is within the organization's environment.

Connect vulnerabilities with critical assets: Incorporate the systems, sensitive data and business processes that could be affected.

Understand exposure: Assess how accessible vulnerable assets are and the potential attack paths leading to them.

Track attacker activity: Incorporate current threat intelligence and evidence of exploitation as conditions evolve.

Account for compensating controls: Understand how existing safeguards affect the likelihood and potential impact of exploitation.

Retest and verify fixes: Confirm, through retesting and pre-production review, that remediation or mitigation produced the intended reduction in exposure.

Together, these factors turn scanner output into a focused remediation strategy and give security teams a stronger basis for communicating priorities across the organization.

Effective vulnerability management services help organizations prioritize the vulnerabilities that represent the greatest risk and direct remediation resources accordingly. By combining vulnerability data with exploitability, asset criticality, exposure, attacker activity and existing controls, security teams can turn a growing volume of findings into clear, defensible priorities and measurable risk reduction.

Leveraging best-of-breed technologies, LevelBlue helps organizations focus remediation efforts on the issues most likely to impact their business, while dashboards track progress and support compliance with standards such as PCI DSS, HIPAA, NIST and ISO. For organizations that need additional support moving from identification to resolution, LevelBlue also offers Patch Management and Remediation as a Service capabilities that accelerate risk reduction across both traditional and non-traditional assets. Organizations working through Wayfinder Frontier AI Services findings can further extend that approach through LevelBlue’s Remediation Sprint and Application Resilience Program, which provides developer-focused remediation and independent validation of fixes.

Title: The Vulnerability Playbook Is Broken: A CISO’s Cheat Sheet To AI-Era Cybersecurity
Context: When a fix does exist, attackers can use frontier AI to analyze it shortly after it is published and build exploits targeting systems that haven’t yet applied it
Full Text:
Vulnerability remediation has been following the same outdated playbook: A scanner finds a vulnerable component, a ticket gets filed, a developer gets assigned. Then a pull request gets reviewed, and a pipeline runs. Then weeks or months later, the vulnerability is closed. That playbook assumed one thing: We have time.

We no longer do.

Exploitation Before Disclosure: The Structural Shift

Over the past year, frontier AI models have changed the daily calculus for security and DevOps leaders. AI developers have reported that their most capable models can autonomously find software vulnerabilities and develop working exploits. That puts components with no upstream fix, such as end-of-life packages and abandoned libraries, at particular risk.

Crucially, the assumption that disclosure precedes exploitation no longer holds, and frontier AI is accelerating that shift. The window between a flaw existing and being actively exploited has collapsed – in some cases to nothing at all.

With the clock at zero, remediation is fundamentally a speed problem, and mean time to remediate (MTTR) no longer favors the defender. If your workflow depends on a human pause at every step – manual triage, pull request reviews, sequential approvals – it will struggle to keep pace.

You cannot fight machine speed with human delays.

Where Today’s Approach Breaks Down

As the industry confronts machine-speed threats, new problems have emerged that many remediation workflows were not designed to handle.

When No Fix Exists. When frontier AI discovers vulnerabilities in end-of-life components, or chains findings into exploits with no corresponding CVE, remediation tools that depend on upstream fix availability have nothing to apply. There is no patch to apply. There is no version to bump to.

When The Fix Arrives Too Late. The mirror image is equally dangerous. When a fix does exist, attackers can use frontier AI to analyze it shortly after it is published and build exploits targeting systems that haven’t yet applied it. Every hour between fix availability and fix deployment is an open exploitation window. The organizations that understand this treat fix deployment speed as a security metric, not an operational convenience.

When a Fix Exists and You Are Running a Self-hosted Environment. Securing self-hosted or hybrid environments is a shared responsibility between vendor and customer. While vendors regularly release critical security patches and updated remediation capabilities, keeping these platforms secure requires active, ongoing updates. Staying current on supported releases ensures your environment benefits from the latest protection against emerging threats.

In our view, none of the AI-era problems mentioned above can be closed by any single tool. Closing them requires a system – one built deliberately across five interconnected layers.

The Required Approach: A Five-Layer, Self-healing Architecture

Matching machine speed requires an architecture that can support it in a machine-automated way, with minimal requirements for human attention. We call this a Self-Healing Software Supply Chain – five critical layers, each addressing a different part of the problem, each one complementing and completing the next.

Prevent – Block risk before it enters. While this layer doesn’t directly solve the problems above, it helps keep new ones from forming. Before you can address what’s already inside, you need to stop adding to it. Flag something before it enters. Swap it automatically for a compliant version, so development keeps moving.

Detect – Find what’s already inside. Conduct regular scans of the different components in your pipelines – packages, binaries, containers, AI models. Detection must operate at the binary level, not just at the manifest level, to catch issues that manifest scanning can miss.

Prioritize – Focus on what can actually be exploited. Not every finding is a real risk in your specific environment. Contextual and reachability analysis help identify the exploitable vulnerabilities in your codebase – so remediation effort lands where it matters.

Remediate – Close the gap automatically. This is where a single approach is rarely enough:

Remediation agents draft fixes for first-party code, with a developer reviewing each change. That review is an important safeguard, but tracking what each agent changed, why, and under what policy is a real challenge at scale.

Hardened package providers manufacture patches for the exact version you run, but automatically getting those patches to every build while adhering to your policies is a separate delivery problem.

Automatic remediation allows you to automatically intercept the artifact request at the repository layer and serve a verified patched version in its place – designed to avoid pipeline disruption. For supported package types, ask for version 1.2.3, receive a fixed 1.2.3, recorded automatically, under policy. Source fixes from multiple providers, such as hardened package vendors and your own patches. Avoid locking into one vendor. This is only possible when a single, universal repository layer sits between every build and the packages it requests.

Prove – Make every action auditable. A fix that produces no evidence is a risk, not an asset. Every remediation action must generate a cryptographically signed record – what was fixed, when, under which policy. The same is true for what was not fixed. Every waiver or exception should be tracked, including the remediation plan, so teams can confirm the follow-through is completed. Ideally, the process generates evidence automatically, so nobody has to assemble it by hand afterward.

Traceability extends past the fix itself. Every dependency in your release should stay under your custody. You can reproduce a build, trace a fix to its source, or swap a provider without losing your history. Lose that lineage, and you depend operationally on decisions someone else made for you.

Seven Properties That Make a Self-Healing Software Supply Chain Work

The five layers above work best when they follow the right properties. In our view, these are the minimum design requirements for a self-healing supply chain.

Automated remediation. Remediation runs automatically, under rules your team sets. Humans govern it through policy, not through manual approval on every action.

Policy-driven. Every remediation action is designed to operate within your organizational guardrails, so changes follow the policies you approve.

Auditable. Every remediation action is signed and traced, producing evidence you can use for audits and regulatory reviews.

Machine speed. Remediation works to close the exploitation window as threats emerge.

Frictionless. Fixes are designed to be applied without breaking builds or slowing developer workflows so security can keep pace with delivery.

Integrated in pipelines. A bolted-on solution lacks the context and the ability to act safely, from blocking risk at the door to fixing what’s already inside. Remediation must be part of the system, throughout the software lifecycle, not layered on top of it.

Universal by design. Remediation can draw on fixes from multiple vendors and sources, so teams can choose the best available fix for their specific environment.

Where This Leaves You

This CISO cheat sheet is not about closing every gap perfectly – it’s about building a supply chain that heals faster than attackers can exploit it. When prevention, detection, and remediation work as one continuous system instead of several disconnected tools, the same speed that once favored attackers starts working for you.

Fewer tickets pile up. Fewer patches wait on human bandwidth. The question shifts from “how did they get in?” to “how fast did we already fix it?” CISOs can walk into board meetings with answers instead of open questions. Engineering teams no longer have to choose between shipping fast and staying secure.

Organizations that adopt this self-healing CISO cheat sheet now can turn remediation speed into an operational advantage.

Title: Optimizely Flaw Exploited to Serve Malicious Code to Visitors of 178 Organizations
Context: Read more on software supply-chain attacks: Attackers Hijack Popular WordPress Plugins to Deploy Backdoors Report URI said the real number of affected organizations was likely...
Full Text:
An attacker has exploited a flaw in the website testing platform of Optimizely, a digital experience platform, to plant malicious code that reached visitors of 178 organizations' websites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, according to security researchers.

Scott Helme, a security researcher at Report URI, said that his team found the code in 188 of the 1611 Optimizely snippets it checked. Other affected organizations included Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA and Optimizely itself.

Optimizely confirmed the incident in a November 17 notice, saying an "unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.

It said it had fixed the flaw, removed the injected code and taken steps to secure affected user accounts.

What the Malicious Code Did

The attacker inserted code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, a custom-code field that runs on every page, and left the rest of each snippet untouched. The tampered files were still served from Optimizely's trusted content delivery network with its certificate, Report URI explained.

The injected JavaScript swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's own, and Report URI said those wallets had received about $7,040 by 19:25 UTC on November 16 before being emptied early the next day.

The code also worked as a card skimmer, capturing card details typed into websites' own forms, though cards entered in hosted payment iframes were out of its reach. It also stole some cookies and page screenshots.

On iPhones and iPads, the JavaScript delivered two iOS exploit kits, which Report URI identified as Coruna and DarkSword. Report URI advised visitors to update to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later.

How the Optimizely Attack Unfolded

The first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC on November 16, and Report URI said all infected files had been cleaned by 23:11 UTC.

The attacker has not been named, but Report URI said one of its wallets had been in use since March 2026, and linked the same actor to an earlier wave of injections through other third-party scripts.

"Supply chain breaches may be an inherent weakness of the web in its current form, but this doesn't excuse organizations from failing to reduce their own attack surface," said William Wright, CEO of Closed Door Security, in emailed comments.

Read more on software supply-chain attacks: Attackers Hijack Popular WordPress Plugins to Deploy Backdoors

Report URI said the real number of affected organizations was likely higher, as it could only check snippets it found in time.

Title: 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour
Context: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the...
Full Text: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether. Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2, manually – no AI required. He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command. "Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote. Meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree." He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery." He went on to claim: "Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does)." Later firmware adds "session control," an authentication mechanism whose strict setting blocks unauthenticated access to most web interfaces. But Meijer found a memory corruption flaw in that protective layer too. He described the final zero-day as a "trivial" pre-auth memory corruption bug which again starts with a segfault but can be wangled into an RCE "with some additional effort." Meijer also considered whether attackers could maintain access after a reset, as seen with implants such as Saltwater and Firestarter. He considered this feasible because the controllers do not use their processor's secure boot features. "In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike – increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food," said Meijer. "Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable – requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid." Meijer's priority for operators was to remove the controllers' direct internet exposure, rather than spend scarce resources on piecemeal patching. He said the vendor's advice following the attacks on European supermarkets and blood banks in recent weeks – rotating creds, applying patches, enabling strict session control – was insufficient given the flaws in the controllers' codebase. "This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible," said Meijer. "We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure." The CCB likewise urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately, but also recommended applying patches when they become available. Beyond the liberal use of strcpy(), Meijer criticized the absence of standard exploit mitigations, including stack canaries and position-independent executables. "These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features... requires no engineering work at all," he said. "It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled." The Register asked Danfoss to respond to the findings, but it did not reply. Danfoss has consistently blanked our requests for information since being implicated in at least some of the attacks that affected European supermarkets recently, alongside rival controller vendors Copeland and Dixell. It also did not respond when we asked about its involvement in the attacks on US commissary appliances over the summer, after some alleged that its controllers were targeted. ®

Title: Researchers Detail iPhone Flaw That Let Apps Record Audio Despite Denied Microphone Permission
Context: Neither Apple nor the two researchers who found the flaw report that it was used in attacks
Full Text:
A now-patched flaw in Apple's audio service let apps on iPhones and iPads record audio even after the user tapped "Don't Allow" on the microphone prompt.

The first security updates with the fix came out on August 17. Neither Apple nor the two researchers who found the flaw report that it was used in attacks.

Nik Tsytsarkin of Meta Red Team X published the technical details last week. Mustafa Calap, a security engineer who reported the same flaw separately, published his own analysis the same day.

On iPhones, an orange indicator shows when an app is using the microphone. On one of the researchers' earlier test builds, that indicator stayed off while the app recorded.

In Tsytsarkin's tests, the prompt appeared the first time the app opened. Declining it did not stop the recording, and the prompt did not reappear on subsequent launches.

In the earlier build of his technical analysis, the system logs showed no record of the app using the microphone. They named the audio service itself as the recorder.

His demo video shows the indicator while the test app records with no microphone permission. He wrote that the video "was filmed on a later build that appears to have restored the orange microphone indicator."

Calap's test app recorded while its permission still read denied, according to his detailed write-up. No orange indicator appeared in the Dynamic Island or in Control Center. He does not say which of his two test builds that was.

Neither researcher describes a way for users to check whether an app recorded them before the fix. Calap reproduced the bypass on iOS 26.6, released July 27, and on an iPadOS 27 beta.

The bypass needed an app already installed on the device. His two test apps were sandboxed apps with no added entitlements. Their only privacy key was NSMicrophoneUsageDescription, which makes the microphone prompt appear.

In his tests, recording had to start while the app was in the foreground. Once started, it continued after the app went to the background and after the device was locked. The background version also set UIBackgroundModes = audio.

Both apps were installed from Xcode and never went through App Review. So the tests do not show whether App Review would have stopped such an app.

The Meta analysis compared two iOS 27 test builds. Neither researcher reports testing macOS, tvOS, watchOS, or visionOS, though fixes are listed for those systems too.

The bypass covered microphone capture through the audio service only. It did not give the app other privacy permissions.

These releases fix the flaw, which is tracked as CVE-2026-65339:

iOS 26.6.1 and iPadOS 26.6.1 (August 17), for iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 3rd generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 1st generation and later, iPad Air 3rd generation and later, iPad 8th generation and later, and iPad mini 5th generation and later

iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 (October 26), for iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and iPad 7th generation

macOS Tahoe 26.6.2 (August 17)

macOS Sequoia 15.8 (September 14)

tvOS 27 (September 14), for Apple TV 4K 2nd generation and later

watchOS 27 (September 14), for Apple Watch Series 9 and later

visionOS 27 (September 14), for Apple Vision Pro (all models)

The researchers describe no setting that blocks the bypass, so installing these updates is the fix.

The iOS 27 notes do not list the flaw, nor do those for later iOS 27 updates as of today. Meta's timeline says the fix shipped in iOS 27.0 beta 5 on August 10.

CISA gives the flaw a CVSS score of 5.0 out of 10. The agency's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities does not list it, as of the catalog's update late last week.

Apple's notes for the August 17 updates describe the flaw only as one that may let an app leak sensitive user information.

Tsytsarkin wrote: "That description leaves out the most striking part: the app could record after permission was denied, without the orange indicator appearing."

In his own tests, the indicator was missing only on the earlier build. An app does not decide for itself whether it may record. That decision goes through the Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC) system, which checks which process is asking.

The audio service, called audiomxd, accepted the app's own word about which process was asking. An audit token identifies a process. An app could send the service a token that named audiomxd itself.

The service then treated the app as itself. It took a shortcut meant for its own internal audio and allowed recording without asking TCC. The kernel itself provided the app with the details it needed to impersonate the service.

The fix makes the service check the real caller's identity, which the kernel supplies. Outside callers now need the private entitlement com.apple.private.audio.client-audit-token-override to replace the client identity the service relies on. An app cannot grant itself that entitlement.

Title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
Context: This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java...
Full Text:
Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.

Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.

Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.

Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Phishing scheme exploiting Microsoft outage | Kaspersky official blog
Context: How attackers lure victims to a phishing site Since Microsoft services went down suddenly on Friday and remained unavailable until the end of the workday, operations at...
Full Text:
As you are probably aware, Microsoft experienced a global outage on November 12 that affected Microsoft 365 services, among others. By the morning of November 14, service functionality had been fully restored; however, cybercriminals are still attempting to exploit this news story in their phishing schemes. The email campaign I want to warn you about in this post targets corporate users and is still being detected by our security solutions even today — November 17.

How attackers lure victims to a phishing site

Since Microsoft services went down suddenly on Friday and remained unavailable until the end of the workday, operations at companies that rely on Microsoft 365 as their primary communication tools came to a virtual standstill. Many employees are still unsure whether their services have been restored, and, more importantly, don’t understand the cause of the incident and fear it might happen again. Exploiting this uncertainty and fear, cybercriminals are sending emails with the alarming subject line “Outlook is disconnected after the Microsoft 365 outage”, purportedly on behalf of Microsoft. In these emails, they claim that Outlook, SharePoint, and Exchange Online may not function properly until the recipient reconnects their Office account.

The email contains a verification code and a link that the recipient is supposed to follow to “reconnect”, which in reality leads to a phishing site.

What are the attackers trying to achieve?

The attackers’ website mimics the Microsoft login screen. Of course, there is nowhere to enter the code provided in the email — a code that no one requested. But they warn in advance that it may have expired, so maybe it might be necessary to generate a replacement. The attackers first ask victim to enter an account name, then offer to send a new code, and finally ask to enter it. However, at every step there’s a “Use your password” link.

Apparently, the attackers were trying to create a universal scheme designed to either connect an unauthorized device to a Microsoft 365 account or steal corporate credentials. Particularly telling is the same “outage” message left in the sign-in window, which is supposed to be a standard one rather than one tied to a specific use case.

We’ve already discussed how the device connection scheme — also known as Device Code Phishing —works on the Securelist blog. In short, as soon as the email recipient clicks the “Send code” button, the attackers’ scripts begin connecting an unauthorized device to the victim’s account. Microsoft sends a genuine code; the victim enters it on the attackers’ website, and the attackers relay it back to Microsoft. As a result, all data accessible through the Microsoft 365 account becomes available to the attackers.

And if the victim doesn’t want to go through the trouble of sending the code, they can simply hand over their password — the attackers will find a use for that, too.

How to stay safe

First and foremost, we recommend regularly raising employee awareness about modern cyberthreats (for example, using the Kaspersky Automated Security Awareness Platform), particularly by explaining exactly how modern phishing schemes work. In addition, it makes sense to explain to employees that if they receive any authorization code they didn’t request or expect, that’s a red flag.

And to ensure that phishing emails cause employees less concern, it’s best to block them at the corporate email gateway level. For this purpose, we offer a specialized solution: Kaspersky Secure Mail Gateway.
