Node.js release lines that have reached end of support, including 20, 23 and 25, do not receive a fixed release. Akamai said its telemetry "shows that 61% of networks are running affected Node.js versions."

JFrog Security Research showed that the flaw also reaches FFmpeg through the libjxl library, by way of Brotli-compressed metadata in JPEG XL files. JFrog obtained instruction-pointer control in FFmpeg with a crafted JPEG XL file but did not demonstrate code execution. The same research produced an infinite-loop denial of service in Apache Arrow, which uses Brotli for compressed Parquet data, with a crafted 534-byte input, and crashed a tested ClickHouse server with a single malformed Brotli-compressed HTTP request. Python HTTP clients such as urllib3, requests, httpx and aiohttp are also in scope when the Brotli or brotlicffi package is installed.

Does updating the system Brotli library fix the issue?

It depends on where the software gets its decoder. Programs that load the operating system's copy of Brotli pick up the fix once they restart. Node.js, Bun and other applications that ship with a built-in copy keep the flawed decoder until a fixed release of that application is installed.

Is every .NET, Envoy Proxy or Istio installation exposed?

No. These platforms are exposed only when Brotli decompression is in use.

.NET: Microsoft says an application "is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed," and ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are off by default. Applications are in scope when they use ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient response decompression, or the Brotli APIs in System.IO.Compression such as BrotliStream and BrotliDecoder. NativeAOT and self-contained applications pick up the fix only when they are rebuilt and redeployed. Microsoft says .NET Framework is not affected.

Envoy Proxy and Istio: Envoy Proxy is exposed only when its Brotli decompressor is configured, and Istio users are potentially affected when they enable Brotli decompression, for example through an EnvoyFilter. Istio 1.29 reached end of support on October 15. Its 1.29.9 release includes the fix.

Is PHP affected by CVE-2026-111497?

PHP's official Windows builds are affected, because they include their own copy of Brotli. On October 26, PHP released updated Windows builds that bundle Brotli 1.2.1. PHP names its cURL extension as the route to the flaw in those builds, once automatic decompression of HTTP responses is enabled. cURL keeps that setting off unless an application or HTTP client library enables it. On other platforms, PHP can still reach a vulnerable decoder through the system Brotli library or through the PHP brotli extension, which bundles its own copy and fixed the flaw in version 0.21.1. The PHP source releases are unchanged, and this flaw is separate from the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities covered in our FAQ.

Is CVE-2026-111497 being exploited in the wild?

On October 26, threat intelligence firm ELLIO reported that its sensors recorded an exploitation attempt against CVE-2026-111497. ELLIO said the attempt targeted Node.js 24.22.0 on x86-64 and combined code copied from public PoCs with an original exploit chain. Tenable has not independently confirmed this activity. On October 27, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, with a remediation due date of November 10 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies.

Has Tenable Research classified this vulnerability as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-111497 has been classified as a “Vulnerability of Interest” as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available for CVE-2026-111497?

Yes. Public PoCs for CVE-2026-111497 are available on GitHub. The Imperva Red Team demonstrated code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image after multiple attempts, and has not released that exploit. At least one public PoC on GitHub claims code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 under narrow lab conditions. ELLIO said it reproduced code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64.

How reliable is exploitation of CVE-2026-111497?

According to ELLIO, an exploit has to be tuned to the specific Node.js build it targets. ELLIO reported that an exploit tuned for the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64 produced nothing in 10,000 attempts against Node.js 22.23.3 and 26.12.0, which each need their own memory offsets. Even against the matching build, most of ELLIO's 400 lab attempts against an Express server crashed the worker process instead of returning a shell, but where workers restart automatically, an attacker gets repeated tries. The exploit request ELLIO captured in the wild did not produce a shell in 50 lab attempts against a vulnerable Node.js 24.22.0 target. Imperva also needed multiple attempts to achieve code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 on Linux arm64.

Are patches or mitigations available for CVE-2026-111497?

Fixed versions for Google Brotli, Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, the Python Brotli packages and PHP for Windows are listed in the table above. As of October 26, ClickHouse had merged a fix without shipping a release, and the Apache Arrow issue remained open.

Patching does not reach code that is already running. The fixed decoder takes effect in a process or scheduled job only after a restart, and in a container only after its image is rebuilt and redeployed.

Where patching is delayed, the Patch the Planet mitigation guide and the broccoli2shell.com tracker list temporary steps that reduce exposure:

Blocking requests marked Content-Encoding: br at the proxy or load balancer, so they stop before anything decompresses them. This step does nothing for applications that fetch Brotli responses from attacker-controlled servers, and turning off Brotli compression on an origin server or CDN has no effect on decompression.

Turning off Brotli decoding in HTTP clients. Taking br out of the Accept-Encoding header falls short by itself, since a hostile server can still reply with Brotli-encoded data.

Disabling the Brotli decompressor filter in Envoy Proxy and Istio in both directions. A disabled filter forwards compressed bytes as they arrive, which leaves any downstream service that decodes Brotli at risk.

Removing the Brotli or brotlicffi package from Python environments until a patched version is in place.

Are there any indicators of compromise for CVE-2026-111497?

ELLIO published the source IP address and a payload hash for the exploitation attempt it observed. They are available in ELLIO's blog post.

Has Tenable released product coverage for CVE-2026-111497?

A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-111497 as they're released. This link will display all available plugins for this vulnerability, including upcoming plugins in our Plugins Pipeline.

[R1] Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities Arnie Cabral Mon, 10/26/2026 - 11:07

Tenable Network Monitor leverages third-party software to help provide underlying functionality. Several of the third-party components (OpenSSL, curl, expat, libxml2) were found to contain vulnerabilities, and updated versions have been made available by the providers.

Out of caution and in line with best practice, Tenable has opted to upgrade these components to address the potential impact of the issues. Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 updates OpenSSL to version 3.5.9, curl to version 8.21.0, expat to version 2.9.0 and libxml2 to version 2.15.4 to address the identified vulnerabilities.

Title: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A working exploit for a Linux kernel flaw has been made public before the bug received a CVE identifier or a merged upstream fix.

Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent that report and five others to maintainers and public mailing lists on October 20 and 21, according to analysis published by the Sysdig Threat Research Team on October 24.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported when Sysdig published its analysis, but several flaws still had no fix in any released kernel.

Public Disclosure Creates Patch Gap

ZDI-CAN-33367, the flaw with the public exploit, is a local privilege escalation (LPE) bug in the Linux networking stack that ZDI gave a CVSS score of 7.8. It can allow an unprivileged user to alter the in-memory contents of files they can only read.

It sits in a code path the kernel's fix for the earlier Dirty Frag page-cache flaws missed. Linux support provider TuxCare reproduced a root shell with the public proof of concept (PoC) on AlmaLinux 8 through 10, CloudLinux 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Sysdig said.

Two of the other five, ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, are the highest rated, at 9.0, and affect ksmbd, the kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) server. The first is a remote, pre-authentication flaw that can leak kernel memory and crash systems, while the second requires SMB Direct, a Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) interface and a writable share.

Read more: Rushed Patches Follow Broken Embargo on New Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

Exposure Varies Across Linux Systems

Of the remaining three, ZDI-CAN-34068 is an LPE rated 8.8 in the kernel's VMware graphics driver. Sysdig said there was no patch and only the report's title was public.

The last two are ZDI-CAN-34076, an information leak in the kernel's Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target, and ZDI-CAN-32005, a userspace stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager.

Sysdig said defenders should prioritize by the components they run rather than CVSS scores. It advised unloading ksmbd where it is not needed, restricting port 445 to trusted networks where it must stay and watching for a vmwgfx patch on VMware guests.

For ZDI-CAN-33367, Sysdig said restricting unprivileged user namespaces should block the public PoC, though TuxCare had not validated this, and noted that rootless containers depend on them. AlmaLinux had patched kernels in testing, but not production, by October 23.

The disclosure leaves a fragmented patching picture, but the public root exploit makes ZDI-CAN-33367 the most immediate concern of the six.

Title: Microsoft Issues Emergency Patch Update for Critical .NET Buffer Overflow Flaw
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Microsoft has released out-of-bound (OOB) security updates for its .NET developer platform, which includes a fix for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability.

The tech giant published the updates for .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 Release Candidate 3 on October 25. Platform users have been urged to apply the updates as soon as possible to reduce the risk of compromise.

They contain patches for two newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as well as two flaws that were not fully addressed in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday rollout.

Single updates are available for each of the affected .NET versions and .NET 11 RC2 users should update to RC3 to receive these fixes.

.NET is a free, open-source framework that developers can use to build apps and cloud services. It is managed by Microsoft and is supported on Windows, Linux and macOS operating systems.

Updates Address Critical Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

One of the new vulnerabilities addressed is CVE-2026-111497, which affects .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 across all operating systems.

The vulnerability is contained in the Brotli decompression algorithm, which is used by .NET. It can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory, leading to information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege.

Microsoft said that applications may be affected if they process Brotli-compressed data through ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient automatic response decompression or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs.

The flaw has a critical CVSS Score of 9.2. Users of Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 also need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries to the latest available version.

Brotli was designed by two engineers at Google in 2015 to allow developers to speed up algorithm compression for developers.

Microsoft’s OOB update also addresses CVE-2026-114148, which can allow an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally by exploiting unsafe ownership metadata in affected .NET tarballs.

CVE-2026-114148 affects .NET versions 7-11, but only for Linux systems. For .NET 10 and .NET 11, CVE-2026-114148 affects source-build tarballs only. For .NET 8 and .NET 9, it also affects ASP.NET Core distributions obtained through ASP.NET Core tarballs, including users who do not build .NET from source, the advisory noted.

It has not been assigned a CVSS score at the time of writing but has been reserved by a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA).

In addition, Microsoft has re-issued fixes for two vulnerabilities disclosed in its October 13 Patch Tuesday rollout. These are for CVE-2026-70197, a memory corruption flaw affecting .NET versions 8-11, and CVE-2026-102870, a code injection vulnerability affecting .NET 10 and 11.

Remediation Guidance for Developers

Microsoft issued advice for .NET users on how to update their applications and build environments in light of the updates. These include:

Install the updated runtime for the .NET version for your framework-dependent application, then restart the application

Rebuild and republish self-contained applications with the updated runtime

Rebuild and redeploy containers using updated .NET container images

Obtain the updated source-build artifacts for your .NET version and rebuild your packages to incorporate the tarball ownership fix

For ASP.NET Core tarball users on .NET 8 and 9, update your installation using the refreshed ASP.NET Core Runtime tarball for your .NET version

Title: Blue Initiative Offers Maritime Sector Dedicated Vulnerability Database
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

Title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

Title: PHP Patches Two Critical Unauthenticated RCEs (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): [Updated for CVE-2026-115560]
Context: In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers - and the model that found these is the same kind of model attackers now have, which is the premise behind Evo...
Full Text:
On Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 to fix two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2, that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The PHP security team advises: "There are no complete mitigations; updating is the only safe choice."

These are bugs in the PHP runtime, not in a Composer package. That changes how you detect and fix them, as we explain below

TL;DR If you run PHP that serves web requests (PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed), update to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 today. If you are on 8.1 or older, get a backported package from your distribution or LTS vendor, or upgrade.

What happened

Times are in UTC.

October 20: The PHP security team published an advance notice of a critical security release scheduled for October 21 at 14:00 UTC. It fixes two vulnerabilities assessed as CVSS v4.0 9.2, with the right reserved to release early if details leak or exploitation is seen in the wild.

October 21, before 14:00 UTC: Snyk published advisories for both CVEs, SNYK-UNMANAGED-PHP-21347795 (CVE-2026-109618) and SNYK-UNMANAGED-PHP-21347796 (CVE-2026-109619), to alert customers to the action they will need to take and so that monitored projects get a hit the moment the fixed versions are known.

October 21, 14:00 UTC: The PHP security advisory and the four fixed releases go live. Within about 30 minutes, Snyk's advisories are updated with all relevant details, including affected ranges and fixed versions.

October 21 onward: Linux distributions (which received the patches in advance) start publishing their own advisories. Snyk publishes advisories for them as they appear, for example SNYK-UBUNTU2604-PHP85-21373920. The running list is at CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Update @ October 23: keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0

On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for CVE-2026-115560, a CVE that is reserved but not yet assigned. It describes a partial bypass vector for CVE-2026-109619. The setting that prevents it, session.upload_progress.enabled=0, was already listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619.

PHP is not rushing an emergency fix because the preconditions for exploitation are rare and unlikely to apply to most deployments. An application must configure session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(), while session upload progress is enabled. Applications that never change the serialization handler at runtime can keep the feature on.

The vulnerabilities

Both are in the request lifecycle of the PHP engine, making them reachable before any application code runs. This is one factor that makes these vulnerabilities both widespread and dangerous.

Technical details

CVE-2026-109618, RCE via out-of-memory corruption: Out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup, then treats the invalid data as valid. An attacker who can drive a worker to its memory limit with a malicious request can trigger the interrupt.

CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state: Request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it. In a long-lived worker model that comprises a cross-request use-after-free.

These bugs were found with AI assistance, in a runtime that has been in production for three decades. In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers - and the model that found these is the same kind of model attackers now have, which is the premise behind Evo by Snyk: AI-driven security for the applications that agents run on, not only for the agents themselves. AI-assisted discovery is also why PHP2Shell won’t be the last flaw of its kind, and why response timelines are now measured in hours.

Who is affected

All PHP installations serving web requests are at risk. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, etc. Apache with mod_php is most vulnerable, with a demonstrated exploit in which a single unauthenticated request triggers the attack before application code runs.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, so an unpatched 8.1, 8.0, or 7.4 install is affected with no upstream fix. Given the severity, the PHP security team did publish minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 for people who build from source or have no LTS vendor.

What you should do now

Update. Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Note that 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026, so if you are on 8.2, this is also your cue to plan the next bump.

Check your vendor. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches ahead of release. Pull their updated packages rather than waiting for a source build. A patched distro build can keep an older version number, so check the distro’s advisory or patch level too.

Verify what’s actually running. Check the PHP version on each host and image (php -v or the image tag). Scan results alone can’t confirm that an installation is fixed.

If you cannot update today, PHP lists mitigations that reduce exposure to specific paths without making an install safe: memory_limit=-1 set where applications cannot override it, a low post_max_size, session.upload_progress.enabled=0 followed by a restart of every worker, and on 8.5 fatal_error_backtraces=0. See the relevant advisory for the caveats on each.

Whether or not you have updated, keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0 set until the next regular bugfix release if your application switches session.serialize_handler at runtime. See the update above for details.

On PHP 8.1 or older, upgrade to a supported version or get a backported package from your distribution or LTS vendor. PHP’s source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are a last resort for teams building from source.

The open source side

The PHP security team gave the ecosystem a day's notice with a fixed time, a severity, and no exploitation details. They pre-shared patches with Linux distributions so packaged fixes could be released alongside the source release. They published backports for unsupported versions (7.4, 8.0, 8.1). They told users of a popular volunteer repo (rpms.remirepo.net) that it would not be updated on day one and what to do instead. And their mitigation guidance is very transparent about what each setting does not protect against.

That is what coordinated disclosure looks like when a volunteer-run project does it right. It is also why, at Snyk, we were able to have advisories live before the release and complete shortly after it: a published schedule lets everyone downstream prepare.

Snyk SCA Behavior

Snyk Open Source reads what your application declares in manifest or build files, like composer.json, composer.lock. The PHP interpreter is not a declared dependency. It is installed by a Dockerfile, a distribution package, a platform image, or by hand. A "php": ">=8.2" constraint in composer.json tells you what the application accepts, but not precisely what is deployed.

How the Snyk Platform helps you find exposed PHP

What you use

What you will see for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Snyk Open Source (CLI or SCM integration)

The CVEs themselves are not reported because the PHP runtime is not a regular dependency in your manifest file. For PHP/Composer projects, Snyk shows the application's declared dependencies, which can help you identify which of your projects are PHP applications. The declared PHP version constraint does not tell you which version is deployed.

Snyk C/C++ Unmanaged scanning

Advisories are reported when the PHP runtime is present in your project, and can be filtered by CVE ID.

Snyk Container

PHP installed from Linux distribution packages is reported once the distribution has published its advisory. Some supported distributions have published advisories, which are available in test results (for example, SNYK-RHEL10-PHP84-21392647 and SNYK-UBUNTU2604-PHP85-21373920). We are importing others as they publish, which are available here: CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619. PHP compiled from source, including the official php: Docker images, is not detected by Snyk Container.

Snyk API & Web

Snyk API & Web allows you to scan your applications and APIs and detect if you are vulnerable to the PHP2Shell vulnerability.

Title: Broccoli2shell: Everything You Need To Know About The Critical Brotli Decoder Vulnerability
Context: A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library
Full Text:
A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library. The vulnerability affects multiple widely used technologies, including Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and more. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to trigger memory corruption, disclose sensitive information, crash affected processes, or potentially achieve remote code execution (RCE).

Organizations using affected components to decompress untrusted Brotli-compressed data are advised to prioritize remediation.

CVE-2026-111497 was discovered and reported by Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer (OpenAI Codex Security), with fixes implemented by Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel (Node.js). Ron Masas (Imperva Red Team) demonstrated its exploitability, while OpenSourceMalware and Aikido analyzed its impact on the Python ecosystem.

What is CVE-2026-111497?

Broccoli2Shell (a.k.a Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell) originates from an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, a widely adopted compression component used to reduce the size of HTTP traffic and other data. The flaw occurs when the decoder improperly handles specially crafted compressed data during block-processing operations, potentially writing beyond allocated memory boundaries. An attacker can exploit this behavior by supplying malicious Brotli-compressed input to a vulnerable application, potentially resulting in memory disclosure, application crashes, or arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected process. Researchers have demonstrated successful exploitation against unpatched Node.js environments.

Although initially associated with Node.js, the vulnerability originates in the upstream Brotli C decoder and extends to multiple downstream technologies that incorporate the affected component. Exploitation requires an application or dependency to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data, either through incoming HTTP requests, externally fetched responses, or other untrusted compressed content. Certain HTTP clients and application frameworks may perform decompression automatically when Brotli support is enabled, potentially exposing applications even when Brotli is not explicitly referenced in application code.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

Cloud environments are particularly exposed due to the widespread use of Brotli-enabled components across containerized applications, Kubernetes clusters, API gateways, reverse proxies, serverless workloads, and cloud-hosted web services. Internet-facing applications that process attacker-controlled requests, as well as internal services that retrieve compressed responses from untrusted external sources, may provide exploitation paths. Successful exploitation could enable attackers to compromise application workloads, access sensitive information, disrupt service availability, or execute malicious code within affected containers or runtime environments.

According to Wiz data 91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497, and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances.

Which products are affected?

Additional products that bundle or link against vulnerable versions of the Brotli C decoder may also be affected. Organizations should consult vendor-specific security advisories, particularly for statically linked libraries and embedded dependencies. End-of-life runtime branches should be migrated to supported versions.

Which actions should security teams take?

Organizations should prioritize the following mitigation and remediation measures:

Apply security updates: Upgrade affected Brotli libraries, Node.js runtimes, Python packages, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and Istio deployments to their respective patched versions or later supported releases.

Identify vulnerable cloud workloads: Inventory virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, containers, serverless functions, API gateways, and application dependencies for vulnerable Brotli components. Prioritize internet-facing services and workloads processing untrusted compressed data.

Review application exposure: Identify applications that decompress Brotli-compressed HTTP requests, external HTTP responses, uploaded files, or other attacker-controlled content. Include indirect and transitive dependencies in the assessment.

Rebuild and redeploy affected workloads: Update container base images, dependency lockfiles, and bundled libraries. Rebuild and redeploy affected container images, restart running processes, and verify that patched components are loaded.

Implement temporary mitigations: Where immediate patching is not possible, consider disabling Brotli decompression or rejecting Brotli-encoded requests before they reach vulnerable components. Restrict untrusted compressed responses where feasible. These controls may reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

Strengthen monitoring and detection: Review WAF, application, and network logs for suspicious Brotli-compressed traffic, unexpected application crashes, and anomalous process behavior. Monitor affected workloads for indicators of exploitation.

Title: OpenRouter Drops 3 Providers After Researchers Catch Months of Prompt Theft at AI Hosting Firms
Context: The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had...
Full Text:
Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week.

Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored.

OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said.

The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said.

The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it.

The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack.

The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server.

On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections.

"A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer.

The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found.

The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys.

One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt.

A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab.

A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint.

Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt.

In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings.

OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned.

The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties.

The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week.

Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers.

Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted.

What the Providers Have Disclosed

An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections.

Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated.

A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window.

At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July.

The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts.

Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers.

Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three.

The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week.

What Users Should Do

The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price.

Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check.

Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys.

A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.

Title: Rackspace Spot breach let hackers access customer Kubernetes secrets
Context: The company disclosed the breach in a notification sent to affected customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, stating that attackers accessed parts of the platform on November...
Full Text:
Rackspace warned customers that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform using compromised credentials, allowing them to deploy unauthorized workloads and access Kubernetes secrets in customer clusters.

Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes.

The company disclosed the breach in a notification sent to affected customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, stating that attackers accessed parts of the platform on November 17, 2026, between approximately 00:20 and 22:00 UTC.

Rackspace says it learned of the intrusion on November 18 after receiving a customer report and confirmed that the recipient's organization was affected that same day.

"On 17 November 2026 (about 00:20–22:00 UTC), an unauthorized party used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot," reads the notification.

According to Rackspace, the attackers were able to act as legitimate users in some customer organizations, allowing them to create pods in Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes.

Kubernetes Secrets store sensitive information such as passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys that can be used to access databases, cloud services, and other systems.

Rackspace warned that the attackers could have read any Secret stored in an affected user's clusters, as well as any Spot API tokens or refresh tokens held by that user.

The company says it has since revoked affected tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods, rotated keys, and strengthened access controls and monitoring.

Affected customers have been instructed to reissue their Spot API tokens, replace refresh tokens used in automation tools, download fresh Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their cluster Secrets.

Rackspace also advised customers to analyze logs associated with databases, container registries, Git repositories, cloud storage, and third-party services dating back to November 17 to identify possible abuse of exposed credentials.

The company shared the following indicators of compromise associated with the attack:

IP address: 23.224.79.106

IP range: 23.224.0.0/15

Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes: i1, glm-, and probe

BleepingComputer contacted Rackspace to ask how many customers were affected and whether customer data was stolen, but has not received a response.

The breach also caused an extended outage of the Rackspace Spot administration console, temporarily preventing customers from managing their clusters and rotating potentially compromised credentials.

In a Reddit discussion, Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and Chief Growth Officer of Platform9, which co-developed Rackspace Spot with Rackspace, explained that the company deliberately disabled access while securing its infrastructure.

"I've been instrumental in creating Spot and in its operations to date, and I can tell you that the team and I are incredibly disappointed to have let you down in this way," Raghuram said.

"I know you disagree, but we made the decision that shutting all access down and sanitizing the entire environment is what we can do to best protect everyone using Spot."

After multiple delays, Rackspace announced that service had been fully restored on November 21.

Title: Cyberattack on Austrian Foreign Ministry Exposes Diplomatic Staff Data
Context: A major service disruption can complicate incident response and monitoring, but the available information doesn’t show that attackers exploited the outage to gain access
Full Text:
Austrian Foreign Ministry Hacked, Staff Contact Details Accessed

Hackers accessed Austrian Foreign Ministry records containing staff contact details, including employees at diplomatic missions abroad.

Austrian Foreign Ministry confirmed a cyberattack against its website that exposed staff contact information, including details of employees working at diplomatic missions abroad. The security breach occurred between November 12 and 13, during a global Microsoft outage, and raises questions about the security of government websites and the risks associated with services managed by external providers.

According to the ministry, attackers gained unauthorized access to a website operated by an external service provider. The intrusion was detected on November 13, and authorities said they stopped it immediately.

“”Between November 12 and 13, the foreign ministry’s website, which is operated by an external service provider, was accessed in an unauthorized ​manner,” the ministry said in a statement, adding that it happened ​during a global Microsoft outage.” Reuters reports.

The ministry confirmed that the hack was detected on November 13 ⁠and government staff stopped it immediately.

An investigation by a team of cybersecurity experts found that the intruders had viewed records containing the names and professional contact details of ministry employees. The information covered both staff at the ministry’s headquarters in Vienna and personnel working at Austrian diplomatic missions abroad.

“An investigation by a team of experts ​found that during the unauthorized access, data records were viewed that listed ​the names and work contact details of employees at ministry headquarters as well as at diplomatic missions abroad,” the ministry added.

The Austrian authorities have not disclosed how many records were accessed, whether the attackers copied the information, or how they managed to enter the website. They have also not identified the vulnerability or attack technique used.

The ministry stressed that the incident did not affect citizens’ personal information. According to Austrian public broadcaster ORF, the authorities reported the incident to the Federal Office for Cyber Security and the Data Protection Authority, while also launching additional technical security checks.

“The Foreign Ministry emphasized that it was taking the incident “very seriously.” The integrity of the infrastructure was of the highest priority. The systems were subject to strict security regulations and continuous monitoring, it stated. The incident had also prompted additional technical security checks.” states ORF. “The Foreign Ministry has been repeatedly targeted by cyberattacks. At the beginning of 2020, there was a serious cyberattack that lasted until February. In April 2022, there were cyberattacks involving phishing emails.”

The timing of the incident is also noteworthy. The ministry said the intrusion coincided with a global Microsoft service outage, but it hasn’t established any connection between the two events. A major service disruption can complicate incident response and monitoring, but the available information doesn’t show that attackers exploited the outage to gain access.

Attribution remains another unanswered question. The ministry hasn’t named any suspected country or threat group, and there’s no evidence linking this particular intrusion to a state-sponsored operation.

However, the incident comes against a difficult diplomatic background. Austria has maintained military neutrality but has politically supported Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In July 2026, Vienna publicly accused Moscow of being responsible for a cyberattack against the Foreign Ministry in late 2019 and early 2020, joining eight other EU member states in condemning Russian cyber operations.

“The ministry did not suggest who might be responsible.” states Reuters.

Russia has repeatedly rejected Western accusations of hacking. Diplomatic tensions have also increased following Vienna’s decision to expel four Russian diplomats in October, bringing the total number of Russian diplomats declared persona non grata by Austria since 2020 to 18. Moscow promised an appropriate response and subsequently expelled an Austrian trade delegate working at the country’s embassy in Russia.

“Russia has repeatedly denied Western hacking allegations.” Reuters concludes.

Beyond the political context, this incident offers an important security lesson. Government websites may not host classified information or directly manage critical services, but they can still expose information that attackers can use to target employees, build convincing phishing campaigns, identify diplomatic personnel or gather intelligence about government operations.

The involvement of an external service provider also deserves attention. Outsourcing website management doesn’t outsource security responsibility. Public institutions need visibility into their suppliers’ security controls, access privileges, logging and incident response procedures, and must ensure that these arrangements receive regular independent checks.

Names and professional email addresses might appear to be low-value information, but they can help attackers prepare highly targeted operations. In diplomatic environments, even basic contact details can provide useful intelligence for social engineering and further intrusions.

Protecting government infrastructure also means protecting the people whose information and professional relationships can become the starting point for the next cyberattack.

Title: BADBOX botnet returns with record-breaking 40 billion daily ad requests
Context: BADBOX was first discovered in early 2023 on a T95 Android TV box bought on Amazon
Full Text:
The BADBOX malware botnet has returned following last year's disruptions, generating a record 40 billion fraudulent advertising bid requests per day through infected Android-based devices.

According to HUMAN's Satori researchers, who uncovered and disrupted the latest variant, BADBOX 3.0 had grown into the largest documented ad-fraud operation by daily bid request volume.

BADBOX was first discovered in early 2023 on a T95 Android TV box bought on Amazon. In December 2024, Germany's cybersecurity agencies warned that the botnet had infected tens of thousands of devices.

In March 2025, a large-scale disruption operation took place where HUMAN and Shadowserver cut off more than 500,000 BADBOX 2.0 devices from their control servers, while Google removed 24 apps that spread the malware from Google Play.

Google later sued the botnet's operators, saying the BADBOX 2.0 had infected over 10 million Android-based devices by April 2025.

BadBox returns

However, the previous disruptions didn't stop the BADBOX operators from rebuilding the botnet and setting new records for daily fraudulent advertising bid requests.

"At its height, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform," reports HUMAN.

"BADBOX 3.0's volume was more than three times the volume of the previous record holder, VASTFLUX, and represents a larger peak than the last five years' worth of published Satori investigations combined."

The modus operandi remains the same: infecting cheap phones, tablets, and streaming TV boxes running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) with malware that performs ad fraud and traffic proxying.

The malware performs ad fraud by playing video ads in hidden windows while impersonating legitimate streaming apps to make the requests appear legitimate.

HUMAN also observed fraudulent server-side ad insertion (SSAI) requests that tricked advertisers into believing ads were played on streaming devices, even though no actual device or video ad was involved.

A proxying module also enrolled infected devices in one of 11 residential proxy networks without the owners' knowledge or consent.

One of those networks, PXYEDGE, was identified as the rebranded successor to IpMoYu, a residential proxy service previously linked to BADBOX 2.0.

The researchers say PXYEDGE advertised approximately 200,000 proxy nodes, while their monitoring showed unique connections peaking at around 340,000.

HUMAN says some of the ad fraud traffic was also routed through these residential proxies to appear legitimate and evade anti-abuse filters.

The researchers linked the malware to a specific Chinese electronics manufacturer through its domains, device-specific checks in the code, a factory-installed TV launcher, and a repository maintainer.

The infected devices fetch malware modules from public code repositories, while the same payloads are also mirrored across various hosting platforms for redundancy and to resist takedowns.

HUMAN says it also participated in Google's disruption of the related XCPE malware operation earlier this month, which included taking down multiple C2 domains used by BADBOX 3.0.

Additionally, one of the malware repositories was taken down, while HUMAN says its systems now filter fraudulent advertising traffic associated with BADBOX 3.0.

However, HUMAN warns that the botnet operators are likely to adapt to the latest disruption, as they have done in the past.

Users should only buy certified Android devices from reputable manufacturers and ensure that Play Protect is available and active.

Title: A Single Malicious Webpage Let Researchers Hijack Meta Muse and Access Private Chats
Context: The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack...
Full Text:
A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown.

The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts.

The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes.

Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer.

There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach.

Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage."

In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up.

From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown.

That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent.

The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines.

Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through.

The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in.

The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

Title: Scope down permissions of existing sessions using AWS STS GetScopedCredentials
Context: When you build AI agents, you often want each agent or sub-agent to have only the permissions its tasks require, rather than the full permissions of the session that started it
Full Text:
When you build AI agents, you often want each agent or sub-agent to have only the permissions its tasks require, rather than the full permissions of the session that started it. GetScopedCredentials is a new AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) API that you can use to scope down the permissions of existing temporary security credentials. You can assign each agent, sub-agent, or process its own set of credentials that keep the caller’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity but carry reduced permissions, a shorter session duration, or both.

You can call GetScopedCredentials with the temporary security credentials you already use, such as those from aws login, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance profile, or an AWS Lambda function. In each call, you pass a scope down policy, a shorter session duration, or both. A scope down policy is an inline policy that describes the maximum permissions for the new credentials. The resulting permissions are the intersection of your session’s effective permissions and the scope down policy, so they can only be reduced. Similarly, the session duration you request can’t exceed the remaining duration of the calling session. You can also call GetScopedCredentials again with the resulting credentials to scope down permissions or reduce session duration even further.

GetScopedCredentials is designed as a building block. Because it scopes down permissions on the credentials you already have, you can build it into agent frameworks, services that issue credentials to other components, continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, and your own applications. You can also call it again with scoped-down credentials, so an orchestrating agent can give each sub-agent narrower access than its own.

In this post, we walk through a few common use cases to get you started, show you how to call GetScopedCredentials, and explain how to manage access to it.

Example use cases

You can use GetScopedCredentials whenever a workload needs narrower access than the session that starts it. Examples include limiting what AI agents can do, scoping down permissions based on runtime context, and granting just-in-time access. We cover two of the most common use cases in more detail in this section.

Limit what AI agents can do

When you pass credentials to an agent, the agent can use any permission those credentials carry. An agent decides which actions to take at runtime, often based on prompts or tool output. If its credentials are overly permissive, an agent that makes a mistake can act beyond the task you gave it.

Before you pass credentials to an agent, you can use GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions to only what its tasks require, such as read access to a single Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket. You could also take the opposite approach and keep most of its permissions while removing only the actions the agent should never perform, such as deleting resources. An orchestrating agent can do the same for each sub-agent it starts. Because a scope down operation can only narrow permissions, a sub-agent never has more access than the agent that started it. To help ensure that your agents only have access to the scoped-down credentials, run them in isolated or sandbox environments such as AWS Strands Box.

Scope down permissions based on runtime context

Many workloads run under a single IAM role but need different, narrower permissions for each task they perform. The right set of permissions for a task often depends on information the workload learns only at runtime, such as who sent a request.

Consider a multi-tenant application that stores each tenant’s files under a separate prefix in one S3 bucket. This application uses a single IAM role to serve all its tenants, so the role can access every tenant’s prefix. However, each request should reach only the files of the tenant who sent it, and the application learns which tenant that is only after it authenticates the request. At that point, a trusted credential broker in the application takes the tenant details from the authenticated session and calls GetScopedCredentials with a scope down policy that allows access only to that tenant’s prefix. It passes only the scoped-down credentials to the worker that handles the request, so Amazon S3 denies that worker access to other tenants’ prefixes even though the original role covers them all.

How to call GetScopedCredentials

This section walks through the process of scoping down permissions for an existing session. Before you call GetScopedCredentials, make sure you have valid temporary security credentials and that they have the permissions to call the API. The following identity based policy grants that permission.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sts:GetScopedCredentials", "Resource": "*" }] }

To call GetScopedCredentials, use the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDK for your programming language.

Step 1: Define a scope down policy

Write a scope down policy that describes the maximum permissions the resulting credentials should have. At launch, GetScopedCredentials accepts one inline scope down policy of up to 2,048 characters. You can write a scope down policy in many ways, such as authoring a policy from scratch, reusing or modifying an existing policy, or asking an AI assistant to draft one. This section covers two such approaches.

Option A: Write the policy yourself If you know which actions and resources your task needs, write the policy directly. The following sample policy allows the resulting credentials to only read objects from a single S3 bucket.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*" }] }

Make sure to include every action the task needs, including dependent actions. For example, if your task uses Amazon Athena to query data in Amazon S3, the policy must also allow s3:GetObject on that data, because Athena reads it with your credentials.

To keep most of the calling session’s permissions and remove only a few sensitive ones, use an Allow statement with NotAction. This statement doesn’t grant additional access, because a scope down policy can only reduce permissions. The resulting credentials keep the calling session’s permissions except the actions you list, which makes this a quick way to set guardrails without listing each action a task needs. The following sample policy blocks identity and account management, assuming other roles, and deleting some critical resources.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "NotAction": [ "iam:*", "organizations:*", "account:*", "sts:AssumeRole*", "s3:DeleteBucket", "ec2:TerminateInstances", "rds:DeleteDBInstance", "dynamodb:DeleteTable" ], "Resource": "*" }] }

Option B: Generate the policy with IAM Policy Autopilot You can also use IAM Policy Autopilot to generate a scope down policy. IAM Policy Autopilot is an open source tool from AWS that analyzes the AWS SDK calls in your code and identifies the permissions it requires to run successfully. You can run it from the command line or as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in your AI coding assistant. To install it, see the Getting Started instructions for IAM Policy Autopilot.

We’ll use the following Python code to generate a scope down policy using IAM Policy Autopilot. It records a report’s status in an Amazon DynamoDB table.

import json import logging import os import boto3 from botocore.exceptions import ClientError logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) dynamodb = boto3.client("dynamodb") table_name = os.environ["TABLE_NAME"] def _response(status_code, message): return {"statusCode": status_code, "body": json.dumps({"message": message})} def handler(event, context): try: request = json.loads(event.get("body") or "{}") report_id = request["reportId"] except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, TypeError): return _response(400, "Request body must be JSON with a reportId") if not isinstance(report_id, str) or not report_id: return _response(400, "reportId must be a non-empty string") try: dynamodb.put_item( TableName=table_name, Item={ "reportId": {"S": report_id}, "status": {"S": "READY"}, }, ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(reportId)", ) return _response(200, "Report status saved") except ClientError as error: code = error.response["Error"]["Code"] if code == "ConditionalCheckFailedException": return _response(409, "Report status already exists") logger.error("PutItem failed: %s", code) return _response(500, "Unable to save the report status")

Save the code as report_status.py and run the following command. If the generated policy exceeds the 2,048 character limit, set the max-policy-size and allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size options to 2048. IAM Policy Autopilot then replaces groups of actions with wildcards to fit that size and warns you if it can’t.

iam-policy-autopilot generate-policies ./report_status.py \ --region us-west-2 \ --account 123456789012 \ --service-hints dynamodb \ --max-policy-size 2048 \ --allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size 2048 \ --pretty

IAM Policy Autopilot returns the following policy.

{ "Id": "IamPolicyAutopilot", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:WriteDataForReplication" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-west-2:123456789012:table/*" ] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "kms:Decrypt" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/*" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": [ "dynamodb.us-west-2.amazonaws.com" ] } } } ] }

IAM Policy Autopilot generates a starting policy that can include wildcards, either because specific resources can’t be inferred from the code, such as with the table/* and key/* resources in this example, or because an optional parameter that limits policy size replaced actions with wildcards. Review the generated policies and replace the wildcards with the actions and resources your task should access.

However you create the policy, save it as scope-down-policy.json. If you want to continue calling GetScopedCredentials with the resulting credentials, also include the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in the Allow block of the permission policy.

Step 2: Call GetScopedCredentials

Pass the scope down policy you created to GetScopedCredentials. The following command also uses the optional duration-seconds parameter to limit the resulting session duration and the optional scoped-session-description parameter to record context for the scoped-down credentials. If you omit the duration-seconds parameter, the credentials keep the calling session’s remaining duration.

aws sts get-scoped-credentials \ --policy '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"}]}' \ --duration-seconds 300 \ --scoped-session-description report-status-job \ --region us-west-2

The response includes a new set of temporary security credentials, a SessionInfo element, and some helpful information about session size and contents.

{ "Credentials": { "AccessKeyId": "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE", "SecretAccessKey": "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY, "SessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...", "Expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z" }, "SessionInfo": { "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane", "ScopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane" }, "SessionTokenUtilization": 17, "SessionTokenSize": 724, "ScopedPoliciesCount": 1 }

Notice that the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the SessionInfo element matches the ARN of your calling session. The scoped-down credentials retain the identity of the calling session, including the role session name, session tags and context keys.

The ScopedPoliciesCount value in the response shows how many scope down policies apply to the session. It increases only when a recursive call adds a new scope down policy and not when a call only shortens the session duration.

Each GetScopedCredentials call is logged in AWS CloudTrail. The following event, shortened for readability, shows the call from this example.

{ "eventVersion": "1.11", "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "principalId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:janee", "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane", "accessKeyId": "ASIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE", ... }, "eventTime": "2026-10-12T02:55:00Z", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventName": "GetScopedCredentials", "awsRegion": "us-west-2", ... "requestParameters": { "policy": "{\"Version\":\"2012-10-17\",\"Statement\":[{\"Effect\":\"Allow\",\"Action\":\"s3:GetObject\",\"Resource\":\"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*\"}]}", "scopedSessionDescription": "report-status-job", "durationSeconds": 300 }, "responseElements": { "credentials": { "accessKeyId": "ASIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE", "sessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...", "expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z" }, "sessionInfo": { "scopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane", "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane" }, "sessionTokenUtilization": 17, "sessionTokenSize": 724, "scopedPoliciesCount": 1 }, "readOnly": false, ... }

The scopedSessionDescription value in the CloudTrail event records the text you passed to the API call earlier. Later calls made with the scoped-down credentials show the scoped down session’s access key ID in userIdentity.accessKeyId, which can be used to trace back to its immediate parent session.

Step 3 (optional): Scope down the credentials again

You can call GetScopedCredentials recursively with the scoped-down credentials to narrow permissions or reduce session duration even further. You can apply a maximum of three scope down policies to a session, and each new scope down policy intersects with all prior ones. Recursive calls that only shorten the session duration and don’t add a scope down policy don’t count toward this limit. For a recursive call to succeed, every earlier scope down policy must allow the sts:GetScopedCredentials action.

Managing access to GetScopedCredentials

You can control access to the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in all relevant policy types. You can also use the sts:DurationSeconds condition key to limit the session duration of scoped-down credentials, and global condition keys such as aws:PrincipalArn, aws:PrincipalTag, and aws:SourceVpce to restrict who can call the API and from where.

Availability and request quota

GetScopedCredentials is available in all AWS commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. The API has a dedicated request quota of 200 requests per second per account in each Region at launch. You can use scoped-down credentials with most AWS services. For a list of services that aren’t supported, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference.

Conclusion

GetScopedCredentials gives you a building block for reducing permissions at runtime. This is particularly helpful when you want to give each agent, sub agent or workload only the access it needs.

For more information about GetScopedCredentials, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference. To learn how permissions are evaluated for scoped-down credentials, see Permissions for GetScopedCredentials and Policy evaluation for requests within a single account. Now go build!

Executive Summary

Unit 42 has tracked and responded to numerous waves of vishing attacks conducted by Com-affiliated threat actors in recent months. The attacks have led to data theft and extortion attempts. This activity has targeted data-rich industries, such as financial services, healthcare and legal services. Targeted organizations were primarily located in the U.S., UK and Australia.

Attribution for this broad activity includes:

Named actors such as Bling Libra (aka ShinyHunters)

Activity clusters CL-CRI-1116 (aka Redact, formerly BlackFile), CL-CRI-1147 (aka Pink), CL-CRI-1182 (aka Falcon), CL-CRI-1192 (aka Helix)

The newly uncovered CL-CRI-1264 (aka Vortex) and CL-CRI-1274 (aka Cinder), which overlap with activity Google tracks as UNC6671

This article details:

Our observations of persistent Com-affiliated threat activity since August 2026 based on unique telemetry analysis and incident response engagements

The different named actors and activity clusters we track, including unique observations not previously disclosed

Insights on victimology

Review of attacker tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs)

Allusions to future activity as we head into 2027

Background

Since early 2026, we have responded to numerous data theft and extortion attempts that we have attributed to Bling Libra and other Com-affiliated threat actors. More details on the typical playbook used by the attackers can be found in the Tactics, Techniques and Procedures section of this article.
