Latest Insights

Emerging Activity Cluster CL-CRI-1264 (Vortex)

In September 2026, we identified a new activity cluster that we track as CL-CRI-1264. The tradecraft used by the attackers largely follows the wider playbook used by Com-affiliated threat actors, but a few traits set it apart. Most notably, we observed this activity primarily targeting healthcare, pharmaceutical and other medical organizations.

Attackers associated with CL-CRI-1264 establish initial access through vishing, where they pose as internal IT support and direct employees to servers using subdomains tailored to each targeted organization. These servers act as adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) proxies that pass user credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) approvals to the attackers in real time. Attackers have targeted employees on both their corporate workstations and personal mobile devices.

We have observed attackers behind CL-CRI-1264 enrolling an unauthorized MFA device within minutes of authenticating to establish persistence. In multiple instances, the attackers have reused a single device named Pixel 10a across compromised accounts. They have also automated data exfiltration using Python scripts (python-httpx User Agent) to target Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive and SharePoint content.

Following exfiltration, the attackers have sent Microsoft Teams messages directly to employees at victim organizations, claiming data theft and directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site.

Emerging Activity Cluster CL-CRI-1274 (Cinder)

In September 2026, we identified another new activity cluster that we track as CL-CRI-1274. Similar to other activity detailed throughout this report, the attackers used vishing for initial access and avoided re-prompting for Duo MFA by replaying a persistent “keep me signed in” session token. They then replayed that same session token from proxy infrastructure.

From there, they used scripted access through python-requests (python-requests/2.34.2) and the Microsoft Graph software development kit (SDK) to collect and exfiltrate data from the victim’s SharePoint and OneDrive environments. Afterwards, the attackers used a compromised account to send extortion messages internally via email and Microsoft Teams, ultimately directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site.

Malicious Browser Extension

During an investigation attributed to another activity cluster, CL-CRI-1192 (which Google tracks under UNC6671), we identified a malicious browser extension (manifest version 1.6.111) named Google Chrome.

The extension was not on the Chrome Web Store. It was downloaded from an attacker-controlled server at oskeysetup[.]com and required the victim to manually sideload it using Developer Mode. Naming the extension Google Chrome helps disguise the browser's built-in warning banner (Google Chrome started debugging this browser) when the extension is active.

This domain's registration information closely resembles attacker infrastructure previously disclosed by Google and ReliaQuest in relation to the activity that we track as CL-CRI-1192.

This browser extension performs several malicious actions:

Installs global keyloggers

Steals local/session storage and IndexedDB data across all sites

Harvests authentication cookies (targeting Microsoft and Google accounts)

Scans pages for QR codes to capture login/MFA tokens

Streams webcam feeds

Furthermore, this browser extension implements a full command-and-control (C2) remote control module via Chrome DevTools Protocol (chrome.debugger). It allows operators to perform the following activities:

Capture hidden screenshots

Dispatch input events

Steal clipboard contents

Allow remote site navigation

We pivoted on this file and identified an additional browser extension also masquerading as Google Chrome (version 1.6.112) that communicates with the same C2 server. Both files share the same hard-coded API key.

We assess with moderate confidence that the attackers associated with CL-CRI-1192 developed this malicious browser extension as an alternative method to extract credentials from desktop and laptop devices running Chromium-based browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge. The extension might also be shared with and used by other Com-affiliated attackers, although we currently have no evidence to suggest this.

We recognize Kevin Pham for his detailed investigation into this browser extension in a September 2026 write-up.

Victimology

Our telemetry shows sustained campaigns by Com-affiliated threat actors accelerating significantly around August 2026. The victims share a common profile: they hold large volumes of high-impact corporate data where exposure carries severe regulatory, legal or market consequences. Financial services, healthcare and legal organizations were primary targets, though activity spans across other industries.

Rather than targeting generic mailboxes, actors systematically sought individuals or systems responsible for high-value files, documents and databases. These attacks focused on:

Legal and corporate strategy: Actors targeted partner communications, firm strategy, executive compensation and pending contracts. They explicitly threatened to publish client agreements and confidential casework.

Financial and investment records: Attackers prioritized private investment portfolios, deal pipelines and large-scale cloud data warehouses. They occasionally exfiltrated tens of millions of customer relationship management (CRM) and recruiting records.

Healthcare and life sciences: Attackers targeted cloud data platforms containing patient records and proprietary research. To maximize pressure, actors broadcast extortion notices across internal chat channels and threatened regulatory reporting.

The most targeted organizations have distributed workforces, centralized single sign-on (SSO) and extensive cloud collaboration platforms. They are also predominantly based in English-speaking countries. We have observed actors repeatedly targeting the same organization, sometimes returning weeks after a failed attempt.

Who Is Being Targeted: Industries and Countries

Our monitoring of domains linked to Com-related activity showed that their targeting shifted from financial services to healthcare in early September 2026. Figure 1 shows that these attackers targeted financial services organizations about twice as often as healthcare organizations in August 2026, but healthcare overtook financial services in September, around when we first observed CL-CRI-1264 activity. Healthcare continued to be the most targeted industry in October 2026, alongside financial services. Attackers also frequently targeted construction, high technology and transportation and logistics organizations.

Figure 2 shows that between August and October 2026, most targeted organizations were based in the U.S. However, we observed increased targeting of Australian organizations beginning in late September 2026. Australian organizations made up less than 1% of observed subdomains in August and September, rising to about 13% in October. Organizations in Australia are now the second most targeted.

Tactics, Techniques and Procedures

Infrastructure and Tooling

A key characteristic of Com-affiliated threat actors is their use of apex domains that pose as SSO portals, IT support pages and passkey configuration services. These domains often host short-lived subdomains that impersonate target organizations, such as {company}.mfaregister[.]com. We actively track this infrastructure, conduct threat hunting for identified domains and publish key findings as Timely Threat Intelligence (TTI) in our GitHub repository.

Across Com-affiliated cases, we have identified similarities in hosting infrastructure, attack chains and victimology. In some cases, these actors also share tooling, such as Doko's Panel, an operator-controlled AiTM phishing kit.

As previously reported by Push Security, some Okta-targeting variants of the kit replace the panel's default backend.php handler with the renamed endpoint api_FyekIDWY.php. We observed this endpoint on multiple domains associated with Com-affiliated cases.

In at least one financial services case, telemetry recorded a full AiTM sequence from credential entry to an MFA number-match prompt, indicating a likely successful session capture, as shown in Figure 3.

Domains consistent with Com-affiliated infrastructure have also been observed in campaigns that use different techniques to target victims. For example, Microsoft reported oskeyregister[.]com in its research into passkey-themed social engineering.

Building on this reporting, we identified Cloudflare Pages URLs following the pattern connect-pages-{company}.pages[.]dev that redirect to company-specific subdomains such as {company}.oskeyregister[.]com. These findings reflect the broader Com ecosystem, which comprises several activity clusters that frequently share infrastructure but can vary slightly in their tradecraft.

Beyond shared infrastructure, recurring patterns in the registration and deployment of tooling associated with Com-affiliated threat actors provide additional opportunities to identify related domains. Table 2 shows common registration patterns observed across this activity.

Attacker Playbook

We did not observe a standard playbook employed by Com-affiliated threat actors. Rather than employing custom tools, the threat actors primarily leveraged native cloud utilities and selectively limited executions and persistence deployments.

Intrusions typically begin with vishing, in which threat actors pose as IT staff resolving an authentication issue and direct the victim to a phishing page tailored to their organization. After the AiTM kit captures credentials and session tokens, the attackers quickly enroll their own MFA devices, misuse cloud utilities and, in some cases, deploy malicious browser extensions to exfiltrate data and extort victims.

Using the harvested authentication data, Com-affiliated threat actors authenticate to victim environments, typically routing through residential proxy networks and commercial VPNs. They then seek to establish multi-layered persistence, enumerate sensitive data and exfiltrate data from cloud platforms. We observed the following techniques across Com-affiliated threat actors:

Persistence

Enrolling unauthorized MFA devices and workstation objects

Generating cloud infrastructure temporary credentials

Authorizing unapproved third-party OAuth applications or data-sync utilities

Staging secondary accounts or harvesting redundant credentials

Discovery and Defense Evasion

Monitoring authentications, permissions and mailboxes

Modifying calendar settings and mailbox rules

Clearing security alert events

Rotating infrastructure

Exfiltration

Using open-source tools such as Rclone and cloud storage platforms

Exfiltrating via native SaaS and REST APIs or scripted HTTP-based exfiltration

Moving data via SaaS to SaaS transfers

Conclusion

Earlier this year, our 2026 Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report found that extortion incidents in 2025 not using encryption (at 78%) dropped below the 90% range for the first time in several years. This trend has continued into 2026 and we don’t expect a slowdown. Cybercriminals like Bling Libra and other Com-affiliated threat actors are pivoting away from encryption, enabling them to move at greater speed across their intrusion lifecycle while still achieving their objectives.

Another plausible motivation for the shift away from using encryption is to fly below the radar of law enforcement officials, given their crackdown on ransomware operators in recent years. However, shifting away from using encryption no longer seems to be enough to keep them under the radar. This is based on the reported arrests of suspected Bling Libra members such as “Rey” and “Umbreon” that occurred in proximity to the group’s claims of a breach of the FBI.

Recent arrests also include a person who allegedly ran Bling Libra’s extortion site.

Going forward, organizations must:

Tighten help desk verification processes

Transition to phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys)

Implement browser extension allowlists

Establish visibility into identity actions

Alert on unauthorized data exports to mitigate the threat activity described in this article

Title: Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers
Context: In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS...
Full Text: Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses. On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information. Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand. Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers. “We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register. “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.” Mastercard previously said that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program. According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said. It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker. Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text, and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26. “This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he said. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.” Customer data has left the building The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published. All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security company Sentra. In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker said, adding that this is his company’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.” Qubole’s parent company Idera did not respond to The Register’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®

Title: Incident Response at Machine Speed: What Black October’s Record Case Volume Reveals About Today’s Threat Landscape
Context: Organizations are also rapidly adopting AI tools, integrations, and services of their own, expanding the attack surface that their adversaries could exploit
Full Text:
The scale and severity of cybersecurity activity in October 2026 was unprecedented. Arctic Wolf Aurora Incident Response handled 78% more non-Arctic Wolf customer cases than the average month, and sophisticated network intrusion incidents, including ransomware, for non-Arctic Wolf customers rose by 96%, accounting for nearly all of the growth. Attackers aren’t just more active. They’re more dangerous.

But given how quickly the threat landscape is changing, October being our busiest month on record for our Aurora Incident Response team isn’t an anomaly, but rather the start of a new normal.

With a growing volume of disclosed vulnerabilities and the speed with which attackers are exploiting them, defenders should not expect conditions to become less demanding anytime soon.

As we saw from the PHP2Shell and Java4Shell disclosures that dominated recent headlines, attackers appear to be using AI to research targets, identify vulnerabilities, create phishing lures, and run campaigns at a scale that wasn’t possible just a few months ago. Organizations are also rapidly adopting AI tools, integrations, and services of their own, expanding the attack surface that their adversaries could exploit. Together, these behaviors are contributing to a higher volume of incidents and creating more opportunities for attackers to gain access.

From AI-Enabled Attackers to AI-Enabled Malware

But it’s not just AI adoption, or using AI to develop threat tactics and techniques, that is creating this frictionless environment for attackers. Malware itself is starting to use AI during attacks. Rather than carrying all of its instructions from the start, some malware now includes a lightweight loader that reaches out to an LLM for guidance while it runs. In Arctic Wolf’s malware samples we analyzed, we observed Large Language Model (LLM) API calls during execution, showing that AI is increasingly becoming part of the attack chain itself, not just a tool attackers use beforehand.

Today, these uses are relatively simple. We’ve seen malware use LLMs to generate file names, customize payloads, and create convincing social engineering messages on demand. But the same approach could evolve to support more advanced capabilities, such as adapting to security controls, tailoring attacks to specific victims, or helping attackers navigate an environment after initial access.

That creates a challenge for defenders. Traditional malware detections focus on what’s stored on disk, which means they can miss logic delivered in real time through an AI service. In order to build resilience against these kinds of AI-embedded malware, defenders need to monitor runtime behavior more closely, including unexpected processes making outbound connections to LLM platforms or AI APIs. This requires organizations to have full visibility into their environment.

AI has already changed the threat landscape by making sophisticated attacks easier to pull off. Techniques that once required deep expertise are now within reach for a much wider range of attackers, and those attackers can operate at a faster pace and larger scale than ever before. October’s incident data reflects that shift.

For our non-Arctic Wolf customers, business email compromise (BEC) incidents remained relatively steady, but more complex attacks surged. Ransomware cases rose by 77%, pre-ransomware cases rose by 55% and network intrusion incidents as a whole rose 96%.

These advances suggest that as more threat actors gain access to advanced capabilities, organizations are facing a growing volume of serious and potentially damaging attacks. Thankfully, we have insight into who these newly resource-enabled attackers are targeting, how they’re tailoring their attack patterns, and which threat groups are the most active.

More Attackers, More Opportunities for Compromised

The attack patterns observed in October reflect the reality that social engineering, external remote access, and exploitation of internet-facing systems were the most common attack vectors in Aurora Incident Response engagements. AI is helping attackers make these techniques more effective. Phishing messages can be personalized in seconds. Reconnaissance that once took days can be completed in minutes. Attackers can scan large portions of the internet for vulnerable systems and quickly focus their efforts on organizations that appear easiest to compromise.

The ransomware groups most frequently observed in October included Akira, Qilin, INC, DragonForce, and Settra.1 Organizations across legal services, manufacturing, real estate, software development, and financial services accounted for the largest share of incident response cases. These industries continue to attract attacker attention because of the sensitive data they manage, the operational disruption they can suffer, and the financial leverage they often present during an attack.

Organizations do not need to slow AI adoption, but they do need to prepare for an environment where attackers can operate at machine speed. Understanding internet-facing assets, maintaining strong identity controls, reducing unnecessary exposure, and regularly testing incident response plans all become more important as the pace of attacks increases.

Cyber resilience depends on knowing how to respond when prevention fails. The organizations that recover fastest are often the ones that prepared before the incident occurred, established clear escalation paths, and practiced how they would respond under pressure.

1 Threat actor attribution reflects Arctic Wolf’s assessment based on October 2026 incident data and may evolve with new evidence. References to threat actor identity are analytical judgments, not statements of legal fact.

This blog reflects my own views as of the publication date and includes forward-looking statements about technology trends. Actual outcomes may differ based on attacker behavior, customer environments, and broader market and regulatory developments.

Title: n0n extortion gang leaks data of JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard customers
Context: In JPMorgan Chase's case, it tweeted that although it believed "the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and...
Full Text:
Data belonging to customers of three of the biggest companies in global finance has been leaked online, after hackers breached third-party service providers working for JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard.

The finance companies have all acknowledged that security incidents have occurred at unnamed third--party companies, after the n0n extortion gang named all three on its dark web leak site earlier this week.

In JPMorgan Chase's case, it tweeted that although it believed "the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses" there had been "no disruption" to its services.

Mastercard also said that its payment network had not been affected, and that cardholders could continue to use their cards.

According to Visa, the breach occurred at an unnamed third-party provider based in Asia Pacific.

n0n claims to have stolen "hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions" related to JPMorgan Chase. All three of the corporations were given 48 hours to negotiate with the extortion gang, but none of them paid. So, n0n published data on its website exposing the details of thousands of customers.

News of the security breach impacted the share prices of all three companies, after a jittery week of high-profile technology outages in the United States.

According to Reuters, the leaked JPMorgan Chase data included more than 16,000 customer email addresses, and what appeared to be the email addresses of some 124 employees of the bank. Some of the customer information included phone numbers, and post codes.

Clearly scammers and fraudsters could exploit information like that in a variety of ways, including by contacting members of the public claiming to be employees of their bank.

Meanwhile, according to a Cybernews report, the leaked Visa data includes details of over 6000 premium card holders who are signed up to Asia-Pacific dining programmes, including names, phone numbers, the messaging apps they use, and restaurant booking details.

n0n is believed to be a Russia-based extortion gang, and despite only having been operating for a couple of months has already managed to claim the scalps of approximately 200 corporate victims.

Security researchers say n0n has typically broken into organisations using valid login credentials, harvested by info-stealing malware or obtained by credential-stuffing VPNs and poorly secured remote desktop (RDP) services, before using legitimate admin tools to gather data. It is not yet known how the vendors in this case were compromised.

Of course, financial institutions are very experienced at securing their own infrastructure. Where they appear to have fallen down on this occasion is through the use of third-party marketing agencies or loyalty scheme operators who have been less diligent in securing their systems.

You are only as safe as the weakest link in the chain. And customers don't really care whose server it was that leaked their data, when they entrusted it to your care in the first place.

The advice for concerned Chase, Visa or Mastercard customers is simple: be wary of unexpected emails, texts or calls claiming to come from your bank. It would not be a surprise at all if scammers exploit the breach by mentioning it to customers, and offering compensation, or inviting members of the public to "verify" their account.

If you are unsure, contact your bank directly using its published number.

Title: Bell Canada says 'agentic' hacker stole enterprise customer data
Context: Bell told BleepingComputer that it has not yet identified the threat actor responsible for the attack
Full Text:
Bell Canada has confirmed that an "agentic" threat actor breached its systems on November 17, 2026, and stole enterprise customer data, including information from a system used to order and provision telecommunications circuits.

Bell is one of Canada's largest telecommunications providers, offering wireless, internet, television, and enterprise networking services.

BleepingComputer first learned of the incident after receiving a tip from a customer who shared a breach notification sent by Bell's Information Security Team.

According to the notification, an unauthorized party accessed a pre-production environment of Bell's Maximo system, which the company uses to order and provision telecommunications network connections.

Bell warned that information belonging to the recipient's organization may have been stolen, including business contact information such as names, job titles, corporate email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses.

The potentially exposed data also includes information contained in ticket titles and some IP addresses associated with network elements or systems, along with limited contextual information.

However, Bell said the affected dataset did not contain credentials, highly sensitive personal information, PDFs, file attachments, or other supplementary information stored in Maximo.

When contacted by BleepingComputer, Bell confirmed the intrusion and said that an "agentic threat actor" had accessed multiple systems and stolen enterprise customer data.

"Bell is investigating a cybersecurity incident that occurred on November 17 in which an agentic threat actor accessed some of our systems, including a system used for ordering and provisioning circuits, and exfiltrated some enterprise customer data," Bell told BleepingComputer.

"Upon learning of the breach, we immediately contained the incident and secured our systems. There has been no impact to customer services."

The company's description of the attacker as "agentic" suggests that AI-powered tools were used during the breach.

Bell says it is sharing indicators of compromise (IOCs) and threat-hunting information with enterprise customers and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS).

However, Bell has not publicly released the indicators of compromise and has not responded to BleepingComputer's request to share them so other organizations can check their environments for related activity.

Bell told BleepingComputer that it has not yet identified the threat actor responsible for the attack.

"We currently do not know the attribution," Bell said.

Bell has not disclosed how many enterprise customers were impacted or the total amount of data stolen.

In its customer notification, Bell urged organizations to remain cautious of unsolicited requests and social engineering attempts by individuals impersonating the telecommunications provider.

Title: Report: Attackers Are Increasingly Using AI Attack Frameworks
Context: ” Threat actors are also integrating AI into commodity cybercrime platforms to help unskilled crooks launch sophisticated attacks
Full Text:
Threat actors are expanding their use of multi-agent AI attack frameworks, according to researchers at Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG).

The researchers have observed attackers abusing open-source pentesting frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI, which can fully automate large portions of attacks.

“Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally,” GTIG says. “Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions.

Current attacks using these tools are noisy and fairly easy to detect, but GTIG believes this will change in the near future.

“Notably, while these frameworks are capable of significantly compressing attack timelines to machine speed and achieving operational objectives, they currently trade stealth for velocity,” the researchers write. “Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces; while these artifacts increase the likelihood of detection and mitigation, these tools remain highly capable of achieving operational objectives. As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity.”

Threat actors are also integrating AI into commodity cybercrime platforms to help unskilled crooks launch sophisticated attacks.

“The Jieyou phishing service, an active Chinese-language PhaaS platform first observed in March 2026, is primarily used by cybercriminals to deploy and manage highly convincing phishing campaigns, with a particular focus on e-commerce fraud,” GTIG says. “The service introduced an LLM chatbot assistant in its June 2026 backend update. This chatbot allows threat actors to easily configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands, significantly lowering the technical barrier for deploying campaigns....The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier. Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly.”

Title: Bazuka Android Malware Uses Fake Screen Overlays to Hide Credential Theft and Device Control
Context: " ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate LLM
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unknown Android malware framework called Bazuka that offers large language model (LLM) integration for victim management and control at scale.

Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it discovered the threat in late October 2026 during an investigation into an NFC-relay banking Trojan.

"Bazuka is a full malware framework," ThreatFabric said in a technical report. "A dropper/downloader, a core, and 23 modules cover overlays, keylogging, 2FA and SMS interception, remote control, and crypto-address swapping."

One notable aspect of the malware that distinguishes it from the rest is a novel overlay technique that allows the trojan to take a screenshot of the home screen or lock screen, and display that as an overlay on demand to cover up malicious activities taking place in the background.

Another perhaps not-so-surprising element is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the control panel to help operators identify victims of interest and manage infections. It supports both locally hosted models and models accessed through an API.

One of the sample prompts provided by the author refers to a score, indicating an operator can likely request the AI model to score victims and determine how attractive they are as targets. The panel also supports the following capabilities -

Create accounts for traffers, who are cybercriminals responsible for driving victims to malware using various lures

Build droppers containing the malware with options to choose the kind of permissions specified in the Android manifest file likely in an attempt to bypass Google Play app review process

This indicates that the dropper apps can be distributed via at least two distribution channels: through traffers, who can use social media ads or bogus sites to trick users into downloading them, and Google Play Store.

One of the droppers containing the malware masquerades as a premium, adult-friendly version of TikTok (package name: "com.tiktok.premium"). Two different variants of the Bazuka attack chain have been observed -

A dropper, which asks the victim for permissions to install applications from third-party sources and then proceeds to download a standalone APK ("com.tiktok.premium.pro") that serves as the stager

A downloader that directly downloads the main payload

It's suspected that the stager is the same as the downloader, whose main responsibility is to retrieve the core and supplementary modules necessary for a particular campaign, and then launch them.

"Once the core and required modules are loaded, Bazuka operates as a keylogger and a classic overlay trojan, monitoring the text entered by the victim and displaying an overlay at the right moment," ThreatFabric said. "All functionality is controlled by commands from C2 [command-and-control]."

The core module is the orchestrator, maintaining communication with C2, loading additional DEX modules, dispatching commands, collecting device information, and managing permissions and component updates. Like other Android trojans, it abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) shell commands and the operating system's accessibility services to request permissions and grant them automatically.

"Important components of the core include mechanisms for enabling Wireless Debugging and completing the pairing process," ThreatFabric explained. "The core can open the system settings screen, find the relevant menu, enable Developer options, and then enable Wireless Debugging."

"When this mode is enabled, it also intercepts the PIN, which is then used to establish a TLS connection to the ADB daemon."

Furthermore, the core component counters detection by Google Play by disabling the protection component through the accessibility services API. It is also equipped to launch a self-destruct mechanism that clears local storage, deletes the database, and disables the application completely.

Communication with the C2 server takes place over two WebSocket channels -

Control, which is used to issue commands

Data, which is used to exfiltrate data and screen capture streams

Bazuka supports 23 modules that enable comprehensive data and cryptocurrency theft -

call_forwarding, to manage call forwarding through USSD commands

clip_monitor, to act as a clipper and substitute cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard with attacker-controlled ones

contacts, to collect contact information

device_control, to manage the device over the ADB bridge and execute commands as shell commands

file_manager, to access the file system

input_recorder, to act as a keylogger and capture all text entered into a target application, as well as identify bank card numbers, wallet addresses, and passwords in user input

location, to determine a victim's location using GPS, cell tower positioning, and Wi-Fi

media, to capture photos and stream camera video and microphone audio

oem_power, to open system and OEM settings for power saving, background operation, and autostart

optics, to facilitate remote control, screencasting, and phishing overlays

preflight, to perform preliminary checks of the runtime environment

proxy, to implement a reverse TCP proxy

push, to create and manage local Android notifications

screen_control, to capture the lock screen PIN, text password, and unlock pattern through accessibility services

self_adb, to implement an embedded ADB client

session_ui, to display phishing HTML overlays

smsmessage, to access SMS messages and extract potential verification codes, send SMS messages, and attempt to delete messages from the device

system_checker, to check the runtime environment and implement anti-analysis measures

tapread-nfc_module, to interact with contactless bank cards

toast, to display text messages on the device's screen

twofa, to capture one-time verification codes

uninstall_shield, to counter attempts to uninstall or force-stop the application

ussd, to send USSD requests from the victim's device and receive responses from the mobile operator

The malware has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. However, the panel has been found to display UI elements in a mix of English and Russian.

"ADB bridging is becoming a standard feature of modern banking trojans," ThreatFabric said. "While it is not there yet for Bazuka and its current architecture, this is a very concerning sign, as it allows malware to obtain various privileges covertly and deploy independent modules that can survive removal of the host application."

"Another equally concerning feature is the use of LLM chats directly within the control panel. AI agents are used to identify victims of interest."

ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data

Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate LLM. Last week, Zimperium zLabs research team detailed another sophisticated and rapidly evolving Android malware called ArcticRAT that supports 129 distinct commands and incorporates LLM APIs into its data exfiltration pipeline to extract high-value financial intelligence from stolen SMS messages and app data.

"What initially began as a targeted spyware operation aimed at users of 11 specific cryptocurrency apps has morphed into an enterprise grade, AI-powered, Remote Access Trojan (RAT)," researchers Rajat Goyal and Fernando Ortega said.

Infection chains make use of malicious sites impersonating Google Play app listings to convince users to install the dropper app. Unsuspecting users are redirected to these pages through malvertising, smishing, or third-party forums. The apps masquerade as popular brands (e.g., Amazon and TikTok), cryptocurrency applications, and generic file managers.

Once installed, the app abuses Android accessibility services to establish remote control, automate fraudulent activity, and leverage AI to parse and "clean" exfiltrated data. It uses TCP sockets to communicate with the C2 infrastructure.

An initial reconnaissance step is used to build a host profile, which then dictates the C2 server to dynamically select the relevant attack payloads to deploy. At a high level, the malware supports the following features -

Initiate a real-time video transmission from the compromised device

Abuse accessibility services for full remote control

Serve fake extortion overlays and deceive victims into making cryptocurrency payments

Make use of LLMs to process harvested SMS messages and look for financial, banking, and trading apps through hard-coded prompts that ask the model to take the role of a professional SMS analyzer and device app analyzer, respectively

Capture credentials, authentication codes, and private communications

Serve overlays to steal device lock screen pattern, PIN, or password

"The malware requests VPN service privileges to null-route network communication on the victim's device, effectively blinding Google Play Protect telemetry during the staging phase," Zimperium said.

"To prevent the user from interfering with these operations, ArcticRAT employs a defense evasion tactic known as a "Black Screen" overlay. When the attacker is navigating banking apps via Hidden VNC (HVNC) or auto-approving system permissions, the malware draws a completely black, un-dismissible view over the screen and drops the brightness to zero. To the victim, the device appears locked or powered off."

Recent versions of ArcticRAT have also been found to abuse the native Wireless Debugging mechanism to initiate a privileged shell session on the victim machine and execute commands, including enabling or disabling accessibility permissions, verifying lock screen PIN or pattern, and displaying a black screen to conceal background operations.

"By abandoning hardcoded attacks in favor of real-time Hidden VNC (HVNC), raw TCP command-and-control (C2), and aggressive defense evasion overlays, the malware achieves complete device takeover," Zimperium said.

Title: Two Incidents, One Lesson in Trust
Context: But dig a little deeper and you’ll notice that criminals didn’t get in through brute force or exploiting a zero-day vulnerability
Full Text:
Optimizely unfortunately suffered two incidents in nine months, so clearly they must be doing something wrong and the answer to that is to buy a bigger firewall.

But is that really the answer?

One incident started with a phone call. The other started with a flaw in a signup form and ended with malicious code served to visitors of the BBC, CNN, Zoom, and HSBC. On the surface they have nothing in common. But dig a little deeper and you’ll notice that criminals didn’t get in through brute force or exploiting a zero-day vulnerability. They exploited trust. And when trust is the attack surface, your workforce is both the target and a critical line of defense.

February: It's Good to Talk (To the Wrong Person)

On February 11, a threat actor got in touch with Optimizely to say they already had access to its systems. They weren't bluffing. According to the company's own breach notification, the way in was a "sophisticated voice-phishing attack." Someone picked up a phone, and the person on the other end said the right things.

Optimizely says the attacker couldn't escalate privileges, install software or plant backdoors, and what left the building was basic business contact information. SecurityWeek reported that the systems touched included internal business platforms such as Zendesk and Salesforce. Although Optimizely didn't name the group, the tactics seemed consistent with that of ShinyHunters.

While it’s easy to downplay that it’s “just” contact data, it’s valuable information that can be used to craft even more convincing phishing emails or phone calls. A breach of business contacts isn't the end of an attack. It can often be the reconnaissance phase of the next one, aimed at somebody else.

November: The Script Everybody Trusted

On November 16, Scott Helme and the team at Report URI spotted malicious JavaScript in Optimizely files used by 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, Salesforce, and GitLab. Optimizely told BleepingComputer the attacker had abused a flaw in its account signup flow, which let them insert code into customers' Project JavaScript.

The payloads included card skimmers, crypto wallet address swappers, and routing that pushed iPhone users towards an exploit kit.

Not one of those 178 organizations was breached in the traditional sense. Their own systems were fine. They had simply trusted a vendor's script.

To be clear, there's no public evidence that the February and November incidents are connected. One was social engineering, the other a software flaw. But that’s kind of the point. They are two very different routes to one destination.

The Inbox Is Not the Only Door

For years, security awareness was quietly treated as a synonym for "don't click the dodgy link in the email."

Email is still the most popular avenue, but look at where the attacks this year on Optimizely actually came from. A phone call, a helpdesk and CRM platform, and a trusted third-party script running in a browser. Not one of those is an inbox.

That's the reality for most organizations now. Work happens across email, Teams, Slack, Zoom, SMS, voice calls, shared documents, and a long tail of SaaS tools, each with its own notifications, its own login prompts, and its own sense of "this is internal, so it's safe." And that’s before you factor in the increasing number of AI agents.

Vishing groups ring the helpdesk pretending to be an employee. They message staff on Teams pretending to be IT. They follow up an email with a phone call to make it feel real. The more channels we use, the more places trust can be borrowed.

This is why collaboration security matters. Protecting all channels across wherever people talk. They need to have the same defenses to protect them against social engineering whether it comes through an email, a chat message, or a voice note.

Why Training Matters More Than Ever

The February breach is the obvious case of a convincing voice and a person who wanted to be helpful. While you want your helpdesk to be helpful, you need to equip them with the skill to pause when a call, a message or a request seems a bit odd and verify it through a trusted channel.

The recent November breach initially appears like a purely technical problem. Which is partly true. Consider what happens next when customers of 178 organizations now have reason to be worried about their card details. Criminals know that a worried person makes for an easier target. Expect "your account may have been affected, please verify your details" emails, texts and calls, because every high-profile incident is followed by a wave of opportunistic phishing riding on its coattails. Stolen business contact data, like the kind taken in February, makes those follow-ups more targeted and more believable.

Therefore training has to change shape. Annual click-through modules about suspicious emails won't be enough when the threat is an authoritative and polite voice claiming to be from IT, or a Teams message from a "colleague" asking you to approve an MFA prompt. Simulations need to reflect the channels people actually use. Coaching needs to happen at the moment, not once a year. The goal isn't to turn everyone into a security expert. It's to build a culture where checking is normal and nobody feels silly for saying "I'll call you back on the number I've got."

But training isn't a magic bullet either. People will make mistakes, or overlook issues, especially when the attack arrives on a platform they believe is safe. That's why the human layer and the technical layer have to work together to catch what they can across every channel, and trained people who catch what slips through, with each one feeding the other.

What Security Leaders Can Do This Week

Train for all your channels, not just the inbox. Run vishing simulations, especially for helpdesk and support teams who are paid to be helpful and are therefore prime targets.

Make call-back verification a habit. Any request to reset credentials, approve MFA, or move money gets verified through a known number or channel, never the one the request came in on.

Extend protection to collaboration tools. Treat Teams, Slack, and other platforms as attack surfaces, with the same scrutiny you give email.

Brace for the follow-up phish. After any big public incident, warn staff and customers that scam messages exploiting it are likely, and tell them how you will and won't contact them.

Know your third parties. Inventory the scripts and SaaS platforms you trust, monitor what they do, and rotate credentials and tokens when a vendor has an incident.

Make reporting easy and blame-free. The colleague who says "I think I just spoke to a scammer" within five minutes should be celebrated as a win, never shamed for making a mistake.

Trust Is the New Perimeter

Optimizely isn't unique, it's simply a well-known name. The lesson is that trust is now the thing attackers exploit, whether it's trust in a voice on the phone, a message in Teams or a script on a web page.

That's why at KnowBe4 we think about securing the whole workforce. Attack Simulation & Training builds the instincts people need across every channel, Email & Collaboration Security protects email and the platforms where work really happens, and Agent Security looks after the AI agents that increasingly sit alongside your staff. Each layer makes the others stronger.

None of it replaces a person who stops, thinks and says "hang on a minute."

Title: AI-Driven Attacks Are Here. Five Steps CISOs Should Take Now
Context: This open-source attack framework works with almost any LLM, and threat actors began experimenting with it against organizations within weeks of its release
Full Text:
Earlier this year, Claude Mythos Preview showed the security community what a frontier AI model can do when it’s pointed at software, finding and linking vulnerabilities far faster than defenders had ever seen up to that point. Access to that model stayed tightly controlled, but ARTEX has recently removed that corporate barrier for attackers. This open-source attack framework works with almost any LLM, and threat actors began experimenting with it against organizations within weeks of its release.

Although the developer later removed the project from GitHub, the code was quickly mirrored elsewhere and remains accessible. More importantly, we’re seeing these techniques attempted against customers. Arctic Wolf is tracking the emerging use of self-hosted agentic penetration testing frameworks like ARTEX, including AntiFox, operating from public cloud infrastructure. In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were linked to confirmed malicious activity targeting internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments.1 There is no indication the hosting provider was aware of or involved in this activity.

We’re seeing the effects of these enhanced offensive AI capabilities in our own case data. In what some industry leaders are calling ‘Black October’ due to the spike in vulnerability disclosures and threat activity, Arctic Wolf Aurora Incident Response handled 78% more non-Arctic Wolf customer cases than the average month prior, and although Business email compromise (BEC) activity remained relatively flat, more complex attacks surged. Network intrusion attacks, including ransomware, rose by 96%, meaning that attackers aren’t just more active. They’re more dangerous.

CISOs know AI is changing the threat landscape, and our case data reflects that shift. To adapt their security operations to keep pace with this shift, security teams should focus on five areas.

Reset Your Response Timelines

Most incident response plans created pre-AI, or even prior to this year, assume there will be enough time to assess what’s happening, gather the right stakeholders, and make containment decisions before an attacker causes significant damage. Increasingly, that’s not the case, especially in large organizations with long chains of approval. Because AI is helping attackers move faster, organizations need to remove as much friction from their response plan as possible, which means deciding in advance how a security team can take action without waiting for approval.

Map Everything Attackers Can See

AI-driven tools can scan thousands of potential targets at once and quickly identify the easiest path into an environment. That’s why there’s never been a better time for defenders to take full inventory of what systems, applications, and services they use are exposed to the internet. With a full inventory, security teams can prioritize taking action on the exposures that are likely to be targeted first.

Strengthen Identity Controls

Social engineering and external remote access ranked among the most common attack vectors in our October engagements, and AI is making both easier to execute at scale. An attacker can now generate extremely convincing phishing messages, and thus targeted campaigns, in seconds using publicly available information. That makes strong identity controls absolutely critical in today’s security landscape. Organizations should prioritize phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, regularly review their remote access tools and old or inactive accounts, as well as apply the same level of scrutiny to their service accounts and API keys. Those often carry extensive permissions but receive far less oversight than human users, making them an attractive target for attackers.

Monitor Behavior at Runtime

Some malware now contacts an LLM during execution to retrieve instructions on demand, which means some of the script may not exist until the malware is already running. The problem is that traditional controls can miss these kinds of attacks, and defenders may not be paying close attention to their AI services. These signals can be correlated across endpoints and network activity, but they usually occur outside of normal business hours, so organizations need the ability to investigate and respond continuously with 24×7 detection.

Practice Before You Need It

Teams that have already worked through their response process generally spend less time figuring out roles, decisions, and communications when a real incident occurs. Leaders need to regularly schedule tabletop exercises built around AI-driven scenarios, especially as new offensive capabilities go live, and test how their team handles a fast-moving attack, like a ransomware precursor or a large data theft. Security leaders also need to confirm that they have an incident response partner ready to engage quickly when something happens.

Building Resilience at Machine Speed

The fundamentals of security haven’t changed. Organizations still need strong identity controls, visibility into their environment, tested response plans, and the ability to detect suspicious behavior quickly. What has changed is the speed at which attackers can operate. As AI continues to compress the time between compromise and impact, security teams need to make sure their people, processes, and technology can keep up.

That’s why Arctic Wolf has built the Aurora Superintelligence Platform and the Aurora Agentic SOC. Our approach has always been grounded in helping organizations operationalize the fundamentals of security. That means maintaining visibility across their environment, strengthening identity security, continuously monitoring for signs of compromise, and ensuring skilled responders are ready when an incident occurs.

The addition of AI and agentic capabilities allows us to help customers execute those tasks faster and at greater scale, and our 2026 Agentic Security Operations Report outlines the impact we’ve measured. Over the past year of the Aurora Agentic SOC, investigation volume has increased 21%, while alert volume has been reduced by 19%, and we’ve shortened the time from an alert-generating event to an actionable ticket by 36%.

At the same time, agentic AI now resolves 60% of investigations, allowing human analysts to provide oversight when necessary. As attackers increasingly use AI to identify exposures, move laterally, and accelerate their operations, we’re delivering the technology designed to help defenders rapidly understand their environment, prioritize risk, investigate suspicious activity, and take action before a threat turns into a business disruption.

The future of security operations will be defined by how effectively organizations combine machine-speed analysis with human oversight. Organizations that can pair strong security fundamentals with trusted AI-driven operations will be best positioned to reduce risk, respond faster, and build resilience against the next generation of threats.

Title: Mapping the AI threat landscape: MITRE ATLAS comes to Elastic Security
Context: 6 supports MITRE Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems (ATLAS), MITRE’s knowledge base for attacks on AI systems, in addition to MITRE ATT&CK
Full Text:
Elastic Security 9.6 supports MITRE Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems (ATLAS), MITRE’s knowledge base for attacks on AI systems, in addition to MITRE ATT&CK. ATLAS covers prompt injection, jailbreaks, stolen model API keys, and poisoned agent tools. In Elastic Security 9.6, prebuilt detection rules for AI platforms and generative AI (GenAI) tooling will ship with ATLAS mappings already applied, so rules provide the AI-related context out of the box. MITRE recently announced that ATT&CK Enterprise will add AI-enabled systems as a new platform, drawing in part on ATLAS content. However, ATLAS remains MITRE’s dedicated, frequently updated AI threat knowledge base. A new coverage table shows which ATLAS tactics and techniques your rules already address, scored in its own view rather than averaged into your ATT&CK numbers. The rule creation form and Elastic Agent Builder also understand ATLAS. Behind it all is a new managed MITRE data service in Kibana.

We’ve supported MITRE ATT&CK since the initial version of Elastic Security, and we’ve extended that support over the years with ATT&CK mappings on prebuilt rules and features, like the coverage overview page.

What is MITRE ATLAS?

MITRE ATLAS is a knowledge base of the tactics and techniques that adversaries use against AI-enabled systems. It's maintained by MITRE and shaped by real-world observations and security research from across the industry and academia. ATLAS is modeled directly on ATT&CK, so the structure will feel familiar to users: tactics to describe what an adversary is trying to achieve, plus techniques and sub-techniques to describe how they go about it.

MITRE ATLAS versus MITRE ATT&CK

ATLAS and ATT&CK use the same structure, but they describe attacks against different kinds of systems.

MITRE ATLAS

MITRE ATT&CK

What it covers

Models, training data, and agents

Hosts, networks, identities, and cloud infrastructure

Structure

Same structure, reusing ATT&CK tactics and adding AI-specific ones, like AI Attack Adaptation and AI Model Access

Tactics, techniques, and sub-techniques

Update cadence

Monthly content releases

Roughly twice a year

In Elastic Security

Prebuilt rule mappings, coverage overview tab, rule form, and Agent Builder

The goal of ATLAS is to give defenders the same thing that ATT&CK did a decade ago: a common, evidence-based vocabulary for a class of threats that they can use to assess their own vulnerabilities. And ATLAS complements ATT&CK, rather than replacing it. Attacks on AI systems rarely happen in isolation. An adversary might use familiar intrusion techniques to get access and then, once inside, turn to AI-specific techniques. Mapping detections to both frameworks, like some of the detection rules we’re shipping, gives users a more complete picture of an attack, including the infrastructure it propagates and the AI systems it targets.

For Elastic Security users, this means a clear view of how well your detections cover the AI systems in your environment, measured on its own terms instead of mixed into your ATT&CK numbers. As your organization adopts large language models (LLMs) and AI services, in addition to autonomous agents, you can see which AI-specific threats your rules already address and find gaps before an attacker does. Our prebuilt detection rules for AI platforms and GenAI tooling now carry ATLAS mappings alongside ATT&CK, so this coverage view is populated from day one.

How MITRE ATLAS works in Elastic Security

In Kibana’s 9.6 release, we will implement support for ATLAS in the ways that customers have come to expect from the MITRE ATT&CK data. A single rule can carry mappings from both frameworks in its threat field. Plus, they sit side by side in the UI, so a user can view coverage counts or external links to MITRE reference data in the same way that they always have. Beyond the addition to our prebuilt rule mappings, we’ve also introduced:

A new coverage overview table. Mirroring MITRE’s own matrix visualization, so customers can see which threat tactics and techniques their rules target.

Manual rule create/edit UI support. The classic detection rule creation form, updated to give customers a visual way to add both ATT&CK and ATLAS mappings to their custom rules or to edit existing prebuilt rules to enrich potential alerts.

AI rule creation. The newly introduced rule creation workflow now supports adding both ATT&CK and ATLAS mappings to rules, where appropriate.

Agent Builder workflows. Elastic Security's Agent Builder skills now understand ATLAS, too, so you can ask an agent which AI threats your installed rules cover or have it recommend prebuilt rules for specific ATLAS tactics and techniques.

How Kibana serves MITRE ATT&CK and ATLAS data as Saved Objects

In the past, we’ve stored our own version of the MITRE ATT&CK framework within Kibana, derived from artifacts released by MITRE itself via Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX) datasets. We’d generate a local artifact via a script and ship it within our stack or serverless release bundles. This method largely worked for users, but it also limited us in some key ways, in that we couldn't easily support specific ATT&CK versions or more than one MITRE framework.

The generated MITRE artifacts were large enough that we had to lazily load them in the UI so they didn’t blow up our webpack chunk size. If we wanted to search through the entities at all, we’d have to load in the entirety of the data and search using basic array operations. The updating process of these artifacts was also tied to stack releases, causing occasional delays and version misalignments for customers who pick up new prebuilt rules as soon as they ship.

With MITRE ATLAS support, we saw a way to both add a new feature and tackle some of this long-standing tech debt by introducing a new managed MITRE data system. We still generate a similar artifact from the STIX datasets, but we now ingest the entities into Saved Objects to serve them to any consuming features via a data client and an API. This allows us to query and filter MITRE data in the same way that we do any other Saved Object, supporting a number of new feature opportunities, some of which (like MITRE ATLAS) have already been implemented.

We’ve also expanded the fields on the entity schema itself, adding new information, like an entity's full description, its revocation status, its version, and more. This provides us a much richer context to work with when building tools for users to integrate MITRE data in their workflows and to keep it up to date in their custom rule mappings.

The managed approach also opens the door to move away from packaging the artifact with Kibana releases themselves and to follow the more frequent prebuilt rule release lifecycle and delivery method, so the incongruencies of version mismatches won’t be an issue for those customers who want the latest and greatest as soon as they’re released. This matters more for ATLAS, which ships monthly content releases.

What’s next for MITRE framework support in Elastic Security

Our goal is to keep building on the managed MITRE data service, giving customers the most up-to-date threat information in the workflows that they already use and building new ways to understand their coverage. A few of the areas we're exploring include:

More frameworks. The data model was built to hold multiple MITRE matrices, which makes it straightforward to bring in others, like ATT&CK for Industrial Control Systems (ICS), as customer needs grow.

Smarter search for AI-assisted workflows. Every MITRE entity now carries its full description, providing valuable context for agent reasoning. We're experimenting with semantic search, so AI-driven features, like AlertZero, can use the latest tactics and techniques most relevant to a given behavior, instead of relying on a model's possibly outdated knowledge base. This update provides higher-quality output on a broader set of models.

Faster framework updates. Decoupling MITRE data from Kibana releases so new ATT&CK and ATLAS versions arrive on the same schedule as the prebuilt rules that reference them. This matters as ATLAS ships monthly and ATT&CK’s AI platform arrives in 2027.

We'd love to hear how you're putting ATLAS to work. If you have feedback on the new coverage view, the rule form, or the mappings in our prebuilt rules, reach out via our Slack Community or the Discuss forum.

Title: JPMorgan Confirms Customer Data Breach Following Third-Party Compromise
Context: JPMorgan has confirmed a data breach following a cyber-attack on third party vendors used by the financial institution
Full Text:
JPMorgan has confirmed a data breach following a cyber-attack on third party vendors used by the financial institution.

The investment banking giant, part of the JPMorganChase group, revealed on X on November 19, at 13.29 GMT, that it believes attackers accessed certain marketing data held by the impacted vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.

“There is no disruption to our services. Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” JPMorgan wrote.

The firm added that the incident is not related to a service disruption on November 16, which it said was caused by a software bug in its on-premise hardware systems.

Chase, which is the consumer and retail banking arm of JPMorganChase, issued the same statement on its X account on November 19.

N0n Ransomware Claims Attacks on JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard

The notification came after the ransomware group N0n listed the financial institutions JPMorganChase, Visa and Mastercard on its data leak site.

Reuters reported that Visa and Mastercard confirmed they had experienced data breaches as a result of a third-party compromise. Visa said that no payment data has been impacted while a Mastercard spokesperson revealed that the breach affected non-payments information from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program.

None of the compromised third-party vendors have been named, so it is unknown at the time of writing if the incidents are related.

Following JPMorgan’s data breach notification on November 19, N0n reportedly released data relating to customers of the three banks, stating that they had each missed a 48-hour deadline to pay its extortion demand.

Title: Vendor data breach exposes Chase, Visa, Mastercard customer info
Context: Morgan Chase warned it suffered a data breach after a cyberattack at a third-party service provider exposed customers' personal information and marketing data
Full Text:
J.P. Morgan Chase warned it suffered a data breach after a cyberattack at a third-party service provider exposed customers' personal information and marketing data.

The bank said the incident didn't disrupt its services and is unrelated to a service disruption that occurred earlier this week.

"We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack," reads the firm's announcement on X.

"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses."

J.P. Morgan Chase Bank is the largest U.S. bank by assets, with about $4.1 trillion as of June 2026. Its consumer banking division reports about 78 million active digital customers.

Visa and Mastercard separately confirmed third-party incidents in statements to the media, though they have not confirmed any impact on customers.

The two firms are major global payment network operators with presence in more than 200 countries, handling annual transaction volumes of multiple trillion USD.

"Visa is aware of these claims. They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," a Visa spokesperson told BleepingComputer.

"Visa's systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week."

Mastercard told BleepingComputer that they "were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program."

Mastercard's spokesperson assured that "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards."

"At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed."

n0n ransomware claims the attack

On November 11, 2026, the n0n ransomware group claimed responsibility for an attack on Qubole, suspected to be the third-party provider the payment services use.

Qubole is a cloud data analytics company owned by Idera, used for cloud data analytics, automated processing, real-time analysis, and reporting.

Between October 14 and 26, 2026, the hackers used compromised Qubole credentials to access customers' AWS environments through IAM roles the companies had previously configured to grant Qubole access.

Allegedly, they stole 53.9 GB across 30,743 files directly from Qubole, including customer contracts, pricing records, staff and trial-user information, and production data.

Additionally, they claimed to hold nearly one petabyte of data from Qubole's customer networks.

n0n leaked the claimed Chase, Visa, and Mastercard data on its extortion site on November 16, 2026.

The hacking group claimed it contacted Qubole and some of the affected companies before public reports from Sentra and Wiz detailed the attacks, but their extortion demands were ignored.

BleepingComputer contacted Qubole for a comment on the threat actors' allegations, but we have not received a response as of publication.

Title: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard Report Third-Party Data Breaches After N0n Claims
Context: JPMorgan said the attackers may have accessed marketing information held by its service providers, including customer names and email addresses
Full Text:
JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose third-party data breaches after the N0n extortion group claims to have stolen customer information.

The disclosures involving JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard highlight a familiar but often underestimated security problem: the risks introduced by third-party service providers. All three companies have confirmed incidents involving external vendors after the N0n extortion group claimed it had stolen customer information and published data allegedly taken from their systems.

The important distinction is that the companies haven’t reported breaches of their own payment infrastructure. Instead, the incidents appear to involve information held by outside providers, showing how a security failure at a supplier can expose data belonging to major financial institutions and their customers.

JPMorgan said the attackers may have accessed marketing information held by its service providers, including customer names and email addresses.

“Based on our ​investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names ‌and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly.

The bank stressed that its services weren’t affected and that the incident had no connection to the technical problems some customers experienced earlier in the week. Where necessary, it plans to contact affected customers and offer free credit monitoring.

Visa confirmed that the incident it was investigating involved a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company said its own systems hadn’t been affected and that there was no evidence that payment information, including card numbers, had been exposed.

Mastercard also acknowledged a security incident at an external provider. The company said the exposure involved a limited number of email addresses belonging to a small group of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefits program. It stressed that the information wasn’t related to payments and that its payment network remained fully operational.

The N0n group had listed the three companies on its leak site on November 16, claiming to have obtained customer engagement and marketing data. It subsequently published the allegedly stolen information and marked the companies as having refused to pay. The group’s claims should be distinguished from the information independently confirmed by the companies.

The scale of the alleged exposure is significant. According to Reuters’ review, the JPMorgan-related files contained more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some associated with phone numbers and postal codes. Researchers also identified what appeared to be 124 email addresses belonging to bank employees.

The Visa dataset reportedly contained thousands of customer email addresses, phone numbers and marketing campaign records, mainly relating to Asia-Pacific markets. The available information also suggests that the exposure wasn’t limited to customer contact details, although the authenticity and completeness of the files remain important considerations.

Neither JPMorgan, Visa nor Mastercard has identified the affected service providers or disclosed the total number of customers involved. This leaves important questions unanswered, including how attackers accessed the providers’ systems, how long they maintained access and what security controls failed.

Even when attackers don’t obtain card numbers or account credentials, names, email addresses and phone numbers can be valuable. Criminals can use this information to create convincing phishing messages, impersonate financial institutions and target customers with fraudulent calls or messages. A message that includes a person’s name and references a genuine banking relationship is much more likely to attract attention.

For this reason, third-party risk management needs to go beyond contractual security requirements and periodic questionnaires. Organizations should know what information suppliers can access, limit the data they share, review access privileges and require timely incident reporting. They should also verify that providers apply appropriate security controls and have effective procedures to detect and contain intrusions.

The N0n group emerged in September and has listed roughly 200 alleged victims on its leak site. Its claims against the three financial companies show how cyber extortion can affect organizations through their suppliers, even when their core infrastructure and services remain operational.

Title: Report: Threat Actors Are Refining Their Use of AI Tools
Context: In addition to integrating AI into their attacks, threat actors are also taking advantage of the growing popularity of AI tools to launch social engineering attacks
Full Text:
Recorded Future warns that threat actors continue to use AI to accelerate their attacks, making traditional techniques such as phishing, supply-chain compromise, and extortion more effective. Both state-sponsored threat actors and criminal gangs are using these tools, with at least one attack operating almost entirely without human intervention. While fully autonomous attacks are still rare, the researchers expect this to change as AI tools improve.

“As agentic techniques mature and diffuse across the threat landscape, autonomous and orchestrated campaigns are likely to become more frequent, alongside a growing underground market for illicit access to commercial models and rising ‘noise’ from low-level automated intrusions that complicate the detection of serious threats,” the researchers write.

In addition to integrating AI into their attacks, threat actors are also taking advantage of the growing popularity of AI tools to launch social engineering attacks.

“Attackers are spoofing the landing pages of popular AI developer tools, standing up fake utility pages, and impersonating products such as OpenClaw with fraudulent wallet pages designed to steal crypto assets,” the researchers write. “These attacks increased significantly after March 2026, demonstrating that threat actors are taking advantage of the increased interest in AI to deliver malware. AI-related lures have been used in the ‘ClickFix’ campaign, which delivers malicious pop-up messages on compromised sites, as well as in search engine optimization (SEO) poisoning techniques that target users searching for AI-related websites. The prevalence of these campaigns demonstrates the long-established trend of opportunistic cybercriminals taking advantage of hype or fear, uncertainty, and doubt (FUD) around a newsworthy subject.”
