Full Text:
Executive Summary

Agentic cyberattacks are no longer theoretical. In 2026, frameworks such as ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI moved from research and red team use into real-world attacker operations.

Our research shows that these frameworks are gaining adoption quickly. Across GitHub and Internet-exposure data, we found thousands of forks and more than 4,000 publicly visible servers, alongside growing interest in these tools within underground communities.

The underlying attack techniques, however, are mostly familiar. The real change is how quickly and autonomously attacks can be executed: agents can chain tools and attack stages, work in parallel, and adapt when blocked. For defenders, this makes broad visibility and multiple layers of protection across the attack chain increasingly important. Cato combines existing inline security controls with Agentic Threat Prevention (AGTP), designed to identify attack progression and help stop likely next steps before the attacker reaches its objective.

Agentic Attacks Are No Longer Theoretical – They Are Here

For more than a year, the cybersecurity industry has been asking the same questions: Are autonomous AI-driven attacks really possible? When will they move from research environments into real-world operations? And how much of the threat is real versus hype?

Throughout 2026, controlled testing started to answer that question. OpenAI disclosed models bypassing isolation during cybersecurity evaluations and reaching the internet, while Anthropic reported similar incidents. In July, Cato demonstrated an agentic attack stack reaching Domain Administrator in a controlled Active Directory environment in 40 minutes from a single high-level prompt, with most planning and execution handled autonomously. The capability was no longer hypothetical.

Over the past few weeks, however, the question has changed. We are no longer asking only whether agentic attacks can happen. We are now seeing threat actors actually use agentic offensive frameworks in real operations.

In October, researchers investigating attacks focused on Japan uncovered a CyberStrikeAI environment configured with 44 specialized agents spanning reconnaissance, exploitation, persistence, C2, exfiltration, and reporting. The activity involved at least 19 organizations, including 16 in Japan, with multiple targets processed in parallel. Deep compromise was limited to a smaller number of targets, but the case demonstrated how agentic tooling can automate attack operations at scale.

At roughly the same time, Microsoft observed the China state-aligned actor Storm-0940 using ARTEX to automate attacks against hundreds of organizations globally. Some successful attacks progressed from initial targeting to privileged cloud access in less than three hours. ARTEX was also used during activity associated with the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise, while the FBI later reported that the compromise enabled access to more than 2,250 downstream tenants.

ARTEX is not an isolated case. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported threat actors using other open-source agentic frameworks, including Cairn and HexStrike, during real incident-response engagements. Since late August 2026, they observed these tools being used across multiple stages of the attack lifecycle, including lateral movement, database exploitation, and preparation for data exfiltration.

By November 13, the shift was significant enough for the FBI to publish a FLASH warning that a variety of malicious actors had weaponized ARTEX to automate multiple stages of cyber intrusions at machine speed. The FBI also highlighted financially motivated attacks against South Korean financial institutions that resulted in the exfiltration of personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people.

Agentic offensive frameworks have moved from GitHub projects and controlled security research into the hands of real threat actors.

Four Popular Open-Source Agentic Offensive Frameworks We Examined

There are already dozens of AI-enabled offensive-security projects available publicly, ranging from experimental research agents to full multi-agent penetration-testing platforms. For this research, we chose to focus on four popular, free, open-source frameworks that have attracted significant public attention and have also appeared in real-world attacker activity: ARTEX, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI.

These frameworks are not identical, but they share a common idea: reducing the amount of manual work required from the operator. Instead of executing every step of an intrusion themselves, an operator can provide a goal while the framework uses one or more agents to reason about the environment, select tools, execute actions, interpret results, and decide what to do next.

ARTEX is an autonomous, multi-agent penetration-testing and offensive platform that divides activity across specialized agents and translates high-level objectives into executable actions. Its original GitHub repository was removed in October 2026 following widespread abuse, but the code continued to spread through forks and localized versions. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant have observed ARTEX being used by both financially motivated and suspected espionage actors during real intrusions.

ARTEХ dashboard interface displayed in a GitHub repository, showing system activity, token consumption, active nodes, traffic exchanges, and security findings

Cairn takes a somewhat different approach. Rather than defining a fixed set of penetration-testing roles or workflows, Cairn is designed as a general-purpose state-space search engine. An operator provides a starting point and a goal, while multiple workers explore possible paths toward that goal using a shared graph of facts and intended actions. Penetration testing was the first domain in which the framework was validated, and Cairn has since been observed being operated by threat actors during real incident-response investigations.

Cairn in action with a goal and target, showing its reasoning process and discovered facts during a CTF task

CyberStrikeAI is a broader offensive-security platform combining multi-agent orchestration, MCP-based tooling, knowledge retrieval, attack-chain modeling, a web console, and integrations with a large number of security tools. It also includes capabilities such as WebShell management and built-in C2 functionality. In October 2026, researchers examining attacker infrastructure found one CyberStrikeAI deployment configured with 44 agents, with work distributed across reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, persistence, command and control, exfiltration, and automated reporting.

CyberStrikeAI dashboard in action, showing vulnerability severity, active tasks, tool executions, recent security findings, and system capabilities

PentAGI, developed by VXControl, is a multi-agent penetration-testing framework designed to take a target and goal and break the operation into tasks handled by specialized agents. Those agents can invoke established offensive tools such as Nmap, Metasploit, and SQLmap inside isolated environments rather than requiring the operator to manually coordinate each tool. GTIG and Mandiant have observed PentAGI being abused in the wild, including operations that progressed beyond reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning into active intrusion and persistence.

PentAGI in action during a demonstration by its creator, showing the chat interface coordinating agents to execute assigned web security tasks

We selected these four because they give us a useful sample of the broader ecosystem: they are popular, actively discussed, publicly accessible, and provide enough observable data to study their development and adoption over time.

From GitHub To The Attacker’s Toolbox

One way to understand how quickly these frameworks are spreading is to look at two different signals: developer/community activity on GitHub and Internet-facing deployments.

The GitHub numbers already show substantial interest around the four agentic frameworks we examined. As of November 15, 2026, PentAGI had more than 34,000 stars and 5,300 forks, CyberStrikeAI had more than 8,600 stars and 1,900 forks, and Cairn, despite being created only in April 2026, had already accumulated more than 5,100 stars and 1,000 forks. ARTEX is more difficult to measure because its original repository was removed, but four surviving copies together accounted for more than 10,000 stars and 7,700 forks.

This does not mean that newer agentic frameworks have replaced established offensive frameworks. In fact, the GitHub activity shows very different lifecycle patterns. Sliver remains actively developed, with more than 900 commits and 20 releases during the last 12 months, while Havoc is archived and had only two commits during the same period, despite continuing to gain forks.

GitHub activity only tells us part of the story. We also searched for publicly reachable deployments using open-source intelligence and Internet-search platforms such as Shodan and Censys.

The Internet-exposure data shows that these frameworks are not limited to GitHub repositories or research environments – they are already being deployed on publicly reachable infrastructure. But deployment is only one part of the picture.

To better understand how quickly interest in these tools is growing, we also looked at their activity on GitHub. Rather than relying only on stars, we focused on forks and development activity: forks give us an indication of how frequently projects are being copied and picked up by others, while commits help show how actively the frameworks themselves are evolving.

Forks, however, tell us mainly about interest and distribution. They do not tell us whether a project is actively being developed. To look at that side of the ecosystem, we examined the number of commits made to each framework month by month.

The development activity shows a much more dynamic picture than fork counts alone.

CyberStrikeAI was developed at a particularly high pace through much of 2026, peaking at 476 commits in July. PentAGI also went through a period of intensive development between April and July before activity dropped sharply. At the same time, Sliver shows that established offensive frameworks are far from disappearing: despite being released years earlier, it recorded 906 commits during the last 12 months.

Havoc represents the opposite end of the spectrum. Its repository is archived and recorded only two commits during the period, yet it continued to accumulate forks – showing that development activity and continued interest do not necessarily move together.

ARTEX stands out with a sharp increase toward the end of the period, although its commit history requires additional caution. Because the original repository was removed and our ARTEX dataset combines surviving copies, some of the visible commit history was imported into those copies and predates their creation.

Beyond adoption and development activity, we also looked at where the publicly visible infrastructure for these frameworks is hosted.

Geographic Distribution of Publicly Visible Agentic Framework Servers:

Across ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI, and Cairn, our searches identified more than 4,000 publicly visible servers, with the largest concentrations appearing in the United States, China, and Hong Kong.

As a closer look at ARTEX, the following view is based on Shodan data only. It gives a useful snapshot of where publicly visible ARTEX infrastructure is concentrated, but it should not be treated as a complete count. Our broader searches returned higher numbers because they also included other Internet-search engines and data sources.

This is only the infrastructure that was publicly exposed and indexed by Internet-search platforms. The actual footprint could be significantly larger, as private, firewalled, short-lived, or otherwise non-indexed deployments would not appear in these results.

The geographic distribution reflects hosting location only; it does not indicate who operates the servers or whether they are being used maliciously.

Taken together, the data shows an ecosystem moving at different speeds: new agentic frameworks are attracting significant attention and, in several cases, rapid development, while established offensive frameworks continue to maintain their own communities and operational relevance.

We also found signs that these frameworks were attracting attention in underground communities before much of the recent public reporting around their abuse appeared. On October 6, 2026, a user on a dark-web forum explicitly asked for help learning CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike, and PentAGI.

That post appeared more than two weeks before Microsoft’s October 21 ARTEX report, and several weeks before Google/Mandiant’s October 30 research, Eye Security’s November 12 incident report, and the FBI’s November 13 ARTEX warning.

The interest in learning and experimenting with these agentic offensive frameworks was already present in underground communities before they became the focus of widespread public threat reporting.

Old Tradecraft, New Operator

So far, the techniques used by these frameworks are mostly familiar. They scan, exploit known vulnerabilities, steal credentials, move laterally, establish persistence, deploy webshells or C2, and exfiltrate data.

The tools are familiar too. CyberStrikeAI integrates more than 100 existing security tools, including Nmap, Nuclei, SQLmap, Metasploit, Mimikatz, BloodHound and Impacket. PentAGI also relies on established penetration-testing tools, and ARTEX has been observed orchestrating existing offensive tooling during real intrusions.

What is different is the way these tools are used. An agent can take a result from one step, immediately decide what to try next, test several paths in parallel, and change approach when something fails.

The ARTEX incident investigated by Eye Security is a good example. After obtaining API keys, the agents started using them within minutes. When rate limiting blocked the activity, they changed their approach within roughly three minutes. They also modified an existing reGeorg tunnel to work in a load-balanced environment, changed user-agent strings to get around access controls, and tested several ways to escape from a container.

We saw similar behavior in our own Agentic Attacker research. In one run, the agent created custom vulnerability probes after standard probes failed. In another, it changed its collection workflow when the environment did not behave as expected, and it also built an SMB-based path for moving data through an existing foothold.

None of this means that AI is suddenly inventing completely new attack techniques. The bigger change is that it can combine existing techniques, adapt when blocked, and keep moving toward an objective with much less human involvement.

Cato Protection

The fact that agentic frameworks rely heavily on familiar offensive techniques also means that defenders are not starting from zero. Cato already provides multiple layers of protection against the infrastructure, tools, and behaviors used throughout these attack chains, including threat intelligence and reputation-based blocking, IPS protections, malware prevention, and identification of suspicious behaviors such as internal discovery and lateral movement.

On top of these existing controls, Cato Agentic Threat Prevention (AGTP) is designed to address the agentic nature of the attack itself. By correlating activity across the environment, identifying attack progression, and applying inline protections against likely next steps, AGTP helps contain an attack before an autonomous agent can continue progressing toward its objective. In other words, while the attacker may move faster and adapt more frequently, the defensive approach also needs to operate across the full attack chain rather than relying on a single indicator or signature.

What This Means For Defenders

Agentic offensive frameworks are evolving quickly, and the barrier to using them is getting lower. New frameworks continue to appear, existing projects can be forked and modified easily, and increasingly capable low-cost and open-weight models are making these capabilities accessible to a much wider group of operators.

That makes relying on static protections alone increasingly difficult. Defenders need multiple layers of protection and broad visibility across the attack chain – from malicious infrastructure and exploitation attempts to C2 activity, lateral movement, credential abuse, and data exfiltration.

The tools may keep changing, but the goal for defenders remains the same: detect the attack as it develops, understand how the different stages connect, and stop it before the attacker reaches the objective.

Title: New EggStreme Malware Variant Goes Silent to Evade Security Tools in Government Attacks
Context: " The end result is that the changes allow it to bypass static signatures and heuristic detections built around the EggStreme malware framework when it was first exposed in...
Full Text:
The suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group behind the sophisticated EggStreme malware has rebuilt its toolkit as it continues to target government organizations in the Philippines.

"When attackers are exposed, the cheap response is to rotate," Bitdefender said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "A file hash changes with every recompile, a domain costs a few dollars, and a new IP address costs less."

"The EggStreme operators did more than rotate – the agent we now see uses a different network protocol, has an enhanced command set, and comes in a passive variant that never beacons out. The infrastructure appears to be moving away from the one certificate authority that tied its older servers together."

The end result is that the changes allow it to bypass static signatures and heuristic detections built around the EggStreme malware framework when it was first exposed in September 2025.

Delivered via an as-yet-unknown initial access vector, EggStreme's defining characteristic is the use of DLL sideloading to execute payloads. It features multiple components as follows -

EggStremeFuel (aka RawCookie), which conducts system profiling and deploys EggStremeLoader

EggStremeLoader, which sets up persistence and decrypts and executes EggStremeReflectiveLoader

EggStremeReflectiveLoader, which executes EggStremeAgent

EggStremeAgent (aka Gorem RAT), the core component and a full-featured backdoor that enables system reconnaissance, lateral movement, data theft via an injected keylogger called EggStremeKeylogger, and reverse shell and file upload/download capabilities via a secondary backdoor called EggStremeWizard

It's worth noting that some components of the framework, such as EggStremeFuel and EggStremeLoader, have been put to use by another cluster tracked by Palo Alto Networks as CL-STA-1048 between March and September 2025.

The latest findings from Bitdefender show a significant retooling of EggStreme's capabilities, including removing the keylogger from every agent build observed since then. Within two weeks after public disclosure, the threat actors are also said to have made other changes -

The method EggStremeFuel uses to protect its configuration

EggStremeLoader's cryptography and payload format, moving from RC4 to RC5 and to a custom cipher by the end of October 2025

Added commands in EggStremeAgent that facilitate Active Directory reconnaissance, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) querying, TCP traffic forwarding, and execution of PowerShell, Portable Executable (PE), .NET assembly payloads

Moving from a single certificate authority to campaign-specific certificate authorities

In addition, where lateral movement previously relied on Impacket-like tooling and on EggStremeAgent itself, newer incidents make use of an unmanaged system that sits outside of the organization's endpoint management but is still reachable by other workstations to stage the payloads and launch them via DLL sideloading using a Visual Basic Script (VBScript) file remotely run over Server Message Block (SMB).

Some of the newer builds have been found to run in passive mode by opening a listening port and waiting for the operator to connect in as opposed to contacting an external command-and-control (C2) server.

There is also some evidence that the attackers have also targeted Taiwan, but it has been treated with low to medium confidence.

"The speed of the loader changes says as much about the operators' maturity as about the cost of exposure," Bitdefender concluded. "The build-time design appears to be what makes rebuilds this fast. What they did not change is how they operate: sideloaded DLLs under system library names, staging through file shares, running from memory, and requiring mutual TLS."

Mustang Panda Targets Philippine Government Using ASEAN Summit Lures

As of late October 2026, Philippine government officials have also been targeted by Mustang Panda, a prolific China-aligned cyber espionage group, using ASEAN Summit lures to deliver PlugX using established tactics like DLL sideloading.

Mustang Panda attack chain

"The package impersonated a Laos–Philippines bilateral meeting agenda from the Lao Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Dream Research Labs said in a report published last week.

"It named five officials and referenced plausible diplomatic priorities, requesting that the reader provide confirmation before the summit. Behind it was a delivery chain that installed PlugX remote-access malware while displaying the decoy agenda."

Earth Alux Uses Stealthy Tradecraft to Strike Southeast Asia

The disclosure comes as a China-nexus threat actor tracked as Earth Alux (aka Ink Dragon, Jewelbug, REF7707, and UAT-11587) has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has assigned the activity the designation TGR-STA-0049 (formerly CL-STA-0049).

"The defining signature of the threat actor behind the activity is the targeting of government entities, combined with the use of advanced custom payloads that are designed for high-stealth intelligence collection operations, with an emphasis on evading security detection tools," Unit 42 researcher Tom Fakterman said.

Attacks mounted by the group have historically deployed an advanced backdoor known as FINALDRAFT (aka Squidoor) since 2023. However, it has since expanded its malware arsenal to include two previously undocumented remote access trojans (RATs) called PerfectPioneer RAT (in July 2025) and KUKURAT (in March 2026).

Initial access to target networks is achieved via exploitation of vulnerable, unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers to deploy web shells like ASPXSpy and Godzilla, which are then used to deploy the RAT payloads. Alternatively, Earth Alux has leveraged phishing emails using decoy PDFs and lookalike domains to compromise victim hosts.

PerfectPioneer RAT is a Go-based malware that's launched via three different methods -

DLL sideloading to launch a malicious DLL that reads, decrypts and executes XOR-encrypted shellcode containing the RAT

Decoy installers for Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect that installs the legitimate program but also writes the malware to disk and executes it in the background

Disguising executable files as PDF documents in phishing emails that, once launched, opens a decoy PDF document while the malware is launched in the background

The malware supports a number of features that enable the operator to gain remote control of the infected host. It facilitates file operations, shell execution, process management, keylogging, SOCKS5 proxy, screenshot capture, Window enumeration and manipulation, and CPU and memory utilization monitoring.

PerfectPioneer RAT execution chain

It also ensures a connection to the C2 server remains active at all times and systematically cleans up temporary files and runs garbage collection if memory usage exceeds 100 MB to minimize forensic traces.

Furthermore, select variants of the malware come with an "isDangerousCommand" feature to avoid running administrative commands that would be highly destructive or noisy, thereby allowing it to be detected by security programs installed on the host. These include rm, curl | bash, wget | bash, and powershell -e, among others.

KUKURAT, in contrast, functions as a modular implant that's executed in networks already compromised by PerfectPioneer RAT. Written in C++, the backdoor implements its functionality as a separate DLL module that's loaded dynamically at runtime directly from the C2 server.

This allows the malware to be highly evasive and adapt its capabilities on the fly in response to shifting operational objectives. It supports the following features -

Send system information and receive a configuration from the C2 server

Take screenshots

Log keystrokes

Enumerate and terminate processes

Perform file operations

Execute shell commands via cmd.exe and PowerShell

Conduct lateral movement via PsExec

Carry out SMB credential brute-forcing

Run Beacon Object Files (BOF)

Facilitate local privilege elevation

Ensure the malware remains active by means of a standalone watchdog executable

What's more, KUKURAT initiates bogus, legitimate-looking activity on the endpoint to camouflage and cover up its tracks based on a command issued by the threat actor. This includes -

Generate 10 decoy HTTP requests per operational cycle to randomly selected domains that are extracted from a hard-coded list of 15 popular websites using randomly generated URL paths with an aim to blend C2 communications

Mimic legitimate Google Chrome browser behavior by writing random data to the registry path HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\BrowserCrashRecovery, reading the data back, and deleting the key

Create temporary files with random names and randomized content inside the system %temp% directory, and delete them

"Both PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT use HTTP/3 as the primary method for communicating with C2 infrastructure," Unit 42 said. "While the adoption of HTTP/3 is rare across the broader malware landscape, its deployment in this campaign reflects an emerging trend among advanced threat actors."

The attacks have also been found to leverage established tools like PsExec, WMI, and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) to move laterally across compromised enterprise networks; collect credentials using Mimikatz, ProcDump, and SharpDPAPI; compromise Domain Controllers to deploy KUKURAT on local endpoints; and exfiltrate sensitive data such as files and emails.

"Through the deployment of KUKURAT and the PerfectPioneer RAT, the attackers behind this activity are actively evolving to stay ahead of traditional network defenses by implementing protocol-level evasion via HTTP/3 and QUIC over UDP," Unit 42 concluded.

"What makes this group particularly evasive is the extensive effort invested in maintaining operational security and remaining hidden on compromised endpoints. The group demonstrates a mature understanding of modern defensive ecosystems. They have even gone so far as to embed hard-coded administrative safety switches within their binaries to prevent their own operators from running loud or destructive commands that might trigger security alerts."

Title: Suspected Chinese APT Rebuilds EggStreme Malware After Exposure
Context: A suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group rebuilt parts of the EggStreme malware framework after it was exposed by Bitdefender
Full Text:
A suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group rebuilt parts of the EggStreme malware framework after it was exposed by Bitdefender. The company said the timing suggested its report was a likely trigger.

Bitdefender detailed the changes in an update to its cyberespionage research, first published in September 2025. It made no new attribution claim. It assessed with high confidence that the operation targeted multiple Philippine government organizations and with low to medium confidence that it targeted Taiwan, calling the latter a lead, not an established fact.

In the original research in September 2025, Bitdefender found a Chinese APT group had compromised a Philippines-based military firm using the EggStreme fileless malware framework.

What the Operators Changed

EggStremeFuel, one of the framework's components, changed how it protected its configuration in a build compiled 12 days after the original report, Bitdefender said.

Two weeks after that, the operators compiled a loader with a new cipher and payload format. That cipher was replaced again by late October 2025, swaps Bitdefender said offered little real protection but still defeated detections built for the old cipher.

The EggStremeAgent backdoor dropped its previous protocol for raw TCP connections still secured with mutual TLS, in which both sides present certificates.

Newer builds added Windows domain mapping and in-memory PowerShell, and none of those analyzed carried the keylogger. Two of them ran in passive mode, waiting for the operators to connect rather than calling out. Bitdefender first saw these builds after the report, though some were compiled earlier.

Bitdefender said the framework's design, which let operators swap capabilities with a new build, appeared to explain the speed.

Read more on Chinese cyberespionage: Suspected Chinese Malware Supplier Tied to Three Hacking Campaigns

What Defenders Can Still Track

Older EggStreme servers traced back to one certificate authority, created in 2019 and linked to 32 domains. No new domains appeared under it after the report. Newer activity suggested a shift to campaign-specific ones, which Bitdefender said was unconfirmed, though some links between old and new infrastructure remained.

Despite the rebuild, four behaviors stayed constant: DLL sideloading (getting a legitimate program to load malicious code), movement through file shares, in-memory execution and mutual TLS. Bitdefender said the operators "spent at the tools level and kept their methods."

Bitdefender's recommendations included restricting built-in Windows tools an environment did not need, detecting DLL sideloading by library name and location, finding unmanaged machines that could still reach workstations and watching for new inbound listeners on workstations.

The company argued that exposure could cost operators more than one campaign, since tooling is often shared. It said that raised a question about handing such operations to autonomous AI tools, where the chance of discovery was high, though its data did not test it.

Title: LABScon26 Replay | Governing Just-in-Time Intelligence: AI, Dual-Use Capabilities, and the Limits of Guardrails
Context: For policymakers, AI providers and threat researchers, this talk offers a historical lens on how offensive capability spreads and a starting point for thinking about how to...
Full Text:
In his LABScon 26 talk, Mauro Vignati, Advisor on Digital Technologies of Warfare at the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), argues that guardrails cannot address the deeper problem with frontier AI. Advanced cognitive capabilities are now distributed through the same on-demand, as-a-service model that has shaped industry, and later cybercrime, for seventy years. That model was designed for industrial efficiency, not for technology this powerful.

Vignati traces the model back to Toyota’s post-war just-in-time production system, built on the principle that customers get only what they need and pay only for what they get. The IT needed to coordinate that system helped give rise to application service providers and eventually to software-as-a-service. Cybercriminals later adopted the same logic for crimeware and ransomware, and hacktivists for DDoS campaigns. In each case the people taking part needed no technical skill of their own.

Model-as-a-service differs from its predecessors because the capability is dual-use at the source, supplied by private technology firms largely independent of who the end users are or what they intend. Vignati explains why criminals who tried to build their own AI systems have largely turned to wrapping commercial ones instead, leaving the legitimate economy to carry the cost of training and infrastructure. He then draws on cybernetics’ law of requisite variety, the principle that any system regulating another must match its complexity, to argue that AI governance has no simple fix. In its place he proposes a layered framework for deciding what a model can do, for whom and under what conditions.

His warning is that as long as the industry keeps offering powerful general-purpose models, criminals and activists will continue to parasitise commercial services.

For policymakers, AI providers and threat researchers, this talk offers a historical lens on how offensive capability spreads and a starting point for thinking about how to govern it.

About the Author

Mauro Vignati is Advisor on Digital Technologies of Warfare at the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). His work focuses on the militarisation of digital space and AI, the exploitation of the cognitive domain as a means of confrontation, and the impact of digital technologies in armed conflict on civilians, critical infrastructure and society. He has more than 20 years of experience in cybersecurity and previously spoke at LABScon 2022.

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

Title: EggStreme Malware: Rebuilt Under Scrutiny
Context: TL;DR: After we published our first EggStreme research in September 2025, we kept monitoring this malware family, and the development we have seen since justifies an update
Full Text:
TL;DR: After we published our first EggStreme research in September 2025, we kept monitoring this malware family, and the development we have seen since justifies an update. Documenting advanced persistent threat (APT, a state-aligned intrusion team) operations matters because these operators depend on staying unseen: once their tooling is public, defenders can hunt for it and find intrusions before they reach their objective. After we published our research, the operators revised their malware architecture and infrastructure, and the timing suggests our report was a likely trigger.

Twelve days after our report, they changed how EggStremeFuel protects its configuration. The loader’s cryptography and payload format followed 14 days later, and they appear to have moved away from the single certificate authority that once linked their servers. Based on our analysis, we assess with high confidence that the operation continues to target Philippine government organizations, with multiple victims. Based on our analysis of the samples, Taiwan is targeted as well, at low to medium confidence. The attribution is unchanged from our first report: a suspected Chinese APT group. This is a technical assessment based on the evidence available to us, not a statement about the involvement of any government.

I’d like to thank my colleagues, Victor Vrabie, Adrian Schipor, and Martin Zugec, for their invaluable contributions to this research.

EggStreme Since Our First Report: Rotation Versus Rebuild

Our first EggStreme analysis (Bitdefender EggStreme research, September 2025) described a multi-stage fileless framework. “Fileless” means the malicious code runs mostly from memory and leaves little on disk for file scanners to find. The framework had six named components: EggStremeFuel, EggStremeLoader, EggStremeReflectiveLoader, EggStremeAgent (a backdoor with 58 commands), EggStremeWizard and EggStremeKeylogger. We kept tracking the operation after we published. This article covers what changed - it does not explain the framework again, so readers who want the baseline should start with the first piece.

An APT operation succeeds only while it stays unseen. The objective is long-term access: months of quiet collection, not a quick payoff. Public analysis threatens that. Once a framework is documented, security teams can hunt for it, find intrusions already underway, and end the operation before it achieves its objective. For operators, exposure puts the whole mission at risk, so they respond by changing what defenders now know.

When attackers are exposed, the cheap response is to rotate. A file hash changes with every recompile, a domain costs a few dollars, and a new IP address costs less. The EggStreme operators did more than rotate - the agent we now see uses a different network protocol, has an enhanced command set, and comes in a passive variant that never beacons out. The infrastructure appears to be moving away from the one certificate authority that tied its older servers together. Each change broke static signatures and heuristic detections built around the framework as we first described it.

David Bianco’s Pyramid of Pain is a useful way to think about this (David Bianco, “The Pyramid of Pain”, March 2013). The pyramid ranks indicators by how much it costs an attacker when defenders detect them. Hash values sit at the bottom, then IP addresses and domain names, then network and host artifacts, then tools, and tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) at the top. For readability, this article groups the bottom three tiers together as “trivial” indicators. Mapped onto those tiers, the EggStreme operators did three things. They rotated hashes, IPs and domains (trivial). They changed payload paths, configuration formats and a firewall rule name (artifacts). They reworked Fuel, the loader and the agent (tools). The behaviors stayed largely the same: DLL sideloading, lateral movement through file shares, in-memory execution and mutual TLS. In other words, the operators spent at the tools level and kept their methods.

Three things made this operation easy to track when we published our first article: the hashes of known samples, a payload decryption method that worked across intrusions, and a single certificate authority that led to the whole server fleet. The operators have since worked on all three.

Our first article went out on September 17, 2025. The first Fuel build with the new configuration format was compiled on 2025-09-29, twelve days later. The first loader build in the newer format followed 14 days after that, with a compile timestamp of 2025-10-13 07:35:48, and was observed in the wild the next day. No new domains have appeared under the legacy certificate authority since.

We tracked some minor changes to the agent before our report, but most of the major changes, including the infrastructure, were first observed after it was published (compile timestamps on some agent builds are earlier, so we date them by first sighting, not by build date).

Some of this speed comes from how the framework is built. EggStreme is not runtime-pluggable: operators cannot load new capabilities into a running implant on the fly. Capabilities are compiled into each build. Our build artifacts show that, from one common codebase, the operators choose at build time which capabilities to include, omit, or swap. The keylogger is the clearest example: it is missing from every newer agent build we have analyzed. Ciphers are another. The loader moved from the RC4 stream cipher (which encrypts data one byte at a time) to the RC5 block cipher (which encrypts fixed-size blocks) in a build dated 2025-10-13, and to a custom cipher by 2025-10-28, about two weeks later.

The agent’s transport differs between generations. Within a generation, builds share the same architecture and protocol, while cryptography, configuration and capability change per campaign. This design is what makes the rework affordable. Changing the cipher or dropping a module does not require a new framework, only a new build.

The infrastructure changed as well. The older EggStreme servers could be mapped from a single certificate authority (CA, the entity that signs TLS certificates) generated in 2019. Searching for that CA’s key identifier returns 32 linked domains. Newer activity suggests a move toward campaign-specific certificate authorities, with certificates and keys embedded directly in each binary, removing that single pivot point. Some pivots remain. Development servers stage certificates for domains before they go live, one development IP is shared across a set of domains, and some legacy domains reappear in the newer setup.

Above: The EggStreme build timeline shows which changes came before and after our initial report.

EggStreme Attribution and Victimology

Our first article attributed the EggStreme operation to a suspected Chinese APT group (Bitdefender EggStreme research, September 2025). This update makes no new attribution claim. The reason we treat the newer activity as the same operation is technical continuity, which is documented in the sections that follow.

Several domains from the legacy infrastructure appear again in the newer setup. One of them, mepintei[.]com, connects the EggStremeFuel activity to the loader and agent activity. Before, we tracked those as two separate clusters. Older-format loader containers, the kind the first article described, are still in use and now carry the newer agent builds, so the two generations meet inside single samples. Delivery still relies on DLL sideloading, the same pattern the first article documented. Within the newer generation, every loader variant uses the same plaintext string KERNEL32 as both key and initialization vector (IV, the starting value a block cipher chains from) in its cryptography.

On victimology, we assess with high confidence that the operation continues to target Philippine government organizations, and that there are multiple victims. Based on our analysis of the samples, we also assess with low to medium confidence that Taiwan is targeted. Readers should treat that finding as a lead, not an established fact. We do not name victim organizations, and we do not publish a victim count. This broadens the target description from the first article, which covered a single Philippine military company.

EggStreme Lateral Movement: Same Strategy, New Mechanics

In the first article, lateral movement relied on Impacket-like tooling and on EggStremeAgent itself. Impacket is an open-source Python toolkit for remote Windows administration that attackers often use to execute commands (What Is Impacket, TechZone).

The operators also used the Stowaway proxy, an open-source multi-hop proxy tool that routes traffic through compromised hosts. They gained execution by injecting a Netlogon script, a logon script that domain-joined machines fetch from a shared folder, into a compromised share. The overall strategy has not changed: stage the payload on shared storage that the targets already reach, then trigger execution remotely. What changed is the mechanics.

In the more recent case, the operators staged on an unmanaged system: a machine outside the organization’s endpoint management that other workstations could still reach easily. That system hosted Visual Basic Script (VBS) files, small scripts run by Windows’ built-in script host, along with an EggStremeFuel package. The package had three parts: a legitimate executable, a malicious DLL (dynamic-link library, a code module that Windows programs load at run time) for that executable to sideload (T1574.002 DLL Side-Loading), and a configuration file.

What is DLL Sideloading?

DLL sideloading places a malicious library next to a legitimate, often signed, program that loads a library of that name at startup. The program runs normally and loads the attacker’s code with it, which helps the malicious code blend into expected process activity. Bitdefender’s explainer on the topic is What Is DLL Sideloading, TechZone.

The operators ran the script remotely over SMB (Server Message Block, the Windows file-sharing protocol) (T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares). The script copied the Fuel package to the target (T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer) and set persistence through a run key, a registry value that Windows executes automatically at user logon (T1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder). Execution itself went through the Windows Script Host (T1059.005 Visual Basic) and a batch file (T1059.003 Windows Command Shell).

These are the elements we observed in the command activity:

Observed Element

Detail

Purpose

reg add run value

Value StandaloneUpdater under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, pointing to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\OneDrive\setup\logs\StandaloneUpdater.exe

Persistence at logon, for the logged-on user only

attrib (hide and unhide)

C:\Users\Public\Officelog.bat

Execution wrapper

WScript.exe

Script-based execution and copy

Each name was chosen to look routine. StandaloneUpdater.exe imitates the naming of OneDrive’s own updater component. The genuine file is OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe, which sits under C:\Program Files\Microsoft OneDrive\ on a per-machine installation and directly under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\OneDrive\ on a per-user one. The staged copy uses a shorter name and sits two folders deeper, in setup\logs, which is the mismatch to watch for (T1036.005 Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location). prncnfg.vbs is a real Windows printer administration script, documented by Microsoft under System32\Printing_Admin_Scripts (Microsoft Learn, “prncnfg”). Officelog.bat suggests Office logging. Toggling the hidden attribute (T1564.001 Hidden Files and Directories) keeps the staged files out of default directory listings when they are not in use.

We saw the same method on multiple machines in the same network. The pattern suggests that valid credentials (T1078.002 Domain Accounts) and a reachable share were enough. The hashes in the indicator of compromise (IOC) tables will be stale by the next campaign. The pattern will probably still apply: an unmanaged host serving scripts, SMB-triggered execution, a run key under a familiar-looking vendor path.

Above: EggStreme lateral movement flow.

Defender action: Alert on WScript.exe or cmd.exe running scripts from C:\Users\Public\, and on run-key values that point into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\OneDrive\setup\logs\ or any OneDrive subfolder that is not the vendor’s installed updater path.

EggStreme v1 and v2: What Changed and What Varies

Two kinds of change are easy to confuse in what follows. One is the step from the framework we described in the first article (v1) to the newer generation (v2). The other is the variation we see between campaigns within v2, where builds of the same generation differ from each other. The following table helps clarify what changed and what varies.

Component

v1 (first article)

v2 (newer generation)

Varies between campaigns within v2

EggStremeFuel

Configuration encrypted with RC4, filename as key

Configuration encrypted with AES-256-CBC, key embedded in the binary and obfuscated; C2 traffic still RC4 with a per-run random key

C2 addresses and the configuration file

EggStremeLoader

Payload decrypted with RC4, keyed from part of a consistent file path

RC5-32 CBC, then a custom CBC cipher; KERNEL32 as key and IV; new payload file layout with the key in the first 8 bytes

The decryption routine (two variants so far), the payload hiding location, the sideloaded DLL name; each payload file carries its own key

EggStremeAgent

gRPC over mutual TLS; 58 commands; keylogger injected per user session

Raw TCP with mutual TLS (wolfSSL) plus an AES-256-CBC layer; certificates embedded; streamlined configuration; command IDs 21 to 88 with Active Directory reconnaissance and in-memory PowerShell; no keylogger

Infrastructure

Behavior

DLL sideloading, share-based lateral movement, in-memory execution

The same

Almost everything that defenders could key on at the file, protocol and infrastructure levels changed between v1 and v2, and keeps changing between campaigns. The behaviors stayed constant across both.

EggStremeFuel: Configuration Encryption Upgraded, C2 Unchanged

EggStremeFuel is mostly unchanged. However, one significant change is how it protects its configuration, and the first build with the new configuration format has a compile timestamp of 2025-09-29, twelve days after our first article.

The earlier Fuel decrypted its configuration with RC4, using the configuration filename as the key. The newer builds use AES-256-CBC, with the key and IV embedded in the binary. The IV is stored in plaintext in several places in the binary as 1234567890ABCDEF. The key is hidden by a custom obfuscation routine and recovers to:

15c7ab53f7cfec92512844244fb09c2f07c2e9aea42b604c31fb78633248a825

The newer configuration we recorded sits at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Notifications\wpndatabase.dat (MD5 8ad958676e67ff70d1b2b95851de6d5d). The name imitates the Windows notification database in the same folder, which is wpndatabase.db, a SQLite database that Windows keeps under that path on current builds. The malicious file differs from the genuine one only in its extension. Moving from a filename-derived RC4 key to an embedded AES key means that knowing a configuration file’s name no longer helps decrypt it. The analyst needs the specific binary. The loader changes, described next, follow the same pattern across components: decryption keys now travel with the build, not with anything an investigator can see on disk.

Fuel’s C2 traffic still uses RC4, with a key generated randomly on each run. Without the per-run key captured from memory, recorded Fuel traffic cannot be decrypted from static analysis alone, so packet captures will show sessions but not their content.

The newer Fuel configurations and binaries point to C2 infrastructure that includes mepintei[.]com, along with 45[.]115[.]225[.]73, 109[.]248[.]24[.]84 and 149[.]104[.]109[.]230. mepintei[.]com also appears in our records of the agent’s original infrastructure.

Defender action: Treat any non-Windows process that reads or writes %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Notifications\wpndatabase.dat as suspicious, and when an EggStremeFuel infection is suspected, capture process memory before remediation, because the per-run RC4 traffic key exists only there.

EggStremeLoader: New Ciphers and a New Payload Format

The loader has one main job: stealth. It decrypts the next stage and places it in memory without leaving a readable payload on disk. We identified four new loader samples soon after the first article, each with major structural changes and a different cryptographic algorithm. The IOC list shows one RC5 build dated 2025-10-13 and three custom-cipher builds dated 2025-10-28, which is about six weeks after publication.

Cipher Progression

The first build in the newer format has a compile timestamp of 2025-10-13 07:35:48 UTC, 14 days after the first new Fuel build. We observed it in the wild the next day, so we consider that timestamp reliable. In this build, string protection moved from XOR (a simple bitwise scrambling with a repeating key, easy to reverse) to RC5-32, the variant of RC5 that uses 32-bit words. It runs in CBC mode (cipher block chaining, where each block is mixed with the previous encrypted block before encryption) with PKCS#7 padding (a standard scheme that fills the last block to full length). Both the key and the IV are hardcoded in plaintext as KERNEL32.

About two weeks later, the scheme changed again. The builds stamped 2025-10-28 replace RC5 with a custom 8-byte block cipher, still in CBC mode with PKCS#7 padding. We call this first custom cipher variant A. In variant A, each byte of a block goes through a simple position-dependent transform, and the result is XORed with the previous ciphertext block. The payload path is still decrypted with KERNEL32 as both key and IV. Payload files work the same way, except that the key is the first 8 bytes of the file itself, stored unencrypted, and those bytes also serve as the IV. The file layout also varies within variant A: in one of the four builds, the block after the key holds a skip count instead of the payload size, and that many junk bytes, which the loader skips without decrypting, sit before the DLL. A decryptor therefore has to match both the cipher variant and the file layout.

Variant A stayed in use unchanged for at least a week. All four builds from 2025-10-28 to 2025-11-05 use the same algorithm, so one decryption routine covers them all. By mid-December 2025 the operators had replaced it with a second custom cipher, variant B. Variant B decrypts each block with four rounds of byte-wise subtraction, byte rotation and byte swapping, and undoes the chaining by subtracting the previous ciphertext block instead of XORing it. Both builds we have, from 2025-12-16 and 2026-05-14, use the same algorithm, and variant B handles keys and IVs the same way as variant A.

Neither custom variant offers real protection. Because the key and the IV are identical, variant A's key cancels out: every block except the first of each encrypted message decrypts with the same fixed constant (01 04 07 0A 0D 10 13 16) and no secret at all. In payload files, all of the DLL except its first 8 bytes therefore decrypts without any key, and those 8 bytes are the standard start of a PE (Portable Executable, the Windows executable format) header. Variant B looks more complex, but mathematically it reduces to a fixed byte rotation plus an 8-byte constant, so a single known 8-byte block is enough to decrypt the entire payload. For both variants, even that is unnecessary: brute-forcing each byte position separately (2,048 trials in total) recovers the payload from the ciphertext alone. In practice, none of this is needed, because both variants store the key next to the data it protects: each payload file begins with its own key, so it contains everything needed to decrypt it. What the cipher swaps defeat is detection and tooling tied to a specific routine, not analysis.

The thread through all of this is the operators’ move from RC4, which the earlier loader builds used to decrypt payloads, to RC5 and then to the custom ciphers. Every variant in the newer format shares three traits: CBC chaining, a key-scheduling step (the routine that expands the short key into per-round values), and PKCS#7 padding removal.

New Payload File Structure

The newer loader also reads a new payload file layout, and that layout has stayed the same since October 2025:

Offset Length Content 0x00 8 Decryption key, plaintext 0x08 8 Encrypted; decrypts to the size of the embedded payload 0x10 N Encrypted embedded payload, ending with the EggStremeAgent component

The key sits in the first eight bytes of the payload file, in plaintext, rather than hidden inside the loader. Because the file carries its own key, one payload can be opened by any loader build that uses the same routine: variant A covers four builds. That adds resilience for the operators, who can swap out a loader build without re-encrypting the payload it carries. The plaintext key is a design choice, not carelessness, and as shown above, the cipher adds little protection on its own.

What the Payload Encryption Does and Does Not Protect

With the earlier loader, a consistent file path and an RC4 key derived from part of that path unlocked payloads across intrusions. An analyst who had reversed one loader could decrypt payloads recovered from other environments. The newer format looks different but offers little more protection. Each payload is encrypted with a routine that differs between variant A and variant B, so a decryptor or signature written for one does not match the other. But every payload file carries its own key, so an analyst who has the file and identifies the variant has what is needed to decrypt it.

Above: Decryption in v1 versus v2: one method opened payloads from every intrusion; in v2 the routine differs between variants, but each payload file carries its own key.

Two things do: content that does not match the extension, and a non-system process reading them at startup. systemZones.res alone accounts for five distinct payload hashes, so the operators reused that path across intrusions even as the contents changed.

Old and New Formats in the Wild Together

The older format has not disappeared. We still see older-format containers, which hold the payload size, EggStremeReflectiveLoader and the agent, carrying newer agent builds. They are encrypted with RC4 under keys that differ from the first article’s: Windows, svchost and, in one case, a key built from the first four bytes of the C: volume serial number. That last variant makes the payload (MD5 197be742fc81bbc87e5f66d1a4a9af92) harder for a researcher to decrypt, because its key depends on the machine it was built for.

The two formats running side by side support the compile-time modularity reading. The operators did not migrate everything at once. They chose the container format and cipher per build.

To help other analysts, we are publishing a Python implementation of the custom cipher used by the newer-format loaders. It takes KERNEL32 as key and IV, derives an 8-byte schedule from them, and decrypts in CBC mode with PKCS#7-style padding removal. It implements variant A. Treat it as a reference for that variant: variant B uses a different routine, and for payload files the key and IV are the first 8 bytes of the file, not KERNEL32.

def key_setup(key, iv): ks = bytearray(8) for idx in range(8): ks[idx] = ((3 * idx + 1) ^ iv[idx] ^ key[idx & 7]) & 0xFF return ks def decrypt(data): key = b"KERNEL32" iv = b"KERNEL32" assert len(data) % 8 == 0 ks = key_setup(key, iv) out = bytearray() prev = bytes(iv) # IV seeds the chaining for off in range(0, len(data), 8): ct = data[off:off + 8] # inner transform vec = bytearray(8) for idx in range(8): k = ks[idx & 7] temp = (idx + k + 7) & 0xFF vec[idx] = ((ct[idx] ^ temp) - k) & 0xFF # XOR with previous block (CBC chaining) out += bytes(vec[i] ^ prev[i] for i in range(8)) prev = ct # save ciphertext for next block # PKCS-style padding removal pad = out[-1] if 1 <= pad <= 8 and all(b == pad for b in out[-pad:]): out = out[:-pad] return bytes(out)

Defender action: Hunt for processes that read Alarm00.wav, appmain.sdb, expmain.sdb, systemZones.res, Feeds.tmp or msinfo32.dll from the paths above when the reading process is not the expected Windows component, and during incident response, always collect the sideloaded DLL together with any payload file found.

EggStremeAgent: Rebuilt Networking, Leaner Configuration, More Commands

EggStremeAgent is the backdoor at the end of the chain. The newer builds differ from the first article’s agent in four areas: how the configuration is stored, how the agent talks to its operators, which commands it accepts, and which modules it carries. Several of these builds carry compile timestamps between March and May 2025, but we first observed them after our first publication. This section therefore describes how the agent differs from what we first documented.

Configuration

Configuration decryption varies between samples, which fits the per-build approach seen in the loader. Some samples still use RC4 keyed from the configuration file’s full path, but with a changed configuration format. Others use RC5-32/12 (32-bit words, 12 rounds) in CBC mode with PKCS#7 padding. In those, the key and IV come from the eight-character filename without its extension. For example, the configuration at %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Comms\Unistore.db is keyed with Unistore. Most of the newer configuration files we recorded sit at %SYSTEMROOT%\system32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Crypto\Crypto.db, a location that looks like part of the system’s cryptographic store. We recorded seven distinct hashes for that one path.

The decrypted configuration has fewer fields than before. It holds a six-character uppercase victim ID, a sleep interval, the C2 (command-and-control, the attacker server the implant talks to) domain and the port, separated by ###:

<victim id>###50###fsstore[.]org###443

When no configuration file is present, the agent uses a hardcoded fallback configuration. TLS certificates are now embedded only in the binary. The agent no longer fetches them from an external configuration. That small change also feeds the infrastructure story: each binary carries its own trust material, which is what makes per-campaign certificate authorities practical.

Transport

The first article’s agent communicated over gRPC, a remote procedure call framework that runs over HTTP/2. The newer builds drop gRPC. They use raw TCP sockets (T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol) wrapped in mutual TLS through the wolfSSL library, a compact open-source TLS implementation often embedded in small software.

What is mutual TLS?

In ordinary TLS, only the server proves its identity with a certificate. In mutual TLS, the client presents a certificate too, and each side rejects the connection unless the other’s certificate is signed by an expected authority. For an implant, this means a scanner or researcher who connects to the C2 server without the implant’s client certificate gets no response worth analyzing.

On top of TLS, the agent adds a second encryption layer: AES-256-CBC (the Advanced Encryption Standard with a 256-bit key, in chaining mode) with keys and IVs hardcoded in the binary (T1573.001 Symmetric Cryptography, alongside the TLS layer’s T1573.002 Asymmetric Cryptography). Because of the double wrapping, intercepting the TLS session (for example, with a TLS-inspecting proxy that holds a trusted certificate) still leaves the analyst looking at AES ciphertext.

Expanded Command Set

The core command set from the first article remains. We see command IDs from 21 to 88, and the same ID can mean different things in different samples, which is another sign that each build is compiled to its own specification. Title: Who protects the antivirus? How we secure Malwarebytes itself
Context: The evidence is accumulating: In July 2025, Google reported that its AI agent Big Sleep discovered a critical SQLite flaw (CVE-2025-6965) that attackers already knew about
Full Text:
An antivirus is also software, and it can have weaknesses of its own.

That makes antivirus development particularly demanding. The product must safely handle files that may be hostile, run reliably across very different Windows environments, and resist attackers who try to abuse its privileges or shut it down completely.

Imagine a piece of malware that can disable your antivirus and leave you unprotected. That’s exactly what we as engineers work to prevent.

The attack surface of a privileged process

You might wonder why vulnerabilities matter for a desktop application that runs locally.

Our software runs with high privileges, so it has access to the entire system. That access is what lets it protect the system from exploits, data theft, and ransomware. It also makes our software an attractive target. An attacker who can disable our protection, or abuse it to gain those privileges, has a much easier path to taking over the system.

Two layers, one critical boundary

At a basic level, Malwarebytes has two layers: a user interface running as the signed-in user, and a background service running as SYSTEM. They communicate through COM (Component Object Model), a built-in Windows mechanism that lets one program call functions in another program, even one running in a separate process.

The UI can’t do much on its own. When you add an exclusion, restore a file from quarantine, or pause real-time protection, the UI only asks, and the SYSTEM service does the work. Those are exactly the operations malware would like to perform: excluding its own folder from scanning or turning protection off.

And malware doesn’t need our UI to act. Any process running as the same user can write its own COM client and call the same methods. So on every call, the service must answer two questions: who is really calling, and is this caller allowed to do this specific operation?

This is just one small example of an attack surface we keep in mind and protect. An antivirus has many more, and every fix to any of them has to preserve protection, performance, and system stability.

AI is making vulnerabilities cheaper to find

Finding a vulnerability usually involves four stages, and AI now speeds up every one of them:

Identifying possible weaknesses

Preparing test code and an environment

Running the tests

Analyzing the results before trying again

AI is a multiplier not just in development or business processes, but in finding vulnerabilities as well.

AI can explain unfamiliar code, generate diagnostic programs, and interpret compiler errors, logs, and debugger output. That lets people attempt investigations that used to be beyond their skills or would have taken far longer, even though a model alone still can’t reliably compromise an antivirus.

An experienced Windows engineer already understands privileges, process boundaries, and common security mistakes, and they know which assumptions to question. AI turns those questions into tests without the engineer having to write every variation by hand. It can build a diagnostic client and repeat the same test under different user accounts, integrity levels, and configurations, while the engineer decides whether the results show a real security failure.

The next step is already here: agents that combine a model with code navigation, build tools, a debugger, and a test environment. They propose a hypothesis, generate a test, observe the result, and refine the investigation in a loop. The hard part is still verification: telling a suspicious pattern apart from a real weakness. But a few years ago, none of this was possible.

The evidence is accumulating:

In July 2025, Google reported that its AI agent Big Sleep discovered a critical SQLite flaw (CVE-2025-6965) that attackers already knew about. Google says this stopped attackers from exploiting it.

Mozilla confirmed 22 security-sensitive bugs found through its collaboration with Anthropic and fixed by Firefox 148. Mozilla rated 14 bugs from the work high severity.

HackerOne reported a record 46,947 vulnerability submissions in March 2026, 76% more than a year earlier, with the share of valid, exploitable findings holding steady at about 25%.

In November 2026, OpenAI reported that an autonomous AI pipeline running an unreleased model built working root exploits for 948 unique Linux kernel local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities in a single scan.

Vulnerabilities will be found in greater numbers and at greater speed, and teams need to be ready.

Finding is only half the problem

Discovering is easier, but fixing vulnerabilities still takes substantial engineering effort, and the industry is already feeling the gap. HackerOne’s 2026 report found that the backlog of valid, unresolved findings grew 131% in two years, even though critical issues are being resolved faster than before.

If discovery speeds up and remediation doesn’t, the backlog grows, and open vulnerabilities present an opportunity for an attacker.

For a security company, the goal is to get ahead of the pace of discovery, and that takes dedicated resources and focus.

How we keep pace: prevent, detect, fix, learn

The inter-process boundary from the example above is just one of many areas attackers may target, and new ones appear as the product grows. At Malwarebytes we approach security as a continuous engineering process.

Prevent

Security by design. Before writing code, we build a threat model for each new feature: how could it be attacked, what privileges can it reach, and where does it accept untrusted input? Each component gets only the privileges its job requires, so a flaw in one part can’t easily lead to a full system compromise.

Zero trust between components. No component trusts another by default. Even our own processes must authenticate and be authorized on every privileged request, so a compromised or spoofed caller can’t ride on someone else’s trust. This is the per-call check the SYSTEM service runs in the two-layer example above.

Minimize the attack surface. Every interface we expose is something an attacker could probe, so we expose as few as possible. Features that aren’t needed are turned off, and privileged operations are reachable only through well-defined, authenticated entry points.

Secure development practices. Our engineers follow secure coding standards that define how to handle memory, untrusted input, and privileged operations, and which unsafe functions and patterns are not allowed. These rules are enforced in code review and by automated checks, not left to individual judgment. The compiler is part of our defense too: strict warning levels catch risky code at build time, and built-in protections such as stack protection, control-flow integrity, and address randomization make any remaining bugs much harder to exploit.

Detect

Static and dynamic analysis. Memory-safety bugs such as buffer overflows and use-after-free errors are among the most common causes of arbitrary code execution. Static analysis catches dangerous patterns before code runs; dynamic analysis catches memory and runtime errors as they happen in our test builds.

An AI vulnerability scanner. We built an internal scanner using modern AI models for source code analysis. It reasons about context and follows untrusted data through the code.

AI security review on every pull request. A dedicated AI agent reviews every pull request purely for security: unsafe memory handling, missing validation, privilege-boundary problems, and more. Engineers still do the regular review, but every change, however small, gets security attention.

Fuzzing and hostile testing. Malware authors craft files to attack scanners, so our file parsers, unpackers, and inter-process communication (IPC) interfaces are tested with malformed data, huge data streams, and fuzzed input on every release build.

Company-wide pipelines continuously scan our repositories for exposed secrets, vulnerable dependencies, and insecure configurations.

Fix

Structured triage. Every finding, whatever its source, is validated and reproduced. We then establish what an attacker would need to do to exploit it, give it a CVSS score, and assign an owner with a deadline based on that severity.

Safe fixes. Let’s imagine an authorization vulnerability between layers is found. The obvious response is to add an additional check. In practice, that check is often tricky to get right. An antivirus is made up of many components that authenticate each other; some start at boot, and some run in the kernel. If one piece breaks, the whole product can fail.

In a large codebase with years of history, even a small patch can cause a blue screen of death (BSOD), slow the system down, or break features for millions of users at once. A security fix has to preserve protection, performance, and stability.

AI-assisted remediation. AI helps our engineers investigate suspicious code, test hypotheses about exploitability, and explore possible fixes. Engineers review every change to confirm it fixes the root problem without introducing regressions.

Safe delivery. Fixes reach users through cryptographically signed updates, with critical security fixes released first.

Learn

A vulnerability isn’t closed when the patch is merged. For each fix, we add a regression test and put the triggering input into our fuzzing corpus. We search for the same bug pattern elsewhere in the code, analyze why the flaw was introduced, and update our scanner rules, fuzzing targets, and coding guidelines. We also track time to remediation, so we can make sure that fixes are shipped on time according to their severity.

What this costs us

Running Prevent, Detect, Fix, and Learn as a continuous loop isn’t free, and we accept the costs on purpose.

The tradeoff on people is time.

Security work takes roughly 10–20% of every sprint. We guard that time, so it isn’t pulled into new feature development.

The tradeoff on AI review is noise.

AI pipelines review pull requests, scan source code, and propose fixes, but an engineer still checks every finding and proposal. Each month, as the models and our process improve, the agent raises fewer false alarms.

The tradeoff on testing is volume.

Every fixed vulnerability gets its own tests, so the same flaw can’t quietly return. That’s more tests to write, run, and maintain, but a regression in a security fix is a flaw we’ve already paid for once.

The tradeoff on runtime checks is execution time.

Verifying who is calling across the boundary, locking down our files, folders, and processes, and hardening installs and updates all add a little work to every operation. We accept that overhead so every task runs securely.

What this means for you

You won’t see most of this work, but it protects you every day:

Protection that holds up under attack. Malwarebytes is designed so that malware can’t switch it off, tamper with it, or turn its privileges against you. We protect every point where attackers might try, from how components talk to each other to our own files and processes.

Fixes don’t trade one problem for another. Every security fix has to keep protection, performance, and stability intact.

Fixes reach you safely. They arrive as cryptographically signed updates, with critical security fixes first.

Fixed stays fixed. Each fix gets a regression test, and we look for the same bug elsewhere in the code.

Security comes first

AI has lowered the cost of finding vulnerabilities, for defenders and attackers alike, and that shift isn’t slowing down. For a product that runs with the highest privileges on a machine and protects millions of users, the only durable answer is to keep up with, and get ahead of, the discovery of flaws. That’s why at Malwarebytes we treat security as one continuous loop—prevent, detect, fix, and learn—where every finding makes the next release stronger.

When your application protects other applications, its own security deserves the same attention as the threats it detects.
