Title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
Context: But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers
Full Text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

Title: Europe’s 2027 Cyber Compliance Year: What’s Fixed, What’s Moving, and What One Incident Looks Like Under Four Laws
Context: DORA's first round of threat-led penetration testing (simulated attacks on live systems) is underway, and the list of tech providers it supervises directly is due for review
Full Text:
On Dec. 11, 2027, the EU's Cyber Resilience Act applies in full, and every new connected product placed on the European market will need security built in and a CE mark to prove it. That is the date most 2027 planning decks lead with. It is also the only big date of the year that is truly fixed.

Around it, almost everything else is in motion. NIS2 is being amended while three member states still haven't passed it. DORA's first round of threat-led penetration testing (simulated attacks on live systems) is underway, and the list of tech providers it supervises directly is due for review. The UK's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill is weeks or months from becoming law, with its duties phased in after that.

So the useful question for 2027 isn't "what's due when?" It's "which of these dates can I build on, which might move, and which depend on things that aren't ready yet?" This 2027 cyber compliance guide sorts all four regimes that way. It then follows a single cyber incident through all four laws at once, because that is where the overlap actually hurts.

The four laws in brief

The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) regulates products: hardware and software with digital elements sold in the EU. Manufacturers must design them securely, handle vulnerabilities for a set support period and report actively exploited flaws.

NIS2 regulates organizations: "essential" and "important" entities in 18 sectors, from energy and health to managed IT services. It requires risk-management measures, incident reporting and accountability for senior management. As a directive, it works through national laws.

DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act, regulates the financial sector's ICT resilience. It has applied since January 2025, and for banks, insurers and other financial entities it takes precedence over NIS2. It also lets EU financial supervisors oversee critical tech providers directly.

The UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill updates the UK's 2018 NIS Regulations. It brings managed service providers, data centres and designated critical suppliers into scope for the first time and tightens incident reporting. It doesn't apply in the EU, and the EU laws don't apply in the UK, but a UK company selling products or services into the EU can face all four.

What's fixed: the dates you can build on

These are in force or set in law, and nothing on the legislative calendar is likely to move them.

CRA reporting is already live. Since Sept. 11, 2026, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting their products: an early warning within 24 hours and a fuller notification within 72, submitted through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform. The European Commission is explicit that this covers products already on the market, not just new ones. If your 2027 plan still lists CRA reporting as a future task, it's a year late.

The CRA applies in full on Dec. 11, 2027. From that date, the essential security requirements, technical documentation, software bill of materials (SBOM) and CE marking apply to products placed on the EU market. Products already on sale before then are caught by these requirements only if they are substantially modified afterwards. Open-source software stewards also pick up reporting duties on the same day.

DORA's first testing cycle closes in January 2028. Financial entities designated as significant must run threat-led penetration testing at least every three years. DORA has applied since Jan. 17, 2025, so the first cycle runs out in January 2028, and 2027 is when most of those tests will happen. Each one involves live production systems and often the entity's critical tech suppliers.

NIS2 is live in 24 member states. Where a national law is in force, the obligations already apply: registration, risk-management measures, 24-hour early warnings for significant incidents and management accountability. 2027 isn't a NIS2 start date for most of the EU. It's the second year of supervision.

Talk to Cyble about 2027 Cyber Compliance readiness and see how exploitation intelligence fits into your CRA and NIS2 reporting process.

What's moving: rules being rewritten while you comply

NIS2 is being amended before it's finished. France, Ireland and Spain still had no national NIS2 law in force in November 2026, and the Commission referred late countries to the EU Court of Justice in July. France's National Assembly passed its bill at first reading on Nov. 17, 2026; it still needs a joint committee of both chambers.

Meanwhile, the Commission's January 2026 amending proposal would add a small mid-cap category that moves many companies from "essential" to "important," standardize ransomware reporting data and let a cyber posture certificate count as proof of compliance. The Commission is aiming for political agreement in early 2027, and member states would then have a year to transpose the changes. Plan against today's national law; budget for a second update in 2028.

The Cybersecurity Act is being replaced. The same package proposes a new Cybersecurity Act (often called CSA2) that would let the EU name third countries that pose a cyber risk and restrict high-risk suppliers of key ICT assets used by NIS2 entities. If adopted in the form proposed, that becomes a supply-chain question for every NIS2 organization.

Incident reporting may get a single front door. The Digital Omnibus simplification package proposes one entry point for reporting incidents under several EU laws. The Council's Oct. 21, 2026 position favors a national single entry point in each country plus an EU information point run by ENISA. It's still a proposal, so the separate channels remain the ones that count in 2027.

DORA's supervised-provider list is due for review. EU financial supervisors designated 19 critical ICT third-party providers, including AWS, Microsoft and Google Cloud, in November 2025, and are expected to reassess the list during 2027 using 2026 data. A provider that lands on it gets direct EU oversight; its financial-sector customers get new contract and exit-planning questions.

The UK Bill is close but not yet law. The House of Lords finished with the Bill on Nov. 2, 2026, and it went back to the Commons over two amendments peers had made. Royal Assent is expected between late 2026 and spring 2027. Most duties then arrive through secondary legislation, and a House of Lords Library briefing says commencement may run through 2028. Medium and large managed service providers will have three months from commencement to register with the Information Commission (the renamed ICO).

What depends on infrastructure that may be late

The CRA's Dec. 11, 2027 date is fixed. What isn't fixed is whether the machinery for meeting it will be ready.

Harmonised standards. Most manufacturers would prefer to show compliance by applying harmonised European standards, which give a legal presumption of conformity. As of late August 2026, no CRA harmonised standard had been cited in the EU's Official Journal for any product category, and the cross-product standard covering all the essential requirements isn't due until 2027.

Notified bodies. Products in the CRA's "important class II" and "critical" categories need a third-party assessment from a notified body. So do "important class I" products, such as password managers, VPNs, browsers and smart home devices, unless the manufacturer fully applies a harmonised standard or certification scheme. The rules for designating these bodies have applied since June 11, 2026, but none had been designated by late June, and the target of having enough of them by Dec. 11, 2026 is a best-efforts goal.

Put those together and the practical deadline for many manufacturers is earlier than December 2027. If a class I product can't rely on a published standard, it may need a notified body, and assessment slots are likely to fill up well ahead of the deadline. The safe assumption is that standards arrive late and assessors are scarce: start the technical file and risk assessment now, and book an assessor as soon as one is designated for your product category.

One incident, four clocks

Comparison tables make these laws look like separate tracks. They stop being separate the moment something goes wrong. Here is a single, hypothetical incident and every reporting clock it starts.

The setup. A UK-headquartered managed service provider runs IT for European customers, including a bank in the EU. It also sells its own remote-management agent, the software installed on every customer machine it looks after. At hour zero, it discovers that attackers used an unknown flaw in that agent to push ransomware across several client networks, including the bank's.

Clock 1: DORA, for the bank. The bank must decide whether this is a "major" ICT incident. If it is, the initial notification to its financial supervisor is due within four hours of that decision and no later than 24 hours after the bank became aware. An intermediate report follows within 72 hours of the initial one, and a final report within a month after the last intermediate report. The bank can't write any of them without facts from the provider, which is why DORA requires ICT contracts to include help during incidents.

Clock 2: NIS2, for the provider. Managed service providers are in scope of NIS2. A provider based outside the EU that serves EU customers must name a representative in a member state and answers to that country's authority. For a significant incident, NIS2 requires an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within a month.

Clock 3: the CRA, for the provider as a manufacturer. The flaw is in a product the provider sells, and it's being actively exploited. Under the CRA, that means an early warning within 24 hours, a vulnerability notification within 72 hours and a final report within 14 days of a fix being available, all through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform. The provider must also tell affected users.

Clock 4: the UK Bill, once commenced. As a medium or large managed service provider, the company would also owe the UK regulator an initial notification within 24 hours and a full report within 72. If personal data was exposed, GDPR's 72-hour breach notification makes it five clocks.

One hypothetical incident: reporting deadlines under DORA, NIS2, the CRA and the UK Bill

Three lessons fall out of the timeline. First, the earliest deadline belongs to the customer, not the company that was breached: the bank's four-hour clock depends on information from the provider, so provider contracts need a customer notification commitment measured in hours, not days. Second, each law uses a different trigger, whether "major," "significant" or "actively exploited," so the same event can be reportable under one law and not yet under another. Third, the facts are the same in every report. Keep one incident record and map it to each format, rather than writing four reports from scratch at 3 a.m.

Reality check: what enforcement actually looks like

Search for NIS2 or DORA fines and you'll find confident lists of six-figure penalties. Most can't be traced to a regulator. Here is what can, alongside claims that keep circulating.

Claim

Status

What the record shows

Austria's FMA fined Western Union International Bank €42,000 under DORA (July 14, 2026)

Verified

Repeatedly late incident reports under DORA's reporting rules

Romania's DNSC fined a public body 50,000 lei, about €10,000, under NIS2 (Sept. 29, 2026)

Verified

Missing the deadline to notify the authority that it was in scope

Germany's BSI fined a cloud provider €850,000 under NIS2 (February 2026)

Not traceable

Widely repeated; independent trackers found no published NIS2 fine as of July 2026

"Most CRA obligations apply from September 2027"

Wrong

Reporting applied from Sept. 11, 2026; everything else from Dec. 11, 2027

"DORA's compliance deadline is in 2026"

Wrong

DORA has applied since Jan. 17, 2025

Two lessons. The first verified fines are about process, not breaches: a late report and a late registration. Supervisors are starting with the obligations that are easiest to prove, so registration deadlines and reporting clocks are where 2027 risk is most concrete. And the ceilings, up to €10 million or 2% of global turnover for essential entities under NIS2, are a long way from any penalty actually imposed so far. Use the ceilings to size the risk, not to predict the bill.

A 2027 plan in six moves

Map exposure by entity and by product. NIS2, DORA and the UK Bill attach to what your organization is. The CRA attaches to what it sells. A UK software company with EU banking customers can be inside all four. List every legal entity and every product, then the regimes each one triggers.

Build one reporting matrix and rehearse it. For each regime, record the trigger, the deadline, the recipient and the format. Then run the four-clock scenario above as a tabletop exercise and time how long it takes to decide whether an incident is "major," "significant" or "actively exploited."

Rewrite supplier contracts around hours. Your customers' clocks may start before yours. Agree customer notification times in hours, make sure financial-sector contracts carry DORA's required incident-assistance terms, and require component suppliers to tell you about exploited vulnerabilities fast enough for your own CRA reporting.

Run the CRA as two projects. Reporting is live and operational. Product compliance is a December 2027 engineering project: risk assessments, technical files, SBOMs, support periods and, for some products, a notified body. Don't let the second wait on the first.

Build to today's law and watch the drafts. Comply with the national NIS2 law in force now, and track the amendments, CSA2's supplier restrictions, DORA's provider review and the UK's commencement regulations without engineering to drafts that may change.

Get registrations right. The first verified NIS2 fine was for a missed registration notice. Check NIS2 registration in every country where you operate, and if you're a UK managed service provider, have your registration ready for the three-month window after commencement.

The question that starts the CRA clock

One phrase in the CRA deserves more attention than it gets: "actively exploited." A vulnerability in your product isn't reportable just because it exists. The 24-hour clock starts when you know it's being used in attacks. That knowledge rarely comes from inside your own engineering team. It comes from exploitation seen in the wild, chatter on criminal forums, proof-of-concept code and attacks on other organizations running the same component.

That makes threat intelligence a compliance input, not just a security one. Cyble tracks vulnerability exploitation, dark web activity and attacker infrastructure across the open, deep and dark web, which is the evidence a manufacturer needs to know when its clock has started and to show regulators why it reported when it did.

Frequently asked questions

What cyber compliance deadlines fall in 2027?

The main fixed date is Dec. 11, 2027, when the EU Cyber Resilience Act applies in full, including essential security requirements, SBOMs and CE marking for products placed on the EU market. DORA's first three-year cycle of threat-led penetration testing also runs through 2027 and ends in January 2028. NIS2 amendments and the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill's commencement are expected but not yet fixed.

Do UK companies have to comply with the CRA, NIS2 and DORA?

Yes, if they sell into the EU. The CRA applies to any product with digital elements placed on the EU market, wherever the manufacturer is based. NIS2 can apply to UK providers serving EU customers, which must appoint an EU representative. DORA applies to EU financial entities and reaches UK tech providers through contracts and, for critical providers, direct oversight.

When will the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill take effect?

Royal Assent is expected between late 2026 and spring 2027. Most duties will then be brought in by secondary legislation, possibly in phases through 2028. Medium and large managed service providers will have three months from commencement to register with the regulator.

Does DORA replace NIS2 for banks?

For financial entities, DORA is the sector-specific law and takes precedence over NIS2 on ICT risk management, incident reporting, testing and third-party risk. A bank reports major ICT incidents under DORA's timelines, not NIS2's.

Has anyone been fined under NIS2 or DORA?

Yes, but the verified fines are small. Austria's financial regulator fined a bank €42,000 under DORA in July 2026 for late incident reports, and Romania's cybersecurity directorate fined a public body about €10,000 under NIS2 in September 2026 for a late registration notice.

Title: Handling the NIST 800-171 Rev 3 Transition
Context: However, the current requirements for defense contractors, found in DFARS 252
Full Text:
The June 2026 proposed FAR CUI rule requires Revision 3 of NIST Special Publication 800-171 for contractors safeguarding Controlled Unclassified Information. However, the current requirements for defense contractors, found in DFARS 252.204-7012 and 252.204-7021, stipulate Revision 2. This creates a transition period between the two revisions, where defense contractors may need documentation for both revisions, until multi-year contracts with Rev 2 fade out.

What differs in Rev 3

Rev 3 is a restructured set of requirements, sourced from the federal catalog of security and privacy controls (NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5). Three major changes stand out:

More families. Rev 3 organizes requirements into 17 families, versus the 14 used in Rev 2. Planning, System and Services Acquisition, and Supply Chain Risk Management are new.

Merged and withdrawn requirements. Many Rev 2 requirements are folded into other Rev 3 requirements, forming structured lists instead of single-sentence requirements.

Organization-defined parameters. Rev 3 leaves blank variables, such as event types, frequencies, and time periods, to be defined by you or a government customer.

The overall effect is larger, more detailed requirements with more assessment objectives, leading to more documentation that forms more complete processes.

The four-step transition

The good news is that moving from Rev 2 to Rev 3 does not mean starting over. If we walk through the steps to transition an organization from Revision 2 to Revision 3, we can see how this works.

Step 1: Relocate Rev 2 requirements

Rev 3 uses an expanded format. A Rev 2 requirement often becomes a list item inside a different Rev 3 requirement. Build a map from each Rev 2 objective to its new home before anything else.

Rev 2 spread the topic of malicious code protection across three requirements: 3.14.2 (protect at designated locations), 3.14.4 (update the mechanisms), and 3.14.5 (periodic and real-time scans). Rev 3 collects all three into one requirement: 03.14.02. The image above shows where each Rev 2 objective lands. Objective 3.14.2[a], which identifies the designated locations, has no Rev 3 match.

Step 2: Take credit for previous work

Some Rev 2 assessment objectives don't directly satisfy Rev 3 assessment objectives, but some small adjustments will often get us there. The assessment language changed, but actions from a Rev 2 Huntress resource may still meet Rev 3 requirements.

In the 03.14.02 example above, you'll see that some of your Rev 2 efforts require fact-checking to see if they line up with the new language:

Rev 3 gets more specific about where malicious code protections must be implemented. If you identified designated locations for malware protection during your Rev 2 implementation and didn't cover all "system entry and exit points," you might have a gap.

Rev 3 also points to "configuration management policy and procedures" as the documents governing malware updates. If policies and procedures don't describe updating malicious code protections when new releases are available, you may have some edits to make.

The malware scanning objectives (3.14.5[a] through [c]) from Rev 2 should satisfy their Rev 3 counterparts. Take credit for work you've already completed!

Step 3: Apply the DoD ODPs

Some Revision 3 requirements provide blank values so an organization can define frequencies, time periods, and other parameters. After 800-171 Rev 3 was published, the Department of Defense published a set of their own parameters for contractors to use in nonfederal systems.

03.14.02 has one blank parameter: how often the malicious code protection mechanisms scan the system.

A value that is stricter than your current practice means a configuration change. In the case above, Managed Antivirus settings can supplement real-time protection with scheduled weekly scans. This frequency is already specified in the Huntress Baseline Configuration created to meet Revision 2 requirements.

Step 4: Attack the gaps

Rev 3 adds requirements and objectives with no Rev 2 equivalent. Backfill them last, once steps 1 through 3 show what is actually missing.

03.14.02 has one new item: configure the mechanisms to block, quarantine, or otherwise mitigate detected malicious code. While Huntress Managed EDR and Microsoft Defender work together to block malicious code, automatic host isolation could easily be one of your "other actions." Existing actions we already include in Huntress CMMC resources address this, and so the "gap" is really documenting how your Revision 2 implementation meets this new requirement.

How Huntress is handling the transition

Huntress has partnered with DEFCERT to chart an upgrade path to 800-171 Revision 3. This includes an updated Shared Responsibility Matrix, Operations Plan, SSP statements, and evidence. Since Revision 2 remains important for existing contracts, any new documentation will map back to Rev 2.

Title: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand
Context: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument...
Full Text: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security. The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data. The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government. The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters. The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month. A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers. For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected. While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand. At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens. In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US. Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators. Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless. Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not. What the judgment does not confirm While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public. "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest. "We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed. "That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now." The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026. The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users. The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals. A government spokesperson said: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public. "A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data. "Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so. "Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies." Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

Title: European Commission Confirms AI-Assisted Cyberattack Disrupted Services
Context: Regnier has not named the AI tool used in the attack, but the disclosure came roughly two weeks after the European Union’s cybersecurity arm CERT-EU warned of threat actors...
Full Text:
The European Commission has confirmed falling victim to an AI-assisted cyberattack that disrupted several of its services.

Hackers hit the European Union’s main executive body in late October, and the attack has been largely contained. The investigation into the incident continues, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said during a press conference.

“As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings, as they come,” Regnier said.

The attack was detected on October 22 and was confirmed on October 26. The investigation has found no evidence of a data breach affecting the Commission’s staff, Regnier added.

According to Politico, the hackers potentially compromised large amounts of data and caused disruptions that lasted over 10 days. Impacted services included the Commission’s HR platform Sysper, medical reimbursement system MyPMO, and translation systems.

While Regnier has confirmed that the hackers used an AI tool during the attack, he did not attribute the incident to a known group and said he was not aware of the Commission receiving a ransom demand related to the attack.

Regnier has not named the AI tool used in the attack, but the disclosure came roughly two weeks after the European Union’s cybersecurity arm CERT-EU warned of threat actors using the AI-powered penetration-testing framework Artex to target its constituency.

“We assess that Artex’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors, resulting in more frequent, faster, and more scalable automated attacks with a higher success rate,” CERT-EU said.

Artex is one of the AI frameworks that threat actors have been increasingly leveraging in attacks, and has been used to hack Barracuda, Railway, ConnectWise customers, and other organizations.

Title: European Commission confirms AI-generated cyberattack disrupted its systems
Context: The European Commission has confirmed it was hit by a cyberattack that misused a publicly available AI tool and forced the institution to take several of its applications offline
Full Text:
The European Commission has confirmed it was hit by a cyberattack that misused a publicly available AI tool and forced the institution to take several of its applications offline.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier gave the confirmation at Thursday’s midday press briefing in Brussels. Politico was the first to report the attack, in an exclusive published earlier that day.

Reporters used the Q&A session to press Regnier on which systems were hit, whether staff data was stolen and who was behind the attack. On the AI angle, Regnier said that “following our investigation, we can confirm that this was an AI generated cyber campaign,” describing it as “a misuse of an AI tool.” Later in the session he added that “it was an AI tool that is publicly available.”

He did not name the tool, and he did not address a reporter’s request to confirm that it was a Chinese AI tool used to identify vulnerabilities.

Regnier opened his answers with a general statement on AI and security. “While AI can of course help to detect vulnerabilities and prevent cyberattacks, it can of course be misused for cyber operations,” he began, adding that “no one is immune to this.” He also mentioned the action plan on cybersecurity and AI that the Commission presented in July, noting it “shows that we are very well aware of what’s going on around us.”

Detected in October

According to the spokesperson, the incident “was detected on the 22nd of October and it was confirmed following the initial investigation on the 26th of October.” The Commission then opened an investigation and took preventive steps.

Among those steps, the Commission “temporarily took down several applications” as “a protective and preventive measure,” Regnier explained, and “most of them have since then been restored.” He did not say which Commission services were targeted.

The Commission is in “close contact with both CERT-EU and the European Data Protection Supervisor,” he added, and the investigation is ongoing.

No sign of a staff data breach so far

Asked whether personal data had been taken, Regnier responded that “at this stage of the investigation, we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.”

He would not say whether the attack has ended, though “many elements have been contained, so that’s the good news.” Conclusive remarks, he made plain, would have to wait until the investigation wraps up.

One reporter asked whether the attackers had demanded money. “I’m really not aware of any ransomware request made to the Commission, so definitely not,” Regnier replied.

“So on the attribution, I will not go there,” Regnier said when asked who was behind the attack, citing the ongoing probe. When a journalist asked what the attackers wanted, he answered that “it’s not a question for me, that’s more a question for the threat actor.”

He also declined to say whether the Commission used AI tools to defend itself, explaining that for security reasons he would not go into “the measures we’re taking and which tools we’re using.” On whether other EU institutions had been compromised, he replied, “I’ll not speak on behalf of other institutions, I only speak on behalf of ours.”

CERT-EU warned about ARTEX

Politico reported that CERT-EU detected the attackers using ARTEX, a publicly available AI tool for finding weaknesses in IT systems.

CERT-EU had warned about ARTEX on 5 November, describing it as “an AI-powered penetration-testing framework” whose original repository was pulled in October after reports of misuse, though forks are still available. The agency said it had seen similar AI-driven activity against the EU bodies it protects, highly likely involving ARTEX, and cautioned that “ARTEX’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors.”

A journalist wanted to know why the Commission had said nothing about an incident that took place weeks earlier, until Politico broke the story.

Regnier argued that measures taken against a cyber campaign stay out of public view “for them to be effective.” The Commission followed what he called “the processes as per usual practice,” informing CERT-EU, the European Data Protection Supervisor and the affected services within the institution.

“There was no hiding whatsoever,” he insisted. “It’s just the Commission taken and following the usual procedural steps.”

Reporters also wanted to know whether the incident deserved the “huge” label Politico had given it. “I’m not going to qualify the scale and extent of this cyber attack,” Regnier told the room. “It is a campaign, so there was a series of incidents indeed, and that’s all I can share with you at this stage.”

Title: European Commission HR hit by cyber attack
Context: ” ARTEX has been known to SOC operations since GitHub first released the tool in July, but widespread misuse of the tool prompted GitHub to make it unavailable on October 8
Full Text:
Barely a week after the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned companies of the cyber attacker interest in an open source penetration testing tool called ARTEX, the European Commission has confirmed that attackers armed with that tool broke into its HR systems.

The attack, which Commission officials detected on October 22, forced them to shut off much of the access to the systems for more than 10 days.

“As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications and most of them have since then been restored,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Thursday. “We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.”

During a news media briefing, a transcript of which was provided to CSOonline, he said that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) was informed of the attack, “so there was no hiding whatsoever.”

Regnier would not go into detail about the attacks, given that the matter is still being investigated, but he did say, “it is a campaign, so there was a series of incidents.”

In an email, Commission officials added, “we are also preventively checking other systems while staying in close contact with CERT-EU and the EDPS.”

ARTEX popular with attackers

The November 13 FBI statement about ARTEX, described as an autonomous penetration testing framework, said that the tool is becoming very popular with attackers.

“Since at least August 2026, a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI advisory said. “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale.”

Although ARTEX can handle a wide range of pentesting functions, it appeared to be primarily used in the Commission attack to search for and locate credentials.

The FBI said that ARTEX can “automatically map effective permissions of Azure credentials–SAS tokens, Service Principals, Kudu credentials, Storage Account keys–using sub-second capability checks.”

ARTEX has been known to SOC operations since GitHub first released the tool in July, but widespread misuse of the tool prompted GitHub to make it unavailable on October 8. “Despite this action, ARTEX remains widely accessible through independent routes and mirrors on code-sharing platforms,” the FBI said.

Uses different tactics

Brian Levine, a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, added that ARTEX’s AI-fueled tactics are different from what many cybersecurity teams are used to.

“ARTEX doesn’t need to steal your keys. It finds the ones you left lying around, like a SAS token in a code repo, a storage key in a config file, or a Kudu credential nobody rotated. Then it tries each one against every door in under a second,” he said. “Picture a burglar walking the block at 3 a.m. and checking every car door handle. He isn’t breaking glass. He’s taking inventory of what you left unlocked and AI lets him work a thousand blocks at once.”

Companies need a secure fallback

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, said he was unimpressed with the Commission’s attempts to tell EU citizens that all was well.

“The Commission says it has no evidence of a breach affecting its staff ‘as a whole,’ which is very different from saying that there is no evidence of a breach affecting any of the staff,” Kenney said. “The wording doesn’t give me much comfort.”

Kenney also said that the attackers’ decision to target HR was not an accident, and that the Commission’s decision to temporarily shut down some systems may have inadvertently helped the intruders.

“When payroll, leave, and medical reimbursement systems go down, people start using spreadsheets, email and manual approvals. Those workarounds often have weaker access controls and worse audit trails than the systems taken offline,” he said. “Enterprises need to define a secure fallback process before the attack, because improvising one often leads to greater exposure.”

HR systems a prize

Levine also said that the choice of an HR victim was understandable.

“HR systems are a prize. Names, home addresses, pay grades and health insurance records for EU civil servants make a ready-made targeting list for espionage and social engineering,” he said. “Whether or not data left the building, every Commission employee should prepare to receive a very convincing phishing email soon.”

His advice to CISOs: “Get secrets out of code and pipelines and rotate anything that has been exposed. Give every token and service principal only the access it needs, so a found key opens a closet, not the vault. Put cloud admin interfaces behind private access.”

Title: From posture to root cause: Investigate OpenShift compliance with Elastic Agent Builder
Context: On Elastic Cloud Serverless, these capabilities are available on supported project feature tiers (such as Serverless Security Complete)
Full Text:
A single Elastic Agent on each cluster polls OpenShift Compliance Operator APIs every 60 seconds. An Elastic Agent Builder agent on top of that data can tell you what change failed the compliance control. Every scan and check result lands in Elasticsearch, as do the remediations, so the agent answers questions (like, Which clusters failed checks this week? Why did a control start failing, and when?) in plain English. The rules that the scanner marks as manual get evaluated with Common Expression Language (CEL) custom rules, and a scheduled workflow in Elastic Workflows annotates the result back to the manual rule in the cluster. Rescans and remediation patches run through those same workflows and pause for your approval. Everything in this post is on GitHub, including the integration package and workflows, along with the manifests.

The Compliance Operator scans each OpenShift cluster against configured profiles covering the CIS Benchmarks, National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53 moderate (the basis for Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program [FedRAMP] authorization), the Australian Essential Eight and more, and then stores the results on that cluster. For one cluster, that’s fine, but across a fleet, nobody has a single view. A rule that passed last week starts failing after a deployment, and a scheduled scan silently fails to trigger. But the only way to find out is to log in and run oc get compliancecheckresult cluster by cluster.

Why OpenShift compliance is hard to track across a fleet

Scan results stored on each cluster

The Compliance Operator runs scans on each OpenShift cluster and stores the results locally. This approach works across a few clusters, but as the fleet grows, it becomes difficult for OpenShift administrators to maintain visibility across each cluster.

A compliance rule that had previously passed might start to fail after a new workload deployment or a cluster upgrade. Similarly, a scheduled scan can fail to trigger, due to unresolved dependencies. Without a central view of compliance scan status and results, these failures go unnoticed until an OpenShift administrator logs in to the cluster and manually checks, using commands such as oc get compliancecheckresult and oc get compliancescan.

In this blog post, we explore how this challenge can be addressed by ingesting OpenShift compliance data into Elasticsearch, giving platform and security teams a unified way to track compliance posture and investigate drift across the fleet.

Manual compliance rules tracked outside the cluster

Not all compliance rules are automated, so they need a manual assessment. Platform teams usually track these rules and their status in shared spreadsheets or Confluence pages. Those trackers sit apart from the scan results, and someone has to update and reconcile them with each cluster’s findings.

Organizational controls add another layer. A team may exclude certain controls from specific clusters because of internal requirements or operational needs. Without a central record, it’s hard to determine which controls apply to which cluster and why an exception exists, and that’s exactly what an auditor will ask.

Compliance reporting spread across clusters

With scan results spread across clusters, security teams have to find their own way to aggregate the data before they can build a report. Auditors can ask for reports at regular intervals, so this aggregation repeats every cycle. Each report draws on scan output and manual rule status, along with documented exceptions that live in different places. Pulling all of that together can leave gaps.

Centralizing OpenShift compliance data in Elasticsearch

Elastic Agent Builder lets you build interactive AI agents on top of your compliance data. Teams can query compliance posture across their entire fleet in plain English, investigate why specific controls failed, and safely trigger remediations with human-in-the-loop approvals, rather than combing through endless scan JSON or switching between cluster consoles.

A custom Elastic integration collects compliance scan data from each cluster and sends it to Elasticsearch. It uses the HTTP JSON input to query the OpenShift Compliance Operator APIs and retrieve scan results, in addition to ingesting them into Elasticsearch. During ingestion, compliance data is parsed and normalized, making it easier to search, build dashboards, set up alerts, and generate compliance reports.

With the data centralized, the next step is to make it easy for platform and security teams to work with it. Together, the integration and the agent turn compliance data into something that teams can interact with directly instead of static dashboards. The agent helps the team to find the information it needs and decide what to investigate next.

The following diagram illustrates the high-level architecture of the entire workflow discussed in this solution:

Note: The proof of concept (PoC) in this solution has been tested with OpenShift Local version 4.22, Compliance Operator 1.10.0, and Elastic Serverless. On Elastic Stack deployments (self-managed or Elastic Cloud Hosted [ECH]), both Agent Builder and Workflows require version 9.5 or later and an Enterprise subscription. On Elastic Cloud Serverless, these capabilities are available on supported project feature tiers (such as Serverless Security Complete).

Elastic also offers a free, 14-day Elastic Cloud trial to help you get started.

How to ingest OpenShift compliance data into Elasticsearch

We deploy Elastic Agent directly on each OpenShift cluster using a single integration policy. Every 60 seconds, the agent queries the Compliance Operator API endpoints via HTTP JSON and ships the raw scan records into Elasticsearch data streams across your entire fleet.

The integration reads three Compliance Operator resources:

Resource / API

What it provides

compliancescans.compliance.openshift.io

The scans configured in the cluster, including scan name, phase, and result.

compliancecheckresults.compliance.openshift.io

Individual check details, including rule name, status, and severity.

complianceremediations.compliance.openshift.io

Available remediations for checks, including their current state.

Because the HTTP JSON integration appends time-series documents to a data stream on every polling cycle, three Elasticsearch transforms (scans, checks, and remedy) continuously collapse each stream into dedicated latest-state indices (ospm-compliance_-latest). The checks transform deduplicates events by cluster and check resource name (metadata.name). This ensures that checks evaluated across different node roles (such as master and worker) are preserved without creating duplicate records across repeated scan cycles.

The agent queries these latest-state indices for current posture and uses the raw time-series data streams for historical investigations.

The following diagram illustrates the compliance scan data ingestion workflow from multiple OpenShift clusters into Elastic:

Note: This is a custom-built integration and isn’t officially supported by Elastic Support.

Deploy the OpenShift compliance integration in Kibana

The custom integration is a zip file package that has all the required components. To deploy the package, you can upload the package directly using Kibana UI.

The integration follows the standard Elastic package specification and bundles all the required Kibana and Elasticsearch assets into a single archive. When uploaded through the Kibana UI, the package registers three data streams with dedicated ingest pipelines, configures prebuilt dashboards, sets up latest-state index views, and installs the continuous Elasticsearch transforms that maintain current compliance posture:

OpenShift Security Posture Management │ ├── 1. Dashboards (kibana/dashboard/) │ ├── [OpenShift Compliance] Posture Overview │ ├── [OpenShift Compliance] Overall Results │ └── [OpenShift Compliance] Auto Remediations │ ├── 2. Data Views / Index Patterns (kibana/index_pattern/) │ ├── ospm-compliance-*-latest │ └── logs-openshift_security_posture_management.compliance* │ ├── 3. Data Streams (data_stream/) │ ├── compliance_check_results (with Ingest Pipeline) │ ├── compliance_scans (with Ingest Pipeline) │ └── compliance_remediations (with Ingest Pipeline) │ └── 4. Elasticsearch Transforms (elasticsearch/transform/) ├── checks ├── remedy └── scans

Download the integration from the GitHub repository.

The video below walks through deploying and configuring the custom OpenShift Security Posture Management (OSPM) integration package in Kibana Fleet. It covers setting the three compliance endpoints for scans, check results, and remediations, setting the 60-second polling interval, and mapping the orchestrator.cluster.name field from the agent's environment variables.

Configure the Compliance Operator API endpoints and polling interval

The integration has three data collection endpoints that cover compliance scans, check results, and remediations. Each endpoint builds the OpenShift API URL from environment variables that Kubernetes sets in the pod, so the same configuration works on every cluster.

For compliance check results, the URL looks like this:

https://${env.KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST}:${env.KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT_HTTPS}/apis/compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1/compliancecheckresults

The integration polls each endpoint every 60 seconds by default. You can change the interval to match how fresh you need the data to be.

When the configuration is complete, create an Elastic Agent policy with these settings and deploy it on your OpenShift cluster to start collecting compliance data.

Deploy Elastic Agent on each OpenShift cluster

To deploy the agent and the integration:

In Kibana, create or update an Elastic Agent policy and add the OSPM integration to it. Confirm that the API endpoints and polling interval match your environment.

The integration automatically enriches each event with orchestrator.cluster.name using the CLUSTER_NAME environment variable configured on the agent.

Generate an enrollment token to be passed along with the Fleet URL endpoint.

Replace the token and Fleet URL in the following reference YAML, and deploy the Elastic Agent on the cluster.

In Fleet, check that the agent is healthy.

Once healthy, add the OSPM integration policy to the agent to start polling data.

In Kibana, open the integration’s data streams. Confirm that documents are arriving and that each one carries the expected cluster name in orchestrator.cluster.name.

Repeat these steps for every OpenShift cluster that you want to monitor, and set the matching cluster name for each environment.

To collect OpenShift compliance data, deploy Elastic Agent as a single-replica deployment on each OpenShift cluster. The manifest below runs the agent with Fleet enrollment enabled and mounts a persistent volume to preserve agent state across pod restarts. It also injects the CLUSTER_NAME environment variable. The integration uses this variable to tag every ingested event with orchestrator.cluster.name, ensuring that multi-cluster scan results remain separated in Elasticsearch.

Complete Kubernetes manifests and role-based access control (RBAC) are available in the GitHub repository.

How to automate manual OpenShift compliance rules with CEL

Starting with Red Hat OpenShift Compliance Operator version 1.10.0, CEL-based custom rules are generally available (GA). Using this feature, create a CustomRule object for rules tagged as Manual.

For example, the compliance rule accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens is common across the profiles ocp4-cis and ocp4-high. Using a CEL expression, check whether any pods have the property spec.automountServiceAccountToken set to true:

apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1 kind: CustomRule metadata: name: custom-accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens namespace: openshift-compliance spec: id: xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_rule_accounts_restrict_service_account_tokens title: "Service account tokens should not be automounted unless required" severity: medium checkType: Platform scannerType: CEL expression: | pods.items.all(p, !has(p.spec.automountServiceAccountToken) || p.spec.automountServiceAccountToken == false ) failureReason: "A pod has automountServiceAccountToken set to true" inputs: - name: pods kubernetesInputSpec: apiVersion: v1 resource: pods

Note: In the custom rule above, spec.id is mapped the same as in the original rule with status of Manual.

Custom rules cannot be evaluated directly on their own; they must be enabled through a TailoredProfile object. To execute the checks, bind this TailoredProfile to a ScanSetting using a ScanSettingBinding.

For example, create a TailoredProfile named custom-ocp4-manual-rules for the custom CEL rule custom-accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens:

apiVersion: compliance.openshift.io/v1alpha1 kind: TailoredProfile metadata: name: custom-ocp4-manual-rules namespace: openshift-compliance spec: title: "Custom CEL automation for shared manual rules (cis/e8/high)" description: "Each rule is evaluated once; rationale documents which native profiles it should be patched back to." enableRules: - name: custom-accounts-restrict-service-account-tokens kind: CustomRule rationale: "applies-to: cis,high"

Using a similar pattern, CEL checks for all the rules tagged as MANUAL can be evaluated.

Note: CEL-based evaluation only supports platform type rules.

In the Elastic Workflows for live OpenShift cluster actions section, we define a workflow that reads scan data from these custom rules ingested into Elasticsearch and uses it to annotate MANUAL rules on the OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) cluster based on their custom scan status. Because the OpenShift Compliance Operator automatically propagates custom annotations from Rule custom resources (CRs) to their corresponding ComplianceCheckResult objects during scan runs, these evaluated statuses are automatically ingested into Elasticsearch on the subsequent scan cycle.

Build the OpenShift compliance agent in Agent Builder

Agent Builder lets you build purpose-driven AI agents connected to your Elasticsearch data. It provides four core building blocks (instructions, skills, tools, and connectors) that govern how the agent reasons and queries data, along with how it interacts with external platforms.

In this post, we build a custom OpenShift compliance agent, which reviews compliance scan data and identifies noncompliant clusters. It also evaluates failed compliance rules. Using tools, it can also trigger compliance scans and apply auto-remediation patches. Plus, it can generate operational reports.

The goal of this compliance agent is to let platform and security teams query compliance data in natural language, without writing custom queries or manually correlating results across clusters.

The following diagram illustrates the anatomy of the OpenShift compliance agent:

Set the compliance agent’s instructions and guardrails

Configuring an agent in Agent Builder starts with custom instructions, which become part of the system prompt. They set the persona and reasoning habits for everything the agent does, in addition to the guardrails. For an OpenShift compliance agent, the most important decision is what level of actions the agent is allowed to perform. This agent uses a strictly precautionary role. It reviews and queries ingested compliance data and can apply remediation patches or trigger scans on the cluster with user approval. It treats the data in Elasticsearch as the source of truth and asks for any unstated detail, such as the cluster name or scan identifier, rather than assuming defaults.

The instructions are structured in Markdown across six focused sections (goal, steps, guardrails, domain context, output conventions, and edge cases):

Section

What it covers

Goal

The agent only handles OpenShift compliance; the ingested Elasticsearch data is the source of truth.

Steps

Confirm scope, retrieve data with the provided tools, verify the results, summarize, and then ask before acting.

Guardrails

No change without explicit approval; only the provided tools; no invented IDs or remediation; and off-topic requests are declined.

Domain context

Rules that the model cannot infer from the data, such as the custom scan and how manual checks are reported.

Output conventions

Timestamps in local time, plus the ingested and original timestamps for Elasticsearch data; sources are cited.

Edge cases

Missing input means ask; a failed or empty tool result is stated, never read as "compliant."

This excerpt from the directives and guardrails shows the tone:

# Guardrails - **Cluster Mapping**: Cluster name provided by the user must match orchestrator.cluster.name exactly as recorded in compliance data. - **Silent Exclusion of Custom Scans**: By default, completely omit and suppress any scan or check result where scan_name contains custom (case-insensitive *custom*). Do NOT list, mention, or show an "Excluded custom scans" section or table in the output. Filter them out completely silently. Only include them if the user explicitly requests custom scans. - **Handling Manual Rules**: Treat OpenShift's base status MANUAL as manual review. If a custom automated evaluation exists, read manual_scan_status (PASS/FAIL) and last_manual_scan timestamp and report that custom evaluation separately. If absent, report "no manual scan annotation recorded". - **Strict Read-Only Workload Investigation**: When investigating which workload or pod caused a rule to fail, the agent operates in strictly read-only mode. The agent must NEVER mutate, patch, or change application workloads. It identifies the root cause and user attribution, and provides the remediation steps for the OpenShift administrator to execute. - **Safety**: Never execute live cluster changes or scans without presenting the plan and receiving explicit user confirmation. - **Concise Communication**: Answer directly and concisely using clear Markdown tables. Do not ask follow-up questions or offer unsolicited next steps unless clarification is strictly necessary to answer the prompt.

The instructions also carry domain context that a model cannot infer from the data. In OpenShift clusters, a custom scan bound to the custom-ocp4-manual-rules tailored profile tests manual rules. The agent leaves it out of summaries and counts unless the user asks for it.

For manual checks in the other scans, the agent reports two statuses side by side: the original status (MANUAL); and the manual scan status from the annotation that a scheduled Elastic workflow writes back to the cluster. Putting these rules in the instructions keeps them in one place, so no tool or skill needs to repeat them. Also, the whole block is static, with no timestamps or session IDs, so prompt caching keeps working.

Add skills for posture, failure investigation, and reporting

Custom instructions are loaded on every turn, making them ideal for general guardrails and domain context. However, adding detailed task workflows to system instructions creates unnecessary prompt overhead. Instead, define modular skills that the agent loads dynamically when the user request matches the skill description.

The OpenShift compliance agent uses four skills, each covering a single responsibility:

Skill

Reads from

What it does

Posture summary

Latest-state indices

Summarizes current scan results, pass and fail counts, failed controls by severity, manual check status, and remediation state.

Failure investigation

Raw data streams

Explains why a check failed or when it started failing, using history and remediation records. Kubernetes log correlation comes once audit logs are ingested.

Live cluster actions

Live cluster, through workflows

Reads live state, triggers a rescan, and applies or reverts a remediation, always after user approval.

Reporting

Latest and raw data

Produces reports, trends, and scan comparisons, and creates dashboards after user approves.

Each skill includes a description specifying its purpose and trigger criteria. Below is the description for the Posture Summary skill:

Summarize OpenShift compliance posture, scan execution status, check results, manual rule evaluations, and remediation states from latest-state indices (ospm-compliance_*-latest).

Each skill defines its own trigger conditions, available tools, workflow rules, and decision trees, along with output standards, execution steps, examples, and edge cases. For example, the manual check logic described in the previous section is implemented as:

Manual Rules & Custom Automated Evaluations When manual rules are requested, call ocp_compliance.list_checks_by_status with status: "MANUAL". For every manual check, inspect both the base OpenShift status and the custom evaluation annotations: Report the base status as MANUAL. If manual_scan_status contains a value (e.g. PASS or FAIL), present it separately as: "Custom Evaluation Status: (last evaluated at <last_manual_scan>)". If both manual_scan_status and last_manual_scan are empty/null, explicitly state: "No manual scan annotation recorded" (indicating it still requires manual verification). Do not interpret or alter values beyond what the data fields show.

Custom ES|QL tools for querying compliance data

Skills tell the agent how to approach a task, but executing those steps requires tools to query data and perform actions. Because compliance scan data is normalized and stored in Elasticsearch, the agent uses targeted tools to search current posture and historical trends. Following are the tools configured for the compliance agent:

Tool

Type

What it does

ocp_compliance.get_scan_status

Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL)

Lists the scans on a cluster with result, phase, and timestamps.

ocp_compliance.list_checks_by_status

ES|QL

Lists checks with a given status, including manual scan annotations for manual checks.

ocp_compliance.list_remediations

ES|QL

Lists auto remediations with their apply flag, state, and target object.

ocp_compliance.get_rule_details

ES|QL

Looks up a specific compliance rule from latest-state data.

ocp_compliance.search_audit_logs

Index search

Searches the OpenShift cluster audit logs ingested into Elasticsearch cluster.

ocp_compliance.search_compliance_history

Index search

Offers open-ended search over the raw event history.

Elastic Workflows for live OpenShift cluster actions

Although large language models (LLMs) excel at reasoning and synthesis, you don't want an AI model improvising arbitrary mutations against a live OpenShift cluster. Elastic Workflows solves this by executing deterministic, YAML-defined steps that run identically every time. When exposed to Agent Builder as tools, the agent decides when to invoke a workflow based on your prompt but cannot alter its underlying execution logic, ensuring strict guardrails around cluster interactions.

Four workflows handle the live cluster interactions supported by the agent, alongside a scheduled automation workflow that reconciles manual rule annotations:

Workflow name

Agent tool

What it does

openshift-compliance-query-live-workload

ocp_compliance.query_live_workload

Executes a strictly read-only HTTP GET request against the live OpenShift API to inspect objects and pinpoint the offending resource.

openshift-compliance-read-live-state

ocp_compliance.live_read_state

Reads the live state of one ComplianceScan, ComplianceCheckResult, or ComplianceRemediation directly from the OpenShift API.

openshift-compliance-trigger-scan

ocp_compliance.trigger_scan

Reruns an existing ComplianceScan on the live cluster by setting the rescan annotation.

openshift-compliance-set-remediation-state

ocp_compliance.set_remediation_state

Applies (apply: true) or reverts a native ComplianceRemediation on the live cluster.

Annotate custom compliance Rule resources

N/A

Each workflow tool has Require user confirmation set to Always, so Agent Builder pauses and asks to approve every call.

Connect Elastic to the OpenShift API with the Kubernetes connector

The Elastic Kubernetes connector provides secure connectivity between the Elastic Stack and OpenShift API endpoints, allowing workflows to interact directly with cluster resources.

The service account token configured for the connector must follow the principle of least privilege, scoped strictly to the operations required by the workflows.

The connector needs patch permissions on the Compliance Operator custom resource definitions (CRDs), so workflows can trigger scans and apply remediations. Investigations need more than that; the agent has to read pods and service accounts, along with RBAC bindings, to find the workload behind a failed check, which also means read-only access to cluster workloads. You can grant both in two ways:

Approach

Permissions granted

When to use

Dedicated connector service account

Bound to the OpenShift view or cluster-reader ClusterRole for read-only workload queries, plus a scoped role granting patch on compliancescans and complianceremediations in compliance.openshift.io.

Production. The connector’s access is separate from the agent’s and can be audited and revoked on its own.

Extend the existing agent service account

Adds get and list on pods, serviceaccounts, and rolebindings to the existing elastic-agent-ospm ClusterRole.

PoCs and lab environments, where standing up a second service account is more setup than the exercise warrants.

The example below generates a token for the existing elastic-agent service account:

oc create token elastic-agent -n elastic-agent-ocp --duration=720h

Note: When deploying across multiple clusters or staging environments, ensure that connector-id in the workflow matches the specific Kubernetes connector configured for that cluster.

OpenShift compliance agent demo: From failed control to root cause

The demo below follows the OpenShift compliance agent across an end-to-end investigation scenario. It shows how the agent summarizes multi-cluster posture and flags rule failures. It also demonstrates how the agent uses Elastic Workflows to query live pods without leaving the chat interface. From there, the agent correlates OpenShift audit logs in Elasticsearch to trace the exact user and deployment that caused the policy drift and documents the timeline into an Elastic case. And it shows how execution guardrails block unauthorized or destructive cluster commands.

Conclusion: OpenShift compliance monitoring at fleet scale

The OpenShift Compliance Operator does the essential work of auditing cluster configurations, but keeping a multi-cluster fleet compliant shouldn't require juggling spreadsheets or hunting down failed pods manually, nor should it force you to scramble before every audit.

Centralizing compliance findings in Elasticsearch and putting Agent Builder on top shifts the experience from static dashboards to active, evidence-backed investigation. Teams can query posture across clusters in plain English and automate manual checks with CEL and scheduled workflows. They can also trace policy drift down to the exact OpenShift user and timestamp, all while keeping humans firmly in control of live cluster changes.
