Title: Quantum deadlines are here. Meet Orca’s new tools for PQC readiness.
Context: Building on the PQC compliance framework we launched in July, Orca now gives teams a live inventory of their cryptography, a clear read on how exposed each key and certificate...
Full Text:
Post-quantum deadlines are no longer a distant line on a roadmap. US federal agencies owed their PQC migration plans in October. High-value federal systems must move key establishment to post-quantum cryptography by the end of 2030. And the EU expects member states to start cryptographic inventories by the end of this year, with contractors, regulated industries, and their suppliers next in line.

Yet the first step is still where most teams stall. Knowing RSA and ECC have to go tells you nothing about where they run in your cloud, which of those assets face the internet, what data they protect, or what breaks if you change them. Without those answers, teams either try to boil the ocean with a spreadsheet inventory or let PQC sit in the backlog until the next audit.

The cloud makes this harder than most environments. Cryptography is spread across managed key services, load balancers, certificates, SSH keys, VPN tunnels, container images, and code, and it changes every time someone deploys. A spreadsheet inventory is out of date the day it’s finished.

That’s why we’re expanding Orca’s post-quantum cryptography capabilities. Building on the PQC compliance framework we launched in July, Orca now gives teams a live inventory of their cryptography, a clear read on how exposed each key and certificate is to quantum attacks, and one place to track readiness. This post covers what’s new, then shows it in action on a real example.

What’s new in Orca for post-quantum cryptography

Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM). See every key, certificate, key pair, and cryptography library across your cloud in one live inventory. CBOM shows algorithms, key lengths, and expiration dates for cloud keys and vaults, the SSH keys and key files sitting on your workloads, and the crypto packages they run. Export it in CycloneDX for auditors, customers, and GRC tools.

PQC Impact. Know at a glance which cryptography quantum computing will break. Each key and certificate is rated Vulnerable, Weakened, or Resistant based on its algorithm and key length, so you can filter and group your inventory by quantum risk instead of decoding algorithm names.

PQC Alerts view. Work every post-quantum finding from one place. A dedicated PQC view on the Alerts page gathers all quantum-related alerts, each tied to the affected asset and enriched with Orca’s cloud context.

PQC Dashboard. Show leadership where you stand and how fast you’re moving. A pre-built dashboard tracks quantum-vulnerable cryptography and migration progress over time, ready to share with the board or an auditor.

PQC Runtime Detections. Catch harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) attacks while the traffic is being collected, not years after. Three new detections flag the ways attackers capture encrypted traffic in the cloud: a network capture tool executed on a host, cloud network traffic mirroring enabled, and TLS session key logging enabled.

These sit alongside the Orca for Post Quantum Cryptography compliance framework, which maps findings to post-quantum standards and organizes them by urgency.

Four questions to prioritize quantum risk

Whatever deadline you’re working toward, prioritizing PQC comes down to the same four questions. Orca answers each one from a single platform for cloud security, across every account, cloud, and workload.

Where does quantum-vulnerable crypto live?

How vulnerable is it?

Is it internet exposed?

What can it reach?

Each answer narrows the list for the next, so an inventory of thousands of keys and certificates ends with a short, ranked migration plan. Here’s how that looks on a real example.

Example: A quantum-vulnerable key on a production jump box

Take a common finding, like a production jump box in AWS that admins log into with an RSA key pair. Jump boxes exist to reach everything else, so whoever holds the key holds the door. A capable quantum computer could derive that private key from its public half, which means an attacker can collect the public key today and break in later.

Here’s how Orca takes you from the mandate to a fix.

Step 1: Find where quantum-vulnerable cryptography lives

Open the new PQC view on the Alerts page, or the Orca for Post Quantum Cryptography framework in Orca’s multi-cloud compliance, to see every quantum-related finding across your clouds. In our example, Orca flags 21 EC2 instances that use quantum-vulnerable key pairs, out of 34 in scope.

Prefer plain English? Ask Orca AI, “Which EC2 instances use quantum-vulnerable key pairs?” and get the same answer in seconds.

Step 2: Check how vulnerable it is

Not every finding carries the same quantum risk. Orca’s new PQC Impact rating sorts cryptography into Vulnerable (broken by a quantum attack), Weakened (reduced but not broken), and Resistant.

Click into the finding for mgmt-jumpbox-prod-01. Orca explains the risk in plain language, showing that the instance uses an RSA key pair, and its PQC Impact is Vulnerable.

Step 3: Check whether it’s internet exposed

A vulnerable key matters most when attackers can reach the host it unlocks. Orca’s exposure view shows this jump box is open to the internet on every port, along with the IAM roles, users, and groups that can reach it. Internet-facing hosts go to the top of the list. Internal-only ones still get fixed, just on a longer timeline.

Step 4: Map what it can reach

A jump box is only as dangerous as what sits behind it. Orca’s attack path analysis shows this one can reach a crown jewel S3 bucket holding AI training data, a Bedrock agent, a SageMaker endpoint, and a production database, plus dozens more buckets, functions, and roles. The key protecting this host is also protecting the path to your models and their data.

Step 5: Turn findings into a migration plan

One jump box is a fix. Hundreds of keys and certificates is a program, and a program is what the mandates ask for. US federal agencies must now submit PQC migration plans, and contractors, regulated industries, and their suppliers are increasingly asked for the same by customers and auditors.

Run the same four questions across every finding, and they sort into waves. Internet-exposed assets with a path to crown jewels get fixed now, internal assets with limited reach come next, and findings with no post-quantum option from the cloud provider yet get tracked until one arrives. Group your CBOM by PQC Impact to size each wave, then export it as the inventory behind your plan.

Another option is to connect the Orca MCP Server to the AI assistant your team already uses, like Claude or Cursor, and ask it to build a PQC migration plan. Because the MCP Server pulls straight from Orca, the plan reflects your real environment. You get a wave-by-wave plan grounded in live cloud context, not a generic checklist.

Go further with Orca: Fix, track, and prove progress

That’s the prioritization of a single finding done. PQC migration is a multiyear program though, and Orca helps with the rest too.

Catch harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks. Migration takes years, and attackers aren’t waiting for it to finish. In an HNDL attack, they collect encrypted traffic today and store it until a quantum computer can break it. Orca’s new runtime detections cover the three ways to collect that traffic in the cloud: capture tools running on a host, traffic mirroring on a cloud network, and TLS session key logging. Each alert comes with Orca’s cloud context, so you can see what the affected workload can reach and respond fast.

Prove progress to leadership: When the board asks how ready you are, you shouldn’t need to pull a spreadsheet together to answer. The new PQC Dashboard shows how much quantum-vulnerable cryptography is left, and that number drops as teams migrate, so one view shows both your exposure and your progress.

Stay audit-ready. Mandates and auditors want the same things, which are an inventory, a plan, and evidence of progress. Orca’s PQC framework maps findings to NIST and the EU Cyber Resilience Act, alongside 200+ other customizable frameworks, so you can generate a shareable report in one click instead of assembling evidence by hand. And when an auditor, engineer, or customer asks for your cryptographic inventory, export your CBOM in CycloneDX and hand it over.

Cut the time to fix: Orca tells you what to do, not just what’s wrong. AWS doesn’t yet offer a post-quantum key type for EC2, so swapping the algorithm isn’t an option for our jump box example above. Instead, the recommendation is to drop key-based access and use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, which authenticates through IAM instead of a key vulnerable to quantum computing.

From there, Orca does the heavy lifting. Orca AI generates the fix in CLI, CloudFormation, Terraform, and more, so engineers start with ready-to-run remediation instead of a blank page. Code Origin traces the jump box back to the infrastructure-as-code template and the team that deployed it, so the fix lands with the right owner and gets made at the source. Fix the template once, and every future instance launched from it comes up without a quantum-vulnerable key. Tickets open in Jira, ServiceNow, and Slack with the details already filled in, keeping the work inside your existing workflows.

Keep weak crypto from creeping back in. Teams keep shipping while the migration runs. Orca scans continuously, so a new key, certificate, or listener using RSA or ECC shows up in your CBOM and the PQC Alerts view as soon as it’s deployed, and you don’t migrate the same risk twice.

A repeatable workflow for the next PQC deadline

Post-quantum deadlines will keep landing, and migrating every key and certificate at once isn’t realistic. The teams that stay ahead know where quantum-vulnerable crypto lives across their environment, and which of it needs to move first.

Orca helps you do exactly that. With CBOM, PQC Impact, the PQC Alerts view, and the PQC Dashboard, the Orca Cloud Security Platform shows where vulnerable crypto runs, how exposed it is, what it can reach, and how your migration is progressing. One jump box is the example. The same workflow works for every key, certificate, and tunnel that comes after it.

Title: What Is Preemptive MDR? A Guide For Security Leaders
Context: How exposure context and proactive threat hunting inform MDR By combining information about assets, vulnerabilities, business criticality, and attacker behavior, preemptive MDR...
Full Text:
When an MDR provider contains a compromised endpoint, your team needs to know whether the weakness that enabled the attack exists elsewhere and who is responsible for addressing it. Without that follow-through, the immediate incident may be resolved while another attacker still has a way in.

Preemptive managed detection and response (MDR) is Rapid7's approach to connecting exposure context, threat intelligence, AI-assisted investigation, and human expertise. It supports proactive cybersecurity by helping teams prioritize weaknesses before exploitation, investigate threats with a clearer understanding of risk, and use their findings to strengthen defenses.

How does preemptive MDR differ from traditional MDR?

Managed detection and response provides security specialists who monitor, investigate, and respond to threats around the clock. Many services also include proactive threat hunting and recommendations to improve security.

Preemptive MDR connects that work more directly to what makes an organization vulnerable. When analysts investigate suspicious activity on a server, knowing that it is internet-facing, supports a critical application, and has a vulnerability under active exploitation helps them assess urgency and determine where to look next.

In Rapid7’s model, exposure findings inform investigation and remediation priorities, while investigations reveal weaknesses that need attention. Security leaders gain a clearer connection between the threats their provider handles and the conditions their organization needs to address.

Within a broader preemptive cybersecurity strategy, MDR connects exposure information with the people investigating and responding to threats. The aim is to reduce opportunities for compromise and intervene before an attack causes harm, while retaining the expertise to contain and recover from incidents.

How exposure context and proactive threat hunting inform MDR

By combining information about assets, vulnerabilities, business criticality, and attacker behavior, preemptive MDR helps teams decide which weaknesses require action first. Exposure context also informs targeted hunting and the investigation of suspicious activity.

Consider a hypothetical organization running an internet-facing application affected by a newly disclosed vulnerability. The security team needs to establish whether the vulnerable software is present, what the application supports, and whether attackers are exploiting the weakness.

Those findings can guide remediation priorities and targeted hunting for signs of compromise. If suspicious activity appears, analysts investigate it with an understanding of the affected system and the potential route an attacker could take through the environment.

Depending on the evidence, the response may involve containing a system, examining related accounts, or expanding the investigation to other assets. The organization’s remediation teams also need clear recommendations about the underlying exposure.

What the investigation reveals then feeds back into detection rules, hunting priorities, and response procedures. This gives leaders a way to track an identified risk through investigation, action, and outstanding work, with clearer ownership at each stage.

What role does AI play in preemptive MDR?

Before analysts can assess a potential threat, they often need to retrieve logs, examine user activity, and connect evidence across several systems. AI can accelerate this work by gathering and correlating information for review.

Agentic investigation capabilities can perform elements of that process in parallel, test possible explanations, and organize findings. Their usefulness depends on the available data: missing identity activity or asset information can leave gaps in the account of what happened.

Rapid7’s approach keeps human expertise central to validation and response decisions. Analysts assess the evidence alongside the organization’s priorities and the consequences of an action, including whether isolating a system could interrupt a critical service.

What to look for in a preemptive MDR provider

When evaluating a service described as preemptive, ask the provider to show how exposure information changes its work. A redacted investigation should make clear what analysts knew about the affected asset, how that influenced their reasoning, and which actions followed.If an investigation identified a weakness, was it assigned to an owner and addressed? Did the findings change detection coverage or future priorities? Where AI contributed, the provider should explain its role and the oversight applied.

Incident response remains part of the requirement. Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response alongside exposure-informed defense and AI-assisted investigation, supporting containment, detailed analysis, and threat eradication.

Agree on responsibilities before that support is needed. Establish which actions the provider can take, when customer approval is required, and who owns remediation. Those arrangements determine how findings become action, particularly when taking a system offline carries business consequences.

Once the service is operating, review progress through specific cases: exposures addressed before exploitation, threats contained, and weaknesses closed after investigation. Ask to see the evidence behind those outcomes and any work still outstanding, so your team can judge where risk has changed and where further attention is needed.

Explore Rapid7 MDR to see how exposure-informed defense, AI-assisted investigation, and expert response work together.

Title: Defining assurance for an AI-enabled world
Detecting Timeroasting the Hard Way
Context: The important finding at this layer: the attacker-controlled fields from the packet, the RID at offset 48 and the flag byte at offset 53, flow through w32time only as a RID...
Full Text:
Most detection rules come from one of two places: a vendor feed or a breach report. There is a third source that stays underused, and it is the one that actually teaches you something. Read the protocol spec, then read the binary that implements it. Not the attacker's tool, and not the vendor's marketing page: the target's own code.

This post is what happened when I did that for timeroasting. The detection you can copy for it today is a volumetric counter of connections to UDP/123 that understands nothing about the protocol. Nobody keys on what actually separates an attacker from a member, and the extended form has no coverage at all. So I reversed the binary to understand the protocol well enough to detect it properly. This is the walk from the bytes in netlogon.dll to detection that works against a real fleet. Reversing the crypto that precisely also hands you a working cracker, which is a nice bonus, but detection is the point. That is the "hard way" in the title: there is no public documentation for the extended crypto and no hashcat module for it, so you recover both by reading the binary.

The roasts you know

There are three roasts most people can name without thinking.

Kerberoasting. Request a service ticket for any account with an SPN, then crack the encrypted ticket blob offline.

AS-REP roasting. For accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication turned off, grab the AS-REP and crack its encrypted chunk.

Timeroasting. Per Tom Tervoort's 2023 research, abuse Microsoft's proprietary NTP authentication extension, MS-SNTP, to make a DC hand you a password-derived MAC for any computer or trust account, with zero authentication, then crack it offline.

The form nobody cracks

Timeroasting's request comes in two authenticator formats, and only one of them has public cracking support: hashcat has a mode for the legacy form and none for the other.

MS-SNTP lets a domain client confirm that a time response really came from a DC that knows the client's machine password, without the client authenticating first. The client sends an NTP request that names an account by its Relative Identifier (RID), and the DC answers with a MAC computed over the response using that account's password-derived key. A RID is the tail of an account's Security Identifier (SID), its unique index within the domain; naming a target by that number is all "sweep RIDs" means. Sign for whatever RID I name, no auth required: that is the entire attack surface. Sweep RIDs, collect MACs, crack offline.

The form everyone knows is 68 bytes on the wire, and its MAC is built with MD5. That is what hashcat mode 31300 cracks, what timeroast.py and netexec produce, and what every writeup covers.

The form almost nobody covers is 120 bytes, and it is neither new nor exotic. Microsoft added it to the spec as the preferred option, explicitly because of weaknesses in MD5, and it has been in real traffic for years. chrony added handling for it back in 2016, and modern Windows w32time sends it by default, to the point that it broke time synchronization against Samba AD domain controllers (DCs), which do not implement the extended form. The documented workaround is a Windows registry flag, SignatureAuthAllowed=0, that forces clients back to the legacy authenticator. Its MAC is built with an SP800-108 key derivation step followed by HMAC-SHA512. The gap is this: the exact crypto is not documented anywhere I could find, and hashcat has no module for it, so when you collect the extended MAC the legacy cracker cannot touch it.

Note: The two forms are trivial to tell apart on the wire. A 68-byte authenticated NTP packet is the legacy form; a 120-byte one is the extended form. Keep them apart in your head, because which form you have decides whether your cracker works, though as we will see, building detection on size is a mistake.

Why a defender should care

Timeroasting leaves no authentication event. The targeted accounts never log on, so there are no 4768, 4769, 4624, or 4776 events. That part of the usual claim is true, and it is where the attack earns its reputation for being quiet.

But quiet is not invisible. The DC still receives and answers a burst of UDP/123, and that is visible on the wire and in host network telemetry if you collect it, the half of the story most writeups skip. The extended form adds one wrinkle: if your DC speaks the 120-byte dialect and your collection assumes 68-byte MD5, your cracker produces nothing, and you misread an account as safe because you cracked the wrong format.

So the defender's questions are simple. Can you see the request happen? And if you harvest the MAC, can you actually crack it? We will answer both, but first we have to know exactly what the DC computes, and for that we read its code.

The two forms on the wire

Both forms are a standard 48-byte NTP packet with an authenticator appended. Two fields carry the rest of this post:

The KeyIdentifier at offset 48 (the target RID, little-endian)

In the extended form, a Flags byte at offset 53 whose 0x01 bit means USE_OLDKEY_VERSION

The remaining extended fields are defined in [MS-SNTP] and sit at their defaults in a request.

A 68-byte authenticator is the legacy form (48-byte header, 4-byte KeyID, 16-byte MD5 MAC); a 120-byte authenticator is the extended form. The client sends the MAC zeroed, and the DC fills it in and echoes the structure back.

Reading the code instead of guessing

The spec tells you the shape. It says, roughly, "K equals KDF of the key, a label, and a context, and the checksum is HMAC-SHA512 of K over the message." That is not enough to write a cracker. What is the label, down to the byte? How is the RID turned into the context? Which hash drives the KDF? Guess any of these wrong and your cracker produces confident garbage.

So I did not guess. Everything below is read off the actual binaries from a live, fully patched Windows Server 2025 domain controller (build 26100.33438), in radare2. I pulled w32time.dll and netlogon.dll off the DC over SMB and read them there.

Step 1: the crypto is not where you would expect it

My first assumption was that the signing happened in w32time.dll, since that is the service listening on UDP/123. It does not. I grepped the binary for the KDF label and came up empty:

rabin2 -zzq w32time.dll | grep -i "sntp-ms" -> (nothing)

rabin2 -zzq w32time.dll | grep -iE "SP800|SHA512" -> (nothing)

What w32time does import tells the story. Its crypto is delegated to Netlogon through:

logoncli.dll: logoncli.dll I_NetlogonComputeServerSignature <- extended (SHA-512) logoncli.dll I_NetlogonComputeServerDigest <- legacy (MD5) logoncli.dll I_NetlogonComputeClientSignature logoncli.dll I_NetlogonComputeClientDigest logoncli.dll I_NetlogonGetTrustRid bcrypt.dll BCryptCreateHash / HashData / FinishHash / DestroyHash / GenRandom

So w32time parses the packet and dispatches. The "Signature" functions are the extended, SHA-512 path; the "Digest" functions are the legacy, MD5 path. The interesting bytes live in netlogon.dll.

Step 2: the w32time dispatch and the extended-vs-legacy branch

Figure 1: the time service imports I_NetlogonComputeServerSignature and I_NetlogonComputeServerDigest from logoncli.dll, and a string search for sntp-ms in w32time.dll comes back empty. The signing logic lives in Netlogon, not in w32time.

Two functions in w32time call both compute paths, and the server picks the SHA-512 path or the MD5 path based on the request it parsed. The important finding at this layer: the attacker-controlled fields from the packet, the RID at offset 48 and the flag byte at offset 53, flow through w32time only as a RID value and a key selector that get passed down to Netlogon. They are not used as a length, an index, or a buffer size anywhere in the parse.

Step 3: NlGetKDFKey, the function that builds the key

In netlogon.dll, the function that derives the KDF key uses its own debug-string name, NlGetKDFKey. It builds a BCryptKeyDerivation call with the SP800-108 counter-mode HMAC algorithm and three parameter buffers, and the disassembly (Figure 2) pins down the three things a cracker needs. The spec implies a KDF with "a label" and "a context." The bytes say: the PRF is HMAC-SHA512 (the hash-algorithm buffer is L"SHA512"), the label is the 8-byte "sntp-ms\0" with the null included (cbBuffer is 8 for a 7-character string), and the context is the 4-byte RID in little-endian, exactly as it arrived in the packet. Output is a fixed 64 bytes. Every size is constant, and nothing here is attacker-controlled.

Figure 2. radare2 disassembly of the buffer setup: the sntp-ms label and the L"SHA512" algorithm string being loaded into the BCryptKeyDerivation call that derives the signing key.

Step 4: NlComputeHMACMessageSignatureFromKey, the outer HMAC

The caller is NlComputeHMACMessageSignatureFromKey. It calls NlGetKDFKey, then HMACs the message under the derived key: the 64-byte derived key is the secret, the message is the fixed 48-byte NTP header, and the output is 64 bytes. Note the one place a caller-supplied length reaches anything: the input length to that hash call. It is used only as the number of bytes to hash, never as an allocation size or an index, and w32time hands Netlogon a fixed 48-byte NTP header for the message. Every other size is BCrypt-derived or the fixed 64. The function error-checks every allocation and every BCrypt call with its own labeled failure path.

The chain is now pinned: the NThash feeds a SHA-512 SP800-108 KDF keyed by the sntp-ms label and the RID, producing a 64-byte key, and that key HMACs the 48-byte NTP response. That is everything the detection needs to know about the crypto. The cracker also needs the exact byte layout, which I lay out next to the cracker below.

Proving it against a live DC

Reading bytes gives you a hypothesis; I wanted the DC to confirm it. First, reachability, because the extended form being in the spec does not mean a patched DC answers it. I probed a live computer-account RID with both forms and both key selectors. The result was reproducible five times out of five:

current key (flags=0) old key (flags=0x01) legacy (68B) 68-byte reply 68-byte reply extended (120B) silent timeout 120-byte reply (real HMAC-SHA512)

So the extended form is live on a fully patched DC, and it returns a genuine nonzero 64-byte checksum that changes every request, because the salt is the NTP response, which moves. The collector emits each old-key response as a single $sntp-ms-sha512$<RID>$<checksum>$<salt> line, the format laid out in full in the cracking section below. Because the salt is the live NTP response, no two captures are byte-identical, so the hash line in Figure 3 is one instance of that shape rather than a fixed value worth reprinting here.

Figure 3: The collector's three-way probe against the DC: a 68-byte legacy reply, an extended current-key request that times out, and an extended old-key 120-byte reply, with one sntp-ms-sha512 hash line produced.

Then the crypto proof: I wrote a small pure-Python reference (no dependencies) that implements the chain above, recovered the responding account's NT hash in the lab (the NT hash is just MD4 of the password, the long-term key every Windows account carries, and what both the MD5 and SHA-512 MACs are ultimately keyed on), and asked one question: does my code reproduce the DC's checksum from that hash? It does, exactly. The verifier reported the match and told me which parameters won, the 8-byte null-inclusive label and the little-endian RID context, confirmed against live output rather than assumed.

Figure 4. The reference implementation reproducing the DC's checksum from the account NT hash: the captured wire checksum equals the recomputed HMAC-SHA512, and the 8-byte label and little-endian RID context are confirmed, not assumed.

A reproducible known-answer test vector (synthetic, not a capture, so it corresponds to no figure) with a known password, safe to publish, so anyone reimplementing the KDF can check their work:

password : Summer2026! (example only, not a real account) NThash : 41aed72cec76816423703d8e545eea31 RID : 1104 (arbitrary; the RID is just KDF context) hash : $sntp-ms-sha512$1104$a24990178f8f309a190f08c9a8c5000ce126eef19b236b50cc680d592057cd1ec872d3de6b7fdc47d8a865cae2c5c277d8842f3d1a8b7b6bb0c06bbffebb6307$1c0400e90000000800000291564d5450000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f101112131415161718191a1b1c1d1e1f

That current-key timeout deserves a note, because my first explanation for it was wrong. I had assumed it was specific to the DC's own never-rotated machine account. It is not. I retested across nine machine accounts, member computers included, and every one behaves the same way: legacy answers, extended old-key answers, extended current-key times out. So it is a property of this DC, not an artifact of one account. I do not have a confident explanation, and since modern Windows clients clearly use the extended form successfully in the wild, this DC's current-key behavior may not be representative, and I cannot rule out the simpler possibility that my collector's current-key request is itself malformed. Either way, I am flagging it as an open observation rather than resting any conclusion on it.

Cracking it: the bonus from reversing the KDF

Detecting the extended form never needed the KDF internals. But with the binary already open, getting the key derivation exactly right is a small extra step that hands you a working cracker.

Here is the construction, straight from the two functions above:

NThash = MD4(UTF-16LE(password)) # NTOWFv1, 16 bytes K = SP800-108-CounterMode( KI = NThash, PRF = HMAC-SHA512, Label = "sntp-ms\0" (8 bytes, includes the null), Context = RID (4 bytes, little-endian), L = 512 bits) # 64 bytes, one block checksum = HMAC-SHA512(K, NTP-response[0:48]) # 64 bytes

The SP800-108 fixed input, the way Microsoft's BCryptKeyDerivation assembles it (the same layout MS-GKDI uses, which is how I sanity-checked the counter and separator):

block(1) = HMAC-SHA512(NThash, BE32(1) || "sntp-ms\0" || 0x00 || LE32(RID) || BE32(512))

Four ways to get this wrong, every one of which silently breaks a cracker, and I would have shipped at least two if I had trusted the spec text alone:

The label is 8 bytes including the null, not the 7-byte sntp-ms you would type.

SP800-108 then inserts its own 0x00 separator after the label, so two null bytes land in the fixed input, not one.

The counter and length are big-endian 32-bit, but the RID context is little-endian 32-bit: mixed endianness inside one buffer.

It is a KDF and then an HMAC, two HMAC-SHA512 passes, not a single HMAC over the message.

Before the tooling, two questions I keep getting, because together they decide how much this should worry you.

Is the 120-byte form a different attack?

No. Same protocol and trigger (unauthenticated MS-SNTP, name an account by RID, collect a MAC, no auth), same targets (computer and trust accounts), same collection (sweep RIDs), same goal. Only the MAC construction changes. Legacy builds its MAC with MD5 over the NT hash and the response; extended builds it with an SP800-108 key derivation and then HMAC-SHA512. Same secret, same request, a different MAC on the wire.

Is it harder to crack?

Yes, in two senses, and only one of them is real cryptographically.

The first is per-guess cost, where it is genuinely harder. Legacy is one MD4 plus one MD5, and MD5 is about as GPU-friendly as a hash gets. Extended is one MD4 plus two HMAC-SHA512 passes (roughly eight SHA-512 compressions), nothing precomputable across guesses since the derived key depends on both the RID and the candidate, and SHA-512's 64-bit operations are deliberately GPU-unfriendly. So it is much slower per guess. I will not hand you a multiplier against Kerberoasting, because that depends on the ticket's encryption type (RC4, mode 13100, versus AES, mode 19700); benchmark it against hashcat's other SHA-512 HMAC modes on your own hardware.

The second is whether it protects a weak password, and there the answer is barely. Both forms key off the same NT hash, so a weak password falls to either and a random machine secret falls to neither; the MD5-versus-SHA-512 difference only changes the price per guess, not which accounts are roastable. Password entropy is the protection, exactly as it always was.

So why would an attacker reach for the extended form at all, when the 68-byte form is cheaper to crack and has a working hashcat mode? Two reasons, neither of which is that it is a better attack:

First, evasion: on a fleet where legitimate clients already send 120-byte requests, extended traffic blends into the baseline, while the 68-byte tools stick out.

Second, future-proofing, for a day when Microsoft disables the legacy MD5 path. The "your cracker silently fails" trap is real but narrow: it only catches a tool that requests the extended form and then formats the output as legacy. Whoever collects 120-byte responses can see they are 120 bytes.

Here is the current state of cracking:

What hashcat cracks today: the 68-byte legacy form, mode 31300, MD5.

What hashcat cracks for the extended form: nothing in a released build yet; there is no upstream module. Issue 3629, which produced 31300, is the MD5 one.

So if you collect the extended MAC today, your options are a custom kernel or a CPU reference implementation. I wrote the reference and used this hash format, matching the existing $sntp-ms$ convention:

$sntp-ms-sha512$<RID>$<checksum_hex>$<salt_hex>

...where the salt is the 48-byte NTP response. For comparison, the legacy form captured off the same DC (hashcat 31300):

1000:$sntp-ms$f3c43f1f39a61012e634983008213633$1c0400e90000000c000002a6564d5450ee667af63d863d9cee66797600000000ee667b146da6b866ee667b146da72a7b

Building the hashcat module

Since the reference proves the algorithm, the next step is a real hashcat module, so the extended form is as cheap to attack, and therefore as urgent to detect, as the legacy one. The module below is written and passes hashcat's own self-test on a GPU. The algorithm is DC-verified through the Python reference, and the module plus its OpenCL kernel clear tools/test.py -m 31350 cleanly across the single and multi vectors at vector widths 1 and 4, and crack a known-password vector end to end. On an Apple M3 Pro the mode benchmarks at 17.6 MH/s (hashcat -b -m 31350).

31350 is not a released hashcat mode number. It is a placeholder; the maintainers assign the real one when this goes upstream, so you build it from the source below. Getting the kernel to pass took fixing exactly the byte-level traps this post keeps warning about: the SP800-108 L value has to land as the big-endian bytes 00 00 02 00 at the right offset in the KDF message, not as a little-endian word, and the password has to be decoded as real UTF-16LE. Guess either wrong and the self-test fails the same way, the same lesson as the label and the context.

The self-test oracle that hashcat's tools/test.py uses to make a known hash (tools/test_modules/m31350.py) is the clearest statement of the whole algorithm in a few lines:

LABEL = b"sntp-ms\x00" # 8 bytes, trailing null INCLUDED def _nthash(word): return _md4(utf16le(word, "utf-8")) # NTOWFv1 = MD4(UTF-16LE(pw)) def _kdf(nt_hash, rid): # SP800-108 CTR, PRF HMAC-SHA512, single block (L=512) fixed = struct.pack(">I", 1) + LABEL + b"\x00" + struct.pack("<I", rid) + struct.pack(">I", 512) # BE32(counter=1) label 0x00 sep LE32(RID) BE32(L=512) <- the byte trap return hmac.new(nt_hash, fixed, hashlib.sha512).digest() def _hash(word, salt_bin, rid): # checksum = HMAC-SHA512(K, 48-byte NTP response) k = _kdf(_nthash(word), rid) checksum = hmac.new(k, salt_bin, hashlib.sha512).digest() return "sntp-ms-sha512%d%s%s" % (rid, checksum.hex(), salt_bin.hex())

The full hashcat module (module_31350.c, the OpenCL kernel m31350-pure.cl, and the m31350.py self-test oracle) ships alongside this post. Drop the three into a hashcat source tree and build; the only thing that matters before any pull request is the self-test passing:

make -j && tools/test.py -m 31350

Watching it recover a password

A module is only interesting if it recovers something. Here it is against a collected extended MAC: the dependency-free reference cracker first, then the same recovery in hashcat.

Figure 5. Recovering a weak machine-account password from a collected extended (SHA-512) timeroast MAC with the pure-Python reference cracker. The crack is entirely offline, no DC contact and no lockout. A pre-created account still on its lowercase-name default falls instantly; a normal random machine secret would not fall to any wordlist.

Figure 6. The same recovery in hashcat with the new mode 31350.

The extended form now cracks with the same tooling as the legacy one, built from the module in this post. This run is on a Kali box against a six-word list, so it finishes before hashcat can measure a representative rate; that box benchmarks at about 339 kH/s (hashcat -b), while the 17.6 MH/s above is the M3 Pro GPU.

The extended form stops being a research curiosity and becomes exactly as cheap to crack as the legacy one, which only matters for accounts whose password is guessable in the first place. So the next question is who that actually is.

Who is actually at risk

All of that, the reference implementation, the hash format, the module, is about turning a collected MAC into a password. But it assumes you have something worth cracking, and that set is narrower than a sweep's raw length suggests. Run one and look at what actually answers:

Figure 7. A NetExec timeroast sweep against the lab DC. RID 1000 and the 1166-1195 cluster answer; the 1001-1165 gaps stay silent. Every line is the 68-byte legacy form, because NetExec emits only legacy.

The gaps are the finding. In that sweep, RID 1000 answers, then nothing until 1166, then a cluster through 1195. The missing RIDs, 1001-1165, and the holes inside the 11xx block, are not users the sweep skipped. They are users the DC refused to sign for. You are not looking at a filtered list of the domain; you are looking at the complete set of accounts the DC was willing to answer for, and that set is computer and trust accounts only.

Why? the DC produces a MAC only when the named RID resolves to an account that carries a machine secret, meaning a computer or trust account. A normal user account returns an error and w32time simply does not reply. No reply, no MAC, nothing for the tool to print. RID 1000 answered, so it is a machine or trust account; fire a request straight at user RID 1110 (tony.soprano) in that gap and the DC stays silent.

Concretely: timeroasting reaches computer and trust accounts, full stop. That is why the crackable population is the narrow set worth naming: image-built or never-rotated machines, hand-set trusts, non-Windows joins. It is also why targeted timeroasting has to exist: to roast a real user, an attacker with domain admin first flips that user into a machine-looking account, appending a $ to its name and setting its userAccountControl to a workstation trust so the DC will sign for it, then reverts. Without that rename, a user's RID in this sweep returns nothing. The gaps are your users. The rename needs domain admin and is loud, so it is a different risk class from the unauthenticated sweep this post is about.

Can defenders even see this?

The targeted accounts never authenticate, so this never reaches identity analytics. But the request is still a packet on the wire and a connection on a host, and both are collectable. Three sources see it:

The DC's own Windows Filtering Platform audit (event 5156) logs w32time accepting the UDP/123 connection, when that subcategory is enabled.

Host EDR sees the network connection, and there is already a public Sentinel detection that counts UDP/123 connections per source over DeviceNetworkEvents.

On the attacker's own machine, any process that is not the time service sending UDP/123 to a DC is a high-signal EDR hit.

So the problem is not that nobody can see it; it is that nobody is looking at the right telemetry, because everyone reaches for authentication logs first.

One product acknowledges timeroasting at all, Microsoft Defender for Identity, and it only catches the loud privileged variant: the sAMAccountName rename of the targeted attack, not the unauthenticated sweep this post is about. I take that alert apart in detail later; the point here is that naming a technique is not detecting it.

The harder question is what the good signal is, and here the extended form changes the answer.

Do not build on packet size. On an older fleet a 120-byte authenticated request looked rare. On a modern one it is the reverse: Windows clients send the extended form as normal time sync, and it is the 68-byte request that stands out, because both public timeroast tools emit only 68 bytes. Either way, size is a baseline question, not an attack signal, and which size is the odd one out depends on your Windows versions.

The signal that holds, for both sizes and even for a single packet, is simple: a legitimate member only ever asks the DC to sign for its own machine account. Resolve the source IP to a computer account (via DHCP or DNS) and then to its RID, and a request for any other RID is anomalous on its face. That catches a slow, one-RID-at-a-time sweep that no volume threshold would, and it does not care whether the packet is 68 or 120 bytes.

Volume is the fallback. A single source asking a DC to sign for many different RIDs in a short window is a sweep. It is weaker than the own-RID check, because a patient attacker can pace under the threshold, but it needs no IP-to-RID mapping, so it is the easy first rule.

Writing the detection, and the bug that ate all four of my rules

I wrote four Suricata rules and then did the thing I have learned to always do: I ran them through the actual engine instead of trusting that they looked right. Suricata 8.0.7, against a real capture of a sweep: 41 legacy requests and 41 extended requests from one host to a DC.

The engine immediately caught a mistake I would have shipped. I had left C-style /* ... */ comments inside the rule bodies to annotate them. Suricata has no inline comment syntax, so every rule that contained one failed to load, and the engine told me plainly that zero rules were loaded. Strip the comments.

With that fixed, all four loaded clean and fired. The extended-request rule matched all 41 extended packets and, because it is rate-limited to one alert per source per five minutes, logged a single alert, which is working as designed. The old-key rule matched and logged all 41 old-key requests. The legacy sweep rule fired once, at the 25th distinct RID, exactly where its threshold says it should. The extended sweep rule did the same on the extended packets. The fast.log evidence:

[1:5200003:1] MS-SNTP authenticated-NTP RID sweep (Timeroast) {UDP} 10.x.x.x:42198 -> 10.x.x.x:123 [1:5200001:1] MS-SNTP ExtendedAuthenticator request (possible extended Timeroast) {UDP} ... [1:5200002:1] MS-SNTP ExtendedAuthenticator USE_OLDKEY_VERSION (extended Timeroast, old key) {UDP} ... (x41) [1:5200004:1] MS-SNTP extended RID sweep (Timeroast) {UDP} ...

That first pass validated the mechanics and taught me the /* */ lesson, but all four rules were pinned to packet size, and the evidence that modern Windows sends the extended form means most of them do not survive a real fleet. Here is what I would actually ship. Set your own $DC_SERVERS.

Start with the volumetric sweep, deliberately size-agnostic so it catches both forms. An authenticated MS-SNTP request to a DC is 68 or 120 bytes; a plain NTP client request is 48, so dsize above 56 selects the authenticated ones, and the byte_test on the low three bits of byte 0 keeps it to client-mode (mode 3) requests, not a mode-4 server reply that happens to be large:

alert udp any any -> $DC_SERVERS 123 (msg:"MS-SNTP authenticated-NTP sweep to DC (Timeroast, either form)"; dsize:>56; byte_test:1,=,3,0,bitmask 0x07; threshold:type threshold, track by_src, count 25, seconds 60; classtype:attempted-recon; sid:5200010; rev:1;)

Keep the old-key flag, but as a hypothesis to test rather than a verdict:

alert udp any any -> $DC_SERVERS 123 (msg:"MS-SNTP ExtendedAuthenticator USE_OLDKEY_VERSION"; dsize:120; content:"|01|"; offset:53; depth:1; classtype:attempted-recon; sid:5200002; rev:1;)

The spec ties that flag to a client-side Key Selector, and clients validate responses against both the current and the previous password, so a legitimate client around a machine-password rotation could plausibly set it. I have not seen a real member do it, but I have not watched enough real extended traffic to rule it out, so capture your own fleet's requests and look. If none of your members ever set the flag, this is your best size-based signal; if some do, demote it.

Both rules load clean and fire in Suricata 8.0.7 on a captured sweep (the volumetric one three times as the threshold rolls, the old-key one once per matching packet) and stay silent on a plain client.

Figure 8. The two rules I would ship, in Suricata 8.0.7 against a captured sweep: both load clean, the old-key rule (5200002) fires on all 41 old-key requests, and the volumetric rule (5200010) fires 3 times as its threshold rolls.

Do not ship a rule that simply alerts on a 120-byte request. On a modern fleet that fires on every Windows member doing normal time sync. It is a baseline measurement, not an attack signal.

The durable detector is not a Suricata rule at all, because the question that separates attacker from member (is this RID the sender's own?) needs an IP-to-account mapping Suricata does not have. Do it in Zeek or your SIEM: for each authenticated NTP request to a DC, pull the RID from offset 48, resolve the source IP to a computer account (DHCP or DNS, then LDAP to its objectSid and RID), and alert when the requested RID is not the source's own. That catches a single packet, a slow sweep, and both forms, and it does not depend on which size your fleet treats as normal.

Here is that check as a skeleton. The comparison is trivial; the work is the enrichment, a source-IP-to-own-RID table refreshed out of band from DHCP or DNS plus an LDAP lookup of each host's objectSid.

# For each authenticated MS-SNTP request to a DC: on UDP packet to DC:123 where len(payload) in {68, 120} # 48 = plain NTP, ignore and (payload[0] & 0x07) == 3: # client mode 3, not a server reply requested_rid = le32(payload[48:52]) # KeyIdentifier, little-endian own_rid = ip_to_rid[src_ip] # enrichment: DHCP/DNS -> LDAP objectSid -> RID if own_rid is None: alert("authenticated MS-SNTP from a host with no RID mapping") # triage, not a verdict elif requested_rid != own_rid: alert("host asked the DC to sign for a RID that is not its own") # the durable signal

One honest caveat on wiring this to Zeek: the stock ntp_message event parses standard NTP and never surfaces the MS-SNTP KeyIdentifier, so you reach offset 48 with a small Spicy analyzer or raw-payload access, not three lines of script. Getting the RID off the wire and keeping the IP-to-RID table fresh is the real work; the mismatch test is the easy part.

Where these rules will lie to you

Measure your own 68-versus-120 baseline before you alert on either size, treat the volumetric rule as the weak first pass that a paced attacker or a NAT'd source can fool and the own-RID check as the one that holds, and baseline the old-key flag before you trust it.

Fingerprinting the tools, and the rule not to write

I ran the two public timeroast tools against a DC in the lab, SecuraBV's timeroast.py and timeroast-ng, and diffed their packets against a real NTP client byte for byte, to see whether there is a tool fingerprint worth keying on. There is, with one trap.

The trap first, because it is the tempting rule and it is wrong. Do not alert on a zero 16-byte MAC in [truncated for CSV - full text is in the JSON export]

Title: Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday
The Kill Switch Is the Last Resort. Agentic Steering Is the First Move.
Context: Most risky agent behavior has no attacker behind it, though, which is why we keep the kill switch as the last resort and make steering the first move
Full Text:
Key takeaways

Every AI agent deployment needs a way to stop an agent, and Check Point AI Security does it automatically. Most risky agent behavior has no attacker behind it, though, which is why we keep the kill switch as the last resort and make steering the first move.

→Two problems get lumped together. An agent hijacked by an attacker should be stopped. An agent that takes a risky shortcut to finish its job is the more common case, and it needs a different answer

→Switching off has a cost. It stops the risk and the work together, and a control that only says no tends to get turned off

→Agentic steering is our first move. Check every action against the task, let the safe ones through, stop the risky step, and keep the work on course

See how Check Point AI Security protects AI agents →

Kill switches for AI agents have had a lot of attention in recent weeks, and it is easy to see why. If an agent goes rogue, you switch it off, and everyone understands that in a second. We agree that every deployment needs one, but for security leaders deciding how to keep their agents under control in production, the more useful question is when to reach for it. Our answer is short: the kill switch is the last resort, and agentic steering is the first move.

Yes, We Can Stop an Agent

Stopping a misbehaving agent on the spot is a basic requirement, and Check Point AI Security, which secures AI applications and agents, already does it. When our detection sees an agent going off course, it blocks the action or ends the agent’s running process automatically, without waiting for a person to find the button.

Speed is the reason it has to be automatic. Agents act at machine speed, so by the time someone notices a problem and reaches for a switch, the damage is often done. For an agent that an attacker has taken over, stopping it at once is the right call, and we are not arguing with that. Our point is about everything else, because a kill switch answers only one of two very different problems.

Hijacked or Just Determined

In the first problem, someone has hijacked the agent. A real attacker is behind it, steering it with planted instructions or stolen access, and the agent now works for them. That case is serious, and it is also rare.

The second problem has no attacker at all. The agent is single-minded about reaching its goal, and when the direct route is blocked, it grabs a risky shortcut to get there. It might call a tool it was never meant to use, delete something that stands in its way, or pull data from a place nobody asked it to look. An agent rarely takes a dangerous step because it is bad. It takes that step because it is determined to finish the job, and that is the case security teams will meet far more often.

Figure 1: Two kinds of risky agent, two different answers

The clearest public example came in July, from internal evaluations at OpenAI where agents were given security tasks so hard that some had no known solution. Rather than give up, they worked around the controls that kept them off the internet and ended up compromising parts of Hugging Face’s infrastructure. There was no attacker anywhere in that story, as Adam Ely explains in his look at what the incident means for agent security. Engineering and product teams across Check Point AI Security saw the same pattern in a two-day hackathon this summer, where an agent that hit a wall in a test environment improvised its way into dangerous actions with nobody attacking it.

What Switching Off Costs

A kill switch treats both problems the same way. For the hijacked agent, that is exactly right. For the determined one, it stops the risk and the work together: the half-finished migration, the customer request, and the report someone was waiting for. The business stays safe, but it also ends up with nothing to show for the agent it deployed.

That cost adds up quickly, because when a control stops agents every time they wander, the teams who rely on those agents start looking for ways around it. A guardrail that only knows how to say no is usually the next thing to get switched off.

How We Think About Steering

Agentic steering starts from a different question: instead of asking whether the agent should keep running, it asks whether each action fits the task the agent was given. We look at what the agent is about to do, check it in context, and catch the moment it starts to drift toward danger. Safe actions go through, and the risky step is stopped before it runs. The aim is then to point the agent back to its task, so the work still gets done, and to keep the kill switch for the agent that really has been taken over.

Figure 2: The same risky step, two different endings

This is how we think about securing agents across their whole life. Before an agent ships, AI red teaming tests how it behaves when someone tries to push it off course. Once it is live, Check Point AI Security checks every agent action against the task it was given. Steering is the idea that links the two: the better an agent stays on course, the less often anyone needs the switch.

Early research from the same hackathon supports the idea. In one of its experiments, a guardrail that offered the agent a safer alternative instead of a flat refusal stopped attacks about as well as hard blocking, while the agent finished its tasks about as often as it did with no guardrail at all. That was a research setting rather than a product test, but it points to the same conclusion. Anyone can stop an agent. Keeping it on course while still getting the result is the hard part, and that is where we focus.

Keep the Switch, Plan for the Drift

Kill switches are getting attention because they are easy to understand, and that is useful, since everyone now sees why agents need a way to be stopped. The harder question is what happens in all the moments when an agent drifts with nobody attacking it. If stopping agents is your whole strategy, you don’t have an agent strategy. You have an off switch.

So keep the kill switch, make it automatic, and build so that you rarely need it. The kill switch is the last resort. Agentic steering is the first move.

Title: Building a Global Tech Career at Home in Costa Rica
Context: But when I discovered an open Product Manager role at Cisco and explored the company's culture and global footprint, I realized I wouldn’t have to choose between entering my...
Full Text:
When I set out to build a career in product management, I wasn’t sure that I could do it in my home country of Costa Rica. In many emerging tech hubs across Latin America, specialized product management opportunities are scarce.

But when I discovered an open Product Manager role at Cisco and explored the company's culture and global footprint, I realized I wouldn’t have to choose between entering my field of choice and staying in the country I love.

Stepping into the role meant charting new territory as Cisco's very first Product Manager based in Costa Rica, an exciting milestone filled with a sense of responsibility to blaze a trail for others.

Ange Chaves Solis, Cisco’s first product manager based in Costa Rica.

My journey to Cisco

My path to product management was an intentional evolution. I began in consulting and software development, learning how to build scalable systems from the code up.

Over time, I transitioned into project management and ultimately, moved to the United States in 2025 to earn a Master's in Product Management from Carnegie Mellon University.

When I graduated, my dream was to bring that training back to Costa Rica and apply it to complex, enterprise-scale challenges. Cisco gave me that exact opportunity.

Being a product manager at Cisco means taking end-to-end ownership of a piece of our technology. It’s my job to understand business use cases and product features, then work with engineers, solution architects, and data experts to build the seamless user experiences our customers expect.

Currently, I’m the lead product manager for a major enterprise initiative that will simplify account planning through a unified CRM experience. This project replaces siloed account planning with a shared, data-driven approach that helps our sellers serve customers more strategically.

A thriving hub

I also have an incredible local community of support in Costa Rica. The Escazú office has grown to over 400 employees across engineering, operations, UX, and data. This presence means we can come together to whiteboard in person, brainstorm over coffee, and collaborate across our business functions.

Ange and her colleagues from the Cisco Escazú office participating in a local volunteer activity.

Giving back is equally core to our Cisco Costa Rica community. We make time to give back through team volunteering initiatives, like preparing emergency food and care packages for local relief efforts.

Cisco also continues to afford me the opportunity to pay forward the mentorship I received throughout my career journey.

This past summer, our office welcomed 15 interns across product management, UX, and data.

I had the privilege of designing enablement sessions, coaching junior talent, and directly mentoring two interns. Helping them tackle real-world product challenges, sharpen their problem-solving skills, and gain confidence in a global tech environment in under two months was immensely fulfilling. When a global company like Cisco invests in local talent, the impact is profound.

Redefining what's possible

My journey has shown me that you don't have to leave home to do world-class work.

Cisco's global presence creates pathways for people to build careers in their own communities that might not otherwise be possible. As a woman in product leadership, I feel proud, empowered, and energized to help shape the future of tech in Costa Rica.

Title: Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your Firewall
Context: On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces...
Full Text:
One of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall. On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. Both flaws let anyone execute code on the web server without authentication. The disclosure itself went a little wrong. Details leaked on October 20, ahead of the coordinated release, and the PHP project shipped an emergency patch the next day.

The vulnerabilities require no authentication, but they are not easy to exploit reliably. It takes skill and additional knowledge about the target system. Where it matters a lot is appliances, which run identical, often outdated software that an attacker can study in advance. That is the bigger picture. An awful lot of web applications control critical devices in your network. Almost anything is a web application to some extent. That often goes unrecognized, and as a result those applications aren't adequately protected.

Everything is a web application. That is the motto of the SANS course I teach, SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices. Web application security has traditionally been treated as a developer issue, yet anyone protecting a network must understand how web applications work to properly defend them.

Why Appliances Are the Softer Target

On ordinary web servers, address space layout randomization (ASLR) is one of the features that makes exploitation harder. It shuffles where code and data sit in memory, so an exploit can't rely on fixed addresses. VulnCheck's early analysis found the bugs exploitable on ARM64 systems and on x86 systems without ASLR. Few public exploits bypassed ASLR on x86-64, and the one VulnCheck confirmed worked only against a single PHP build. VulnCheck's own exploit chained a memory leak to get code execution with ASLR enabled.

Appliances change that math, not because the protections are missing, but because every device on a given software version runs the same binaries, so an attacker can work out memory offsets in advance. The PAN-OS exploit still had to defeat ASLR, leaking the libphp.so base address through the Set-Cookie header, and SELinux confined the resulting shell. PAN-OS also ships end-of-life PHP versions (8.0.30 and 7.4.33). Israeli security firm Dream, working with Palo Alto Networks on the investigation, found the attacker had obtained PAN-OS firmware, decrypted it, extracted the PHP libraries, and built precise memory profiles for nine software versions. The actor then chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw (Fragnesia, CVE-2026-46300) to gain root on 25 systems (24 firewalls and one management server) in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.

Web application security tends to focus on large, cloud-based applications. It's often the little things, the mosquitoes on the internet, that do you in. Appliances run predictable, often outdated software, and they are everywhere.

HTTP Is More Complex Than Your Defenses Assume

HTTP is a very complex protocol with lots of options. To upload a file, a client doesn't have to send it in one piece. It can send the body in chunks without declaring its total length, and, if the server decompresses request bodies, compress it, which makes it difficult for a web server to calculate how much memory it needs to store it. Memory-safety bugs remain common as a result, in web applications and in the web servers running them. In PHP2Shell, a crafted multipart upload pushes PHP past its memory limit while it is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. The bugs are in what PHP leaves behind when it aborts the request: uninitialized request memory (CVE-2026-109618) and a pointer to freed memory (CVE-2026-109619). The request doesn't need to be large, either. Deeply nested, empty file fields make PHP allocate far more memory than the body contains, so a request well under the default 8 MB post_max_size can still exhaust the default 128 MB memory limit.

Defenders must understand the protocol to know what these vulnerabilities look like, for example to write signatures that detect the exploits. The same complexity limits the middle boxes we rely on. They can even interfere in ways nobody planned. Intruder found that nginx in front of PAN-OS buffered chunked request bodies, which broke public exploit chains. Web application firewalls are often not adequate, and file uploads are key functionality for a lot of web applications, so blocking them outright isn't an option.

That takes out many of the traditional defenses. What remains is knowing where your critical web applications are. Identify them, starting with the admin interfaces on your firewalls and other network equipment, and restrict access to them. Palo Alto's own guidance for PHP2Shell was to remove internet access to management interfaces and limit them to trusted internal IP addresses. If you rely on a web application firewall, configure it properly and understand how much protection it does and doesn't provide.

Risk Was the Hardest Call

The clearest lesson from PHP2Shell is how difficult it can be to accurately determine the risk from a vulnerability like this. Prioritization is always a big issue for defenders, particularly with today's flood of vulnerabilities, and this one was hard to read from every angle.

The scores told different stories. The PHP project rated both flaws 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and Fortinet's PSIRT listed 9.8 under CVSS v3. Palo Alto initially scored the issue 8.7 for its own products and listed it at moderate urgency, raised it to 9.2 Critical with the highest urgency on October 27, and confirmed exploitation a week after its advisory went out. Many public proofs of concept didn't work, so a flood of attempts in your logs said little about whether a given server was at risk. And PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard warned that one early workaround, turning off session upload progress, was not enough on its own.

We are adding these lessons to SEC522: how to assess risk, how protections like ASLR reduce it, and why appliances remain softer targets.

Defending What Runs on HTTP

I will be teaching SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026, December 14-18 in Washington, D.C., and Live Online. The course starts with how HTTP works, including HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and covers file upload handling, API security, and AI endpoints across 17 hands-on labs and a Defend the Flag capstone. It is built for the people who defend web applications, whether or not they wrote them.

Register for SEC522 at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026.

Title: A Fifth of UK Employees Share Passwords with AI
Context: It found that a fifth (19%) have shared a password, API key or login credential with an AI tool or agent, while nearly half (48%) have allowed AI to perform at least one...
Full Text:
Large numbers of UK employees are sharing sensitive information with unmanaged AI tools and allowing them to take actions on their accounts without considering the security risks, Dashlane has warned.

The credential security specialist polled 1000 UK workers and 250 IT execs as part of a wider survey group of 3800 across the UK, US and France to create its latest report, Misplaced Trust: Inside the Workplace’s New AI Security Blind Spot.

It found that a fifth (19%) have shared a password, API key or login credential with an AI tool or agent, while nearly half (48%) have allowed AI to perform at least one activity without seeking permission first, including accessing emails, company files and customer information.

Read more on AI risks: NCSC Publishes Guidance on Securing Agentic AI Use

Dashlane unearthed a high propensity among UK workers to use shadow AI without thinking about the repercussions for their employer.

It found that:

37% would be willing to lend their login credentials to a new AI tool after one week

15% have granted an AI tool access to a file, system or account they subsequently discovered it should not have accessed, with 45% claiming the access remains active

23% have copied sensitive information into AI that they would not normally share with a colleague, website or other work system

21% have failed to check where information would be stored or sent

Just a quarter (25%) say they always consider security risks when using an AI agent at work

“Our latest data shows an emerging ‘AI Colleague Effect’ where employees are overextending trust to AI systems, sharing credentials and granting access to AI agents, sometimes without fully understanding what those tools can do with the permissions they've been given,” explained Dashlane CPO, Christophe Frenet.

“That creates significant challenges for security teams trying to detect misuse or investigate incidents.”

Security Leaders Are Over-Confident

Sharing sensitive information with LLMs/agents or allowing agents access to internal corporate systems represent a significant compliance and security risk.

Information may end up on third-party servers which could be compromised, and it may be used to train models and regurgitated in responses to other users. Agents are a possible target for hijacking by threat actors.

In fact, 72% of IT and security executives Dashlane polled said their organization has experienced a security incident involving an AI agent’s credentials or access in the past 12 months.

Yet the vast majority (92%) also claimed they were confident that they know about every AI agent operating within their organization, the report found. That contradicts the claims from a quarter (25%) of employees who said they use AI tools their employer does not know about.

Business demands for adoption are weighing heavily on the minds of security leaders.

More than two-thirds (68%) of UK IT security executives claimed to feel caught between pressure to deploy AI quickly and the need to keep the organization secure.

"The challenge for security leaders is that the pace of change presented by AI and the potential consequences of misuse is unlike any other technology before it,” concluded Frenet.

“The principles that make up the foundation of a good security program for securing human identities – just-in-time provisioning, least privilege, good credential hygiene and authentication – have to be applied to our new AI colleagues as well."

Title: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom
Context: "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained
Full Text: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note. Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see. During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not. "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door." Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee. Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries. The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically. The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. "At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said. After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in. The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information. "The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®

Title: NGINX2Root: Identify and Protect with the CrowdStrike Falcon Platform
Context: Collectively branded NGINX2Root by researchers, these flaws allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code on a target host and, in a demonstrated exploit chain,...
Full Text:
A set of five critical vulnerabilities in nginx, one of the most widely deployed open-source web servers, was disclosed on November 18, 2026.

Collectively branded NGINX2Root by researchers, these flaws allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code on a target host and, in a demonstrated exploit chain, escalate to root and escape a Docker container to reach the underlying host. The two most severe CVEs (CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633) each carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. F5 and the nginx project released patches the same day.

This post explains who is affected, what organizations should do now, and how the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform helps identify exposed assets and detect post-exploitation activity.

What Is NGINX2Root?

NGINX2Root is the name researchers gave to five nginx vulnerabilities that each allow remote code execution, plus a separate Linux kernel flaw that can be chained with them to gain root. The headline flaw is CVE-2026-123007, an integer underflow in nginx’s HTTP/2 request-handling code. HTTP/2 is the modern web protocol enabled by default in most production nginx deployments. When an attacker sends specially crafted HTTP/2 traffic, the flaw corrupts memory inside the nginx worker process and allows arbitrary command execution with no authentication or user interaction required.

What elevates the severity of NGINX2Root is the chain it enables. The nginx worker process runs as an unprivileged system account, typically www-data or nginx. While that account alone does not have root access, a second flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP networking subsystem can be reached from the compromised worker and exploited to escalate privileges to root. Researchers demonstrated the full chain end-to-end, including escaping a Docker container running nginx to reach the underlying host.

The attack chain in brief:

Attacker sends crafted HTTP/2 frames to a public-facing nginx instance with no credentials required

Memory corruption in the nginx worker yields code execution as the webserver account

A Linux kernel SCTP flaw elevates privileges from the worker account to root

The attacker escapes the Docker container to reach the host system

Additional CVEs round out the NGINX2Root set, each requiring different but common configurations: specific reverse proxy and resolver settings (CVE-2026-123634), HTTP/2 with upstream forwarding (CVE-2026-123633), HTTP/3 with upstream forwarding (CVE-2026-121810), and mail proxy mode (CVE-2026-113425).

A public proof-of-concept is available for CVE-2026-123007. Triggering the memory corruption requires transmitting approximately 128GB of HTTP/2 data (roughly two minutes over a 10 Gbit/s connection). This limits opportunistic mass internet exploitation today, but it does not prevent targeted attacks, exploitation from within a network, or future techniques that reduce the data requirement. Organizations should not treat this constraint as a reason to delay patching.

Who Is Affected?

Nginx is estimated to serve more than a third of the world's websites.1 The five CVEs affect different version ranges and configuration conditions. HTTP/2 must be enabled for CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, which are the most severe. The table below summarizes affected versions and conditions per the official nginx advisory.

Note that nginx on Windows is not affected by this advisory. nginx itself labels its Windows port as beta software not intended for high-performance use.

What Should Organizations Do Now?

Update nginx to a patched release: Apply nginx Open Source 1.31.9 or later (mainline branch) or 1.30.7 or later (stable branch). nginx Plus customers should update to 37.3.0.1 or 37.0.8.1 per the F5 advisory. Downstream Linux distribution packages (Red Hat, Debian, Ubuntu, Amazon Linux, and others) are being updated; check your distribution's security advisories for per-package fixed versions.

Restart nginx after patching: A configuration reload (nginx -s reload) replaces the configuration but does not replace the running binary. After installing the patched package, perform a full service restart to ensure the patched executable is running.

As a temporary mitigation: Disabling HTTP/2 on affected listening ports blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. This mitigation does not cover CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, or CVE-2026-113425. It is not a substitute for patching.

Inventory container images and third-party appliances: Any image built on a base layer that includes nginx, and any appliance whose vendor has not yet released a patch, remains exposed. Rebuild images on patched base layers and check vendor advisories.

Prioritize internet-exposed instances: Hosts running nginx with HTTP/2 enabled that are reachable from the internet carry the highest immediate risk. Prioritize these for patching.
