Title: Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
Context: Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France
Full Text:
Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.

Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.

The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation.

Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done.

Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet.

A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name System

To understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory.

DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy.

And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications.

In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. Cloudflare launched our public DNS resolver 1.1.1.1 in April 2018 to give back to the Internet. Our goal was to make a fast, reliable, privacy-first consumer DNS service available for free to everyone. We succeeded. 1.1.1.1 is among the fastest DNS resolvers in the world, including in Europe. Cloudflare's resolver doesn’t collect any user data, let alone sell it to advertisers. 1.1.1.1 has always been one of our favorite examples of Cloudflare fulfilling its mission to help build a better Internet.

1.1.1.1 is one of many public resolvers that anyone can use. In addition to 1.1.1.1 and Quad9’s 9.9.9.9, some of the other best-known public resolvers include Google’s 8.8.8.8 and Cisco’s OpenDNS. Just because these services are offered for free doesn’t mean they’re easy to provide. A well-run global public DNS resolver is an extraordinary engineering feat, built to securely and privately resolve hundreds of billions or even trillions of queries a day across a globally distributed network of hundreds of server locations.

As Quad9 notes, there are many other DNS resolvers available to users, many of them offered by essentially anonymous services whose practices are unknown or undocumented. It’s easy to change your DNS resolver, and people do so for a variety of reasons including performance, reliability, or to access specific security features.

Why public DNS resolvers should not be required to block

Rightsholders have a legitimate interest in preventing online piracy. But trying to address online infringement through public DNS resolvers is fundamentally the wrong approach.

Among other things, such blocking is ineffective. Think back to the analogy of an operator finding a phone number in a directory. If a court wants to shut down an illegal business, forcing the directory operator to cross the business's name out of the phone book doesn't actually close the business. The storefront is still open, the products are still there, and anyone who already knows the address, or uses a different phone book, can walk in.

The same is true for the Internet. DNS resolvers are just one link in the transmission chain. The only way a DNS resolver can “block” content is by declining to return the IP address for a particular website. But a public DNS resolver cannot remove the actual infringing content from the Internet, nor can it take down the servers hosting it.

Because of this, blocking by public DNS resolvers is remarkably easy to bypass. Any Internet user who wants to reach a blocked site can circumvent the block in less than a minute simply by switching to one of the thousands of other DNS resolvers available online. In fact, users don’t even need a resolver at all to reach infringing content if they already know the underlying IP address. Unsurprisingly, while blocking via public resolvers may inject some friction for some users when accessing content, there is no evidence that it actually reduces the total amount of online infringement that occurs.

In addition to being ineffective, as we’ve written previously, DNS blocking is a blunt instrument that causes collateral damage. Because DNS operates at the domain level, a resolver cannot block a specific infringing video or file; it must block the entire domain. This affects all content on that domain, whether legal or illegal. It is also entirely opaque to the user: when a resolver is forced to block a domain, the website simply fails to load. The user receives no explanation or legal notice, making it impossible to know if the site is down for maintenance, if their network is broken, or if the site was blocked by a court order.

The problem is substantially worse with respect to public DNS resolvers. Because public resolvers operate globally, any blocking will naturally cross borders, meaning that a single country could dictate what content is accessible around the world. For example, while the EU-dedicated DNS resolver DNS4EU operated by Whalebone blocks in response to country-specific orders, it does so across the entire EU. Efforts to reengineer public DNS resolvers to allow for more localized blocking would fundamentally alter the service, harming performance and resilience, undermining user privacy, and fragmenting the open Internet.

For these reasons, Cloudflare, Google, Cisco, and Quad9 have all opposed efforts to mandate blocking by public DNS resolvers, with some success. Several years ago, courts in Germany ruled in favor of Cloudflare and Quad9, rejecting requests to require DNS blocking. More recently, a French court rejected penalties against Cloudflare for failing to block through 1.1.1.1, finding that other actions we had taken through our CDN and reverse-proxy service were sufficient to comply with the underlying order.

Undeterred, rightsholders have continued to press for blocking by public resolvers with a level of determination that is hard to explain. A recent study found that the majority of online piracy in Europe is hosted in Europe. If rightsholders want to genuinely address online infringement, there are far better places to focus their efforts — most notably by requiring the hosting providers who actually store the pirated files to take them down.

Forcing public DNS resolvers out of markets hurts the Internet

The French court’s penalty order against Quad9 represents the culmination of these rightsholder efforts. As a small non-profit that only offers a public DNS resolver, Quad9 had no alternative methods for demonstrating compliance with the order. The French court therefore granted rightsholders’ request to issue penalties for non-compliance, forcing Quad9 to undermine its own service or leave the country.

Quad9’s withdrawal from France represents a genuine loss for the Internet. In the short term, removal of Quad9’s resolver is likely to cause immediate and potentially severe disruptions to Internet access. Because of the way their service is set up to preserve privacy, Quad9 has no way to know who exactly is using its resolver, let alone to directly communicate to them about the upcoming withdrawal of services. That means that individuals, hospitals, universities, and government offices all may be caught unaware when the resolver stops working. Again, because of how DNS resolvers work, those users will not receive a detailed error message explaining what happened — their Internet will simply stop working. The problem will be even worse when devices like security systems or thermostats are hardwired to use Quad9’s resolver. Fixing these issues may be slow or even impossible.

More generally, driving Quad9 out of France does absolutely nothing to prevent online infringement, but it does leave everyday Internet users with fewer safe, reliable options, particularly ones like Quad9 that also protect users from phishing and malware. Taking established public DNS resolvers away forces Internet users to fall back on the default resolvers offered by their ISPs (which may monetize their browsing data), try lesser-known resolvers operated by anonymous or less trustworthy organizations, or run their own resolver. The irony is that Quad9 and Cloudflare are being pulled into court precisely because we are transparent, reputable organizations. Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web.

The way forward

If nothing else, we hope that Quad9’s announcement may serve as a wake-up call to rightsholders and policymakers that seeking to block infringement at every layer of the Internet has real costs.

We believe there are far better ways to work together to fight piracy without compromising the integrity of the Internet, and Cloudflare continues to pursue innovative collaborations to that end. Our collective efforts in addressing online infringement would be put to better use in seeking to have such content removed at the hosting provider, which would both achieve a more durable solution and avoid collateral damage to the Internet.

In the meantime, we will keep resisting misguided efforts to require blocking by public DNS resolvers. Along with Google and Cisco, we have appealed the Belgian order that would impose penalties on us if we do not start DNS blocking by January 2027. We hope to get a resolution before the end of the year that would avoid another situation like the one Quad9 faces now in France.

We have grave concerns about the disruption that would be caused if additional resolvers are forced to withdraw from markets, and we will continue to advocate against that possible result.

Title: During the Microsoft 365 Disruption, Not A Single Email Was Lost
Context: As a result, not a single email was lost, and every email was scanned for threats before reaching end users Adversity is where resilience proves itself A disruption of this...
Full Text:
Email stopped being “just email” a long time ago. It carries invoices, password resets, approvals, and the sign-in checks that open other services. So when Microsoft 365 service was disrupted for roughly 24 hours, organizations felt the impact right away.

During this downtime, the 90,000+ customers who rely on Check Point WorkSpace email security to protect their mailboxes turned to us for support. Here is what we saw, what we did to keep their email safe and flowing, and what we’re improving.

What our customers needed

When messages couldn’t be delivered to mailboxes, we held them safely until delivery could resume. Our team worked around the clock, across every time zone, to ensure that no email would be lost and that no email would be delivered unless it had been cleared as safe by our security layers. As a result, not a single email was lost, and every email was scanned for threats before reaching end users

Adversity is where resilience proves itself

A disruption of this scale puts every part of the cloud ecosystem under pressure. Our protections continued to operate as designed, while the event reinforced two important learnings about continuing to build resilience in an increasingly interconnected world.

First, outages can have effects far beyond the affected platform. Delays extended into the broader email ecosystem, including mail destined for Gmail users, as queues increased and delivery slowed. The takeaway is simple: organizations cannot assume that a disruption affecting one cloud provider will remain isolated to that environment.

Second, resilience requires the ability to absorb unexpected demand. As queues grew, our platform continued protecting messages while our DevOps team proactively scaled capacity to accommodate the exceptional volume. We’re building on that resilience with additional automation and dynamic capacity management, further reducing the operational intervention required during extreme events.

Attackers follow outages

Disruption creates confusion, and criminals use it. After outages like this, we expect fake support messages, bogus “recovery” links, help-desk impersonation, and payment fraud. Under pressure to keep people working, teams may also be tempted to loosen security controls. That is exactly the moment attackers hope for.

What to do now

Keep multi-factor authentication and other controls on. Log any emergency changes, and reverse them once service returns

Verify every password reset, access request, or payment-change request through a second channel

Give staff an approved backup way to communicate, so they don’t turn to personal email or apps

Tell staff never to sign in through a link in a “recovery” message

Once service is back, review sign-ins and admin changes made during the outage

The bigger picture

This is not the first outtage this year. Undersea cable cuts, the PHP2Shell vulnerability, and a major AWS outage all showed the same thing: too many organizations depend on the same few providers, for email and for the identity checks that open everything else.

Resilience is an ongoing engineering journey of adding redundancy to critical components and analyzing each component’s behavior when other parts of the system fail. This Microsoft 365 outage gave us a rare opportunity to test the system in such rare circumstances.

Title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
Context: “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says
Full Text: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack. The good news? It was all part of a test. The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.” “Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report. If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face. Google did not respond to The Register's questions. According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.” Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.” Turns out it existed. “We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said. “When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.” Four test scenarios The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent. In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection. After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions. After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255, a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says. In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident, Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test. In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said. Next time: kill switches at the ready A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One of them tried a SQL injection, and multiple claimed to be Epoch staff on the helpline. They also attempted to bypass a CAPTCHA check. Finally, the fourth scenario on October 29 and 30 kept the agents contained in a sandbox, with no internet access and no copy of Epoch’s website. They were, however, offered a decoy switch and told it would turn off the firewall. In all three runs, the agents switched the decoy off and obfuscated its address to bypass Gemini’s safeguards. On one, the agent rebuilt the switch’s address from positions of words it had saved earlier. The real firewall blocked the agents’ traffic throughout all of these tests. At this point, Trajectory stopped its tests, and said it won’t run any future experiments until it has a risk management plan in place, with signoff from its CEO and CTO, along with approval from any outside systems that the models could “reasonably” target. Tests will also include real-time automated monitoring and kill switches, and Trajectory said that it’s setting up a system to notify any organizations affected by these experiments. Interestingly, Trajectory co-founder Peter McIntyre told us that the testing firm “ran a similar test with another frontier model, and it did not exhibit the same misalignment as Gemini 4 Argon.” However, this was not a controlled comparison. “Our report covers one model's behavior, and was designed as a stress test to see whether that model would exhibit similar misalignment under duress, not a measure of how often different models behave this way,” McIntyre told The Register. Overall, the testing firm noted that the agents’ behavior “show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely.” Trajectory says that it's developing a set of safety standards, and recommends that anyone else running misalignment tests use fully isolated sandboxes. ® Correction: Epoch only consented to one of the tests, scenario three. The original version of this article said that it consented to all of the tests.

Title: Ignite 2026: Building the frontier ecosystem
Context: They are also available in Foundry
Full Text:
Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, delivered the opening keynote at Ignite in San Francisco this morning. Here is an edited version of his remarks.

This week is about two things: First is how we capitalize on new capabilities that are growing exponentially. And second is how do we build the capability to deal with the consequences of these exponentials.

At times like these, I always find it helpful to be grounded in our mission: To empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. In today’s world, that means building a frontier ecosystem. We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large.

For us, that comes down to three things: Keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring your control of your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust.

And so, our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three core architectural principles.

Copilot

Copilot is the new OS for work. Copilot brings together all the new form factors of human-computer interaction, whether it is Chat, Cowork, Code or Autopilot, into one experience. It also brings together the disparate categories of knowledge work, coding and business process. That is why we have all of Office with its richness built into Copilot. And underlying it is a model system that matches the right intelligence to the right context to the right form factor to accomplish the task.

Home gives you one place to start, whether you need a quick answer or want to assign and complete complex, multi-step tasks. Code brings the power of an infinite SaaS factory to every individual. It lets you build your own custom SaaS apps, dashboards and much more. And Autopilot is an autonomous agent that keeps moving your work forward 24×7 in all the places where you and your team collaborate.

Underlying all this is Work IQ. You can think of this as the most important database for any organization, with a deep understanding of people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats and projects that make up the fabric of work.

And we are going further. We are extending Copilot for specific roles: sales, legal, finance, service. We are organizing the skills, connectors and plugins for these roles across the entire surface area of Copilot.

And that includes third-party systems, too. In fact, today we are announcing new plugins for business applications, starting with Dynamics 365. And it is not just Dynamics. We are very excited to partner with Salesforce to bring Salesforce to Copilot.

And we are going beyond that as well. Up until now, we have mostly been in a single player world of people and their agent loops and swarms. But the time has come for a true multiplayer form factor, where people, their agents and other people are all driving towards a common goal, with shared context. This is Copilot Workspaces:

YouTube Video

Click here to load media

Microsoft IQ

The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain and continuously improve its own intelligence. Essentially, we are taking the system we built underneath Copilot and externalizing it as a first-class platform that embodies your organizational intelligence as an asset that you continuously build and control.

We are bringing together all of the data you have across Fabric, Foundry and Microsoft 365. And, of course, all the third-party context too. Microsoft IQ comes with hundreds of new connectors we are announcing today, so agents can get the full enterprise context where business gets done. And all this rich context manifests as business plugins that can be shared and inherited across the organization.

Models

For us, it is about mapping intelligence to a given task, with the best economics. This is something we can uniquely do in the context of real-world tasks by tuning our products, harness and tools, and the model system, end-to-end.

And today we are thrilled to announce Microsoft-Decision-1.1, which is now generally available and ready for enterprise deployment. We have added multimodal support. And we have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster. Already, more than 4,000 customers have used it. And we ourselves are using it for core tasks like routing, data labeling, personalization, content filtering and hundreds of other use cases.

Foundry of course has all the most popular closed and open weight models, too. We are very excited to bring GPT 6.2 to Foundry. It is a great model that sets a new bar for AI in professional work. And today we are announcing that Meta’s latest models are all coming to Foundry as well.

We are also innovating at the frontier with our own MAI model family that is both compute-efficient when it comes to pre-training and token-efficient when it comes to product deployment. Our goal is to put additional points on the frontier curve informed by real world task-performance.

And we are going further. We are announcing MAI Licensed Weights, meaning our trusted customers will now be able to get access to Microsoft AI model weights through our Frontier Co.

Today, we are introducing lots of new models. But I want to highlight two in particular:

First, Code. We are introducing our new flagship family of agentic coding models: Code 2. Code 2 is at the frontier of cost-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. It excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multifile implementation, repo-wide reasoning and UI at a fraction of frontier cost.

Code 2 Flash is designed for fast, high-volume work like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes and rapid iterations. It brings near-flagship quality for a much lower cost. These models are both generally available today on GitHub Copilot, both in the model picker and as part of Copilot Fusion. They are also available in Foundry.

We are taking the same approach in cyber. Cyber 2 Flash is our most capable security model yet. It is a flash-sized model that delivers performance ahead of frontier models at a fraction of the cost per task. And, just as we have done with coding, we are co-designing the model with the tools and systems where it will be used. We are integrating Cyber 2 with Perception.

Agent 365

Successfully deploying AI systems starts with making sure you have observability at every layer of the stack. That is where Agent 365 comes in. It is a control plane that extends your existing governance, identity, security and management systems to the agents in your enterprise. We already have over 50 million agents in Agent 365.

And it includes FinOps, too. As AI scales, every organization needs a clear line between what it spends and the value AI creates. That is why today we are announcing Agent 365 Business Analytics. You can think of it as your ERP system for AI usage. You can see exactly what is driving spend. You can connect spend to outcomes to drive business value. And you can optimize ROI across different scenarios.

Security

The next thing I want to talk about is how you take the environment you have set up, from Copilot to IQ to Agent 365, and secure it. And that is where Perception and our security stack comes in. We are building an end-to-end trust platform. We are helping customers both secure their AI deployments and use AI to strengthen their security posture.

Perception is a complete agentic security system with teams of red, blue and green agents that run through playbooks to deliver security outcomes at machine speed, with you always in control.

Essentially, think about it like this: red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks and green team agents fix and remediate. With Playbooks, you can compose teams of agents to tackle complex jobs and trigger them to take action autonomously.

Perception helps connect all the signals, sensors and actuators across your identity, client, cloud, apps and agents to intelligence to secure your end-to-end environments. And I am very excited to share that Perception is now generally available.

In addition to the work we have been doing across our products, we are also working across the ecosystem to ensure everyone can innovate at speed and scale, safely. Today, we can see almost everything models touch. But we cannot see what happens inside the model. And what the model tells us about itself is not independent evidence. These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable. We need to be able to examine what AI sees and does, verify its actions independently and control what it is allowed to do.

That is why today we are also announcing the Microsoft AI Transparency Initiative.

There are three parts to this: First, we will expand our collaboration in NIST’s Agent Standards Initiative, drawing on its research to help lead the development of open, industry-wide standards for AI transparency, security and governance.

Second, we are taking a full ecosystem approach. Together, we can enable AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Already, 40 organizations are working with us on defining and applying these standards.

Third, we are working to incorporate the same standards in our products, including MAI models, Foundry and Copilot. Our ambition through our research, our product work and our ecosystem is to help establish an open industry standard that makes AI safer, more transparent and more accessible.

Cobalt 200 VMs

Underneath all of this is unbelievable silicon. We are building a heterogeneous platform working across the ecosystem to bring you all the latest innovation. We are also advancing our own hardware systems, co-designing silicon, servers and infrastructure to get more from every watt, chip and datacenter.

We just announced Maia 300, which will deliver 40 percent more tokens per watt compared with leading GPU-based systems. Azure Boost and Azure Integrated HSM move critical infrastructure and security functions into purpose-built silicon. And today we are announcing general availability of our next-generation Cobalt 200 VMs, which are our highest-performing general-purpose VMs with leading price-performance.

So, that is a quick walk through some of our news. When you look at all that is coming, it is clear that we are entering an era of ubiquitous intelligence. Title: Security for the agentic era, powered by Microsoft Perception

Full Text:
In this article

A new cyber stack, built to fight AI with AI

Delivering agentic security at Microsoft Ignite

Secure your foundations

Defend with agents

Secure agentic insiders

Changing how security work gets done

Explore what's new

A year ago, finding a serious, exploitable vulnerability was slow and expensive work done by elite security researchers. That’s no longer true. Over the past 12 months, frontier AI models have become remarkably good at discovering and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and similar levels of capability are quickly becoming available in open weights models with limited cyber guardrails. Attacks that once required specialized resources are now within reach of almost anyone.

We saw what that looks like in a single week this fall when PHP disclosed two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, flaws that let an attacker take control of a server with a single request over the internet.1 At the time of disclosure, tens of millions of internet-facing PHP services were running affected versions. Nearly two weeks later, about 29 million services remained vulnerable. Behind those servers are banks, healthcare providers, energy companies, and much of the infrastructure the internet runs on. And that same day brought five other major disclosures across the industry.

Explore coordinated agents and shared intelligence with Microsoft Perception

Turning a flaw like the PHP one into a working attack once took a specialist team months. Within roughly a day of PHP2Shell’s disclosure, security researchers had developed a working, weaponized exploit. By the following week, that research had expanded to cover additional PHP versions and configurations. The time from discovery to exploit is shrinking from months to minutes.

The physics of cybersecurity are changing, and fast.

AI is amplifying risk. Attackers can now find and exploit gaps faster than defenders can close them.

Attacks are becoming fully automated. AI has moved from assisting attackers, to executing their tasks, to planning and running entire campaigns on its own.

Agents are the new insiders. While not inherently malicious, they perform tasks and business workflows at machine speed, around the clock, and have broad access to data, apps, tools, and other agents. Like any insider, they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

What we built for humans does not scale for AI. Frontier Transformation starts with business outcomes and a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. To help organizations bring their ideas to life and innovate safely in the agentic era, we need a new cyber stack, built for agentic security.

A new cyber stack, built to fight AI with AI

The Microsoft cyber stack has three layers:

Signals, sensors, and actuators. This foundational layer is powered by sensors and actuators in Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Sentinel, the network, the operating system, the browser, and our hyperscale cloud. Sensors tell you something is wrong. Actuators let you do something about it: contain a device on the network, revoke an identity’s access, or block an agent at the authorization layer. And because we know we’re not the only security solution provider in your environment, we connect to the wider ecosystem through more than 500 connectors. Together, Microsoft and partner sources produce more than 165 trillion signals a day,2 which, enriched by Microsoft and customer threat intelligence, fuel the context layer.

Context. This layer organizes those signals, together with each customer’s own environment, into agent-ready, real-time understanding of the digital estate that is optimized for precision, recall, and token efficiency.

Agents, harness, and models. On top are specialized security agents that work together as teams through playbooks, directed by a harness, and a multi-model approach that uses the right model for each task, designed to ensure effective and efficient security outcomes, at scale.

Delivering agentic security at Microsoft Ignite

At Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re delivering innovation across every layer of the stack. It starts with Microsoft Perception, now generally available.

Perception brings the top of the stack together. It orchestrates red, blue, and green team agents through playbooks, working together in a closed loop to deliver security outcomes. Red team agents simulate attacks from an attacker’s perspective before a breach occurs. Blue team agents detect, triage alerts, and investigate attacks, freeing analysts to focus on the critical decisions that matter most. Green team agents fix and remediate.

Perception is built to help security teams move at machine speed, drive outcomes rather than tasks, and automate while staying in control. Your team sets the guardrails and signs off on high-impact actions, and automated triggers launch playbooks when an incident meets the criteria you set. New cost management dashboards and a cost estimator help you track AI usage, forecast spending, and connect costs to measurable security outcomes.

Agents are only as good as what they can see and what they can do. That’s why we are investing as much in the foundation as in the layers above it.

Read the Microsoft Perception Tech Community blog

Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, generally available for core capabilities, is part of that foundation. ISOC brings security information and event management (SIEM) capabilities, user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA), threat intelligence, and threat protection and disruption together so you can start your journey to the agentic security operations center (SOC). Eligible Defender Suite, Microsoft 365 E5, and Microsoft 365 E7 customers receive all Microsoft Sentinel SIEM features, 90-day default data retention for Defender data, more than 500 connectors, reduced ingestion rates, and a built-in data lake. The complete breadth of SIEM capabilities is now in preview.

Learn more about the latest updates in Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel

Read on to learn how Microsoft Perception, ISOC in Defender, and new capabilities across the stack work together to help customers secure their foundations, secure agentic insiders, and defend with agents.

Secure your foundations

Defending against AI-speed attacks starts with closing the doors attackers walk through first, and the scale of that work is increasing. In 2026, more than 96,000 vulnerabilities3 have been published to the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) Program, more than double 2024’s roughly 40,000 and more than 20 times the level of 2010,4 driven in part by AI-assisted vulnerability discovery tools.

Yet only 26% of vulnerabilities in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog were remediated in 2025, as remediation typically extends into weeks and months. AI finds those gaps faster than teams can close them. Today we’re announcing new capabilities to help.

Strengthen your security foundation with Perception. In preview in January 2027, new AI Readiness Initiatives in Perception turn Secure Now guidance into actionable plans with shared progress tracking, helping organizations close critical security gaps, and prepare for AI adoption. Initiatives focus on scenarios that help reduce AI-amplified risk such as modernizing authentication and deploying monthly updates.

Prioritize and reduce exposure with Perception agents and playbooks. Focus on the risks that matter most and coordinate remediation using threat intelligence and business context. Two new playbooks bring together green team agents, including the Posture Prioritization Agent, now generally available, and the Risk Reduction Agent, now in public preview. Coverage spans Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud.

Vulnerability shielding, available in preview, helps protect vulnerable assets from exploitation by applying targeted, temporary protection to buy defenders time before they can apply a permanent patch. During routine operations the Risk Reduction Agent proactively suggests shielding when patches aren’t immediately available. During an active attack, vulnerability shielding helps reduce exposure to certain vulnerabilities by applying targeted, temporary protections while organizations prepare immediate remediation. In supported scenarios, these protections can include adjustments to network accessibility and permissions to help limit exposure.

Secure data across humans and agents with Microsoft Purview. Enhanced data classification drives precise protection with less manual effort, generally available in January 2027. Also entering preview in January: grounding protection for Copilot based on sensitive information types, which lets customers adopt Copilot without labeling every file first, and expanded data loss prevention (DLP) controls for prompts to Copilot and local agents running on Windows, which help protect sensitive data from leaking while customers use AI. Learn how Microsoft Purview accelerates data protection for the AI era.

Defend with agents

A SOC where people work through a queue of alerts by hand can’t keep up with increasingly autonomous attacks. Perception brings specialized red, blue, and green agents, and playbooks that automate common SecOps workflows, so defenders can get ahead.

Stop threats at machine speed with new Perception playbooks and agents. Accelerate threat detection, investigation, and response with new playbooks and four blue team agents, now generally available: Alert Triage Agent, Attack Investigation Agent, Detection Authoring Agent, and Threat Intelligence Agent. Helping teams move from detection to response faster, with less manual effort.

See it in action: Watch agents triage an incoming alert, investigate the attack end to end, and then improve detection rules that help identify similar threats in the future.

Stay ahead of attackers with new Perception playbooks and agents. Proactively find and validate weaknesses with playbooks that coordinate red team agents, including the Recon Agent, now generally available, and the Web App Pen Test Agent, now in preview, helping security teams identify and address vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.

See it in action: think like an attacker with the Protect web app playbook, which runs a pen test against your app, surfaces the weaknesses that matter, and drives the fix through to your code in GitHub.

Use Perception in your flow of work. Teams can now invoke Perception playbooks in Defender, connect through Model Context Protocol (MCP) and APIs to SIEM, security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR), and IT service management tools, and bring in signals from AWS, Okta, and Salesforce. These integrations are in preview.

We are also expanding the preview of Codename MDASH, our agentic code scanner, which helps customers find and fix vulnerabilities. MDASH can now analyze repositories up to 5 GB, run in regulated clouds, and MDASH code scans can be used by the Web App Pen Test Agent to prioritize and fix vulnerabilities. MDASH adds more of the MAI Cyber family, including MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash and MAI-Cyber-2 in preview,5 improving efficiency while maintaining the quality of security findings. Learn more about MAI-Cyber-2.

Sign up to explore Codename MDASH with optional MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash access

Secure agentic insiders

Agents are the new insiders. They operate continuously, collaborate with other agents, change shape, and pursue goals in ways that can surprise the people who deployed them. To mitigate this risk we must discover agents, onboard them to management, secure and contain them, and do it continuously—even as their behavior and context change. Building on our October 2026 announcement, at Ignite we are introducing new capabilities to help customers secure agentic insiders, around the clock.

Continuously contain agentic insiders with new Perception playbooks and agents. Investigate and remediate AI posture risks and anomalous agent behavior with new playbooks and green team agents. Microsoft Entra ID Governance dynamic permissions grant task-scoped, time-bound access, while Conditional Access dynamic controls adjust protections as risk changes. These capabilities remain in limited preview.

Discover, govern, and secure agents with Microsoft Agent 365 and Microsoft Entra Suite capabilities for agentic insiders. Discovery expands by 35 local agent types, to 60 in total, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot, plus third-party cloud agents on AWS and Google Cloud. Discovered agents receive a Microsoft Entra Agent ID and can be governed with Conditional Access. Intune policies contain supported local agents on the device. Additionally, Microsoft Autopilot agents get their own Agent user account and ID, so admins can enable Conditional Access, ID Protection, and access governance to the work an Autopilot does under its own identity. Defender and Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention protect runtime and sensitive data access, and Dynamic Agent Risk assesses each agent’s exposure, blast radius, and runtime behavior. Available in preview.

While these capabilities can enable customers to secure and contain agents, they will not give them insight into how the model behind an agent behaves. Without that visibility it is hard for customers to answer three basic questions about consequential AI activity:

What was the AI asked and authorized to do?

What happened between the request and the outcome?

Can we independently verify it?

That’s why Microsoft is announcing the next phase of our commitment to responsible AI: the AI Transparency Initiative. We believe every organization should be able to see what its AI accesses and does, independently verify those actions, and control what it is permitted to do, whatever model or provider it runs on. To that end, we are expanding our participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) SI Agent Standards Initiative,6 plus drawing on our own research to develop open, industry-wide standards for AI transparency, security, and governance. We’re shaping this approach with more than 40 organizations including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard, and Volvo Cars. And we will implement this work across Microsoft AI models and products, including Microsoft Foundry and Copilot.

The more agency we give AI, the more transparency we should expect in return.

Sign up to help shape the AI Transparency Initiative

Changing how security work gets done

AI is changing how attacks happen, and how security work gets done. Developers, IT, and security teams now share responsibility for building, managing, and securing AI, so Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Agent 365, and Perception share the same signals and context. Inside the SOC, analysts need agents to defend at machine speed, which is why we’re building agentic security into the tools they already use.

Technology alone won’t get us there. Securing our own environment through the Secure Future Initiative has taught us a great deal, and our Frontier Security Engineers, services teams, and partners are working side by side with customers to put those lessons to work.

Join us at Microsoft Ignite, online or in person, to learn how Microsoft Perception, ISOC in Defender and new capabilities across the stack can help secure your organization at machine speed. We’d love to see you there.

Qualys ROCky for Gemini Enterprise, now available on Google Cloud Marketplace, allows you to ask your vulnerability, asset, and risk questions, get an answer ranked by real risk, and act on it, without leaving Gemini Enterprise.

With the introduction of frontier AI models, vulnerabilities are now being discovered and weaponized at machine speed. Unfortunately, most security teams still triage at human speed. A typical enterprise carries thousands of open findings and can fix only a small fraction of them, yet leadership still expects a straight answer to a simple question: Are we keeping up? Getting that answer usually means exporting a scan, building a spreadsheet, and losing an afternoon.

Today, we are live with Qualys ROCky for Gemini Enterprise. It puts your Qualys vulnerability, asset, and risk data one question away, right inside Gemini Enterprise, and it can even take the next step in the process for you, with a person in control of any changes to an asset.

Your Program, By Conversation

The agent turns interactions with the Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Platform into a conversation. Four things it does well:

Ask about your data. “Which of my internet-facing hosts is the biggest risk?” “Are we exposed to Log4Shell?” “What is tied to ransomware?” Whatever your risk management question, you get an answer from your subscription in seconds, in plain language, rather than a raw export.

Prioritize by real risk. Ask what to fix first, and the agent returns a worklist ranked by the Qualys Enterprise TruRisk score. It surfaces the handful of vulnerabilities that are actively exploited, listed in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, or associated with ransomware, and it explains why each one matters. Half a day of specialist triage becomes a two-minute, defensible decision.

Remediate with confirmation. When you are ready to act, the agent stages a patch job in TruRisk Eliminate and shows exactly what will deploy, patch stability, and to how many assets. Nothing changes a host until you explicitly say yes. You go from finding to fixing in the same conversation, with a clear record of who approved what.

Prove you are keeping up. Ask for your mean time to remediate, how your open CISA KEV backlog is aging, or how current your scan data is, and the agent answers on demand, in the terms boards and auditors expect.

Qualys ROCky for Gemini Enterprise answering “What should we fix first?” against live Qualys data: a worklist ranked by risk, with CISA KEV, weaponized-exploit, and malware context and the affected hosts for each fix

A Day in the Life

An overdue critical patch shows up on a Windows fleet. A security lead asks the agent, “What is our exposure and what should we do?” The agent names the vulnerability, shows the affected hosts ranked by risk, and recommends the patch. The lead says, “Stage it for my Windows hosts.” The agent stages the job, shows the target set, and waits. The lead confirms, the job deploys, and a follow-up question confirms it completed. One conversation, start to finish.

Qualys ROCky for Gemini Enterprise summarizes critical exposure against live Qualys data: open detections broken down by severity, with the affected hosts listed below.

Confirmed Before Anything Changes

An agent that can read your security data and act on your hosts has to earn trust before it earns adoption. Three principles are built in from the start.

The agent stages a patch in Gemini Enterprise and stops for a decision: “This job is currently disabled, and no changes have been deployed to your hosts. Do you want to deploy this patch now?” Nothing changes a host until a person confirms.

Every request runs under the signed-in user’s own Qualys entitlements. People see exactly what they are allowed to see in Qualys, and nothing more. The agent does not pool all users behind one shared account, and one customer’s data is never visible to another.

Actions are confirmation-gated. The only steps that change a host are staging and deploying a patch job, and deploying always requires an explicit, single-use confirmation. The agent moves at machine speed on the reading and the ranking, and it stops for human validation on anything that changes a host.

Your data stays in your control. Answers are computed against your Qualys subscription through the same Qualys APIs your teams already rely on. There is no separate copy of your risk data to manage.

Where It Runs

Qualys ROCky runs inside Gemini Enterprise and is available on Google Cloud Marketplace, so your teams can reach it in the environment they already work in, with the sign-in and controls your organization already manages.

“Bringing Qualys ROCky to Google Cloud Marketplace will help customers quickly deploy, manage, and grow the conversational AI assistant on Google Cloud’s trusted, global infrastructure,” said Dai Vu, Managing Director, Marketplace & ISV GTM Programs at Google Cloud. “Qualys can now securely scale and support enterprises using Qualys ROCky to manage and patch vulnerabilities through natural language queries within Gemini Enterprise.”

See It for Yourself

No team has time to fix everything. ROCky helps your team spend its hours on the risk that can actually hurt the business, and prove the program is working while it does. It brings the Qualys TruRisk platform to where your teams already work, and keeps a person in control of every change.

Qualys customers: Find Qualys ROCky on Google Cloud Marketplace, or contact your Qualys representative to see it run against your own environment.

Title: Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open
Context: A new experimental Windows 11 build previews security features including an Intune-controlled Remote Lock, while a beta build clears away another relic from the halcyon days of...
Full Text: A new experimental Windows 11 build previews security features including an Intune-controlled Remote Lock, while a beta build clears away another relic from the halcyon days of Windows Phone. The security changes include viewing and individually removing passkeys stored on FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) security keys, plus a preview of the Microsoft Pluton Cryptographic Provider. For enterprise administrators, though, Remote Lock is the main attraction. Finding a lost Windows device has been around for years, and you can also remotely wipe a device to prevent data from falling into the wrong hands. Remote Lock lets an administrator lock a managed device through Intune without wiping it. The instruction takes effect at the device's next check-in. Windows signs out of every active session, hides every sign-in option, and shows a locked screen. The lock survives restarts and the device going offline – only an administrator can lift it remotely. Microsoft's documentation spells out the restriction: "There is no offline or local unlock. No PIN, password, local admin, or web sign-in works on a locked device; unlock arrives only through Intune." Once the lock is applied, even stolen credentials won't restore access through the normal sign-in screen. The user's account itself is not affected; this applies only to the specific device. Though still in preview, the feature will allow IT teams to respond non-destructively to a report of a missing device. It doesn't erase data or isolate the device from the network (Microsoft directs admins to other Intune controls if that is required). The lock doesn't block Safe Mode, Windows Recovery Environment, or booting from external media. Microsoft advises keeping BitLocker enabled to protect the data. Now for the beta build, where Microsoft, in time-honored fashion, gives and takes away. The latest Windows Insider build hammers another nail into the coffin of Microsoft Maps. The Maps app was removed from the Microsoft Store and made nonfunctional in July 2025. Now Offline Maps settings are following it out, as Microsoft retires the Windows UWP Map control and Windows Maps platform APIs. The original Maps app dates back to Windows Phone 7 and appeared on the desktop with Windows 8. It continued through subsequent versions before Microsoft stopped preinstalling it with Windows 11 version 24H2. For those with a nostalgic streak, it's another piece of Windows Phone disappearing off the map. ®

Title: The risks of device code authentication for AI coding agents
Context: Detection and disruption availability depend on the supported configuration, required telemetry, identity integration, and deployment prerequisites
Full Text:
In this article

From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agent

How the attack works

One approval, four ways the impact can spread

Turning a phishing attempt into a Defender signal

Mitigation and protection guidance

References

Learn More

Device code phishing has become a recurring route to account takeover. Instead of stealing a password, an attacker persuades someone to approve a sign-in on a legitimate site simply by entering a code. The resulting access often can reach email, files, or other cloud services, depending on the account and the permissions granted. Notable earlier campaigns such as EvilTokens show how readily this technique can be scaled to do real damage. Microsoft worked hard with partners in industry and law enforcement to disrupt EvilTokens in September 2026.

That led us to a different question: what else can an attacker do with a phished device code authorization? What happens when the same trick targets an AI agent rather than a mailbox?

We used GitHub Copilot CLI as an illustrative example. Depending on its configuration, it can work with code, run commands on a user’s machine, retain context across sessions, and allow an active session to be steered remotely. Like many command-line tools, it supports the OAuth device flow for sign-in. The phishing technique itself is not specific to GitHub or Copilot CLI: any public client that supports the device flow can be abused the same way, and the attacker chooses the requested scopes when starting the flow.

We explored this scenario in a controlled lab simulation. A victim test account approved a GitHub device-code request initiated by an attacker client we controlled. With that approval, we were able to analyze four possible outcomes:

Steer an active Copilot CLI session remotely, if the user has enabled remote control and organization policy allows it, and, subject to local permissions and approval settings, have the agent run commands on the user’s machine.

Add misleading entries to the agent’s memory that could influence later interactions.

Read Copilot CLI sessions that were synchronized to the cloud.

Access private repositories available to the affected account.

These are proof-of-concept results showing how existing features, working as designed, could be abused after a phished authorization; they are not attacks we have observed in the wild. These outcomes require the victim user to approve a device code request initiated by the attacker; each outcome also depends on the account permissions and enabled features described below.

Later in this post, we show how Microsoft Defender helps detect these attacks by connecting phishing attempts with GitHub authentication activity, and how organizations can disrupt suspicious access to protect affected identities.

From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agent

The OAuth device flow helps clients such as command-line tools sign in without displaying a full browser. A client requests a short code; the user enters it on the service’s verification page; the requesting client receives access after approval. In device code phishing, the attacker starts the request and persuades someone else to approve it.

Microsoft has reported device code phishing against accounts in several campaigns, including Storm-2372, an AI-enabled campaign in 2026, and EvilTokens. Those cases motivated us to examine a different target: a coding agent that can work with repositories and, when remote control is enabled, expose an active session to remote interaction.

The remainder of this post describes a controlled GitHub Copilot CLI simulation; we have not observed the four outcomes below in those campaigns or in the wild.

How the attack works

Figure 1. A user approves a legitimate GitHub device-code request that was initiated by the attacker-controlled client. Conceptual illustration.

Initiate: The attacker starts a device-code sign-in request. In our simulation, we used the Copilot CLI client, but any device-flow client could be used.

Lure: The attacker sends the short code and GitHub verification link to the user, for example under the pretext of an IT request or a Copilot license check. The verification page is genuinely hosted by GitHub; the legitimate domain alone does not establish who initiated the request.

Approve: The user opens the GitHub page, signs in if needed, and approves the request. This is the social engineering step.

Sign in: After approval, the attacker-controlled client completes the sign-in automatically.

Operate: The attacker can act within the permissions granted to the application and the resources available to the affected account.

The request behind the code

The following example shows the initial HTTP request to GitHub’s device authorization endpoint. The Copilot CLI client identifier is public; it is not a client secret. The attacker sends the short code returned by GitHub to the user. Once the user approves it, the requesting client signs in without another manual step.

GitHub Device Code Authentication (Simplified) Endpoint: GitHub Device Authorization Endpoint Client ID: Requested scopes:

The request looks legitimate

The user signs in on the real GitHub site, not a lookalike page. A familiar domain therefore cannot tell the user whether the request was theirs. An authorization also appears under a legitimate application name; the name alone cannot distinguish the attacker-controlled client from an expected sign-in.

One approval, four ways the impact can spread

The device code approval was only the starting point. What an attacker could do next depended on the account’s permissions, enabled features, memory settings, and whether an active session could be controlled remotely.

Figure 2. Four possible outcomes in the lab, each subject to the account’s permissions and enabled features. Conceptual illustration.

1. An attacker can steer an enabled remote session

Copilot CLI supports remote steering of an active interactive session when the user has enabled remote control for that session and organization policy allows it. In our lab, the attacker-controlled client used the test account’s authorization to interact with a remotely controllable session. The agent ran a command on the test machine, subject to the session’s approval prompts and local operating-system permissions. This demonstrates misuse of an authorized remote-session capability working as designed; it is not unauthenticated remote code execution and does not apply when remote control is disabled, the session is not running, or the machine is offline.

Figure 3. Remote-session misuse is bounded by the local machine’s permissions and approval controls. Conceptual illustration.

2. Memory can carry the attack forward

Copilot Memory can retain repository facts and user preferences. In the simulation, we added misleading entries using the agent’s /memory command. If those entries are used in later interactions, the effects can outlast the initial sign-in. The behavior depends on which memory features and policies are enabled.

Figure 4. Misleading memory can affect later agent interactions. Conceptual illustration.

3. Synced sessions reveal earlier context

Where cloud session storage is enabled, we could read the test account’s synced Copilot CLI sessions, including sessions from before the simulation. They may contain code snippets, file paths, architecture discussions, and other work context. For Copilot Business and Enterprise, availability depends on the organization’s session-storage policy; syncing a session does not itself enable remote control.

4. Repository access follows the account

In the lab, the authorization let us access private repositories available to the test account. The request included the repo scope along with read:user, read:org, gist, and codespace. These scopes are chosen by the client that starts the flow; the resulting repository access reflects the requested scopes and the account’s permissions, not a property of Copilot CLI itself. The potential exposure is bounded by the account’s repository access, which can include application code and infrastructure definitions.

A phishing message, a click, and a GitHub authorization can each look unremarkable on their own. The challenge for defenders is recognizing when they belong to the same attempted takeover. The legitimate verification page is part of the story, not evidence that the request was safe.

Turning a phishing attempt into a Defender signal

Microsoft Defender helps organizations detect and respond to device code phishing targeting GitHub accounts. With the GitHub Enterprise Cloud connector enabled in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, organizations gain visibility into GitHub activity that can support investigations of suspicious authorization patterns.

As part of our research, we developed two detections for suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing, covering attacks delivered through email and Microsoft Teams.

These detections correlate suspicious messages and clicks with subsequent GitHub OAuth token creation and regeneration events, helping identify potentially unauthorized Copilot CLI authorizations that might otherwise appear legitimate. Microsoft Defender XDR customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below.

Microsoft Defender coverage

Observed activity

Tactic

Microsoft Defender XDR: Suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing via email

Suspected device code phishing delivered through email, potentially resulting in unauthorized GitHub Copilot CLI access.

Initial Access / Credential Access

Beyond detection, we also developed a disruption action for GitHub Enterprise Managed Users (EMU). This action suspends the affected managed identity through the organization’s identity provider, interrupting the attacker’s access. We validated this capability in our research environment.

Responders should also review and revoke unexpected OAuth authorizations, verify that access is blocked, and investigate potentially affected sessions, repositories, and saved memory.

Together, these capabilities help security teams move from identifying a potential phishing attempt to containing the affected identity. Detection and disruption availability depend on the supported configuration, required telemetry, identity integration, and deployment prerequisites.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Make the approval rule clear to everyone who uses developer and AI tools: enter a device code only for a sign-in you initiated yourself. An unexpected request to “verify” GitHub or activate Copilot should be treated as a phishing attempt, even if the page is hosted on github.com. GitHub’s own verification page warns users never to use a code sent by someone else.

Configure Safe Links policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 for email and verify Safe Links protection for Microsoft Teams. These protections can help with malicious links and provide investigation context; a legitimate GitHub verification URL still requires the user to recognize an unsolicited code request.

Review GitHub Copilot CLI session settings. For organization-provided seats, GitHub’s “Store local sessions in the Cloud” policy determines whether sessions can be stored and remotely controlled. Choose the least permissive setting that supports your workflows. Remote control also requires an active, online interactive session.

Review authorized OAuth applications in GitHub account settings and revoke authorizations that are unexpected or no longer needed. Limit repository access with appropriate organization roles so an affected account cannot reach more code than its work requires.

If Copilot Memory is enabled, use GitHub’s memory-management controls to review and remove suspicious repository facts or user preferences. Disabling memory does not automatically delete entries already stored, so review the saved content during incident response.

Connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps and validate the activity available in your environment before relying on it for investigations.

Remember: A legitimate sign-in can still be the wrong one

The most striking part of this simulation was how little needed to look suspicious. The user visited the real GitHub site and approved a normal-looking request. Yet the approval belonged to a client the user had not started. From there, the consequences depended on what that identity could access and which Copilot CLI capabilities were enabled.

That is why this is more than a story about a code. As AI agents gain access to repositories, session history, and local tools, the impact of a phished authorization increasingly depends on what those agents can reach.

A legitimate verification page does not mean the request is safe. Users should approve only device-code requests they initiated. Organizations should regularly review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorizations, restrict Copilot session and memory settings to what their workflows require, and validate GitHub activity visibility in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps to support investigations.

Ultimately, protecting against device code phishing requires both user awareness and the ability to connect suspicious authorization activity to the phishing attempt that preceded it.

Title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
Context: Details: First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing...
Full Text:
This seems like a good thing:

Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

[…]

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

Alternate link.

Details:

First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.

Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.
