Title: Flightageddon grounds the nation.
Context: Kaspersky warns that a remote code execution vulnerability in Telegram’s newly launched widgets feature may have been exploited in the wild to deliver WebRAT, a Rust-based trojan also known as Salat Stealer. Cybersecurity firm Forescout Technologies reports that publicly available artificial intelligence models can...
Full Text:
U.S. airline operations return to normal. Microsoft unpacks last week’s outage. Commerce Secretary Lutnick defends less stringent export controls on advanced AI chips. Italy fines Meta 887 million dollars for privacy violations. Telegram’s new widgets may deliver a RAT. The FBI warns of ARTEX pen testing abuse. Refrigeration controllers see opportunistic scanning. Publicly available AI models dramatically accelerate vulnerability discovery. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Patrick Coughlin, CEO and Co-Founder of Savi Security, sharing how shopping fraud has industrialized in the AI era. A refrigerator company learns it’s secretly leading the laundry revolution.

Today is Monday November 16th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

U.S. airline operations return to normal.

U.S. airline operations are largely returning to normal following a rare four-hour nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA on Friday, November 13, which caused thousands of cancellations and stranding travelers into the weekend.

Officials confirmed the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack, attributing it instead to aging telecom infrastructure and legacy hardware. Specifically, an L3Harris contractor upgrading copper wire to fiber replaced a Cisco 600-series router manufactured between 2001 and 2006. The faulty router began flooding the network with login attempts, spreading instability across 17 FAA facilities and prompting the agency to halt flights out of an abundance of caution while 3,500 planes were airborne.

In response, the Trump administration increased its funding request for air traffic control modernization to $30 billion, noting that a previous $12.5 billion allocation is insufficient. However, Democratic lawmakers pointed out that only $1 billion of those initial funds have been spent so far, demanding accountability at an upcoming congressional briefing.

Microsoft unpacks last week’s outage.

Microsoft has traced last week's nearly 24-hour global Microsoft 365 outage to a latent Windows defect in its cloud networking gateway servers. According to Redmond's preliminary incident report, the bug, introduced via a server-specific fix deployed back in July, caused severe "lock contention," where competing internal processes exhausted processor and memory capacity on newer, multi-core hardware.

The defect remained hidden for over three months until a shift in Microsoft Teams traffic collided with a 14 percent reduction in server capacity. As servers crashed, automated failover systems rerouted connections to healthy endpoints, triggering a cascading failure that rendered over 80 percent of servers unresponsive and severely disrupted Exchange Online.

Engineers eventually mitigated the crisis by rolling back the faulty connection-handling update and gradually restoring traffic. While Microsoft confirms customer Windows devices were unaffected and require no configuration changes, the incident underscores how automated recovery mechanisms can inadvertently amplify systemic cloud failures.

Commerce Secretary Lutnick defends less stringent export controls on advanced AI chips.

According to The New York Times, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been advocating for less stringent export controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips, rules that directly affect Southeast Asian data centers with financial ties to his former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.

While the US bans the direct sale of cutting-edge Nvidia chips to China, Chinese tech firms can legally rent computing power from facilities in countries like Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. Lutnick, who transferred leadership and ownership of Cantor Fitzgerald to his sons, has pushed to limit new regulations to only seven countries, exempt existing data centers, and require government notifications rather than strict licenses.

Cantor Fitzgerald has arranged major financing for several of these data center operators, including Singapore-based Bitdeer, which plans to supply Nvidia computing power to Chinese tech giant Tencent. National security analysts and Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns over potential conflicts of interest and warned that narrower rules will allow Beijing to easily bypass restrictions.

Conversely, a Commerce Department spokeswoman stated that Lutnick bases his policy decisions strictly on US national interests, does not discuss department matters with his sons, and has complied with all federal ethics agreements. Furthermore, proponents of a lighter regulatory touch argue that overly broad restrictions could stifle American innovation and harm US companies like Nvidia.

Italy fines Meta 887 million dollars for privacy violations.

Italy’s data protection authority has fined Meta 805 million euros, roughly 887 million US dollars, for accessing Android users’ photos, videos, and metadata without specific consent or proper notification.

According to the regulator, the violation stems from Facebook’s gallery suggestions feature, introduced in 2023. The app bundled camera roll access into a single, generic authorization prompt, leaving roughly 20 million Italian users unaware they were permitting Facebook to scan their personal galleries for post ideas. Regulators noted the infringement remains ongoing for users who have not updated their apps, and cited Meta’s lack of cooperation during the investigation when calculating the penalty.

Meta announced it will appeal, calling the fine disproportionate. Moving forward, Menlo Park must implement a separate, transparent consent prompt detailing how gallery data is accessed and how users can opt out.

Telegram’s new widgets may deliver a RAT.

Kaspersky warns that a remote code execution vulnerability in Telegram’s newly launched widgets feature may have been exploited in the wild to deliver WebRAT, a Rust-based trojan also known as Salat Stealer. According to the Russian security firm, visiting compromised Telegram channels triggered a hidden PowerShell script to install the malware, which steals cryptocurrency wallets and Telegram account data.

The alert follows proof-of-concept videos from researchers at V12 demonstrating exploits against Telegram’s Android and Windows clients, which they attribute to running the QuickJS JavaScript engine without a sandbox.

While Kaspersky advises users against launching widgets until patched, Telegram CEO Pavel Durov dismissed the claims, stating users cannot be hacked merely by receiving a message and confirming that server-side patches have already resolved the underlying scenario.

The FBI warns of ARTEX pen testing abuse.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation has issued a Flash notice warning that threat actors are increasingly weaponizing ARTEX, an open-source, artificial intelligence-driven penetration testing framework, to execute rapid, global cyber intrusions. Since at least August 2026, attackers have used the tool to target sectors including finance, government, defense, and healthcare, compromising over two thousand downstream tenants in a ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply chain breach and stealing data on roughly 67,000 individuals from South Korean financial institutions.

Released on GitHub in July 2026, ARTEX plugs into external large language models to automate reconnaissance and exploitation, enabling some intrusions to achieve privileged access in under three hours. According to the FBI, attackers predominantly pair the framework with Chinese-origin models like DeepSeek Flash due to low costs and minimal guardrails.

Although the creator removed the original repository in October following widespread abuse, community forks and commercial variants continue to proliferate. The Bureau notes that ARTEX’s speed leaves defenders little time to respond, urging organizations to bolster defenses on overlooked portals and third-party integrations.

Refrigeration controllers see opportunistic scanning.

Threat actors began attempting to exploit newly disclosed vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers less than two hours after the flaws went public, according to security firm VulnCheck.

Researchers uncovered 14 flaws, each capable of yielding root privileges, after similar controllers were targeted in an October attack on 700 French supermarkets that France attributed to Iran. While nine vulnerabilities affect older firmware, five impact the latest builds, including predictable daily passwords derived from the device's exposed MAC address. Because Copeland ended support for the XWEB EVO line in March 2026, these flaws will not be patched.

VulnCheck’s sensors detected opportunistic scanning targeting unauthenticated flaws on November 12 and 13. With nearly 2,000 hosts exposed online, researchers urge operators to isolate these legacy devices behind a VPN and migrate to supported models.

Publicly available AI models dramatically accelerate vulnerability discovery.

Cybersecurity firm Forescout Technologies reports that publicly available artificial intelligence models can dramatically accelerate vulnerability discovery in critical infrastructure software on a tight budget.

Using a custom AI-assisted research harness to examine 10 popular TCP/IP stacks, Forescout researchers compressed roughly nine months of work into just 90 hours, combining 10 hours of AI scanning with 80 hours of manual validation. The effort uncovered 99 flaws, including 66 zero-day vulnerabilities, at a static analysis cost of roughly $935, or $2.58 per finding. (Researchers noted binary analysis proved six times costlier and twice as slow as source-code review.)

Forescout VP of Research Daniel dos Santos warned that while AI still requires human expertise, it fundamentally alters vulnerability economics, allowing defenders and attackers alike to find embedded software bugs faster and cheaper.

Monday business briefing.

Venture capital and mergers and acquisitions in the cybersecurity sector remain heavily focused on artificial intelligence, cloud security, and managed services, according to recent industry announcements.

On the funding front, Israeli AI detection and response platform Daylight led the pack with an $80 million Series B round backed by Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Fellow Israeli startups also saw major investments as Bay emerged from stealth with $50 million, cloud backup provider Dreeze raised $33 million, and SecOps platform Brava secured $15 million. Meanwhile, US firms Lazarus AI and WhiteMatter raised $43 million and $20 million respectively, and Italian automation startup CyberKord closed $3 million.

In M&A activity spanning four countries, compliance platform Vanta agreed to acquire Israeli agentic security firm Pillar Security, while Cogent acquired AI penetration testing startup Specular. Elsewhere, ShorePoint absorbed federal contracts from Coalfire Federal, while managed security and consulting consolidation saw acquisitions by Brite, ASI Solutions, Entech, and Saepio.

A refrigerator company learns it’s secretly leading the laundry revolution.

Stirling Marathon, a modest appliance maker in Elora, Ontario, recently learned it was poised to revolutionize the North American laundry industry. There was just one minor catch: the company only makes refrigerators, freezers, and coolers.

According to CBC News, the sudden surge in fame was courtesy of an artificial intelligence scam. Fraudsters blended legitimate company marketing photos with AI-generated footage on YouTube to hawk a fictitious "bombshell" washing machine called "the Keel."

Customer service representative Jordan Cuddihy first realized something was amiss on a Wednesday morning after fielding puzzled inquiries from across the continent, and watching hopeful bargain-hunters physically show up at the facility. A quick Google search revealed the phantom appliance, prompting YouTube to eventually pull the plug on both the video and the channel. For Stirling Marathon, it was a brief, unsolicited brush with industrial disruption, proving that in the age of AI, you don’t actually need to manufacture a product to generate buzz.

And that’s the CyberWire.

How to Find Shadow AI Apps Built With AI App Builders
Context: The Orca Research Pod built and attacked real applications on several of these platforms, then measured which signals actually survive across templates and across our own...
Full Text:
Key findings: How to detect AI-built apps

Somebody in your organization has built an application with an AI app builder. It is running on one of your domains, it talks to a database holding real data, and it went through no procurement, no architecture review and no deployment process. You have no record of it because there was never a step at which a record would have been created.

From the outside these applications are close to invisible. They look like ordinary websites. Most of them run on the builder’s own infrastructure rather than in your estate, so there is no workload of yours to scan, and the ones that do reach a domain you own can be fronted through your own CDN, which erases the hosting fingerprint you would have matched on.

From the inside they are findable. The Orca Research Pod built and attacked real applications on several of these platforms, then measured which signals actually survive across templates and across our own customer fleet. Before you can secure these apps, you need to get visibility into AI systems running in your cloud, and these signals are where that starts. What works:

Packages the builder’s own scaffolding writes into the repositories it generates, some of which are provably inert anywhere else

Commit metadata, which is the most durable anchor available, because content gets edited and commit history does not

Build output that survives compilation into the files a visitor actually receives

DNS records on custom domains, though only some of them find anything

Cloud identities and resources a builder creates when a developer wires it to your own data services

Just as important is what does not work, because a detection rule built on the wrong signal produces noise that buries the real finding. We measured that too.

And the thing you are looking for is not the application on its own. It is the application together with the database behind it.

Signal 1: builder packages already in your software inventory

Start with packages, because you are almost certainly collecting them already.

One of the builders writes its own npm packages into the projects it generates. On its own that would not mean much, since a dependency list is full of things a developer chose deliberately. What makes these different is that they cannot function anywhere else. One of them activates only when a platform-specific environment variable is present, and renders only on that platform’s own domain.

Nobody would install it on purpose. It is residue. So if it is sitting in a repository in your estate, that project was created and run inside the builder.

That makes this the cheapest signal available. You are not adding a data source, you are writing a query against something you already have. Three details decide whether that query works.

Match any one of the packages, never all of them. The builder does not write an identical list into every project. Across three real applications, two of its packages appeared in all three, one appeared in a single project, and one in none. A rule that insists on the full set matches nothing at all.

Match the prefix, not the exact name. Package inventories commonly store the version inside the name, so an equality check silently returns zero and a perfectly good approach looks like a dead end.

Accept that one builder gives you nothing here. It ships no proprietary package whatsoever, and that is not a gap waiting to be filled, it is simply how the platform works. Its repositories carry one small configuration file and an HTML file with a default image URL. That is the entire surface.

Why builder names, editor libraries and HTTP headers produce false positives

Search for the builder’s name and you will find noise, occasionally spectacular noise.

One builder’s name is a common English word. A package with exactly that name appears in hundreds of organizations, and essentially every one of them is something else: a Linux device manager, an embedded key-value store, a chat framework, a ride-sharing company, a repository of torque specifications. Another builder’s name turned up in one company’s DNS as a run of records pointing at private addresses. Their internal naming scheme generates codenames as adjective plus adjective plus noun, and the builder’s name happened to sit on the adjective list.

The same vendor that writes those useful packages also publishes ordinary editor libraries that any developer might install. Those appear across many times more organizations than the proprietary ones do, and they indicate nothing whatsoever. A rule that counts them is measuring library popularity, not AI-generated software.

Then there is the shortcut that looks free: grep your stored HTTP response headers for builder names. Nothing new to collect, and the data is already there. When we measured it across the fleet, every single match was a Content Security Policy frame-ancestors entry, which means the site’s owner permits their own site to be embedded inside the builder’s interface. That is close to the opposite of what you wanted to know. It produces a list of companies that integrated with a builder, not companies that built something with one.

We dropped two header-based approaches for the same reason. Both told us where an application was hosted rather than who wrote it, and hosting turned out to imply the builder in a tiny fraction of cases.

Whole words and exact values, then. Never substrings. That one discipline is the difference between a rule your detection team keeps and a rule they mute within a week.

Signal 2: commit metadata and bot authors

Anything you can find inside a file has a shelf life. We know because our own research notes have been wrong twice in the same direction: markers we had treated as the primary tell for one builder are absent from every template we have generated since.

Commit metadata does not drift like that.

Two of the builders we studied commit generated code under a dedicated bot identity, one of them with more than 180,000 public commits to its name. A developer can open a generated file and delete a marker in ten seconds. Rewriting the authorship of an entire repository is a different kind of act, and almost nobody bothers.

Two things make this better than it first looks. In the AI-built repositories we examined, effectively every commit belonged to the bot, so the proportion of bot commits is a triage signal in its own right. When it sits at one, nobody has ever opened that application by hand.

And the baseline is clean. Across the distinct commit authors visible in our fleet data, not one was a bot of any kind. This is not a needle you have to separate from a haystack. There is no haystack.

Not every builder hands you this. One of them commits under the developer’s own identity and leaves nothing behind at all, which is worth knowing before you invest in collecting it.

Signal 3: builder markers that survive into compiled build output

A marker in a source tree tells you about a repository. A running application has been through a bundler, and most of what identified it in source is gone.

A few things do survive, and those are the ones that matter for anything already serving traffic. Across the builders we looked at, the survivors included a runtime error-reporting hook attached to the global object, asset URLs pointing back at the builder’s own domain, a default social-preview image URL, and, on one platform, a generator tag naming the builder in the page’s own metadata.

That last one is the best of them. It is a single line in an ordinary source file, it was present in both applications we generated on that platform, in source and in compiled output alike, and tens of thousands of public files carry it. It is also the one marker with no file of its own, which is why anyone auditing a repository by eye walks straight past it.

Which markers survive is specific to the template, and this is where re-verification matters most. Before you ship a rule, generate a fresh application on the platform and confirm your marker is still in the output. One of ours was not, and we only caught it because somebody rebuilt the test application instead of trusting notes written months earlier.

When you go looking, check application roots, web document roots, build output directories and container image layers. Then check user home directories, which is not optional. The real applications we studied lived under somebody’s home directory rather than in a tidy system path. Agentless scanning can read these locations, home directories included, without installing anything on the workload.

Signal 4: DNS records on custom domains

A custom domain gives you a DNS record to match, and for one builder that works well: your own records resolving into the platform’s dedicated address space, plus a verification record with a fixed prefix.

The detail worth carrying forward is which half of that does the work. Matching the builder’s hostname in DNS values found us a couple of organizations. Matching its dedicated addresses found an order of magnitude more.

For a builder with no address space of its own there is no equivalent. Its custom domains resolve into general-purpose cloud ranges shared with millions of other tenants, which you cannot match on without drowning in false positives, and its default hostnames live in the builder’s own zone, so they never enter your DNS at all. Until somebody pays for a custom domain, there is nothing there to see.

Signal 5: cloud identities that show an AI-built app’s blast radius

When a developer connects one of these builders to a data service in your own cloud, the builder provisions named artifacts inside your account. We reproduced this end to end across several integration paths: an identity holding read access to specific buckets, a query-service identity with permissions over a data catalog and a results bucket, catalog databases and tables describing your data, and, on another cloud, a service account with storage roles including one that could write.

What makes this the clearest evidence available is not that it names the builder. It is that the policy and the catalog entry tell you exactly which of your data an AI-generated application can reach. Every other signal in this post finds an application. This one measures the blast radius. Left unreviewed, a builder-created role can quietly join your list of overly permissive cloud identities.

It is also the least universal. One of the builders we studied provisions nothing in your cloud on any path, so there is no equivalent to go looking for.

Pair every AI-built app with the database behind it

What you are hunting is not the app on its own. It is the app together with the database behind it, and neither half is the risk by itself. Because the data is where the exposure lives, it pays to find and protect sensitive data across your cloud, so you already know what an AI-built app could reach when you find one.

Be careful how you find that second half, because a database client in a dependency list is not a database. Applications generated by one builder declare a client for a specific managed Postgres and then never use it, because it is template boilerplate rather than a decision. Of three real ones we took apart, one kept everything in memory, one used a completely different database, and one ran its own.

The reverse is just as common. An application on another platform that genuinely did have that managed Postgres attached carried no trace of the vendor anywhere in its source, because the connection string is injected at deploy time and the code only ever names an environment variable.

So the applications that declare a database and the applications that have one are two different sets, and neither bounds the other. Only an observed connection string or hostname proves the database is real. Whatever your rules record, give both halves a shared key from the start, so an analyst is handed one finding rather than two unrelated ones. Ours carries one, and it is the single field we refused to ship without.

It is worth being plain about severity, because it decides whether any of this is an alert or an inventory entry. A default-configured application on these platforms keeps its data off your premises with row-level security enabled, and does not leak on its own. Treat what you find as inventory and AI security posture management, not as an incident. Escalate when a builder artifact sits next to a secret on a scanned asset, or when the builder has been wired into your own cloud data. A database reachable through a generated function holding an administrative key, which is what we walked through in part 4 of this series, is a real finding. A generated to-do list is not. Drawing that line is how you prioritize the risks that matter most, instead of treating every generated app as an emergency.

A six-step checklist for finding AI-built apps in your estate

The platform-specific values are the one thing you have to supply, and all of them are either published or observable from a single generated application: the vendor’s package scope, its address ranges, its bot commit address, its asset domains.

Query your package inventory first. Prefix match, fire on any one of the set, and exclude the vendor’s general-purpose libraries.

Look for bot commit authors across your repositories, and treat a repository with a bot-only history as generated until somebody shows you otherwise.

Search your document roots and build outputs for the markers that survive compilation, not the ones that only ever existed in source.

Check DNS values against the builder’s address space, not just its hostname.

Audit your cloud for identities named after a builder that hold data permissions, then read the policy to see what they can reach. Whole words only.

Join every hit to its database, then re-verify your markers against a freshly generated application before you trust any of it. Ours drifted twice.

None of this is exotic work. The signals sit in data most estates already collect, and the reason these applications stay invisible is not that they hide well. It is that nobody has gone looking with the right query. The one thing that will not keep is the query itself, so whatever you build, put a date on it.

How Orca helps you find and secure AI-built apps

Everything above is a method you can run yourself, with queries you write and re-verify as the builders change. Orca AI AppGen Security helps you uncover apps built with AI tools and brings that discovery into the Orca Cloud Security Platform, so security professionals can protect builders and enable their organizations to grow using AI.

For every app it finds, Orca maps risk across the app’s APIs, integrations and data access. That keeps the application and the data behind it together as one finding, which is the pairing this research argues for.

Findings are prioritized by business impact in the same risk model as the rest of your cloud estate. A generated to-do list stays an inventory entry. A builder wired into production data moves to the top of the queue.

Title: ‘123456’ has been the world’s most popular password for 7 out of the last 8 years
Context: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the...
Full Text: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime. NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way. “Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.” Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either. According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place. “We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present. AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised. The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA. But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example. Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends. “Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years. The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said. We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg, the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®

Title: Ubuntu gets AI-generated security fixes for those feeling brave
Context: We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive
Full Text: Canonical is offering Ubuntu Pro users an opt-in channel for AI-generated security patches, deploying bots to help tackle the growing pile of vulnerabilities other bots are uncovering. Canonical's VP for "Excellence Engineering," Pierre Guillemin, gave the second keynote at the recent Ubuntu Summit, introducing the Edge archive, an optional repository of security fixes generated by the company's Surge framework. As the announcement describes it: "We built Surge, a multi-agent orchestration framework for CVE remediation and backporting, and have reached a high level of confidence in its capabilities. We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive." Edge offers patches before extended testing and qualification are complete, allowing users to assess them themselves. Canonical says updates delivered through the normal security channels will remain human-validated. Ubuntu Summit now runs twice a year. Last week's Ubuntu Summit 26.10 followed a rather unfortunately timed server outage for the company. At the previous such event in June, the company announced a move into agentic AI, but this new one is bolder still. Guillemin noted that "October 2026 saw almost as many CVEs as all of 2025." Surge is a "multi-agent orchestration framework" to remediate vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace. In other words, not the kernel, but even so, it is ambitious. The idea is to use a group of different LLMs to triage new vulnerabilities, find existing fixes, use multiple competing models to backport them to the versions in Ubuntu, and run automatic testing on them. Then a different group of "judging models" will evaluate the fixes and look for consensus. When candidates are chosen, they pass through normal Ubuntu package testing. If there are edge cases, low confidence scores, deadlocks, or other problems, then the process will be escalated to the staff of Canonical's security team. It's an attempt, as Guillemin put it, "to use AI to fight AI" – cooperating groups of LLMs patching their way through the ever-increasing flow of security holes. Even so, this is a remarkably courageous tactic (at the risk of using a famous British euphemism). It's an opt-in feature of Ubuntu Pro, Canonical's security and support subscription – although as we reported in 2022, Pro also has a free tier, so security researchers and the community can try Edge out, study it, and report their findings. We do sympathize with companies struggling against a rising tide of bot-powered security hole discovery. In theory, corporate funding can pay for faster fixes than a volunteer community can offer, but even for commercial vendors these are testing times. As we reported when Debian turned 30, surveys suggest that Ubuntu is about a third of the world Linux user base. Some of those users will be intrepid enough to try this, and that will end up being informative for the whole FOSS world. Those with long memories will remember the last time Canonical used the same edgy nomenclature. Back in July 2013, it launched a crowdfunding campaign for an Ubuntu smartphone. The campaign didn't raise enough money. ®

Training Cybersecurity Students in Real-World Environments
Context: Over three years, students progress from foundational concepts to enterprise technologies, hands-on labs, certifications, and increasingly complex projects that mirror the...
Full Text:
When students begin a career in cybersecurity, they quickly discover that security rarely exists in isolation. Networks, cloud services, remote access, monitoring, troubleshooting, and business continuity all intersect, and practitioners need to understand how those pieces work together.

That reality shapes how GIBZ Academy, a Fortinet Academic Partner in Switzerland, approaches cybersecurity education. Over three years, students progress from foundational concepts to enterprise technologies, hands-on labs, certifications, and increasingly complex projects that mirror the environments they will encounter in the workplace.

The result is an approach built on a simple principle: Students should have the opportunity to work with cybersecurity as it is actually used before they enter the workforce.

Cybersecurity Across the Curriculum

At GIBZ, cybersecurity is not confined to a specialized topic at the end of a student’s studies. It is integrated throughout the three-year curriculum, allowing students to build their understanding progressively as they develop broader IT and networking skills.

That structure matters. Cybersecurity is difficult to understand when it is separated from the systems it is designed to protect. Students need to understand networking, infrastructure, access, applications, and operations, as well as how to secure them.

To support that approach, GIBZ has incorporated Fortinet content into two core modules: IM_S4 Enterprise Security focuses on network security, including FortiGate administration and FortiAnalyzer. IM_S6, Enterprise Security II, builds on that foundation with more advanced topics, such as troubleshooting and SD-WAN.

The program also introduces students to ethical hacking and network defense, giving them opportunities to consider cybersecurity from multiple perspectives. They learn how attackers approach systems, how defenders respond, and how enterprise technologies are used to mitigate risk.

Learning on Enterprise Technology

One of the defining features of the GIBZ program is its use of technologies students are likely to encounter in professional environments.

Before partnering with Fortinet, the school used open-source firewall platforms such as OPNsense and pfSense to teach networking and security concepts. Those platforms provided a solid foundation for learning, but the partnership gave GIBZ the opportunity to place students directly in front of enterprise security technology and the capabilities they are likely to encounter in the field.

Students work with features such as web filtering, antivirus scanning, advanced threat protection, proxy functions, SD-WAN, FortiAnalyzer, and other capabilities used in modern security operations.

The difference goes beyond the technology itself. Students learn how enterprise security is configured, managed, analyzed, and troubleshot, rather than learning firewall concepts only in theory.

From Student Project to Security Architecture

GIBZ student Miguel Fernandes demonstrated this progression in his diploma thesis, in which he designed and implemented a multitenant captive portal solution using multiple Fortinet technologies.

The architecture used FortiAuthenticator as a VM within a dedicated FortiGate vDOM environment, with FortiAnalyzer providing centralized logging and FortiManager scripts automating branch-site provisioning for multiple tenants. FortiADC provided Layer 7 application delivery and web application firewall protection within the authentication flow.

The project required multiple security and networking components to work together. Guest users connected through Wi-Fi and were directed to the hosted captive portal, where their credentials were validated by FortiAuthenticator. After authentication, users received controlled, time-limited internet access.

For a student project, the significance is not simply the number of Fortinet products involved. It is the architectural thinking required to integrate authentication, routing, logging, automation, application delivery, and security controls into a single working solution.

That is the difference between learning how a technology works and learning to solve a problem with it.

The Lab Experience

Hands-on learning plays a central role in that progression. GIBZ currently has two physical labs equipped with 12 FortiGate 40F devices and plans to expand the lab environment by adding switches and access points, giving students additional opportunities to explore wireless networking and zero-trust network access.

The physical equipment adds another dimension to the learning experience. Students work directly with devices, ports, cabling, configurations, and the practical constraints of managing physical infrastructure.

GIBZ also uses structured Fortinet labs to introduce students to the technology. As their skills develop, students can progress from guided virtual exercises to physical hardware and then to more complex projects that integrate multiple technologies and concepts.

For Miguel, that progression made the learning experience meaningfully distinct from traditional classroom instruction. “The Fortinet labs allowed me to work in hands-on, realistic environments with clearly structured tasks, a completely different experience from traditional classroom learning,” he says. “I could work at my own pace, take more time on challenging tasks, and didn’t have to wait for others to move forward.”

The value of that approach extends beyond familiarity with individual products. Students have opportunities to make mistakes, investigate what went wrong, and develop the confidence to work through unfamiliar problems.

Certifications That Validate the Learning

Certifications provide another measure of that progression. Three GIBZ teachers, along with 14 students, have earned Fortinet certifications. Six students have also earned higher-level Fortinet certifications.

For students, those credentials provide a way to demonstrate knowledge and practical experience with technologies recognized across the industry. For instructors, they offer an additional way to align classroom learning with professional expectations.

Miguel saw that connection firsthand, particularly through his work with SD-WAN and ADVPN. "Through this program, I gained deep knowledge of Fortinet products, especially SD-WAN technology and ADVPN. These are complex, modern networking concepts that I was able to explore in detail and really understand from the ground up."

The experience also strengthened his sense of career readiness. "Fortinet is one of the most widely adopted network and security vendors, with a constantly expanding Secure Fabric ecosystem. Many companies rely on Fortinet, which makes this knowledge directly relevant and valuable for my career."

Bringing Education Closer to Industry

GIBZ sees its partnership with Fortinet as a way to bring education closer to the technologies, skills, and expectations students will encounter after graduation.

That connection extends beyond the classroom. Some GIBZ students already use Fortinet technologies in their own companies or with customers through organizations such as IT-Point and InfoGuard. Those connections matter because cybersecurity education must align with workforce requirements. Employers need graduates who understand network operations, security controls, and how modern systems are evolving. Students need opportunities to build those skills before they are expected to apply them professionally.

GIBZ also aims to expand industry engagement across the Swiss states of Zug, Schwyz, Nidwalden, Obwalden, and Lucerne. InfoGuard and IT-Point are expected to support Fortinet events, helping connect students, educators, and local industry players.

In a field facing an ongoing shortage of skilled professionals, those connections can help bridge the gap between education and employment. Students gain a clearer view of the work they are preparing to enter, while industry can engage with developing talent earlier in the pipeline.

Looking Ahead

GIBZ expects interest in cybersecurity to continue growing. Many students currently study systems engineering with a focus on cybersecurity and show strong interest in areas such as network defense and ethical hacking.

The school is also exploring ways to expand its curriculum to include security operations. GIBZ is interested in developing a new module on SOC operations that leverages Fortinet eSOC capabilities. This would enable the school to introduce students to additional areas of security practice, including monitoring, investigation, incident response, and operational workflows.

That would build naturally on the progression already underway in the program: from networking and security fundamentals to enterprise technologies, to hands-on troubleshooting and architecture, and eventually to the operational processes used by security teams.

GIBZ offers one example of what that approach can look like. By integrating cybersecurity across the curriculum, providing students with access to enterprise technology, combining virtual and physical labs, supporting industry certifications, and strengthening connections with employers, the school helps students build practical skills before they begin their careers.

For many students, their first meaningful encounter with cybersecurity need not wait until after graduation. At GIBZ, it is already part of the classroom experience.

Title: Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code?
Context: Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited
Full Text: October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application. Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. Pillar’s OpenCode disclosure in October showed how a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could execute commands on a developer’s Windows or WSL machine during authentication. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet. Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded. A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work. In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100. These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first. Security has to become every developer’s responsibility Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them. Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase and checked against what users should be allowed to do. A new approach to securing your code CodeRabbit Secure uses semantic analysis to understand your codebase and reason about it the way a security engineer would, tracing requests and checking whether permissions and business rules are enforced. Agents investigate potential attack paths and verify findings independent of the developer or agent that wrote the code, while CodeRabbit Agent generates reviewable fixes. Three main use cases that improve your code security: this works across the SDLC: reviewing each commit in a new PR and flag its security risks; finding vulnerabilities across the repo with a Deep Scan; rechecking code with incremental scans and validating findings at runtime. Find vulnerabilities already in committed code Deep Scan examines the repository, including older paths outside the latest PR. Agents map entry points, access controls, and sensitive operations, then investigate across functions and files. Linked repositories, when configured, supply context from shared services and libraries. A separate agent challenges each suspected vulnerability, checking reachability, exploitation conditions, and safeguards that could disprove it. I tried CodeRabbit Secure Deep Scan against ast-grep and was impressed by its precision. Proving vulnerabilities before flagging them makes every finding far more actionable. Herrington Darkholme, creator of ast-grep Review incoming changes before merge PR security reviews assess each incoming change, including agent-generated code, for vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable in the existing application. CodeRabbit’s Security Architecture Review examines how architecture-level changes affect permissions, sensitive data flows, and trust boundaries. The Security Blast Radius map connects changed components to their dependencies and the code that relies on them, helping reviewers trace the potential security impact beyond the PR diff. On GitHub, administrators can enable CodeRabbit Security check and require it through branch protection or a ruleset. It blocks merges when PR security comments at or above the configured severity threshold remain unresolved. Recheck code as it evolves and validate findings at runtime Each Deep Scan builds an attack surface map of the repository, showing which security-relevant entry points have been verified, which have gone stale as the code changed, and which have never been examined. Delta scans then check changed files and areas of the map that are out of date or unverified, so teams know how much of the codebase has been security-reviewed and when it was last reviewed. Individual findings can also be rechecked to determine whether a fix addressed them. For eligible Deep Scan findings on GitHub Cloud with CodeRabbit Cloud, runtime verification generates a reproduction guide and can run it in an isolated environment to confirm whether the vulnerable path is reached. Results are “reproduced”, “not reproduced” or “inconclusive” for the tested revision and environment, however a failure to reproduce may not mean the finding is fixed. Carry the investigation through to a fix Developers can ask CodeRabbit Agent to implement a fix and open a PR, then inspect the finding, proposed fix, and supporting evidence. Teams can also configure severity thresholds to create Jira or Linear tickets automatically and track remediation in their existing workflow. Connecting the vulnerability finding, its supporting evidence, and a proposed fix helps engineering and security teams act while the context is still fresh and carry the change through review, testing and release. Teams can use CodeRabbit Agent to act on that context or easily hand it off to your preferred coding agent with a shareable markdown file. What a million-dollar initiative surfaced CodeRabbit recently committed up to $1 million in free Deep Scans to help organizations find and fix hidden vulnerabilities. In Deep Scans created over a 10-day period in early November, CodeRabbit Secure recorded about 53,000 High or Critical findings across some 2,000 organizations. More than 10,000 findings have already been fixed, including 1,049 rated High or Critical. Some of the security fixes implemented by CodeRabbit included preventing: embedded JavaScript in a repository document’s metadata from running arbitrary code. email subject lines from being interpreted as executable templates and running JavaScript with an API server’s privileges. unauthenticated transfer requests from injecting SQL and triggering unauthorized database operations. As agents produce more code and attackers become more capable, investigation using semantic analysis needs to become a regular part of how software is built and maintained, alongside existing security checks. Find vulnerabilities in your code before an attacker does As attackers use AI agents to investigate unfamiliar systems and adapt their next move, engineering and security teams need the same capacity to investigate their code and carry findings through to tested fixes. Title: New Huntress Security Insights Report & Reporting Center
Context: We renamed it because it has been completely redesigned and now contains information on security posture and other key stats in addition to threats discovered
Full Text:
Huntress has built a reputation for delivering outcomes without all the noise. But on the flip side, we haven't always been great at showing all the work happening behind the scenes. We've received consistent feedback from partners and customers that our reporting could be improved.

It's time for that to change. That's why we've been hard at work rebuilding our reporting capabilities from the ground up. We've quietly rolled out several updates over the last few months, and today we're taking things further with a completely redesigned set of monthly and quarterly reports, plus a better way to find and manage them. Here's a quick summary of what's new, with more details below:

Updated Security Insights Reports (formerly called Threat Reports)

NEW One Page Summary

NEW Investigations View

Meet the Security Insights Report (formerly the Threat Report)

You may know this one as the Threat Report. We renamed it because it has been completely redesigned and now contains information on security posture and other key stats in addition to threats discovered.

This is our primary monthly and quarterly org-level report, and it's built to answer the question partners and customers ask us most:

"What has Huntress actually done for me lately?"

Intended for IT and security professionals, it provides a detailed picture of the outcomes delivered by each Huntress product an organization has.

Here's what's new:

A visual overhaul. The report now uses a horizontal, card-based layout instead of the old portrait format, built for screen sharing and dropping straight into a slide deck for a QBR. Your logo and brand color now carry across the cover and every page.

A new Executive Summary up front. You'll see a protection funnel (events analyzed, signals detected, signals investigated, incidents reported), analyst notes from the Huntress SOC, and a trailing incident trend line, all on the first page.

Full breakdowns by product. Managed EDR, Managed ITDR, Managed SIEM, and Managed ISPM all get their own space in the report now, so it actually reflects everything Huntress protects for you, not just endpoints.

Two new EDR pages. Firewall Status Monitoring gives you a snapshot of endpoint firewall health, and External Recon shows your externally visible attack surface: open ports, risky exposed services, and the kind of low-hanging fruit attackers look for first.

A cross-product Incident Summary page. Every incident from the reporting period now rolls up into one place, broken down by severity and product.

We're rolling out the Security Insights Report now, and it will become available in your portal as the rollout progresses. You'll find it where you access today's report in your portal: click Reports. For the next few months, you'll receive both the legacy Threat Report and the new Security Insights Report to ensure you have time to transition any existing workflows.

One Page Summary for Non-Technical Stakeholders

Not every stakeholder wants (or needs) the level of detail in the Security Insights Report. That's what this one is for.

Think of Dr. Lee, a dentist whose practice is managed by a managed service provider (MSP). He doesn't need a breakdown of signals investigated by product. He needs to know his practice is protected, in plain language, on one page. That's exactly what this report gives him: the layers of protection Huntress has in place (EDR, ITDR, SIEM, and so on), an easy-to-understand summary of what was investigated and contained, and a quick view of how Huntress and his MSP kept his organization protected during the period.

It's delivered each month automatically via an emailed link, and it's always available in the "Reports" section of the portal. Partners can hand it straight to their end customers. It doesn't replace the Security Insights Report above, but it complements it, giving you a one-page option for the people who just need the non-technical headlines.

Investigations View

A few weeks ago, we rolled out the new Investigations View to give you a full chronological timeline of every investigation our SOC runs, including the ones closed as benign. If you'd like to learn more, take a look at the Investigations View announcement here.

What's next

This is a big step, but it's not the finish line. Here's what we're already working on:

An account-level Security Insights Report, giving MSPs and internal IT teams the same redesign, rolled up across all the organizations they manage.

More customization through the Reporting Center, so you can configure recipients, branding, and content directly from the new hub.

A more advanced ISPM compliance report, a dedicated, deeper report for compliance and audit needs, separate from (and in addition to) the ISPM posture page that's already part of the Security Insights Report today.

Updated Reporting Center with New tabs organizes reports by type, so you can go straight to the one you need instead of scrolling through a single long list. And informational callouts on each report type explain what it's for, who it's for, and what's inside, so you know exactly which one to send before you send it. This will be helpful as we continue to roll out additional reporting options in the future.

We want your feedback

This is an important step toward making Huntress more transparent about the work happening behind the scenes, but it's not the last one. If you have requests, ideas, or feedback on any of these reporting updates, let us know at feedback.huntress.io.

We're listening. And we'll keep evolving the Huntress portal to make our work—and your value to your customers—even clearer.

Title: The AI Arena: Huntress CTF 2026 Retro
Context: Figure 3: "Time trial" mode showing Hall of Fame speeds Highlights from Huntress Capture the Flag 2026 This year's competition featured hands-on malware analysis, threat...
Full Text:
It's that time of the year again! No, not cybersecurity awareness month, Black October, of whatever they're calling it these days. It's the fourth installment of the Huntress Capture the Flag (CTF) competition.

Over the last three years this event has drawn fierce competition. This year's event was no different, with 2,715 registered users and 1,602 teams.

But what was different this year? If your answer isn't AI, you're likely living under a rock. By now, AI can chew through a classic CTF challenge before you have time to refill your coffee. So this year, we leaned into that reality and built the Huntress CTF around it: through a special AI Arena.

Participants could bring Claude, another model, or no AI at all, then decide how much they wanted to put their new tooling to work. We provided the stage, complete with tokens, so competitors could experiment without racking up a hefty bill.

But most importantly, our goal wasn't to just let models submit flags: we wanted to help players hone their skills around directing, validating, and working alongside AI during technical investigations. And, as we'll highlight below, participants came up with some pretty neat results.

But first, what's Capture the Flag again?

Capture the Flag, or CTF, is a cybersecurity competition built around solving technical challenges and finding a hidden "flag," usually a unique string of text. Players earn points by locating and submitting those flags. But getting there is the real work, and involves a good level of technical expertise, a little bit of creativity, and a lot of drive.

The Huntress CTF as a whole started with a simple question during cybersecurity awareness month planning four years ago: how do we give people more than another reminder to turn on MFA or stop reusing passwords? We wanted to create something people could actually dig into, learn from, and come back to throughout October. The answer was a CTF that brought defenders together for a full month of hands-on problem-solving.

Figure 1: This year's CTF Leaderboard

A challenge might ask competitors to untangle an obfuscated malware sample, pull apart an executable, trace suspicious activity through logs, or spot the clue buried in a web application. The goal is for players to feel like they're working through the same kinds of puzzles that show up in real investigations.

CTFs are a useful place to build technical instincts without the pressure of a live incident. They reward persistence, curiosity, and the willingness to change course when one idea goes nowhere. Some people compete for points, prizes, and a place on the leaderboard. Others are there to sharpen their skills and learn from the community.

How does AI change the whole concept of CTF?

Teams are increasingly using AI models in CTFs to make sense of unfamiliar code, test ideas, and automate routine analysis. Some competitions now even put autonomous agents on the scoreboard.

This year, Huntress fully leaned into the use of AI; but we tried to do so tactfully. While AI is changing CTF competitions, it hasn't made human competitors obsolete. AI models can help a team get unstuck or move through routine analysis, but it doesn't guarantee a flag. AI tools can still misread a challenge, produce broken code, or confidently send players down the wrong path. The strongest use is often collaborative, with a human operator making the judgement calls, bringing important context into the challenge, and verifying information.

Figure 2: A snippet from a participant's (team.dev) custom scoreboard tracking tiny timing differences between their solves and submissions and those of other teams

As one way to help players see the speed at which teams were solving challenges, we included a "Hall of Fame" that would list every player's fastest solve times in the "Time Trial" mode. The aim here was to encourage players to optimize their engines even more.

Figure 3: "Time trial" mode showing Hall of Fame speeds

Highlights from Huntress Capture the Flag 2026

This year's competition featured hands-on malware analysis, threat hunting, and other exercises based on real-world malware samples, CVEs, and active exploits. A few of our favorite challenges included:

SHA1-Hulud: "SHA1-Hulud" (by Nordgaren) is a reverse-engineering CTF challenge. Solvers got one password-protected ZIP with a single executable, and had to reconstruct a runtime-generated flag while working around anti-debugging and self-modifying code.

In this challenge, the flag wasn't encrypted anywhere in the binary: only a chain of SHA-1 "mined" nonces were stored, and replaying the hash chain at runtime would regenerate the bytes.

Most classic reverse engineering shortcuts (like static string extraction, breakpoints, or memory dumps) were purposefully blocked. Instead, solvers had to look at the bigger picture of the entire key-derivation pipeline and reproduce it without disturbing the program.

Framework Roulette: This was a multi-stage web security CTF challenge. Players had to find and exploit a different vulnerability in each of six live applications, adapting across several frameworks and languages.

Framework Roulette served as the CTF Web Track's final exam, bringing the month's bug classes together in one ranked challenge. As seen in Figure 4, each player tackled six different stacks, each hiding a different flaw.

Figure 4: Each of the vulnerable apps with different weaknesses in the Framework Roulette challenge

Each app yielded a flag fragment, which players had to assemble in order. The difficulty here came from having to adapt quickly.

Unique Write-ups This Year: Another interesting part of the AI Arena was seeing competitors document not just their answers, but the systems they built to reach them. Those write-ups became useful extensions of the CTF itself: they gave other players a way to compare approaches, revisit challenges after the event, and learn from the tradeoffs behind each solve. The bland3man 2026 CTF Huntress writeup site

SU Pack's AI Arena write-up packet

Integris even created a cool video on the Sha1-Hulud challenge:

Together, these player-created resources show what made this year's format different. The AI Arena rewarded speed and automation, but the strongest teams also built durable workflows, checked their results, and shared what they learned with the wider CTF community.

A successful CTF year

Thanks to everyone who played Huntress CTF 2026 and helped make this year's competition such a lively place to learn, experiment, and compete. The AI Arena showed that new tools can change how quickly we work, but curiosity, careful validation, and sharing what you learn still make the difference. From creative solutions to detailed player writeups, the community made this CTF more than a leaderboard. We're grateful you joined us, and we're already looking forward to building on what we learned together next year.

Title: Tenable One Adversary View brings Claude Mythos’ adversarial reasoning to your environment

Full Text:
Tenable One Adversary View is now generally available. Powered by Claude Mythos, it reads your scan data like an attacker would and tells you what to fix first.

Key takeaways

Adversary View is generally available. Tenable One customers with Tenable Hexa AI can run it today, with nothing new to deploy.

Tenable Hexa AI applies Claude Mythos’ adversarial reasoning to data you already collect. It works across the findings from your existing scans and plugins to find vulnerability chains and attack-path choke points.

Break more attack paths with fewer fixes. Adversary View ranks every fix by how many attack paths it stops, so your team can prioritize actions that cut off the most attacker progress.

Virtually every security team works from the same question: What can we fix next to reduce the most risk? Tenable One is designed to answer this question every day with attack path analysis, which uses rule-based logic to continuously map how attackers could reach your critical assets.

Tenable One Adversary View, now live for all Tenable Hexa AI users, adds a deeper, point-in-time check on top of it. Tenable Hexa AI uses Claude’s Mythos-class model to reason like an adversary across your existing scan data, working through how findings combine instead of matching them to predefined rules. Then it points you to the fixes that cut off the most routes.

When Tenable previewed Adversary View in September, we promised a way to see your environment the way an attacker does. If you’re a Tenable One customer with Tenable Hexa AI, you can run it today.

Vulnerability management programs must adapt to AI-accelerated discovery

AI is reshaping vulnerability management by accelerating vulnerability discovery and the creation of working exploits.

For security teams, every new CVE makes it harder to answer the question: “What do we fix next?” These teams still need to understand whether a new CVE applies to their environment, whether they can validate it, and whether anyone is exploiting it. Only then can they start to prioritize it against the thousands of other vulnerabilities across their environment.

But an attacker doesn’t start with a CVSS-sorted spreadsheet of your vulnerabilities. Attackers read the environment to determine which hosts talk to each other, what services are exposed, and which accounts are reachable. Then they reason about how to get from an entry point to a valuable asset.

Severity-based prioritization doesn’t operate that way. A netstat entry, a mapped network drive, or a line buried in plugin output may not be a critical finding on its own, but together they can form a dangerous attack path.

Spotting those combinations across every vulnerability, at this volume, is more than any team can do by hand. Keeping up requires automated attack path analysis, assisted by frontier AI, for prioritization and remediation.

What Adversary View does

Adversary View, accessible in Tenable Hexa AI, looks at your assets from an attacker’s viewpoint. Point Adversary View at a set of assets you already scan and ask how an attacker could move through them.

Tenable Hexa AI uses Claude Mythos to apply adversarial reasoning, building an on-demand graph of your environment from your existing vulnerability scan data, with no new sensors or agents needed, and returns:

Ranked vulnerability chains, with each hop backed by scan evidence

Choke points, and a prioritized list of what to fix, ordered by how many paths each fix closes rather than by severity alone

Remediation and reporting includes patches and configuration changes for each route, plus a Jira ticket, remediation dashboard, or shareable PDF report

Attack path analysis and Adversary View cover different jobs. Attack path analysis watches your environment continuously and flags paths based on pre-defined rules as they form.

Adversary View is the on-demand deep read: Scope it to a business unit or a tag, and Tenable Hexa AI reasons through that slice of your environment the way an attacker would.

Adversary View in action

We ran Adversary View across a production environment of hosts, and it found and prioritized numerous paths to a crown-jewel asset. The top-ranked path starts at an internet-facing host, moves through a workstation and a domain controller, and ends at a Windows Server 2016 box still vulnerable to EternalBlue, the exploit behind WannaCry.

Adversary View also found a short list of fixes that closes nearly all of the paths: patch two servers (a domain controller and a second Windows Server 2022 box) and you block Server Message Block (SMB) traffic from the internet into the internal network. That one firewall rule closes 32 SMB connections that offer a direct path from the internet into the internal network.

Adversary View is a capability within Tenable One that analyzes existing scan data to identify viable vulnerability chains and the specific routes an attacker could take through connected assets. It is accessed through Tenable Hexa AI and operates as a point-in-time inspection. To begin, the user opens Tenable Hexa AI and selects the Adversary View card. This triggers the agent to analyze scan data and construct a graph of asset connections. The scope can be set to all assets or narrowed to specific tags, IP ranges, or business units. Once submitted, Tenable Hexa AI offers to tag the scoped asset group for future reference. After confirming your scoped assets, Adversary View deterministically builds a map and applies reasoning to discover vulnerability chains without relying on predefined rules. The model interrogates the asset graph step-by-step to identify paths an attacker could traverse. The output includes an executive summary that identifies structural chokepoints and the fixes that are aimed at reducing the most risk. In the example shown, Tenable Hexa AI identified and ranked seven viable attack routes reaching crown-jewel assets. The top-ranked route traces an attacker’s movement from an internet-facing workstation to an EternalBlue-vulnerable server. Each step in a route is backed by actual scan output, including active network connections (NETSTAT_CONN) and specific CVEs, grounding findings in real data. A “What to Fix” section provides tailored remediation recommendations for each route, specifying control changes that disrupt the attacker path across multiple hops. Users can interact with Tenable Hexa AI through follow-up prompts to prioritize fixes and assess risk reduction before applying patches. Tenable Hexa AI is designed to surface the top highest-leverage actions that eliminate maximum exposure. From the conversation, users can create a Jira ticket or Exposure Response initiative directly, with Tenable Hexa AI collecting the technical details needed and allowing the user to define scope before pushing findings into the IT Service Management (ITSM) console.

How to run Adversary View in your environment

Here’s how to run the same analysis on your own assets.

Start a conversation. Open Tenable Hexa AI and click the “Adversary View” tile, or ask for an Adversary View in your own words.

Set your scope. The demo uses the “All Assets” option. In your own environment, you can target tags, IP ranges, operating systems, or a business unit. Tenable Hexa AI offers to tag the scoped assets so you can rerun the same analysis later.

Confirm and let it run. Click “Confirm”. Tenable Hexa AI builds a map of how your scoped assets connect, then uses Claude Mythos to reason across that map and the raw scan evidence behind it. The analysis takes several minutes and keeps running in the background if you leave the panel.

Read the summary. Results open with an executive summary that includes the top vulnerability chains in your environment and the fixes designed to stop them.

Inspect a route. Each ranked route shows its hops on a graph, with the scan evidence behind every hop, from SMB sessions and netstat connections to specific CVEs.

Find the fixes that matter most. Each route lists patches and configuration changes that help to stop attacks. Ask Tenable Hexa AI follow-up questions to see which fixes close the most routes at once.

Turn it into tracked work. Ask Tenable Hexa AI to open a Jira ticket or track your remediation efforts by creating a dashboard. It gathers the technical details, then pushes them into your IT Service Management (ITSM) console.

Generate a report. Have Tenable Hexa AI generate a PDF and download it straight from the chat. The report summarizes all findings and top actions so you can share results across teams.

Prompts to try

Show me an adversary view for assets tagged “production”.

Show me the shortest path from any public entry point to a Critical ACR asset.

Show me the top 3 choke points and explain why each ranks where it does.

If I could only patch 5 assets this sprint, which ones should I pick to close the most vulnerability chains?

Prompts to follow up with

Create JIRA tickets with the top fix and assign them to respective owners.

Ensure MacOS assets are in the appropriate Smart Group to ensure remediation of [CHOKE POINT] in the next patching window.

Create a downloadable PDF for all discovered vulnerability chains.

How to get started with Adversary View

Before your first run, check that you have:

A Tenable One Foundation or Tenable One Advanced license

“Frontier AI Model Access” turned on in Tenable Hexa AI’s settings by your admin

A role with access: Adversary View is on by default for administrators and scan managers, and custom roles need the right permissions

Scans covering your target assets with the options “Override normal verbosity” enabled and “Report as much information as possible” selected

Get more details about Adversary View

Ready to see which of your vulnerabilities an attacker could chain together, and which fixes stop them?

Read the documentation

Existing customers: Open Tenable Hexa AI in Tenable One and click the Adversary View tile.

Google Project Zero to Cut Disclosure Deadline to 30 Days by 2028
Context: It also argued that severity should not set disclosure timing: "A vulnerability's severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its...
Full Text:
Google's Project Zero has scrapped its "90 + 30" disclosure policy and will publish vulnerability details 90 days after reporting them, whether or not a fix exists, before cutting the disclosure deadline to 60 days and then 30 days.

Project Zero outlined the changes in a November 13 post and tied the changes to AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

Project Zero said, "We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year."

Project Zero Replaces 90 Plus 30 Policy

Under the new policy, dubbed Full X, Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities X days after reporting them to vendors. The policy begins as Full 90, moves to Full 60 on February 2, 2027 and reaches Full 30 on January 3, 2028.

The 30-day 'soak time', the grace period and the variant policy have been removed. Three exceptions remain: vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild, bugs whose details have already been made public and cases where vendors ask Project Zero to publish the details.

Project Zero said 'soak time' was no longer meaningful because attackers can almost immediately work out bug details from a patch.

Vendors consulted by Project Zero warned that an immediate change could expose unfixed bugs, push them to fix Project Zero's reports ahead of more severe ones or lead some to stop trying.

Defenders Pressed to Close the Patch Gap

Ivan Milenkovic, VP of risk technology at Qualys, told Infosecurity that Project Zero had "removed the snooze button on responding to issues." Pointing to Project Zero's finding rate, he said: "This describes an arrival rate that most patch programmes were never built for."

For organizations, he said, patching monthly now means you're slower than disclosure. He called the vendors' objection to an immediate change to the disclosure policy "a fair response, but the alternative was letting attackers set the deadline."

Read more on vulnerability disclosure: N-able Rushes Out N-central Fixes After 33 Zero-Days Go Public

Project Zero said its new policy was intended to encourage vendors to reduce the patch gap, the period between a fix becoming available and users installing it.

It also argued that severity should not set disclosure timing: "A vulnerability's severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users."

The group said it would still track whether bugs were fixed, but that fix status would no longer decide when technical details were published.
