Title: Investigating vault particles with Claude
Context: We’re sharing another finding from Anthropic’s biology research lab: the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells
Full Text:
We’re sharing another finding from Anthropic’s biology research lab: the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells. Vaults are large, hollow barrels of protein found in cells across the tree of life, and their function is still unknown. Below, we describe how Claude helped at each step of this research: searching across sequence literature, optimizing a method of isolating particles, and mapping the vault’s structure. More information is in our preprint, which we’ve submitted to bioRxiv; we’ll update the link as soon as it goes live.

Biological cells were first detected in 1665, but more than three and a half centuries later, much of how they work remains unknown. Until relatively recently, the existence of some crucial components, let alone their function, was controversial. Even today, more than a third of the roughly 4,400 genes in one of the most comprehensively studied cells, the bacterium E. coli, remain poorly understood. Another such enigma is the vault particle.

A vault particle is a large, hollow protein shell found in nearly all the cells in our body. It was discovered in 1986 by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha, but its function remains elusive. At roughly three times the mass of a ribosome, it’s one of the largest known molecular complexes in eukaryotes—organisms with complex cells, such as mammals (as opposed to simple, usually single-celled “prokaryotes,” such as bacteria). Vaults take their name from their shape. When observed under an electron microscope, the ribbed shell reminded Dr. Rome and Dr. Kedersha of the vaulted ceiling of a cathedral. In mammals, the shell is made of 78 copies of the major vault protein, arranged as two identical halves joined at the middle.

Vaults are found across most of the eukaryotic tree, from slime molds to humans, so scientists believe that they must do something useful. Researchers have proposed various functions, including transporting molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm, protecting cells from toxic compounds such as cancer drugs, and supporting innate immunity, but none of these proposals have been conclusively confirmed. Other studies have shown that mice lacking vaults still survive, which suggests that vaults may be necessary only under specific environmental conditions. Still, the question remains: why would evolution retain something so large if it didn’t have an important function?

Interested in whether Claude could help make progress on this long-standing open problem, our biology research team has been investigating vaults. We haven’t yet determined their biological function, but we did find that many more vault proteins across the tree of life, including those in prokaryotes and the bacteriophages that infect them, can assemble into complete vault-like particles. Related proteins had already been found in the genomes of both prokaryotes and phages, but to our knowledge no one had shown that they assemble into vaults.

A vault in a prokaryotic cell gives researchers a simpler system to study. Compared with mammalian cells, bacteria are quick to grow, which makes it easier to investigate where vaults came from, what their basic structure looks like, and what, if anything, they contain. Studying the bacterial relatives of human proteins has been informative before. Bacterial versions of cGAS–STING signaling, gasdermins, and viperins revealed the microbial origins of these human immune defenses. In those cases, their function in humans was already known. For vaults it is not, and their prokaryotic relatives may help reveal it.

Here, we describe how we uncovered the molecular structure of a vault from a bacteriophage. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Like all viruses, they hijack their host cells to make their proteins, so this vault would be built inside a bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. The vault is built from 96 copies of a single protein, compared with 78 in human vaults. By duplicating part of the protein, we engineered the vault to be even larger. Together, these results shed light on how such complexes assemble and suggest how they could be adapted for biotechnology—for example, as nanocapsules for delivering enzymes.

This work also demonstrates our team’s wider aim: to speed up research in fundamental biology by building Claude into every step of the process. Under our direction, Claude searched protein databases, designed the DNA constructs, optimized the isolation method, and processed the microscopy data. As a result, a vault purification that conventionally takes three days took us about 90 minutes, and a first structural model was ready 34 hours later, which we estimate would normally have taken us weeks.

Despite this progress, there is still much to be learned about these perplexing structures. When we shared the structure with Dr. Rome, whom we brought on to advise us on this research, he said:

Figuring out the function of vaults is still enormously challenging. I am pleased that Anthropic has so much good data. Now, other people will be working on this problem … The broadness of Anthropic’s finding[s] suggests that it is going to be a complicated function and an interesting ride.

Our lab is releasing these findings early to continue to show the scientific community how Claude can be used for discovery. You can read more about our results and methods in our preprint, and we will be releasing the structures and additional data soon.

A vault-like structure in prokaryotes

We uncovered the vault structure using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), in which many copies of a particle are flash-frozen and imaged with an electron beam, before being combined into a single 3D model. The vault is built from 96 copies (48 copies per half) of a single phage protein, which we call L05, with a combined mass of about 9.5 megadaltons. By contrast, the mammalian version has 39 copies per half. The phage-derived vault is also shorter and wider: roughly 54 nanometers long and 45 wide, compared with 67 by 40 in mammals. Despite being shorter, it encloses about 25% more volume because it is more spherical. The protein chain that makes up its wall is built from seven repeating segments stacked end to end, rather than the nine in mammalian vaults, and its end caps are flatter. It’s among the largest protein shells ever identified in prokaryotes.

One notable feature of its structure is how the caps close. A wall 48 copies around must narrow toward the pole, and it does so in three steps, like a tiered dome. In every group of three neighboring copies, one ends at the first step, one at the second, and one continues to the tip. The three copies are identical along the wall, but take different shapes (conformations) in the cap.

Given that we can make this vault in the lab and isolate it quickly, we also experimented with altering its structure to learn more about how these proteins assemble. Working with Claude, we made 15 altered versions of the protein, most with changes at the points where neighboring copies touch. Some single changes near the cap were enough to prevent the shell from closing: in place of sealed vaults we saw open, rosette-like particles, which shows that this region is needed to seal the shell.

We also tried making the vault even bigger. Ordinarily, the wall is built from seven repeating segments. When we copied two of them, giving the protein nine—the same number as in the human vault—it assembled into even larger vault particles, increasing the enclosed volume by approximately 20%. These experiments demonstrate how vaults could have changed size over their evolutionary history by duplicating pieces of their own wall without disrupting how they assemble.

Finding, isolating, and mapping a new vault with Claude

Part of the reason vaults have remained unexplained for 40 years is that they are missing from the organisms biologists rely on most for genetic experiments, including baker’s yeast, fruit flies, and nematode worms. In mice, which do have vaults, animals that are bred without a vault partner protein or the vault RNA develop normally, leaving no obvious defect to follow up. In recent years, bioinformaticians identified distant relatives of the vault protein in prokaryotes, but it wasn’t clear whether these proteins formed vaults.

Our team set out to answer that question. The research required several steps: surveying genetic sequences to find where vault proteins occur across the tree of life, producing and isolating the most promising candidates to test whether they actually assemble into vault-like particles, and determining the structure of one of the particles to see how its chains fit together.

We began by using Claude Science to search for the vault protein’s relatives across a database of about 15 billion predicted proteins. They turned out to be rare but widely distributed, present in 29 major groups (phyla) of bacteria and four of archaea (the other main group of prokaryotes) but in less than 1% of species with a sequenced genome. We then chose 44 of these proteins and tested each in a cell-free system to see which genes yielded full-length protein and how much. We chose the proteins, and Claude turned each protein sequence into DNA tailored to the host cell, added the control sequences that switch a gene on, and prepared the designs for ordering. We moved the best performers into living E. coli bacteria, where 15 of 24 produced soluble protein.

Next, we needed to isolate the particles. The conventional method, developed for eukaryotic vaults, spins the sample through a tube of increasingly dense sugar and takes approximately three days. To speed this up, we decided to try size-exclusion chromatography. In this process, the sample flows through a column of porous beads. In a process called fractionation, small molecules get stuck in the pores, while the vaults, which are too big to enter, come out first, in what’s known as the void volume.

Claude first argued against taking the chromatography approach, because clumps of misfolded protein come out in that same void volume. We went ahead anyway, and Claude helped make it work by recommending a specific column as well as methods to track the vault protein and check whether particles had formed. Claude then proposed loading the contents of ruptured cells straight onto the column with no purification beforehand. We were reluctant at first because these columns are expensive, and the raw contents of ruptured E. coli cells can clog them or cause contamination. But we were willing to test an unconventional idea, and it worked.

We are not the first group to isolate vaults on sizing columns, but our optimized method takes about 90 minutes from cells to microscopy grid instead of days. Under an electron microscope, seven of the 15 proteins had assembled into vault-like particles.

Cryo-EM confirmed the vault shape for four of those seven, two from phages and two from bacteria. We chose one of the phage proteins, L05, for the detailed structure described above because it was among the best at forming complete, closed particles. Determining a biomolecular structure often takes weeks or months of manual work with specialized software. We directed Claude through the whole process. Working in an internal multi-agent harness with access to internal compute resources, Claude set up an open-source processing software (RELION) and ran each step, while we advised on the analysis decisions. A first full model was ready in 34 hours, and the final maps were ready about a week after processing began.

Claude also pointed out a feature of the structure we can’t yet explain. A pocket partway up each of the 96 protein copies holds a small molecule that shows up clearly in the map but that we haven’t been able to identify. Claude found that its shape resembles coenzyme A, a common helper molecule that cells use to shuttle chemical groups around. If it is coenzyme A, or something similar, it would be an early hint at a possible function.

A new way of doing science

For us, this was a dramatically different way of doing science. None of us had worked with a protein assembly this large, and we had limited experience in structural biology. We took the project on anyway, because Claude could make up for what we didn’t know and rapidly perform analyses that would otherwise have taken us much longer.

In under four months, we screened dozens of candidate vaults, prepared samples for the microscope, and solved the first vault structure found in prokaryotes. Most of this work could be achieved by a typical lab with access to existing Claude products. Only the cryo-EM analysis, which used hundreds of GPUs in parallel to save time, required more computing resources than might be available to an academic institution.

Working this way also showed us where Claude needed improvement. A protocol it wrote called for a growth medium containing an additive that interferes with getting DNA into cells, which set the project back by two weeks. Early in the cryo-EM processing, it skipped a standard step and produced a flawed map blended with its mirror image, and we told it to stop improvising (“Please let’s do normal things unless they don’t work”).

We have used what we’ve learned to inform Claude’s development. We shared our lab notes with the ML researchers who train Claude, so they could see where the model went wrong. This has informed the kind of data Claude learns from. Over the course of the project, Claude got much better at these tasks as new models arrived, making seemingly fewer errors in DNA construct design and better identifying potential pitfalls in experiments. In areas we knew well, we caught mistakes quickly, but they cost us time in areas we didn’t. Overall, we found that the benefits of working this way far outweighed the drawbacks, and Claude has become integral to our work.

So far, we have made these vaults only in E. coli, and have yet to test whether they form in the bacteria and phages where they’re naturally found. More work is needed to determine the function of these particles, and our work only deepens the mystery. As Dr. Rome put it:

Will we find out that they are all doing the same thing? Or will we see an evolutionary development of vault function? Maybe they are doing the same thing as human vaults, and that is also very interesting.

We will continue our research into the function of vaults, and will share more as this work progresses.

Work with us

We are releasing the details of our work in our preprint. If you have an idea for what these vaults might be doing, or a system in which to test it, we would like to hear from you: mdurrant[at]anthropic.com, nicholasp[at]anthropic.com.

Title: What one organization revealed about AI agent risk
Context: A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents With early access to Sysdig AI Defense, one software development company spent a month looking at AI agent usage across their enterprise
Full Text:
A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents

With early access to Sysdig AI Defense, one software development company spent a month looking at AI agent usage across their enterprise. Below is what they found.

Citizen developers are generating code

At this organization, 50% of the employees using AI agents work outside of the engineering department. Marketing, human resources, sales, legal, and finance all used AI agents daily, and they aren’t just chatting with them. Among the non-engineers using agents, an average of 42% of them had an agent run code, a build, a package install, or a cloud or cluster command.

A finance employee building tools likely doesn’t possess the same security knowledge as an engineer, nor are they likely to have the same reviews in place by default. But that shouldn’t stop them from creating. Organizations should watch installs and CLI calls and provide an approved, sandboxed path for them to build.

Tool calls are running without human approval

People turn off prompts to keep their work moving, and although it isn’t generally a sign of carelessness, it can open organizations up to greater risk. More than 60% of this organization’s tool calls ran without a human approving them — 52% screened by Claude Code’s auto-mode classifier instead of a person, and 9% with permission prompts intentionally turned off (YOLO mode).

But the answer to minimizing this risk isn’t blocking everything or turning a blind eye. Organizations need to understand their risk profiles at different levels, and allow tools, agents, and extensions based on what they can reach and change.

The agent’s account of its own actions isn’t enough

For every tool call this organization’s agents logged, the kernel captured seven processes. While an agent’s log may help a user debug a session, it’s not meant to be used as audit evidence because the agent writes it. The kernel sees what actually ran at the process level, regardless of the tool or API used. However, additional data shows that the security team needs both to see the full picture. For example, when an agent read a credential file, the agent’s log had no entry 82% of the time. However, the kernel logged every read.

Connecting unverified extensions to agents

Nearly half (47%) of the MCP servers in use came from third-party registries or vendors for this organization. Each server is a trusted relationship that only takes one line of config to connect to an agent, and once connected, it has access. Servers can also update silently in the background, so the one you trusted last week may not be the one running today.

Matching models to tasks

More than 50% of the organization’s AI spend went to duplicative processes and capabilities. With visibility into which models are used, scoped to the team and user behind each agent, organizations can tie model choice to the task and cut duplication.

What else is in the full report

This is only a fraction of what one month of agent activity uncovered. Dig deeper to discover:

How often security-relevant detections are triggered.

A risk-tier framework for allowing agents and extensions by what they can reach

Real alerts from the deployment, including a possible data exfiltration, an unapproved model provider, and a change to cloud permissions.

What model tiers employees are actually using day to day.

A risk reduction table you can hand to your team.

Odds are, AI agents are already running in your organization. The question is whether you know where they’re running, and whether you can see what they’re doing. Read the full report to see what this organization found and how you can start closing the gap.

Title: Democracy without a safety net.
Context: Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in financially motivated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, and power stations, by 2028. Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day...
Full Text:
CISA scales back its Election Day role. Google takes down a massive Android TV botnet. The UK warns of AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure. German lawmakers face potential spyware threats. An AI-enabled infostealer ranks its victims. Ivanti patches more exploited zero-days. NATO launches cyber war games in Estonia. A Harvard breach exposes data linked to 850,000 email addresses. Our guest is Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, on protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. Democracy is calling. And texting.

Today is Tuesday November 3rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

CISA steps back from the midterms.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is taking a dramatically reduced role in today’s midterm elections, abandoning the coordinated national election security operation it has maintained since 2018, the New York Times reports.

Under the Trump administration, CISA has lost roughly a third of its workforce, scaled back intelligence sharing, and discontinued election-specific cybersecurity assessments. There will be no national election security war room or scheduled press briefings, leaving state and local officials with less federal support for responding to cyber threats, technical disruptions, and disinformation.

CISA insists it's fully prepared, pointing to regional teams available to assist election officials and hundreds of security-related engagements.

Former officials disagree, warning that the retreat leaves dangerous gaps in nationwide threat awareness and coordination.

States have significantly strengthened their election defenses since 2016, including expanded use of paper ballots. But experts say the federal government's ability to identify and communicate threats that cross state lines has substantially weakened.

Google dismantles a set-top-box botnet.

Google says it has dismantled a massive botnet built from more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes shipped with malware already installed.

The botnet, dubbed XCPE, allegedly originated with Chinese manufacturer Videostrong Technology, which Google says secretly turned customers' devices into residential proxies, renting their internet connections to third parties for activities including advertising fraud and other cybercrime.

Google severed ties with Videostrong and took legal action against the infrastructure controlling the botnet. Researchers say the disruption could also cut off access to more than 10 million additional compromised devices.

The malware wasn't limited to streaming boxes. Researchers also found it on Android-based healthcare equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage.

Google says it has addressed the weakness that allowed the malware to activate during initial device setup. The case highlights a troubling supply-chain threat: devices compromised before customers even plug them in.

The UK’s NCSC warns of likely attacks on critical infrastructure.

Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in financially motivated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, and power stations, by 2028.

In its annual State of the Cyber Nation report, the NCSC also predicts Russia and China will routinely incorporate AI into their cyber operations.

Agency chief Richard Horne says the danger isn't necessarily new attack techniques, but AI's ability to discover and exploit existing vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed and scale.

He criticized organizations for running outdated systems, postponing security upgrades, and failing to monitor their networks.

The British government is responding with new investments in cyber defenses, AI security research, and vulnerability detection.

Horne warned that organizations face a choice: invest in resilience now, or risk serious disruptions to essential services later.

Warnings from Apple prompt German authorities to highlight potential spyware.

German authorities are warning lawmakers and prominent public figures about possible spyware attacks following a new round of threat notifications from Apple.

Germany’s federal cybersecurity agency, the BSI, confirmed that members of parliament and other notable individuals received alerts indicating they may have been targeted by sophisticated surveillance software.

Apple sent similar warnings to users in 99 countries. The company doesn't identify suspected attackers or confirm whether targeted devices were successfully compromised.

The spyware involved in these campaigns can potentially steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information, sometimes exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction from victims.

German officials say they're taking the warnings seriously and advise recipients to assume their devices may be compromised.

It's unclear who's responsible for the latest campaign, or whether any German officials were successfully hacked.

A new infostealer uses AI to identify the most valuable victims.

Researchers at Cisco Talos have uncovered a new infostealer that uses artificial intelligence to analyze stolen data and identify the most valuable victims.

Dubbed Volta-Autodoxer, the malware collects passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, payment information, and cryptocurrency credentials. It also targets active sessions on platforms including Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox.

But Volta goes beyond simply stealing data. It conducts additional searches through victims' accounts, gathering information about their locations, habits, and purchases to build detailed personal profiles.

The malware then submits that information to commercial AI models, asking them to act as intelligence analysts and produce structured assessments that help attackers prioritize targets.

Volta defaults to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, with fallback options including Moonshot AI's Kimi and Google's Gemini.

Researchers haven't confirmed the malware has been deployed in the wild, but its design demonstrates how AI could make traditional credential theft more targeted and efficient.

Ivanti patches additional Connect Secure zero-days.

Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day attacks since early October. Attackers chained a privilege escalation flaw and a file upload vulnerability with an authentication bypass bug patched last month, enabling unauthenticated root-level code execution. Researchers at Volexity say the attackers avoided deploying malware, instead repeatedly exploiting devices to execute commands and tampering with logs to hide their activity. CISA has ordered federal agencies to patch the authentication bypass vulnerability by Friday. More than 5,000 Connect Secure instances remain exposed to the internet.

NATO’s Crossed Swords cyber exercise kicks off in Estonia.

NATO's Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence has launched Crossed Swords 2026 in Tallinn, Estonia, bringing together more than 250 participants from over 40 countries.

The exercise focuses on coordinating offensive and defensive cyber operations with conventional military and special operations missions, where timing can be critical down to the minute.

This year's exercise introduces a dedicated AI agent track, allowing participants to build, deploy, and work alongside autonomous systems while maintaining human oversight. The training environment also incorporates OpenAI's Daybreak cyber defense technology.

Military cyber operators, threat hunters, forensic specialists, and command staff are participating, alongside civilian partners helping integrate critical infrastructure protection into operational planning.

Crossed Swords has grown significantly since its beginnings in 2014, reflecting the increasing importance of coordinating cyber capabilities with traditional military operations.

A data breach at Harvard exposes more than 850,000 email addresses.

A data breach at Harvard University exposed personal information associated with more than 850,000 email addresses, according to breach notification service Have I Been Pwned.

Attackers compromised Harvard's Alumni Affairs and Development systems in November 2025, stealing names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, dates of birth, donation details, and other biographical information.

Harvard says the affected systems did not contain Social Security numbers, passwords, or payment card information.

The ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed responsibility and published a 1.1-gigabyte archive of stolen data in February after Harvard reportedly refused to pay a ransom. Harvard has not publicly attributed the attack.

The incident was part of a broader series of university breaches, with Princeton and the University of Pennsylvania also reporting compromises involving donor information in November 2025.

Title: Simplify Operations and Strengthen Protection with Fortinet AI-Driven Secure SD-WAN
Context: Learn how Fortinet AI-Driven Secure SD-WAN simplifies operations, improves application performance, and strengthens protection across distributed networks.
Full Text:
IT teams managing distributed networks face growing pressure to deliver reliable application experiences while protecting an expanding attack surface. Cloud adoption and generative AI (GenAI) are increasing demands on the WAN, while shadow AI, the use of unsanctioned AI applications and services, creates visibility, data protection, and governance challenges. Emerging technologies such as quantum computing also pose long-term risks to data confidentiality. Manual troubleshooting and fragmented visibility make it harder to address these challenges and keep pace with business requirements.

When application performance degrades, determining the cause can require extensive investigation. Teams must examine WAN conditions, overlay connectivity, routing, and security policies, often across multiple locations. Routine configuration changes add to the workload, consuming resources that could otherwise support strategic business initiatives.

Fortinet AI-Driven Secure SD-WAN addresses these challenges by converging intelligent networking, AI-powered security, and automation on a unified platform. Built on FortiGate firewalls and the FortiOS operating system and accelerated by purpose-built ASICs, it helps organizations simplify operations, strengthen protection, and improve application performance while mitigating emerging AI and cryptographic risks.

Accelerate Troubleshooting and Streamline Network Operations

Resolving connectivity and performance issues requires actionable insight into what is happening across the network. Fortinet brings AI assistance to SD-WAN operational workflows to help IT teams move more efficiently from investigation to corrective action.

FortiAI-Assist supports VPN diagnostics, network troubleshooting, and guided remediation. AI assistance in FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer simplifies alert triage, overlay preparation, and policy analysis, helping teams investigate reachability and path selection with current device information and historical analytics.

For example, when a branch experiences intermittent application access, engineers can use AI-assisted diagnostics to assess tunnel health, routing behavior, and relevant policies. Supported workflows allow administrators to review proposed fixes and authorize one-click execution, reducing manual effort while preserving operational control.

AI agents for SD-WAN further streamline operations by generating configurations, validating syntax, and creating policies through natural-language prompts. These capabilities help teams accelerate deployment preparation and reduce repetitive work, allowing engineers to focus on validating business requirements and maintaining consistent configurations across sites.

Improve Application Performance with Proactive Insights

Reliable connectivity requires continuous visibility into the conditions that affect application delivery. Latency, jitter, packet loss, and bandwidth utilization can degrade the user experience even when links remain available.

FortiAIOps combines predictive modeling, anomaly detection, and dynamic baselines with real-time monitoring of WAN service-level agreements (SLAs) to help IT teams identify emerging performance issues. These insights enable earlier investigation of congestion, abnormal behavior, and recurring SLA violations.

Teams can trace affected application traffic through the SD-WAN device and assess link conditions to isolate potential bottlenecks. Application-aware steering and failover select paths based on configured policies and SLAs, helping maintain a consistent application experience as network conditions change.

Together, contextual insights and policy-based path selection enable organizations to respond to performance issues more efficiently across distributed locations.

Strengthen Protection and Control AI Application Usage

GenAI adoption introduces new visibility and control requirements. IT teams need to understand which AI applications employees are using, distinguish approved services from shadow AI, and enforce consistent policies across the branch network. Unsanctioned AI tools can expose sensitive information, create compliance gaps, and introduce unmanaged third-party risk.

Fortinet AI-aware application control and shadow AI detection provide visibility into GenAI usage, helping teams identify unsanctioned applications and enforce granular, per-user controls. Integrated FortiGuard AI-Powered Security Services protect network traffic, while FortiAI-assisted policy reviews help identify redundant rules, unused policies, and potential security risks for correction by administrators.

Quantum computing poses a separate, long-term challenge for organizations that need to protect sensitive data over extended periods. Advances in quantum computing could render some current cryptographic methods vulnerable. In harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks, adversaries collect encrypted data today with the intention of decrypting it when the necessary capabilities become available.

Fortinet supports the long-term confidentiality of data in transit through quantum-safe tunnels. Hybrid key exchange combines classical and post-quantum algorithms to help defend against emerging threats while enabling a practical transition to post-quantum cryptography. These capabilities help organizations adapt their protection as application usage, AI governance requirements, and cryptographic risks evolve.

Title: PHP2Shell: what we know about the threat two weeks later | Kaspersky official blog
Context: The first attack exploiting this vulnerability was recorded on October 26, so don’t put off installing the updates
Full Text:
Late October brought several unsettling cybersecurity stories all at once. Among these were two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, which potentially affected about 70% of websites worldwide. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — dubbed PHP2Shell — could let attackers execute code on a server remotely, without authentication.

On October 21, PHP’s developers released emergency patches for the supported PHP 8.2–8.5 branches and for the unsupported PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Experts predicted that attacks on vulnerable servers would start within 15 minutes of the updates going public. Amazon even reported exploitation attempts four days before the patches came out. With all this in the news, some organizations sounded the alarm early. For example, in several countries, government service websites were taken offline as a precaution. Even Wikipedia’s project management and bug-tracking system suspended service.

Nearly two weeks have passed since the updates came out, but according to Censys data, of the 46 million scannable servers running a vulnerable PHP version, 29 million still contain the flaws. Right after the patches were published, we broke down each flaw in detail and explained what companies and everyday users should do. In this post we cover what’s known about the threat today, and what extra steps businesses need to take.

What happened after the PHP2Shell patches

The news about critical PHP vulnerabilities set off a flurry of reactions. Researchers noted a large number of exploitation attempts, and fresh exploits kept appearing in batches — courtesy of AI. A Palo Alto Networks unit even reported a PHP2Shell attack on a government agency in Europe, though it later retracted that statement. Solid evidence of how these vulnerabilities can actually be exploited only emerged later. On top of that, a third, unpatched one turned up.

A vulnerability with no patch

On Friday, October 23, the PHP team warned about a new vulnerability — CVE-2026-115560 — which can be used for remote code execution. But attackers can only pull this off on systems with an “unusual combination of configuration and application code”. That configuration is so exotic that the developers decided against an emergency patch, and will close the vulnerability on the regular schedule. In the meantime, they advised users to disable the session.upload_progress.enabled INI option.

First signs of PHP flaws being exploited

Let’s get back to the more serious threats. The most substantial confirmation of PHP2Shell exploitation in real-world attacks only came on October 24. Honeypot servers run by Adel Karimi of Perplexity running PHP 8.4.26 and presenting ordinary web pages recorded successful attacks from two IP addresses. The observed exploit chain was consistent with CVE-2026-109618. There’s an important caveat, though: the researcher’s honeypot ran the Apache mod_php module, which is the configuration most convenient for attackers.

Later, on October 26, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. That confirmed the threat isn’t just theoretical.

Real-world breaches with PHP2Shell

On October 26, the technology company Dream reported that 25 firewalls and management servers had been compromised in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Three of them were in an environment presumed to be linked to U.S. government agencies. The attackers combined PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel vulnerability dubbed Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300). Upon gaining full administrative control, they were able to extract the password of an LDAP service account and steal the listing of users and groups, full network configuration, and private keys.

Dream initially didn’t name the device vendor. In its October 29 update, though, the company stated that the systems were Palo Alto Networks devices running certain versions of PAN-OS. The vendor confirmed attacks on management interfaces exposed to the internet. It urged customers to close public access to those interfaces, limit it to trusted internal IP addresses, and install patches.

Why there are so few incidents

Exploits are multiplying, but no wave of breaches has materialized, and the possibility of mass compromise of PHP servers remains unconfirmed. Even in the Palo Alto case, the scale of the attack was minimal: out of about 19 000 devices found, the attackers picked just 240, which were running software versions their exploit could handle.

As it turns out, the existing PHP2Shell exploits aren’t one-size-fits-all. To exploit the vulnerabilities in a given environment, attackers have to account for the exact PHP build, memory settings, request handling, and application specifics. Still, the danger remains, so don’t neglect protective measures.

How to stay safe

The key advice stays the same: update. You can find the latest versions of the language on the PHP website. But installing patches isn’t enough. You also need to run a thorough audit of your systems and check every component that runs on PHP for signs of compromise.

Why install the second round of PHP updates?

Five days after releasing the emergency patches, the PHP developers published another round of fixes. The reason is that the updates that fixed PHP2Shell didn’t cover the CVE-2026-111497 vulnerability in Brotli, a third-party library. Exploiting this flaw can lead to code execution when PHP processes a specially crafted compressed response from an external server. The builds from October 25 include a patched version of the library. The latest PHP versions are 8.2.35-1, 8.3.36-1, 8.4.27-1, and 8.5.12-1. The first attack exploiting this vulnerability was recorded on October 26, so don’t put off installing the updates.

Threat detection

Possible signs of a PHP2Shell compromise include unusual POST requests that contain multipart/form-data media type, suspicious combinations of PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and upload parameters, atypical request sizes and request bursts, and HTTP 500 errors accompanied by PHP out-of-memory messages.

Title: Cato CTRL Research on Suspected Iranian MuddyWater Activity Using Israel Tax Authority Lures and SimpleHelp
Context: The table below maps vendor-documented features to potential attacker use and business impact
Full Text:
Executive Summary

We investigated a campaign targeting Israeli organizations through phishing emails impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. The activity has been observed since September 2026. Government-themed domains and a verification page lead recipients to ZIP archives containing executables disguised as tax-related documents. The campaign abuses SimpleHelp, a legitimate remote monitoring and management tool, to enable attacker-directed remote access.

The lure exploits a routine business task and can reach finance, accounting, and administrative staff across sectors. We suspect a connection to MuddyWater based on its documented use of SimpleHelp and targeting of Israel.

Key Findings

The campaign uses Israel Tax Authority impersonation and government-themed domains to distribute ZIP archives to Israeli organizations.

The payload is presented as a tax-related document but is a SimpleHelp executable.

Cato telemetry recorded threat prevention alert against campaign web infrastructure. The event demonstrates prevention of that request, without establishing a completed remote-access session.

Attack Flow

Figure 1 summarizes the delivery chain. Remote access depends on successful execution and activation of the SimpleHelp component.

Figure 1. Tax authority impersonation leads to a SimpleHelp executable. The dashed final step represents potential remote access following successful execution.

Technical Details and Analysis

This activity was previously described in public reporting by CyberIL. Our investigation examined the campaign’s delivery infrastructure and use of SimpleHelp.

From a tax themed email to a verification page

The attack begins with a phishing email impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. Recipients attempting to access the supposed personal area are directed to a lookalike site and prompted to complete a CAPTCHA-style verification step before downloading a ZIP archive.

The infrastructure uses names such as document-govil[.]com to resemble the official Israeli government namespace, gov.il. The string govil is part of a separately registered domain and does not indicate government affiliation.

The verification page in Figure 2 displays a checkbox, a Continue button, and the password 123123. This presentation reinforces the appearance of a protected document-delivery process.

Figure 2. Verification interface used in the tax authority lure.

A ZIP archive delivers the executable

Following the verification step, the download is presented as a tax-related archive. Figure 3 shows Israel_Tax_Authority.zip in the browser download history. The investigation also identifies an archive named document.zip.

Figure 3. Download of Israel_Tax_Authority.zip.

The agency-themed naming continues inside the archive. The executable shown in Figure 4 is named רשות המסים בישראל.exe, meaning “Israel Tax Authority.” A recipient expecting a tax document is instead presented with a program to run. The payload inventory also includes document.exe.

Figure 4. Executable named רשות המסים בישראל.exe presented under the tax authority pretext.

SimpleHelp provides the remote access capability

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote support software. In this campaign, it is used as the remote-access component behind the document lure. The research identifies 129.121.120[.]121 as associated command-and-control infrastructure.

Successful deployment can allow an operator to connect to the endpoint and continue the intrusion using the software’s built-in capabilities. The table below maps vendor-documented features to potential attacker use and business impact. It describes capabilities rather than observed post-compromise actions.

These capabilities are described in SimpleHelp’s feature documentation, Toolbox Guide, and Remote Access Guide.

The activity involved social engineering and abuse of legitimate RMM functionality. Our findings and SimpleHelp’s assessment are summarized in the disclosure section below.

Mapping the infrastructure with FOFA

We searched FOFA for the two observed HTTP ETag values. The search returned eight service records associated with 129.121.120[.]121, including records for document-govil[.]com and document-govil[.]online, as shown in Figure 5. Both domains displayed “Coming Soon” pages served by nginx.

Figure 5. FOFA results linking the two domains to 129.121.120[.]121. The eight results are service records on one IP.

Public reporting on SimpleHelp abuse

Group-IB previously documented MuddyWater’s use of SimpleHelp, providing context for our attribution assessment. Sophos, CISA, and Huntress have also reported separate ransomware incidents involving SimpleHelp exploitation or abuse.

Attribution Assessment

We suspect MuddyWater involvement based on the combination of Israeli organizational targeting, locally tailored authority impersonation, and delivery of legitimate remote-access software through phishing. HarfangLab documented an October 2023 MuddyWater phishing email linking to a SimpleHelp installer. Proofpoint documented Hebrew payroll lures in March 2024 that led Israeli recipients through PDF links to ZIP archives containing Atera installers.

Earlier campaigns also used institution-themed Egnyte subdomains and Hebrew filenames related to scholarships and tourism. These examples show a recurring approach of adapting recognizable Israeli identities and routine business tasks to persuade recipients to install remote-access software. The current campaign follows a similar pattern through Israel Tax Authority impersonation and tax-themed filenames.

The February 2022 joint government advisory identifies MuddyWater as a subordinate element of Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security.

Disclosure Timeline

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. Based on the evidence reviewed and validation with SimpleHelp, we did not identify exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability or compromise of SimpleHelp’s own infrastructure in connection with this campaign. The activity investigated involved social engineering intended to induce users to deploy SimpleHelp configured to connect to attacker-controlled infrastructure, consistent with the broader abuse of legitimate RMM tools by threat actors.

SimpleHelp confirmed that both samples identify themselves as SimpleHelp Remote Access Client version 5.4.5. Based on the information we provided, SimpleHelp assessed the activity as apparent malicious use of an older release and stated that it had not seen evidence indicating exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability. SimpleHelp offered to investigate associated infrastructure and assess available action, requesting server addresses or hostnames, observation timestamps, and supporting evidence through a private file request. We subsequently shared the relevant server list with SimpleHelp.

Title: Stop Chasing CVEs: Start Governing Software Dependencies
Context: Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six...
Full Text:
A new vulnerability disclosure can set off a familiar chain of work. You check whether or not an application uses the affected component, determine whether the vulnerable code is reachable, find a fixed version, test the upgrade, and get it into production. Then the next advisory arrives.

Known vulnerabilities need to be understood and remediated. But a process built around chasing CVEs one at a time can leave teams reacting to risk after a dependency has already entered their software.

It also leaves important questions unanswered:

Is the package malicious?

Is its license acceptable?

Is the project still maintained?

Can its origin be verified?

Does the dependency meet the organization's requirements?

A CVE is a useful signal, but it is not a complete measure of component trust. Teams need to govern the software dependencies they use across the SDLC, from selection and approval through ongoing monitoring and remediation.

CVE Remediation Is Necessary. It Is Not the Whole Strategy.

The CVE system gives security teams, developers, vendors, and researchers a shared way to identify known vulnerabilities. But a CVE record or score does not show whether vulnerable code is reachable in an application, whether a dependency is direct or transitive, or whether a safe upgrade is available.

Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six weeks. Those gaps can make it difficult to rank findings and decide where engineering time will reduce the most risk.

Teams need to treat CVEs as one input and weigh them alongside component use, available fixes, and application context.

Disclosure Starts the Remediation Cycle

When vulnerability management centers on incoming CVEs, teams begin responding after disclosure: identifying affected versions, tracing dependencies, and coordinating upgrades. By then, a component may already appear across applications, build environments, and releases, adding to the remediation backlog.

Component risks also extend beyond CVEs. A package may be malicious, poorly maintained, or incompatible with licensing requirements. Finding those issues earlier can help teams avoid broader changes, release delays, and retesting.

AI Is Increasing the Pace of Discovery and Consumption

AI is changing how quickly teams find and use software components. A developer might ask a coding assistant to add a feature, accept its suggestion to use a new library, and move on to the next task. The package can become part of the project before anyone has checked whether it is maintained, allowed by policy, or appropriate for that use. Consequently, teams must absorb a higher volume of vulnerability disclosures while simultaneously tracking which components enter their codebase and why.

A large Spring security disclosure illustrates the downstream scale. In August 2026, Sonatype tracked 91 CVEs across Spring and related projects. At the time of publication, Sonatype Guide reported 148,608 affected components, including components that bundle vulnerable Spring code. The disclosure does not establish that AI caused those vulnerabilities, but it shows how broadly a vulnerability can affect software that depends on an ecosystem.

Teams responding to disclosures at this scale need to determine:

Which applications include the affected components, directly or transitively?

Which vulnerable versions are present or deployed?

Which components pose the greatest risk in their environment?

Which upgrades will address the vulnerabilities without causing unnecessary disruption?

Discovery can move faster than downstream teams can locate, assess, and upgrade affected components. As AI-assisted vulnerability research develops, vulnerability intelligence and remediation processes will need to keep pace.

Teams also need visibility into what is in their software, where it came from, how it is used, and who owns decisions to keep, upgrade, replace, or accept it. That context helps turn a stream of findings into work that can be prioritized and acted on.

Component Risk Goes Beyond Vulnerabilities

A component can create risk even when it has no known CVE. A more complete assessment considers several dimensions:

Malware: Has the package or release been compromised, or does it contain malicious behavior?

Licensing: Is its license compatible with the project's obligations and intended use?

Maintenance: Is the project maintained, and can the team rely on its release and support practices?

Provenance: Can the component's source and history be verified?

Policy: Does it meet the organization's requirements for approved sources, versions, and use cases?

Each scenario demands distinct evidence and action: fixing vulnerable releases, instantly blocking malicious packages, scheduling replacements for unmaintained libraries, legally reviewing licenses, or verifying provenance prior to approval.

Treating every issue as another scanner finding can obscure those differences. Component governance gives teams a way to define which qualities matter, set expectations before adoption, and assign an appropriate response when a component falls outside them.

Govern Dependencies Before and After Adoption

Governance works best when it is part of normal development, rather than a review that begins after a release is ready.

Teams can make it practical by connecting policy to the component lifecycle:

Define acceptable use. Establish requirements for sources, licenses, maintenance, provenance, and known security risks. Set policies that reflect how components will be used and the impact of a failure.

Evaluate before adoption. Check candidate components against those requirements before they become dependencies. Give developers and AI tools clear, approved choices where possible, so the compliant path is also the easy path.

Maintain a record of use. Track component identity and version, origin, dependency relationships, and the applications or releases that include it. This context helps teams understand the reach of a new advisory or policy change.

Monitor for change. A component's status can change after adoption. New vulnerability information may emerge; a project may become inactive; a release may be compromised; or an organization's policy may change. Reassess components as new evidence arrives.

Route decisions to owners. Define who handles upgrades, replacement, license review, and exceptions. Record the reason for an exception and when it should be reviewed again.

Scanning and patching remain essential, but connecting them to a broader decision framework lets teams weigh vulnerabilities against exposure, exploitability, available fixes, and business context. Meanwhile, malware alerts, licensing issues, and maintenance risks can be routed directly to the appropriate decision-makers.

Effective open source policy enforcement aligns with risk severity. Known malware warrants immediate blocking, licensing queries require review before distribution, and unmaintained low-risk components may receive temporary exceptions. Explicit thresholds, designated owners, and time-bound exceptions enable consistent standard application without unnecessary escalations or blanket bans.

Timing is critical. Providing developers and AI tools with trusted, policy-approved component options during dependency selection allows teams to address risk before it is built in. Identifying flagged components later in release pipelines forces teams to reverse decisions already embedded across repositories and applications.

Move From a Findings Queue to Better Decisions

Software teams will continue to receive CVEs, and they should continue to remediate vulnerabilities that put their applications at risk. But a growing list of CVEs is not, by itself, a strategy for choosing and managing software components.

A stronger approach starts earlier and continues after adoption. It helps teams select components that meet their needs, understand where those components are used, detect changes in their risk, and respond according to clear policies. That can reduce avoidable surprises and help engineering teams spend less time reconstructing dependency context during an incident.

The goal is not to eliminate vulnerability work. It is to make that work part of a more complete way to govern software components — one that accounts for security, licensing, maintenance, provenance, and policy throughout the software lifecycle.

Sonatype Nexus One platform helps put that strategy into practice and gives teams the data to assess open source dependencies. With trusted component intelligence and policies built into development workflows, teams can make better decisions about what they use and respond more effectively when the evidence changes. Context: ” Investigators can settle attribution only from a session record, and they need the answer after the session ends
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why audit trails record a developer when an AI agent acted, how entitlement scope differs from action attribution, and the five facts a session record needs to show which agent ran a query and whose credentials it used.

An AI agent ran the query. The audit trail says a person did.

Why does an audit trail attribute AI agent activity to a person?

An AI agent connects with credentials issued to a person, so the audit trail records the person.

For example, at two in the morning, a database connection opens and a query runs against a production table. The audit trail records the username of a developer who was asleep at the time. A coding agent made the connection with the developer credentials while it worked through a task the developer had assigned before logging off.

Nothing in the log entry separates the developer from the agent. By its own standard, the log is complete. It still cannot answer the question an investigator will ask: Who ran that query?

In the Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report: The AI Enforcement Gap, Gal Diskin, Vice President of Research and Head of Delinea Labs, noted that actions taken with AI credentials “are very hard to distinguish between the AI and the human that launched them with existing tools and audit log limitations.”

Access models and audit trails were designed for human actors

Access models assume that the person who holds an account is the person who uses it. Until recently, that assumption held. A username answered two questions at once: Who held the access, and who used it. Audit trails follow the same design, so they record the username as the actor.

AI agents break that assumption. The account holder and the actor can now differ, and security teams need a way to talk about each one.

Entitlement scope is what an identity is permitted to reach. A developer with access to the production customer database has that database in scope, whether the developer or an agent opens the connection. Reviewers settle entitlement scope during an access review, before any session begins.

Action attribution identifies which actor used the entitlement and what that actor did. Attribution separates “the developer ran the query” from “a coding agent ran the query with the developer credentials.” Investigators can settle attribution only from a session record, and they need the answer after the session ends.

The agent never receives an entitlement of its own. It works with the entitlement already issued to the person who started it.

AI agents carry entitlements without the judgment behind them

A person receives an entitlement because someone decided that person could be trusted with access. An agent receives the same entitlement, but nobody made that decision about the agent. Nothing checks the agent against the original approval. The session record is the only place to find out what the agent did with the access it inherited.

How can security teams tell whether an AI agent or a person performed an action?

Security teams can tell only when the session record captures the initiator separately from the username. If the record captures only the username, the person and the agent look identical.

The Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report shows how often agents reach past their tasks. Of the IT and security leaders surveyed, 87% said an AI tool or agent at their organization accessed, or likely accessed, sensitive data beyond what its task required in the past year. Only 36% said their organization can always trace a sensitive AI access event back to a named human authorizer.

Example: overprivileged AI agent access

What happened. A developer asks a coding agent to look into a spike in failed customer logins. The developer has access to the production customer database for on-call work, so the agent has that access too. The agent pulls full customer records, including email addresses and phone numbers, and saves them to a file on the developer laptop. The task needed only login counts.

What the audit trail showed. The database log lists the queries under the developer username.

Why the evidence fell short. The log cannot show who pulled the records, which agent acted, or what instruction the agent followed. Without those facts, the reviewer cannot tell whether a person or an agent decided to export customer data, and the security team cannot decide who owns the response.

What should an AI agent audit trail record about each session?

An authorization record shows who approved an agent. A session record shows what the agent did with that approval; an AI agent audit trail needs both. At a minimum, the session record should capture five facts:

the identity that held the entitlement

whether a person or an AI agent initiated the session, and which agent

the resources the session reached and the actions taken on each resource

each path the agent used to reach a resource, including paths outside the Model Context Protocol (MCP)

a record the security team can reach and search during an investigation

AI agent activity can bypass MCP, so audit coverage cannot depend on MCP-only monitoring. MCP is a common standard for connecting AI agents to tools and data, but an agent with a database credential does not need it. The agent can open a database connection on its own, and a monitoring approach that watches only MCP traffic will never see that connection.

How does Delinea record AI agent activity?

Delinea records AI agent activity at the gateway, where the agent connects to the resource. When Delinea identifies the agent, the session record names both the person who held the entitlement and the agent that acted on behalf of that person. The record captures both names regardless of how the agent reached the resource.

Delinea built agent attribution by extending the gateway that already recorded human sessions. The developer and the coding agent appear in the same record, so investigators can review human and agent activity in one place.

AI agent attribution is the first step toward AI agent guardrails

Frank Vukovits, Chief Security Scientist at Delinea, framed the issue the way an auditor would: “Saying the AI agent did it is not a defensible answer.”

After a session ends, investigators use the session record to learn who ran the query. The gateway identifies the agent when the connection opens, so the same information can limit what the agent can do in the first place. Security teams can write entitlement rules for the agent itself. The developer keeps access to the production customer database, and the coding agent working for that developer does not.

Phil Calvin, Executive Vice President of AI Innovation at Delinea, tested an agent-specific rule which he documented in the blog "Your AI agent doesn't need to go rogue; it just needs you to be over-privileged". The gateway enabled him to write to a database and blocked the agent working for him from doing the same. His results show what a rule written for the agent can do.

In our conversations with security teams, we hear a consistent pattern. Teams want to audit which agent acted and which identity the agent used, but the larger concern is keeping agents out of critical production systems until the organization has a reason to trust them. Until that trust exists, the gateway can keep agents away from the most sensitive resources.

Title: Why I Sleep Out for Covenant House
Context: When you meet me now, you see a career at Cisco, a title, a life that looks like it worked out
Full Text:
When you meet me now, you see a career at Cisco, a title, a life that looks like it worked out. What you do not see is the teenager I used to be.

At sixteen, I was working long hours to keep a roof over my head and going to school at night. That experience is part of my story, but it was never the whole story. I had dreams. I had potential. I had a future worth fighting for, even when my circumstances made that future hard to imagine.

That is what I wish more people understood about young people experiencing homelessness. They are not defined by where they sleep. They are funny, creative, determined kids who want what we all want: To feel safe, to belong, to be loved, and to build a meaningful life.

They do not need us to decide who they are based on what they are going through. They need us to believe in who they can become. Sometimes, all it takes is one person who believes in you.

When I think about my own journey, I know what it feels like to need a second chance, a helping hand, and someone to see the person you are beyond your circumstances.

That is why Covenant House means so much to me. More than a safe place to sleep, it offers stability, guidance, education, and adults who care and believe in young people's potential.

Why I sleep out

Every year, Cisco employees come together to support Covenant House through Sleep Out, giving up the comfort of our beds for one night to raise awareness and funds. For me, it is deeply personal. When I sleep outside, I am reminded of the uncertainty of not having a safe home. I also know that when morning comes, I can go back inside and take a warm shower. For the youth we support, that certainty is not always there.

Monica during an interview at the Pennsylvania 2026 Sleep Out.

I have served on the board of Covenant House Pennsylvania and helped lead Cisco's Sleep Out efforts. At last year’s Pennsylvania Sleep Out, the Cisco team raised $95,000, contributing to the overall $1 million raised for Covenant House by Cisco in 2026. Our total impact since partnering with Covenant House in 2014 has reached over $18 million.

What moves me most is not the dollar amount. It is what those dollars make possible. A safe bed. A caring adult. A chance to keep going in school. A path toward independence. A young person starting to believe that tomorrow might look different.

You do not have to change someone's entire world. You just have to help open a door.

How you can be part of it

Anyone can be part of this mission. Join a Cisco Sleep Out team. Make a matched donation. Invite your colleagues. Spread the word about the cause and invite friends and family to donate.

Consider hosting a Sleep Out at home with your own family. Spend an evening talking about what it means to have a safe place to sleep. You can turn one night into a family experience while raising money that helps young people get the support they deserve.

I know what it is like to be that teenager. When I look at the youth Covenant House serves, I do not just see the challenges. I see potential: Future colleagues, leaders, parents, and people who will change their communities and the world.

I cannot say exactly where I would be if my life had unfolded differently. But I know how much a little stability, a helping hand, and someone believing in you can mean when you are young and trying to find your way.

Maybe that somebody can be you.

Title: The ROI of Agentic Remediation: Real-World Results with Wiz Green Agent
Context: When an active zero-day like the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability breaks, security tools light up within minutes, flagging critical production risks that demand an immediate fix
Full Text:
When an active zero-day like the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability breaks, security tools light up within minutes, flagging critical production risks that demand an immediate fix. And while AI has accelerated how quickly vulnerabilities are discovered, fixing them still waits on human coordination.

However, implementing that fix extends far beyond the security team and becomes an organization-wide initiative. Security teams discover the risk, but they don't own the code, the infrastructure, or the deployment pipelines. Resolving the issue requires coordinating across three distinct teams, each with their own set of priorities:

Security: Wants to eliminate exploitable risk immediately.

Engineering: Wants to maintain shipping velocity without breaking dependencies or spending time figuring out the right fix.

Cloud / Platform Operations: Wants to preserve uptime and infrastructure stability.

With each team working in their own workflows and against their own roadmap, remediation becomes an expensive game of cross-departmental ping pong. Tickets bounce between teams, developers waste hours determining the environment-specific fix, and Mean Time to Remediation (MTTR) grows.

To close this gap, organizations need a bridge between runtime context and developer execution so fixing becomes automated and continuous. Here is how leading teams use Wiz Green Agent to eliminate the three core bottlenecks of remediation, the ROI they achieve, and how that work builds towards a self healing cloud.

The Three Bottlenecks that make remediation hard

Finding the right owner for the Issue

Before a team can investigate or fix a risk, they run into the first hurdle: who actually owns the vulnerable asset? In dynamic multi-cloud, hybrid, or AI environments, that answer is hard to come by. A production container might have been deployed through a shared pipeline, authored by an engineer who switched teams months ago, or spun up across accounts with missing tags and with a CMDB that’s out of date. When ownership isn't clear, Issues sit unassigned in backlog queues or bounce between Platform, DevOps, and AppSec teams trying to determine whose repo or service an issue belongs to.

That delay in finding an owner stretches out remediation cycles before work can even begin.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent eliminates the ownership guessing game by connecting signals from across your entire environment. By analyzing repository commit history, Wiz Project assignments, service catalogs, CMDB integrations, and cloud logs, Green Agent automatically identifies the Suggested Assignee: the specific developer or individual best positioned to act.

Security teams can assign the issue to the right owner with one click directly inside the Issue drawer, ensuring Issues land with the person who can actually merge the fix.

This analysis is how teams like Rogo, an enterprise AI platform for financial institutions, eliminate manual cross-team detective work while maintaining rapid development velocity across AWS and GCP:

With the Green Agent it's surfaced automatically in the Wiz Issue and is incredibly valuable in finding the right person so our developers can quickly remediate.

Eric Tu, Product Security Engineer, Rogo

Understanding risk at the root cause

When a critical security Issue hits a developer’s queue, they want clear, actionable answers on what they need to fix, where it lives in code, and how they need to fix it so they can get back to shipping new features. Getting to those answers starts with tracing it back from runtime to code to understand the root cause.

That means confirming the workload is actually exposed, verifying the vulnerable package is reachable, and locating the originating repository, Dockerfile, or commit that introduced it. Doing that forensic legwork by hand for every alert is slow and repetitive, and at cloud scale, with AI pushing more code into production every week, it's where the bulk of triage time goes before the fix can begin.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent automates that entire investigation under the hood. For each Issue, it reasons across the Wiz Security Graph to evaluate runtime exposure, identity access, and code-to-cloud mapping to understand the root cause. It confirms whether the risk is truly exploitable and recommends whether to remediate or adjust the severity to keep developers focused on high-priority risks, then pinpoints the exact file and line in the source code responsible for the vulnerability.

As a result of Green Agent’s AI investigation engine, Fireblocks, the digital asset and blockchain infrastructure provider, cut daily operational triage time by more than 70% and now reaches same-day resolution on critical risks.

Green Agent explains the full context; it shows us all of our workloads and the exact remediation path for any issue. All the remediation paths are really clear... Before Red Agent, Green Agent, and the Cloudflare integration, we used to have manual processes for triage. Now, we get clearer findings and faster remediation that reduce the amount of manual hours of operation needed.

Roy Weiss, Principal DevSecOps, Fireblocks

Turning alerts into actionable fixes for developers

Even with the right owner assigned and the root cause identified, the final friction point is execution: turning that Issue into merged code.

Handing an engineer an alert with a link to a generic CVE bulletin forces them to context-switch away from their sprint, research potential patches, and figure out how to write the fix without breaking existing dependencies. Developers are focused on building and shipping product features; for remediation to move at the speed of AI engineering, the specific environmental fix has to meet developers directly in their everyday workflows.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent closes that loop by generating prescriptive, environment-specific remediation. It provides code or Terraform changes needed down to the exact line, and surfaces 1-click Pull Requests or handoffs to coding agents so developers can simply review, validate, and merge. For teams building with AI, Green Agent also exposes its remediation context via API and the Wiz Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, allowing developers to pull Green Agent’s remediation recommendations directly inside their agentic IDEs to accelerate fixing.

By meeting developers where they work and removing the manual research burden, project44, the global supply chain visibility platform, accelerated their remediation velocity by 10x while keeping engineering focused on roadmap priorities:

AI has enhanced coding velocity for engineers; the Green Agent from Wiz offers a similar increase in velocity for security engineering work.

Matthew Blackert, Security Operations Manager, project44

Our Wiz enablement with Engineering showed us what's possible when you remove the noise: engineers fixing real risk instead of validating false positives.

Mihajlo Jankovic, Security Operations Analyst II, project44

Closing the Remediation Gap

Remediation speed is no longer limited by how fast security can find risks, it’s defined by how smoothly security context converts into developer action.

By eliminating the context gap, automating ownership attribution, and delivering 1-click code fixes, Wiz Green Agent transforms remediation from a cross-team tax into an automated, closed-loop workflow.

Title: Artificial intelligence and cyber intrusion
Context: Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process
Full Text:
In 2028, the AI-cyber threat landscape facing the UK has almost certainly increased. Geopolitical tensions highly likely remain high, and nation states are almost certainly leveraging AI-powered cyber capabilities to project power and achieve strategic objectives.

State-sponsored actors, such as China and Russia, highly likely remain the greatest threat, through their developing AI capabilities. China, despite some quality lag in its chip development, has made significant strides in AI capabilities, with a focus on developing its own indigenous technologies. However, the increasing efficiency of AI models has reduced its dependence on cutting-edge western chip technology.

Meanwhile, it is highly likely that Russian cyber actors have leveraged open-source AI models, adapting and retraining them to suit their intelligence requirement needs, rather than developing in-house capabilities from scratch. This approach has allowed Russia to maintain a significant cyber capability without investing heavily in AI research and development. This has highly likely led to an increase in pre-positioning, espionage and intellectual property theft against UK interests.

The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal. Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally.

In 2028, it is likely that attackers will apply AI-cyber capability against known vulnerabilities in CNI legacy tech and the new opportunities in the attack surface provided by the deployment of AI tools within CNI. The use of AI within CNI has almost certainly presented an increased attack surface for adversaries to exploit. UK CNI has likely seen an increased volume of sophisticated attacks as the result of AI-cyber tools, some combatted by defensive AI tools, but implementation of defensive capabilities in UK CNI lags behind offensive ones.
