Title: Drei Tage it-sa und eine Frage, die uns nicht loslässt: Wer hat Zugriff auf was?
Context: Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Detection- und Response-Workflows sind wichtig, doch in einem KI-gestützten Angriffsszenario ist es bereits zu spät, wenn man darauf wartet,...
Full Text:
„Wenn Sie uns fragen würden, wie viele Service Accounts oder KI-Agenten wir in der Organisation haben, bekämen Sie je nachdem, wen im Security-Team Sie fragen, eine andere Antwort.” Ein CISO sagte uns das auf der it-sa 2026. Und wissen Sie was? Er war nicht der Einzige. Drei Tage lang drehte sich in Nürnberg alles um KI, Regulierung und Souveränität. Doch die Gespräche, die blieben, drehten sich um etwas viel Grundlegenderes: Welche Identitäten haben in der Organisation Zugriff auf was, und wie wird dieser Zugriff abgesichert?

Diese Frage ist der rote Faden, der sich durch viele Gespräche zog, nur jedes Mal in anderer Verkleidung: mal als KI-Thema, mal als Compliance-Thema, mal als Souveränitätsfrage.

Was wir über die Trends und Herausforderungen gehört haben, die die IT-Security-Welt gerade beschäftigen, wollen wir Ihnen nicht vorenthalten.

Silverfort, it-sa Expo&Congress 2026

Drei aktuelle Trends von der it-sa 2026

1. KI-Angriffe: Wer sie nicht erkennt, hat sie trotzdem.

Jeder CISO beobachtet genau, wie Angreifer KI als Waffe einsetzen. Die Zahlen bestätigen das: Laut der Bitkom-Studie „Wirtschaftsschutz” gehen 82 % der Unternehmen davon aus, dass Angreifer verstärkt KI einsetzen. Gleichzeitig bestätigen Schlagzeilen, dass KI-Angriffe zunehmen. Tempo und Umfang, in dem sie sich entfalten, machen sie für Verteidiger derzeit so herausfordernd.

Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Detection- und Response-Workflows sind wichtig, doch in einem KI-gestützten Angriffsszenario ist es bereits zu spät, wenn man darauf wartet, dass SIEM- oder SOAR-Erkennungen etwas Verdächtiges melden. KI-Angriffe spielen sich in Minuten ab, schneller als jede Triage und schneller, als ein Mensch etwas rechtzeitig korrelieren kann. Das Einzige, worauf jeder Angriff weiterhin angewiesen ist, ob KI oder nicht: der Missbrauch von Identitäten. Auch der beste KI-Angriff braucht am Ende einen Zugang, ein Passwort, ein Token, einen Service Account. Auf der Identitätsebene wird ein Angriff sichtbar, wenn man jede Anmeldung und jede Zugriffsanfrage im Blick hat und in Echtzeit entscheidet, ob sie fortgesetzt werden darf.

2. Compliance & NIS2: Ein Dauerprojekt.

Auf die Frage, was die EU-Richtlinie NIS2 bei Security-Teams konkret verändert hat, kam am Stand am häufigsten diese Antwort: „Wir arbeiten dran.” Das Gesetz gilt in Deutschland seit Ende 2025. Laut einer TÜV-Rheinland-Umfrage haben aber nur 14,3 % die Pflichten vollständig umgesetzt. Fast jeder Dritte (30,8 %) antwortete auf die Frage nach dem Umsetzungsstand sogar mit „weiß nicht”.

Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Unternehmen müssen bald nachweisen können, dass sie die Pflichten einhalten. Ein Großteil der NIS2-Compliance beruht auf starken Identity-Security-Kontrollen, etwa: alle privilegierten Konten identifizieren, MFA einführen, nicht-menschliche Identitäten wie Service Accounts prüfen, Remote-Zugriffe wie RDP und SSH schützen, granulare Zugriffsrichtlinien für alle kritischen Systeme und Anwendungen etablieren und mehr.

Die gute Nachricht: An der Einsicht fehlt es nicht. 60,3 % der Befragten halten NIS2 für wichtig oder sehr wichtig für mehr Resilienz. TÜV-Rheinland-Experte Michael Silvan sagt: „NIS2 ist kein Bürokratieprojekt. Es ist eine Chance, Sicherheitsstrukturen so aufzubauen, dass sie im Ernstfall wirklich tragen.” Wer jetzt auf der Identitätsebene gründlich Bestandsaufnahme macht, hat bei der Umsetzung einen Vorsprung.

3. Souveränität: Wer abhängig ist, kann nicht souverän entscheiden.

„Digitale Souveränität” war auf der it-sa an jeder Ecke Thema, und fast jeder wünschte sie sich. Aber: Der Bitkom „Cloud Report 2026″ zeigt, wie weit Wunsch und Wirklichkeit auseinanderliegen: 85 % halten Deutschland für zu abhängig von US-Cloud-Anbietern. 71 % beziehen heute Cloud-Angebote aus den USA, bevorzugen würden das nur 8 %. Als größtes Hindernis für einen Wechsel nennen die Unternehmen Lock-in-Effekte. Und das ist ein Sicherheitsthema, nicht nur ein Infrastrukturthema: Laut demselben Report sagen 87 % der Unternehmen, dass es souveränen Cloud-Angeboten internationaler Anbieter an Transparenz bei Datenverarbeitung und Zugriffsrechten fehlt.

Warum das für CISOs wichtig ist: Ohne diese Transparenz lässt sich die Frage, um die es in diesem Beitrag im Kern geht, nicht beantworten: Wer hat Zugriff auf was? Souveränität ist im Kern eine Frage der Kontrolle: über Ihre Daten, Ihre Schlüssel und Ihre Logs und darüber, wer entscheidet, wenn es darauf ankommt. Unsere Einschätzung: Jede Abhängigkeit ist auch ein Zugriffspfad und ein potenzieller Single Point of Failure. Wer nicht weiß, wo seine Abhängigkeiten liegen und wie schwer ein Wechsel wäre, kann im Ernstfall nicht entscheiden, sondern nur reagieren.

Die gute Nachricht: Die Bereitschaft wächst. 37 % würden für eine Cloud, die Daten ausschließlich in Deutschland und geschützt vor ausländischem Zugriff verarbeitet, inzwischen Nachteile in Kauf nehmen. Bitkom-Präsident Ralf Wintergerst sagt: „In den Cloud-Markt könnte in den kommenden Jahren mehr Bewegung kommen, wenn sich Unternehmen einen Wechsel zutrauen und gezielt nach Alternativen mit klarem Souveränitäts-Profil suchen.”

Der gemeinsame Nenner: Unternehmen erkennen, dass die Basics wichtiger sind denn je

Auf den großen Bühnen ging es wie zu erwarten um KI, in den Gesprächen am Stand jedoch um Basics. Auf die Frage nach alten Konten begegnete uns Ehrlichkeit: Das bleibt eine Daueraufgabe, die Security-Teams lösen wollen, um identitätsbezogene Lücken zu schließen. Das deckt sich mit der Bitkom-Studie: Angriffe richten vor allem deshalb Schaden an, weil sie nicht erkannt werden (59 %), Systeme falsch konfiguriert sind (57 %) und das Identitäts- und Zugriffsmanagement Lücken hat (55 %). Die häufigsten Schadensursachen seien „keine besonders ausgefeilten oder exotischen Angriffe, sondern blinde Flecken im eigenen System”, so Bitkom-Präsident Ralf Wintergerst. Oder, wie es unser CISO vom Anfang sagte: „Wie viele Service Accounts wir haben? Kommt drauf an, wen man fragt.”

Aus Identity-Security-Wahrheiten werden Prioritäten für 2027

Bei allem Gerede über neue Kategorien und neue Lösungen: Die Konzentration auf die Basics bringt viel, während Security-Teams erst lernen, wie KI-Angriffe ablaufen. Die meisten Sicherheitsstrategien setzen auf klassische Detection-and-Response-Szenarien und auf Schwachstellenmanagement. Doch in einer Welt, in der Angreifer KI als Waffe nutzen, müssen Organisationen verhindern können, dass Angreifer überhaupt erst eindringen und Schaden anrichten. Und so bleibt jedes Mal dieselbe Grundfrage: Wer hat Zugriff auf was, und was kann diese Identität tun, sobald der Zugriff gewährt ist? Das sind Ihre Prioritäten für 2027:

Jede Identität sichtbar machen, auch die nicht-menschlichen (NHIs) und KI-Agenten. Erfassen Sie Service Accounts, API-Schlüssel und Tokens, die Ihre KI-Agenten nutzen, und löschen Sie, was niemand mehr braucht. Beginnen Sie mit Sichtbarkeit und erweitern Sie von dort aus um Kontrollen, die zur Laufzeit durchgesetzt werden.

Jeden Zugriff prüfen, und zwar in Echtzeit. Gemeint ist wirklich jeder Zugriff: ob Mensch oder Maschine, in der Cloud und on-prem, auch auf Altsystemen. Und Echtzeit heißt wirklich Echtzeit, denn KI-Angriffe arbeiten in Maschinengeschwindigkeit, ihr Angriffsweg schrumpft auf Minuten. Nur eine Prüfung, die mithält, hindert Angreifer, ob KI oder Mensch, daran, mit dem Zugang, den sie zu missbrauchen versuchen, etwas anzurichten.

Nachweisen können, wer worauf zugreifen darf. Dokumentieren Sie Zugriffe so, dass Sie Ihren NIS2-Stand belegen können, und kennen Sie Ihre Abhängigkeiten. Das ist Ihre Roadmap für Geschäftsleitung und Budgetrunde.

KI-Angriffe auf der Identitätsebene stoppen: So geht es nach der it-sa 2026 weiter

Wir haben uns gefreut, Sie in Nürnberg zu treffen, und wollen das Gespräch darüber fortsetzen, wie Sie Ihre Identitätsebene zur stärksten Verteidigungslinie machen. Es mag abgedroschen klingen, zu sagen „Identität ist der neue Perimeter”, aber es stimmt: Einen Perimeter gibt es eigentlich gar nicht mehr, und Angreifer haben nur dann Erfolg, wenn sie in Ihre Umgebung gelangen.

Bei Silverfort erforscht unser Team, wie KI-Angriffe ablaufen und warum KI-Angreifer Identitäten so gern ins Visier nehmen. Wir teilen unsere Erkenntnisse gern ausführlich mit Ihnen, ob wir uns auf der it-sa gesprochen haben oder diesmal nicht zusammengekommen sind.

Vereinbaren Sie ein Gespräch, um den Austausch fortzusetzen, oder stöbern Sie in unserem AI Attack Readiness Kit, um selbst loszulegen.

Title: CREST Urges Whole-Ecosystem Approach to Financial Cyber Resilience
Context: CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and...
Full Text:
Cyber resilience in financial services should be built across the wider ecosystem of institutions, supervisors and specialist providers rather than treated solely as each institution's own responsibility, a new framework has argued.

CREST, the global non-profit accreditation body for the cybersecurity industry, said its whitepaper, Cyber Resilience in Financial Services: A Whole Ecosystem Approach, provides a maturity pathway for jurisdictions to assess their capabilities and coordinate improvements across three domains.

The paper, published on October 29, argued that weaknesses in shared infrastructure, technology providers, cyber firms or public authorities can undermine resilience across the wider financial system.

CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience

Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and demonstrating their controls work under pressure.

Financial supervisors are tasked with setting proportionate expectations, overseeing individual firms and understanding systemic risk, while cyber service providers are expected to deliver specialist advice, assessment, threat intelligence, testing and response capabilities.

The framework maps each domain through five stages of cyber maturity, with the three pathways planned together. Institutions progress from incomplete basic hygiene to advanced, threat-led assurance and continuous improvement. Supervisors move from mapping their sectors and establishing mandates to adaptive, cross-sector oversight, while providers progress from unvalidated services to specialist financial-sector capabilities.

CREST said the pathways are illustrative, not a new compliance standard. Its three priorities were ecosystem-wide measurement of maturity, a common language across the three domains and faster development wherever one part of the ecosystem lags.

Read more on financial-sector cyber regulation: FCA Updates Cyber Incident and Third-Party Reporting Rules

Framework Calls For Multi-Year Cyber Maturity Programs

CREST suggested supervisors or other market participants set out multi-year programs so the three domains develop in parallel, warning that requirements outpacing readiness can produce limited assurance. Its roadmap begins in years one and two with institutions mapping critical services and closing urgent hygiene gaps while supervisors publish a baseline and strategy.

Years three to five would bring independent assessment and risk-based testing for institutions, tiered requirements from supervisors and independent accreditation for providers. Years five to 10 would focus on threat-led penetration testing where proportionate, system-wide exercises and a diverse community of accredited specialist providers.

The whitepaper also warned that moving prematurely to mandate the highest international accreditations could shut out local providers where no route to accreditation exists. It pointed to measures including mentoring, partnerships, training and CREST's Cyber Accelerated Maturity Programme (CREST CAMP).

"Financial institutions, supervisors and cyber service providers each have a distinct role, and the strength of the system depends on their capability developing together," said CREST CEO Nick Benson.

Title: Reports of SIEM's Death Have Been Greatly Exaggerated
Context: Lean on a partner for the threats that look bad anywhere, and build your own detections for the things only your team would know are off
Full Text:
There's a phrase I keep hearing in cyber circles lately, at in-person conferences, on LinkedIn, pretty much everywhere:

"SIEM is dead."

I get why it's catchy. But SIEM has died more times than a soap opera villain, and it keeps showing up for next season. Before SIEM, it was the perimeter that was dead. Then antivirus. Then passwords. (Passkeys are coming for them, but plenty are still living on sticky notes under keyboards.)

Here's where I land: the way a lot of companies have been buying and feeding their SIEM deserves to go away. SIEM itself doesn't. So before anyone orders flowers, let's look at what's actually changing.

Follow the money (and the marketing)

There's so much cybersecurity marketing out there that it's hard to tell which tools and controls matter against today's threats. Every booth on the expo floor has "AI" printed on it somewhere. Some of it is impressive. Some of it is a chatbot wearing a trench coat.

"X is dead" is about the oldest trick in the marketing book. If the old category is dead, you'd better buy the new one. It makes for a great keynote slide. It also skips the question I'd want answered first: what was the old thing doing for us, and do we still need that done?

For SIEM, the job was visibility across the environment, catching attackers, running investigations, and keeping records for compliance. Attackers are still here. So are auditors. The open question is whether there's a smarter way to do it.

The "send it all" era

For years, the big legacy players (think Splunk and QRadar) priced on how much data you ingested and how much you stored. That model let them charge what they charged.

And the advice that came with it was always the same: send everything. Firewall logs, DNS queries, DHCP renewals, every time a printer had feelings. Get it all in, and figure out what's useful later.

Later almost never came. What came instead was a giant bill, a pile of alerts nobody had time for, and a very expensive junk drawer.

If your vendor makes more money every time you send another log, of course they'll tell you to send more.

The market has caught on. Cisco bought Splunk, and IBM sold its QRadar SaaS business to Palo Alto Networks. When the biggest names in a category start changing hands, something is shifting.

Enter the AI-native challengers

That market shake-up opened the door for a wave of AI-native SIEMs and security data lakes. The newest pitch I keep hearing goes something like:

"Why store everything yourself? Leave the logs where they are. Our AI will call your sources' APIs, pull what it needs on demand, and only keep the signals that matter."

I'll be fair. That sounds great, and some of the thinking behind it is smart. Nobody enjoys paying to store terabytes of noise, and using AI to pick out signal is a useful idea.

The problem is the bill.

You swapped a storage bill for a token bill

When AI is querying everything on demand, you're still paying. You've just moved the cost from storage to compute, specifically the tokens it takes to pull, parse, and reason over that data each time. During an active incident, when you're firing off question after question, that meter moves fast. It's like cutting the cable bill and then signing up for nine streaming services.

Also, tokens right now are about as cheap and subsidized as they'll ever be. AI providers are pricing to win market share, and that won't last.

We've been here before: Moving everything to the cloud was going to save us all a fortune, remember? For plenty of companies it did, right up until the egress fees and surprise invoices showed up and someone had to go hire a FinOps team. Prices settled at their real level. I expect AI inference to follow a similar path.

Cost isn't the only catch, either:

Retention: If the source system only keeps 30 days of logs, then so do you, which hurts when you find out about a breach on day 45.

Availability: Your investigations depend on someone else's API being up and free of rate limits, usually at the exact moment you need answers.

Compliance: Telling an auditor or your cyber insurance carrier "we can go fetch it if we need it" makes for a tough conversation.

A better approach: store what matters, keep what you're required to keep

In my opinion, the best way to get real security value out of logs sits somewhere between hoarding everything and storing nothing. Only store the logs that matter.

That's how we approach it at Huntress. Our smart filtering removes logs that aren't security relevant before they ever hit storage, so you're paying for signal and not chatter. The logs that drive detections and investigations stick around.

Filtering doesn't mean ignoring compliance. If HIPAA, PCI DSS, CMMC, or your cyber insurance policy says you need certain records for a certain amount of time, keep them. Those logs might not catch an attacker in real time, but after an incident they're how you show you did things right.

When I talk with teams about this, I usually suggest running every log source through a simple filter:

Detect: Does this help us spot or investigate a threat? Keep it.

Prove: Does a regulation, auditor, or insurer require it? Keep it.

Drop: Neither? Drop it. Nobody's going to miss the printer logs.

The bill shrinks, sure. The bigger win is fewer false positives, faster investigations, and analysts who spend their day hunting threats rather than scrolling past junk.

So where does AI belong?

AI isn't the bad guy here. It absolutely has a place in a modern SIEM. What I care about is whether it's running on every log, all the time, with the meter spinning, or whether someone decided where it actually helps.

Once you've filtered down to security-relevant data, AI gets a lot more useful and a lot cheaper, because it has far less to dig through.

Correlation is where I think it shines most. A VPN login from a country the user has never been to is interesting on its own. Now add an encoded PowerShell command running on a server that same account touched ten minutes later, and then a new inbox rule in their Microsoft 365 account forwarding mail to an outside address. Separately those are three data points. Together they're an incident. Pulling EDR and ITDR telemetry together with the logs coming in from across the rest of IT, and lining it all up into one timeline, is a great job for AI.

It also helps with the grunt work of an investigation, like summarizing what a user did in the last 24 hours instead of handing an analyst 4,000 raw log lines. It can add context during triage, such as whether an IP has a bad reputation or whether this process normally runs on this host. And it can write up findings in plain English for the people who don't speak fluent ES|QL, which is most of leadership and every auditor I've met.

In every one of those cases, AI shows up after the filtering, at a specific point where it helps someone make a better call. Detections and real SOC analysts still decide whether something is malicious. That control is what keeps things predictable. You know where AI is being used, so you have a decent idea what it'll cost, and it isn't dreaming up alerts out of nowhere, which keeps false positives down.

Who owns what? The shared responsibility nobody puts on the sales slide

SIEM is one piece of the bigger SecOps picture, alongside EDR, identity threat detection, security awareness training, backups, and an incident response plan you've hopefully tested at least once. So when you're figuring out what to run in house and what to hand to a partner, keep in mind that even with a managed SIEM, some of the work stays with you.

Cloud providers figured this out years ago. AWS will lock down the data center, but if you leave an S3 bucket open to the internet, that one's on you. Managed SIEM works the same way.

What your partner should handle

Some activity looks malicious in pretty much any network. Credential stuffing. A user getting hammered with MFA prompts until they finally tap "approve." Shadow copies getting wiped. Someone dumping credentials out of memory with Mimikatz.

This is where you should be able to fully lean on a partner like Huntress. Our SOC sees attacker tradecraft across hundreds of thousands of environments, so when a new technique or IOC pops up in one place, we go looking for it everywhere else. One internal team can't get that view on its own. Detection engineering, tuning, 24/7 triage, and active remediation (isolating hosts, killing sessions, locking accounts, cleaning up persistence) are all things we own, across endpoint, identity, and SIEM. We don't just hand you a pile of alerts.

What only you can catch

Then there's the stuff that could be totally fine or a huge red flag, and the only way to know is whether your team expected it.

A remote access tool you didn't approve. ScreenConnect showing up on a workstation could be your help desk. It could also be an attacker, or a "helpful" vendor, setting up shop. Only you know which RMM tools are sanctioned in your environment.

A new admin account. Was that new domain admin part of a change ticket, or did it just appear on a Friday afternoon?

An off-hours login to a critical system. For one company that's the overnight batch job. For another it's the first sign someone has the keys to the ERP.

A service account wandering off its usual path. Service accounts are supposed to run in the background, not log into the VPN from a laptop. If one shows up in your VPN logs, someone may be using its credentials as a side door.

Firewall rule or group policy changes outside a maintenance window. If nobody on your team made the change, someone else did.

Your approved software list, your change calendar, and your maintenance windows live with your team. We can tell you a service account just logged into the VPN. Only you can say whether Jim from IT set that up as a "temporary" workaround three years ago.

That's where your own saved queries and custom detections come in. You know what "weird for us" looks like, so you write the logic, and you decide what to do when it fires. The SIEM gives you the data in one place to do it.

Response is a team sport, too

A partner like Huntress can stop the bleeding and clean up after it. But some calls only you can make. Do you take the production line offline? Notify customers? Loop in legal, the insurer, or HR? Which servers can be isolated on a Tuesday afternoon, and which ones need a phone call first?

Get your own leadership, IT, legal, and HR on the same page before an incident. Decide who owns which calls, who gets the phone call, and which actions are pre-approved. With Huntress, you choose where and how we respond in your environment, so those decisions carry straight through to how we act. Revisit them after every incident. Trust me, you don't want to be figuring out who's allowed to disable the CEO's account at 2 a.m.

The partnerships I've seen work best aren't "set it and forget it." It's more like "set it, tell us what matters, and we'll both sleep better."

So, is SIEM dead?

Nope. If there's one thing I'd want you to take away, it's to be intentional.

Be intentional about what you store. Keep the logs that help you detect and the ones that help you prove, and drop the rest. Be intentional about where you use AI. Point it at the spots where it sharpens the picture, like tying endpoint, identity, and log data together, instead of running it everywhere because you can. And be intentional about who's watching for what. Lean on a partner for the threats that look bad anywhere, and build your own detections for the things only your team would know are off.

The question I'd ask isn't whether SIEM is dead. It's whether yours is earning its keep.

Title: Zero Standing Privilege: Give the Next CVE Nothing to Inherit
Context: On October 17, Amazon Threat Intelligence observed the first attempt to exploit PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP, the programming language behind many websites
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why new CVEs outpace patching, how a foothold inherits standing privilege, and how just-in-time access and secrets management limit what one exploit can reach. Includes five questions to test your environment.

On October 17, Amazon Threat Intelligence observed the first attempt to exploit PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP, the programming language behind many websites.

The PHP maintainers shipped fixes four days later, on October 21. Any vulnerable server that an attacker exploited before the server was patched could have given up the database passwords, API keys and cloud tokens the server held.

New vulnerabilities now arrive faster than organizations can patch them. Zero standing privilege limits what each exploit can reach

On October 23, Delinea published “PHP2Shell: The aftershocks will be identity attacks,” which covers which secrets to rotate first and how to prepare for the attacks that follow.

This blog covers the pattern behind PHP2Shell. New exploits now arrive faster than patching programs can absorb them, so organizations need a defense that does not depend on knowing which flaw comes next. Zero standing privilege (ZSP) gives an attacker nothing standing to inheritno matter which system the attacker breaks into first.

PHP2Shell was one of three vulnerabilities in the news during the week of October 19. On October 21, CISA added Plex2Shell, a chain of four vulnerabilities that gives attackers code execution on Plex Media Server, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Plex had fixed the flaws in early August, yet the Shadowserver Foundation counted more than 36,000 exposed servers still unpatched in early September. Researchers also published a working proof-of-concept exploit for a critical, unauthenticated flaw in Fortinet FortiSIEM about a week after Fortinet shipped the fix.

More exploits are likely to follow before the month ends. The pattern matters more than any single bug. New exploits arrive at a rising pace; defenders get less time to respond to each one, and some systems go months without a patch.

Vulnerabilities now arrive continuously

The 2026 data show the same acceleration. CISA added 247 vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog between January 1 and October 1, more than the 245 it added in all of 2025. Since June 10, CISA has given federal agencies three days to remediate most new KEV entries, down from 21 days for most 2025 entries. Even under the longer deadlines, organizations took a median of 43 days to fully remediate KEV vulnerabilities in 2025, according to the Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report.

The Google Threat Intelligence Group recorded an average of 11 zero-days a month from January through August, up from 8 a month in 2025. The October Microsoft Patch Tuesday release fixed more than 1,400 CVEs, the largest release since the program began. Only a fraction of those CVEs will be exploited, but an attacker needs only one.

AI now speeds up both the discovery of flaws and the development of exploits. In June, Microsoft Vice President of Engineering Tom Gallagher said AI-assisted vulnerability discovery was enabling bug hunting “at a speed and scale previously unseen.” Amazon Threat Intelligence wrote that AI-assisted analysis “makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit.”

The pace of new vulnerabilities is likely to keep climbing. No patching program, however well run, closes the gap between disclosure and deployment to zero. Patching remains essential, and organizations should fix KEV entries first. A strategy that depends on patching faster than attackers can find and weaponize flaws will lose over a long enough timeline.

A foothold inherits whatever privilege is standing

Each of the three exploits gives an attacker the same thing: code running on a system the organization trusts. Security teams call that position a foothold. What happens next depends less on the vulnerability than on what the compromised system can reach. Field Effect made the same point about Plex2Shell, noting that further impact “depends on the permissions assigned to the [Plex Media Server] service account and the resources accessible from the host.”

A web server running PHP often holds database credentials, API keys and cloud tokens in its configuration or environment. A SIEM collects logs from across the environment and often stores the credentials it uses to access monitored systems, making an unauthenticated SIEM flaw a high-value target. Management consoles and orchestrators often hold administrative rights over the systems they manage.

Standing privilege is access that an identity holds at all times, whether or not anyone is using it. The vulnerability gets the attacker in the door. Standing privilege decides how far the attacker gets.

An AI agent ran the full attack chain in July

A July incident at Hugging Face showed what happens when exploitation no longer needs a human at the keyboard. An AI agent running in an internal evaluation at a frontier AI lab escaped its sandbox and ran a four-and-a-half-day campaign, roughly two and a half days of which it spent inside Hugging Face production infrastructure. Hugging Face reconstructed the campaign from roughly 17,600 recovered agent actions.

The agent got in through two flaws in a dataset-processing pipeline. One flaw handed the agent the secrets and tokens stored in the environment of a production pod. Nearly every escalation after that ran on standing credentials: a shared broker credential bound to cluster-admin, a VPN key built for automation and tokens for source control. The agent went from code execution in a single pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under 13 hours. None of the escalations Hugging Face describes involved a human login, so stronger authentication for people would not have stopped them.

Hugging Face named “short-lived credentials” among its defensive priorities. After the incident, Hugging Face rotated credentials across its infrastructure and rebuilt the broker with a separate credential for each cluster.

Machine-speed attackers are likely to chain together the weaknesses that PHP2Shell, Plex2Shell and the FortiSIEM flaw expose: find a foothold, harvest what is standing and move. The foothold is the part defenders can’t always prevent. The standing privilege is the part defenders can remove.

ZSP works whichever CVE lands next

ZSP means no identity, whether AI agent, human or machine s, holds privilege it isn’t actively using. Just-in-time (JIT) access puts ZSP into practice. An identity requests access for a specific task, and an access platform grants that access for a limited time and revokes the access when the time ends. ZSP doesn’t depend on knowing which vulnerability attackers will exploit next, which is why ZSP fits an era in which new vulnerabilities arrive continuously.

The graphic below compares the same foothold in three scenarios: with standing privilege, with JIT Admin and JIT Access added, and with short-lived secrets added.

The model is illustrative, and the entry point is identical in each scenario.

Layer 1: JIT Admin removes standing root from hosts

An exploit usually runs with the permissions of the process it compromises. Researchers ran the Plex2Shell exploit, for example, as the Plex Media Server service account. The attacker’s next move is to escalate to root, the account with full control of a Linux or Unix server, or to local administrator on a Windows server. Standing root and local administrator rights turn one compromised server into many, because an attacker with those rights can read the SSH keys, service-account passwords and other credentials stored on the server.

JIT Admin replaces standing admin rights with elevation on demand. An administrator requests privilege for a task, the system checks the request against policy and grants the privilege for a limited time and records the elevation. Delinea Privilege Control for Servers (PCS) replaces standing root and local administrator rights with just-in-time elevation for specific commands.

PCS also enforces multi-factor authentication (MFA) at server login and again at privilege elevation. On a host that PCS protects, an exploit finds no standing admin rights to inherit, and PCS records each failed escalation attempt.

Layer 2: JIT Access limits spread across infrastructure

Once an attacker holds a foothold, the attacker’s next move is lateral movement: using credentials found on the first system to reach other servers, databases and clusters. In the Hugging Face incident, one shared broker credential gave the agent cluster-admin on two Kubernetes clusters within one second.

Delinea Runtime Authorization grants access to servers, Kubernetes clusters and databases per identity, per resource and for a limited time, so an attacker with a stolen credential reaches one resource for a limited time. The Runtime Authorization proxy injects credentials into each connection, so the client does not hold the credential and a compromised host has no stored credential to steal. Network access alone no longer grants access to a resource. A compromised application host or management server does not inherit access to every resource the host can reach on the network, and Runtime Authorization logs each connection it brokers.

Layer 3: Delinea Secret Server shrinks what an attacker can steal

PCS and Runtime Authorization limit where an attacker can go. Delinea Secret Server limits what the attacker finds on arrival. Secret Server brings privileged-account vaulting and workload secrets management together, so workloads (the applications and services that run without a person at the keyboard) retrieve credentials at runtime instead of carrying static values in environment variables and config files.

Secret Server rotates service-account and database passwords, API keys and other secrets on a schedule or after each use. Secret Server also issues dynamic credentials. Secret Server creates each dynamic credential on demand for a single workload, and the credential expires after a set time.

Secret Server doesn’t make a compromised host blind. An attacker with code execution can still read whatever credentials are present on the host at that moment, which is why the earlier Delinea blog—PHP2Shell: The aftershocks will be identity attacks—advises treating each secret a compromised server could read as stolen. What Secret Server changes is the value and lifespan of what the attacker reads.

Continuous CVE discovery demands continuous identity discovery

Vulnerability management identifies which systems are exposed. Identity security identifies what an attacker can reach from a compromised system. Security teams cannot reduce standing privilege they haven’t found. Machine and service identities are often the hardest to find. Hugging Face wrote that it had “wrongly provisioned” its broker with one credential shared across clusters and bound to cluster-admin. An inventory of privileged machine identities is the kind of check that surfaces a credential like that before an attacker does.

Delinea Continuous Identity Discovery uses AI to find human, machine and AI identities across the environment and flag the identities that hold standing privilege.

What ZSP doesn't fix

ZSP doesn’t patch a vulnerability. The flaw is still there, the exploited process still runs and an attacker with code execution can still do whatever that process is permitted to do. Patching, configuration hardening, network restrictions and detection all remain necessary. After the incident, Hugging Face closed both code-execution paths, blocked pod access to cloud metadata and added detection, in addition to rotating credentials.

ZSP does a different job. ZSP shrinks what the exploited process is permitted to do and how long the process holds that permission, so the window between disclosure and patch carries less risk.

Five security questions to ask about your environment

If an attacker compromised one of your internet-facing or management systems today, such as a web server, a SIEM or an orchestrator, what admin rights and credentials could the attacker reach from that system?

How many human, machine and AI identities hold standing privileged access, and when did your team last inventory those identities?

Does any single credential grant admin rights across more than one system, cluster or environment?

How long would a stolen service-account password, API key or token stay valid?

When the next exploited CVE lands on a product you run, how quickly can you tell which privileged identities and secrets the affected system holds or can reach?

Each question your team cannot answer points to standing privilege that an attacker could inherit.

Plan for the exploit that arrives before the patch

Prevention will sometimes fail, and sometimes the patch will arrive after the exploit. The organizations that fare best are likely to be the ones that removed standing privilege, not the ones that patched fastest every time.

Privilege Control for Servers keeps a foothold from escalating to root on hosts. Runtime Authorization limits how far the attacker can move across infrastructure. Secret Server shortens the life of each credential the attacker steals. Together, the three products apply ZSP across human, machine and AI identities, which helps one compromised system stay one compromised system.

See how Delinea applies Zero Standing Privilege and just-in-time access.

The next CVE is already being found. Make sure it finds nothing standing.

Title: Integrate Aquasec and Prometheus for Greater Visibility Into Runtime Security Operations
Context: Platform Aqua Platform Runtime Powered Cloud Security Monitor behavior, detect exploitable risk, enforce policy and contain threats across the application lifecycle
Full Text:
How does the Aquasec and Prometheus integration work?

The integration uses two separate configurations to make diagnostic metrics available to Prometheus.

Aquasec Platform monitoring

Administrators enable Prometheus under Administration, Integrations, Monitoring Systems in the Aquasec Platform.

The configuration supports an optional bearer token and a configurable data collection interval. Aquasec makes diagnostic metrics available at the specified interval, including the number of connected Enforcers and Gateways, images waiting to be scanned, images being scanned and images that failed scanning.

The integration also provides metrics for successful and failed user logins, defined Image Assurance Policies, Runtime Policies and Firewall Policies.

These metrics help teams understand the operational state of their Aquasec environment and identify patterns that may require attention.

Aquasec Enforcer monitoring

For more detailed runtime monitoring, Aquasec provides a Prometheus Metrics Exporter for Aquasec Enforcers and VM Enforcers.

Administrators enable the exporter under Settings, Enforcer, Prometheus Metrics Exporter. The exporter uses port 8995 by default, although this can be changed. The Metrics Exporter advanced setting must also be enabled for the relevant Enforcer groups.

The exporter exposes several categories of metrics, including:

Resource utilization: CPU and memory usage at the host and Enforcer levels, helping teams monitor the resources consumed by runtime protection.

Enforcer health: Enforcer version and type, active container counts, enabled functions and Gateway connection status.

Runtime security activity: File related events detected or blocked by runtime controls, malware scanning activity and behavioral detection event counts.

Security operations: Audit activity, event processing errors and host or image scanning results.

For Kubernetes deployments, Aquasec’s documentation provides an example using a local Prometheus server with service discovery to collect metrics within a cluster. A remote Prometheus server can use federation to collect metrics across clusters. Standalone Aquasec Enforcers and VM Enforcers do not require the local cluster deployment step.

This architecture allows organizations to monitor Aquasec metrics across distributed environments while maintaining the runtime enforcement capabilities that operate inside protected workloads.

Title: Shadow AI Across Government: It's Three Problems, Not One
Context: That only works if you can see which path people are actually taking
Full Text:
Most agencies and contractors now have a generative AI (GenAI) policy. Far fewer can tell you what their people are actually running.

That gap has a name. Like shadow information technology before it, Shadow AI is what happens when AI tools, services, and components enter an organization outside the processes meant to govern them. The difference is that shadow IT mostly showed up as an unapproved application.

Shadow AI can create risk at three points:

Data that leaves your environment.

AI-generated code your developers commit.

AI models and other components your builds pull down.

Those three are usually discussed as one risk. They are not. They have different failure modes, different owners, and almost no overlap in the controls that address them. An organization can have an excellent acceptable-use policy and still have no idea which AI models are running inside its own software.

None of which is an argument against adoption. The productivity gains are real, and the organizations getting the most from these tools are not the ones that tried to ban them. They are the ones that made the sanctioned path the easiest path to take. That only works if you can see which path people are actually taking.

Here is what each problem is, who owns it, and what closes it.

The Adoption Already Happened

Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that 45% of employees are now regular users of AI on corporate devices, authorized or not — up from 15% a year earlier. Two thirds of those users accessed AI services through non-corporate accounts, which means the activity is largely invisible to the organization paying for the device.

Shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action in the report's data loss prevention findings. And the most common category of data sent to external AI services is source code.

That last detail is the one worth sitting with, because it connects all three problems. Source code leaving is a disclosure problem. The same assistant that received it returns code and dependency choices that come back in. And the models behind these tools increasingly arrive as components inside your own applications.

One behavior, three exposures.

Problem One: What Goes Out

This is the problem most policies already address, and the one most people mean when they say Shadow AI. An employee pastes contract language, personnel data, or controlled unclassified information (CUI) into a public chatbot to summarize or rewrite it.

Ownership: Security and privacy teams, records officers, and acceptable-use policy owners.

Controls: Provide a sanctioned platform people prefer, use data loss prevention and network controls, name approved services, and give staff practical guidance.

Verizon's findings show why prohibitions alone may not work: employees may turn to personal accounts, moving AI use further out of view rather than stopping it.

For Department of War (DoW) components, this is already written down. DoW Instruction 8430.01 bars entering non-public departmental information into generative AI services unless the service resides on departmental systems and is approved for departmental use. Both conditions, not either.

What does not close it: anything in your software supply chain toolchain. No repository control, bill of materials, or scanner sees a developer paste code into a browser. If a vendor tells you otherwise, press on exactly which telemetry they are reading.

Problem Two: What Comes Back In

Your developers are using coding assistants. The output is unverified input, and the accountability for it does not transfer to the tool that produced it.

DoWI 8430.01 is explicit on this point for defense work: AI-generated code is treated as unverified, and developers and their teams remain fully accountable for what they ship. It also asks software efforts to maintain a record of the models, versions, and significant datasets used to generate or test software, kept with the software evidence package and treated as analogous to a software bill of materials (SBOM).

The subtler issue is that a coding assistant does not only write code. It chooses dependencies. An assistant suggesting a package is making a supply chain decision on your behalf, at a speed and volume no review process was designed for, which is a different problem from whether the code it wrote is correct. We covered that specific question in more depth earlier this month.

Who owns it: engineering leadership and application security.

What closes it is treating assistant output as you would a pull request from an unfamiliar contributor. Human review, software composition analysis (SCA) on everything it introduces, and a record of which models were in the loop, which is both a DoW requirement and the only way to answer the question later.

Problem Three: What Your Builds Pull Down

The third problem is the least discussed and the hardest to see after the fact: AI models and machine learning packages entering your environment as components.

Sonatype calls components retrieved straight from public repositories, bypassing the repository manager, shadow downloads. Sonatype Research Labs audited 9,658 Hugging Face requests across a set of customers in the first half of 2026, as part of our Beyond Traditional Packages report. Nearly 7% were blocked or rejected by policy. Of the 674 models blocked, 55% were stopped on model acceptability and 18% on security grounds, which says models are raising governance questions traditional policies were not built for.

A model is not like a library. It arrives as opaque weights, it may carry a license with terms on how its output can be used, and its published name tells you very little about what it was built from — open models are routinely fine-tuned, merged, quantized and re-released under a new publisher. Three federal exclusion orders now name a single model developer and reach products "developed using" its implementations, which makes model provenance a procurement question and not only an engineering one.

Who owns it: platform engineering and whoever runs your repository manager.

What closes it: one governed path in. Route model pulls through a proxy repository so every request is visible in one place, block direct downloads from the corporate network, and lock client configuration so the path cannot quietly be bypassed. Sonatype Firewall can then audit or quarantine models at that boundary before a developer gets them. Start in audit mode to see what your teams are actually pulling, then move to quarantine. At scan time, Sonatype Lifecycle flags a model as a derivative and names the foundation model it came from, and the AI Models Usage dashboard shows which applications are using models, with lineage, commit hash and publishing date.

That last piece matters for a reason beyond engineering. Joint guidance on AI and machine learning supply chain risks, co-sealed by the National Security Agency and seven other national agencies, tells organizations to require an AI bill of materials from vendors as a condition of procurement. Asking your suppliers for something you cannot produce yourself is a difficult position to hold.

What To Do About It

Pick your lane. These are three different jobs and they rarely belong to the same person.

If you own policy. Name specific sanctioned services rather than categories, and pair the policy with a platform people prefer to the alternative. Then confirm your inventory obligation is being met. OMB Memorandum M-26-05 makes each agency head responsible for the security of software on the agency network and directs agencies to maintain a complete inventory. Models are software.

If you own compliance. The obligations people associate with the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) did not go away when Phase 2 was suspended. DFARS 252.204-7012, NIST SP 800-171 and Supplier Performance Risk System scoring are unchanged, and annual affirmations remain in effect. An attestation that does not match the environment is the exposure, and that gap is exactly what undeclared AI tooling creates.

If you own the platform. Start with visibility, not enforcement. Put a proxy in front of model pulls, turn Sonatype Firewall on in audit mode, and spend two weeks looking at what comes back before you block anything. Most teams are surprised, and the surprise is the business case. Then make it continuous — an inventory taken once begins decaying the day it is produced, and the reason to route intake through a single path is that the record maintains itself rather than becoming an annual exercise.

Shadow AI is no longer a question of whether people will adopt these tools. They already have. The question is whether you can identify:

Which services receive your data.

Which models help write your code.

Which models run inside the software you ship.

Three questions, three owners, one answer: you can only govern what you can see.

Tom Tapley specializes in securing software supply chains for Federal environments, bringing deep expertise in aligning agency security, compliance, and operational requirements with modern technology solutions. With a proven track record in supporting mission-critical systems, he bridges the gap between evolving federal mandates and scalable, secure software practices.

Title: Cisco and PSA Singapore Collaborate to Power the Next Phase of Tuas Port with AI-Driven Operations
Context:
Cisco and PSA Singapore (PSA) will accelerate the next phase of Tuas Port’s transformation into a digitally resilient, AI-driven port of the future.
More RSS Fee
Full Text:
News summary:

Cisco and PSA to develop an AI-powered observability and incident management platform at Tuas Megaport to strengthen the port’s digital resilience.

The platform brings together live data from across PSA’s applications, infrastructure, and network into a single view, using AI to map how systems interact, pinpoint root causes of disruptions, and recommend fixes to keep port operations running smoothly.

This initiative supports PSA’s multi-year digital transformation journey under Cisco’s Country Digital Acceleration (CDA) program.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29, 2026 — Cisco and PSA Singapore (PSA) will accelerate the next phase of Tuas Port’s transformation into a digitally resilient, AI-driven port of the future. The companies today announced a strategic collaboration to develop a proof of concept for an AI-powered observability and incident management platform at Tuas Port, currently the world’s largest fully automated container terminal.

The collaboration is part of Cisco’s Country Digital Acceleration program, through which Cisco partners with the public and private sector to advance national digitalization priorities and support Singapore’s digital agenda.

Digital resilience has shifted from a strategic advantage to an everyday necessity across industries, including modern port operations. Cisco research underscores this, revealing that the average annual cost of downtime per organization has climbed to US$300 million. Outages affecting critical systems like the Terminal Operating System (TOS), which manages the movement, storage, and tracking of cargo, can disrupt port operations and business continuity. The new platform is designed to reduce and eventually pre-empt these unplanned outages.

Enabling Predictive, AI-Powered Operations

The platform, powered by Cisco, unifies real-time performance data from PSA’s applications, infrastructure, and networking systems into a central view. By using AI to map how different services and infrastructure interact, it helps technical teams quickly identify which services are affected during an incident, diagnose the root cause, and receive recommendations to resolve issues in real time.

Built in, cloud-native security helps protect the port’s critical infrastructure against modern threats, preventing unauthorized access and flagging unusual network traffic.

"Digital resilience is fundamental to the reliability and efficiency of global supply chains. At PSA, we continually explore new technologies to strengthen operational resilience and deliver service excellence. Our collaboration with Cisco reflects a shared commitment to advancing innovation in port operations while reinforcing Singapore’s position as a trusted global hub for trade,” said Nelson Quek, Regional CEO, SEA,PSA International.

"As critical infrastructure becomes more complex, organizations need the ability to see, understand, and act across their entire technology stack in real time. We are committed to providing PSA with AI-powered observability and security to transform their operations, delivering the critical infrastructure for the AI era," said Bee Kheng Tay, President, ASEAN, Cisco.

Building on Tuas Port’s strong digital foundation, this collaboration advances PSA’s multi‑year digital transformation journey through next-generation solutions. The platform will be implemented first at the Tuas Port Phase 2 Living Lab, which provides a real-world platform to test, validate, and refine innovations that support the port’s continued development as it expands towards full completion in the 2040s.

Title: Sandbox Flipped to ‘Danger-Full-Access’: Unauthorized AI Relays Create Risk for Organizations
Context: Threat Hunter has found the relay in use across a dozen organizations since early 2026
Full Text:
Key findings

An unauthorized relay service has been observed installing the genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code CLIs on enterprise systems and then reconfiguring them to route every request through third-party infrastructure instead of the vendors' own servers.

The service has been active since at least early 2026, and has impacted systems at a dozen organizations, most of them in mainland China, as well as multinational subsidiaries based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Affected sectors include industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals, and data center services.

Delivery relies on a fileless PowerShell or bash setup script that is fetched from a lookalike domain by a one-line command that users appear to run themselves shortly after a legitimate install of the Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, so the download looks like a normal companion step rather than an attack. The reconfiguration disables the CLI's execution sandbox entirely, enables network access for the write sandbox, replaces the user's real API credentials with relay-issued tokens, and disables telemetry and error reporting.

On at least one host, the script forced the user to log out of their legitimate Anthropic session and deleted their authentication environment variables before reissuing relay-controlled credentials.

There is no evidence so far that the relay operator has abused this level of access, but a potential risk is that the configuration it installs would let it read every prompt, file, and secret passed through the agent and run commands with the user's full privileges.

The relay's backend infrastructure has rotated across at least eight domains over the observation period, all impersonating OpenAI- or Anthropic-branded chat services.

Overview

AI coding agents such as OpenAI's Codex and Claude Code read files, write code, and run commands on the machines where they are installed. One of the safeguards they employ is a sandbox that is meant to limit what they can do. However, Symantec's Threat Hunter Team has identified an unauthorized relay service that provides access to OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code command-line coding agents, mainly in markets where the vendors do not officially operate, primarily mainland China. Rather than building its own client software, the service repurposes the genuine CLI tools. It installs them normally, then rewrites their configuration to switch sandboxing off, in Codex's case by setting it to “danger-full-access,” and routes every request through its own servers instead of OpenAI's or Anthropic's.

This is not a vulnerability in Codex or Claude Code. The tools are behaving as designed once their configuration has been changed.

Threat Hunter has found the relay in use across a dozen organizations since early 2026. There is no evidence the operator is currently abusing its position, but the configuration changes it makes strip out the safeguards that are meant to contain an AI coding agent, potentially exposing any organization whose employees use it to security risks.

Usage

The organizations where this relay has been observed span industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals, and data center services. Most are based in mainland China, though the list also includes the Chinese operations, and in some cases the home-market operations, of multinational electronics and petrochemical firms based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Most instances appear to be a workplace where an employee or the organization itself wanted to use a Western AI coding assistant that is not officially sold in their market and so turned to an unauthorized reseller to get it.

Tooling

Installation and delivery

The service does not distribute a modified or trojanized client. Users run a legitimate npm install

-g @openai/codex, npm install -g codex-cli, or npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

shortly before the override occurs, within minutes to roughly half an hour.

A fileless PowerShell or bash setup script, fetched with a one-line iwr -useb <url> | iex or curl | bash from a lookalike domain such as vibe.aiok[.]me, checks whether Node.js and the target CLI are already installed, installs them silently if not, and only then applies its own configuration. Because the script performs a real, working installation of the genuine tool, the installation looks routine to the user and to most monitoring tools.

We did not observe any automated or exploit-based delivery. The one-line command embeds a relay-issued API key and the relay's own endpoint, and the script is written for interactive use (it prints progress messages in Chinese and tells the user to re-run it in an elevated PowerShell session if it lacks administrator rights), which indicates that users copy a ready-made command from the relay or its reseller and run it themselves, although we have not seen the page or message it was copied from.

Configuration override

The script's actual purpose is to rewrite each tool's configuration file: ~/.codex/config.toml for Codex, or ~/.claude/settings.json for Claude Code. It replaces the base_url (or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) with a domain the relay controls, swaps in a relay-issued API key formatted to match what the CLI expects, and establishes both as user-scope environment variables so the change survives a reboot without further action from the operator. It also sets the CLI's sandbox mode to full access and enables network access for the write sandbox, disabling the isolation that is meant to limit what an AI agent can do on the host. Telemetry and error reporting are disabled at the same time, which would also suppress any usage signal that might otherwise reach OpenAI or Anthropic.

sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access" network_access = "true" DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1

Credential replacement

On one host, the script went further before applying its own configuration. It ran claude /logout, deleted the ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variables, and then ran claude /login. That sequence clears out a legitimate, already-authenticated session so it cannot override the credentials the script is about to install. Whether this step runs in every deployment of the script or was specific to that host was not established.

claude /logout Remove-Item Env:ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, Env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue claude /login

Geolocation check

Several hosts show the script querying the Windows locale setting immediately after installation. This is consistent with a service confirming it is running on a system in the region it serves before completing setup.

reg.exe QUERY "HKCU\Control Panel\International\Geo" /v Nation /reg:64

Possible business model

Why an operator would want this degree of control over a client-side relay is unclear. Bypassing the regional restrictions that keep Western AI vendors from selling directly into certain markets is the simplest explanation, but it does not require disabling a CLI's sandbox or establishing persistent credentials that survive a reboot. Reselling capacity below market rates is another possibility: the Claude Code keys issued by the relay were formatted sk-ant-oat01-, the prefix Anthropic uses for subscription-based OAuth tokens rather than sk-ant-api03- pay-per-use API keys, which is consistent with, though not proof of, a relay pooling flat-rate subscriptions and splitting the capacity across many customers. Fraud involving stolen credentials or payment cards, and resale of the prompts and files that pass through the relay, are also plausible and cannot be ruled out with the evidence available.

Significance

To be clear about what we have and haven't observed: the configuration changes described above were observed; the risks that follow from them are potential.

The geography of this activity tracks the practical reality that OpenAI and Anthropic do not officially sell their coding agents into mainland China, which creates demand for unauthorized resellers regardless of who ultimately operates them. The organizations affected here look less like chosen targets and more like workplaces where individual employees found and used such a service to get access to tools they wanted.

That demand does not make the risk any smaller. A relay in this position sees every prompt, file, and secret an employee sends to the agent, and can alter or fabricate every response it returns. With the sandbox disabled and network access enabled, a malicious or compromised response could execute with the full privileges of the user's account. None of the evidence reviewed here shows the operator exploiting that position, but the architecture would support it if the operator's intentions or security changed.

The credentials this service issues do not stay confined to the AI agent, either. Because they are established as user-scope environment variables, any other tool on the same machine that reads those variables can pick them up, extending the exposure well beyond the coding assistant that first prompted an employee to install the service.

Protection

For the latest protection updates, please visit the Symantec Protection Bulletin.

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.

Organizations concerned about unauthorized AI relay use should also watch endpoints running Codex or Claude Code for the following:

Changes to base_url or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in a CLI's configuration file.

sandbox_mode set to "danger-full-access" in ~/.codex/config.toml.

OPENAI_BASE_URL, CODEX_API_KEY, or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN set as user-scope environment variables outside an approved deployment process.

A PowerShell iwr | iex or bash curl | bash invocation run shortly after, or in place of, npm install -g @openai/codex or @anthropic-ai/claude-code.

Traffic from AI CLI tools to destinations outside an allow-list of approved AI service endpoints.

Title: How we detect frontier model misalignment
See the Real AI Experience with Cato DEM
Context: From “AI Is Slow” to Knowing Where to Investigate Detecting poor performance is only the first step
Full Text:
AI is becoming part of everyday work. Employees rely on services such as ChatGPT and Claude to research, create, and solve problems, while developers increasingly use AI-powered tools like Cursor and coding agents in their development workflows.

As employees increasingly rely on AI to work more productively, the AI experience is becoming a critical part of the digital experience IT teams are expected to support. Slow responses, failed interactions, or inconsistent performance can disrupt workflows and undermine the productivity gains AI is meant to deliver.

The challenge is that IT may have limited visibility into the AI interaction itself. Teams may not know there is a problem until employees start complaining.

Cato Digital Experience Monitoring (DEM) addresses this visibility gap with AI Experience Monitoring, providing IT teams with live visibility into AI latency and failures, along with the context they need to investigate performance problems.

AI Is Becoming Critical to Everyday Work. Can IT See When It Fails?

As AI becomes embedded in daily workflows, its performance increasingly affects employee productivity. An employee waiting on ChatGPT or Claude, or a developer relying on an AI coding tool, expects that interaction to work quickly and reliably.

That creates a new digital experience for IT teams to support.

But knowing that an AI application is reachable does not necessarily tell IT whether the actual AI interaction is performing well. Teams may only learn about slow responses or failed interactions when a user opens a ticket saying, “Claude is slow today.”

Then the investigation begins. Is the issue associated with a particular AI service or model provider? Is it concentrated at a specific location? Does it affect users accessing the service in a particular way?

The challenge for IT is no longer simply whether employees can reach an AI service. It is knowing whether the AI experience is working well, before employees must tell them it isn’t.

Traditional Application Monitoring Can Obscure the Real AI Experience

Monitoring an AI application is not the same as monitoring an employee’s interaction with the AI model.

GenAI applications such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor generate many different types of network traffic. The agentic portion of that traffic, including conversational interactions with AI models and traffic from coding agents, can be mixed with software downloads and updates, authentication requests, licensing and configuration calls, telemetry, and other background activity.

Measuring all this traffic together can create a noisy representation of the actual AI experience. For example, a large application download may affect usage figures even though it has nothing to do with an employee’s conversation with an AI model. Performance measurements can similarly mix model-provider latency with unrelated application activity.

As a result, IT can see application traffic without getting clean answers to two fundamental questions: How quickly is the AI responding, and how often are AI interactions failing?

To understand the real AI experience, IT needs to separate this AI traffic from the surrounding application noise.

Isolate the AI Traffic That Matters with Cato DEM

Cato DEM addresses this challenge with AI Agent Experience Monitoring.

Instead of treating all traffic generated by a GenAI application as a single experience, Cato isolates the AI portion of that traffic, the interactions with AI model providers, including conversational traffic and traffic from coding agents such as Claude Code. By separating these AI interactions from downloads, updates, authentication, telemetry, and other background traffic, Cato gives IT a clearer view of the experience that matters to users.

The capability focuses on two fundamental indicators: latency, showing how quickly the AI service is responding, and errors, showing how often AI interactions are failing.

IT can examine performance by application and model-provider domain to identify where degraded experiences are occurring. At launch, coverage includes ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, with additional AI services to be added over time.

And because AI Agent Experience Monitoring is built directly into Cato DEM, AI performance becomes part of the same digital experience monitoring environment IT teams already use.

Instead of waiting for someone to report that “AI is slow,” IT gains live visibility into the AI traffic itself.

From “AI Is Slow” to Knowing Where to Investigate

Detecting poor performance is only the first step. IT also needs context to narrow the investigation.

Cato provides a dedicated AI Agent Experience Monitoring drill-down, where teams can analyze latency and errors by model provider, domain, and site. They can also see how employees are accessing the AI service.

Cato DEM also shows how users access AI services, whether through a browser, terminal, script, or coding tool. For example, IT can distinguish between someone accessing Claude through a browser and a developer using a coding tool such as Claude Code.

Consider that complaint: “Claude is really slow today.”

Without AI-specific experience visibility, IT starts with a broad application-level investigation where model interactions are mixed with other Claude traffic. With Cato DEM, teams can focus on latency and failures in the actual AI traffic and then use provider, site, and client context to narrow the investigation.

This turns a vague user complaint into a much more focused performance investigation.

Cato DEM measures the network experience of that traffic; it does not monitor what an AI agent does.

Catch Poor AI Experiences Before They Become User Complaints

AI is becoming another digital tool employees rely on to get work done. Cato DEM gives IT teams the visibility to support that experience proactively.

Teams can identify slow AI interactions without background application traffic obscuring the picture. They can spot failed interactions through error monitoring. And when something goes wrong, the provider, site, and access context give IT operations and network teams a more focused starting point for troubleshooting.

Most importantly, this visibility lives within DEM alongside the performance data that the performance data teams already monitor. IT can extend the same operational approach used to support other employees’ digital experiences to AI services, making them part of everyday work.

As AI becomes increasingly important to employee productivity, waiting for users to report poor performance is no longer enough. Cato AI Agent Experience Monitoring helps IT see the real AI experience, so teams can find slow or failing AI before users must tell them something is wrong.

Title: CCoP 2026: Strengthening Cyber Resilience Across Singapore’s Critical Infrastructure  by Yusri Mohamed Yusop
Context: The attack path extends beyond the CII environment An attacker may first compromise a user account, remote-access system, engineering workstation or management server before...
Full Text:
Singapore’s Cybersecurity Code of Practice for Critical Information Infrastructure 2026 marks an important shift in how CII owners must think about security.

The focus is no longer limited to protecting the designated CII environment itself. CCoP 2026 places greater emphasis on Board and senior-management accountability, visibility into systems connected to CII, continuous monitoring, behavioural baselining, threat hunting and evidence that security controls are working as intended.

For security leaders, the challenge is clear: attackers do not respect organisational or network boundaries.

The attack path extends beyond the CII environment

An attacker may first compromise a user account, remote-access system, engineering workstation or management server before moving toward the systems that deliver essential services.

CCoP 2026 reflects this reality by extending security requirements beyond the designated CII itself. The Code distinguishes between enterprise systems, CII interconnected systems, and the CII systems that deliver essential services, with new Section 12 requirements focused specifically on systems that connect to or communicate with CII.

This means CII organisations need more than a static view of what should exist. They need to understand what is communicating, how identities and systems are behaving, and whether suspicious activity is progressing toward critical infrastructure.

Where Vectra AI can support CCoP readiness

Vectra AI supports CII organisations in the areas where visibility, detection, investigation, and response are most important.

“CCoP 2026 reflects today’s evolving threats to critical infrastructure. Vectra AI supports 31 of the 38 clauses relevant to its capabilities within the Code’s 53 clauses, helping organisations detect threats earlier and respond before critical operations are disrupted.”

— Hock Leng, Vice President of Sales, APJ, Vectra AI

See what is communicating with CII

Based on our clause-by-clause assessment of CCoP 2026, Vectra AI directly or supportively aligns with 31 of the Code’s 53 clauses. That alignment is strongest across visibility, monitoring and detection, threat hunting, incident response, OT monitoring and interconnected-system security. Alignment does not mean Vectra AI alone satisfies each clause, but that its capabilities can directly support or strengthen the required control.

Detect abnormal behaviour earlier

Section 6.2 requires CIIOs to establish normal operational and network activity, monitor deviations, correlate cybersecurity events, and trigger alerts for investigation. The Code also recognises that attackers may use less-monitored areas as stepping stones toward CII.

This aligns closely with Vectra AI’s core capabilities. The platform analyses activity across network, identity and cloud environments to identify abnormal behaviour, correlate related events, and prioritise the entities that present the greatest risk.

Instead of presenting analysts with disconnected alerts, Vectra AI helps show how an attack is progressing and what requires immediate attention.

Support threat hunting, investigation and response

CCoP also places greater emphasis on proactive threat hunting and incident readiness.

Vectra AI provides enriched metadata, behavioural context, and investigation workflows that help analysts search for hidden activity, reconstruct attack paths, and determine whether a cybersecurity incident is underway.

When response is required, integrations can support native actions such as isolating a host, restricting a compromised account, or blocking malicious traffic. These capabilities strengthen the technical execution of incident response, while the CIIO retains ownership of its response plan, regulatory reporting, forensics, and recovery processes.

Supporting OT and interconnected environments

Many CII environments include OT, legacy systems, and devices that cannot support endpoint agents.

Vectra AI can passively monitor visible traffic in these environments without requiring agents on sensitive systems. This is particularly relevant to the requirement in Section 10.2 to monitor OT-to-enterprise data flows for anomalies, as well as Section 12.7 requirements to investigate suspicious activity across interconnected systems.

Additional controls are still required for areas such as endpoint logs, virtualisation infrastructure, patching and formal reporting to CSA, but Vectra AI can provide an important layer of behavioural visibility across the communication paths attackers may use.

Start with the visibility gap

For CII organisations preparing for CCoP 2026, a practical starting point is to ask:

Do we know every system that communicates with the CII?

Can we detect when a valid identity or trusted system begins behaving abnormally?

Can we show what the security team saw, investigated, and did in response?

Vectra AI does not replace the governance, certification, IAM, patching, backup or regulatory-reporting controls required by CCoP. Its role is to help CII organisations see attacker behaviour earlier, investigate faster and produce stronger operational evidence that their detection and response controls are working.
