Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling. A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users. Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems. The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider. Tailworm targets Tailscale. Ohio’s Auditor of State investigates a cyberattack. A suspected ransomware attack disrupts Israel’s largest vehicle importer. Norway raises their cyber risk level to high. Our guest is Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, discussing AI exploits and identity containment. AI science needs a spam filter.

Today is Wednesday October 28th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling.

Two Democratic senators accuse the Trump administration of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling as Congress considers renewing a controversial intelligence program.

Senators Ron Wyden and Adam Schiff say the administration missed a September deadline to release findings from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court concerning Section 702 of FISA.

The court reportedly found that intelligence agencies used filtering tools to search Americans’ intercepted communications without required safeguards, including approvals and documentation.

Section 702 expired in June, but surveillance continues under a court authorization lasting until March.

The administration has promoted the program’s effectiveness while keeping the ruling classified, despite earlier promises to release it.

Civil liberties organizations are urging Congress to withhold reauthorization until the findings become public.

Wyden and Schiff have demanded an explanation by November sixth.

The dispute raises a fundamental question: How can Congress evaluate the legality of government surveillance when critical findings about that surveillance remain secret?

A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users.

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a suspected surveillance operation targeting users of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service.

According to Reuters, researchers at TrendAI found that an Israeli advertising technology company, Discover-Tech, was aggressively bidding for ads targeting Starlink users in more than 100 countries.

The company was particularly active in conflict zones, including Syria, Yemen, Libya, and South Sudan, where legitimate advertising demand is limited.

Researchers believe the activity was designed to exploit data leaked through online advertising auctions, potentially allowing operators to identify, locate, and track Starlink users.

TrendAI initially identified the operation only by the codename Shadow-Earth-79, reportedly declining to name Discover-Tech over legal concerns.

Citizen Lab and Confiant independently identified the company, prompting Google, Comcast, and others to remove it from their advertising platforms.

Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems.

Attackers are already probing for vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems following the disclosure of a critical security flaw.

Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit a SQL injection flaw and potentially take complete control of affected systems.

Oracle released a patch on October twentieth, urging customers to update immediately.

Security firm Defused says its honeypots detected attempted exploitation on October twenty-seventh, although Oracle has not confirmed active exploitation in the wild.

Shadowserver has identified more than 670 internet-exposed Oracle E-Business Suite instances, mostly in the United States. It’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

The activity follows previous attacks against Oracle enterprise software, including a campaign by the Clop extortion gang that exploited a separate E-Business Suite vulnerability to target major corporations and universities.

The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider.

The FBI has seized the domain of Virtualine, a so-called bulletproof hosting provider accused of supporting cybercrime, money laundering, and the distribution of child sexual abuse material.

Operating under several names, Virtualine openly advertised hosting services for illegal activities, promising to ignore abuse complaints and law enforcement requests.

According to the Justice Department, the company continued supporting a forum distributing illegal content even after receiving complaints from international authorities. Prosecutors also allege Virtualine helped the forum’s operators establish another site and attempted to launder cryptocurrency payments.

No arrests or criminal charges were announced.

The seizure follows international crackdowns on similar providers linked to ransomware operations. But researchers warn that disrupting these services often simply pushes criminal customers toward replacement providers, rather than eliminating the underlying market.

Tailworm targets Tailscale.

Tailscale is rolling out fixes for a collection of security vulnerabilities that researchers say could allow attackers to move rapidly through private networks.

Dubbed Tailworm, the findings from Cyberdione Labs include eleven issues affecting Tailscale and the open-source headscale server.

Four vulnerabilities involve Tailscale SSH, where improper privilege handling could allow an attacker with access to one compromised device to gain root privileges on other authorized servers.

Researchers demonstrated automated attacks spreading between vulnerable machines in less than a second per hop, without user interaction.

Tailscale emphasizes that exploitation requires existing network access and depends on SSH policies. There’s no reported exploitation in the wild.

The company has published security bulletins and remediation guidance. Organizations are advised to review SSH access policies and disable unnecessary forwarding.

Ohio’s Auditor of State investigates a cyberattack.

Ohio’s Auditor of State is investigating a cyberattack targeting its web server, potentially involving foreign state actors.

Auditor Keith Faber says security monitoring detected and isolated the threat, prompting officials to take the server and online accounts offline.

The incident was not ransomware, and officials have found no evidence that personal or government financial information was compromised. Payment data is stored separately.

State and federal law enforcement are investigating. A temporary website is planned, and audit clients experiencing payment disruptions will receive a grace period.

A suspected ransomware attack disrupts Israel’s largest vehicle importer.

A suspected ransomware attack disrupted operations at Colmobil, Israel’s largest vehicle importer, delaying vehicle deliveries and services.

Israel’s Ministry of Transport disconnected the company from government registration systems as a precaution, while customers reported delays involving Mercedes-Benz vehicles.

According to sources cited by Calcalist, the ransomware group SETTRA was responsible and demanded payment. Industry sources say Colmobil paid the ransom, though the company has declined to confirm either claim.

Colmobil says it has restored operations and that the incident did not affect vehicle systems or manufacturers.

The attack highlights the automotive industry’s growing dependence on interconnected digital infrastructure, from vehicle registration and payments to maintenance and diagnostics.

While researchers have demonstrated attacks against connected vehicles, there’s no evidence this incident involved attempts to remotely control cars.

Norway raises their cyber risk level to high.

Norway’s National Security Authority, or NSM, has raised the country’s cyber risk level to high, publicly disclosing its assessment for the first time.

The agency reports a threefold increase in successful cyber operations against Norwegian organizations over the past six months, with some incidents posing serious national security risks.

Defense, aerospace, critical infrastructure, and their suppliers face particularly elevated threats, including reconnaissance, attempted intrusions, ransomware, and denial-of-service attacks.

Officials also warn that artificial intelligence could accelerate attacks by helping adversaries identify vulnerabilities more efficiently, although such AI-enabled activity hasn’t been documented in Norway.

NSM is urging organizations to strengthen defenses immediately, emphasizing phishing-resistant authentication, network segmentation, improved monitoring, vulnerability management, and supply chain security.

The agency says stronger organizational defenses can help reduce the country’s overall cyber risk.

AI science needs a spam filter.

Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research, but it’s also creating a rather inconvenient problem: scientists are increasingly struggling to separate genuine discoveries from AI-generated nonsense.

Science journalist Dalmeet Singh Chawla warns that generative AI is overwhelming academic journals with questionable research, leaving publishers’ integrity teams struggling to keep up.

The irony is that AI has already demonstrated extraordinary scientific potential.

In 2020, Google’s DeepMind developed AlphaFold, a system capable of predicting how proteins fold into the shapes that determine their biological functions.

Within a year, AlphaFold predicted 200 million protein structures, work that would have taken an estimated hundreds of millions of years using traditional laboratory methods.

The achievement helped earn its creators a Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

So AI can dramatically accelerate scientific discovery. Unfortunately, it can also accelerate the production of questionable science.

Apparently, the scientific method now needs a spam filter.

Title: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A virtual desktop service provider in Japan has told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by hackers.

GMO Internet’s Onamae.com service is delivered via a network of tens of thousands of servers operated by the firm and is popular with foreign-exchange traders.

However, the firm was forced to suspend the service on October 21 after discovering the day before that “malicious programs” had been installed in “some customers’ server environments.”

A security alert claimed that some information may have been accessed and that as many as 26,739 servers may have been impacted. Some reports suggest the hackers may have accessed trading accounts and made unauthorized transactions.

An extortion email sent on October 21 demanded a ransom of around eight billion yen ($50.7m).

Read more on ransomware attacks in Japan: Japanese Railway Operators Hit with Weekend Cyber Attacks

Having refused to pay the ransom, GMO Internet was notified by its attackers that they would deploy ransomware on October 27 as 12pm. As a result, it advised its customers to perform a full virus scan on their devices, back up all data, and then disconnect their PC from the internet and turn off the power.

In the meantime, GMO Internet has been asking for customers to ship their PCs so that its security team can investigate.

“As of [October 27, 11:59], no malware (including ransomware) has been detected in the devices that have been analyzed,” it explained.

“However, the analysis is still ongoing, and we have not yet confirmed the security of all customer devices. More devices from customers are expected to arrive in the future. We will proceed with the analysis as soon as they arrive.”

Japan Inc Under Fire

“This demonstrates how a vulnerability in a remote access service can have consequences far beyond the compromised system,” said Suzu Labs chief security evangelist, Phillip Wylie.ㅤ

"Attackers don’t necessarily need to deploy ransomware to cause significant damage. If they can steal sensitive information, compromise accounts, and threaten to publicly release data, they already have multiple ways to pressure an organization.”

Wylie added: "The biggest takeaway is that preventing the initial compromise is important, but limiting what attackers can do once they gain access is equally critical.”

The breach is the latest in a string of security incidents impacting Japanese firms this year. Organizations as diverse as Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (eight million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million) have suffered major data breaches.

Title: AI Is Turning CISOs Into Business-Risk Translators, Says Nvidia’s Head of Cyber
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
In the AI era, cybersecurity leaders must explain how AI-related risks connects to business goals and help executives understand who is responsible for accepting those risks, according to Nvidia’s head of cybersecurity policy, Mark Weatherford.

Speaking at ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Weatherford argued that the broad adoption of AI in the workplace, including in cybersecurity workflows, has transformed the CISO role from a security gatekeeper to a business-risk translator.

As organizations weigh AI adoption, CISOs must help executives understand the tradeoffs and clarify who owns the risk, he said.

Weatherford recalled a board meeting where a CISO struggled to explain the relationship between security and the business. Ultimately, the board challenged the CISO on their understanding of the company’s business model. This event, he said, had a negative impact on the perception the board had of the CISO’s credibility and ability to protect the business.

Weatherford said the exchange taught him that CISOs need to understand how their organizations generate revenue, not only how to protect them.

He added that business perspective is especially important as organizations weigh the potential benefits and risks of AI.

For instance, boards may worry that moving too slowly will cost them competitive advantage, Weatherford said, while moving too quickly can mean deploying tools without appropriate controls or an understanding of the risks.

While he argued that CISO rarely owns the business risk from deploying things like AI, he emphasized that modern CISOs must interpret that risk and make sure leaders understand who owns it.

Balancing AI Innovation With Cybersecurity Risks

Weatherford described two main challenges CISOs face with AI.

First and the “pace of technological change” makes their work more challenging.

Second, CISOs need to focus both on “security for AI and AI for security,” protecting the AI systems their organizations deploy while also considering how AI can support security operations.

Combined, these challenges mean traditional cybersecurity approaches may no longer be sufficient, he argued.

“If you’re not doing pentesting 24/7, 365, you’re probably behind the curve,” he said.

Weatherford also cautioned against investments driven by “fear of missing out.”

Leaders, he said, should do business due diligence before spending heavily on AI. CISOs can contribute by preparing concrete proposals for reducing risk. He recommended putting together a short plan that describes the proposed work and the resources it would require.

Vendor evaluation is another area where CISOs need to apply judgment. Weatherford said he looks for AI-native products that address security problems, rather than older products with AI added on.

He urged CISOs to consider supply-chain dependencies, too. Multiple vendors may depend on the same suppliers, creating single points of failure that can affect more than one product or service. Some dependencies may sit several tiers down the supply chain, beyond the suppliers an organization knows it relies on directly.

Weatherford’s advice for keeping pace with these changes was to stay curious and keep learning and even relearn things as technologies evolve.

For instance, he encouraged CISOs to “learn one new thing every week,” suggesting focusing on one AI topic at a time, such as model context protocol (MCP), prompt injections or sandboxing.

Finally, Weatherford recommended CISOs to join and create formal and informal peer communities. He mentioned that he created a CISO Exchange Network in which he invited CISOs from Nvidia’s major partners, customers and suppliers, where they share experience, concerns and tips.

Title: Building a Career at the Biggest Company You’ve Never Heard Of
Context: The program offers a structured foundation for a sales career with internal mobility, and it provided the launchpad to a sales career I never imagined
Full Text:
I’d just finished business school at The University of Warwick when I joined Cisco in 2015 through the Cisco Sales Associate Program (CSAP).

This pathway wasn’t well-known among U.K. university graduates, but it’s a world-class early-in-career talent sales program at Cisco. The program offers a structured foundation for a sales career with internal mobility, and it provided the launchpad to a sales career I never imagined.

What’s CSAP?

CSAP is a three-month boot camp followed by six months of hands-on experience, and from day one, I was thrown into the deep end. I got to work with some of the U.K.’s biggest media clients as a Virtual Sales Account Manager, attending meetings about how Cisco enables some of the U.K.’s most famous TV programs and radio stations to thrive — including popular shows like “Love Island.”

After three years in Global Virtual Sales (GVS), including a stint as Team Leader, I transitioned into a Commercial Sales field role. There, I owned strategic engagements with major media clients and led a team of Virtual Sales Account Managers.

When the pandemic hit, I shifted focus to finance, legal, and high-end retail sectors, including some of the world-famous department stores in the U.K., such as Selfridges. Cisco fully supported my move by setting a flexible schedule that helped me balance learning with new responsibilities.

Stepping into my dream roles

I’ve always known I wanted to lead, and Cisco’s culture of promoting from within made that ambition feel achievable.

About three years ago, I stepped into my first leadership role, leading nine account managers across London and the southern regions of the U.K. and Ireland. This was the most excited (and nervous!) I’d been moving into a new role, but it was 100 percent the right move for me. My leader at the time really encouraged me to go for it and threw his support behind me. He helped me identify gaps in my skills and experience and worked closely with me on my development, something you often find here at Cisco.

GSX, Las Vegas, 2026. This annual sales conference provides the time to learn and connect!

Then, in December 2024, a role I’ve wanted since very early on in my career became available: Theatre Lead for Global Virtual Sales and Engineering, UK and Ireland. It was the role directly above the one I was currently in, and when I went for it, I made sure I took the advice of my Cisco mentors. In January 2025, I began the role, overseeing four First-Line Managers and a team of 31 Account Executives.

This is probably my sixth role within Cisco, and I’ve had the opportunity to work under seven or eight different managers, learning from each along the way. That’s why I’ve stayed at Cisco for so long — although it’s one company, the opportunity to learn, develop, and grow is immense!

Planning for your next career move?

For those looking to advance their career, my tip is this: It’s important to be proactive and honest about your ambitions with your managers. There are always options to pivot and grow. Leaders here understand that you won’t stay in one role forever, and that flexibility is key.

2026 Team Sports Day. A time to bond and enjoy some friendly competition!

I’ve experienced firsthand the incredible variety and the freedom to explore new roles, without ever leaving the company. If I ever feel ready for a new challenge or want to try something different, I know I can easily move to another role.

I also strongly believe that you’re in charge of your own career. My leaders have supported my goals, but ultimately, it’s up to me to take ownership. Cisco offers a wealth of internal resources for aspiring leaders, including self-guided courses on platforms like Mindtickle, Skills Studio, and LinkedIn Learning, as well as formal leadership training. The company also recently launched Time to Grow, which gives all employees four dedicated hours each month to build new skills and explore emerging technologies.

Another great thing about Cisco is the people you meet on your journey. Early on, I sought advice and connected with people across the business, simply by messaging them and asking for a coffee. Plus, I’ve made some of my best friends through CSAP and the wider company. I’ve been to Cisco birthdays, holidays, weddings, and even christenings!

Looking back, I’m grateful I chose Cisco over other paths I considered. The variety, culture, and opportunities here are unmatched. It truly is the biggest company you’ve never heard of, and I’m proud to be part of it.

Then he asked people to keep their hand up only if AI had actually done something for them, like sending an email or booking a meeting, and about half the hands went down. In his words: “We’re used to getting answers from AI, but we’re moving to an era where AI can actually do things for you.” Getting an answer and letting AI act are very different decisions. Once AI is acting, we need someone to decide what it’s allowed to do and who is accountable when something goes wrong. He also shared that Cisco cut its partner support cases from 4 million a year to 400,000: “By fixing the root causes, we have reduced them by 90 percent.” Fix the reasons people open cases first, then use AI to close the rest faster. Title: Why so many AI security programs start with the OWASP Top 10
Context: What OWASP is The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is a nonprofit foundation with a global community of security practitioners
Full Text:
When an auditor or an RFP asks how your organization handles AI risk, the OWASP Top 10 lists are often a core part of the checklist behind the question. Cato AI Security is built to address the risks on two lists.

What OWASP is

The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is a nonprofit foundation with a global community of security practitioners. It publishes free security guidance, and volunteers lead its projects and local chapters worldwide.

Its GenAI Security Project publishes several lists. Two of the most widely used are the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2026) and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026). Each list ranks the 10 most critical risks that an AI security program should cover. Many security teams treat the lists as an industry standard and plan their AI security work around them.

The LLM list covers applications with a model embedded inside them, where risks include prompt injection and sensitive data leaking in a response. The agentic list covers what changes once agents plan tasks and call tools on their own.

The OWASP lists give each AI Security team the same set of risks to work from:

App developers use them as a guide to the risks their applications should avoid.

Security vendors build their products around them.

Auditors use them to assess the risk in an AI platform.

Buyers use them to evaluate AI security platforms.

Mitigating those risks is a responsibility shared by the security vendor and the teams that build and run your AI apps and agents. A security platform can stop some risks on its own. Others also need work in the app, the data pipeline or the agent platform.

How Cato AI Security maps to OWASP

Cato AI Security covers the risks on both lists in three ways:

Direct protection: Cato stops the risk in line, before the AI application or agent acts.

Shared protection: Cato reduces the risk and works with your app developers on the rest.

Platform evidence: Cato logs every AI interaction in an audit-ready format, so your team can investigate and show auditors what happened.

Cato AI security runs AI Security for Users, Applications, and Agents with unified visibility, context, and control, so the same inspection and policy applies to every risk below. The OWASP risks fall into three groups.

Supply chain risks

AI apps and agents rely on models, MCP servers and skills that someone else built. If one of them is compromised, every agent that uses it inherits the problem. OWASP lists this as Supply Chain (LLM04) and Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities (ASI04).

A security team can’t set a policy for tools it can’t see. Cato protects against supply chain risk by discovering MCP servers and skills connected to agents and coding tools, including ones IT never approved, and applying policy to each one.

Prompt injection and sensitive data exposure

Attackers can hide instructions in content a model or agent reads and make it act against your policy. Employees can also paste API keys or personal data into an AI app. OWASP lists these as Prompt Injection (LLM01), Agent Goal Hijack (ASI01) and Sensitive Information Disclosure (LLM02).

Cato AI Security protects against prompt injection and data exposure through runtime guardrails on AI agents and the custom applications your teams build. It inspects each prompt and response in line, along with the results tools send back to an agent. Cato blocks prompt injection and jailbreak attempts before the model or agent acts.

The same inspection finds sensitive data in prompts and responses and in files attached to AI apps.

Tool misuse and excessive agent access

An agent with access to tools can change records and run commands. If it has more access than it needs, one bad instruction can cause serious damage. OWASP lists these as Excessive Agency (LLM03), Tool Misuse and Exploitation (ASI02) and Unbounded Consumption (LLM06).

Cato AI Security lets your security team name the tools, MCP servers and skills an agent may use, and block or monitor each one. Your security team can also set limits on how much apps and agents spend on model usage.

Where your team’s work starts

Some risks sit partly outside the traffic path. For these types of risks, Cato AI Security works alongside your team or provides platform evidence:

Data and model poisoning (LLM05): Cato AI Security detects manipulated context in live interactions, while your data pipeline owners protect training and fine-tuning data.

Rogue agents (ASI10): Cato AI Security keeps an inventory of agent activity and applies policy to each agent in line, while your agent platform owns the kill switch.

Cato’s AI interaction logs sit beside network, cloud access security broker (CASB) and endpoint data on one platform, so an analyst doesn’t have to pull logs from separate tools to investigate.

We’ll go through the OWASP lists with you and map them against the apps and agents you run today, one use case at a time. You’ll see our coverage for each risk and how we work with your team to mitigate each one.

What Happens Next: Turn Cloud Security Assessment Findings Into Action

October 28, 2026

Adrian Pascual

BLOG

5 min.

Cloud security assessments are good at finding problems. Once the assessment is over? That’s where things can get complicated.

An assessment may identify excessive permissions, exposed data, insecure configurations, gaps around AI or weaknesses in how an application is protected. The report gets delivered, everyone agrees the findings are important and then a much harder question comes up: Who actually owns fixing this?

That answer matters, because a cloud security finding is rarely just a “cloud problem.”

TL;DR – The real value of a cloud security assessment is what follows the report: contextual prioritization, assigning ownership and resolution of the findings.

Cloud findings can be as complex as cloud environments themselves, with multiple stakeholders and responsible parties.

Contextual analysis and prioritization require cross-functional conversations and collaboration.

Turning findings into action that often requires expertise beyond the team that performed the original assessment.

Start With The Environment

It might seem natural to assume that a “cloud finding” means “cloud security” owns remediation. Reality often dictates a much different view.

Some issues may be superficial, such as an unrestricted security group on an isolated dev instance. The cloud security team can probably fix this one without broader coordination. Other issues may involve multiple stakeholders and require engineering support from a team of domain experts before they can be truly considered fixed.

One of the universal realities of cloud security is how interconnected everything has become.

Take an identity finding in a cloud environment: An overprivileged service account maintains persistent credentials and lacks a defined rotation policy. At first glance, it might seem straightforward. Bring in the identity team, scope the permissions and enforce least-privilege policies.

But what if that service account has access to unencrypted personally identifiable information (PII) or financial records that are subject to Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) regulations? Now data security matters. And so does compliance.

What if the same identity is also connected to a customer-facing application programming interface (API) gateway that serves production traffic? Now the application security team needs to get involved. Possibly the developers as well.

Now let’s complicate it even further. What if an AI service is using that service account to pull training data or take action based on customer inputs? Now AI security enters the conversation and compliance adds additional checks.

The blast radius has now extended beyond the cloud platform, into identity and access management (IAM), through data security, across compliance in multiple ways and into model integrity, prompt injection risks and data lineage obligations.

And if there is evidence that the exposure may already have been abused, the conversation may quickly move toward the security operations center (SOC) or incident response team.

The cloud team who initially received the finding of “an overprivileged identity” is now responsible for remediation across multiple teams.

The original finding has not changed. The context around it has. That is why one team cannot realistically be expected to solve every security issue uncovered during an assessment. Understanding the complete environment touched by a finding will help determine who actually owns remediation.

What’s the Best Process to Determine Ownership of Cloud Security Remediation?

The best way to determine who owns what is to know who’s who among your experts and lean into that expertise. I tend to think about this process the same way I think about tools. You would not use a screwdriver to hammer a nail into a wall. You use the right tool for the job. Security expertise works the same way. The value of a finding depends entirely on whether the right person is interpreting it.

If the assessment uncovers significant identity weaknesses, involve someone who understands identity architecture and access controls.

If the findings involve sensitive information, data governance, classification or exposure, bring in data security expertise.

If application architecture is contributing to the risk, involve the application security team.

If the concern is operational detection or evidence of compromise, involve the SOC or incident response team.

If AI is part of the environment, there may be entirely new questions around identities, permissions, applications, data access and governance.

Not every finding will involve five different teams. However, organizations that avoid assuming the team that finds the problem is automatically the team best equipped to solve it tend to resolve findings faster and more effectively. Ownership clarity accelerates remediation. Ambiguity stalls it.

What if My Team Lacks the Experts Needed to Analyze Findings?

This is more common than most organizations admit and it is not a failure. It’s simply a resourcing reality.

Many security teams operate lean. They have strong generalists who keep operations running, but they do not have deep specialists in every domain an assessment might touch. Identity architecture, data governance, application security and AI security are just a few of the distinct disciplines within the larger cybersecurity knowledge sphere and very few organizations staff all of them internally.

The risk is in treating findings as resolved when the team analyzing them does not fully understand the implications. A generalist reviewing an identity finding might close it as low-priority because the immediate access looks limited, while a specialist would recognize that the same misconfiguration creates a lateral movement opportunity across the environment.

There are a few ways organizations navigate this gap:

Engage External Specialists for Targeted Analysis: A third-party assessment partner can provide the domain expertise a finding requires without the overhead of a full-time hire. This is particularly effective for complex identity, data security or AI-related findings where internal knowledge may be thin.

Build Relationships Before You Need Them: Organizations that establish partnerships with specialized security firms ahead of an assessment can move faster when findings land. The alternative (scrambling to find expertise after a critical finding surfaces) introduces delays at potentially inopportune times.

Use Findings to Identify Capability Gaps: If every assessment produces findings that sit unresolved because no one internally can fully interpret them, that pattern is itself a finding. It reveals where the organization needs to invest, whether through hiring, upskilling or advisory relationships.

Separate Interpretation From Remediation: Even when internal teams will execute the fix, the initial analysis and prioritization can come from external expertise. This keeps remediation timelines tight while ensuring findings are understood in full context before action begins.

The goal is to have a path to the right answer for every finding, whether that path runs through internal teams, external partners or a combination of both.

How Do I Determine Which Findings to Fix First?

Now you have identified the environment and stakeholders for your findings. So you should simply tackle them based on severity score, right?

Not quite.

At this stage, contextual analysis continues to matter. This is also where many remediation processes lose steam.

A finding tells us something exists. A severity rating tells us how someone scored it. Neither of those tells us what to do about it or more importantly: what happens if we do nothing.

Once we understand the environment around a finding (the systems it touches, the data it exposes, the access it enables, etc.) and we know who needs to be involved in the remediation process, then we need to answer some pointed contextual questions:

Does it need to be fixed immediately?

Do we have all of the information or are there outstanding unknowns that require additional investigation?

Do we have a process for coordinating between all involved teams?

Are there mitigating controls already in place?

Is the risk understood and accepted?

Is the finding pointing to a deeper, systemic weakness or architectural design flaw?

What is the risk if we do nothing or postpone the fix?

Answers to questions such as these provide a much more useful prioritization outcome than simply labeling something High, Medium or Low and moving on.

The Assessment Is a Starting Point

An assessment report can document hundreds of findings. Your auditors need your reports. That alone does not necessarily make the organization safer, yet there is a tendency to view the final report as the end of an assessment.

There is a different way to see it: Real strides in security posture maturity are made when the report becomes the basis for a clearer understanding of the environment and creating a practical path forward:

Finding → Context → Priority → Owner → Action

The strongest security programs succeed by deciding what each finding means, bringing the right people into the conversation and then doing something about it.

Finding the issue is important, but knowing what to do next is where the real value begins.

FAQs

What is blast radius in cloud security?

Blast radius describes how far a single security finding can extend across an environment. An overprivileged service account, for example, can span identity, data security, compliance and application security — turning one finding into a cross-functional remediation effort.

What is the difference between a severity score and contextual risk?

A severity score rates a finding in isolation. Contextual risk accounts for what systems the finding touches, what data it exposes and what happens if you do nothing. Effective prioritization requires both.

Should you use the same team for assessment and remediation?

Not necessarily. The team that identifies a finding may not have the domain expertise to resolve it. Separating interpretation from remediation ensures findings are fully understood before action begins.

Any change large enough to invalidate the assumptions of your last assessment. Common triggers include mergers and acquisitions, major workload migrations, new AI platform deployments and security incidents that reveal gaps in detection or access controls.

What happens if cloud security findings go unresolved?

Unresolved findings compound over time. Configuration drift widens the gap and institutional knowledge degrades. What started as a single misconfiguration can become a systemic exposure across identity, data and application layers.

PHP2Shell Won't Be the Last. Here's Where the Next One Will Show Up First.
Context: The first question every team faced was where PHP was answering requests, and whether someone could exploit it right then and there
Full Text:
On October 17, Amazon's honeypot network logged a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt from an anonymized IP address. Yet, public disclosure was still four days away.

By the time PHP got its fixes in on October 21, the technical details had already leaked, proof-of-concept exploits were in wide circulation, and more exploit attempts were being logged left and right. The issue was that there were two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in the PHP engine itself (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS v4.0 9.2) -- what we now know as PHP2Shell.

Our own Security Research team covered what happened and what you should do: which releases to move to, which mitigations you could put in place to reduce exposure until you were able to update, and where each part of the Snyk platform sees the problem.

This post now picks up where our Security Research team left off. We want to talk about what the response taught us: where this kind of exposure lives and comes from, why answering fast depends on the work we’d done months earlier, and why the next one is already on its way.

Why was PHP2Shell a problem for teams with clean code?

Well, because the vulnerabilities live below the code. And what does that mean? Both of the mentioned CVEs happen in the request lifecycle of the PHP engine, which makes them reachable before any application code actually runs. On Apache, with mod_php, an exploit needed but a single unauthenticated request.

Now, think about that for a second. You probably had careful reviews, clean code, plus a neat and tidy dependency tree, all sitting above the actual problem. The first question every team faced was where PHP was answering requests, and whether someone could exploit it right then and there.

The question was about running applications. The very same question attackers will always start with.

Which inventory tells you where PHP is running?

Each type of inventory tells you part of it.

PHP reaches production via a Dockerfile, a distribution package, a platform image, or manually. A "php": ">=8.2"constraint in composer.json tells you what an application accepts, and then the deployed version depends on which of those routes installed it. Container scans see PHP installed from distribution packages once each distribution publishes its advisory, and PHP compiled from source, including the official PHP Docker images, falls outside that view. (Once again, our research team's post maps exactly which Snyk view sees which slice of this reality.)

Then there's the version string. VirusTotal fingerprints roughly 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, and only about 1.1 million of them announce a version, so roughly four out of five hide it. Their summary is one of the cleanest lines we've read on the subject anywhere: "If you only search for a version string, you only see the fraction of the problem that volunteers it."

The gap between what your inside-out views know and what actually answers from the outside is where the real risk lies. Attackers hit your URL, and PHP2Shell is the purest case of that we’ve seen. Anyone probing for it ends up asking the same question: Does PHP answer on this URL?

What did the response look like from the outside in?

The head start: before PHP's 14:00 UTC release on October 21, Snyk had advisories live for both CVEs, so monitored projects would get a hit the moment fixed versions were known. Within about 30 minutes of the release, those advisories included affected ranges and fixed versions, and distribution advisories followed as each distribution was published. That covered what Snyk Container and Unmanaged scans could tell you.

Three questions ran through Snyk API & Web:

Where is PHP running? Discovery enumerates the assets on your domains and fingerprints their technology stack. Set the Tech filter to PHP, and you get every discovered host and endpoint where PHP was identified, with its risk rating, score, and last-seen date. Version numbers come later, from the hosts themselves. As our research team put it, before you can patch, you need the list.

Can someone exploit it? Within 24 hours of PHP's release, the full scan profile tested for PHP2Shell, and teams could run that check on their own as a custom profile for a fast answer across every PHP target.

Did the fix hold? Run the same custom profile after patching, and pair it with your distribution's advisory or patch level, because a patched distribution build can keep an older version number.

So, Discovery --> targeted check --> patch --> re-test: probe, observe, and infer, against a clock that now runs in hours. And that’s exactly the most concerning part, what we care about the most. For teams already running Snyk API & Web, the hard part was done before October 21: their domains were mapped, and their applications set up as targets. When the check was there, the response took only a filter and a quick scan.

For us, that’s one of the main returns on having continuous outside-in testing: the work that answers at day one gets done months before that.

If PHP2Shell is detectable from the outside, what was the hard part?

Time.

In May, we laid out the distinction on which COS is built. Heuristic-detectable vulnerabilities show themselves to deterministic tools: throw payloads at a running application or API, observe the responses, and infer. Context-dependent vulnerabilities (BOLA, cross-tenant leakage, and chained business logic) carry no signature at all, because they live in the gap between what an application is supposed to do and what it actually does.

Once it was known, PHP2Shell became testable from the outside, which puts it squarely in that first class of heuristic-detectable vulns. The hard part, the constraint, was the gap between a disclosure and having a check running against everything you expose. That gap is the attacker’s window to exploit, and this time it opened four days before disclosure eventually did.

The disclosure kept moving, too. On October 23, the PHP project described a partial bypass (CVE-2026-115560) that applies when an application switches its session serialization handler with ini_set() before starting the session, with upload progress enabled. Its preconditions are rare, and whatever you concluded on Wednesday still needed a second look by Friday. A point-in-time answer ages in days.

Why won't PHP2Shell be the last?

There are three reasons for that. Due to the nature of how they were found:

Because they were found with AI assistance, in an engine that has served the web for three decades. Our research team put it plainly: "In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers." And the kind of model that found these vulnerabilities is the kind attackers now have in their hands.

The stronger cadence. Manoj Nair, Snyk's CTO and Chief Innovation Officer, described it in September: "The kind of severe flaw that AI now surfaces in widely used software, the sort of find that used to arrive once or twice a year and reset everyone's quarter, is landing several times a week in what I'm seeing."

The much faster clock. CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, drew two lessons from PHP2Shell that apply well beyond it. Defenders "should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation." And "the time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons," because AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or an advisory into a working exploit. His advice for critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems: "measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours."

What does being ready for the next one take?

Strip out the product names, and it comes down to four properties. Judge any approach by them (ours included). Don’t think about product names, but how it all comes down to four properties. And you should judge any approach with these (ours included!)

An inventory that exists before the advisory does. Built from the outside in and kept current, so a new disclosure starts with a filter.

Checks that ship in hours. The gap between an advisory and a running test is the attacker's window. Measure it.

Re-tests on demand. The same targeted check, run again until the fix holds.

Testing that needs no signature. Heuristics catch what someone has already described. Everything else takes reasoning: testing that works out what your application is supposed to do, then goes after the gap between that and what it actually does.

As for Snyk, here’s how that maps to what we offer.

Snyk API & Web carries the first three: Discovery, an engine the team keeps current as disclosures land, and targeted profiles you can run and re-run. Continuous Offensive Security adds the fourth: AI Pentesting reasons about your application the way a pentester would, Agent Red Teaming engages the moment recon spots an LLM in the stack, and Dynamic Testing, the Snyk API & Web engine, covers the heuristic classes underneath, continuously. In our platform's terms, that's Validate: continuously attack your applications to prove fixes held and show what's still exploitable.

Then there's posture. At The AI Security Panel: Unfiltered on October 14, Manoj asked the question we keep coming back to: "When an autonomous attacker is going to attack you, why don't you attack yourself?" That question is the whole premise of COS. On our side, the work is shrinking every single gap in this story: from advisory to running check, and from check to confirmed fix.

Where will the next one show up first?

Which engine, and when, is anyone's guess now. Where it shows up first is easier to call: at your URL. That's where your testing should already be.

Title: Snyk UNFILTERED: Inside Our First-Ever Customer Summit
Context: Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job Detection is no longer the bottleneck
Full Text:
What happens when you bring security leaders from some of the world's most forward-thinking organizations into one room, close the doors, and invite them to speak candidly about what's working, what's breaking, and what they’re still working out?

That’s what we set out to find with Snyk UNFILTERED, our inaugural Customer Summit. Held in San Francisco ahead of the launch of Evo Agentic AppSec and the AI Security Summit, Snyk UNFILTERED was designed to feel nothing like a conference.

We brought together a small group of security leaders from our customer community for an afternoon of candid discussions, interactive debates, and peer-to-peer exchanges. With no traditional presentations, product demos, or carefully rehearsed talking points, the summit gave attendees the freedom to share their experiences without attribution. What followed was an open exchange of ideas about the challenges and opportunities shaping the future of AI security. Leaders compared notes on real rollouts, real roadblocks, and real questions they have not yet figured out, with a level of transparency that is hard to find at traditional industry events.

From the growing backlog of vulnerabilities to the governance of autonomous agents, attendees challenged assumptions, compared real-world experiences, and explored questions the industry is still answering. And that's where the most valuable conversations began.

Five key takeaways that stuck with us

Five themes kept resurfacing over the afternoon, across every table and every discussion:

1. When AI writes the code, who owns the risk?

If an engineer prompts an AI tool to build an agent skill and that skill causes an issue later, who is at fault? The room kept coming back to the importance of guardrails: clear controls and ownership that hold up even when no human typed the line.

2. The AI conversation has grown up

Just a few months ago, the questions were about cost and token usage. Now leadership wants to know the return on investment, what AI is really costing, and where to set budget caps. AI has moved from experiment to line item with scrutiny to match.

3. Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job

Detection is no longer the bottleneck. The questions have moved to how teams fix issues, how fast they can fix them, and how they reduce human error within the loop. Fixes that stall in review, testing, and merge were a shared frustration.

4. Risk can come from anywhere

When everyone on a team has access to AI, vulnerabilities can come from anywhere. Democratizing AI also spreads responsibility, and attendees talked about how to keep everyone accountable without slowing anyone down.

5. Humans can only do so much

Teams are limited by how much people can review and approve. Leaders are open to trusting agents, but only with controls that an agent cannot bypass, and with governance designed for machines rather than adapted from processes built for people.

From UNFILTERED conversations to the future of AI Security

Snyk UNFILTERED was just the beginning of an important week in San Francisco. The challenges discussed behind closed doors at UNFILTERED reflected a broader shift happening across the industry: security teams are moving beyond simply identifying risk toward enabling organizations to build, innovate, and operate safely at AI speed.

The next morning, we launched Evo Agentic AppSec, and the AI Security Summit brought builders, researchers, investors, and CISOs into the same building. The questions from the customer room about fixing at speed and governing agents were carried straight into those conversations. Hearing those challenges directly from customers shapes what we build next.

The best conversations don't end when the event does

The leaders in the room are navigating enormous change. They’re balancing innovation with accountability and securing technologies that evolve faster than the processes designed to govern them. What made the afternoon valuable was their willingness to talk openly about what they haven’t solved yet. Spaces like that are rare, and we plan to keep creating them.

Snyk Unfiltered is part of our commitment to bringing our customer community together through candid conversations and shared learning, and this was the first of many.

In-app surveys capture feedback

In-app surveys add the team's own perspective on that work. The default questions focus on value: the most valuable thing someone has done with Claude recently, how Claude changed the time that work took, which use of Claude a teammate should copy, and, if the team lost access tomorrow, what would break or slow down first. Admins can customize or remove questions and choose who receives a survey, when it runs, and where it appears. Members see it as a short card after a reply in the tool they’re already working in.

Responses appear on the survey page as they arrive, and admins can export them to a spreadsheet. In-app surveys can now be enabled for organizations that use customer-managed encryption keys, and for organizations that set one retention period for all data, surveys and their responses are deleted on that schedule.

In-app surveys are treated as your data, so Anthropic accesses them only as necessary to operate the service.

Pooled group budgets put spend where the work happens

Pooled group budgets give a group one shared monthly budget, so people who use Claude heavily are less likely to hit an individual limit early in the month while others leave budget unspent. Member limits still work as a guardrail against unusually high individual use. Every request counts against both, and a member stops at whichever runs out first. When someone hits a limit, they can request more from inside Claude, and the request goes to admins for review. The setup suggests an amount based on the group's recent usage, and admins with billing permissions receive email alerts at 50%, 75%, 95%, and 100% of a budget.

IDC Research (IDC), a global leader in technology intelligence for more than 60 years, worked with Anthropic to bring IDC Quanta into Claude, available to IDC customers today. IDC has also rolled Claude out across the company, where teams use it every day.

Applying market research has traditionally meant reading through long reports to get to the answers a customer needs, such as a vendor shortlist or a competitive brief. Now, an IDC customer describes the market, strategy, or purchase they're working on, and the IDC Quanta MCP connector for Claude returns finished analysis built on IDC's trusted forecasts and data.

What customers can do with IDC Quanta in Claude

IDC Quanta, an AI-powered technology intelligence platform that helps customers do better work, faster, with credible, verified intelligence from IDC’s proprietary data and research. In Claude, IDC Quanta enables customers to benchmark performance, size markets, choose vendors, and shape strategy. It’s as simple as a customer describing the question they're working on, and Claude answering it using IDC's intelligence.

The questions that users ask vary by role, but they tend to look like this:

Competitive briefs: A corporate strategy lead asks Claude for a competitor brief. Claude returns the competitor’s positioning, market share, product capabilities, and recent acquisitions, cited to IDC's research. A job that used to take a day’s worth of research is complete in minutes.

Vendor shortlists: A CIO evaluating procurement software asks Claude which vendors are the best fit based on her existing architecture and unique business requirements. Claude returns the top three by IDC's procurement database and MarketScape research as an Excel scorecard, ready for the evaluation team to act on.

Analysis of their own numbers: A CFO uploads next year's IT budget, and asks how it compares to IDC's forecast. Claude returns where the two differ, and by how much, while updated data stays private to the customer.

IDC Quanta works wherever the customer already uses Claude, including the Claude app on desktop and mobile, Cowork, and the Microsoft Office add-ins. It gives Claude the same data and definitions an IDC analyst works from, so a market share or growth rate matches what IDC would publish, and each answer cites the IDC document or dataset it came from.

How IDC uses Claude internally

IDC has also put Claude to work across the company, where its engineers, product, marketing and sales teams are using it daily to build, plan, and sell. A clear example of the difference it's making is in engineering: IDC's engineers rebuilt the internal data repository its analysts use for research in three weeks instead of an estimated three months, and since they began using Claude Code for testing, bugs in the code they ship have come down significantly.

Engineering was the first team to adopt Claude, and the rest of the company has followed. Here's how they're using it:

Building and testing software: Product managers use Claude Code to build working prototypes before engineering starts, which has cut the time it takes a feature to reach engineering from months to weeks. Engineers use it to run tests in parallel, and a code review that once filled five days is done in about 30 minutes.

Planning and strategy: Product teams give Cowork their research and internal files, and it writes the first draft of the plan. Planning sprints that took three weeks now take three days. Writing a new test to check that code works now takes about 20 minutes, down from days.

Optimizing sales: IDC's sales team runs a tool built with Claude that reads an export from the company's CRM. In minutes, it tells each rep which of their deals have stalled and which are worth chasing.

Producing marketing content: IDC's content marketing team built an assistant in Claude to draft much of its marketing content. It optimizes the content for search and AI answer engines (SEO/AEO), and checks it against buyer personas and IDC's own research. From there, the team edits, proofs, and publishes the work, publishing content faster than it could on its own

“Assessing the impact of a competitor’s acquisition used to mean a market intelligence professional spending hours pulling multiple reports, synthesizing the findings, and turning them into an executive-ready brief. Now, they can open Claude, ask what that acquisition means for their business, and get a board-ready analysis in minutes, grounded in IDC’s research and more than 15 billion data points,” said Lorenzo Larini, CEO, IDC. “We brought IDC Quanta into Claude because that’s where many of our customers already work, giving them a faster, more intuitive way to put IDC’s trusted data and research to work.”

“IDC has spent 60 years helping leaders make better technology decisions, and now it’s using Claude to rethink how its teams work and how it delivers value to its customers,” said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer, Anthropic.

Title: The strategy behind the shield.
Context: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has unveiled CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, a strategy aimed at strengthening national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure resilience against cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats. CISA has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively known...
Full Text:
CISA unveils its 2030 cyber strategy. PHP2Shell exploits are in the wild. HHS preserves healthcare security requirements. Microsoft offers buyouts amid its AI spending spree. A cyberattack disrupts New Mexico hospitals. Google’s Finnish data center plans hit an environmental roadblock. Blue Initiative tracks maritime vulnerabilities. A Chinese national faces charges in a $37 million cryptocurrency scam. Our guest is Cal Al-Dhubaib, host of the new Authorized Intelligence podcast. Anthropic’s prospectus includes an existential disclaimer.

Today is Tuesday October 27th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

CISA plans to defend, harden and prevail.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has unveiled CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, a strategy aimed at strengthening national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure resilience against cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats.

The plan rests on three pillars. Defend focuses on securing networks, operational technology, software supply chains, and emerging technologies, including quantum computing and advanced AI. Harden emphasizes turning threat intelligence into action, improving risk prioritization, and accelerating incident response. Prevail seeks to strengthen national resilience through regional partnerships, emergency communications, and coordinated planning.

The strategy also prioritizes resilient 5G and 6G networks and satellite communications.

CISA will review its existing capabilities within 60 days, deliver an implementation plan within 180 days, and report on its progress within a year.

PHP2Shell is officially under active exploitation.

CISA has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively known as PHP2Shell, to its catalog of actively exploited flaws. The bugs could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable systems.

Researchers observed widespread exploitation attempts before patches were released October 21, though early attempts reportedly failed. Subsequent honeypot activity confirmed successful exploitation in the wild.

Federal civilian agencies have until Thursday to patch their systems.

HHS scales back plans to eliminate privacy and security certification requirements.

Federal health regulators have scaled back plans to eliminate privacy and security certification requirements for electronic health records, following widespread objections from healthcare providers and industry groups.

The Department of Health and Human Services’ final rule eliminates 14 health IT certification criteria, down from the 34 originally proposed. All 13 core privacy and security requirements will remain intact, including standards for authentication and access controls.

Commenters warned that eliminating those safeguards could shift security responsibilities onto healthcare providers, particularly smaller and rural organizations with limited resources.

However, the rule does eliminate transparency and risk-management requirements for AI-powered clinical decision support tools. Those provisions required developers to disclose information about their systems’ capabilities, limitations, and potential risks.

HHS says the changes will save health IT developers more than $1.5 billion in regulatory costs.

Most provisions take effect December 28, with others following in January.

Microsoft offers buyouts amidst AI-driven growth.

Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to approximately 60,000 employees, roughly 27 percent of its workforce, as it balances soaring AI infrastructure spending with efforts to control costs.

The offers cover eligible workers in the United States, Canada, India, and Britain, including some employees at the vice president level.

Microsoft expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion in the September quarter, driven largely by data center investments supporting AI services.

The company previously offered voluntary retirement packages in April and announced 4,800 layoffs in July.

Some engineering, sales, and marketing teams are excluded from the latest program. Eligible employees have until early December to decide, with departures scheduled for December 31.

Microsoft says the initiative will provide flexibility as the company reshapes its workforce around AI-driven growth.

New Mexico hospitals divert patients following a cyberattack.

A cybersecurity incident disrupted operations across the University of New Mexico Health System on Monday, forcing ambulance diversions, canceled appointments, and temporary restrictions on hospital access.

The disruption affected New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center, leaving the state without its highest level of emergency trauma care. Other healthcare providers stepped in to accommodate additional patients.

Employees reported hearing messages broadcast through hospital computers claiming that student, employee, and patient information had been stolen. Those claims have not been verified.

The health system declined to discuss the incident’s nature or scope, citing an active law enforcement investigation. The FBI confirmed it was assisting.

Hospitals and clinics began gradually resuming operations Monday afternoon, although the full extent of the disruption remains unclear.

Cleared trees halt development of a Google AI data center in Finland.

Google’s massive AI infrastructure expansion in Finland has run into an environmental backlash after the company cleared hundreds of thousands of trees without completing required environmental assessments.

At one site in northern Finland, an estimated 250,000 trees were removed across 815 acres. Conservationists estimate another 150,000 were felled at a second location.

Finnish regulators have ordered work stopped at both sites. Google has apologized, saying it acted according to its understanding of local regulations.

The controversy threatens to complicate Google’s €13 billion investment in Finnish data centers, part of a broader AI infrastructure boom attracted by the country’s cool climate and abundant energy.

Supporters point to jobs and tax revenue. Critics question the environmental costs, electricity demands, and limited economic benefits.

More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding tighter regulation and compensation for affected communities.

Google says it will comply with regulators and plans to replant trees.

Blue Initiative tracks vulnerabilities affecting ships, ports, and maritime infrastructure.

A coalition of cybersecurity and maritime organizations has launched Blue Initiative, a free public database tracking vulnerabilities affecting ships, ports, and maritime infrastructure.

The project helps operators identify and prioritize security risks across IT and operational technology systems.

The database currently contains nearly 30,000 vulnerabilities, including more than 2,000 rated critical and over 580 known to be exploited.

Users can search, filter, and receive alerts about vulnerabilities, while researchers and industry partners review entries and contribute new findings.

A Chinese national faces federal charges in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment scam.

A Chinese national has been extradited from the Netherlands to face federal charges in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment scam that defrauded at least 174 Americans of nearly $37 million.

Prosecutors say 44-year-old Zheng Zhao participated in an international fraud network operating partly from scam centers in Cambodia.

The scheme allegedly involved contacting victims through social media, dating sites, and text messages, building relationships, then persuading them to invest through fraudulent cryptocurrency platforms.

Investigators say the stolen money moved through American bank accounts to the Bahamas, where it was converted into Tether cryptocurrency and transferred to wallets controlled in Cambodia.

Eight alleged co-conspirators have already pleaded guilty.

Zhao faces a money laundering conspiracy charge carrying a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

Anthropic’s prospectus includes an existential disclaimer.

Anthropic is preparing to go public, and its pitch to investors comes with an unusual warning: the company’s products could potentially threaten human civilization.

In its 335-page IPO filing, Anthropic devotes 93 pages to potential risks, ranging from employee retention and computing costs to AI systems developing beyond human control.

The company warns that increasingly autonomous models could conduct cyberattacks, spread misinformation, help develop dangerous weapons, or take harmful actions without human intervention.

There’s also the possibility that AI development could outpace Anthropic’s ability to evaluate and safeguard its own technology.

And then there are more conventional business concerns, including expensive data centers, regulatory scrutiny, and dependence on major customers.

Anthropic argues that its commitment to AI safety makes it uniquely positioned to manage these dangers.

So, the investment proposition is essentially this: help us build extraordinarily powerful AI, and we’ll do our best to keep it from ending civilization.

Not your typical prospectus.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Full Text:
Last year at Ignite, we introduced the concept of Frontier Transformation and how it is different from any technology-led pursuit, because it requires us to focus on business outcomes first. It starts with a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. There is no path where this notion of infinite cognitive compute replaces human purpose. Frontier Transformation is an opportunity for a wholesale reinvention of how you think about your unique ideas coming to life and how your organization can thrive in your industry.

Over the course of this past year, we have been leading our customers to focus on the three durable traits that are required for successful transformation: human ambition, intelligence and trust. We are taking a platform approach toward enabling the same: Copilot as the place to call home for interacting with AI to empower human ambition; the Microsoft IQ platform to compound and amplify your intelligence from within while protecting your unique differentiation; and Agent 365 to enable Trust and Observability at every layer of the stack so that you can govern, manage, secure and get business value and return out of the capabilities you deliver.

Our latest earnings are another important marker on that journey. Behind the numbers are thousands of customers, partners, developers and employees putting AI to work in meaningful ways. We have so many inspiring stories from our customers that highlight these outcomes, and below are some of our favorites.

Empowering human ambition with Copilot

Volkswagen has scaled Microsoft Copilot to more than 330,000 employees as it expands the role of AI in decision-making and knowledge-based processes across the enterprise. Building on Copilot Chat adoption that reached more than 300,000 monthly active users, employees are now using Copilot with Work IQ for more advanced scenarios, bringing greater organizational context to decision-making and knowledge-based work. Volkswagen is also working with Microsoft to further scale its Intelligent Data Foundation on Microsoft Fabric to make data easier to find, understand and use across the entire company. With this investment, Volkswagen is demonstrating how companies have evolved from using Copilot as a productivity tool to an operating system to empower human ambition.

Following a successful pilot, Fujitsu is scaling Microsoft Copilot across its global workforce of approximately 100,000. Copilot usage has surpassed 90%, and the company is using the tool to connect employees with specialized agents and business systems. AI agents are already automating roughly 75% of initial responses and triage for a service desk that receives nearly 300,000 inquiries annually, while new agents are supporting work across sales, systems engineering, procurement, finance and accounting. As customer zero, Fujitsu is using Copilot as the front door to a multi-agent work environment and using insights from its own AI adoption to better serve its customers.

KOHLER is using GitHub Copilot to transform software development, with one organization improving code releases by 25% and reducing error defects by 75%. These engineering breakthroughs are part of a broader effort to embed AI processes across the company, spanning IT, finance, marketing, supply chain and operations. Microsoft Copilot has reached 98% adoption, saving an average of 2 to 5 hours per month as employees are making informed decisions and getting answers faster in the flow of their work. Employees across the company have also created more than 3,000 agents to date, with hundreds active daily.

At Krafton, Microsoft Security Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR are helping the security team respond to a growing volume and complexity of threats. The global gaming company automated key parts of security operations, from alerting and investigation to reporting, combining Microsoft Security solutions with its own systems and data to quickly gather context that helps distinguish real threats from false positives. This approach is having immediate results: security alert recognition time has fallen by approximately 95% to less than one minute, investigation work that previously took tens of minutes now takes about three minutes and roughly 95% of report creation has been automated. By taking on repetitive work, AI is giving Krafton’s security professionals more time to focus on responding to real threats and making critical security decisions.

To accelerate discovery across decades of scientific data, NASA is making complex information easier to explore through Microsoft Copilot. NASA employees are using Copilot to sift through massive amounts of academic literature and streamline daily tasks, and specialized assistants are helping researchers navigate complex Earth science data through natural language, extending access to information that once required significant technical expertise. Hydrology Copilot, for example, can analyze variables like precipitation and soil moisture to help communities better understand water conditions, prepare for droughts and anticipate flood risks, while automatically performing calculations and analyses.

To transform frontline work, Williams, a US natural gas company, is using Microsoft Copilot to help employees spend less time searching documents and completing manual processes, and more time on critical field operations. Copilot helps teams generate plans, interpret procedures, assess regulatory requirements, troubleshoot issues and complete safety reporting, while employees can create agents tailored to their own workflows. Demonstrating that the person closest to a problem is often the best one to solve it, one operations technician built an anomaly detector using Copilot that compares equipment data against baseline statistics and alerts teams to potential issues before they become costly or dangerous. Since deploying Copilot, AI adoption at Williams has grown from single digits to more than 90%, helping employees accelerate operations, improve reporting and compliance and identify equipment issues earlier.

Bristol Myers Squibb has rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 25,000 employees, reaching 96% adoption, and is now putting AI agents to work across everyday use cases such as document review and project management in support of the company’s mission to bring more medicines to more patients faster. One agent, called RABIT, analyzes meeting transcripts, surfaces action items and delivers insights directly within employees’ workflows.

Facing rising patient demand and financial pressures, Brown University Health is using Dragon Copilot to give clinicians more time to focus on patients. The health system adopted Dragon Copilot, and an early pilot across 420 clinicians found users spent less time on after-hours documentation and reported lower cognitive burden. Building on that experience, Brown University Health deployed Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Studio across departments, which led to the creation of more than 24 AI agents to support clinical workflows, hospital policies, patient access and operations. These AI solutions are not only supporting clinicians in the flow of their work but also helping to improve the patient experience and access to care.

Microsoft IQ compounds and protects your intelligence

BNY has made AI part of how its employees work through Eliza, its in-house AI platform built with Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Copilot and GitHub Copilot – with plans to add Work IQ. More than 300 solutions now run on Eliza, ranging from inquiry management to client onboarding, and 100% of employees have been trained on the platform. Across the bank, that scale is translating into meaningful results: client transaction inquiries are being resolved 80% faster and AI-assisted client onboarding is 20% faster on average.
