That's defense in depth: none of them is enough alone, none of them is redundant, and together they cover each other:

OpenShell is prevention. Hard limits, enforced below the agent. It decides what's possible at all.

Prempti is judgment. It understands the agent's actions, can stop the obvious stuff early, and ask a human when something looks off.

Falco is ground truth. It sees what ran, no matter how it got there, from a place the agent can't reach.

So, who watches the watchmen? Something the agent can't touch. OpenShell and Prempti stand right next to the agent, and that's exactly why they're useful: they can stop things before they happen. Falco stands outside, and that's why it's useful: it sees everything that happens, including what happens to the watchmen.

Try the three watchmen workflow

Everything is in the demo repo. You need Docker 28+, a Just command runner, and the OpenShell CLI and gateway. nix develop gives you all three, and just gateway starts a local gateway.

just gateway # once: local OpenShell gateway just falco # terminal 1: Falco with the OpenShell rules just openshell # terminal 2: Claude Code in a sandbox, with Prempti just prempti-logs # terminal 3: Prempti's verdicts

No Anthropic API key? Run the simulated evil agent instead and watch Falco light up:

openshell sandbox create --name evil --no-keep --from openshell-claude-prempti \ -- bash -c "$(cat test/evil-agent.sh)"

test/kill-prempti.sh and test/hijack-prempti.sh replay Scene 5 the same way.

We tested this on macOS (Apple Silicon) with colima, OpenShell 0.1.2, Falco 0.45, and Prempti 0.2.1.

One thing we learned running real sessions: Claude Code does a lot in the background (telemetry, claude.ai connectors, a plugin-marketplace clone). OpenShell's policy blocks all of it, as it should, and Falco reported every blocked connection and credential probe: about 160 alerts in a session where nothing bad happened. Three Claude Code environment variables in the entrypoint and a few narrow rule exceptions brought that to 0. Tune detection against real agent sessions, not just the attacks you script.

No single layer was enough: each caught something the others missed. The demo is repo available, so you can run the scenarios yourself and see what each layer catches and misses

Title: Using Codex for education at Dagster Labs
Context: Because our users come from varied technical backgrounds, we’ve found it essential to meet each persona at the right technical depth
Full Text:
At Dagster Labs, we produce a lot of technical educational content for data engineers, machine learning engineers, and analysts to better understand how to use Dagster, an open source workflow orchestration framework. Because our users come from varied technical backgrounds, we’ve found it essential to meet each persona at the right technical depth.

In this post, I’ll share how we use OpenAI’s Codex to accelerate documentation, translate content across mediums, and even measure how complete our docs are.

The power of CONTRIBUTING.md files

To make it easier for our community members and internal engineers to contribute documentation, we overhauled our CONTRIBUTING.md file. To our surprise, we had inadvertently significantly improved the utility of Codex. It turns out there is serious value in clearly outlining the hierarchy, structure, and best practices for writing documentation in your code base. Both for humans and robots.

# Contributing documentation ## Content ### Links #### Use full paths instead of relative links Docusaurus doesn't always render relative links correctly, which can result in users seeing intermittent 404s when accessing those links. Use full paths instead of relative links, like this: ``` For more information, see "[Defining assets](/guides/build/assets/defining-assets)". ``` instead of this: ``` For more information, see "[Defining assets](defining-assets)". ``` #### Use non-trailing slash links to Dagster docs e.g. use `/guides/build/assets/defining-assets` instead of `/guides/build/assets/defining-assets/`. **Context:** Links to Dagster docs with trailing slashes automatically redirect to non-trailing slash links. While that's helpful for docs links we don't control, too many redirects on our own pages can confuse search engines and cause SEO issues. ### API documentation ...

Codex is only as good as the scaffolding you give it. A well-structured CONTRIBUTING.md becomes both documentation for humans and a map for AI.

Codex for understanding

Beyond writing docs, Codex can act as an always-available code explainer. For developer advocates and technical writers, this has been invaluable. In open source projects, or projects with many engineers, it can often be difficult to stay up-to-date on all of the features being developed, and how they work. This is especially true for smaller teams of developer advocates and technical writers. We’ve found that some of the best assistance Codex provides is through explaining pull requests, or pointing it to a part of the codebase and asking for an explanation.

A tip we’ve found here is to leverage the gh command from within Codex to explain pull requests. Ask it to review the PR description and diff, summarize why the feature was implemented, and explain how it should be exposed to end users.

The power of the mono repo

This might be a controversial opinion, but I’m a big fan of mono repos. When context is key, having everything accessible in a single repository makes it so much easier to get access to what you need, and in the case of Codex, this means complete context: code, docs, and examples all in one place.

While some people have expressed concern about tools like Codex failing to scale with repositories, I’ve found this not to be the case. By making use of file references within Codex (@) you can give Codex the initial sub directory or file to start with before further exploration. And there are some serious benefits to having your framework code alongside your documentation in a single repository. This setup lets us prompt Codex to read framework code and draft initial documentation scaffolds that we can then refine.

Here’s an example where we prompted Codex to review an existing pull request, and add a section to the documentation on how exactly these environment variables are useful when configuring your deployment.

>_ You are using OpenAI Codex in ~/src/dagster To get started, describe a task or try one of these commands: /init - create an AGENTS.md file with instructions for Codex /status - show current session configuration and token usage /approvals - choose what Codex can do without approval /model - choose what model and reasoning effort to use ▌ Review the changes made in pull request 32557 using `gh pr diff <number>`, review the environment ▌ variables that were introduced and already exist for configuring the gRPC server, then update ▌ docs/docs/deployment/oss/oss-instance-configuration.md page to outline the configuration options. > I’ll fetch the diff for PR 32557 and scan for added/updated gRPC-related environment variables, then cross-check with existing env var usage in the repo. • Ran gh pr diff 32557 | sed -n '1,200p' • Ran gh pr diff 32557 | sed -n '200,400p' • Explored └ Search DAGSTER_GRPC_[A-Z_]+ in dagster Read api.py, code_server.py, oss-instance-configuration.md Search DAGSTER_CODE_SERVER_[A-Z_]+ Read constants.py Search DAGSTER_(REPOSITORY|SCHEDULE|SENSOR)_GRPC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS| DAGSTER_GRPC_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD in dagster Read proxy_server_manager.py > Next, I’ll expand the gRPC servers section of the instance configuration docs to include API gRPC server variables and communication timeouts/limits, keeping style consisten ...

You can find the pull request that was produced by this session at dagster-io/dagster # 32558.

Translating between content mediums

Different personas prefer different learning formats, but the underlying ideas are often the same. Because of that, we produce a variety of content mediums: blog posts, tutorials, online courses, YouTube videos, and more. The core content of these materials can often be the same, just presented differently depending on the target persona.

Codex works exceptionally well at translating between these mediums. For example, taking a tutorial and producing a transcript for a YouTube video. Or taking a low-level tutorial, and abstracting it slightly for a blog post. In the below screenshot you can find an example prompt used to take one of our example projects and produce a video transcript. This approach saves hours of rewriting while keeping our messaging consistent across channels.

>_ You are using OpenAI Codex in ~/src/dagster ▌Review the example project: examples/docs_projects/project_dagster_modal_pipes ▌and produce a video transcript to teach users the core Dagster and Modal concept ▌covered. Break the transcript into sections, and include code snippets to be ▌showcased in the video. The prose of the script should be fun but professional. ▌Save this to MODAL_VIDEO_TRANSCRIPT.md. > I’m going to scan the example project to understand its structure and code before drafting the video transcript. • Ran └ bash -lc 'ls -la' bash -lc 'ls -la examples/docs_projects/ project_dagster_modal_pipes' bash -lc "rg --files examples/docs_projects/ project_dagster_modal_pipes | sed -n '1,120p'" • Explored └ List project_dagster_modal_pipes Search rg --files examples/docs_projects/project_dagster_modal_pipes Read README.md, definitions.py, __init__.py, resources.py, constants.py, feeds.py, pipeline_factory.py, summarize.py, config.py, transcribe.py, hello_dagster.py, verify_cloud_mount.py • Added MODAL_VIDEO_TRANSCRIPT.md (+335 -0)

See the full video transcript here!

Evaluating documentation coverage

One of the more experimental ways we’re using Codex is as a proxy for human understanding.

By using documentation as the source-of-truth, and base context for Codex, we can have it generate code. For example, people often use Dagster for running and observing their dbt data models alongside other data processing code.

By prompting Codex to reference the documentation and produce the code for this project, we can then run a test suite on the resulting code to check that it operates as expected. If it works as expected we can assume that our documentation has adequate coverage of the required content. If Codex can generate working code purely from our documentation, it’s a strong signal that humans can as well which becomes an indirect measure of documentation completeness.

Summary

All in all, the Dagster team has found Codex to be immensely helpful for creating, reviewing, and translating education content. It has enabled us to scale beyond our original capacity, helped us ensure that we have adequate documentation coverage as the framework evolves, and more importantly, it has made it so that we can more easily support our community.

Codex has underscored how important context and structure are. For us, that means refining our documentation architecture so both humans and AI can navigate it easily. This feedback loop, powered by AI, has improved both how we create content and how users generate framework code. As AI tools evolve, the line between documentation, code, and automation will blur. Teams that treat documentation as structured data will have a major advantage.

Title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
Context: We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation
Full Text:
On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

What happened

GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

Immediate remediation

After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Background: how we serve GLM 5.3

Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMs and smaller, faster, safer models.

The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).

Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.

Issue one: misconfiguration

On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.

This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence. We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.

Issue two: SGLang bug

In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Here’s what was happening before.

When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path (Req.set_finish_with_abort) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.

In disaggregated mode such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was finished, not whether it was rejected. A rejected request reported itself as live. So:

Bootstrap. The router told the decode node the prompt length (8 pages in the diagram). Decode reserved 8 KV pages for the request.

Prefill admission. The prefill admission queue admitted any request where req.finished() was False. A rejected request stored its rejection in to_finish, not finished_reason, so finished() still returned False. The rejected request was admitted.

Prefill forward pass. Rejection had already replaced the prompt with a one-token placeholder. Prefill ran a trivial forward pass on that one token.

KV transfer. Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete.

Decode admission. Decode's admission queue had the same finished() check, so it accepted the handoff.

Decode attention. Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations.

Response. The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400. prompt_tokens matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. It arrived faster than an 8-page prefill should take, and it contained content from other users' KV pages.

Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue #30233 on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.

GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.

Ongoing hardening effort

This bug belongs to a class of KV cache memory-safety bugs that Cloudflare has been working to address for several months. In each case, a page is freed, reused, or read while something else still has a claim on it. We see two common causes.

The first is page lifetime within a single node. Several tasks on a decode node can hold the same page at once: token generation, offload to host memory, the KV transfer receiver, and the abort and error paths. If one of them frees the page while another is still using it, a new request can be given that page while it is still being read or written. Our earlier fixes for decode offload (#24226, #30899) and double release on grammar errors (#30937) were of this kind.

The second is a race across nodes. When a request is aborted while prefill is still writing its KV cache to decode over RDMA, the writes already sent cannot be recalled. If decode frees those pages right away, those pages can be given to another request, and the late writes land in that request's KV cache. Cloudflare has contributed to the effort to fix this race through proposed fixes (#31357, #38961) and a reproduction script (#32564). In both cases the result is corrupted output, or one user's data in another user's response, with no error raised. The bug in this incident was different: a rejected request went through the handoff every time, rather than by a timing accident. But it had the same result: decode reading pages this request never wrote. None of these covered the failure in this incident in which prefill rejected the request, and decode never learned of it.

Since the incident, we have:

Extended deferred release to hold prefill's source pages as well, and to cover every failure type, not just aborts. We proposed it upstream as #38961, which was superseded by #40645, #41402, and #41404.

Deployed bounded Mooncake transfer batches (#32758, from the SGLang community), so no single transfer call can outlast the release timeout.

Changed our load balancer so a client disconnect no longer aborts a request mid-transfer. It holds the prefill connection until prefill finishes and the decode connection until the first token, then closes both.

Added a check to every disaggregated deployment change: KV pool size measured against context length, deferred release on both roles, transfer batch bounds inside the release timeout, and all required patches applied.

All of these changes were released to our disaggregated production deployments.

Working with the SGLang team

We met with the SGLang maintainers at RadixArk on September 10, the day after the incident. We agreed that RadixArk would investigate the race conditions we had reported, upstream the integrity-checking idea, and build reproduction tests for this class of bug.

The following have landed on SGLang main to address this incident and related KV cache race conditions, and all but one are included in v0.5.22. Operators running disaggregated SGLang should update to v0.5.22 or backport these patches as needed.

What we recommend to other operators

If you run SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode, we recommend the following:

Measure your KV pool and compare it to your context length, on every prefill and decode node, from the engine's startup log, after every change to weights, quantization, parallelism, or memory fraction. If the pool is smaller, lower the context length to fit. Do not rely on a proxy to enforce the limit, and do not assume the engine will reject what does not fit. This is the check we did not enforce.

Upgrade to a build that includes #36988 and #38935 (v0.5.22 or later), so an over-length request is rejected before handoff regardless of pool size. This is the engine-side fix, and it is the backstop for the day your check in step one is wrong.

Run with deferred KV release on both roles (default after #41023), and bound your Mooncake transfer batches so a single timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded tail of writes.

Turn on corruption detection where your model supports it. --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum and --kv-canary do not yet cover every model architecture. Check your logs to confirm requests are being verified. We are working with the SGLang team to extend both checks to more architectures, including GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.

Ensure your proxy is not generating unnecessary aborts. Configure your load balancer to allow requests to proceed up to the first token, so that you do not trigger an abort that requires cross-node coordination.

Longer term

Integrity by construction

Configuration checks and lifecycle fixes reduce the number of ways a page can be misused. They do not make misuse impossible, and this incident is a reminder that the next bug will have a shape we have not seen. The durable answer is for the engine to detect, at read time, that a request is about to attend over a page it does not own, and fail that one request rather than return someone else's data.

We built a prototype of this over the summer and described it in August. Every physical KV page carries a tag that changes when the page is reallocated, each request records the tags it expects, and the mapping is checked before decode reads the cache. In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues.

The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in #39500 is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer.

Integrity by mathematical impossibility

RDMA copies data directly from one node’s memory to another’s. It’s vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when it’s finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system.

Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods. Topaz enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of Meerkat’s QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed.

We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLang’s distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove — as far as possible — that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps.

Coordinated disclosure

We are publishing this report as part of a coordinated disclosure. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.

Read more at the post from the SGLang team.

If you find a security issue in Workers AI, please report it at hackerone.com/cloudflare.

Title: PHP2Shell Is a Wake-Up Call for Every Business Leader
Context: AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw...
Full Text:
AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw being found and a flaw being exploited keeps shrinking. Today, we have more known vulnerabilities than at any point in history, and they’re being exploited faster than ever. Nearly 87% of exploited vulnerabilities in 2026 have been exploited before or on the day they were disclosed, up from 48% in 2024 and just 19% in 2018, according to zerodayclock.com, a neutral, independent observatory for cybersecurity telemetry.

More code, more bugs, and AI-aided discovery have all influenced this volume. The systems exposed are often the same systems that run revenue, operations, and customer relationships. Leaders now need to focus on something bigger than prevention alone. They need to build cyber resilience, the ability to withstand an attack, continue operating, and recover quickly. Every organization is racing against the clock to build that resilience.

We saw this play out recently during a week that saw multiple high-profile vulnerabilities and security incidents emerge in rapid succession. PHP2Shell, the name given to two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in PHP, became one of the most visible examples of how quickly newly disclosed flaws can become immediate operational risks. Researchers using frontier AI models identified the flaws and worked with the PHP Foundation to prepare fixes, but details leaked before the planned release. Patches were pushed early, but between the time the vulnerability was disclosed and the patch was available, exploitation attempts began appearing almost immediately. Our Arctic Wolf Labs researchers used aggregated, anonymized telemetry from across our customer community to spot spikes in scanning activity and to analyze exploitation attempts and uncover attacker payloads tied to PHP2Shell. Labs also replicated attacker techniques in controlled environments.

Those findings fed new detections, threat hunt queries, and immediately valuable customer remediation guidance, but detection and response work like this is most effective when an organization already knows what it needs to protect. While PHP2Shell captured much of the industry’s attention, it was only one example in a week that underscored how quickly new exposures can emerge across technologies and attack surfaces. The broader lesson is that organizations need resilience before the next disclosure arrives, and that the time to build cyber resilience into an organization’s ecosystem is now. Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic, warned on X following the PHP2Shell disclosure that security leaders need to prepare their boards as soon as possible for the new threat landscape.

“As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better. security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)” — Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic

Organizations best positioned during that window already knew where PHP ran in their environment, which of those systems faced the internet, and how quickly they could patch, restart, and verify each one. A flaw in a system you cannot see cannot be fixed in the hours that matter. Those are the basics boards need to fund. Because the gap between discovery and exploitation will keep shrinking, the organizations that win the race against the clock are the ones that build that foundation of continuous visibility into their attack surface and disciplined exposure management before the next disclosure arrives.

Machine Speed Is the New Normal

AI accelerated both sides of the PHP2Shell situation timeline. The underlying flaws in the code had reportedly been in PHP for years, and turning them into a usable exploit required a level of complexity that would have been extremely difficult and time-consuming for most researchers to achieve on their own. Attackers gain the same AI efficiencies defenders do. They’re using AI to write malware, build exploits, find vulnerabilities, and automate actions. This means the gap between a flaw being disclosed and being exploited will keep narrowing. Patching alone cannot keep pace when that gap is just a few hours long.

In many circumstances, a vulnerability is disclosed before a patch is available. PHP2Shell showed us that. In those moments, security leaders need a way to detect exploit attempts and respond effectively. Machine speed meets that moment, especially when an exposure is widespread, and security leaders should recognize that machine-speed attack and defense are the new normal.

That shift has implications far beyond the security team. Cyber risk now deserves the same level of ownership, accountability, and investment as financial and operational risk. Boards and executive teams need to treat security as a business issue, not just a technical one. That starts with the fundamentals, including maintaining an accurate inventory of assets, applying patches on a defined timeline, enforcing strong identity controls, and maintaining continuous visibility across the environment. These aren’t new security practices, but they become far more important as AI compresses response timelines. You can’t remediate a vulnerability in hours if you don’t know the system exists.

The Four Fundamental Principles of Threat Protection for the AI Era

Vulnerabilities aren’t the only path to a breach. Initial access comes from social engineering (which is scaling with AI), internet-facing misconfigurations, and internet-facing vulnerabilities. Once an attacker is inside, more internal exposure means faster movement. We want to close the opportunity through configuration health and security hygiene.

Security fundamentals only work when teams can operationalize them consistently.

Exposure management strategies turn security hygiene upkeep into a repeatable process. Start with full visibility of your attack surface, including shadow IT and configuration gaps. Then connect asset management with vulnerability and patch management so each cycle improves on the last. Find known and hidden assets, assess them in the context of one another, identify where vulnerabilities are present and controls are missing, and mitigate the highest impact exposures first.

True resilience requires a continuous cycle of risk mitigation over time. Fewer exposures mean fewer opportunities for attackers, and organizations of every size can better defend against AI-driven threats with AI-driven defense and expert oversight. That means operating at machine speed with experts overseeing the work, and it requires knowing your environment, maintaining strong security fundamentals, and responding quickly when new threats emerge. In an era of machine-speed attacks, resilience belongs to organizations that can move just as fast.

Security operations must evolve as well. Human-only processes can’t keep pace with the speed and volume of modern threats. At the same time, fully autonomous security without oversight introduces its own risks. AI should handle most of the volume of investigation that slows down teams, while experienced analysts focus on validation, judgment, and the genuinely complex threats that require context. We’ve built Arctic Wolf around that principle. Our patent-pending Swarm of Experts™ combines specialized AI agents with expert human oversight, allowing us to operate at machine speed. Large teams of AI agents perform investigations, analysis, and response activities at scale, while experienced security experts remain involved where judgment matters most.

Leaders also need to prepare for the reality that one day, their organization may fall victim to AI-driven adversaries, with tested response plans and the ability to restore operations quickly. As the threat landscape rapidly evolves, this scenario appears increasingly likely, especially for businesses that lack the resources to staff their own security team.

We built Arctic Wolf for moments like this one. Internal staffing around the clock is difficult and costly, even for large organizations. Attackers don’t care about holidays, and AI cares even less. That’s why a partner matters. By combining AI-driven automation with expert human oversight, we help customers respond with speed and confidence when new risks emerge. Through our global partner ecosystem, we’re bringing that capability to organizations around the world and helping security leaders turn cyber risk into cyber resilience.

PHP2Shell won’t be the last vulnerability to remind us how quickly the threat landscape can change. This isn’t a risk to sleep on or push to next year’s budget. The time to act is now. The organizations that come through these moments will be the ones that understand their environments, maintain strong security fundamentals, and can respond decisively when new threats emerge. There has never been a better time to get proactive about cyber resilience.

This blog reflects the author’s views as of the publication date and contains forward-looking statements and opinions about technology trends. Actual outcomes may differ based on attacker behavior, customer environments, and broader market and regulatory developments.

SUNNYVALE, Calif., October 26, 2026 – Proofpoint Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced it is joining the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) vendor ecosystem. The new integration enables Microsoft 365 customers to layer Proofpoint’s market-leading Core Email Protection API into their existing Microsoft security environment and view Proofpoint detections directly within the Microsoft Defender portal.

This milestone builds on Proofpoint’s growing integration with Microsoft services and extends that interoperability into the ICES ecosystem to deliver a more unified security experience. Proofpoint’s integration with Microsoft’s native protection adds human-centric threat detection for more comprehensive, layered protection against email-based threats.

“Organizations rely on both Microsoft and Proofpoint to protect their most critical communications and data,” said Tom Corn, Executive Vice President and General Manager, Threat Protection Group at Proofpoint. “By extending Proofpoint’s interoperability across ICES, we’re delivering a more unified security experience that strengthens defense-in-depth and simplifies operations for our shared customers. This milestone reflects our commitment to joint customers worldwide.”

A Unified Security Experience for Microsoft Customers

Through the ICES integration, Microsoft customers can view Proofpoint’s API-based detections directly within the Microsoft Defender portal. This reduces friction for security operations center (SOC) teams by minimizing context switching and streamlining investigative workflows.

Key customer benefits include:

Integrated visibility: Security teams can see Proofpoint detections alongside Microsoft detections in a single console, accelerating investigations and improving response times.

Layered protection: Powered by advanced AI from Proofpoint Nexus, Proofpoint’s Core Email Protection API enhances Microsoft’s native controls with 99.999% detection efficacy, delivering true defense-in-depth against phishing, business email compromise, ransomware, and other sophisticated email-based attacks.

Operational efficiency: Streamlined workflows reduce analyst burden and enable faster, more coordinated threat response.

“Our focus is on building a cohesive defense fabric that drives real efficiency for security operations centers, anchored in Microsoft Defender,” said Oz Wilder, Partner Director for email and collaboration security, Microsoft. “The ICES ecosystem enables customers to adapt and scale with the evolving threat landscape. By integrating with Microsoft Defender, Proofpoint helps deliver a more consistent and simplified security operations experience for shared customers in Microsoft Defender.”

Partnership Momentum Accelerates

Proofpoint protects more than 1.8 million Microsoft customers worldwide, making its participation in ICES a natural evolution of the partnership and a commitment to delivering tightly integrated security experiences.

With industry-leading, human-centric threat detection and a proven record of protecting enterprise email at scale, Proofpoint brings depth and interoperability to the Microsoft security ecosystem.

Title: Meet the Huntress Neighborhood Watch Program

As a managed service provider (MSP), you protect dozens of businesses. Maybe hundreds. But who’s protecting you?

It’s the question most MSPs don’t have time to ask. Your team has remote access to everything. Your tools hold the keys to your customers’ networks. Your own environment is exactly the kind of target attackers dream about, because one way in can mean many ways out.

And you’re the one who’s supposed to have this handled.

That’s why we built the Neighborhood Watch Program.

What is the Huntress Neighborhood Watch Program?

The Huntress Neighborhood Watch Program is a collection of programs and resources designed to help elevate the broader security community. To kick things off, we’re making the Huntress Managed Security Platform available to any MSP for internal use at no cost to keep your own house secure, even if you’re not a Huntress partner. This includes our human 24/7 SOC team, threat hunting and everything else we’ve added to our platform over the last few years.

Getting started with our Neighborhood Watch Program takes about an hour of your time. We’ll ask you to spend 30 minutes with our team to get an understanding of how our platform works followed by setting up your account and deploying our technology through a trial.

Give us an hour of your time and we’ll protect the internal devices at your MSP, no strings attached.

More importantly, we’re just getting started.

We will continue making investments like this to help keep our industry more secure while we build a healthy business. Giving back and growing revenue do not need to be mutually exclusive, and we’re so excited to share our ideas of how the Huntress Neighborhood Watch Program will evolve as we further our mission of bringing cybersecurity to the 99%.

Get Free NFR Licenses

Why protect your own environment first?

Because your risk isn’t just yours.

When an MSP gets compromised, the damage doesn’t stop at your front door. It can reach the customers who trust you. That’s a different kind of weight than a normal business carries.

There’s a second reason, and it’s less scary but just as real. You shouldn’t deploy a platform you’ve never lived with. You need to know how the alerts read at 2 p.m. on a Tuesday. You need to know what it’s like when the SOC reaches out. You need to know what your techs think after a month of using it.

Running Huntress internally lets you check the things that matter:

Product fit for the way your team works

Alert quality and noise

How the SOC investigates and communicates

Reporting you could show a client

The real operational effort of keeping it running

You don’t have to take our word for it. You can see it for yourself.

What’s included in Neighborhood Watch?

You get access to the Huntress Managed Security Platform, backed by our 24/7 SOC. That means expert SOC analysts monitoring, investigating, and responding around the clock, so your small team isn’t doing it alone.

Here’s how the platform breaks down:

Endpoint protection and response: Managed Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)

Identity protection: Managed Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR)

Security operations and compliance support: Managed Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)

Human risk reduction: Managed Security Awareness Training (SAT)

Identity hardening: Managed Identity Security Posture Management (ISPM)

Endpoint hardening: Managed Endpoint Security Posture Management (ESPM), currently in early access

How the program works

Three steps. No guesswork.

Request access. Fill out the internal license request form.

The Pwn Request Reckoning: What Still Works Against GitHub Actions
Context: Checkout protections, read-only cache tokens, and event policies close the paths that made exploitation trivial
Full Text:
For years, pull_request_target has been the canonical Pwn request vector: a workflow trigger that runs with repository secrets, yet can be triggered by anyone who opens a pull request from a fork. In 2026, GitHub responded with platform changes that make the default-case exploit significantly harder..

These changes represent real progress. Checkout protections, read-only cache tokens, and event policies close the paths that made exploitation trivial. But they don't eliminate the vulnerability class. They shift it. Attackers who previously exploited any pull_request_target workflow now need to find explicit opt-ins, outdated checkout versions, unprotected triggers, or script injection.

In Part 1 of our GitHub Actions research, we laid out the threat model and core defenses, and Part 2 covered AI-powered actions. This post updates that threat model for 2026: what GitHub's changes actually protect against, where the gaps remain, and how defenders need to adjust. The audit checklist at the end covers what to look for in your own workflows.

The 2026 Security Overhaul: Timeline of Changes

Recognizing the endemic risk posed by Pwn requests, GitHub spent 2026 systematically closing the gap through a phased rollout of platform-level protections and action updates.

Date

Milestone & Action Taken

June 18, 2026

Release of actions/checkout@v7.0.0, blocking fork code checkouts by default in untrusted triggers (pull_request_target, and workflow_run triggered by pull requests).

June 26, 2026

GitHub introduces read-only cache tokens at the platform level for untrusted triggers, preventing cache poisoning attacks.

July 20, 2026

Backported fork checkout protections across all active major versions of actions/checkout (v2.8.0, v3.7.0, v4.4.0, v5.1.0, and v6.1.0; v1 excluded). Workflows referencing mutable version tags (e.g., @v4) inherit these defenses automatically.

September 10, 2026

Fine-grained cache controls via cache-mode reached General Availability (GA).

September 17, 2026

Workflow Execution Protections reached GA, enabling fine-grained event policies and actor rules.

December 2, 2026

[Scheduled] GitHub begins enforcing the default event policy that blocks pull_request_target in public repositories without an explicit event policy. The rule has been in evaluate mode since September 17. Private and internal repositories are not affected.

Residual Risk: What Still Works

While this sequence of platform updates significantly strengthens default security configurations for GitHub Actions, they don't remove all risk.

The December 2 enforcement is a default, not a ban. Maintainers whose automation depends on pull_request_target (labelers, preview deploys, fork CI with secrets) will add an event policy that allows it. Those are exactly the workflows that handle untrusted input with elevated privileges. The default policy also doesn't apply to private and internal repositories or to workflow_run. The rest of this section covers how these surviving workflows can still be exploited.

SHA Pinning: The Security Paradox

One of the most disconcerting findings in our research is how standard supply chain hardening advice - specifically pinning actions to exact commit SHAs - can inadvertently bypass GitHub's platform defenses.

# "Security-hardened" workflow: SHA-pinned for supply chain safety - uses: actions/checkout@08eba0b27e820071cde6df949e0beb9ba4906955 # v4.3.0

Because GitHub's backported protections rely on logic embedded within actions/checkout itself, pinning to SHA values prior to the July 20, 2026 backport release means the workflow runs legacy code without any safety checks. Our empirical testing across workflow triggers confirmed this discrepancy: referencing mutable tags like @v4 (resolving to v4.4.x) or pinned versions such as @v4.4.0 remain protected, whereas older versions like @v4.3.0 or SHA-pinned references to legacy releases (such as @08eba0b... resolving to v4.3.0) offer no protection.

To maintain protection, security teams using SHA pinning must ensure their refs are updated to match or exceed the minimum patched release versions: v2.8.0, v3.7.0, v4.4.0, v5.1.0, v6.1.0, or v7.0.0+.

Custom Checkout Scripts and Third-Party Actions

A second gap concerns workflows that bypass actions/checkout altogether. GitHub's protections are implemented within the action's code - any alternative method of fetching code operates unrestricted. Direct CLI invocations sidestep protections entirely:

- env: GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }} PR_REPO: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name }} PR_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} run: | # Any one of these fetches fork code without actions/checkout's protections # Bypass 1: Direct git clone git clone "https://github.com/${PR_REPO}" pr-code && git -C pr-code checkout "${PR_SHA}" # Bypass 2: gh pr checkout (runs in the base repo's workspace) gh pr checkout "${PR_NUMBER}" # Bypass 3: gh repo clone gh repo clone "${PR_REPO}" fork-code

Third-party checkout actions implement their own git logic, so they don't inherit these protections. Any of them configured with a PR head ref will check out fork code unrestricted.

Unprotected Privileged Triggers

GitHub's checkout protections only cover pull_request_target and workflow_run:

Pwn requests triggered in other event types besides pull_request_target (such as issue_comment) will not be blocked by this change. Further hardening of additional events may be explored in future releases.

GitHub changelog

This creates an inconsistent security boundary: GitHub's cache controls explicitly treat issue_comment as a low-trust trigger, while checkout protections do not. Workflows using issue_comment for bot commands (/deploy, /test, /cherry-pick) remain fully exploitable with checkout v7 - no allow-unsafe-pr-checkout flag required:

on: issue_comment: types: [created] jobs: deploy: if: github.event.issue.pull_request && contains(github.event.comment.body, '/deploy') runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 with: ref: refs/pull/${{ github.event.issue.number }}/merge # Checks out fork PR code

Other privileged triggers have the same gap. repository_dispatch also runs with secrets, and it's exploitable when a workflow uses attacker-influenced payload data to choose a checkout ref.

Until GitHub extends checkout protections, these workflows have to enforce their own authorization, and it needs to hold from the moment the event fires until the code runs:

- Verify who triggered it. For comment commands, check the commenter's actual repository permission (getCollaboratorPermissionLevel, write or above). Don't rely on author_association, which doesn't reflect current permissions. For repository_dispatch, limit who holds a token that can send the event, and don't treat the payload as proof of who sent it.

- Pin what was approved. refs/pull/N/merge is mutable, so an attacker can push a malicious commit after a maintainer comments /deploy. Check out the exact head SHA, and abort if the PR was updated after the comment was posted.

- Treat the event payload as untrusted input. Validate comment arguments and dispatch payload fields against a strict, anchored allowlist regex, and pass them to the shell through environment variables, never through ${{ }} interpolation.

Script Injection: Pwn Request Without Checkout

A common misconception is that pull_request_target vulnerabilities require checking out fork code. In reality, attackers can achieve code execution without any checkout step, through script injection.

When workflow authors interpolate event context directly into shell commands using ${{ }} expressions, GitHub substitutes the value into the script before the shell runs, so attacker-controlled data becomes part of the command itself:

on: pull_request_target jobs: greet: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: echo "Thanks for PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

An attacker simply crafts a pull request with a malicious title:

"; touch /tmp/pwned; echo INJECTED #

The quote closes the string, the semicolon ends the echo, and everything after it runs as a new command with the job's secrets and token. None of GitHub's 2026 changes touch this: there is no checkout to block, and the vulnerability lies in how the workflow handles untrusted input.

The fix is to never interpolate untrusted input into a script. Pass it through an environment variable instead, so the shell treats it as data:

- env: PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} run: echo "Thanks for PR: $PR_TITLE"

The double quotes around $PR_TITLE matter. Without them, the shell still word-splits and glob-expands the value.

Persistent Data Channels: Beyond Cache Tokens

GitHub's read-only cache tokens protect the Actions cache service, but workflows can still exchange data through channels that remain unaffected.

Artifact Poisoning

The upload-artifact and download-artifact actions operate independently of cache tokens. The classic attack chain uses an unprivileged pull_request workflow to upload attacker-controlled build outputs, then a privileged workflow_run to download and execute them:

# .github/workflows/build.yml - unprivileged, runs the fork's code name: Build on: pull_request jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - run: npm ci && npm run build # Attacker-controlled - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 with: name: build-output path: ./dist/ # .github/workflows/deploy.yml - privileged, has secrets name: Deploy Preview on: workflow_run: workflows: ["Build"] types: [completed] jobs: deploy: if: github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4 with: name: build-output path: ./dist/ run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }} # Fetches the fork run's artifact github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - run: ./dist/deploy.sh # Executes attacker-controlled file env: DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }} # Exposed to attacker code

This is exactly the workflow_run scenario checkout v7 was built to block, and it doesn't help here. The privileged workflow never checks out fork code; it downloads it. Unlike cache entries, there's no platform equivalent that marks artifacts from untrusted runs as tainted, so any workflow that downloads and executes artifacts from a less-trusted run inherits the risk.

Self-Hosted Runner State

On non-ephemeral self-hosted runners, filesystem state persists between jobs. Local package manager caches (~/.npm, ~/.cache/pip), build directories, and installed tools live on the runner's disk, outside the Actions cache service, so read-only cache tokens don't cover them. Attacker code running under an untrusted trigger can write to these locations and poison the next trusted workflow scheduled on the same machine, including release and publish jobs. Use ephemeral runners, which are wiped after each job, for any workflow that untrusted events can trigger, and keep untrusted and trusted workflows in separate runner groups.

The Misconception That Won't Die

Many security teams believe they have another safeguard in place: the "Require approval for all external contributors" setting under Settings -> Actions -> General. If enabled, fork PRs need maintainer approval before workflows run. Problem solved, right?

Not quite. That setting only gates pull_request workflows, which run the fork's own workflow YAML. For pull_request_target, GitHub considers the workflow definition trusted (it comes from the base repository), so the approval setting doesn't apply and the run starts immediately.

The irony cuts deep: pull_request_target is the more dangerous trigger (secrets access, write tokens), yet it's the one that skips the approval requirement. If a pull_request_target workflow needs a human gate, put the privileged job behind an environment with required reviewers, or restrict who can trigger it with Workflow Execution Protections actor rules.

Explicit Opt-In: allow-unsafe-pr-checkout

Finally, developers who need to interact with fork code can explicitly disable checkout protections by enabling the allow-unsafe-pr-checkout flag:

- uses: actions/checkout@v7 with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true # Re-enables untrusted fork checkouts

While the parameter name is deliberately alarming, determined development teams or third-party workflows may still employ it to maintain legacy automation, effectively reopening the exact same execution vector as before. Security teams should pay special attention to any use of this flag.

What Changed

To sum up, GitHub's 2026 security rollout deserves credit. Default event policies, checkout protections, and read-only cache tokens make the trivial Pwn request (fork, PR, profit) significantly harder. Starting December 2, pull_request_target will no longer run in public repositories unless an event policy explicitly allows it. Cache poisoning through the Actions cache is mitigated. These are real wins.

But the vulnerability class isn't eliminated. It shifted. What remains exploitable: explicit opt-ins via allow-unsafe-pr-checkout, SHA-pinned versions predating the July 2026 backport, custom checkout scripts that bypass action-level controls, script injection requiring no checkout at all, unprotected triggers like issue_comment and repository_dispatch, artifact poisoning chains from pull_request to workflow_run, persistent state on non-ephemeral self-hosted runners, and private or internal repositories, which the default policy doesn't cover. The attack surface shrinks, but what remains is harder to spot.

What To Do About It

Start by auditing what you already run, then get ahead of the December 2 enforcement.

Audit Your Workflows

Wiz Code automatically scans GitHub Actions workflows for Pwn requests, script injection, version gaps, and risky configurations to cover this residual attack surface. Alternatively, use open-source tools like zizmor or even these basic grep searches to start the audit:

# Flag risky triggers, unsafe checkouts, outdated checkout versions, artifact downloads, # self-hosted runners and event data in expressions (env: usage is safe), then review each hit grep -rnE 'pull_request_target|workflow_run|issue_comment|repository_dispatch|allow-unsafe-pr-checkout|self-hosted|download-artifact|gh (pr checkout|repo clone)|git (clone|fetch)|refs/pull|actions/checkout@v(1|2\.[0-7]|3\.[0-6]|4\.[0-3]|5\.0|6\.0)([^0-9]|$)|\$\{\{[[:space:]]*github\.(event\.|head_ref)' .github/workflows/

In addition, run this script to resolve each SHA to its release tag, then compare against the patched versions:

tags=$(git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/actions/checkout) grep -rhoE "actions/checkout@[0-9a-f]{40}" .github/workflows/ | cut -d@ -f2 | sort -u | while read -r sha; do tag=$(echo "$tags" | grep "^$sha" | sed 's#.*refs/tags/##; s#\^{}$##' | sort -V | tail -1) echo "$sha ${tag:-UNKNOWN - not a release tag, check manually}" done

Preparing for the December 2 pull_request_target Enforcement

Starting December 2, the default event policy will block pull_request_target in public repositories that have no explicit event policy. workflow_run is not affected, and neither are private or internal repositories. Before that date:

Check policy insights to see which pull_request_target runs would be blocked.

Decide per workflow whether it actually needs pull_request_target. If not, move it to pull_request. If a privileged follow-up step is still needed, a workflow_run workflow can handle it, but it must treat the PR run's artifacts as untrusted data, never execute them.

For workflows that legitimately need fork access, create an explicit event policy and use workflow file targeting to allow pull_request_target only for those files. Treat every file on that allowlist as high-risk: run it through the audit above before adding it, and re-audit whenever it changes.

AI Agents Don’t Stop at the Device. Your Security Program Shouldn’t Either.

October 26, 2026

GuidePoint Security

By Chris Hughes, VP Security Strategy, Noma

BLOG

5 min.

AI agents don’t need an exploit to cause damage. They just need permission, something most security teams already granted, one login at a time.

Why Is This Suddenly a Governance Problem?

AI agents have moved from experimental to running daily workflows on employee devices. Developers use coding agents to inspect repositories, run terminal commands and open pull requests. Business users deploy productivity agents to search documents, draft emails and update CRM records, extending both with MCP servers, skills and connectors often installed from public registries in minutes, with no review process.

No single action here is dangerous on its own. The agent inherits permissions to everything the employee running it can reach: credentials, browser sessions, internal systems, even production infrastructure and a config edit or a linked account can extend that reach before security has any record of the change.

The device isn’t the end of the story. A coding agent that starts on a laptop can call a homegrown service or cloud API. A productivity agent can move from local files into a SaaS platform in the same task. The device is where the agent launches, not the boundary of what it can reach.

TL;DR – AI agents can use an employee’s access to carry out tasks across enterprise systems. Individually authorized actions can combine into data exposure risk or destructive changes that single-event controls miss and the full sequence often runs beyond the device where the agent started.

Key Takeaways:

Agents already operate with the same access as the people running them, extended further by MCP servers, skills and connectors.

Risk usually comes from a sequence of individually legitimate actions, often crossing from the device into SaaS and homegrown systems.

Closing the gap means extending the visibility security teams already have on the endpoint into one model that follows an agent everywhere it goes.

When Does Legitimate Agent Activity Become Risky?

An agent can use an approved application, act on behalf of an authenticated user and make permitted API calls while still exposing sensitive data or making destructive changes. The risk becomes clear only when you look at how those actions connect across the full session.

Consider a desktop agent handling routine CRM follow-ups: one lead record contains instructions to email account history and contact details to an external address. The agent follows those instructions, though they came from the record rather than the user. The query, the data access and the email tool were each authorized on their own. Only connecting the untrusted instruction to the data pull and the outbound send reveals how a routine task became data exposure, starting on a device and ending through a SaaS application.

Agent risk is often distributed across a sequence of actions that each look fine in isolation and increasingly, across more than one environment.

What Are the Recurring Failure Modes?

A few patterns show up again and again as organizations adopt agents:

Shadow agents and configuration drift

Employees install a new assistant or MCP server to finish a task, then move on, leaving the configuration behind long after anyone is tracking it.

Personal account connections

Agents can authenticate through personal accounts on the same device used for work, creating a path for company data to cross identity boundaries outside enterprise administration.

Excessive permissions

A connector added for one read-only task can just as easily expose write, delete or administrative functions the job never required, a pattern OWASP names directly as Excessive Agency in its Top 10 for LLM Applications.

Supply chain exposure

Every MCP server, skill and connector an agent uses can be misconfigured, compromised or quietly updated after it was first reviewed.

In one documented case, a widely used coding CLI was found uploading entire local repositories, commit history included, to the vendor’s own cloud storage, independent of what the model had actually read.

Prompt injection and tool poisoning

Agents process natural language from sources they don’t control: web pages, tickets, code comments, tool responses. For example, instructions hidden in an MCP tool’s own description can silently redirect an agent’s actions.

None of these require a sophisticated attacker. They’re the result of giving autonomous software the same reach and access as a trusted employee, without the judgment a human applies.

Extending Endpoint Visibility Across the Full Agent Estate

Endpoint-focused discovery and control are the right starting point: they tell security teams which agents, MCP servers and skills are actually running on employee devices.

The opportunity is to carry that same visibility to where an agent’s activity actually goes. In the CRM example above, the agent launched from a desktop, but the exposure happened when data moved to an external recipient through a SaaS-based email tool. Connecting an agent’s local footprint to its identity, destination and behavior across SaaS and homegrown systems is what turns endpoint visibility into full protection.

Security teams get the most value by extending what they already have on the endpoint with a unified policy model and behavioral baseline that follows an agent into every environment it reaches, so the same identity, rules and audit trail apply wherever the agent runs.

How Should Security Teams Respond?

Locking agents down entirely isn’t realistic. The goal is bringing every agent, wherever it runs, into one governance model that builds on endpoint visibility.

1. Build a live inventory across every environment

You can’t govern agents, MCP servers and skills you don’t know exist. Discovery should cover what’s actively running and what’s configured but dormant, since a dormant component can become active the moment an agent invokes it.

2. Apply least-privilege access control consistently

Govern which MCP servers, tools and skills agents can use based on identity and group membership and scope permissions to individual tools and actions so access to a system doesn’t automatically include write, delete or admin rights.

3. Set business-defined boundaries that follow the agent, not the environment

Some risk depends on cumulative effect, not any single action, like a refund agent with no daily cap. Those limits need to hold regardless of where the agent is invoked from.

4. Detect and stop risky behavior across the full session

An agent may encounter a prompt injection, retrieve sensitive data and attempt to send it outside the company minutes later through a connected SaaS application. Security needs to connect those actions and intervene while the task is underway.

5. Establish ownership and identity context from day one

Know who owns each agent, whose credentials it uses and which tools and skills are approved for that user or group, with ownership, review status and approvals managed under one model.

6. Build toward a single control plane

As agents show up in new places, from endpoint devices to SaaS platforms to homegrown systems, the organizations getting this right consolidate around one policy model and one behavioral baseline that extends their existing endpoint investment to follow an agent wherever it runs.

So Where Do You Go From Here?

Effective agent governance brings discovery, identity-based access control, business-defined boundaries and runtime enforcement into one model across endpoint, SaaS and homegrown agents, extending the visibility security teams have already built rather than replacing it.

This is the kind of work GuidePoint Security helps organizations operationalize: connecting existing identity, endpoint and access governance programs to cover agents and the systems they reach, with consistent policies and a clear process for responding when activity becomes risky.

The organizations managing this well are the ones who treated agent governance as one identity and access problem from the start, covering endpoint, SaaS and homegrown agents under a single model rather than solving each surface on its own.

Agents aren’t going away and neither is the access they’ve already inherited. The question isn’t whether to let employees use them. It’s whether security has one consistent answer, across every environment, to what those agents can reach, what they’re allowed to do and how you’d know if that changed.

Today, we're releasing the Claude for Nonprofits plugin, a set of skills and connectors built with ~30 nonprofits. It helps teams set up Claude responsibly with their organization's context and policies, supports fundraising from research through reporting, and takes on the operational work that stretches small teams. We're also planning to extend Claude Corps (opens in new tab), our program for placing early-career fellows in U.S. nonprofits, through a partnership with Taproot (opens in new tab).

As a public benefit corporation, Anthropic has a responsibility to make sure our products are accessible and useful to organizations working on the world’s hardest problems. Last December, we launched Claude for Nonprofits (opens in new tab) with discounts of up to 75%, connectors for Blackbaud, Candid, and Benevity, and a free AI Fluency course built with GivingTuesday. More than 25,000 nonprofits now use Claude in their work. Most of those organizations are small, local operations: more than 75% of them have fewer than 10 Claude seats. We think today's update will have the biggest impact on these organizations.

We’ve spent the last year working directly with nonprofits to meet their needs. We expanded nonprofit plans to the same models as our standard Team and Enterprise plans, lowered the Team plan minimum to orgs with as few as two people, and included Claude Code in nonprofit plans at no additional cost. And during the United Nations General Assembly in September, we launched a new discount of ~90% for verified nonprofits in low- and middle-income countries, bringing standard Team seats to $3/user/month.

Cost is only one barrier. Nonprofits told us two others stood in the way: a lack of people with the skills to put AI to work, and a lack of tools built specifically for how nonprofits operate.

Too few people with AI skills. Claude Corps is placing 1,000 early-career fellows in at least 400 US nonprofits to build with Claude alongside their teams. Hosts include a wide variety of organizations, from large organizations to small, local teams, including food banks, art museums, and veteran support organizations. We’re now planning to extend this program through a partnership with Taproot, which would match nonprofits with experienced pro bono consultants for shorter, project-based work. A growing group of partners can support nonprofit adoption, including Accenture, Boston Consulting Group (BCG), The Bridgespan Group, Civis Analytics, Deloitte, fusionSpan, Idealist Consulting, Myridius, SapienAI, Slalom, v4c.ai, and Vera Solutions. And for teams getting started on their own, we’re hosting two live webinars: Claude for Nonprofits: An Admin's Guide to Data Handling and AI Use Policy (opens in new tab), for admins, on November 10, and Claude for Nonprofits: A Staff Guide to Making Claude Useful on Day One (opens in new tab) on November 12.

Too few tools built to meet nonprofits where they’re at. We built the skills we're releasing today with the nonprofits in our Design Partner Circle. It includes ~30 organizations, from small teams serving one region of the United States to international organizations operating in dozens of countries, working on education, economic mobility, health, humanitarian response, and more. Many are funders themselves. This fall, fundraisers, operations leads, and chiefs of staff at many of these organizations tried early versions of our skills on real work and told us what wasn't working. We brainstormed, iterated, and updated our solution based on what we heard.

What's in the plugin

We’re starting with three areas nonprofits told us were most urgent, especially as year-end fundraising picks up.

Extend your team

Many nonprofits told us the same thing: there are more jobs to do than people to do them, so everyone covers several roles at once. Claude extends your team, so a small staff can work like a bigger one and spend more of its time on the mission.

Marketing: plan a campaign sized to your team’s bandwidth, teach Claude to draft in your organization’s voice, and get a second read on your content before it goes out.

Hiring and people: build a job post with an interview guide and scoring rubric, plan a new hire's first 90 days, and answer staff questions from your own handbook.

Board and leadership: see what skills your board is missing, draft outreach to the candidates you have in mind, get new members up to speed with an orientation packet, and plan the deck for your next meeting.

Set up Claude responsibly: security, governance, and context

Claude works best when it has your organization’s context, including your mission, programs, workstreams, communication principles, and policies, and when your staff have clear rules for working with it. Start by asking Claude to:

Map your organization. Claude asks where you keep each kind of record, like donor data, grant files, finances and policies, and, with memory on, saves that map for each person. It then offers to connect the tools it can't reach yet. Every other skill in the plugin reads the map first, so Claude knows where to look and you don't have to point it to the same source for each task.

Check what your AI policy allows. Staff can ask "Can I use Claude for this?" and get the answer based on your organization's own AI policy. (No policy yet? See the Claude Academy tutorial below.)

Fund your mission

Fundraising is the lifeline for nonprofits, and it matters even more toward the end of the year. It's also time-intensive and process-heavy, which can be challenging for small organizations. The plugin supports the full fundraising lifecycle, freeing up your team's time for the irreplaceable human work, like managing relationships and deciding which opportunities to pursue.

Find the right funders and grants. Research donors, foundations, companies, and surface open grants, with sources cited.

Decide what to pursue. Forward an RFP and get a breakdown on eligibility, requirements, and what it would take to compete.

Write proposals and reports. Turn an RFP into a requirements list and a first draft built from your own material. Grant reports include sources for their figures.

Keep relationships warm. Get a brief before a funder call, a write-up and thank-you note after, and donor updates in your voice. Ask how to re-engage donors and receive a stewardship plan.

Speech models in Ollama
Context: The first speech model is Phonon, a family of small, state-of-the-art text-to-speech models from Gradium
Full Text:
Ollama can now turn text into speech. The first speech model is Phonon, a family of small, state-of-the-art text-to-speech models from Gradium. Speech models are now available for macOS, with Windows and Linux support coming soon.

ollama run phonon "Hello from Ollama."

Unedited output from Ollama 0.40.11 on a MacBook Pro with M5 Max.

Performance on Apple Silicon

On Apple Silicon, Ollama is accelerated by MLX, Apple’s machine learning framework, for state-of-the-art throughput. On a MacBook Pro with M5 Max, Ollama was 35% faster than the next fastest engine, Gradium’s own runtime.

Throughput

Times faster than real time

Measured on a MacBook Pro with M5 Max, generating 45 seconds of speech. Median of 10 runs. Gradium's own runtime, ptts, uses 8-bit weights on the CPU, fp16 on the Neural Engine and f32 on the GPU; Ollama runs the model in bf16.

Ollama’s implementation is just as accurate, matching the word error rate of the reference implementation in Hugging Face Transformers:

Accuracy

Word error rate

Lower is better. 200 sentences from the Seed-TTS English test set, transcribed with Whisper large-v3.

Voices

Choose a voice with --voice, or voice in the API:

ollama run phonon --voice Hadley "Hello from Ollama."

The voices come from Gradium’s voice catalog. ollama show phonon lists them all.
